It's been roughly two years since I've reviewed Starbound on Early Access, and boy, has this game gone through a ton of iterations.  Some of them good, some of them bad.  But since it's finally been officially released, I figured it was time to give the game an up-to-date, proper review.
First off, yes, it's pretty much Terraria IN SPACE!  Heck, with the exception of the space combat/travel segments, you could also say that Starbound is essentially what No Man's Sky should've been when exploring planets.  And unlike No Man's Sky, you can actually meet and interact with other players!
You can travel from the many, many worlds and sectors, each one having their own little secrets and unique mini-biomes to discover though, and that's a great deal of the charm with this game.  And yes, each world is roughly the same size as the worlds you'd find in Terraria, the underground included, meaning that you are going to have a LOT of places to explore.  That part hasn't changed one bit.
However, the exploration process has been streamlined significantly, mostly to make things less frustrating for new players and easier to get into.  That means less grindy chores, less ridiculous resource requirements or vague quest tasks (well, mostly... I'll explain more in a moment), no starting planets that get hammered by huge♥♥♥♥♥asteriods outta nowhere and destroys your starting home (GOD THAT WAS ANNOYING), no starting planets with lava or toxic pools instead of water, less unbalanced enemy encounters, etc.  It certainly makes like easier for the most part, but it does remove a bit of the challenge and that feel of beating the odds when they're stacked against you.
The streamlining does have a fault, though.  Whereas in Terraria you could find over-powered gear and items if you knew where to look, were willing to brave the more dangerous regions, or simply lucked out, you'll rarely encounter situations where it feels like you've 'gamed' the system or discovered an awesome piece of gear.  With the exception of the consumable items and wearable gear, all of your equipment is randomly generated, with stats matching the worlds your on and rarely exceeding it.  There isn't as much variety in the gear either, so don't expect as much esoteric equipment as you'd find in Terraria.
The game now has a campaign to complete.  The unique story missions certainly stand out, both because of how large they are, and how much detail you realize must've gone into designing each mission.  The undersea Hyotl library was the most memorable, if only because I was left admiring how much effort went into designing the whole place, and more importantly, how it's theoretically possible for me to reconstruct it... provided, if I had mastered the wiring system, had infinite construction resources, and no life to speak of.  But the sidequests on the other hand are mostly randomly generated, often have vague instructions, and quickly become repetitive.  The vagueness of certain objectives cannot be stated enough - several times I had to defer to online guides in order to figure out just what did the quest giver mean or where to find and craft the ingredients.  You'll eventually find yourself burning out on any of the sidequests not given on the Space Outpost, possibly only endulging them for the sake of obtaining a new crew member for your starship.
Sadly, the game still has issues with engine optimization.  The issues no longer affect me (unless I'm visiting one of the more crowded settlements or in a big fight), but I've been hearing lots of chatter from other players complaining that the game has a terrible framerate, crashes frequently, or can't even be booted up.  Thus, make the best out of that 2 hour grace period you have after purchase to figure out if the game can even run on your system, or else you might be stuck with a dud for awhile longer.  There are also other glitches abound, but the fact that I can't remember them off the top of my head probably speaks to how minor most of them are.
SUMMARY:
Ultimately, my recommendation is still the same as it was two years ago.  Starbound's gameplay can indeed be fun building your own little town and upgrading your starship, doubly so with some of the higher quality mods out on Steam.  But the game still does feel partially incomplete for some reason.  Perhaps it has to do with the fact that I was one of the earliest players and remember what the original version played like, faults and all, or how many things were significantly altered or even removed.  Remember the tentacle biome, or some of the original bosses?  Or even better, the original quick-inventory system, or how you could actually pause the game when playing alone? Perhaps they'll appear in a future update, perhaps not.
But for now, it's a good game overall, and if you enjoyed Terraria or other similar games, I'm pretty sure you'll enjoy Starbound.

People complain about the RNG, but thats the good part. This game is about making the best out of bad things, it's what gives this game a great atmosphere. Yes, the game is hard. Yes, the game is unfair. Yes, this isnt a casual turn based dungeon crawler. The devs even tell you that:
But damn is this game good. Darkest Dungeon is more than just a rogue-like RPG. It’s an epic story. You will get attached to your characters. Those final blows will be very painful to witness. But finishing off a boss is just as rewarding as losing a member is devastating.
Darkest Dungeon gameplay is slow and methodical, but that does not make it stale. Oh no, the gameplay is as staunch as the droves of monsters you’ll slay. Rushed decisions are unforgiving and Punishing. They will lead to the suffering of your party both mentally and physically. Plenty of stats and plenty of buffs/debuffs to make a fight more tactical
There are so many bosses. So many hours can be spent in this game
Controls are simple, actions are responsive. The UI is very good with enough depth to achieve what you want without any problem. You can literally play the entire game with just a mouse, besides naming your characters.
Amazing, animations are simple but so interactive that they feel alive. Its enough to warrant the purchase of an art book. It’s orginal, somber, but warm enough to set it apart from other dreary titles. It takes you back, draws you in, and provides more than enough character and emotion while remaining true to the art direction. Nothing seems out of place, and at the same time everything feels otherworldly.
Buttersmooth
A solid foundation for a rogue-like game, and more than enough narration and backstory to keep you invested. The story will provide you with everything you need to understand the world and characters.
Crawling through dungeon is really diverse with different enemies, different heroes and different skill sets. There’s tons of upgrades (both town and character) and lots of trinkets to be found, if you stay alive long enough to make use of them. On top of that, there are currently three distinct areas with different enemies and randomized dungeons.
One of the best games ever made. Period.

Oh Darkest Dungeon. My bittersweet companion. That sums it up pretty well but there's so much that goes into it to make it such an absorbing experience.
You begin as an outsider to the bleak affairs of your newly inherited Hamlet; a wretched place where nothing is gleeful, the buildings are ruined and the surrounding environs are corrupted. Four places, the Ruins themselves, the Warrens, the Cove and the Weald, each with their own flavours of unnatural taint. Each requiring specific preparations and favouring different explorers. The wide assortments of classes make up your 4 person party, each baring significantly different contributions to the parties strength and assembling them to compensate for one another's weaknesses, or to compliment one another's strengths makes for an interesting dynamic between different combinations.
Lets take a step back. Gameplay is divided into two parts; plumbing the four aforementioned areas (and a fifth much later) with a small party in order to advance and to loot, and managing the hamlet they return to and your roster as a whole. All the while described by the disembodied voice of the ancestor that caused all the unholiness in the first place and then killed himself, leaving you to piece this broken place back together, in probably one of my favourite pieces of game narration I've ever encountered, it truly adds something to every scenario with his old, affected voice overlaying them.
Delving into the dark places puts you in one of two situations, exploring and fighting, combat is turn based, with each fighter having their own initiative to determine the order of turns, various status effects and weaknesses specific to certain areas make preparation key, as you can only bring a certain amount of limited supplies with you, and how much you can take back as loot is limited by what you have filled your inventory with in the first place. You will not know what will be useful until you have experimented, or guessed, and taking risks is your only option. Combat, despite sounding impersonal in description is made visceral by simply focusing on the combatants. Assaults upon your explorers will not only be physical, but psychological; for each fighter's mind has a breaking point, and deciding whether to focus upon the impacts of physical harm or insanity will never be easy. Exploring you will have the chance to interact with various hazards around these places, using items discerningly can grant you great boons, not doing so can cause great trauma, but loot must be taken, or else you will be returning empty handed. Both aspects of this dungeon delving are unforgiving, and sacrifices will have to be made. Each area eventually presents two powerful enemies that must be hunted down, to cleanse these places and to discover more of your ancestor's dark secrets, each one being hugely different, the Gibbering Prophet who hides behind the pews of an old church to protect himself from the slashes of your melee warriors, or the Alluring Siren who may charm one of your mercenaries to fight alongside her and summons wretches of the sea to do much the same. Each one presents a unique threat.
If and when your explorers return to the hamlet, they will only carry the weight of their mental ailments back with them, a huge variety of afflictions, or strengths, may change not only the way they fight, but the way they act, sometimes outside of your control. The hamlet provides oppotunity for respite, whether by faith, by revelry, or by medicine, to care for your ailing mercenaries. How successful you were outside will determine how much you can improve your hamlet, or indeed restore your warriors. It also provides places to train your warriors, hire new mercenaries and to enhance their equipment, the capacities of each again improves by how much you were able to loot. Again, outside of this place you must choose whether to press your warriors into further danger in order to return with greater, much needed, treasure, or to make a timely retreat whilst you still can.
The atmosphere of the entire world you have entered is crafted to crush and destroy your spirit, the hand drawn art style is flawless in creating a dark impression of even the holiest of things, every sound gives more and more to the grim nature of it all. The lost diaries of previous explorers, the memoirs of your ancestor, the horrific deeds done in his name, the encounters with unique otherworldly terrors like the Collector all come together in blood stained, disease ridden, unholiness like a mixing pot of all that damns.
To take a step back and be less theatrical about it; this game is fantastic, it is challenging, it is absorbing, it is compelling. It has life unlike any other, twisted though it may be.
Right onto the short part of this review; complaints, in fact, it might just be 'complaint'. Singular.
Bosses are repeated three times. Not in immediate succession of course, but of all the bosses in the four primary areas, they are all faced three separate times at heightening levels of difficultly. I personally don't have a problem with this as it's made more interesting by changes in mechanics, addition of more moves to the bosses and new memoirs unlocked after each, however I can see how it might annoy someone less patient.
It also does become hugely difficult towards the end, the fifth area, the Darkest Dungeon itself, is pig-headedly unforgiving. Bring bandages and prepare to be bled.
However, all in all, this game recieves my heartiest of recommendations, and I don't hesitate to say it's the best indie game I have played this year, quite possibly the best game I have played this year overall. Darkest Dungeon you are a 10/10. Red Hook, have my children. I think this may be the longest review I've ever written, and is most certainly the one I thought about the most, let that speak for itself.

I have loved the XCOM franchise since I had no idea what I was doing a child getting extremely frustrated, but the latest version XCOM2, is a major disappointment. The games play is great, the stylistic look is great, the story is great, the strategy and tactical play is great. What is horrible and completely ruins this game despite its obvious potential are the blatant shortcuts taken on fixing key game mechanics. By key game mechanics I mean functionalities that should 100% of the time work. Let me give you some examples of how broken mechanics have literally ended an entire run for me.
- You are supposed to be able to have another action after you move a soldier into a white colored tile correct? Many times I have done exactly this, moved a soldier on their first action into a white colored tile only to have my turn ended completely, effectively starting the unstoppable downward spiral that we all have experience with. Along these same line, the functionality of the camera and cursor are still such crap in XCOM2 that I have tried to move to a specific square but the cursor is so buggy that it is twitching between two adjacent tiles and I have to flip a coin to choose which tile I will end up in...
- Apparently enemies have Xray vision, but only on some occasions. I have been spotted by enemy troops through ceilings, walls, vehicles, you name it. If the door is closed or there is a completely solid barrier between us how can they spot me? With the way that missions timers (crap design choice) work you are forced to rush into enemy groups, but now that can see straight through walls apparently...
-The way that soldiers interact with cover can potentially end your game. Example, I had full cover looking around a lightpost to shoot a flanked enemy. In order to take the fully flanked shot my soldier for some reason needs to take the butt of his rifle to the lamp post to take the shot, effectively destroying his own full cover...he proceeds to miss the flank shot leaving himself fully exposed to take a shot to the face and die. Why are my soldiers destroying their own cover to take shots?
-Gernade throwing mechanics are horribly implemented and have the potential to end a run for you. They do not indicate correctly what they will actually do damage to. We have all been in that situation where you absolutely need to make a kill so you use a gernade, only to have it effect everything way outside of its indicated area of affect making cars and the like destroy the entire map. Multiple times I have thrown a gernade with a generous gap between a vehicle only to have it explode anyways killing either the civilian you are supposed to rescue or the remainder of your squad. If the gernade correctly indicated what they will hit I would have survived many more encounters. On top of this the gernade target mechanic is horrible to use. I use the non tile-snapping gernade mod to help the targetting issues but the inaccurate explosion radius indicator is still potentially game ending.
-And here is the kicker that made me write this review. The saving system is flawed. For some reason I have an autosave of every game I have ever played. When I came to load my most recent game there is no sign of it. I have past games where I was about to die with the autosave. If you are going to impletment an Ironman format your autosave functionality must be 100% functional. This particular run was hands down my fursthest run but it just straight up didn't save my game. I guess this is partially my fault for not making sure to save before I quit, but then why is there an Autosave Functionality at all if my game is not saved. Autosave saves automatically because that is what it is called right? AUTO as in AUTOMATIC, the definition of AUTOMATIC is that it is AUTOMATED. But the AUTOMATIC SAVE is actually not AUTOMATIC.
If you create a game like this where literally one bad move can end all of your progress, you need to make your game mechanics 100% functional, 100%. Not 99% I have been cheated out of my games countless times because of failed game mechanics. I have lost many other games due missed percentages that we as XCOM players are familiar with, and I am not complaining about these, they are part of the game. I am complaining about all the extra time with false announcements and pushed back dates. With all this extra BS how can you release a game with such glaring flaws. I am losing games because of failed mechanic functionality as basic as an autosave functionality. How can you release a game completely dependent on a single moves and have those single moves not 100% functioning correctly? How did this ever get past a test phase? You will lose entire campaigns based on flawed functionalities that you have no control over.
I cannot recommend this game for such a high price if the basic functionalities of the game are causing me to lose enitre campaigns.
Here is a doozy...I finally made it to the final level on Commander Ironman. I am fighting about 6 MECs. I kill most of them off using and big AOE void zone the Commander's Avatar leaving the two advanced MECs standing in the AOE zone. I use two of my Specialists to shut them down so that they take the remaining damage at the end of their turn from the AOE void zone. The first Specialist has a 100% success rate for the hack with a feedback effect of gaining defense and aim boosts. The specialist successfully shuts down the MEC and then takes feedback damage from the MEC...There is no indication that the Specialist will take damage on a failed hack...but then again he didn't fail. The indicator told me that I would only recieve the feedback effect from a failed hack. The hack was a success and I ended up recieving the feedback effect anyway. On top of the that the feeback effect which should not have been triggered, was the wrong one. Ok so now I have one MEC shut down and my Specialist is low health. I can heal him and keep going right? So I go the next Specialist to shut down the second MEC. Same scenario, if I fail a 97% hack then the MEC will gain defense and aim boosts. I successfully complete the shutdown and my Ironman run on the last level is ruined. When I successfully hacked the second MEC my first Specialist again took feedback damage, killing him. On two separate successful shutdown hacks in the same turn, a single Specialist took feedback damage from two seperate targets. There are so many mechanical flaws here it is unbelievable. To top all that off this is an Ironman run on the final level...
Combined Mechanical Errors to End my Furthest Run:
Incorrect feedback effect indicator on MEC 1.
Incorrect feedback effect indicator on MEC 2.
Successful shutdown on MEC 1 causing the incorrect feedback effect.
Successful shutdown on MEC 2 causing the incorrect feedback effect.
Successful shutdown on MEC 1 causing feedback damage.
Successful shutdown on MEC 2 causing feedback damage.
Successful shutdown on MEC 2 causing feedback damage to the wrong target.
I cannot fathom how a cosmetic pack being released so that your soldiers look like clowns is higher priority than fixing the obvious and frequent GAME BREAKING mechanical errors.
Do not buy this game until the price comes way down and the most blatant mechanical errors are fixed.

Better map variety;
more enemy types
enemy stats scale with tier progression
-->more intriguing tactical situations;
-->no boring/repetetive endgame

The Bad:
long load times
occasional stuttering
no improvement on UI (at all)
poor explanation of research, building and everything before it's done
less varied soldier types (no gene mods, mek replacement class only in add-on)
The Ugly:
more emphasis on equipment and soldier exp. progression than on variety on tools
Experimental ammo/armor/heavy w/launchers is an RNG
world map can be really busy (at once and from mission to mission)
exponential difficulty curve between difficulty levels
mod support feels a lazy excuse from Firaxis to avoid additional effort on development (but prove me that I'm wrong Firaxis)

People complain about the RNG, but thats the good part. This game is about making the best out of bad things, it's what gives this game a great atmosphere. Yes, the game is hard. Yes, the game is unfair. Yes, this isnt a casual turn based dungeon crawler. The devs even tell you that:
But damn is this game good. Darkest Dungeon is more than just a rogue-like RPG. It’s an epic story. You will get attached to your characters. Those final blows will be very painful to witness. But finishing off a boss is just as rewarding as losing a member is devastating.
Darkest Dungeon gameplay is slow and methodical, but that does not make it stale. Oh no, the gameplay is as staunch as the droves of monsters you’ll slay. Rushed decisions are unforgiving and Punishing. They will lead to the suffering of your party both mentally and physically. Plenty of stats and plenty of buffs/debuffs to make a fight more tactical
There are so many bosses. So many hours can be spent in this game
Controls are simple, actions are responsive. The UI is very good with enough depth to achieve what you want without any problem. You can literally play the entire game with just a mouse, besides naming your characters.
Amazing, animations are simple but so interactive that they feel alive. Its enough to warrant the purchase of an art book. It’s orginal, somber, but warm enough to set it apart from other dreary titles. It takes you back, draws you in, and provides more than enough character and emotion while remaining true to the art direction. Nothing seems out of place, and at the same time everything feels otherworldly.
Buttersmooth
A solid foundation for a rogue-like game, and more than enough narration and backstory to keep you invested. The story will provide you with everything you need to understand the world and characters.

Oh Darkest Dungeon. My bittersweet companion. That sums it up pretty well but there's so much that goes into it to make it such an absorbing experience.
You begin as an outsider to the bleak affairs of your newly inherited Hamlet; a wretched place where nothing is gleeful, the buildings are ruined and the surrounding environs are corrupted. Four places, the Ruins themselves, the Warrens, the Cove and the Weald, each with their own flavours of unnatural taint. Each requiring specific preparations and favouring different explorers. The wide assortments of classes make up your 4 person party, each baring significantly different contributions to the parties strength and assembling them to compensate for one another's weaknesses, or to compliment one another's strengths makes for an interesting dynamic between different combinations.
Lets take a step back. Gameplay is divided into two parts; plumbing the four aforementioned areas (and a fifth much later) with a small party in order to advance and to loot, and managing the hamlet they return to and your roster as a whole. All the while described by the disembodied voice of the ancestor that caused all the unholiness in the first place and then killed himself, leaving you to piece this broken place back together, in probably one of my favourite pieces of game narration I've ever encountered, it truly adds something to every scenario with his old, affected voice overlaying them.
Delving into the dark places puts you in one of two situations, exploring and fighting, combat is turn based, with each fighter having their own initiative to determine the order of turns, various status effects and weaknesses specific to certain areas make preparation key, as you can only bring a certain amount of limited supplies with you, and how much you can take back as loot is limited by what you have filled your inventory with in the first place. You will not know what will be useful until you have experimented, or guessed, and taking risks is your only option. Combat, despite sounding impersonal in description is made visceral by simply focusing on the combatants. Assaults upon your explorers will not only be physical, but psychological; for each fighter's mind has a breaking point, and deciding whether to focus upon the impacts of physical harm or insanity will never be easy. Exploring you will have the chance to interact with various hazards around these places, using items discerningly can grant you great boons, not doing so can cause great trauma, but loot must be taken, or else you will be returning empty handed. Both aspects of this dungeon delving are unforgiving, and sacrifices will have to be made. Each area eventually presents two powerful enemies that must be hunted down, to cleanse these places and to discover more of your ancestor's dark secrets, each one being hugely different, the Gibbering Prophet who hides behind the pews of an old church to protect himself from the slashes of your melee warriors, or the Alluring Siren who may charm one of your mercenaries to fight alongside her and summons wretches of the sea to do much the same. Each one presents a unique threat.
If and when your explorers return to the hamlet, they will only carry the weight of their mental ailments back with them, a huge variety of afflictions, or strengths, may change not only the way they fight, but the way they act, sometimes outside of your control. The hamlet provides oppotunity for respite, whether by faith, by revelry, or by medicine, to care for your ailing mercenaries. How successful you were outside will determine how much you can improve your hamlet, or indeed restore your warriors. It also provides places to train your warriors, hire new mercenaries and to enhance their equipment, the capacities of each again improves by how much you were able to loot. Again, outside of this place you must choose whether to press your warriors into further danger in order to return with greater, much needed, treasure, or to make a timely retreat whilst you still can.
The atmosphere of the entire world you have entered is crafted to crush and destroy your spirit, the hand drawn art style is flawless in creating a dark impression of even the holiest of things, every sound gives more and more to the grim nature of it all. The lost diaries of previous explorers, the memoirs of your ancestor, the horrific deeds done in his name, the encounters with unique otherworldly terrors like the Collector all come together in blood stained, disease ridden, unholiness like a mixing pot of all that damns.
To take a step back and be less theatrical about it; this game is fantastic, it is challenging, it is absorbing, it is compelling. It has life unlike any other, twisted though it may be.
Right onto the short part of this review; complaints, in fact, it might just be 'complaint'. Singular.
Bosses are repeated three times. Not in immediate succession of course, but of all the bosses in the four primary areas, they are all faced three separate times at heightening levels of difficultly. I personally don't have a problem with this as it's made more interesting by changes in mechanics, addition of more moves to the bosses and new memoirs unlocked after each, however I can see how it might annoy someone less patient.
It also does become hugely difficult towards the end, the fifth area, the Darkest Dungeon itself, is pig-headedly unforgiving. Bring bandages and prepare to be bled.
However, all in all, this game recieves my heartiest of recommendations, and I don't hesitate to say it's the best indie game I have played this year, quite possibly the best game I have played this year overall. Darkest Dungeon you are a 10/10. Red Hook, have my children. I think this may be the longest review I've ever written, and is most certainly the one I thought about the most, let that speak for itself.

Summary:
X-Com 2 is a follow-up sequel to 2012's reboot turn-based tactical game, X-Com: Enemy Unknown, developed by Fireaxis Games. It takes place 20 years after the events of the first title, as we're fighting back against aliens trying to take over the human race.
The simple concept of the story is far from one to be bothered to show any interest in. It's one of the weaker aspects of the game, or at least, I just didn't see myself relating to any of the characters or issues at hand. Had the same problem with the first game. Whilst the characters do have different personalities, they seem one-dimensional and the overall plot is just there. The player is the head of the resistance against the aliens as well as leading the ship the Avenger, who of which we never get to see or hear. It's an attempt to immerse us into the role, but since there's no attachment to any of the other characters or critical moments occurring in the game, it's difficult to place ourselves within the X-Com realm.
The soundtrack's there, and there's honestly some good tunes to fight aliens with, fits the setting, but in no time I was substituting the missions with my own music.
The gameplay is where this title truly shines, and is a major step above its predecessor. Turn-based combat is thought of as a tool of the past in games, simulated in a much-quicker pace in the modern era due to the technology available and gamers shifting more towards the action-packed genre than ever before. X-Com keeps the traditional style of turn-based tactical-combat but they manage to make the battles intense and exciting enough to pull off this old style of gameplay. We're given a handful of soldiers at our disposal, multiple objectives to accomplish, various aliens to take down and keep the game from going dull, and upgrades to our equipment and weapons to feel even more satisfied with taking down the extraterrestials.
Satisfying. That word sums up the game extremely well. Perhaps what makes it so rewarding is finally getting a shot or ability to work in your favor. There's an accuracy penalty due to the cover-based terrain that each unit would take cover behind, as well as other factors like armor or ambushes. No one can hit every shot, and that goes for both humans and aliens, just a matter of getting the right angle and drop on your opponent before they do. After a few solo kills or assists on taking down the aliens, your soldiers level up, or in this military scenario, are promoted. Each promotion nets the new class a choice between two decent abilities. That's right, this game has a class system, and it meshes in well, each with role being quite useful for every mission. Sharpshooter (the sniper), Ranger (close-quarters with shotgun/sword), Grenadier (heavy weapons), and Specialist (healing/hacking). There's also a Psi-Operative class, allowing the players to tap into the psychic abilities that aliens use with a soldier of their own. With the different abilities available, it's recommended to make two characters of each class. Later on, players will be able to take six soldiers out on a mission, so mixing and matching the team is optimal.
Speaking of soldiers, there's plenty of customizing. From nationality to voice to personality, color schemes for armor and weapons as well as patterns. This makes the game even more fun as you can make your family/friends, or just about anyone you want, and send them off to battle to do your bidding. It's possible for soldiers to die or be wounded and thus out of action for a few days-weeks depending on the severity of the injury (how much damage they took during the mission), so a careful approach (and having heals) is the best bet to make it through the rough stages of X-Com 2. Equipment can be developed to further give you the edge on the battlefield, such as different effect grenades, armor, ammo, and healing kits.
On top of researching and engineering (the two factors towards upgrading which will speed up if more engineers and scientists are retrieved), the Avenger ship is able to expand its deck and add new facilities such as workshops and laboratories. Each facility requires power, leading the building of power relays. Picking when and where to build the facility is a pivotal part of the game, and then of course making proper use of them. Things were a little more complicated with facility-building in Enemy Unknown, with bonuses to building the same facilities adjacent to one another, etc., but here it's more user-friendly. Quick tip: If there's a choice between retrieving a scientist or an engineer, take the engineer mission. Scientists are woefully underused in this game, only very slightly increasing research speed, ulnless a laboratory is built and even then the difference I halved when it's fully upgraded, and even t hen only two scientists can be active in a lab.
Naturally, there are costs to upgrading. Nothing is really risk-free here. There are two primary resources: Intel, and Supplies. Intel is used in the black market to get mods for the soldiers, extra supplies, etc.. It can be used to learn more about what the aliens are doing with their Avatar Project (a timely event which is our primary objective to find out more about and prevent), whereas supplies help run the ship, expand map prescence, build items, etc.. There are also various minor resources which can be retrieved by completing missions.
This game sounds complex, but it's been mainstreamed to appeal to a larger audience, and that's a good thing in this particular case. It takes elements from tactical-games, RPGs, etc., and blends them altogether in a finely tuned futuristic-army warfare. The number of strategies and ways to take down enemies are seemingly endless, the graphics are spectacular, and the missions keep you on your toes. Some have said that this series is difficult, and whilst they are challenging, it's certainly not on the same level of Dark Souls, Ninja Gaiden, or brutally unforgiving games. For those that like that kind of challenge, the Iron Man mode is available (which prevents multiple save files from being created and auto saves every other turn), as well as harder difficulties.
Online mode is fun, as it pits you against another human player for a change. You can also be the aliens which makes for an interesting change of pace. It's been a little wonky, though, disconnecting issues, just overall unstable for me, but I'll try again in a week or two.
All in all, X-Com 2 takes what made Enemy Unknown good and improves on it ten-fold. Once you jump into your first mission, you'll want to keep advancing and honing your team to destroy the rebel scum. Or alien scum if you prefer. There have been many reports of the game not running smoothly, crashing or facing many bugs/glitches such as units being unable to move, thus giving the game a much lower score. Whilst that is an upsetting issue, a patch or two later would fix all this, and the dev team are currently doing so (two major patches since release to help alleviate these problems). I myself haven't run into any crashing or game-breaking issues other than the loading screen getting stuck twice in the 40+ hours I've put into it. I haven't finished the game yet, on the last stretch and I've hesitated because I don't want it to end. Some DLC is coming along the way with more customizing, weapons, and story. If this isn't obvious already, and given what little time I have for gaming these days: I highly recommend X-Com 2 to anyone. Personalize it however you want to, fight back for your race, and strategically dominate the playing field.

I've only put in about 10 hours of this but man is this game fun. It's pretty easy to get into and so far most of the community that I've run into has been pretty helpful. The game is definitely early access though, as there are a few issues I have with it.
- There's no really good tutorial yet. There's a video tutorial but that's pretty much it.
- Server browsing is pretty much glorified matchmaking. The servers from what I can tell are auto-generated to accomodate players. This makes it really hard to play with friends. Speaking of that.
- Team balance is completely in the hands of the players. If you and your friend join a server together, it's likely the start of the match will place you on opposite teams to balance. The only way to play together is to "request a team switch". You push a button and it notifies the server that you want to switch teams. If someone on the other team also pushes that button, then you will switch. Otherwise you are stuck on the team assigned to you.
- Some of the ships currently are pretty OP, especially against newer players who don't know what these other ships are capable of. The game has a pretty fluid system of counters and synergies that most people do not yet understand. In all honestly I have yet to run into a ship I thought that there was no way to destroy them, but there are a couple where I know it's next to impossible to deal with them if my team doesn't know what to do.
- The current win objective is zerg-rush friendly. Basically you capture points until you are allowed to warp to their base. Once you do you can start capping their base. There's no way to "uncap" any progress they make. This means a team that just constantly zergs your home base can win even if they all have a KD of 0/5.
- There's no in game friends list that I am aware of. So if you meet players in game who you want to be friends with, there's no way to do so. The game also doesn't support the steam friends feature where you can search for recently played players.
- After each match you are moved back to the home screen, meaning you are booted from the server you were in. No chance of rematch against players you played or just even a chance to play with the same people.
Even though that seems like a big list of negatives, each one only detracts from the experience (for me) in a minor way. I'm also giving them the benefit of the doubt in that it is early access. Most of the things I listed are things that could easily be fixed, so we'll just have to see. In the end though the game is super fun and I played for a few hours in a row right off the bat after getting it because it was just so addicting. In the end I would recommend you get it simply because it is really fun, but if you're looking to get it to play with friends you might want to hold off until they address that issue, or at least make a statement saying they will address it.

XCOM 2. What an experience. Also what the hell does XCOM stand for? Nevermind that.
XCOM 2 is a tactical TBS (turn based strategy) that has a strong focus on contacting and organizing rebellion efforts across the planet, and raising a squad of soldiers from rookies to the most elite soldiers in the galaxy, all in a desperate fight to stop the Advent from meddling with Earth's affairs. It is somewhat similar to the Total War series, because there is a world view where you make strategic decisions, decide what to research, what structures to build on your lone ship; then you go down to the nitty gritty and have to fight the battles you get yourself into.
Let me make this clear immediately: if you are new to tactical TBS games, unless you are playing on the lowest difficulty,
I lost my first campaign in 5 hours, because I thought the default difficulty would be manageable. I was dead wrong. So I started a new game on 'Rookie', the lowest difficulty (with Ironman enabled (no save scumming mode)) and I was doing fantastic... until I ran into my first squad of Sectopods and I lost 5 of my 6 best troops in one day and I proceeded to lose the game less than an hour after that.
On my third playthrough, after about 25 hours, I finally completed the game and got to see the ending... that leaves many questions unanswered. I guess its about the journey, not the destination, right? Right...?
+ Lots of customization options for your soldiers, both cosmetic and tactical. This game rewards players that think tactically about what soldiers and tools are best for each encounter.
+Campaign seems unfair at first, but once you get the hang of it you will find a nice balance of challenge and reward for smart play.
+Diverse cast of alien troops- every time you see a new alien you haven't fought before, you will be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ yourself trying to figure out how you will take it down. 9 very different classes of soldiers. Soldiers rank up and learn new abilities by participating in missions and getting kills, and you have a large influence into what type of soldier they become.
-Lots of bugs. Clipping is very frequent, soldiers of both sides will constantly be shot through walls, or at angles that seem absurd. Also the game seems very slow at times, with constant pauses for several seconds for no apparent reason. You may want to try the mod 'Stop Wasting My Time'. Also can I just say
(Hopefully the bugs will be reduced over time in future patches; I was playing the game through in early March.)
-The ending is very anticlimactic. (MILD SPOILERS) What happens to the Advent? Do they get eradicated for good, or do they retreat from Earth to strike again at a later date? Were the Advent actually bad as everyone thought, or were they working for the greater good the whole time as they claimed?
Note that I have not tried the multiplayer yet, I may update this review at a later date once I give it a test drive.

XCOM 2 returns to the XCOM: Enemy Unknown universe, picking up where humanity has failed to defend Earth and humankind is now living in a big-brother-esk heavy handed rule of alien leaders where propaganda and misdirection keep the general populace under control. Taking up the reins of the XCOM project, your job as
will be to lead guerrilla style missions from your mobile base - a re-appropriated massive alien ship. My first play was a commander difficulty playthrough, save scummed. I'm currently doing ironman attempts to redeem myself from pleb status.
XCOM 2 feels in a lot of ways like everything XCOM:EU
have been. One of my biggest gripes with EU was that the best tactical strategy in almost every mission was to leap frog with strategical overwatch rotations, until you finally popped a pod. With X2, humanity is now on the back foot, and running guerrilla style tactics means that you'll be launching most missions under the cover of concealment. With this you'll be able to start a mission without the aliens being aware you are there, until you either launch an attack or accidentally step into their vision radius - which is clearly marked if you're in a good position. Concealment not only makes the game play faster, but is also a critical tool to use correctly for timed missions - more on that later.
Enemy scaling is vastly improved from my point of view. The difficulty ramped up in appropriate fashion along the way, and felt like it was paced better than EU. In EU I felt like all I needed to do was rush weapons and that doesn't feel like a viable strategy in this game, at least at the more difficult settings. There is occasionally a feeling of difficulty being annoying at times - but good positioning and tactics will take you most of the way.
Soldier skills feel largely improved, I found myself building opposing types for every single soldier type to mix things up - and each variant brings it's own advantages and disadvantages. There is not as many skill decisions where it is completely imbalanced and a non-choice. This means that gameplay is more varied mission-to-mission and feels fresher for longer.
Psi class - it's awesome. Use it, abuse it, love it.
Weapon balancing can sometimes feel off. Rangers have a seriously badass sword to allow them to melee enemies every turn if desired. Unfortunately, much of the time these are simply useless when compared with the shotgun. A lot of this is down to positioning, melee means running deep into enemy lines, which can almost always risk popping another pod (or two if the RNG gods are angry). Another problem with the sword is that it misses. It misses a lot. More often than you would think. In my opinion this weapon should be either a guaranteed hit with an innate chance to have a glancing blow, or higher damage, in order to compensate. Aside from wasting sectoids early on, I found myself using it only in very specific circumstances.
Retaliation missions. Ugh. Some variation on these would be nice. Doesn't help when Central is yelling at you every time a civilian dies. When I consider throwing a mission from the mid game onward and paying the price for it just to avoid it - it's probably not a good thing.
At launch it was apparent that the game did not have a final polish that was expected for a uni-platform game which was already delayed from it's original launch date. Thank goodness for the original delay or this game would have been an unmitigated disaster.
Some of the jank and issues I had on vanilla release:
I've put a lot of time into X2 since launch, putting aside a lot of other games I should probably be playing instead. I love this game, at it's core it is a fantastic strategy game. As more and more patches come out to repair the performance issues my recommendation to buy this will only get stronger.

Ok, so i'm gonna give just a quick initial review on this game. First off, the graphics and gameplay experience... Totally amazing! I'm gonna give just a couple pro's and con's on it, just to settle in the balanced review of what i personally think.
Pro's-
-Graphics: Totally amazing. Unreal Engine 4 is the best engine to work with on a futuristic game like this.
-Gameplay: Really awesome. I love the gameplay in this game. It's something new, and nothing like World of Tanks. Which was what i was thinking it was going to be like going into it.
-Features: Really good: I love the features the game has to offer. The Tech Tree, upgrades, etc. Really balanced.
Con's-
-Purchasable Ships: Now i never seen a game do this before, but the fact that you need to use real money to purchase ships in game, is just beyond stupid. It gives an advantage to people who don't mind spending 8 bucks to buy better ships. Initially when i first got the hang of the game, i seen alot of premium ships. Which obviously outmatched my ship i was using. In my opinion, to overpowered. This is one thing that has to be nerfed. Make it so that you earn the ships in game. Like have an Achievement system that allows you to unlock better ships, and have a premium purchase for upgrades to the ships, like customization upgrades.
-Long Respawn Times: The respawn times are horrifically too long. Over a 40 second respawn time? Seriously? This is one thing that has to be nerfed. It is more better if respawns where 25 or 20 seconds. Not no 40 seconds....
-One Game Mode: I know this is early alpha, and my opinion might be conquered over later on, but only one gamemode is kinda stupid. The only game mode you get to play right now, is capturing enemy bases. Which can span a single match over half an hour if you have a decently balanced room. They should add more gamemodes to the game, like team deathmatch, and free for all to keep the style of gameplay updated so you don't continuously only have to play one game mode constiently. I can see that getting boring really quick.
Other then that, i recommend this game because its pretty awesome. It is in early alpha, so any turn offs that might happen while playing the game is to be expected, just for the simple fact it is not the full version yet...

I have loved the XCOM franchise since I had no idea what I was doing a child getting extremely frustrated, but the latest version XCOM2, is a major disappointment. The games play is great, the stylistic look is great, the story is great, the strategy and tactical play is great. What is horrible and completely ruins this game despite its obvious potential are the blatant shortcuts taken on fixing key game mechanics. By key game mechanics I mean functionalities that should 100% of the time work. Let me give you some examples of how broken mechanics have literally ended an entire run for me.
- You are supposed to be able to have another action after you move a soldier into a white colored tile correct? Many times I have done exactly this, moved a soldier on their first action into a white colored tile only to have my turn ended completely, effectively starting the unstoppable downward spiral that we all have experience with. Along these same line, the functionality of the camera and cursor are still such crap in XCOM2 that I have tried to move to a specific square but the cursor is so buggy that it is twitching between two adjacent tiles and I have to flip a coin to choose which tile I will end up in...
- Apparently enemies have Xray vision, but only on some occasions. I have been spotted by enemy troops through ceilings, walls, vehicles, you name it. If the door is closed or there is a completely solid barrier between us how can they spot me? With the way that missions timers (crap design choice) work you are forced to rush into enemy groups, but now that can see straight through walls apparently...
-The way that soldiers interact with cover can potentially end your game. Example, I had full cover looking around a lightpost to shoot a flanked enemy. In order to take the fully flanked shot my soldier for some reason needs to take the butt of his rifle to the lamp post to take the shot, effectively destroying his own full cover...he proceeds to miss the flank shot leaving himself fully exposed to take a shot to the face and die. Why are my soldiers destroying their own cover to take shots?
-Gernade throwing mechanics are horribly implemented and have the potential to end a run for you. They do not indicate correctly what they will actually do damage to. We have all been in that situation where you absolutely need to make a kill so you use a gernade, only to have it effect everything way outside of its indicated area of affect making cars and the like destroy the entire map. Multiple times I have thrown a gernade with a generous gap between a vehicle only to have it explode anyways killing either the civilian you are supposed to rescue or the remainder of your squad. If the gernade correctly indicated what they will hit I would have survived many more encounters. On top of this the gernade target mechanic is horrible to use. I use the non tile-snapping gernade mod to help the targetting issues but the inaccurate explosion radius indicator is still potentially game ending.
-And here is the kicker that made me write this review. The saving system is flawed. For some reason I have an autosave of every game I have ever played. When I came to load my most recent game there is no sign of it. I have past games where I was about to die with the autosave. If you are going to impletment an Ironman format your autosave functionality must be 100% functional. This particular run was hands down my fursthest run but it just straight up didn't save my game. I guess this is partially my fault for not making sure to save before I quit, but then why is there an Autosave Functionality at all if my game is not saved. Autosave saves automatically because that is what it is called right? AUTO as in AUTOMATIC, the definition of AUTOMATIC is that it is AUTOMATED. But the AUTOMATIC SAVE is actually not AUTOMATIC.
If you create a game like this where literally one bad move can end all of your progress, you need to make your game mechanics 100% functional, 100%. Not 99% I have been cheated out of my games countless times because of failed game mechanics. I have lost many other games due missed percentages that we as XCOM players are familiar with, and I am not complaining about these, they are part of the game. I am complaining about all the extra time with false announcements and pushed back dates. With all this extra BS how can you release a game with such glaring flaws. I am losing games because of failed mechanic functionality as basic as an autosave functionality. How can you release a game completely dependent on a single moves and have those single moves not 100% functioning correctly? How did this ever get past a test phase? You will lose entire campaigns based on flawed functionalities that you have no control over.
I cannot recommend this game for such a high price if the basic functionalities of the game are causing me to lose enitre campaigns.
Here is a doozy...I finally made it to the final level on Commander Ironman. I am fighting about 6 MECs. I kill most of them off using and big AOE void zone the Commander's Avatar leaving the two advanced MECs standing in the AOE zone. I use two of my Specialists to shut them down so that they take the remaining damage at the end of their turn from the AOE void zone. The first Specialist has a 100% success rate for the hack with a feedback effect of gaining defense and aim boosts. The specialist successfully shuts down the MEC and then takes feedback damage from the MEC...There is no indication that the Specialist will take damage on a failed hack...but then again he didn't fail. The indicator told me that I would only recieve the feedback effect from a failed hack. The hack was a success and I ended up recieving the feedback effect anyway. On top of the that the feeback effect which should not have been triggered, was the wrong one. Ok so now I have one MEC shut down and my Specialist is low health. I can heal him and keep going right? So I go the next Specialist to shut down the second MEC. Same scenario, if I fail a 97% hack then the MEC will gain defense and aim boosts. I successfully complete the shutdown and my Ironman run on the last level is ruined. When I successfully hacked the second MEC my first Specialist again took feedback damage, killing him. On two separate successful shutdown hacks in the same turn, a single Specialist took feedback damage from two seperate targets. There are so many mechanical flaws here it is unbelievable. To top all that off this is an Ironman run on the final level...
Combined Mechanical Errors to End my Furthest Run:
Incorrect feedback effect indicator on MEC 1.
Incorrect feedback effect indicator on MEC 2.
Successful shutdown on MEC 1 causing the incorrect feedback effect.
Successful shutdown on MEC 2 causing the incorrect feedback effect.
Successful shutdown on MEC 1 causing feedback damage.
Successful shutdown on MEC 2 causing feedback damage.
Successful shutdown on MEC 2 causing feedback damage to the wrong target.
I cannot fathom how a cosmetic pack being released so that your soldiers look like clowns is higher priority than fixing the obvious and frequent GAME BREAKING mechanical errors.
Do not buy this game until the price comes way down and the most blatant mechanical errors are fixed.

Honestly, after playing this game for years and spending hours upon hours and multitudes of my money I can say that while this is/was a rock solid MMO and I had nothing but fun in it, I cannot recommend it to play to anyone. It's far to dead, the golden has all but faded into ashes at our feet and the few players left either don't care and are merely waiting for the game or are just denying the inevitable.
The PVP used to be awesome, full teams Tiers 1-3 hundreds of players and competition and while there was a meta fun weapons could always be found. Now it's nothing but AAcheron to win and full BK and if you don't have that or a derivitive some othe rplayer will and they'll dumpster your day.
The PvE oh man, where do i begin. Before missions and all those updates it was one of the funnest, most explorative, planned, and beautiful creations I had ever seen in a game like this. But now it's nothing but a shodw of its former self. The enemies were fun, diving was a challenge that required planning and a variety of gear. It was fun to meet up with other knights and plan a party so you could do an entire boss run together. Now, you just need 3 swords, a gun, and one set of armor and you can carry your way through the entire game.

Great concept with a few serious short comings. The initial apprentice dungeons and intermediate veteran dungeons are difficult, yet well balanced and rewarding. This isn't the case for the champion dungeons. I understand the game is based on the concept of "making the best out of a bad situation", but the late game difficulty spike is ridiculous. Basic enemies encountered in champion dungeons are seemingly on par with previous boss fights. My best heroes (max level, equipment, and skills) we're more often than not getting hopelessly roflstomped 2-3 battles in...even on short scouting quests. To make matters worse, management mechanics become increasingly skewed. For example, the weird level cap system prevents heroes from partaking in quests below their corresponding level, making it unnecessarily difficult to train badly-needed replacements and raise funds. Overall, late game play feels less about exploring dungeons/smighting evil  and more about bolstering lost gold and manpower (tedious/unrewarding grinding). After a couple hours of frustration, I threw in the towel. I doubt I have the motivation to finish it in its current state. Total shame, I really enjoyed it up to this point.
I realize Red Hook has plans to implement a short mode. Hopefully they address some of these issues/give the game more mass-appeal. Until then, I can't recommend this to anyone but hardcore RPG fans.....casual gamers stay away!

This game is also suitably challenging with a wide array of enemies and mission objectives.  I would recommend anyone new to the franchise start with the first reboot XCOM as this game starts off as hard as the end of the last.
Now for the bad parts.  The game needs some serious tweaking on the pacing as the game felt very rushed and was quite annoying in forcing you into mission after mission.  I had a lot of trouble with this on the 'normal' difficulty as the pace is unmanageable for how long it took your soldiers to heal.  I quickly had trouble fielding teams for missions as this game is quite hard.  Having a soldier out for 20 days is the equivlent of losing a soldier with the game's pacing.  The game also has some frame rate issues and weird camera bugs.

As a Fallout game, Fallout 4 is completely stripped of its charm, choices and meaningful consequences. I enjoyed the density and detail of Boston, but the soul of a Fallout game is nowhere in sight. The vast majority of my playtime was spent in the settlement system, as thread bare as it was. The 'Better Settlements' mod on the Nexus is far, FAR superior the the Bethesda supplied option, if anyone is interested. I played a good 150+ hours on PS4, purchased it here on Steam a while back (most of my hours were offline, didn't want to bother my friends with the constant coming and going online with modding).
As for this "paid-mods-that-are-not-paid-mods-but-are-mods-that-you-pay-for" argument going on... There's not a whole lot to be said about it other than that. Bethesda, and people who want to defend Bethesda, will try to find new ways to define these Paid Mods so as to bypass one's prejudices, like calling them "Mini-DLC's". You can twist it whatever way you like, these are MODifications to the game that you PAY for. And these mods are simple skins and armors that can be found anywhere on the internet for free. To think that Bethesda would come out of the gate with *these* after the fail of their last attempt, is just pitiful. If, and that's a big IF, Bethesda get started on releasing big mods, game overhaul type of mods of high quality and assurance of updating and maintenance on said mods, then I might begin to warm to the idea of paying for a mod like that. But, this? This is disappointing. Bethesda seem to be losing the good graces of many fans lately. I don't want that to happen, I hope they can turn this around. But I don't see that happening though.

Review after 25 hours:
Pros:
-Fantastic audio/graphics/art/atmosphere/music. Very evocative, striking, memorable. Especially the narrator.
-Satisfying, deep combat system. Finding what party combinations work together is entertaining, as well as learning what you should look out for in different dungeons, etc.
-The "Five more minutes..." effect is strong. Ruined my plans for a good sleep schedhule this christmas.
Neutral:
-The quirk-system is alright, however I do wish the quirk affected the heros' personality and not just their stats.
-I wish the managementsystem outside of dungeons was a bit deeper, but it's passable.
-RNGesus be with you.
Cons:
-Lacklustre story.
-To begin with I was very attached to my different heroes, but this passed quickly. After a few hours you are forced to expand your roster to such a degree that each hero will mean little to you. This dampened my investment in the game, as a hero dying doesn't really matter to me anymore. I would prefer if you had fewer heroes, and each one had a greater signifigance.
-The game is a bit too grindy for my taste.
Conclusion: 8.5/10, would play a lot while listening to podcasts.

What makes this game so unique is the fact it is a puzzle in itself. This isnt like most of the other games that gave you your classic objectives and kicked you in the but expecting you to "get er done". Half-Life required that you used your mind to solve little escape puzzles. These puzzles ranged from, opening an oversized heater vent to activating oversized prones to a massive generator.
Now, lets talk about the dangers. theres alot in half-life that wants to kill you. Oversized fans are sure to turn those bones into processed alien brunch, and lets not forgert about those "Large falls of doom" Miss a ledge and its a long way down complimented by a nice crunch and the sound of your heart monitor flat lining.
Overall this is an amazing game that you must add to your collection. My step dad intoroduced me to it before he passed away, and I still find myself playing this game every now and then. I reccomend you play the game while listening to trance music, it makes it go so much smoother as my stepfather showed me.

I played Trove back in beta, before it was on Steam. It was really fun then, and though it's still fun now, there are some things I wish they had/hadn't changed.
1) In the beta, you could drop items. Now you cannot. This makes trading with other players tedious as you must first travel to a trading post. You can now only store or destroy items.
2) There are too many benches. Crafting is a massive part of this game, but it's very annoying that you must craft a bench to craft a bench to craft a certain item. How about just one bench with a level-tier system for what you can craft?
3) The monetization is stupid. Yes, I know, Trion has to make money somehow, but making some items available only for those willing to pay real money is ridiculous. This is the same nonsense that's plagued F2P games for years. Surely Trion can be more creative than this.
That being said, Trove is still a really fun game. The crafting system is solid and the items are pretty cool. Find a friend to play it with and you can adventure forever. That's actually true, considering the worlds are procedurally-generated. Definitely check this game out.

Gameplay wise, XCOM 2 is a definite improvement over it's predecessor. A lot of the problems i had with XCOM:EU and EW are fixed here. The streamlined base building mechanics are also welcome over the confusing layouts in Enemy Unknown. The character customization is also very detailed, allowing you to create lookalikes of your friends as well as yourself. The story is genuinely interesting too, with the concept of Aliens runnning an oppressive government executed quite well, with high-quality cinematics too.
However, the technical problems are very much present. Various animation glitches, crashes, terrain disappearing, aliens taking too long to respond in a turn, framerate drops etc. If this wasn't a turn-based game, i would have stopped playing a long time ago. i ran this game on an Intel 3970x @ 3.9 Ghz, 2x GTX 970s, 16gigs of RAM and the game running off a high-speed SSD, and the performance was pretty much the same, irrespective of whether SLI was on or off. And by that i mean the game runs poorly regardless of whether sli is on/off.
In it's current state, i cannot recommend this game. My advice for a potential customer would be to wait until the problems have been ironed out before picking this up. Or maybe wait for a sale.

Let's be clear from the start - most of this review is going to be about poor business practices by Chucklefish. Having said that, the game itself isn't worth your money. The content is all extremely repetitive, and if you find yourself checking back for any reason after the initial 5-10 hours, it'll be to see if any updates have taken place. You'll be met with disappointment. Avoid leaving the launcher up when you leave the game, as that trumps up your playtime as well, and Tiy loves to run to Twitter citing higher playtimes as reasons his game must be better than it is.
Now, on to why you REALLY shouldn't play this game:
The company behind it, Chucklefish, is among the most unethical and dishonest companies around. They're setting themselves up to be a miniature Electronic Arts. They're just as greedy, except they produce less.
They released nearly 7 months ago, and thus far have only produced two updates of questionable value, after taking in four million dollars in funding. From the moment of release it has been plagued with excuses for why development stopped, such as taking a month vacation after Steam release, then another 3-4 months so they could move a few members to London for communication purposes (which hasn't solved anything yet), to knocking off early for, "Mario Kart" sessions. Development remains in a state of limbo, and nobody is really sure what's going on.
Luckily, they don't communicate with the Steam community either, so the ignorance is shared among their company and investors. I mean, sure, they make loads of money on the platform, but when it comes to updating the folks that supported their 7 month vacation, you have to paw through every social media site known to man to actually locate information, and when you do, it's usually about everything BUT "Starbound." Wondering when the next update will be? I hope not, because their site, Reddit, and Twitter - the places they direct you to for announcements - contains everything from their new office dog, to employees playing in trash cans, to excuses for ranting on Twitter, such as them being under the influence of surgical drugs following an operation, yet managing to spend the entire day on Twitter.
Speaking of communication, unless it's blind praise, they don't want to hear it, and they WILL censor you. They'll claim they don't, and sure, you'll hear reports of their official websites being highly censored, and probably not think too much about it. "Two sides to every story" you'll tell yourself, until one of their developers comes through Reddit, Steam, and the Chucklefish forums and goes on a massive ban wave of critics, while allowing the harshest fanboys to remain, and you'll quickly learn it's true. The one responsible for the project, Tiyuri, even dedicates a significant portion of his day on Twitter calling all criticism "trolling" in an attempt to garner sympathy. If you head to their forums, they'll label ALL criticism - either done well or blatantly trolling - "flamebait" and lock it immediately... if you're lucky. Often enough, people have been banned for it, regardless of post quality.
There's more, but what I'm trying to say is, no matter what goes on with this game, don't support it. We've already funded the vacations of some of the laziest, most condescending people imaginable. They make promises they can't fulfill, spend most of their free time Tweeting and blogging about wasting time between complaining about the investors critical of them, taking the development money and spending it on other publishing ventures, and generally treating those that supported them with disdain and contempt, whilst simultaneously running off to Tweet about how everyone is mean to them and they don't understand why.
There are PLENTY of good indie companies out there, and Chucklefish is the exception to the rule. Give them your money instead.

I have completed a playthrough of this game, and I wanted to make a review to contrast other reviews that made me hesitant to purchase this game.
I have seen comments that the progression of the game locks you down into one linear path that you must take. This is not true. I am not even very experienced with XCOM games, but I can tell you that even I was able to easily take my own strategic approach to successfully beating the game. Claims that the aliens progress so fast that you are forced into a path of action are not true, and claims that missions have so few turns that they are nearly impossible to beat are also not true.
I had quite a lot of fun making strategic choices. There are times of push and pull, or an ebb and flow, of combat. You must learn when to properly establish an ambush, how to utilize concealment, and how to prioritize targets or utilize specific abilities on properly placed units in the right order. It is a great feeling to watch a well established strategy come to fruition. I think the problem some people have when they say that there aren't enough turns in a mission, is that they don't know how or when to sacrifice moving forward to create a proper kill zone strategy to decisively kill most or all enemies in a single turn. Furthermore, I think these individuals also lack the understanding of when to stop sitting back, and instead to charge forward into open and uncovered positions to dominate the enemy with high-risk-high-reward movements. Even a bull rush charge to an evac zone must be executed with proper decision making and method.
To all the people who complain of imbalance or insufficient time, I disagree strongly. I play a lot of strategy games, and this game is a fantastic strategy game. I was locked in for hours. I looked forward to coming home in the evenings and playing this game for a couple hours before heading to bed. Now that I've beaten it once, I think I'm going to go back through again now that I understand how to play this game better. It's fun, and it is a constant learning curve. As you develop, so will your enemies, and you will continuously encounter new enemies that you must quickly adapt to.
Are you ready to build a squad that has the proper array of abilities and soldiers to overcome any arrangement of obstacles and inconveniences? Ready to find the weak points of your opponents position and species and punish them for it? Eager to mitigate RNG with proper position and ability usage? Resource management to prevent, "not enough minerals," from starving you? Feel good about killing aliens trying to take over your planet? Then get ready for a lot of fun.

This game is the example of a true classic masterpiece. The enviourment is dark, the deaths are very abrupt, and the enimies are ruthless. Half-Life is sure to keep you on the edge of your seat and constantly fueling the feeling of paranoia in the back of your mind.
What makes this game so unique is the fact it is a puzzle in itself. This isnt like most of the other games that gave you your classic objectives and kicked you in the but expecting you to "get er done". Half-Life required that you used your mind to solve little escape puzzles. These puzzles ranged from, opening an oversized heater vent to activating oversized prones to a massive generator.
Now, lets talk about the dangers. theres alot in half-life that wants to kill you. Oversized fans are sure to turn those bones into processed alien brunch, and lets not forgert about those "Large falls of doom" Miss a ledge and its a long way down complimented by a nice crunch and the sound of your heart monitor flat lining.

This has got to be one of my favorite free to play MMOs of all time. It has great coop gameplay which relies on skill to stay alive, and staying alive is very important because it is a PERMADEATH game. It runs in Flash, so its compatible with almost all systems. The graphics are a retro pixelated masterpiece and will definitely bring on the nostalgia. The game has no ending, making it very addictive. This game is still being updated regularly and new content is being added all the time. There are 14 classes to unlock, loads of items to be found, dungeons for all skill levels, and a guild system to help encourage cooperation.
This game is also full of bugs that are difficult to fix, given the nature of the coding. The bugs aren't game-breaking but can get annoying at times. There is an unsolvable issue with memory leaks that will force you to restart the game every hour or so. Spambots advertise for websites that sell items illegally. Do not buy anything from them. The items they sell can be farmed in the game without spending any money. There is a trading system which you can use to buy, sell, trade, or gift items with other players. Do not spend money on items, it is a waste!
Some people, including myself, experience a bit of lag when playing the Steam version of this game. If you have issues such as input delay, I encourage you to give it another shot by playing it at its home,
.
With all that in mind, I still thoroughly enjoy this game and support its development by buying extra vault space and character slots. I would recommend it to anyone who likes skill based shooters and MMORPGs. Did I mention its FREE?!

Great concept with a few serious short comings. The initial apprentice dungeons and intermediate veteran dungeons are difficult, yet well balanced and rewarding. This isn't the case for the champion dungeons. I understand the game is based on the concept of "making the best out of a bad situation", but the late game difficulty spike is ridiculous. Basic enemies encountered in champion dungeons are seemingly on par with previous boss fights. My best heroes (max level, equipment, and skills) we're more often than not getting hopelessly roflstomped 2-3 battles in...even on short scouting quests. To make matters worse, management mechanics become increasingly skewed. For example, the weird level cap system prevents heroes from partaking in quests below their corresponding level, making it unnecessarily difficult to train badly-needed replacements and raise funds. Overall, late game play feels less about exploring dungeons/smighting evil  and more about bolstering lost gold and manpower (tedious/unrewarding grinding). After a couple hours of frustration, I threw in the towel. I doubt I have the motivation to finish it in its current state. Total shame, I really enjoyed it up to this point.
I realize Red Hook has plans to implement a short mode. Hopefully they address some of these issues/give the game more mass-appeal. Until then, I can't recommend this to anyone but hardcore RPG fans.....casual gamers stay away!

This is, to sum it up, one of the best games I've ever played, just like XCOM: Enemy Unknown. It's taken everything from Enemy Unknown and fine-tuned it to perfection. Less fun things like the fighter jets, satellites and panic tracker are gone, and new features such as the character pool where you can put your soldiers to reuse them in later campaigns, the concealment mechanic which allows you to surprise the enemy and ambush them, a line of sight indicator and the ability to heal from a distance with your Specialists rather than having them be close to wounded soldiers are in.
A greater selection of equipment, research, abilities and randomized maps all make for a much deeper and varied experience, and I'm sure I'll be replaying this many times over. Add in good mod support and you have a game that could last forever. With DLC coming soon adding even more content, XCOM 2 is just getting better and better. The only negative things I have to say are that the game's difficulty drops off rather quickly on lower difficulty settings, and that it has its fair share of bugs and performance issues.
Overall, it's the perfect turn-based strategy game and a very good candidate for GOTY 2016, if not one of the greatest games of all time. It's VERY highly recommended for all strategy fans.

So this is my first time taking the time to write a review:
The main takaway from this is, if you liked XCOM 1, buy this game. It's much more cinematic, customizable, and expansive. This is a review after having played 9 hours so far over the free weekend.
Fractured Space is a MOBA shooter game that puts you in the cockpit of your choice of several different ships.  Ships are broken down across three different corporations, and cover the whole range of standard MOBA roles.  There are close-ranged brawlers, quick-moving high damage hunters,  long-range snipers, and even cloaky assassins.  Support ships are also present, offering heals, disarms, and other utility functions to generally support the team.
You unlock new ships by playing with a corporation's ships and thereby gaining xp as you complete battles.  After you unlock them, you then spend credits (also achieved through battles) to purchase the ships for use.  For reference, after about 3 games I had enough to purchase my first ship from the 2nd tier of the corporation I used first.
As with any other MOBA-type game, every ship has its counters, and knowing them is a key to victory.  The development team has done an excellent job of balancing the different ships in their roles, and preventing any one ship from dominating the field.  While snipers may smash brawlers and some other short and midranged ships, they are easily dispatched with assassins and the quick-moving hunters.  I would like to pause and point out that the three "starter ships" as they're referred to, are equally effective as the later tiers of ships.  They just have a different focus and every ship is flown a little differently to maximize it's efficiency.  While skill always plays a role in any fight, bringing the right fleet composition will go a long way to achieving victory for your side.
Personally, I've very much enjoyed my time playing Fractured Space, and have not run into any errors or serious issues as of yet (I will update if I do).  While there are some negatives, the game is already very well-polished and extremely playable.  It is in a far better shape than many games I've played at release, and is currently only in alpha.  I believe this bodes well for the future of the game, and look forward to seeing continued development on the great experience Edge Case Games has offered us.
