This game is legit just a more modern version of Combat Arms. It follows every F2P shooter model that for some reason is pumped out of South Korea and I can only assume this one is backed by Nexon too. It's a fairly basic FPS, it has a really lame over the top cinematic tutorial that tries to make the game way more cooler then it is but fails at even being cool and is just annoying.
Seriously though it has pretty much the same menu as Combat Arms, and has the same business model where you "rent guns". For some reason though as far as I can tell you can buy every gun permanent for free, you don't really have to rent the guns, you can just save up until you can buy them perma. Which makes me wonder why you even have the option to rent. Only explanation I have is that the shop is the one from Combat Arms, because like I mentioned it's almost the exact same menu. Which would explain the rental option despite the business model currently not being geared towards you paying for permanent equipment.
Overall this game is Combat Arms, if you want to see what the games business model will be like in the future look at Combat Arms because that is what this game is. This was obviously some attempt to take that game, put a new coat of paint on it, and rake in a few more years worth of revenue.

Roguelikes or Rogues or whatever the term is have a certain appeal.  That "I like to be punished and die a lot."
But I personally also like to progress.  And this game is too unforgiving too often.  I spent hours training groups to take on the "Darkest Dungeon" the difficult ones, and in seconds they were obliterated.  That isn't fun to me, that's just telling me my time spent was time wasted.
I set the game down for a long time, came back, played through a dungeon...  I watched the stress of my party climb, I watched them one by one freak out, not one of them becoming valorous.  Then they started dying.
Then I remembered why I stopped playing it.
I got 40 hours out of it, but after a few other experiences similar to this (FTL comes to mind), I think I'm done with the "punishing" / "rogue like" genre.
My recommendation is to avoid the frustration.

Great game ! If you like tactical RPGs and Lovecraft, look no further this one is for you !
Darkest Dungeon is quite the challenge, your team WILL die horribly while you wonder why all your healers end up as masochistic screw-ups who damage themselves, this is not a "perfect run" kind of game...
With that said, the mechanics are good and simple enough so that you never feel cheated, the difficulty is not artificial here and you'll need to plan ahead carefully, make drastic choices and level up your characters to be able to get to even the first boss of the game.
DD has elements of Rogue Like (procedurally generated dungeons, random characters and enemy spawns, characters perma-death...) mixed in aswell, every new game will feel different and it has a ton of replayability.
Graphics are really nice, the illustrations really help to set the mood and are faithful to what you'd expect of a story centered around Lovecraftian lore.
All in all, if the game remotely interests you, get it ! You won't be disappointed

I'm going to start by saying that XCOM 2 is everything that XCOM: Enemy Unknown was except done better. If you liked Enemy Unknown or Enemy Within, you should probably just go ahead and buy this game, no questions asked. Now that we've gotten that out of the way, let's get to the nitty gritty.
So in XCOM 2, the game picks up where the first one left off: you lost, the aliens had their way with us and now humanity is controlled by creatures from outer space. This leads to a number of things: no more interceptor battle (yay!), a little bit more limited base building and a lot of turn timers.
At first, I thought I would hate the turn timers, but as I went on I grew to love them. They added the extra level of tension that this game needed to be better than the first. Along with a host of HORRIBLE new enemies, the turn timers prevent the game from being a tedious "move troops forward, then overwatch" crawl like the first one. Then of course there's the Avatar Project. If you don't complete certain missions to delay it, the aliens win. Which is also good as it prevents you from just sitting in one place on the map and collecting resources until you can steamroll anything they throw at you.
While the base building is more limited this time around, they dumped all of their effort into making the combat amazing and deep. The new "stealth" mechanic means that you can sneak around the map until you chose to ambush the enemy. The new armor mechanic means that you have to conserve those grenades for tougher enemies.
Also, the new skill-trees are way more diverse than the first game. Both paths are commpletely viable, as opposed to having certain must-have skills. Plus the sharpshooter is no longer completely broken, so that's a relief. My one minor complaint is that vanilla swords don't scale very well, but mods can easily fix that.
Which brings me to the workshop. The devs designed XCOM 2 to be moddable from day one. In fact, Long War Studios made three mods for the game that were available at launch (all of which are excellent and I highly recommend them). Plus there's an endless stream of new content. I tend to stay away from the ones that change the game's difficulty (such as increasing squad size, turning off timers), but the options are there if you want them.
Now let's talk about the bugs. Yes, there were a lot of issues at launch, but they seem to be getting ironed out over time. The most egregious offender is that framerate in the base is at about half of the combat's. While these glitches/bugs/optimization issues are annoying, they are far from gamebreaking. And let's not forget that Enemy Unknown's camera remains broken to this day. For me, these don't really take away from the experience. If you can't stand anything being out of place, this game may not be for you.
Then of course there's the character pool, allowing you to create and save soldiers/crewmen that will be randomly inserted into your game. There's nothing quite like rescuing Hulk Hogan and having him put to work as an engineer on your ship. Why wasn't this in the first game?
Last but by no means least, the maps are now randomly generated. That's right, the game is finally infinitely replayable without getting the same missions over and over again. I only played Enemy Unknown a couple times and Enemy Within a couple more because of this, but with endlessly generated levels, I will probably never have a reason to stop playing this game.
So in summary, this is a very similar game to Enemy Unknown, but leagues ahead of it in every way. I can't recommend XCOM 2 enough. It's everything you love (or hate) about XCOM turned up to 11 and it will keep me entertained for years to come.

I highly doubt I can say anything that hasn't already been said by countless other positive reviews so I'll just list a few short items and add my recommendations to this awesome game!
1.  Solid turn based strategy that looks beautiful.
2.  Good support in official patches and content release plans so far.
3.  Soldier customization is amazing!
4.  And maybe most importantly for the long term, superb modding support and potential.  If there's something you don't exactly like about the game, you can mod it to your heart's desire.  Fine tune the game exactly to your personal idea of 'fun'.  You can't ask for more than that!
I easily see this game being the first Steam game I put more than 1000 hours into, especially as future content and mods pave the way for more great fun and new adventures!

This game is legit just a more modern version of Combat Arms. It follows every F2P shooter model that for some reason is pumped out of South Korea and I can only assume this one is backed by Nexon too. It's a fairly basic FPS, it has a really lame over the top cinematic tutorial that tries to make the game way more cooler then it is but fails at even being cool and is just annoying.
Seriously though it has pretty much the same menu as Combat Arms, and has the same business model where you "rent guns". For some reason though as far as I can tell you can buy every gun permanent for free, you don't really have to rent the guns, you can just save up until you can buy them perma. Which makes me wonder why you even have the option to rent. Only explanation I have is that the shop is the one from Combat Arms, because like I mentioned it's almost the exact same menu. Which would explain the rental option despite the business model currently not being geared towards you paying for permanent equipment.
Overall this game is Combat Arms, if you want to see what the games business model will be like in the future look at Combat Arms because that is what this game is. This was obviously some attempt to take that game, put a new coat of paint on it, and rake in a few more years worth of revenue.

After my 100th hour, I have finally put an end to the Darkest Dungeon.
As the leper says, a tide rises and a tide falls - I made triumph and I faced defeat, with the latter being the most common. I have forsaken favourite heroes, lost valuable trinkets and relics at the cost of gold and progress. In the end, I found out that I was at a stalemate. "This isn't fair." I said that to myself multiple times, yet I continued to struggle. The feeling of accomplishment drove me. The feeling of success over such a huge crowd of people like me. I didn't give up, despite the stressful and desperate times. And now, I hold the spoils of victory. At what cost...?
Hats off to the developers. At first I saw the game as everyone else sees it - a game. I ignored the story - thought it was some universe where monsters just exist - came out of nowhere, being a trivial thing. On the contrary,  with the journals found and the bosses slain, I find out that the reason for these abominations' existance isn't a given. Someone is behind all of this, and the reason for all of these horrors.
Of course, people are and will be complaining about the RNG or grinding of it but the game is meant to be like that. I haven't seen a game so punishing and unfair before. But here I am, unscathed, actually pretty broken after the final quests, but at least the game teaches you not to falter in front of difficult challenges and situations. You will lose, of course, multiple times at that. But the trick is to keep on trying. And take note from this game and apply it in life.(cliche but a reality)
A note: the devs are working on a comic series about the characters' backstory. So far my favourite one is about the Crusader. You can check them out at the Darkest Dungeon Wiki.
UPDATE: A year later I still find a liking to the game. For those who have surpassed themselves even with New Game +, I suggest trying out the Pitch Black Dungeon mod in the Steam Workshop. The mod makes changes to heroes/monsters/events/items/curios/dungeons, for those seeking even a grater challenge. It's compatible with skins and even additional class mods. It was a breath of fresh air and I felt desperation like I did the first time I tried it. As a community item, it went beyond my expectations.

Post Edit: There are seemingly a large number of people giving unhelpful "dislikes" to a lot of the reviews that recommend the game, and vice-versa. Whether or not you like the game is one thing, but let the buyer choose for themselves. An "Overwhelmingly Positive" review score means something, after all.
A monumentally attractive, refreshingly poetic, and remarkably action-packed entry to an otherwise swamped genre. Passing through the gates of Hell comes Darkest Dungeon, an RTS style RPG with inherently difficult gameplay and a fantastic combination of ability-chaining and pure, old-fashioned luck.
Rather than a simple health and magic/mana/stamina system, DD introduces the Stress mechanic, similar to the Call of Cthulu (an obvious inspiration) board game; after fulfilling quests, the heroes must deal with the longing effects of wading through the mire and watching their companions become spew on the floor for a host of terrifying and objectively "what the ♥♥♥♥" monsters. A careful balance of experienced warriors and fresh-off-the-block newcomers will force you to make decisions based on an outcome you can never accurately foresee...
All the meanwhile, the looming sense of dread compounded by an ultimately idiotic (at least, in character, which abounds in this game) narrator serves to make it an immersive experience, far from my original expectation. Will you switch back and forth between various groupings, or find four heroes you flit under your wing, and do everything possible to maintain their sanity?
All is up in the air in Darkest Dungeon, and if not that, all is lost.

This is my opinion and how I feel about the game.  Please don't post negative remarks about my opinion of the game.  This is my review and I'm not asking for approval of others, nor others opinions on the matter.  Yes the game is in Alpha, and my opinion is based on the Alpha content.  If the game actually releases to a full game I will play it again and review it again.
The first thing that stands out to me is the F2P.  I don't like Free 2 Play becuase of the grind fest that are those games.  F2P also leads to unbalanced games where the game is balanced towards those whom pay vs those that don't (no pay no win).  So far it would seem the game is balanced for those that purchased the game vs those whom didn't only as far as time spent grinding ends up being better ships to kill you with.
There is an introduction video and turtorial about the game however the actual ship controls are really slugish.  Even for the small class ships the controls are really identical to the other ships.  It doesn't feel like a space sim.  The nose, and tail don't drop at all so you can't pull a lot of actual moves.  It really feels like a naval combat with mutliple layers.  The controls are bound and they are in the worst possible key bindings ever.  There are about 6 keys for weapons and systems 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, right and left mouse.  Of those 5 and 6 are port to another zone keys.  1, 2, 3, 4 are system or weapon keys along with left and right mouse.  To make matters worse you're using your w, a, s, d for movement, and space and ctrl for up and down.  So unless you're using your main two weapons/abilities you're gonna have to stop moving to fire.  There is a C for cruse control however it's just engine at full throtle.  Kind of funny since they made the areas really small and packed with astriods.  If your main to weapons and killers switch to another ship that has better main weapons and you'll win just because of crappy control designs.
There is no real point in going up or down as the weapons are mostly AOE, or lock on  missiles.  The rare chance when the fire is skill shot the rate of fire is so high, and range so long that you end up tagging people 90% of the time.
The only map they have isn't a bad concept at all.  However the constant jumping with only a 10 second cool down makes the game more about tactical jumping rather than anything else.  Learn how to jump to another zone and you win.  Each zone is very small for this kind of battle and there is almost no hiding or tactics other than simply go out and attack each other.  The tracking of other ships is super easy as well with the super zoom that allows you to see across the longest map.  The astroids, and small capture the flag bases are always in the same locations.  If you run into any astroid or base you'll get sticky glue syndrom and be stuck for a while.
The main reason I don't like this title is because the ships are so out of balance it's not even funny.  The heavy tank ship can dish out more damage than the attack ship.  It also can move as fast, or faster than the small medic ship.  The range on it's attacks is super long and effective up close as well.  Their are 3 tiers of ships for the heavy as well and only 2 tier for the others.
The developers aren't worried about alpha balancing at all but rather pumping out content regardless of quality.  The medical ships magically turn into non medical ships in the second tier.  Making healing others 100% useless if you want a better ship.  The titan class ships are worthless in battle and there is no way to stop someone from attacking them.  They pretty much get targeted as soon as you start healing.  So healing isn't even possible.  For a healing ship it has so little armor, or health that you end up dying every major fight.
If you know there are going to be 3 types of ships why not balance those 3 types really well then start adding options to them rather than coming out with more over powering of one ship type since everyone is playing it.  Alpha is a good time as any to start balancing your game, and coming out with new content at the same time.  Slight tweaks would fix a lot of bad game play.
The timers for death are out of balance for each class as well.  It's based off how many times you die.  Which is really messed up for thet over powered tank class vs the easy to kill medic class.  So you end up at a 1 to 2 minute timer for medic class, and 1 minute tops for those heavy class tanks.
There is no play with friends or create a game button.  So you have to both hit the luanch button, find the same server join that server, then hope you're on the same team.  If you aren't press f4 and hope someone will switch teams with you.
All in all the game was fun for about 3 hours.  After the new smell wears off it's grind fest, and play the over powered ships to grind.

So I've gotta be a big boy here and admit that my original review, was more of an angry rant than an actual review. It may have taken me way longer to understand the tips and tricks to not having your soldiers die on turn 1, but after a while, I've gotten past the learning curve.
This is a damn good game. I've had so much fun with it in my almost 90 hours as of now. In my opinion, it builds on the foundation of the already great previous entry "XCOM Enemy Unknown" and improves so many aspects.
For starters, the whole timed mission thing. This is one of the biggest criticisms that I've seen of XCOM 2, and honestly, it's an unjust one. The timed mission feature honestly adds to the overall tension of XCOM. If none of the missions were timed it would be as simple as "I'm gonna overwatch till the enemies eventually come this way" (Granted I did this a lot in EU) and when you finally get a mission where it isn't timed, it's almost a relief, but in a good way. The thing is, in XCOM 2, you're no longer a huge military force with unlimited recourses. You're a resistance force and it only  makes sense that you should feel backed into a corner as you fight this overpowering alien menace, and when you do succeed it just makes it that much sweeter.
When it comes to performance I will admit it's not the best, it could've been improved, especially on launch day. However, I feel like I've been one of the lucky ones. I have never had this game crash on me in almost 90 hours, it has hung from time to time but it has never fully crashed. The framerates do dip a bit in certain environments but I'm not exactly running with god tier hardware so honestly the complaints about performance are a bit harsh
I also really have to commend Firaxis for their support of mods. The fact that we had day 1 mods that honestly feel like they integrate perfectly into the vanilla game is astounding! I would seriously recommend installing anything put out by LongWarStudios, those guys know what theyre doing!
My point is, I hopped on the hate bandwagon a bit too early, and I want to think a lot of others did too. It's easy to nitpick every little flaw in a game when you're not enjoying it. At first, I wasn't enjoying it because quite frankly I sucked♥♥♥♥♥ not because the game itself was flawed. The early game, you will be put through a meat grinder, formed into a meat patty, stomped on, then put right back through that meat grinder over and over and over again. The early game is tough as nails, but once you start getting into some of the research development side of things with better weapons and armor, you feel a sense of progression, you can honestly see and feel that you're more powerful. That's something that they did even better than Enemy Unknown in my opinion.
If you liked the first game, I'd recommend picking it up. It's got a bunch of new features you're gonna have to get used to, believe me it takes a while. My biggest gripe with the game is that it does a ♥♥♥♥ing terrible job with its tutorials. However once you learn some of the little tricks on how to take down certain enemies, the best ways to flank, etc, you will feel like an absolute boss, taking down the alien menace and saving the planet!
If you decide to pick up the game, you won't be dissapointed. Good Luck Commander! ;)

RE-EDIT: February 2017 and XCOM 2 inexplicably works again. Strange.
First off, if you enjoyed XCOM1, you will enjoy XCOM2. But wait, performance fixes are needed, and modders are doing a good job patching up what Firaxis has delivered, it is becoming a game. When it came out, it was mostly a storyline, non-canonical at that. Again.
What do I like? The battles work much better, now you can actually sneak about - set up ambushes, and spy on patrols and try to predict where is the best angle of attack. Mostly the same game as XCOM1, but with has an abundance of cutscenes and animations, which is a bit of a problem for some in regards to performance. I manage.
Snake people are back, instead of the thin man concept, they are actually snake people.
Science is still stupid. Always was. If the soldiers given an alien a nickname in the field, that's basically the name that sticks, and you get the animation with the analysis when you initiate the research, not when its done. Well you get it then too - more text, no new content. Lots of loading, nada content. But it was always like that, now its just - IN YOUR FACE. Engineering works much better. There are no MEC's this time around, though. Instead they have more armor, and a hectic game pace.
This game is actually a bit of a challenge.
BUT: There are no factions, like in XCOM1, you just have money handed over to you from more or less irrellevant sponsors. Why of why have Firaxis abandoned the concept of factions - which were brilliant in Apocalypse, when you could pillage, raid and wage war as much against human organizations, as against aliens, and they would gravitate towards XCOM or the alien "masters" (otherwise that game was extremely silly with teddy-bear graphics...)
This game, with its terrorist angle would not be any less of an enjoyment if you could try to make alliances with other resistance groups, could try to convince corporations to lend you aid covertly, or attack these treasonous groups outright for supplies and corvè labour. It is a blunder and missed opportunity that tells me that Firaxis is more interested in mass production than quality.
Then we have damage. You can actually kill everything here. You kan kill every civillian and level all buildings without any consequences whatsoever. Of course there is 1 type of mission where you HAVE TO RESCUE 6 people. Because they are yours. But even here you can safely blow up the rest. This is stupid. In the "olden days" collateral damage, even damage to infrastructure would harm your budget and support. Now maybe, as a terrorist, bombing buildings would not have a totally negative consequence but playing ISIS is completely possible here, and doesnt affect the game at all. And is stupid.
Now, I have to mention that physics is back where it used to be before Firaxis took up the thread. Now objects will not be hanging in empty space if the supporting structure is removed. Killing aliens by blowing up walls and floors, making them fall many stories, or having the roof cave in on them is actually a workable strategy, and this is a huge and welcome improvement. I could not believe why this was not the case in XCOM1.
Now I must also mention the stupid mistakes they have made upon launch. Like smoke grenades actually not providing any game effects at all. Oh you might think you got some defense bonus, but that's just a puff of color you have there. Fortunately, the modders have fixed it, but you HAVE TO get one of those two mods.
Like the sound options; you can tone everything down, but there are some ambient and triggered sounds that DONT RESPOND to your commands in the options. Like the intro music that will still blast you upon launch until the menu appears, like the sound that comes when aliens are revealed, this will always be loud, radios and other sources in game will jabber on. So if you play on a headseat, or late at night trying not to wake others from sleep, be aware of this so you dont go deaf or something.
Also, still there are no bases to be built. Now you fly around in a captured (?) UFO, which is fine for a resistance I guess, but it must get cramped and you loose any possibility of specializing your capacities. So there OUGHT TO be a feature where you build small bases, which would act as your recruitment/training facilities, the listening posts, R&D stations, etc. But there are No such Things. You fly around the world and set up radio towers. Like the analogous radio network would be beyond the capacity of aliens to infiltrate. There are no base attacks either, so this time around Firaxis saved themselves ALOT of work. There are no alien landscapes at all in this game. Very few aliens as well in fact (they are all projections or genetic reworkings, the aliens are gone).
The storyline hints at a dynamic approach with the option to turn against the resistance. This is only in words, there are no such options in the game. It is a uniliear storyline, with very little strategy, and these make up my primary problems; No strategy, no factions nor economics without any diplomacy and very little responsibility.
Tactics work fine, great and much better than last time.
If I can manage to learn, I will make the factions and the ways to deal with them myself. Cause of course without modbuddy this game would be DOA.

I will actually be serious in this review so people who actually want to know the pros and cons of this game can see.
Pros:
- Very smooth gameplay. No long pauses between combat and each turn transitions quite well.
-Character customazation is really fun. The game lets you create the characters backstory, nickname, first and last name, armour, armour patterns and colors, gun attachments, etc. Really creates a bond that keeps you invested in keeping them alive.
-Story is standard humans rise against increasingly difficult alieans in different situations. I haven't made it all the way through the story yet. I will edit it when I do.
-Even though all these joke reviews say that the shot percentage is still against you, I feel like it has been quite balanced out. Way better than the original at least.
-Tougher variations of old enemies really make you think rather than blow past puny sectoids every mission.
-The base management and means of getting supplies has been tweaked and makes budgeting seem more real than last game.
Cons:
-There are an awful amount of turn limited missions. They make you destroy, encrypt, or rescue something in a set time, and if you don't all squad members who didn't evac get left behind. Very frustrating if you play ironman.
-Seems like squadmates panic way too easily no matter how high their will. A tiny complaint, but lots of tiny things add up to become a huge turnoff.
-The difficulty ramp is too high for me at times. I absolutely appreciate and embrace a challenge, but this ramp curves till it's almost a circle. Once you discover the advanced alien units, even once, get ready for them to be in every single mission.
-There are quite a few annoying bugs and some long load times. Trying to start the game can be a chore at times when I click the oberlay to actually bring up the game and the window will pop up, but nothing will be there. I have issues with long loading times between missions, after cutscenes, etc. Also, sometimes the main menu won't let me do anything. The animantions work and I can move my mouse cursor, but I cannot select anything.
Overall: I haven't been able to play the whole game yet, but what I have played, I have loved and will continue playing it. It's a great TBS game and it reminds me of why TBS and shooters can mesh so well.

You can "jump" between zones, but only connected ones.  Right lane to middle, middle to left, and once all are captured, you can jump into the enemy's base zone from one of the "lane" zones.
There are points to capture/defend within each lane and when you are able to level up, you just coast into a friendly captured point and it automatically gives you the boost.
It's pretty cool in my opinion and so far, the ships seem reasonably easy enough to acquire.

In my limited time playing Black Squad, it has a lot of potential to be a great game, so here are a list of good and things they can improve
Pros
- It's not a Pay2Win game. A lot of F2P games allow you to buy better weapons leaving the guys who don't want to spend money at a huge disadvantage. This game is spot on towards competing without disadvantages towards those who don't spend money on ingame items. There are skins and such to buy ingame but does not give advantages to anyone else.
- Sounds are really good, the footsteps are loud so sneaking around is usually the best way to go
Battle (Gamemode) is a very intense and fun gamemode to play
- Most guns are pretty balanced
- Demolition (Gamemode) is really fun
- It's Free to Play
Things to improve
- The Blazer (sniper rifle) is really overpowered in that it's mobility is really high for a one-shot kill. If they reduced movement speed and make it more of a stationary weapon rather than a run and gun one-shot kill then I think that would balance it
- When observing (dead/spectating) teammates, it's hard to tell which is a teammate and which is an enemy. I suggest putting a highlight over teammates much like in CSGO so people know who's an enemy and who's not. Also keeping the minimap up while observing would be beneficial for players that use 3rd party communication services (discord, mumble, teamspeak) to help make callouts to teammates
- In Demolition (gamemode) Bomb timer is 40 seconds and the defuse is 7 seconds. The maps are fairly large and as a Peacemaker (defender) will take a while to clear areas and get to the bomb to defuse. The percentage of winning a round as a peacemaker, especially when stuck at a disadvantage (1v2) and on the other side of the map, is really low. If they increase the timer to say 50 or 60 seconds it would still be competitive and give the Peacemakers a chance to win the round. Either increase the bomb timer or decrease defusal/plant time.
- Would like to see some more gamemodes (maybe Capture the Flag, etc)
- Obviously this is still early access but with time I'd like to see more weapons and cooler, more aesthetically pleasing animations when inspecting weapons
- Not too big a deal, but adding in-game microphone would be beneficial when playing gamemodes such as demolition where communication is key
- Map design is good not great, basic map styles. Some have too many openings it's hard as a Peacemaker to navigate where the enemies are. Keeping it simple will make the game flow much better
Overall this is a fun game that I hope will continue to update and get better.

Even though this game is almost 15 years old and uses a modified Quake engine, it is still one of the most FUN and best shooters ever to be made. In fact all other first person shooters and games in general can learn from Half Life 1. The game world is extremely immersive. There are no level ends, there is no text to read, there are no scores and everyone talks to you without freezing you into a cut scene. All of this makes you feel less like you are a player playing a game, but you are indeed the hero Gordon Freeman. Characters recognize you, talk to you, and you can have them come with you or stay put. Security guards that come with you will shoot enemies (slowly).
The story is that you are silent protagonist Gordon Freeman (you'll feel like him by the end) and you work for Black Mesa, your standard super secret facility. Something goes horribly wrong and uh. The formula is very simple, but they execute it so well that other games have copied it and failed (Doom 3). Needless to say you need to fight your way out through the facility, on the desert (being chased by a helicopter), and everything else would just be a spoiler. There are no levels, no loading screens. Loading is seamless and happens during downtime.
Half Life 1 has simple controls and an optional tutorial level. There are buttons for jumping, crouching (sneaking), using your flashlight (that needs to be off to charge it), shooting, secondary shooting (for machine guns) and "using" things. The game is always in run mode and character speed seems to be fast. Too fast sometimes, but there is that sneak button that will slow you down.
But how is the first person shooting? There is a wide variety of guns and each has a certain joy and usefulness to them. Even the simple pistol is useful for lesser enemies 8 hours into the game. There is a shotgun, a machine gun with grenade launcher, grenades, explosives you detonate, wall sensors with explosives, a harpoon, a laser guided rocket launcher that once it launches you point your cursor and it will turn accordingly, lasers, homing missiles, head crabs and more. An amazing array that you continue to get even up to the final levels areas. To swap weapons you push 6 number keys and press some keys twice to access some weapons like the shotgun / machine gun / harpoon.
You start with a crowbar good for breaking grates, and destroying boxes. Destroying boxes is how you will find most items and ammo. Instead of just finding things scattered on the floor, on shelves or on a desk you need to bash open boxes to find the good stuff. You can also push or pull the boxes too which is nice for puzzle solving and platforming.
The enemies are just as diverse and each one requires you to think and act differently. Since I don't know the name of any enemy I'll fumble through this. The start enemies are lesser creatures that will start on the floor and jump at you. 2 shots from a pistol take them out. There are zombie-ish aliens that take a shotgun or two, but they are easy enough to avoid. Aliens that teleport in and beam electricity at you will cause you to hide, pudgy little alien crawler / hoppers will make you shoot from a distance because they will send out a small shockwave. Standard soldiers that will shoot machine guns, throw grenades and coordinate attacks against you like flanking. Ceiling huggers that are yucky red globs on the ceiling with long rope like tongues that when they catch you, you'll be pulled up and eaten... if you don't shoot them. Giant aliens with homing missiles too. There is a wide variety of enemies and bosses. I can't list them all.
The game also shines with its tricks and traps and will throw a puzzle or challenge at you to keep you thinking. But in this game it doesn't feel like a puzzle or a challenge. It seems natural. There can be a hidden turret where the fun is making your choice how to take it out... Grenade, explosive, shooting it and getting shot in the process, running by it or just not hitting the trip wire to start it in general. Wall sensor explosives, push and pull box puzzles, pushing buttons, hopping hanging boxes over a pit, conveyer belts, using a sky cannon to destroy walls, using turrets, on rails vehicles that you have a lot of control over, water puzzles, high jump pads and so on. There is a lot of variety and it's never the same thing twice.
To sum it up, this is a diverse and VERY FUN game. It has a sense of humor to it and you'll feel like you are Gordon Freeman through the game's well crafted immersion. Puzzles, shooting and challenges all melded together into one fantastic game and I can't say that too often.

I will actually be serious in this review so people who actually want to know the pros and cons of this game can see.
Pros:
- Very smooth gameplay. No long pauses between combat and each turn transitions quite well.
-Character customazation is really fun. The game lets you create the characters backstory, nickname, first and last name, armour, armour patterns and colors, gun attachments, etc. Really creates a bond that keeps you invested in keeping them alive.
-Story is standard humans rise against increasingly difficult alieans in different situations. I haven't made it all the way through the story yet. I will edit it when I do.
-Even though all these joke reviews say that the shot percentage is still against you, I feel like it has been quite balanced out. Way better than the original at least.
-Tougher variations of old enemies really make you think rather than blow past puny sectoids every mission.
-The base management and means of getting supplies has been tweaked and makes budgeting seem more real than last game.
Cons:
-There are an awful amount of turn limited missions. They make you destroy, encrypt, or rescue something in a set time, and if you don't all squad members who didn't evac get left behind. Very frustrating if you play ironman.
-Seems like squadmates panic way too easily no matter how high their will. A tiny complaint, but lots of tiny things add up to become a huge turnoff.
-The difficulty ramp is too high for me at times. I absolutely appreciate and embrace a challenge, but this ramp curves till it's almost a circle. Once you discover the advanced alien units, even once, get ready for them to be in every single mission.
-There are quite a few annoying bugs and some long load times. Trying to start the game can be a chore at times when I click the oberlay to actually bring up the game and the window will pop up, but nothing will be there. I have issues with long loading times between missions, after cutscenes, etc. Also, sometimes the main menu won't let me do anything. The animantions work and I can move my mouse cursor, but I cannot select anything.
Overall: I haven't been able to play the whole game yet, but what I have played, I have loved and will continue playing it. It's a great TBS game and it reminds me of why TBS and shooters can mesh so well.

In my limited time playing Black Squad, it has a lot of potential to be a great game, so here are a list of good and things they can improve
Pros
- It's not a Pay2Win game. A lot of F2P games allow you to buy better weapons leaving the guys who don't want to spend money at a huge disadvantage. This game is spot on towards competing without disadvantages towards those who don't spend money on ingame items. There are skins and such to buy ingame but does not give advantages to anyone else.
- Sounds are really good, the footsteps are loud so sneaking around is usually the best way to go
Battle (Gamemode) is a very intense and fun gamemode to play
- Most guns are pretty balanced
- Demolition (Gamemode) is really fun
- It's Free to Play
Things to improve
- The Blazer (sniper rifle) is really overpowered in that it's mobility is really high for a one-shot kill. If they reduced movement speed and make it more of a stationary weapon rather than a run and gun one-shot kill then I think that would balance it
- When observing (dead/spectating) teammates, it's hard to tell which is a teammate and which is an enemy. I suggest putting a highlight over teammates much like in CSGO so people know who's an enemy and who's not. Also keeping the minimap up while observing would be beneficial for players that use 3rd party communication services (discord, mumble, teamspeak) to help make callouts to teammates
- In Demolition (gamemode) Bomb timer is 40 seconds and the defuse is 7 seconds. The maps are fairly large and as a Peacemaker (defender) will take a while to clear areas and get to the bomb to defuse. The percentage of winning a round as a peacemaker, especially when stuck at a disadvantage (1v2) and on the other side of the map, is really low. If they increase the timer to say 50 or 60 seconds it would still be competitive and give the Peacemakers a chance to win the round. Either increase the bomb timer or decrease defusal/plant time.
- Would like to see some more gamemodes (maybe Capture the Flag, etc)
- Obviously this is still early access but with time I'd like to see more weapons and cooler, more aesthetically pleasing animations when inspecting weapons
- Not too big a deal, but adding in-game microphone would be beneficial when playing gamemodes such as demolition where communication is key
- Map design is good not great, basic map styles. Some have too many openings it's hard as a Peacemaker to navigate where the enemies are. Keeping it simple will make the game flow much better
Overall this is a fun game that I hope will continue to update and get better.

This is the first time I'm writing a review ever because I cannot sit by and abide Bethesda's extreme disregard towards its customers any longer.
There has been a lot controversy surrounding the introduction of the Creation Club(CC) aka "paid mods" and is covered by many other reviews here.What I'm going to talk about is somewhat different.
For those who have bought every FO title made by Bethesda,it has already been well established that each title is left a bug riddled mess with many bugs present since release.You see,Bethesda does not care about fixing bugs and by extension,its customer's experience.They only fix major game breakers/blockers and ignore everything else(which is A LOT!).As long as you can complete the main questline from start to finish,they consider their work done.This results in many issues that add up ranging from side quests that do not execute properly(not getting the rewards or the intended result) to  the game hanging.How would you like to go through a lengthy quest chain only to not get what you earned or the result you sought?If Bethesda expects us to just stick only to the main questline and ignore everything else to avoid the bugs,wouldn't that defeat the purpose of it being open world and a RPG?
The typical Bethesda FO release goes like this:
So,they only release 2 types of patches,one is for new dlc,the other is for game breakers.I tried to give them the benefit of the doubt by assuming that they wanted to wait till after all DLC has been released to handle all the bugs at one go but much time has passed since the last DLC was released and yet no further fixes.This applies to all previous titles as well,you can look up their patch history.The only exception is Obsidian,the creators of FO:New Vegas.Obsidian tried at least to fix further quest bugs but it was obvious that their hands were tied by Bethesda(probably for the reason that bug fixing is not profitable).It isn't suprising as well that New Vegas turned out to be one of the more well received titles among the new FOs given that Obsidian genuinely care about the player experience.
Instead,Bethesda announced they are making FO4 VR and introduced the CC.Does Bethesda seriously expect us to have confidence in FO4 VR when they have not bothered to properly fix the existing game?The CC is the ultimate insult to injury because not only does it show that they prioritze short term gains over the customer experience,their whole stance about it is hypocrtical as well.They claim that one of their goals with the CC is to introduce new quality content that will enrich the player experience yet ironically,they CANNOT BE BOTHERED to fix the myriad of long existing bugs that DETRACT from the player experience.Obvious PR speak to hide their greed.The CC is what they PRIORITIZED their team to do over bug fixing?Wow.
I would not have mind the CC that much if Bethesda had bothered to fix their game in a consistent manner but that is not the case.You can't always take from us Bethesda,you have to give in order to receive at times too and that 100 credits is a spit in the face for what we have to put up with.
There are some who would come to Bethesda's defence by pointing out that there are mods that "fix" those bugs.I take issue with that because of 2 reasons.First of all,they are not fixes but workarounds that usually involve the execution of console commands via mods,as such they can turn out to be awkward and immersion breaking.
The second reason is because I EXPECT Bethesda to do their own job since ultimately only they have all the tools and expertise to handle those bugs.Even modders have commented that some things must be done by Bethesda because all they can make are band-aids.Just like it is fair for Bethesda not to be responsible for issues caused by mods,modders should not be expected to clean up the mess created by Bethesda too.The lack of further fixes shows an absolute lack of responsibility on Bethesda's part.
With the introduction of the CC,I worry that Bethesda is going to double down by selling bug fixes(they have not ruled it out).Remember the aforementioned fixes by modders?Imagine someone makes a better one for sale on the CC exclusively.The only way you are going to enjoy bug fixes that should have been Bethesda's responsibility in the first place is to pony up the cash.If they sell it piecemeal by making it location specific(eg vault 81 quest fixes),you will be looking at forking out a whole bunch because this game has plenty of bugs.That way,Bethesda gets to profit by asking someone else to do their work form them while taking the lion's share at the same time.
TLDR:Do not support a hypocritical company that claims to care about the player experience on one hand but does nothing about the issues that detract from said experience on the other.
Edit(23/11/17):To further prove my point,several updates were released one after another in a relatively short period of time after the release of the creation club.Guess what?The patches were all related to Creation Club.It shows that Bethesda is capable of releasing patches but only for things that matter to them,longstanding game bugs not being one of them.

First of all, I do like the game, but, it has a myriad of problems.
Xcom 2 is just more of the same (with a little less currently) of the first game.
There’s no real innovation, it’s just prettier.
The feature “you get the jump on the aliens” changes nothing, it actually works the same way in Xcom 1. You spot a pod of enemies, engage them the best way possible while you try your best to not aggro another pod, which continues to stay oblivious to the fact that their “buddies” are in trouble.
The story, where is taken on the perspective that we lost the first game, is pretty… lame actually. They re-use basically every plot feature from the first installation but try to keep that sense of wonder which is already lost to people who have played it.
This time around you have a time limit to finish the game, which is somewhat manageable, but still quite limiting. (I didn’t actually let the time expire to see what happens, though).
Classes are okay. Rangers are pretty dope with their swords, even though these can be a coin toss at some points, and Supports’ got a robot that heals.
The worst part are the technical issues. The game is sluggish when compared to the first one. Everything takes too damn long to happen, loading screens, turn ending, environmental damage, camera angle switching when you unleash a barrage of overwatch and whatnot.
But know this. Mods. Mods make everything better.

Darkest Dungeon is a game that is challenging, but fair. The people you command will die and it will be your fault 99% of the time. The enemies will be challenging, but the game gives you time to prepare. You can leave any dungeon at any time, and in combat you can also try to run away during your turn. Regardless of what stage you are in the game you can always train new recruits, with only 2 or 3 successful dungeon runs to catch up to your strongest guys. In my experience what kills your party most is not the bosses, stages, or enemies, but the players own greed and huberus.
Gameplay 7/10
The gameplay follows a pretty simple turn based system. Each turn, each of your people get to make a move once, and each enemy (usually) gets to make a move once. Before battles you can equip your party with trinkets that help in combat, allocate skills for camping and combat, upgrade weapons, prepare supplies for the dungeon run, then go running off into one of the 5 dungeons. One thing I personally liked is that there is no mana, but the opponent also has no mana, so everybody gets to spam. You will often end up changing groups for dungeons, so one of the challenges will be deciding how placement, and abilities will work ingame. Overall the combat is pretty simple.
Music 5/10
The game doesn't have many great songs. The sounds work well in the games atmosphere, but In the whole playthrough there was only 2 moments where i thought the soudtrack was good.
Story 8/10
The story is simple, but good. The real element that makes it shine is the narrator, who has a great speaking voice, but makes horrible decisions which is why you are hiring people to clear dungeons in the first place.
Characters 8/10
The people you hire interact well in the game. It really makes you feel like you are hiring mercenaries and sending them to their deaths.
If you are looking for a long and hard game with a great atmosphere and narration you are in the right place.

DD is actually fairly difficult. I mean, it doesn't start difficult, but as you get into the more advanced dungeons, it is. I actually think that's a good thing. You need to be willing to run away from fights. The only issue with the game is that in order to get a good endgame roster, you need to run a lot of dungeons to amass loot so that you can upgrade your skills and weapons to the top level, which are quite expensive. I don't have a problem with the prices of those upgrades, nor do I have a problem with the amount of loot that drops from dungeons. Instead, I think they should make the inventory items stack higher. More gold, more gems etc per slot. You STILL need to make choices about what to take with you and what to leave behind, but that way you're not leaving 60% of the loot back inside the dungeon once you're finished.
This is however accomplished with a simple config file edit that doesn't really do much about the game difficulty, it just saves you time. I'd just like to see a reasonable increase hardcoded into the game rather than essentially having users set it themselves.
Regardless, even if someone was a bit of a turd and made it so they could carry literally everything in a dungeon back with them, the game would still be difficult because 90% of its difficulties comes from the combat itself. You need to make  choices and think about the likely result of choosing to use one skill versus another. You also need to think about what character classes will go well together. If you don't set yourself up with some kind of system, you're going to have a very hard time of it in the game and lose a lot of characters.

I love games like this, they're goofy, fun, and challenging. There are people who may not consider this as a true "game," but the point of games like these is that they break the mould, and discover new ways to entertain. Also, doesn't usually fail in making you laugh in the end.
Upon starting up the game, I was using a keyboard. Yes, it is difficult, but just like with any game, you learn how it works. It took me a hilarious hour to finish the tutorial. I don't regret it. Went into free roam next to get a better handle on controls, check out the environment. Being each type of bread can present its own difficulties surprisingly. I did connect one of my controllers up to play this, and it is much easier. Although, if you just set your "grips" to comfortable keys close together, it shouldn't be much of a problem to use a keyboard. Going through the game, there are a lot of little things to find, and interact with. At the end of one game session, all that I could see of my little toast was chips, eggs, and jam/jelly sitting in a pile of mass destruction. You can try to skateboard, but I seem to fail that, and just send myself flying. Curiosity sent me into a garbage can. All in all, this is a game you'd love if you like challenging physics, comedy, bread, and a bit of mini sandbox exploration.

Okay now that i've beat the game I can say a few more things about it.
Veterans of EU/EW will be right at home with the basic gameplay of x2 but there are some big changes in it.
Most missons now have a forced timer putting pressure on the player, I actualy like this feature, it adds to the strategy of the game. In EU it was too easy to just sit down spaming overwatch, and in x2 this is somthing that is much harder to do. be it having to get to an objective in eight turns or the VIP missons.
Now the VIP missons is probably where the timer becomes an issue for people due to one thing, for these missons you have twelve turns to do your objective and EVAC, any soldiers left behind are basicly dead (they can be saved down the road in another VIP misson but at that point they would be way behind in rank) these missons are stressful, anoying, and are easily the hardest missons in the game.
The thing is, this game is modable as hell. you can easily remove timers, extended them (my favorite) or just make missons easier, or harder. This so remeber if you have an issue with this game mods will help. and if they don't, steam refunds.

Black Squad (previously known as Viper Circle) is a free-to-play, military-themed first-person shooter video game developed by NS Studio through a team assembled around Park Bo-Hyun, a former producer for Alliance of Valiant Arms, at South-Korea-based NS Studio. The game was released to public in 2013 but went through a complete overhaul afterwards, most notably the setting from near-future to military theme with some elements of modern warfare.
Black Squad pits two teams, Viper Circle and Peacemaker, against each other in various game modes and maps that can host up to 20 players and "large scale" 32-player matches known as Battle Mode and allows players to call for airstrike and artillery support, based on a special combat skill system. Players can choose from many modern realistic firearms and improve their FPS skills.

Overall Rating: 4/10
Gameplay Rating: 6/10 - simple, fun gameplay; no real explanation for essential aspects of the game
Accessibility Rating: 2/10 - no captions/subtitles
So far, this appears to be a Control Points type game where you and your team of 4 other players try to capture stations in different quadrants to gain resources for ship upgrades that ultimately help you capture the enemy station.  Both teams fight for control of these stations and team members must work together to simultaneously capture points for your team and prevent the opponent from capturing for theirs.
Some Alpha stage problems do exist.
- First, it is difficult to get into a server - I often experience a failed join with no explanation as to why that is.
- Second, the basics of the game are in place, such as an initial set of ships and crew, but more are to be added, and there are some aspects of crew arrangement that seem to be placeholders for future functionality only.
- Third, as it is now, I have not seen any real tutorial for out-of-play experience (such as crew, ship selection and upgrading, and tech tree) to explain the details of what is what.
- Finally, the control schema for the game is only accessible outside of gameplay via the Hub interface rather than through game options.
On the plus side, the gameplay itself is fluid when you get into it and the currently available game mode is relatively easy to grasp without a steep learning curve.  Further, there is currently a rudimentary technology tree that offers different ships (and different styles of gameplay) based on an in-game credit system that currently requires no micro payments.
In its early stages, players seem to still be developing tactics for successful team play and I can see this game improving into something both challenging and fun to play with friends over time.
+ You CAN edit options before playing the game.
+ HOH gamers CAN adjust audio controls separately for master volume, music, effects, and voice.
+/- Players with mobility issues can NOT currently rebind keys from inside the game, but the developers will add this feature soon.  For now, check out
if you are comfortable editing game files.
- Subtitles DO NOT exist for this game.
It is playable without captions, but information may be missing.
Further, the instructional video on the Hub screen (when you first open game) is sourced from YouTube and the developers did not caption the video.  Deaf/HOH gamers must rely on Auto-captions for this video.
+ Gamers can communicate in game (both Team and All chat) with an easy-to-read chat system.

This is the first time I'm writing a review ever because I cannot sit by and abide Bethesda's extreme disregard towards its customers any longer.
There has been a lot controversy surrounding the introduction of the Creation Club(CC) aka "paid mods" and is covered by many other reviews here.What I'm going to talk about is somewhat different.
For those who have bought every FO title made by Bethesda,it has already been well established that each title is left a bug riddled mess with many bugs present since release.You see,Bethesda does not care about fixing bugs and by extension,its customer's experience.They only fix major game breakers/blockers and ignore everything else(which is A LOT!).As long as you can complete the main questline from start to finish,they consider their work done.This results in many issues that add up ranging from side quests that do not execute properly(not getting the rewards or the intended result) to  the game hanging.How would you like to go through a lengthy quest chain only to not get what you earned or the result you sought?If Bethesda expects us to just stick only to the main questline and ignore everything else to avoid the bugs,wouldn't that defeat the purpose of it being open world and a RPG?
The typical Bethesda FO release goes like this:
So,they only release 2 types of patches,one is for new dlc,the other is for game breakers.I tried to give them the benefit of the doubt by assuming that they wanted to wait till after all DLC has been released to handle all the bugs at one go but much time has passed since the last DLC was released and yet no further fixes.This applies to all previous titles as well,you can look up their patch history.The only exception is Obsidian,the creators of FO:New Vegas.Obsidian tried at least to fix further quest bugs but it was obvious that their hands were tied by Bethesda(probably for the reason that bug fixing is not profitable).It isn't suprising as well that New Vegas turned out to be one of the more well received titles among the new FOs given that Obsidian genuinely care about the player experience.
Instead,Bethesda announced they are making FO4 VR and introduced the CC.Does Bethesda seriously expect us to have confidence in FO4 VR when they have not bothered to properly fix the existing game?The CC is the ultimate insult to injury because not only does it show that they prioritze short term gains over the customer experience,their whole stance about it is hypocrtical as well.They claim that one of their goals with the CC is to introduce new quality content that will enrich the player experience yet ironically,they CANNOT BE BOTHERED to fix the myriad of long existing bugs that DETRACT from the player experience.Obvious PR speak to hide their greed.The CC is what they PRIORITIZED their team to do over bug fixing?Wow.
I would not have mind the CC that much if Bethesda had bothered to fix their game in a consistent manner but that is not the case.You can't always take from us Bethesda,you have to give in order to receive at times too and that 100 credits is a spit in the face for what we have to put up with.
There are some who would come to Bethesda's defence by pointing out that there are mods that "fix" those bugs.I take issue with that because of 2 reasons.First of all,they are not fixes but workarounds that usually involve the execution of console commands via mods,as such they can turn out to be awkward and immersion breaking.
The second reason is because I EXPECT Bethesda to do their own job since ultimately only they have all the tools and expertise to handle those bugs.Even modders have commented that some things must be done by Bethesda because all they can make are band-aids.Just like it is fair for Bethesda not to be responsible for issues caused by mods,modders should not be expected to clean up the mess created by Bethesda too.The lack of further fixes shows an absolute lack of responsibility on Bethesda's part.
With the introduction of the CC,I worry that Bethesda is going to double down by selling bug fixes(they have not ruled it out).Remember the aforementioned fixes by modders?Imagine someone makes a better one for sale on the CC exclusively.The only way you are going to enjoy bug fixes that should have been Bethesda's responsibility in the first place is to pony up the cash.If they sell it piecemeal by making it location specific(eg vault 81 quest fixes),you will be looking at forking out a whole bunch because this game has plenty of bugs.That way,Bethesda gets to profit by asking someone else to do their work form them while taking the lion's share at the same time.
TLDR:Do not support a hypocritical company that claims to care about the player experience on one hand but does nothing about the issues that detract from said experience on the other.
Edit(23/11/17):To further prove my point,several updates were released one after another in a relatively short period of time after the release of the creation club.Guess what?The patches were all related to Creation Club.It shows that Bethesda is capable of releasing patches but only for things that matter to them,longstanding game bugs not being one of them.

The game is really good, but I would suggest the developers stop making updates. Even if there are great ideas for game mechanics not yet being used, too many of them can ruin a game (i know a thing or two about games...)

First of all, I do like the game, but, it has a myriad of problems.
Xcom 2 is just more of the same (with a little less currently) of the first game.
There’s no real innovation, it’s just prettier.
The feature “you get the jump on the aliens” changes nothing, it actually works the same way in Xcom 1. You spot a pod of enemies, engage them the best way possible while you try your best to not aggro another pod, which continues to stay oblivious to the fact that their “buddies” are in trouble.
The story, where is taken on the perspective that we lost the first game, is pretty… lame actually. They re-use basically every plot feature from the first installation but try to keep that sense of wonder which is already lost to people who have played it.
This time around you have a time limit to finish the game, which is somewhat manageable, but still quite limiting. (I didn’t actually let the time expire to see what happens, though).
Classes are okay. Rangers are pretty dope with their swords, even though these can be a coin toss at some points, and Supports’ got a robot that heals.
The worst part are the technical issues. The game is sluggish when compared to the first one. Everything takes too damn long to happen, loading screens, turn ending, environmental damage, camera angle switching when you unleash a barrage of overwatch and whatnot.
But know this. Mods. Mods make everything better.

Before I get into what makes this such a superb game I feel that I need to breifly address all of the "It's too hard", "This is too grindy" reviews: THAT IS THE POINT!  In fact, the game all but tells you to expect this on the initial start-up.  As someone who has been playing Darkest Dungeon interstitially since the early beta days and seen it undergo many iterations in regards to system and functional design, I can say with 100 % sincerity that these components are part of the game by design, and help to make it the incredible experience that it is.  The bread and butter of this game are its deep, multi-leveled combat system and gorgeously rendered characters and world.  It is very much a game about the overall experience and journey than the ultimate destination.  In short; if you enjoy the gameplay, why would you complain about the fact that there is so much of it?
Now, on to the actual review.  Darkest Dungeon is a turn-based, RPG dungeon crawler with procedurally generated dungeons and a heavy emphasis on making the best of a terrible situation.  Expect a hefty amount of planning prior to your dungeon excursions as you assemble your team of four from an extensive roster of unique (and beautifully realized) character classes, try to find a balance between their positive and negative quirks (essentially random stat buffs or debuffs), outfit them with the best combination of gear, and make sure you have enough provisions to see your team to the end of their mission (without destroying your Hamlet's economy, of course).  There is much to keep track of, but as you complete missions and gain more knowledge you'll quickly find a cadence and breeze through the process.
The dungeons themselves are located in four different regions that all exhibit their own unique challenges.  There are a variety of mission types ranging from exploration to the elimination of specific bosses, each requiring different methods of preparation and potentially, different team compositions.  Mission types may appear a bit "samey" to some, but again, what takes center stage in Darkest Dungeon is the highly refined combat system, and fights make up the bulk of this title's gameplay.  Battles are turn based and the order of action is determined by your character's "Speed" stat, as well as that of the enemies you face.  This means that you never know precisely how the turn order is going to shake out which adds a refreshing, if occassionally frustrating, layer to the gameplay.  Each character class is equiped with unique skills and discovering unexpected synergies amongst your party members is a constant joy.
Your ultimate destination as you continue to build your roster of dungeon divers and rebuild the struggling Hamlet of your Ancestor (impeccably narrated by the incredibly talented Wayne June) is the Darkest Dungeon itself; a series of four highly difficult, pre-built dungeons that will test all of the knowledge you've accumulated up to that point.  These missions are divisive amongst Steam users, but I personally found them to be an enjoyable test of skill, even if the odds of the first two seem artificially stacked against you.
Long story short; if you're looking for a challenging, meaty RPG with a ton of variation, gorgeous artwork and narration, and top-notch gameplay, look no further than Darkest Dungeon.  As the title screen informs you: you will loose heros, you will occasionally feel cheated, you will alway be challenged, but the tools for success are available to you and perseverance is the name of the game.

This game was fun for the first hour or so, and became annoying and boring.
""great shooting mechanics and amazing netcode. Black Squad is a military first-person-shooter game using the Unreal Engine 3 to show realistic graphics and dynamic visuals. Absolutely no Pay-to-Win. Welcome to the best F2P shooter on the market."
Not really, I mean.....
-Tutorial really buggy and feels like the AI talking to you thinks its a joke. Tutorial frequently crashes, and the ending part is really unclear, it took me a long time to figure out what to do.
-Very difficult to figure out how to queue with friends, its not like theres a selection to "Queue w/ Friends". Lets see.... uhh
-Grenade physics are quite bad, the smoke and grenade does not bounce, and you can see through the smoke, I do not know if that is supposed to happen.
-Whenever I select 1920x1080, the screen is completely glitched. Also, the crosshair are very low quality, and "Fixed" does not lock the size of the crosshair, which is annoying.
-The ui isn't user friendly and you can't join a match after leaving.
-
-Animations are poor and not interesting
-Hitboxes are broken
-Players with high ping, poor server optimization
-Weapons are incredibly unbalanced
-Movement feels weird and laggy, not precise
-Headshots feel....weak. It takes several full headshots to kill one player, which doesn't make sense.
-Maps feel poorly designed, poorly clipped and not fun to play, lots of spawn camping, no UI or ways to improve map awareness
-Legit every battle match map is just symmetrical, which for me isn't fun at all.
-Basically stole the "Hold Knife= Run faster" mechanic from CS:GO
-A lot of toxic, smug players who taunt and bad manner you after killing you with a one shot gun or running and gunning...... The main tactic is to run and shoot. There is not much recoil compensation, or spray control needed. I frequently see experienced players getting destroyed repeatedly by a player just running and gunning.
-I didn't notice a report system, and thus cheaters run rampant :)
-Netcode needs major improvement
-UI needs to be optimized and user friendly
-For some reason you can spam crouch
-I don't see movement penalties, if there are any
-Gameplay is boring, stale, uninteresting
-For some strange reason, whenever I respawn or reload my weapon, its only 99% full. If I press R again, it loads another clip into it, which is weird.
-Ping isn't limited well, and enemies with 200+ ping are near impossible to hit.
-Lots of hackers, battleeye? Not much better than VAC, I am afraid.
-Theres are hackers that modify their weapon damage somehow to one shot crates, and a lot of hackers who aimbot and wallhack.
-Hackers, hackers, hackers, LOTS OF HACKERS, using foreign hacks I am quite amused with
-The game isn't very original, its like a old class shooter with poor coding and poor hitboxes and balancing.
-The voice acting is weird, like they aren't serious and taking it as a joke
-Kind of like a mix of COD and CSGO, and not fun at all, like they took all ideas from popular FPS shooter games
-Crates in Battle Match take way too much shots to destroy, and yep, if you guessed it, there are hackers who modify their weapons with HACKS to one shot crates.
-SMG's are insanely powerful, stronger than assault rifles which makes no sense.
It is technically P2P, with xp boosted purchased with money and skins
The game has a lot of potential, and its quite relaxing to play.... but if it isn't improved NOW, I'm afraid it isn't going to be a good game.
I know this game is in Early Access and was just released, but for now, this is what think of it.
Hopefully this dev team won't become money-hungry community-abusive.

If the game would only consist of the tactical fights without the world-map, i would rate it 95%. However the latter one is ruining it for me. Simply going somewhere on the over-map to grab a supply drop can be interrupted any number of times by research completing, other drops to investigate, incoming transmissions, or a variety of alien missions. Meanwhile, the ticker is always running on various dark events the aliens are planning that you’re supposed to prevent.
It’s really stressful. It’s too much. This aspect of the game makes me feel more like a juggler than anything. And I’m juggling too many tasks, and the fun is taking a beating. The main problem is that even for an XCOM: Enemy Unknown veteran in the first playthroughs it's impossible to tell which of the hundrets of decisions you have to make outside the tactical map later turned out to be fatal. Maybe it gets less stressful when you get a feeling for all the resources and factors (more intel? more supplies? more enigneers? more scientists? which mission to choose? which rebels to contact? which dark event to interrupt? more research? communications? avenger defenses? ...? ), but until then it's not about making wise decisions but trial and error.
EDIT: after giving it a second shot, i now see a lot clearer. Just don't expect to understand anything in your first playthrough. The problem is also that you can make at least one fatal decision in the tutorial (not contacting the right rebels), that you will not recover from. This happened to me, which caused alot of pressure and frustration. So this game has its problems, however the tactical map is so enourmously fun and engaging, that it makes up for various design problems. Review changed to positive!

Before I get into what makes this such a superb game I feel that I need to breifly address all of the "It's too hard", "This is too grindy" reviews: THAT IS THE POINT!  In fact, the game all but tells you to expect this on the initial start-up.  As someone who has been playing Darkest Dungeon interstitially since the early beta days and seen it undergo many iterations in regards to system and functional design, I can say with 100 % sincerity that these components are part of the game by design, and help to make it the incredible experience that it is.  The bread and butter of this game are its deep, multi-leveled combat system and gorgeously rendered characters and world.  It is very much a game about the overall experience and journey than the ultimate destination.  In short; if you enjoy the gameplay, why would you complain about the fact that there is so much of it?
Now, on to the actual review.  Darkest Dungeon is a turn-based, RPG dungeon crawler with procedurally generated dungeons and a heavy emphasis on making the best of a terrible situation.  Expect a hefty amount of planning prior to your dungeon excursions as you assemble your team of four from an extensive roster of unique (and beautifully realized) character classes, try to find a balance between their positive and negative quirks (essentially random stat buffs or debuffs), outfit them with the best combination of gear, and make sure you have enough provisions to see your team to the end of their mission (without destroying your Hamlet's economy, of course).  There is much to keep track of, but as you complete missions and gain more knowledge you'll quickly find a cadence and breeze through the process.
The dungeons themselves are located in four different regions that all exhibit their own unique challenges.  There are a variety of mission types ranging from exploration to the elimination of specific bosses, each requiring different methods of preparation and potentially, different team compositions.  Mission types may appear a bit "samey" to some, but again, what takes center stage in Darkest Dungeon is the highly refined combat system, and fights make up the bulk of this title's gameplay.  Battles are turn based and the order of action is determined by your character's "Speed" stat, as well as that of the enemies you face.  This means that you never know precisely how the turn order is going to shake out which adds a refreshing, if occassionally frustrating, layer to the gameplay.  Each character class is equiped with unique skills and discovering unexpected synergies amongst your party members is a constant joy.
Your ultimate destination as you continue to build your roster of dungeon divers and rebuild the struggling Hamlet of your Ancestor (impeccably narrated by the incredibly talented Wayne June) is the Darkest Dungeon itself; a series of four highly difficult, pre-built dungeons that will test all of the knowledge you've accumulated up to that point.  These missions are divisive amongst Steam users, but I personally found them to be an enjoyable test of skill, even if the odds of the first two seem artificially stacked against you.
Long story short; if you're looking for a challenging, meaty RPG with a ton of variation, gorgeous artwork and narration, and top-notch gameplay, look no further than Darkest Dungeon.  As the title screen informs you: you will loose heros, you will occasionally feel cheated, you will alway be challenged, but the tools for success are available to you and perseverance is the name of the game.

What can be said about this game that already hasn't been said a billion times over? If you're looking for a Harvest Moon that Harvest Moons better than the current Harvest Moon (Story of Seasons is good, but it's not on PC), then Stardew Valley is the fix you need. It has your HM basics (farming, finding, and friending) but adds that wonderful Rune Factory favorite (fighting). It's not heavy on the "magical sprite" BS Harvest Moon got into in some of its weaker titles, but the game's resident magical nonhumans are cute and useful and QUIET, which is their main selling point. You have full customization of your character except if you're looking to make them sexually ambiguous, but that's easily countered by the game's casual attitude to same sex relationships (still painfully lacking from HM, so many decades after its inception). The game is rife with adults themes like alcoholism and depression, but still manages to highlight the overall theme of "things will get better with time, effort and patience". Every character is unique and has a story, and it's fun figuring out who's a likable weirdo and who's entirely deserving of a piece of coal during the Winter Festival. I highly recommend this game until a PC version of Story of Seasons or Rune Factory comes into existence, and then I recommend coming back to this, because the creator is still churning out more ways to enjoy this game each year (at least for the foreseeable future).

If you've played more famous MMORPGs and ARPGs than Trove will likely come across as 'casual' and... well that's mostly because it is. But I wouldn't say that in a bad way. While the game mechanics and progression are reasonibly liniar there can be a lot of fun had in going for the next objective, collection or even  just building up your club world.
The crafting system is strong, allowing players to upgrade gear as well as craft mounts, pets, coloured blocks for construction as well as decoration items for your buildings.
There is a cash shop in game for things like mounts and skins, which don't affect gameplay, and you can buy a subscription which gives access to useful crafting items and extra XP for the time it is active, but again it's easy to play the game without it. With the quality of gameplay on offer here I have no issue with dropping a little cash once a month on payday to recompensate the devs that gave us this game.
I'd recommend Trove to anyone who's tired of doing things like Raiding in MMOs but enjoy social gaming, as well as to people that enjoy building and creating in games like Minecraft but would like a little more depth to the combat. At this point I've played for over 400 hours across around 5 months and I'm not looking to stop playing yet.
