Absolutely fantastic game, if you can handle the difficulty and perceive it as a challenge as opposed to something that frustrates you. The best way I can describe it is that it is greater than the sum of its parts, with seemingly simple mechanics that, when combined with each other and with the lore/fluff and amazing voice acting, creates the harsh, unforgiving environment the game promises to deliver right from the start (The game opens with a warning).
That's not to say the gameplay itself is simple by any means. Having a good team composition is simply necessary to survive. You will have to use trial and error to see which abilities and heroes are good in which situations/areas, and to date I have been unable to find any one "broken" team comp that can destroy everything. It is remarkably well-balanced in that respect, which is something I have to tip my hat to Red Hook for.
The only "downside" I find is the grind aspect to the game. After the initial, brutal shock of the game, you will figure out how to survive, how to maximize gold income, which heroes excel in which environments/teams, which trinkets you like, what quirks you like (each hero has positive and negative quirks that influence how they perform in some way)... then you have to grind. As your best heroes are cut down, you must grind to level up their replacements. Sometimes, the gold you gain from a completing a mission barely covers the cost of de-stressing and disease-curing the same heroes who completed the mission. You need a lot of gold, you need a lot of heirlooms, you need a lot of time.
All in all, 10/10. For what the game is, it is fantastic and absolutely worth the buy (I got it on sale but I would be willing to pay full price for it).
Will you rise to the challenge when your suffer crushing defeat by the eldritch horrors? When your favorite heroes are cut down before your very eyes? Or you will you fold like a cheap lawn chair, say the game is stupid or the deck is stacked against you?
Injury and despondence set the stage for heroism... or cowardice. Don't get frustrated! Rise to the challenge! PRESS THIS ADVANTAGE, GIVE THEM NO QUARTER!

Let me change this up a bit now that there's been an update; 17/02/2015
Let me tell you a little bit about Starbound. An indie 2-D early access title developed by Chucklefish studios. They couldn't find an engine that allowed them to do everything they wanted to do with this game, so they made their own. It is early access so there will be bugs, and there will be problems. I will address them in the review, but don't mark this game off your buylist just yet. I'll tell you why It's already worth the price.
Almost everything is generated randomly. This is a wonderful feature.
By random, I mean randomly assembled by randomly chosen parts. You seldom find anything that is ever the same. Monsters and creatures with random parts, sounds and attacks types; and certain attacks paired with certain parts. Trees are randomly assembled, but all drop the same kind of wood except for rarely occurring variants, but this isn't a weakness, honestly. Soil is randomly coloured and tinted, along with weather effects that are randomly selected from a set of interesting phenomena available to the planet, depending on its biome. Replayability is wonderful.
Progression rarely gets as satisfying as it does here. It is always makes a notable change with the user's power level. Admittedly, you have about the same strength if you just go to the next tier solar system, but if you go back to easier ones, (Which I highly recommend) you should be able to handle the creatures with relative ease.
Boss Battles have changed dramatically. There are only two implemented in the current version as far as I can tell, and they're both well fleshed out with suitable arenas and backstory as to why you're fighting them. The fights are needed for progression, and I'll come back to this when I discuss the mission system.
Random NPC villages and structures spawn on your worlds, and this makes for fun dungeoneering with or without friends. A new feature means you cannot just break the blocks of the dungeon from the beginning, adding challenge, as you have to reach the end of the dungeon and disable a shield generator before you have the ability to hoard all that sweet,
decorative loot.
Progression through mining has been overhauled almost entirely. Ores look different in appearance now, and not just in colour. All ores have different textures, except silver and platinum, which look shockingly alike but that sort of adds to their charm. You find a different version of iron in each level of solar system, and you make an alloy out of it later which is stronger than the previous. In the past, you used coal as the alloy material for everything, but now you use all sorts of things to create alloys, from oil to uranium. A very important change is that you don't require an absurd amount of metal to create a set of armour and weaponry anymore, so you don't feel overburdened by mining.
Spelunking is a lot better now, with over a 150 mini-dungeons added. It appears that there is a theme with them spawning, so you'll find the same themed ones on a certain planet's underground, and an entirely different set of them with a different theme on another. Underground exploration is a fair bit more diverse since these micro-dungeons were added. The caves are still a bit bland, but you can get a fair amount of entertainment from killing the creatures, and finding the ores you need is quite satisfactory.
The humour in the game is hilarious, with all sorts of references to various sci-fi series from the past, present and most likely future. The art style is wonderful and the worlds all look lovely. Decoration items are all very well designed. There are all sorts of clever and witty remarks from the NPC's, but they could still do with a fair amount of variety. Their attitude to your character still depends on your selected race.
Modding I hear you ask? Of course it has modding, and it is highly suited for it too. Just be careful with what you install, as there is no in-game mod manager, it will have to be done externally and there are all sorts of game breaking risks, such as character and world corruption.
Let's get onto some of the new features. Your ship, and it's AI. Your ship has a newly implemented progression system, where you upgrade it over time with materials, after purchasing an illega- *cough* -legitimate licence from professional businessmen. Every ship has a S.A.I.L (Ship-Based Artificial Intelligence Lattice) with a different digital representation depending on your race. Your ship, how it appears and how it upgrades is also dependent on your selected race. Your S.A.I.L unit allows for you to upgrade your main mining tool, a matter manipulator, over time with mining speed and mining area. You have a mission system with a tutorial which introduces you with the basics of the game, and a main quest which just helps you allow unlock further progression, such as activating your FTL drive allowing you to travel to other solar systems.
The mission sytem has a special mission for each tier that requires you to obtain a full set of your tier's armour, then you can accept the quest, which will require you to do a dungeoneering mission or a bossfight. You will receive rewards and be allowed to progress to the next sector with its ores. These dungeoneering missions and bossfights are well fleshed out, but there should be more of them and I believe more will be added in the future.
Lastly, 3-D printing and the Tech system. The tech system was used to give you all sorts of useful powers to use throughout your experience, and are now all available without having to find a specific chip. You just obtain a blank tech card from a mission or rarely spawning chests, and you can unlock a tech. You can now equip 4 techs at once. Every tech has a specific slot assigned to it. You get the survival techs which involve passive ability to survive harsh environments, leg slots which involve jumping, such as a double jump. You also have another slot for techs which involve double tapping your directional movement keys activating the ability, and lastly your active ability which can be activated using F by default. In the past you could only have one tech equipped at a time, so this is a great change.
3-D printing is a feature where you use the in-game currency, 'pixels', to learn the schematic of any furnishing item (which there are hundreds of) at a fraction of the printing price. Once you learn the schematic you can print more of it at will, at a price. This is useful for base building and decoration, so I would say it is a good feature.
Currency in the game is another thing. At the moment it is mainly gotten from killing monsters and a certain machine which allows you to turn ores into money. You cannot sell weapons or other things to NPC shopkeepers yet, but you will most likely be able to in a future patch. NPC shops have a theme, you might get a clothing vendor who will sell you clothing specific to their race, or a food vendor who will sell you all sorts of foods. The food making system along with the crop system has been revamped. Foods now only give you buffs depending on their rarity.
For enjoyment purposes - If you're a lone adventurer looking for a singleplayer joyride; or if you're looking for a rollercoaster of recreation to enjoy with your friends - Starbound does it's job, and it does it well.
I'd recommend you to give the game a shot,  it is already worth the money, but you can wait a while longer for  a more developed version before purchasing. In the past I would've hesitated to call this game a beta, but with the new update it is very well done and deserves everyone to try it at least once. If you have some money around and want to help with the Beta testing, definitely give it a bash.
Hopefully I have helped you in your decision for purchasing this game!

1. Incredibly challenging, as the game forces you to make decisions you may or may not like, which gives you a feeling that i cant describe to you

If you've played an Age of Empires game before, you know the formula - the classic RTS game, wreathed in the particular appearances and technological context of a given historical period. In this case, AOE3 heads for the colonial ages of America, and does so to great effect. This game has three modes worth mentioning - multiplayer via LAN connection, single player freeplay, and the story-driven campaign. Playing this game multiplayer with friends is a lot of fun, and I don't think I'd ever get tired of it. Single player outside the story is solid for a while, but probably gets old pretty quickly.
The campaign is where this game shines, particularly compared to the previous two iterations of the series. The campaign is fleshed out with historical characters, a full voice acting cast and a pretty detailed story. You'll get a LOT of hours of gameplay out of this, particularly the complete collection which comes with some very lengthy additional DLCs. Heck, I had already played AOE3 all the way through twice and I still found this purchase worth my money for the extra content I'd never seen.
Super fun game, easy to play, and enough stuff to do where you won't feel bored.

I would recommend this game but only to a narrow audience. You have to be into Rogue-likes; and into the ones which are relentlessly punishing to the player. FTL on hard comes to mind. This is a game where RNGesus is your lord and you can only plan ahead and hope for the best. Some of the people who have written negative reviews aren't 100% wrong. This is a really brutal experience for the player, and without careful management and planning you will fail eventually no matter what. Further, several negative reviews mention the high amount of grind to keep characters from having any negative quirks.
You aren't supposed to keep them from having ANY negative quirks. You are only meant to manage the ones that are the most detrimental. This is a game where you can only win if you let your fighters go a little mad. As to the accusations of it being a grind fest... I dunno; that's always in the eye of the beholder. A grind is only a grind if it's not something you enjoy. If you enjoy consistently punishing dungeon crawling where you may lose everything you've hoped for with a single mistake. It's less of a grind and more like "What I'm doing with my Friday Night".
I would say; if you're on the fence there are always Let's plays. You may get far enough in under 2 hours to try it and refund it but I'm not certain as the game's difficulty only really begins to kick in beyond the First tier of dungeon.
Currently my only problem with the game is that I have to be in a very specific frame of mind to play it, and have restarted twice as I've come back and forgotten what I was doing. It's a minor complaint for a game that totally delivered on it's Early Access promises for me. May revisit and edit my review if my mind changes when I finally complete the titular Darkest Dungeon... but I'm not seeing how I could do a 180 on a game that makes me this happy.

Ok so you heard about this game, you like FPS and you have played many others before and want something new.
Wellcome to Black Squad, CSGO's and CoD's love child, this game will feel very similar to both however it does have its own identity inside the very crowded fps genre, while not replacing the already stablished IPs, Black Squad shows that its got what it needs to be a propper fps worthy of becoming e-sports.
It is known that the game was originally released in Korea and is very famous over there, however, this new release has already left the korean's versions boots and has gone on its own path patching the game periodically with new weapons, and slight changes that have already made the game play differently than its korean counterpart. If you are a FPS vet or just like the genre and looking something good to try out, definately play this game, you are not going to regret it.
And now, because i do enjoy making lists, there you have a nice big list of the Pros and the Cons that come with playing this game:
-Feels like home for Cross-Fire/CSGO players, specially when sniping.
-The only F2P Shooter that isnt P2W.
-Guns are
and you do not have to repair them.

-New Mechanic called Fatal Shots, which are, FaceShots, allowing almost every weapon the potential to kill in 1 headshot provided the bullet lands in the face.

It was on my second hour that I got Howard the Leper.
In the four hours of dungeon running since, I have not found a better character than Howard.  He almost never missed his hits, with each swing of his mighty broadsword cleaving through the undead ranks like butter.  He brought other party members back from the brinks of insanity with inspirational speeches of encouragement.  Using his powerful presence, he intimidated enemies into weakness.  Howard was a hero, a titan, a stone wall that refused to be felled.
Then came the boss fight against the prophet.
Driven to madness, everyone else had died of a heart attack.  The Plague doctor was the first to fall, weak was she from a lack of experience.  The arbolist, while a tad more resilient, eventually succumbed to madness and died under a hail of ruin stone.  The Vestel became the next victim, struck by fear and unable to heal herself effectively.  In the end, Howard stood tall, with nary a health point left and on the brink of insanity.
He didn't live to see the Fall after the Summer.
Now, he resides in the graveyard, among all the overconfident fools who went mad on their first trip.  Even now, though, one can imagine that he is a true testament, an icon, a beacon of hope to those unfortunate enough to traverse this delapidated manor.
God bless you, Howard, and may you rest in peace.

Well as of writing this review I've played it less than an hour and to be honest I didn't acomplish much. While this game is a fun look at physics, as a game it lacks some of the more satisfying things we've come to love.
I consider this to be much more of a test of frustration than anything. The controls are stiff and very hard to use. I've seen people complain about how hard it is with the mouse and keyboard so I opted to use the controller instead, and its still way too difficult for the average person to grasp. It demands motions that your brain isn't familiar with making and gives you very little time to work with it.
Overall it's still a good game, and I plan on dedicating more time to it later, but its just not really fun to play right now.
Pros:
- The graphics are fun, and the music is nice to play to.
- It seems like with a little work it COULD be fun to play.
- As a physics game it is very solid.
Cons:
- The controls are awful. And when I say awful, I mean they are just not intuitive. It seems like there could easily be a better way to work them but they have elected to go with the most difficult non-intuitive choice possible. The only way it could get harder is if you had to order the bread around with your voice.
- The game timer and edibility meter sucks. When you fall on the floor you have mere moments to react before you lose. And I understand "Who wants to eat dirty bread?" But it wouldn't be so bad if the controls weren't such crap to begin with.
- It seems like the difficulty isn't in the placement of obstacles or even the fact that if you get too dirty you are trash, but rather it seems that they have chosen to make the controls as difficult to use as a way to make it a more difficult game, and that takes the competitiveness and fun right out of it. If they made the game's controls a whole lot easier to use and instead ramped up the difficulty with obstacles it would be a more successful game in my opinion. Instead it feels like lazy development.
- You are going to get frustrated, and I mean at epic levels. Once you realize that the reason you cant get somewhere easily isnt because its a difficult game but that moving the bread around sucks horribly you will want to throw your controller out the window.
All in all, I am still recommending this game for two reasons.
1. Some people like these really difficult games and they do have a place in the market, and the game isn't terrible. I imagine if i wanted to dedicate like 12 hours just to learning the controls I could probably master it. The problem with this as I see it is I'm not learning to fly an airplane or drive a car here. I'm playing a video game. When a normal game could be finished in 12 hours and I'm still learning how to move a piece of bread around that might be a problem, but I digress.

This game is the challenging RPG I've always wanted: one where the solution to a tough fight isn't "grind more."
The RNG makes it all the better because you can never be completely prepared for the missions you set out for--you have to count on your own mastery of the game and your ability to deal with the problems that crop up.
I can understand if this isn't your thing, if it's TOO hard or if you're not a fan of RNG. But people who are aware of what the game presents, buy and play the game, and THEN say it's unfair? THAT I don't understand. You can't fault a game for delivering on its premise. Yes, the game can get hard. Yes, you'll be punished by the RNG. But never irreparably so. If you do, that's YOUR fault for pushing your party too far. The game gives you achievements for fleeing combat and abandoning quests for a reason--that's par for the course. And there is never that ONE RNG event that completely kills you. This stuff has to pile up to reeeeally screw you over, and if it does, you have only yourself to blame.
This game is about managing stress--both yours and your party's. If you're up for the task, you'll get a lot out of this game. All that challenge and stress adds up to some of the most satisfying victories you'll ever win. I've never felt more tension in an RPG battle before. This game is pure nail-bitting bliss.
PS - I just noticed you have the option to actually turn off a handful of the game's harsher mechanics, such as failing combat retreats and adjusting enemy crits (ex: if an enemy attack does 7-12 damage, the crit will do a max of 12 instead of double damage). Pretty handy! The only thing you miss out on is one achievement if you choose to do use these options.

Been a fan of the Fallout franchise since 3 was released in 2008. I first played it when I was about 13, loved every second of it. Same thing for New Vegas. Great ideas, passionate developers, endless amounts of fun.
I was already disappointed about Bethesda's release of Fallout 4. I'd give it in its vanilla (unmodded) state, about a 6/10 and that might be a bit generous but I'm not accounting for all of the game-breaking bugs many experienced at launch.
I became even more disappointed to learn Bethesda wouldn't release the Creation Kit for modders until about 6 months after F4's release, for what I can safely assume to be, because they didn't want modders producing what they had in planning for their 'awesome' DLC line-up, which ended up consisting of half settlement expansions (without any fixes to settlements lol).
I became disgusted when Bethesda launched a platform on their site for users to upload mods but they didn't account for one big thing: people could steal mods from an already widely used and accessible platform, NexusMods. Plagiarism ran rampant, prominent modders left the scene entirely taking all of their mods with them, and Bethesda hardly lifted a finger to address it while their saving grace for Fallout 4, the modding community, packed their bags and left without looking back
And now I have absolutely no words for this. The first time Bethesda tried to introduce paid mods, it failed. Miserably. And it backfired on Valve, too. Now that we've seen what the Creation Club is all about, I know without a doubt that any hope and faith I had in Bethesda as a developer is moot. These do not seem to be the same caring people I've been very passionately supporting for the past 11 years since Oblivion.
For every re-release of Skyrim and eventually Fallout 4 that they're charging for, for putting out the Creation Club offering mods that are already FREELY AVAILABLE for money while giving a laughable cut to the people who did all the work, for the lack of transparency and communication from developers to their customers... I don't think I can justify supporting any future releases from Bethesda and I can't recommend Fallout 4 to anyone considering buying it.
You will probably have fun, but not as much as you would from their games that they actually cared about, i.e. every game before Fallout 4. It's a shame to see Skyrim, a true marvel of a game, being milked the way it is and a modding community that's already been sidelined get even more disrespect from Bethesda.
It's taken about 2 years for me to give up on Bethesda and it will take at least twice as long as that to have any trust or faith in them anymore after everything they've done to their fans.

This game is truly great.
The few poor reviews are often from Early Access players, who use to feel overly punished by the RNG. Once you get familiar with the character classes, you will be able to generally assume you will get your lineup through a expedition.

I consider it to be one of the best games I have played in the last severak years. I am  really looking forward to the upcoming expansion, although they maybe should send Guy Davis a check for inspiring them so deeply with The Marquis :)

Everything about it looked like it was going to be a fun, difficult dungeon crawling game with some rogue-lite/like elements that I could dump many hours into. You should want to come back to the game after playing it, not uninstall it.

I'm going to preface this review by saying that I've been playing since the game was in early access so i've seen it go through numerous tweaks and change. That said I CANNOT recommend the final product.
Darkest dungeon is a turn based rpg permanent with rogue-lite elemets where you can recruit characters to go through dungeons and death is permanent.
You have to manage health and sanity. If a character becomes too insane that causes other characters to lose their sanity. After too much insanity, the characters suffers a heart attack and ides.
Characters acquire quirks (buffs/debuffs) at the end of dungeons, interacting with items in the dungeon or even relieving stress in town. All quirks stay with the characters through the game, negative quirks can be removed by spending money, while positive quirks can be locked in, which also costs money.
Now that's I've got out of the way, I can tell you with certainty that this game loses it's appeal very fast and becomes miserable to the point of being anti-fun and here's why:
You have no control over the classes you get to recruit, it's completely left to RNG. Sure, there upgrades availble to increase the chance of having leveled up characters show up and how many total recruits are availble.
Example: Six recruits are availble, two of them may be level 3 while the rest may be level 0, or half may be level 1, or they could all be level 0.
This is tolerable in the early to mid game where team composition isn't as important and just having characters to play with is important because you're bound to lose some as you play and learn the mechanics of each dungeon.
However, this becomes insufferable in the late game where the bosses and dungeons in general require very specific team compositions in order to be beaten.
So, do you need one healer? There's two classes that do that well and one is far better than the other at doing so. It may be weeks (in game) before you one shows up to be recruited and that's translates to hours of grinding and trying to build another viable team, which becomes repititve very, very quickly.
The game isn't difficult in terms of mechanics. The difficulty comes from having to grind for hours to put together a competent team that's gets destroyed due to rng destroyed and having to start all over.
In conclusion, great aesthetics and sound design can't make up for a fundamently flawed game.

YES, PLAY THE GAME, BUT THE GAME IS BAD.
I kick-starter this game. I had a lot of hopes and loved the idea.
Unfortunately, this is one of the worst difficulty designs I ever saw.
The game try to simulate the atmosphere of Lovecraft Myths and do it pretty well. The art of the game is amazing, but the game design really spoil the experience.  They don't want to challenge the player or to make it the difficulty about strategy and well planned actions, is all about luck. The game is 80% based on luck.
The boss fights are one of the worst ideas I ever played. In summary is a monster that attack 4 times in one round with a bunch of objects protecting him.
The worst part on the battles, and that you really fell during the boss engagement, are the reordering of characters turns. This is completely absurd. To the point where sometimes a boss attack four times, and right after 2 of your characters he attacks again! There is no strategy you just keep watching the boss beat your whole team to death. It's not funny, its not hard it's purely bad design.
I get it, the point of the game is to frustrate not entertain, but they did it completely wrong. I am a huge fan of Lovecraft Myths and punitive game design. When done right it is really engaging and an immersive experience. But this game do it wrong. You don't want to try again because you don't fell that you lose because of your own actions you just fell that you were cheated by the game, and that it is exactly what happens.
Dark Souls has the same philosophy of game design but is well execute. That game crushes the player but you want to keep trying because you know was YOUR fault, you mess up. The game is punitive and hard with eh player, but it's fair. Darkest Dungeon is unfair.
'The game designer created a lot of great ideas, such as limiting your party level when exploring dungeons so you don't farm and get over power with easy levels. if you extend to much a fight just to heal your characters the enemy receive support from more minions (that's a really cool idea), but the combat design is really random. You can lose a member of your party against minions if you are just unlucky enough and this will happen.
The main problem with losing your party is the amount of time you need to assemble them. Took me at least 3 to 5 hours to gather a good team with good equipment to go on a boss hunt. See them all being vanished by a random chance based boss is game breaking. Even if you go back "more prepared this time" it is no up to you, it's all about luck. One of the hardest bosses took me 3 attempts. On two of them I was obliterated, the third time I just got lucky, the boss didn't focus my healers and I won easily the fight. I didn't change any of my strategy, I actually was even less prepare since I was already giving up. After that I just stop playing and didn't finish the game. WINNING was even WORSE than losing, because make me realize how bad was the game design and how stupid I was by keep playing such a random based game.
The game could easily be better if the game design focus more on surprising the player instead of using randomness as the lethal weapon. I would have don it completely different. I think boss battles should be more puzzle like instead of a thing that is protected by other objects or creatures that they summon. I would make easier to assemble party so even when you lose by randomness you at least don't have to expend another 5 hours for a second try of the boss. And definitely would make the rules way more logical. The reroll of turn order is bad, like really bad. For what I understand the speed is just an attribute that add to a random number rolled for each character and creature every turn. So don't matter how high is your speed, you will have the chance to just start after an enemy. This looks to work OK until a boss battle where ONE enemy can act 4 times, which becomes 8 times (how they let an enemy act four times in a roll?). Make the enemies unpredictable by actions not by turn order. The whole game has a lot of unpredictability such a party order, negative stats, stress, torch light etc. The turn order changing every single turn is a joke Just because it can break boss battles. At least on boss battle the game design should have the common sense of not letting a boss act 8 times in a roll before your healers can act.
Most of all, the easier way to solve RNG problem is to make it a pseudo RNG. Where chances increase or decrease each time they happen.
Just want to add that another poor decison on game design are the enemies that can attack all your party and stun on a single strike. I already lost 3 boss battles that were easy wins just because 1 of this attacks crit and stun my whole party. After a single lucky skill from an enemy my whole party died one a fight that were already won. It feels liek teh game was not even well tested. Once again, if you lose a party of a high level (lvl 5) prepare to lose at least 5 to 8 hours of your time just to have a second chance.
I really want to say that I recommend the game, even more because I was looking out for it since the kick-starter campaign. The art is amazing. The sound design is great. I love how the music changes when your torch is getting weaker. There is a lot of potential on the party idea and the mechanics, but it is a game to be played once and never get back because it lack the most important thing that a game designer should understand, PLAYER AGENCY. It is very simple, a player's death will never be understand unless the player had enough agency to prevent it. So, unfortunately, and as a huge fan of the idea I would say that you should not buy it for the full price. Get on a steam sale discount.

Basically the same thing except with less mob HP and DMG, NPC's to trade with (Connects to internet to see prices.), and a mode were you have every item and infinite of it. You gain fame whenever you die, And fame can be used for things like guilds, items, and just plain showing off. As for Realm Gold, the purchaseable In-Game currency (Not used in trading, Stat potions are.) Its mainly purely cosmetic items, with a few exceptions. (Xp boosters, Loot drop/tier potions, Backpacks.)

XCOM 2 is a worthy successor to XCOM EU/EW.  Why, simply because I've spent over 80hours in XCOM 2, compared to the 20 in EU/EW.  Now to explain why that is the case....
What most people don't understand the Random Number Generator (RNG) system that is the core of the game.  If you have done some research, or just stalked the forum, you will have heard lots of complaints of how difficult the game is and how unfair it is that they keep missing an 85% shot.  Well 85% to hit almost means 15% chance to miss.  One tactic that worked the last 5 missions isn't guaranteed to work in the next mission.  Just like real life.  The only difference, this is a game built on numbers, some of which we see, while in real life we don't see those number we just get feelings on an outcome based on stimulus.
Once you understand the RNG mechanic you can understand just how inconsistent (random) and unfair it can be.  However, there are mechanics in place to help you.  For example, if you soldier misses a shot they will be given a bonus aim to increase the chance that the next shot will hit.  Did ADVENT get too lucky? The game set an aim penalty to adjust for it.
On the flip side, you can get some really good kill streaks when the RNG numbers are in your favour.
To hate the RNG is to hate XCOM.  RNG to XCOM is like a Duck to water, it makes the game what it is.  It adds tension and excitement then mixes it with frustration, fear and sorrow.  Will this shot hit, will it kill the ADVENT soldier?  What if it doesn't hit?  Am I solely relying on this shot to kill the enemy so I don't get wiped out on the next turn?  My favourite soldier is bleeding out; do I try to revive and heal or pull her out and be two soldiers down?
I'm 80 hours and have seen the winning end just the once, on Rookie (Not so Easy).  I have now progressed on to next difficulty up the list, Veteran (harder than you expect).  There are another two difficulties, which I am not ready to try.
Let's not forget IRONMAN mode!  To make the game even more difficult, enabling IRONMAN will make each decision permanent, preventing you from using a tactic know as save scumming.  Basically, if you make a bad turn and lost a soldier you cannot rely on a save game to undo that turn.  Of course, the game already has a fate mechanic which uses a predetermined amount of roles which makes it difficult for the same action to have a different outcome.
Compare that to rolling a Snake-eye's, then using a time machine to go back to that same event and re-rolling. Guess what? Snake-eyes again!  Except in this game the snakes also have boobs!
I don't feel like I have been able to put across how great this game is and could probably write so much more to try and justify that.  The problem is, I am not a writer, I am a gamer and there are already dozens upon dozens of reviews made by professionals out there.  Go read some!
How I approach XCOM 2, is (that while I do not use IRONMAN) I accept the actions that I have taken.  I learn from my mistakes as the mission progresses, rather than trying to fudge a fix by reverting to a save.  I form a relationship with my soldiers.  I have my favourites and those favourites are usually the first to die.  I morn their loss, then move on.  There is a war to win after all.
I love the random mechanics of producing special weapons; I have no idea what I am going to win, the difference is I know I am going to win and be awarded with something different new.  I love the hacking mechanic when it gives wonderful hack rewards, and then hate it when those hack rewards end up working against me.

Well, I figure that this review will be a little bit obsolete, considering the fact that this game has been out for a long time. Long enough to make it redundant to write a review, but here goes...
The game is hard and unforgiving, like a turn-based Dark Souls, difference being that your hero stands back up in souls. Not so much in this game. As someone who really enjoys creating a comprehensive story for the characters I play as, it is unwise to attach yourself to any individual in this game.
Now, you can look up forums and find advice to help better plan and complete the game, but there are many factors that you have to juggle with your characters (positive and negative) that will greatly influence the effectiveness of these suggested strategies.
Overall, it is a surprisingly deep and immersive game, with some great hand-drawn visuals and atmospheric music. The narrator can be droning, but you can always mute him if it bothers you. This is not an easy game, and it may cause you undue amounts of stress. If you like a challenge, and enjoy spending a long time playing a single game, this might very well be right up your alley.

The customization is a fantastic add (though I wish the female side had been as good) and this is one of the first squad-games where I felt close to my troopers. As for the things I was nervous about going in?  The 'Avatar' counter.. don't worry about it, it isn't as scary as it sounds and you can just play the game.  (That's a good thing, I was dreading that thing, I enjoy playing the long-unrushed-games)  The 'pick dark event and the rest happen' mechanic made me nervous, but they are gerally just for a month (wish that was clearer, but yea, not terrible).  The 99% hti chance missing 'that's XCom'..  so my character, as far as I'm concerned, is 'Dr. Who'.  They are supper-powered baddy invader aliens and I'm Dr. Who - so I didn't just miss on a 1%, I just got a preview of the future and then save-scummed back to my 'real' action.  :)

A mix between CoD & CS:GO, Black Squad is a game with many flaws, yet has the potential to be a newly spawned masterpiece.
Most games I've joined are either A: Fast paced run and gun team deathmatch, or B: Tactically sound plant bomb and defend it round. Again, CoD & CS:GO.
Other than modes, what hurts Black Squad the most is its graphics, interface, and way players and guns are handled.
Graphics are decent for a free to play, but even at highest settings shadows will be boxy and frame rate crashes will be inevitable.
The game's interface, as in the menu, is a mess. While better than a lot of free to plays, I still got lost my first time playing, not knowing how to leave my inventory and enter a game (btw, servers are called channels and there's only one of each so I see no need to even make you pick the one option you have).
Finally, what was a killer for me was the fact that the default assault rifle is nearly as powerful as the SCAR H, a rifle that you must buy and is supposed to be 3 times as deadly. Since everyone has this rifle, everybody uses it, and games become massacres. Sniper rifles don't solve this, and most of them require 2 shots to the head for a kill, 3 on the body. Finally, everybody looks the same, with the Peacemakers and Viper Circle nearly exact copies of each other, only differentiated with bland colors. While this may not sound important, it greatly affects your ability to respond accordingly when the guy that just popped up could either be friend or foe. By the time you figure it out, you're dead, so making the two factions more unique looking would be a great improvement to the gameplay.
Despite all the problems I have listed, I have hope for this game. I believe that this could be the first step to uniting the fans of tactical strategy and fast paced shooters, two kinds of gamers that have been at war for years, under a single title.

Before the Creation Club update - which has instituted a pay-for-mods - my feelings about Fallout 4 were mostly negative. The game itself suffers from a wide range of serious issues: the narrative barely reacts to your choices, a reliance on "radiant" quests show signs of obvious padding, the writing is absolute garbage compared to New Vegas and Fallout 1 & 2, the RPG systems have been dialed back to make it more "streamlined" and, worst of all, the (poorly implemented) addition of settlements is just good enough to show the barebones idea of what could have been an incredibly fun system of collection and construction - if it had been fleshed out.
Now, up until the Creation Club update, I might have recommended picking this game up if it were heavily discounted. The gunplay, at least, is as good as it has ever been in 3D Fallout series, and mods have gone a long way to improving some of the gameplay problems (although none have fixed the narrative's problems.) Now, however, what little incentive you might have had to buy this game is gone. Bethesda wants you to not to pay for mods, but to buy their credits...to pay for mods.
Not only do they want you to pay for content - and not even good content at that, with the current selection at the time of writing being little more than reskins of items and lower-rez versions of existing mods - they want you to do it with "Creation Club Credits," meaning you can't refund things or the like.
Don't bother with this. Go play New Vegas.

In the year elevnty-twelve there was a young lad who had taken on his first RPG. This wonderful game was called Realm of the Mad God. He loved the game with all his heart. Suddenly it was the year 2015. The boy still played day in and day out. For some reason he started to notice less and less content being produced. His world was turning grey. His days were monotonous, shatters after shatters nothing would change. Sure, one day there were a couple turkeys in the realm, but that didn't interest the boy. He just wanted to make Realm great again.
The boy's mind was hallow he felt empty inside. Slowly and slowly he felt less reason to continue his adventure. The lava called to him. "Come here, it's warm in the lava. There's no need to be out there anymore." the lava said. And so the boy walked, with his trusted speed the boy shed his armor and walked. Towards the lava, his world full of sadness he noticed the graves around him. He was following in the footsteps of his friends and guild members. He blended in with the community he followed blindly in their rage.
With his first foot in already, an angel creept out from behind the clouds. The angel's name was Silex and he said, "My son this place will be new again you mustn't throw yourself away." The boy listened and learned about the world of DECA. DECA was unfamiliar to him, yet it felt so close. Like a gentle mother's touch, DECA showed him things he couldn't imagine.

Picked up this game solely on my experience with Enemy Unknown; so...
Is it good, bad, game of the year?
Let me break it down for you:
First thing is that this is turn-based strategy and everything is probabilities so you basically live or die by the math.random function; if either of those are as hostile to your being as 1 bar atomosphere to an Andromdon then you might want to give this a miss.
That said the game has an interesting premise and adds some really great mechanics to what we got in the first game (Acual stealth for one) and the amount of customisation is ridiculous (in a good way). On the whole the gameplay is solid and there's some interesting variety in missions, maps and situations. The plot on a whole is also more engaging and the motives make much more sense (particularly the aliens) then the first game which... I mean... What even?
But it ain't perfect by a long shot.
The game's story sometimes makes the same kind of massive logic leaps that became a hallmark of Enemy Within/ Enemy Unknown fortunately it doesn't detract from the overall plot but will it leave you in in disorientated state for three turns on occasion. Performance is also an issue, the game is still at time of writing rather poorly optimised; part of this is the fact that the game's default priority level is below normal and while that can be fixed, the really annoying stuttering and audio desync during cutscenes can't. There are also a couple of obvious bugs that clearly weren't fixed during the test phase: animation fails (as in enemies sliding across the map, etc), random slow-motion, poor or incomplete nav-meshes, units (particularly GREMILINS) falling thru the map and the enemy AI sometimes going out for a drink and forgeting all about you are all in here. Basically the game feels likes its missing a about a month of polish which will hopefully come in the patches.
In summary, if you enjoyed the first XCOM you'll have fun with this game, if you like turn-based strategy you'll like this game, If you like playing high-stakes poker with the Collectors from Mass Effect you'll love this game. Otherwise, you might want to save your money for the Division.

I've enjoyed this game. When I first started playing, I was hooked and played for hours straight. The art style is just fantastic. I really like the dark setting and just how different the game feels to so many others. Trying to keep as many men alive as possible and optimizing tactics and strategies based on who you have available for a mission makes a grind heavy game feel different enough each mission that it doesn't get boring. The stress level is also interesting and adds a lot to the game. Even after putting lots of time into it and then taking several months off, I still find myself coming back to it. Mostly just on long trips because its so convenient to be able to play a turn based game like this without a mouse. Honestly if you can get it on sale its a great game to have because it can be picked up and continued anytime. You could literally not play for months and pick the game up where you left off and not miss a beat.
The biggest complaint I seem to hear / read about is the RNG. It is there and it can be frustrating to just wipe randomly to a weak mob in a corridor. But I also think that it brings a lot of what this game is supposed to be about. In a game that’s trying to replicate the horrors of what a "real" dungeon crawl would be like, having so much RNG makes sense. If there was no randomness once you optimized your strategy everything would just play out as expected and get boring.
This game isn’t for everyone. If you don’t like the grind or having your party wipe to something that feels out of your control it probably isn’t for you. The difficultly level is pretty high and you won’t ever get tips like aoe attacks are only good to finish an enemy off. So you could continually play poorly and never know any better.
The game was meant to be challenging and random. If you view this as a positive you’ll probably like this game. If it makes you frustrated to lose to the RNG gods after perfectly optimizing everything, I’d pass on this game.

This game has a confluence of flaws that, independently may not be problematic, because it fall apart through gameplay. Let me describe the basic elements independently first.
1) RNG (i.e., randomness) - Most games use this mechanic. From first person shooters to dungeon crawlers alike. This drives dodge, resist, crits, etc. Even things like rearranging the positioning of your line-up which directly impacts what abilities they can use.
2) Rogue - When a character dies they die and stay dead. There is no "mirror" character that then shows up to replace them.
3) Class roles - each character has a role from damage, tank, utility (stuns, dots), and heals.
The first issue is that there is basically ONE class that can really heal -- Vestal. Some other classes have either wimpy or completely inconsistent heals -- if you really need to heal you need a Vestal. There are too issues that arise. 1) You are completely dependent on RNG to get them on the caravan and they rarely come. 2) As you level them up from overuse they won't go on lower level quests. This means you are unable to really get a healthy pipeline of heroes because you are forced to run a lvl 1 quest without a healer because of the last 20 heroes you saw none were a Vestal. Why can't you just run without healers --- see the main issue below.
The MAIN ISSUE with the game is the combination of RNG and ROGUE GAMEPLAY. It goes beyond hardcore to just downright pointless. You might as well get a pair of dice and see if you can roll them 200 times without getting snake eyes. Trust me you'll have more fun doing that than playing this game. Because after countless hours of playing no matter how much you prepare or how strategic you are... you're just going to lose to RNG. I'm not talking about losing that 1 character you really liked. That happened 3 times and it's cool. Just have to rebuild. I mean your A-team with your 8 best trinkets are gone forever to literal randomness -- Crits, Dodges, and more Crits.
This game positions itself as demanding a lot from its players. It is my opinion it uses that claim as a crutch. I think the fundamental gameplay mechanics (damage, health, crits) are flawed and the roster design is poorly thought out. It positions itself as hardcore but really feels more like a game for masochists. So while this has better graphics than rolling a pair of dice 200 times to try and avoid snake eyes... understand that's exactly what you are doing. You are investing hours into a game that will happily wipe it all away because RNG said to. If you are into that -- you'll have a blast.

Ok so I just realized my review from ages ago was set to Friends Only, so here's an updated version. I'll also update it based on the new company, because they're doing much better than their predecessor. I played this game a lot. A LOT. I don't really play it much anymore, but I still recommend it to friends and play with people when they want to. It's a game that I walked into expecting nothing, and was pleasantly surprised. Then it was my life, for about a year. It has a way of hooking people in a way I rarely see, especially considering the game is permadeath. I keep coming back to it when other games lose their luster.
So I guess I'll pick out a couple of things to highlight:
PROS:
There is more complexity to this game than you will initially see. The initial "run around and shoot" transitions into "here, have a skill-based dodging game, reliant on game knowledge and fast reflexes to not lose hours worth of work"
The ability to stockpile resources in your vault to give to your other/future characters makes the permadeath much less painful, as it feels like you're making progress from character to character.
Guilds, join one or make one. They make this game way more fun.
No content is behind a paywall, the game's core is free to play.
CONS:
People hack. There's no pvp in the game, so it doesn't really impact other players too much, but it's frustrating. (The new company seems to be addressing this to some extent, I've heard quite a lot of players have been banned recently)
I used to have a con in here about limited content, but the new company is doing a good job about that too.
You are limited to one character slot and have limited vault space if you don't buy gold (premium currency). The game is a lot more fun with multiple characters, so I'd recommend expecting to spend a few dollars if you get into the game. The beginner's package they offer new players is a pretty solid deal, but still, the game's free to play is limited in that way.
Note for new players:
Realmeye <-- That website that will improve your game experience by a ton, it functions as a player marketplace and has tons of tutorial resources. This isn't an ad or anything, the site's free, and everyone who plays uses it.

First seeing this game, I saw it as minecraft and roblox had a baby. Now with some decent hours on it... its more like it's own thing. It's quite an intriguing spin on the olden style F2P(Free 2/to play) MMO with classes, in game currency, and a CRAP TON of things to do.
To really describe this game... kind of requires a glazed over walk though. It's a 3d building MMO, what did you expect?
It starts out with dungeon-ering about with your first pick of a class, whatever it may be of the doesens of classes to choose from. It really breaks down into ranged or melee, and it's obvious who is who in that respect. There mildly hidden Info icon that looks like a small green button usually in the bottom left corner, which is something you will need consistently. It tells you general info on the general play style and skill names of the class. With your class picked out... the rest for about 13 levels is lots and lots of dungeons. Once you get enough cubits from daily playtime, you should be able to buy something in the in game store. You could buy health potions, new classes, mounts, emblems, (Which are passive equipable buffs) and allies. (Which are equipable pets, also with buffs) Generally what you want to do is increase your overall level, or mastery levels. This is done by doing things such as leveling up the different characters, or classes, learning new recipes or finding new items. Much past that... its up to you to do what you want.
There are specific areas you get certain things for crafting and so forth, but that is more of a side note, even though it's a large part of the game! There's gardening, ring crafting, rune forging, reforging, ya-da ya-da bla bla bla, you get the idea.
To cut the crap, the following are the bare essentials to know.
PROS:
*Expansive, with the constant updates this is no visible end to the content within this game. AKA: LOTS of playtime, for FREE!
*Easy to learn combat with some genuine difficulty sprinkled on top
*Easy time killer... no... MURDERER game. Still for free!
*Great sound track and unique graphics
*Your general dungeon crawling home can be moved with the press of a button
*The building mechanics in game are exceedingly expansive.
*You can craft yourself an entire WORLD to build in and to share with your friends... with enough resource grinding
---If you really enjoy it, there is always the premium mounts, costumes, and inventory expansions, those being VERY USEFUL. You run out of inventory awful quick with all the different things in this game.
CONS:
*Very repetitive if played for more than an hour or so in one sitting
*None of the alternate things to do are heavily encouraged, they are really side quests when compared to dungeon crawling.
*Building is neigh non-existent in the normal world, seeing as whatever you build outside of your set house, seeing as anything you build outside of it can and will be destroyed.
*Your created worlds don't have ores in them, or any wide range of biomes. Those you have to craft. Yes... CRAFT your world's biomes.
*Server side issues like you wouldn't believe, they are bound to be fixed in a reasonable amount of time
*It's in early access, so there is going to be no shortage of bugs, glitches, and crashes. Shocking.
I would say this game needs a fair dosage of work.

I can't believe I didn't review this great title.
I would like the world to know that salient soldier, in an act of godlike generosity, introduced me to the best space game ever.
Forget elite, freelancer, star citizen, no man's sky, space engineers, and anything else that involves space, ships, space ships, and russian space ship captains.
I want you to imagine a game that plays like world of tanks in space, with MOBA skill bars. You make your space tank ship BLINK, so you can capture the red square, and wait 15 minutes for the game to upgrade your weapons. Then, my friends, then you go to the enemy's big red square, and you sit inside their forcefield bubble for X minutes to win.
When I played, the graphics settings page was a work in progress, and so were the controls. You had to play at whatever the awful default graphics were, with whatever cryptic, undocumented controls they had assigned. It was great. Like I was playing mechwarrior online again, minus all my ground out stuff, but with added russians voice acting. The cutting edge frontier of F2P games, that aren't really F2P. The wild west.
It is very important that one plays fractured space with a zen like mindset, and expects failure. You should be HAPPY when you get a kill. This is the next level, my friends. Remember to use your sniper long range backstabs, your close range critical strike, your blinks, and beehive barriers.
11/10, would play for another 20 minutes of my life, but as I have experienced the finest in moba mechanics dressed up as space ships, there's no point. I am simply beyond this game now.
Thank you, fractured space, for teaching me the answer to the riddle of steel.

Picked up this game solely on my experience with Enemy Unknown; so...
Is it good, bad, game of the year?
Let me break it down for you:
First thing is that this is turn-based strategy and everything is probabilities so you basically live or die by the math.random function; if either of those are as hostile to your being as 1 bar atomosphere to an Andromdon then you might want to give this a miss.
That said the game has an interesting premise and adds some really great mechanics to what we got in the first game (Acual stealth for one) and the amount of customisation is ridiculous (in a good way). On the whole the gameplay is solid and there's some interesting variety in missions, maps and situations. The plot on a whole is also more engaging and the motives make much more sense (particularly the aliens) then the first game which... I mean... What even?
But it ain't perfect by a long shot.
The game's story sometimes makes the same kind of massive logic leaps that became a hallmark of Enemy Within/ Enemy Unknown fortunately it doesn't detract from the overall plot but will it leave you in in disorientated state for three turns on occasion. Performance is also an issue, the game is still at time of writing rather poorly optimised; part of this is the fact that the game's default priority level is below normal and while that can be fixed, the really annoying stuttering and audio desync during cutscenes can't. There are also a couple of obvious bugs that clearly weren't fixed during the test phase: animation fails (as in enemies sliding across the map, etc), random slow-motion, poor or incomplete nav-meshes, units (particularly GREMILINS) falling thru the map and the enemy AI sometimes going out for a drink and forgeting all about you are all in here. Basically the game feels likes its missing a about a month of polish which will hopefully come in the patches.
In summary, if you enjoyed the first XCOM you'll have fun with this game, if you like turn-based strategy you'll like this game, If you like playing high-stakes poker with the Collectors from Mass Effect you'll love this game. Otherwise, you might want to save your money for the Division.

Do you like video games? Do you like RTSs? Do you like not having to have 300 apm to keep a constant stream of resources coming in? Then you will like AoE 3. If you don't go hardcore or of Asian descent and play strategy games like a casual (like me) then you will also like this game. What I mean is that the macro from Age of Empires II was VERY watered down in AoE 3. Sure you still need some form of it like all RTSs, but the amount has dropped very much so. And I LOVE gunpowder units. Nothing is more satisfying then seeing 100+ musketiers poppin caps in each other like this is Chicago.
The addition of Home City shipments is another feature that I like. Basically you choose around 20 shipments (they are cards that you put into a deck and you pick new cards everytime you level your home city) gain experience from various actions and once you accumulate enough you gain the ability to call in a shipment to your town center. Cards are also Age related and most can only be used once. The cards can range from calling in military units, villagers, economic shipments and buildings, and upgrades for many different things. And some cards affect all your allies. There is a lot of different strats you can go with a deck.
As I mentioned earlier you have Home Cities for each civ. Basically when you first start the game you choose which Civilization you want to be, then you choose your home city name and your explorer name ( you can put any name you want for both, great feature ) then you go into a game. You gain exp as you finish games, gaining levels for your city. Then you can unlock new cards. Some cards are locked until later levels ( it goes something like 10>25>40 I think) but from what I have since they aren't that much better, still useful though. If you want to play a different civ you have to make another home city for them and can also name that anything you want, along with the explorer, starting back at level one ( Unless you play the DLC, for some odd reason you start at level 10 with 10 unlocks. So just play the Asian DLC since it has everything for the other one and the base game.) Each Civ has different cards available at the start and to unlock although about half are universal.
Onto the gameplay it is mostly the same as AoE 2. With the addition of Trade Routes and Native camps (which supply extra resources and unlocks special respectively) it adds some degree of map control. There probably was already map control on AoE 2 but I know little of how the meta is for it. If there was I'm sure trade routes and native camps add even more since the extra resources are a huge bonus ( They start off giving only Exp and can be upgrade 3 times with the last being a train, another feature I like. And the free exp is HUGE to getting early home shipment points) and natives can harass early on. Natives also don't add to pop limit but you can only train a certain amount. Having more than half of all the trade posts and native camps gives you the option to start a Trade monopoly victory, which gives you victory in 5 minutes if they don't destroy any trade posts/native camps, helps if the enemy is turtling hard. You also can only build one castle and thats from a shipment you get (Russians can build more I believe). And if the wagon it starts off as gets destory you don't get another. Stone was also removed as a resource. Also, cannons and muskets. Pretty much the two man things you will build, or at least for me. Still plenty of archers, cavalry, swordmen, pikemen, etc. A lot of civs have more than one special unit, and they aren't built from the castle only. The population cap is set at 200 and that has mixed feelings but I'm fine with it. The graphics are great even though I run it on low. Haven't played the campaign nor the multiplayer, just skirmishs.
Overall, a great game and a must buy for any RTS fan. Even if it is slightly watered down from AoE 2 the new additions to it and time setting are amazing, great gameplay, and good graphics.
40 dollars though? Damn, definitely worth at at any sales price, but who even buys triple A games over 30? Still worth it at 40.

I dont play it as often as I'd like because it is very difficult and I get frustrated and take breaks.  You walk through a dungeon (over and over) and collect items and fight bad guys, a lot of which are overpowered becuase of this 'stress' indicator.  Your player gets all stressed out from battle and spazzes out usually, although i believe its random.  Usually when stress levels start rising people start dying.  Maybe I just suck but I thought the game was extremely difficult.  When the character gets too stressed you have to leave him to recover whle you go on the next dungeon adventure.  Otherwise they are pretty worthless.  I like the concept here, I just think it might be able to be executed a little better?  The stress thing seems overdone.   Another option is to pick up new characters at the tavern to replace the experienced ones you have now resting from battle stress.  It gets frustrating going through a dungeon with a party you've had awhile and they get wiped to a group of overpowered enemies.  Its a turn based rpg, the animations are similiar to old final fantasy games in battle.  I Like this game, I have not played it enough that I could recommend it.  Thats because I probably just suck at the game, but I feel its way too difficult and the stress thing is too much.  I feel like the gameplay is unbalanced I guess.  It has the potential to be an amazing RPG, but it falls short.  Pick it up maybe if you get a great price on it. In Fractured Space you're taking control of a massive spaceship in a two-team multiplayer battle over strategic points.
The only spaceship i've been playing so far is the Hunter, a ship that is somewhere in the middle in terms of mobility, shielding and firepower. Hunter has an array of turrets which fire in a rapid succession when you hold the LMB. Turrets are positioned on the ship so that they're covering all directions, but you have to keep the enemy directly in front of you and at a certain distance in order to deal maximum damage. The other reason to face your enemy at all times is the elongated shape of the Hunter — you'll make yourself a more difficult target to hit. RMB makes you "blink" through a certain distance in the direction of your crosshair; use it to close distance with the enemy, move in on the objective, retreat, or launch a surprise attack. Hunter is also able to launch missiles and attack drones once in a while.
The "battlefield" is divided into five sectors: two side lines, two bases, and the centre. The objective is to capture the enemy base. Usually the enemy base is heavily protected, and to prepare yourself for the final assault you'll have to capture
- Stations, which heal and upgrade your team's ships
- Mining facilities, which accumulate resources for the upgrades
- And the central station, which provides additional firepower for the whole team

Here be XCOM 2 for all of you tactical fans. It is one of the many games in this franchize which began back in 90ies with XCOM: UFO Defense. I played that version in 2010 and it still holds up. To make my biases clear: I really liked UFO Defense as well as XCOM: Enemy Unknown from Firaxis.
As a handsome customer you must be wondering: Do I want this game? And as a gamer to a fellow gamer I must conclude that if you liked XCOM: Enemy Unknown from Firaxis, you will probably want this game, but if you didn't like XCOM: Enemy Unknown it's not as likely that you'll like this one and here's why:
The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t RNG is still present in this game and now more than ever. Enemies still get free moves when you engage an alien patrol after concealment is broken and while there were a limit on the max amounts of aliens you could engage on a lower than classic difficulty in Enemy Unknown - that's not the case anymore.
In addition; there are timers everywhere in XCOM 2 and that's not even an overstatement as non-timed missions are something of a rarity. Indeed - even the geoscape map has a global timer called the AVATAR project and while there are means to set back the "progress" on the AVATAR project, it can easily overwhelm you in the early stages of the game. I pretty much lost my first 4 games on Veteran (the second lowest difficulty) because of a multitude of a lack of resources, lack of time and lack of competent manpower. It wasn't until I turned off Ironman before I felt that I could properly enjoy the game and have the game become playable which is interesting since the developers recommend you to turn on ironman by default.
I played through XCOM: Enemy Unknown with Ironman on Regular and felt that it was managable, even when I lost some important people, but with all the odds stacked against you in XCOM 2 you'll find that the game is substantially harder than previous titles. Yes, I would even go so far to say that it's much harder than XCOM: UFO Defense. But let me be clear on this: This is still only faithful to Firaxis's: Enemy Unknown - not the older UFO Defense!
Still I found that once I turned off Ironman - I had a greater degree of fun; even though it felt like I was cheating. You still snowball a lot in the later game and can steamroll pretty much any enemies once you get some half decent armor and weapons, although situations are still as brittle as they were in the XCOM: Enemy Within as you meet enemies who can still challenge you.
I've spent the last few days playing XCOM 2 and it's much like that annoying family member who is difficult to get along with, but in your heart you still enjoy spending time with. I definetly recommend it to those of you looking for a challenge after XCOM: Enemy Unknown, but for those of you who really didn't enjoy XCOM: Enemy Unknown - keep walking because this is really more of the same only more unforgiving.

I absolutely fell in love with this game because of it's art style and narration. The theme in general is just dripping lovecraft and any fans of lovecraft will find something nice in this game. It is also a great game for lovers of difficult rogue like experiences. It has a nice and simple turn-based combat system with some interesting positional mechanics. The real meat of the game, though, is the stress inducing nail biting caused by the systems agressive asault on the minds and lives of the player's roster of heroes. As the game goes on heroes are constantly on the verge of heart attacks or on death's door an dthe thrill of lossing a hero at any moment, or possibly come through the assault more emboldened than ever.
A lot of people have critizied the game for beign too hard and too RNG focused. While it is quite a difficult game at times, the difficulty is customizable in the games settings, though I understand a lot of people don't really dig through menus and the game doesn't do an amazing job of makign that information readily available. As for the RNG, for the most part a good deal of it is avoidable, one of the things I see a lot of people complain about is how interacting with various items in the game have such a large chance of just permanently debuffing heroes, however with enough trial and error(or reading the wiki) it can be discovered that there are item interactions which always garuntee positive results from these curios. As for the combat it self, it is very much a necessity to have a full hero roster leveling up because the party will need to be dynamic, either because certain heroes are too stressed to be in a party, the levels have been mismatched, or you need a certain party for a particular quest.
That said, this certainly isn't a game for everyone; it is a lovecraftian experience at it's core. A true lovecraftian experience that doesn't just toss in the tentacles for the sake of weirdness, but actually explores the concepts of true dread and hopelessness. Lovecraft isn't only about tentacled monsters and cultists; it's about the inevitability of failure, the struggle against incredible odds, and the constant reminder that maddess is always scratching beneath the surface, and that's what this game brings.

An addictive, beautiful,
adventure through the cursed lands of your lineage; essentially XCOM meets Fire Emblem, as told by HP Lovecraft, you direct mercenaries of a wide variety of classes as they delve into various dungeons to fight monsters, gain loot and stem the tide of corruption emanating from the titular Darkest Dungeon.
YOU WILL LOSE HEROES. It is pretty much inevitable. Whether they die with a whimper, or in a blaze of glory, the graveyard in your town will become ever fuller as this slow boil progresses; and while this can be a great setback, it'll be up to you to summon the willpower to move on, to find a new recruit and pray they don't meet the same fate. And if they don't die, chances are good that, if their Stress meter reaches full, they'll become Afflicted - becoming Paranoid, Fearful etc., and becoming more of a liability to the party.
Yet for the misery this game can bring, its moments of triumph balance it out; a hero landing a MIGHTY crit, dodging a devastating blow, or passing a Virtue check at full Stress and having a positive Affliction - becoming Courageous or Stalwart in the face of great adversity, pledging to lead your party to victory.
BOTTOM LINE: Get it. Absolutely.
PROS:
+Incredible art design
+Known Lovecraft audiobook narrator Wayne June serves as one of the best narrators in gaming history - on par with that of The Stanley Parable.
+Simple turn-based RPG with a depth as great as the dungeons you'll delve into.
+Those moments of "YYEEEEAAAAAHHHHH" triumph when things go well - because you'll want to savor those times.
CONS:
-RNGesus may screw you over on a whim. Afflictions, your heroes missing attacks while the enemies land horrible crits on you, or you simply won't get a lot of the items you're specifically searching for.
-A VERY slow boil - it could take ages for you to fully prepare to actually venture into the Darkest Dungeon itself, though confidence may be the major factor in deciding if you and your heroes are ready.
-Some setbacks may discourage you from getting back on the horse.

XCOM2 feels like a theatrical rebellion against an unknown alien federation who have enslaved the world. The game looks beautiful and the presentation is top notch right off the bat, whether you skip the Tutorial missions or not. The first (or second if you choose the tutorial) mission will remind you of the same unforgiving gameplay present in XCOM: Enemy Within/Unknown. It still isn't quite as difficult as its grandparents, and that isn't really a bad thing. Watching half of your squad die while walking off the Skyranger didn't really make you feel like an Earth saving super team, and should be remembered when facing this game's difficulty. It is unforgiving in its own right, and rightfully so based on its past.
The squad customization options in XCOM2 completely overtake anything in previous titles, and will allow you to create almost anyone you wish (with mods adding even more to this aspect, but more on that later.) The gameplay is presented and flows in a much better way than XCOM: EW/EU. The action camera returns, bringing you on to the battlefield with your created units and joining in their revenge against the aliens.
Absolute victory is no longer required as it was in EW/EU; and failure in missions will set you back, but not ultimately lead to a game over. I appreciated this as I felt like Ironman playthroughs of the first new title got stale after one mission failure in Classic difficulty lead to complete annihilation.
The turn limits pressed me into a specific way of playing, and although I initially found this exhilirating... I found that without them the game was far more exciting even. I personally believe that they could be re-imagined so that timers on certain missions would only begin to count once the new concealment was broken.
I have heard the complaints about performance and crashing issues; I have been lucky enough to encounter close to none, and the game has run even better since the hotfix. My machine is 8 years old, and hardly matches the maximum requirements.
With the modding built in and an already solid game to build from, the excitement of each new campaign only builds, as my second wave is constructed off of said mods and the experience of the first. To me, this is an improvement over every aspect of the original (new) release, and is already one of my favorite games of the recent generation!

I dismissed this game for a long time, because of the voxel graphics. This game is actually pretty good though. There is a pretty heavy pay-to-win market in effect, but the game is 99% PvE, so it's not really pay-to-win. I say 99% because there is a PvE arena that has just released, but is still a beta build. However, every class is maxed out on level (as with most instanced MMO PvP) to even the playing field. The only advantage higher level players have are the rarer weapons/armors have better bonuses, if those even count in PvP (not 100% sure yet, not many people do arena so I've only played a couple matches). Also there is a player market where you can buy virtually anything that requires cash from other players, though some prices will be steep, as the sellers are usually trying to buy your in-game currencies by spending real money on items that can't be bought without cash.
This game is an MMORPG above all, and it does it well. It's definitely grindy, but the fighting is pretty fast-paced, making it more fun than tedious. Like Minecraft and most MMOs these days, you can craft a ton of items, and also customize your own little plot of land that can be uploaded into any available slot on randomly generated worlds. If you're looking to build bigger, you can create or join a club, and each club can create their own unique world. Also, you can unlock every class with in-game currency, and change on the fly without having to exit and reload the game. While the voxel graphics may be a turn-off for some players, this keeps the game's size small, making it a quick download that can run on almost any computer.
If you're looking for an MMO that offers fast-paced runs, and depth that is fairly simple to learn, yet will keep you addicted and coming back for more, this game is worth a play. Hell, even if fast-paced isn't your thing, you can just sit around, fish, and profit. Or craft items to sell on the market so you can buy some awesome mount/wings. Any approach is viable in this game, and it's all pretty fun.
