Darkest Dungeon is a rougelike and turnbased RPG/DungeonCrawler which I've been following during it's entire early access phase. From back then, the game has developed quite well if you'd ask me... I do believe that the RNG isn't as harsh as it was in the Early-Access-Phase - the game has quite improved in many of it's former flawed points...
The mechanics of the game are quite simple: You recruit a troop of heroes with different abilities, motives, backgrounds and quirks. After that you'll set up a team of 4 heroes, buy some equipment (mostly food and torches) and venture out into one of the 4 corrupted regions of the game, unknowing what awaits you... You'll face traps, monsters and even the primal fears of mankind, such as hunger, stress and darkness, and those are the ones that might kill you over time, if you are not well-equipped enough... Combat is brutal, every fight can be compared to a roll of dices, and you can only influence the "outer borders" of possiblities (e.g. due to guarding abilities and healing). Heroes will die or go insane, you'll have to make sacrifices and make tough tactical decisions as you reclaim the cursed lands of your ancestors, restoring them to their former glory...
The games hand-drawn graphics, excellent narration and music match quite well with the depressing and dark, lovecraftian atmosphere and the mentioned 4 regions are quite variable, featuring many different enemies and bosses for which different tactics are required...
The story is delivered in pieces of dialogue and the intro sequence, and leaves the player curious to learn more about the accursed world of Darkest Dungeon - Every slain boss unfolds another bit of knowledge about the eldritch and wicked areas of Darkest Dungeon. I found the final boss to be an amazing and challenging experience and I daresay: It's one of the best examples for lovecraftian bosses I've ever seen in a videogame!
Even once you get a hang upon the game, there will still be a high difficulty-spike and a VERY strong factor of RNG/luck which may safe or doom an expedition...
In short: If you like playing tactical and turn based RPGs and are able to handle RNG without ragequitting you'll most likely have lots of fun AND lots of bitterness playing this gloomy journey through hell, in the end you can only slightly push the RNG in your favor and even then you MIGHT fail many a time - So good luck if you should buy it!
[EDIT: I finished the main quest on February 17 - And sadly the last quests turned into a constant grind-fest... It somehow felt like the end completely broke the games flow, most likely due to the absurd amounts of grinding I had to do before facing each of the four last quests... If you can handle sh!tloads of grinding and RNG you'll probably still have a very good time, but if those make you angry you shouldn't even dare touching it... It's a real shame that I had to edit this after having a good time during most of Darkest Dungeon (leaving the frequent BS-moments aside)...]

Here be XCOM 2 for all of you tactical fans. It is one of the many games in this franchize which began back in 90ies with XCOM: UFO Defense. I played that version in 2010 and it still holds up. To make my biases clear: I really liked UFO Defense as well as XCOM: Enemy Unknown from Firaxis.
As a handsome customer you must be wondering: Do I want this game? And as a gamer to a fellow gamer I must conclude that if you liked XCOM: Enemy Unknown from Firaxis, you will probably want this game, but if you didn't like XCOM: Enemy Unknown it's not as likely that you'll like this one and here's why:
The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t RNG is still present in this game and now more than ever. Enemies still get free moves when you engage an alien patrol after concealment is broken and while there were a limit on the max amounts of aliens you could engage on a lower than classic difficulty in Enemy Unknown - that's not the case anymore.
In addition; there are timers everywhere in XCOM 2 and that's not even an overstatement as non-timed missions are something of a rarity. Indeed - even the geoscape map has a global timer called the AVATAR project and while there are means to set back the "progress" on the AVATAR project, it can easily overwhelm you in the early stages of the game. I pretty much lost my first 4 games on Veteran (the second lowest difficulty) because of a multitude of a lack of resources, lack of time and lack of competent manpower. It wasn't until I turned off Ironman before I felt that I could properly enjoy the game and have the game become playable which is interesting since the developers recommend you to turn on ironman by default.
I played through XCOM: Enemy Unknown with Ironman on Regular and felt that it was managable, even when I lost some important people, but with all the odds stacked against you in XCOM 2 you'll find that the game is substantially harder than previous titles. Yes, I would even go so far to say that it's much harder than XCOM: UFO Defense. But let me be clear on this: This is still only faithful to Firaxis's: Enemy Unknown - not the older UFO Defense!
Still I found that once I turned off Ironman - I had a greater degree of fun; even though it felt like I was cheating. You still snowball a lot in the later game and can steamroll pretty much any enemies once you get some half decent armor and weapons, although situations are still as brittle as they were in the XCOM: Enemy Within as you meet enemies who can still challenge you.
I've spent the last few days playing XCOM 2 and it's much like that annoying family member who is difficult to get along with, but in your heart you still enjoy spending time with. I definetly recommend it to those of you looking for a challenge after XCOM: Enemy Unknown, but for those of you who really didn't enjoy XCOM: Enemy Unknown - keep walking because this is really more of the same only more unforgiving.

XCOM2 feels like a theatrical rebellion against an unknown alien federation who have enslaved the world. The game looks beautiful and the presentation is top notch right off the bat, whether you skip the Tutorial missions or not. The first (or second if you choose the tutorial) mission will remind you of the same unforgiving gameplay present in XCOM: Enemy Within/Unknown. It still isn't quite as difficult as its grandparents, and that isn't really a bad thing. Watching half of your squad die while walking off the Skyranger didn't really make you feel like an Earth saving super team, and should be remembered when facing this game's difficulty. It is unforgiving in its own right, and rightfully so based on its past.
The squad customization options in XCOM2 completely overtake anything in previous titles, and will allow you to create almost anyone you wish (with mods adding even more to this aspect, but more on that later.) The gameplay is presented and flows in a much better way than XCOM: EW/EU. The action camera returns, bringing you on to the battlefield with your created units and joining in their revenge against the aliens.
Absolute victory is no longer required as it was in EW/EU; and failure in missions will set you back, but not ultimately lead to a game over. I appreciated this as I felt like Ironman playthroughs of the first new title got stale after one mission failure in Classic difficulty lead to complete annihilation.
The turn limits pressed me into a specific way of playing, and although I initially found this exhilirating... I found that without them the game was far more exciting even. I personally believe that they could be re-imagined so that timers on certain missions would only begin to count once the new concealment was broken.
I have heard the complaints about performance and crashing issues; I have been lucky enough to encounter close to none, and the game has run even better since the hotfix. My machine is 8 years old, and hardly matches the maximum requirements.
With the modding built in and an already solid game to build from, the excitement of each new campaign only builds, as my second wave is constructed off of said mods and the experience of the first. To me, this is an improvement over every aspect of the original (new) release, and is already one of my favorite games of the recent generation!

This is more than just a joke game.  This is a masterpiece well worth your time.
CONTROLS:
First of all, personally I like the control system.  For the main story mode hold down a button to select a bread corner, then move it in the direction you want it to go.  Sure there is a short learning curve, but I find climbing and navigating the world with these kinds of control schemes very enjoyable.  The gifs you will find posted by the master players on the community hub are a joy to behold.  Don't be afraid.  Give it a go!
If the controls still bother you there are plenty of game modes, (including a free roam mode) starring different characters who are mostly easier to control than a bread slice.
Gameplay:
The variety is what makes this game stand out against most joke simulators.
There is plenty to do, and the game isn't reliant on humour to succeed.
You can enjoy a Star Wars parody, you can hunt for cheese, you can race baguettes, and you can plate up the dirtiest piece of bread you have ever seen with a smile on your face after skateboarding through dust, ants and falling in the dish water.
This is a unique fun game that deserves a chance.  Give it a go.

Before the Creation Club update - which has instituted a pay-for-mods - my feelings about Fallout 4 were mostly negative. The game itself suffers from a wide range of serious issues: the narrative barely reacts to your choices, a reliance on "radiant" quests show signs of obvious padding, the writing is absolute garbage compared to New Vegas and Fallout 1 & 2, the RPG systems have been dialed back to make it more "streamlined" and, worst of all, the (poorly implemented) addition of settlements is just good enough to show the barebones idea of what could have been an incredibly fun system of collection and construction - if it had been fleshed out.
Now, up until the Creation Club update, I might have recommended picking this game up if it were heavily discounted. The gunplay, at least, is as good as it has ever been in 3D Fallout series, and mods have gone a long way to improving some of the gameplay problems (although none have fixed the narrative's problems.) Now, however, what little incentive you might have had to buy this game is gone. Bethesda wants you to not to pay for mods, but to buy their credits...to pay for mods.
Not only do they want you to pay for content - and not even good content at that, with the current selection at the time of writing being little more than reskins of items and lower-rez versions of existing mods - they want you to do it with "Creation Club Credits," meaning you can't refund things or the like.
Don't bother with this. Go play New Vegas.

This is a very interesting concept and I like the atmosphere of the game.
That being said, in its effort to be dark and oppressive, the game quickly becomes tedious. If the RNG favors you, your character lives another round. If it favors the mobs, a single critical hit takes out one of your characters and your party dies. (Note: I never once successfully retreated from combat.) Permanent debuffs stack up like snowflakes, and just removing a single one from a single character costs a significant share of an entire dungeon run's income. Yes, maybe that's how it would be an a real evil dungeon, but there's a difference between challenging and frustrating. Leveling is also difficult in that it proceeds by jumps - once your characters hit level 3, they can no longer level at all except in level three dungeons, which will stack so many debuffs and stresses on them they'll be useless before they hit level 4 and might have some chance at success.
As you can see, I gave it a fair shot. I felt like I made no progress whatsoever in the 12 hours I played. Every time I managed to get four characters to level 3 and destressed enough to run a dungeon, they were promptly slaughtered and I was back where I started. I'm uninstalling the game.

XCOM 2 reminds me why I didn't quite like XCOM EU when I played it on console.
If you've read around at all, the usual suspects criticizing this game aren't exactly wrong in their gripes about XCOM's core gameplay mechanics:
No pun intended on this game's apparent seeded RNG mechanic (That's a Random Number Generator for you non-nerds).
Seeded RNG would be more like a loaded digital slot machine,
, but anyways...
I love strategy games, so I know quite a bit about the niche, from classic cardboard table tops like Chess, Risk, Catan to old school computer titles like Starcraft, Warfrcat, Z etc. to modern day games like Front Mission, Homeworld, and so forth.
The never ending dice rolls is what takes so much away from this game. No matter what amount of skill a player has in this game, randomness is what sends you spinning out of control, epecially in missions on the harder difficulties.
There is so much work lost through random-chance character deaths and mission losses, that any enjoyment and reward are overshadowed from the amount of frustration and hours of grinding and reattemps.
And I can attest. I completed the last game on its hardest difficulty and played this one on its "Legendary Ironman" mode just to say that I did. So, I can honestly say I gave this game a complete and comprehensive playthrough before criticizing it.
If you've read anything about this game, you'll have picked up on the flame wars in several threads between the highbrow critics and fankids. I suppose I am the former, but the issue is apparent.
However, I am a patient completionist.
As I said, I played the previous XCOM and beat it (Reluctantly, after several attempts) on its hardest difficulty.
It wasn't fun. I did it simply to say I did it.
And now I am playing this one on its "Legendary Ironman" and will beat it (Eventually, after several begrudged attempts). But, I gotta say it's really not fun. Needless to say, its really hard.
But, it's so hard that it's not fun.
I'm just going through the motions for some achievements.
Playing it on its hardest modes only bring out the reasons why its reliance on its All-or-Nothing RNG gameplay is just not fun.
I suppose this is what the game was intended to be like. That's just XCOM, as they say right? You could play it on easy mode, but why buy a new game at 60 bucks just to play it on easy mode a couple of times? Is that worth it?
The gameplay mechanics not only make the game unenjoyable and frustrating, but seems to make alot of things unbalanced as well.
I purchased this game with it's AAA price tag in hopeful expectation that I'd see some refreshing new core gameplay and a better level of enjoyment, but I rolled the 2K's RNG dice and it let me down once again as it has so many times before.
Maybe I am the demographic that XCOM is targeting, along with the other gambling addicts and "masochists"?
I cannot recomend this game with it's current $59.99 price tag and have usually told my friends who are strategy buffs to avoid it, as most wouldn't enjoy it. The majority of whom I know that have tried this or the last XCOM game have been disappointed, unfortunately.
If you really want to try this game I'd say wait for a price drop or give an older XCOM game a go. Preferably try a free demo. Like I said, you might not enjoy this game because of it's core mechanics. It tends to put off many players.
In the meantime, I hope that 2K takes heed from other turn-based tactical games like Square Enix's Front Mission series and reward skill, not gambles.

It's been more than half a year since I've posted this review, and now the game got its first noticeable update since alpha launch early 2014. I will have to see it for myself after which I will update this review accordingly.
22 July 2016
Wow, has it been two years since I first wrote this? Since my last review update, I haven't played the game much. Some things were added, some removed. In the end I wasn't entirely satisfied at first. Recently I've given it another go, what I've seen is a much more interesting game than before.
It took a LONG time, but the game has actually been released today. Yes, the game takes ages to update. But now it's finally of acceptable quality. Therefore you no longer need to wait for new updates per se.
The game plays the same as before, but has become more user-friendly. The game doesn't try to give a "story mode" anymore. Instead it's treating undiscovered content as a new surprise every time you progress, much as I described the old story mode actually felt like.
The "end game" still revolves around your own creativity. If you like building, you'll most likely be pleased with Starbound. Furthermore to get the actual buildings items you need to explore different planets, each having it's own theme based on its biome type.
Progress in the game is signified by the biome type of the world you're on, more dangerous worlds that include acid and lava environments are more challenging than the peaceful forest worlds. Several technologic enhancements can be unlocked which gives the player immunity to acid or the ability to breathe in any environment.
That's Starbound 1.0 in a nutshell. It's actually recommendable now, because you no longer need to wait for (slow) updates which should make the game playable. In the end it did become an enjoyable game, in my opinion.

I cannot describe in words how much this game just blows my mind. Everything in this game is something you gamble.  Everytime you enter a dungeon you wager the money you spend on supplies and upgrades, the gear on your heroes, as well as the heroes themselves.  You could clear it with ease, or maybe just leave with a few scratches and unwanted effects.  Or you could lose everything you've so desperately worked on.  Level 0's become dungeon fodder, desperately throwing them into the unknown at the hope of reward.  Your best trained and equipped become your worst nightmare, constantly faced with the grim chance of them being lost like cattle to the slaughter.  You don't want to send them out.  You shouldn't.  You can't.
But you must.  So you shall.  You set their poor souls on the table and take a gamble with Death, praying so strongly that they are some bit prepared for the horrors that await them.
Ruin has come to your family.

Having played this since it's early days before it's release on steam I think it's time I give this game a proper review. It is an amazingly developed free to play game, with an outstanding developer who pushes out constant updates almost every single friday that fix major issues and bugs, and add in new content that completely changes the game. If you're looking to get this game, don't be thrown off by the fact that it looks like Minecraft. You will have some amazing times with your friends, encounter friendly players just trying to survive, bandits who'll snipe you from across the map, a revolver professional, or those guys who fly around in a helicopter to show off. This game has the most hours in my entire library and still has yet to be surpassed by CS:GO. The singleplayer in this game is amazing, allowing you to build HUGE mansions, or tiny beach houses. The mod community is also hard at work using the new content that is pushed out almost every week to give back to the community something amazing, or something like a bird that smokes weed. Either way this was one of the best free games I've ever played.

XCOM 2 is the sequel to XCOM:EU/EW; the twist is that it's the sequel to a LOSING single player campaign.  The core gameplay of a strategic overlayer and tactical turn-based combat layer both remain, and the tactical game has been polished.  Game mechanics that you didn't know could be improved in the 2012 version have indeed been improved for XCOM 2.
That said, the system requirements are steep.  While that won't matter in the future, it does bear mentioning now.  I built a PC in November 2015 for the release of Fallout 4.  i5-4460, 16 gb PC-1600 RAM, GTX 970 with 4 gigs VRAM.  All I'm trying to do is game at 1920x1080, and my system experiences slowdowns even running at the recommended graphics settings.  XCOM 2 is very poorly optimized, and hopefully future patches will remedy this.
OEM mod support is great, whether you want to change gameplay or just add more customization options for your soldiers.  The character pool lets you create yourself and/or anyone you know (or watch on TV, or in movies, or other games, or read in books, etc) to appear in your campaign, which is awesome.
Overall, this game is definitely worth playing.  I'm about to add a couple more mods and start my third playthrough.  If you've enjoyed any of the base XCOM games, you'll enjoy this.

Creative space survival story that is able to blend perfectly with the MMO genre. The game follows a survivor of a race of knights caught in a war as he/she crash lands on an unknown planet and has to craft gear such as weapons, armors, and shields to fend off predators and survive in this new world. The game has an ever-expanding story mode/campaign, a self-sustained economy that allows players to exchange in-game items with each other for in-game currency or for other items from other games,(which is why this game is so closely attached to the TF2 economy) guilds in which friends and strangers can commune and play together, events in which there are special missions and rewards, and even prize boxes that allow you to obtain cosmetics or branded gear for real-life money. Numerous weapons, armor, shields, and most importantly cosmetics and acessories such as costumes for your knight that conceal your not so good looking battle-armor. If you're looking for a game that has more than one way to advance, this is the game for you.
However, developers have been having internal issues and the consequence of that is a severe lack of content and what feels like an incomplete game. Thos game has potential, but it needs support to get there.

I really, really, REEEEALLY wanted to love this game. I am very into quirky games, I pride myself in checking out all of the strangest, most oddball games on Steam. And I had heard great things about I Am Toast. But sadly, for me at least, this game is almost unplayable. Wacky concept with pretty nice graphics and a TERRIBLE control scheme. Maybe my brain doesn't work in the way it's supposed to for this control scheme to make sense. I even played it mostly with a PS3 gamepad, and I still could not get the hang of it for the life of me. Nothing but frustration. The grip meter depletes too quickly, so you barely have time to hang onto objects. Attempting to flip over the edge of ledges is a chore in redundancy and pain, as the moment you flop onto the ground you are basically dead. You get, what, like 5 seconds at most to find a surface to latch onto after falling to the ground? I'm sorry, but this is not challenging, it's just downright AGGRAVATING.
Just when I thought the controls couldn't get any worse, I attempted Zero G mode. HA!!! A true exercise in futility. Made absolutely no sense whatsoever to me as to how to accurately control the flying toast. Honestly, the controls could have been stellar if they were based more off of the scheme used in Katamari Damacy. Maybe I'm crazy uncoordinated here, but I just can't understand how so many people out there love this game and are able to get the hang of the controls. It's rare in this day and age for me to play a game that is so unique and has so much potential, only to be buried by horrific controls. I feel like it's been a solid 5-10 years since I've played a game with a control scheme as unbareable as this one. It's sad, really, because it simply destroys what I was hoping to be a fresh, original, exciting experience like the first time I played Katamari.

Imagine Call of Duty, if it were developed by Koreans.
TL;DR at bottom.
This game is incredibly well-polished, beautiful, and very fun!
I've got 29 hours logged and I'm definitely not planning on stopping.
Pros:
- *Very little recoil on almost all guns, so gameplay will depend on skill level more than RNG bullet-spread.
- Easy to obtain in-game currency (it takes around 120 games to unlock 1 Assault Rifle if you're using games alone, to obtain currency). Daily logins give you 15k currency (worth 15 games), which saves you approximately 2 and a half hours of TDM grinding. There are also bonuses for logging in every day for a few weeks.
- Finding matches takes around a minute (North American Server, Quick Match), so there's not much downtime on queuing.
- Sounds are satisfying: Headshots are indicated with a "skull-cracking" sound and all guns have unique firing sounds.
- *Silencers and laser sights are completely free! (They come with nearly every gun; Snipers do not have silencers or laser sights). Also, every rifle with "GL" in its name, will also have a Grenade Launcher! Happy noob-tubing.
- *Having the ability to aim down your sights is always a positive thing, especially when it makes a huge difference in accuracy.
- Walking makes you silent.
- *You can try nearly every gun available for 7 days to figure out which gun you want to purchase first (the DLC is split into three parts and is available on the store page. Once activated from the store page, it stays in your inbox for 30 days before it expires or until you activate it in-game).
Cons:
- All grenades are purchasable and are not defaulted with your character.
- Seems like only "Green Smoke Grenade 3 Days" is the only thing available in the Random Boxes; this game is only in Alpha, so that's understandable.
- It's common to see "high-ping players" (a.k.a. laggers) in your game lobbies since the servers are still somewhat limited. This is a problem because they are able to kill players that have exited their line of sight.
Asterisk notes (all points with *):
- When starting out, the recoil is very difficult to notice on most assault rifles; everything seems laser-accurate, leaving little room to blame a death on lag or because the bullet-spread wasn't in your favour. If you're coming from Call of Duty, this game will seem like heaven. If you're coming from CS:GO, you won't have to think about bullet patterns here. The recoil will become more noticeable after more gameplay.
- Everyone (regardless of age, gender, level, etc.) has free access to silencers and laser sights. Silencers hide your position on the mini-map when firing and laser sights have no use (that I'm aware of) other than to look cool. Laser sights are (as stated in-game) invisible to the enemy team, so don't worry about giving away your location by shining the laser into a sniper's eye.
- Grenade launchers do not explode on impact. This is a fair compromise for people who love and hate noob-tubers. Noob-tubers can use grenade launchers to their heart's content (although, you only get two grenades with no way to replenish them unless you respawn or pick up a gun that hasn't used theirs), and people who hate tubers have a fair chance to avoid the explosions.
- I thought I was going to enjoy the Scar-H, but after trying the DLC, I decided to main the RL5.
TL;DR
- Every gun is nearly laser-accurate
- Noob-tubing is fair for both sides
- Black Squad > Call of Duty
- Only BS deaths come from high-ping players

After the initial excitement of getting my hands on a sequel from one of my all time favourite games, I was worried.
Many of the missions started with "Turn Limits" where you had to complete the objective & evac within a certain number of moves or risk failure. I felt this would affect the strategic side of missions and give a rushed feeling, ending up with a mandatory team of 6 Ranger Shotgunners "Rapid Firing" the entire mission at point blank, with fingers crossed behind their backs.
Turns out it wasnt as bad as I'd been told.
On average I'd end missions with at least 3-5 turns left to play with, and that was being relatively cautious and experimental. And many missions give unlimited turns after the objective has been completed.
It does however make you think twice about spending turns setting up a "perfect" ambush for every encounter, and full healing/reloading before seeking out the next batch of enemies, which in XCom EU took a further 3 turns chasing in circles through the Fog of war and took most of the pressure off making the missions easier.
I LOVE the extent of customization and can only hope if theres ever a third X-Com they would expand on this, maybe more faces and voices. I believe alot of games underestimate the importance of making a squad personal to the player.
Very impressed with the "Personality" setting on soldiers that effected their stance and body language, giving them extra attitude AND the naming/customization of weapons! My First Rangers Shotgun was called "SURPRISE!" of which I'd shout a particularly popular "Dexter TV Series" quote, everytime I point blanked an enemy in the face with it.
Absolutely superb game.

It's been more than half a year since I've posted this review, and now the game got its first noticeable update since alpha launch early 2014. I will have to see it for myself after which I will update this review accordingly.
22 July 2016
Wow, has it been two years since I first wrote this? Since my last review update, I haven't played the game much. Some things were added, some removed. In the end I wasn't entirely satisfied at first. Recently I've given it another go, what I've seen is a much more interesting game than before.
It took a LONG time, but the game has actually been released today. Yes, the game takes ages to update. But now it's finally of acceptable quality. Therefore you no longer need to wait for new updates per se.
The game plays the same as before, but has become more user-friendly. The game doesn't try to give a "story mode" anymore. Instead it's treating undiscovered content as a new surprise every time you progress, much as I described the old story mode actually felt like.
The "end game" still revolves around your own creativity. If you like building, you'll most likely be pleased with Starbound. Furthermore to get the actual buildings items you need to explore different planets, each having it's own theme based on its biome type.
Progress in the game is signified by the biome type of the world you're on, more dangerous worlds that include acid and lava environments are more challenging than the peaceful forest worlds. Several technologic enhancements can be unlocked which gives the player immunity to acid or the ability to breathe in any environment.
That's Starbound 1.0 in a nutshell. It's actually recommendable now, because you no longer need to wait for (slow) updates which should make the game playable. In the end it did become an enjoyable game, in my opinion.

To help this, you can upgrade your town, which enables you to remove negative effects from adventures, upgrade their skills, get better equipment and so on.
The gameplay itself is difficult(ish). The whole point of the game is that you get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked during every mission. So if you expect something else, I guess it's difficult. Saying this, it's not all that difficult to keep things running. You can abort missions whenever you feel like it and hiring new adventures doesn't cost anything. I don't even know if it's possible to loose the whole game somehow.
To sum it up: Darkest Dungeon is nice little game and I would recommend it. It might however get somewhat repetitive after a while.

As a big fan of XCOM: Enemy Unknown, I was surprised to see how many things changed with XCOM 2. Along with the new futuristic setting, almost every aspect of the gameplay has been tweaked or modified in some significant way; altogether, it makes XCOM 2 feel wholly fresh and unique – even if not all of the changes are for the better.
What stood out the most early on was the steep learning curve; it wasn't until around the 30-hour mark that I felt like I had a good understanding of how things worked. The “Veteran” difficulty setting struck me as being WAY too hard for a first playthrough. I recommend setting it to the easiest mode, at least for the first bunch of hours.
Of course, the complexity that makes it hard to warm up to is part of what fuels its replay value – there is an enormous amount of depth here. You can modify soldier weapons and some of their stats with special items, equip different kinds of armor, manage research projects and constructions, keep track of limited supplies, manage special development projects and special reseach projects......umm, actually there are TOO many things to keep track of. It reminds me of the excessive micromanagement of the first Mass Effect – the depth is definitely there, but it takes too long to get anything done.
The weakest part of XCOM 2 is the story. It comes across as rather cliché average sci-fi, but at least has a very strong presentation with stylish cutscenes and good voice acting. Visually, the whole game feels “brighter” than Enemy Unknown, but still has the same great use of color and special effects. It's a lot of fun to take screenshots during the cinematic moments in battle – give it a try!
It's easy to compare XCOM 2 to Enemy Unknown and point out its flaws, but at the end of the day the turn-based strategy battles and base-management elements have a similar kind of engaging, almost compulsive appeal with very high replay value. It is intense, entertaining, and will push your intellect to the limit. Just be sure to treat this game the way you would any hostile alien: approach with caution.

Before we dive into my review, lets address something that people seem to misunderstand about this game.  Yes it is hard, but there are different reasons as to why a game gets that distinction.  I see Darkest Dungeon compared to games that have varying facets of difficulty (RNG, requiring memorization of moves, gear grinding, etc). Just because you "like/are used to/pwn hard games" does not mean you're going to like
hard video game.
NEARLY. EVERY. SINGLE. ONE.  Do me a favor, stop and re-read that a few times to let that sink in.  Every time something happens, assume a d10 is being rolled in the background as a significant source of determining whether you succeed or fail.
Yes, the game has some punishing mechanics.  Yes, there are some bosses that if you bring the wrong party composition, you're going to have a really hard time living long enough to even retreat.  But the majority of the difficulty comes from the volume of RNG in this game.  I have 129.4 hrs (currently) logged into this game and I have seen nearly every part of the bell curve when it comes to RNG in Darkest Dungeon.
I was in a champion dungeon, and on the second section in the very first hallway all four enemies critically hit the exact same hero on the first turn.  All of their attacks took place first. Before I could even make single act, one of my maxed out heroes was killed, permanently.
I've only had that happen to me ONCE in my 129.4 hrs of gameplay, but at some point
.  When it does, are you going to rage-quit or is it going to remind you that no matter how awesome your strategy and prep work is, that sometimes a case of bad luck causes you to get wrecked, and that in itself is part of the challenge.
Is this game hard? Yes.  More importantly, is its flavor of hard to
liking?  If the sample above doesn't make you want to completely and utterly rage-quit, you'll have an awesome time.
If heavy RNG isn't your style, you'll end up getting frustrated instead of getting even.
Since you've read this far, I'll keep my praises short :)  This game is outstanding.  The setting, environment, dialog and music all truly capture the dark fantasy, dread and hopelessness this game promised.  Whenever I'm in the mood dark fantasy game, Darkest Dungeon is my #1 go-to.

This is a game I cannot recommend enough to the right kind of person.  Did you like how Dark Souls rewarded you for mastering the system and "getting gud"?  And how it offered little glimpses into the background world through snips of description and tiny clues?  Do you like some minor resource management, weighing the costs of wasted provisions against the risk of underfeeding your heroes on expedition?  Can you appreciate some truly impressive sound and visual design?  Can you overcome terrible adversity?
Are you afraid of the dark?
This game is impressive not for the basic combat or leveling mechanics, but for the tension and the aura surrounding the characters, the mosnters, and the missions.  For the heroes whose little bits of dialogue hint at the people who they are and the people who they were.  For the narrator, whose voice looms heavy with every misstep and every triumph.  For the punishing difficulty, the spirals of stress and hopelessness, when your heroes are on their last legs and one of them is struck nearly dead, and then...
"A moment of valor shines brightest against a backdrop of despair!"
Try it.  Buy it.  Pay attention as you play, and your reward will not be more items or a special sideques, but insight into a world begging to have the surface scratched instead.  "The way is lit, the path is clear; you require only the strength to follow it."

In a game that takes you 10 minutes to get to the toaster and 20 to get in it, this game is a must. Why is it a must? Well, the physics in this game are incredible (get this: bread can actually break ceramic plates.), the idea of this game is amazing, I mean, come on. You're bread. What's more original than being bread? The reason I actually completed the first level was because of the soundtrack. So derpy, fits the mood ("What mood?" BEING BREAD, YOU DUMMY!), and it is pretty comical... An "edibility" meter indicates how edible your slice of bread is. How do you ruin this? Falling on the floor, going into the sink full of water, failing epicly and plummeting to your doom in a litter box, etc.
All you need to do is get to the toaster as fast as you can and with as much edibility as you can! Simple, easy, and straight-up original. Can't find this anywhere else.
This would be a perfect score, however, if the controls weren't clunky as hell, it'd be one point higher. The gameplay involves you moving through a series of household obstacles (like plates, stoves, openable refrigerators, sinks filled with water, the floor, and even crumbs on the counters) to get to a toaster on the other side of the room by using the controls (see controls). The controls kinda tie into the gameplay, hence bumping this down a point. The thing that really irritates me is the grip. Grr. Kinda reminds me of Lara Croft: Tomb Raider Angel of Darkness. It's okay, because it's a long grip time, but gets irritating when you fall a hundred feet to the floor and have to climb back up again. The annoying part about this game is when you first start out, you have to take about 10 minutes to get to the toaster and another 20 getting in it, unless you grasp the controls and mechanics quickly.
Not high definition, but it's not supposed to be. It's a game about manuvering bread. Are you supposed to see every grain of bread on the slice you control?
You control the bread with the triggers, bumpers, and the A B X Y buttons, with the triggers and bumpers to grab and the A B X Y buttons to lock your grasp, useful for pulling things off of counters and watching them crash to the floor. The D-Pad can be used to look around your slice of bread, and the right stick is used for orbiting your slice. The left stick is used for moving around the "limbs", or in this case, corners of your slice. The controls are okay, amid the "I want to move you this way, but you move this way (then when I try to correct you, you fall to the floor and start losing edibility)" type of gig.
The soundtrack, the breaking of ceramic plates, the sound you make when grabbing things. Utter perfection. By "perfection", I mean it perfectly fits the game in it's own little way. Comical, stupid, wierd(, original).
Continue to fail epicly in an attempt to get to the toaster.

I have tried to love Fallout 4. From the onset: the shooting seemed much better & settlements were fun at first. But...
The feeling of eking out life as an outsider in a desperate wasteland was gone, replaced by just endlessly building pointless settlements and becoming the beloved leader of pretty much everyone at once; but I persisted.
The incredible agency & openness one felt in both the wasteland and in the story itself was gone, replaced by a ham-fisted narrative with ultimately very little choices; but I persisted.
The fun dialogue of other Fallout games was gone, replaced by four bland options you have to choose blindly; but I persisted.
The incredible worldbuilding & quests of other Fallout games were gone, replaced by hand-waving the past and just doing whatever seemed to fit; but I persisted.
The many unique & quirky character options along with the massive arsenal of weapons were gone, replaced by a bland options board and making only minor adjustments to existing guns; but still I persisted!
And now, under the guise of paying it forward towards the modding community, Bethesda or perhaps Zenimax has begun to try and earn a hefty profit off of existing mods for even the smallest of items; and now I'm done.
Now I'm just another idiot whining on the internet like it means something! Another poor fool thinking this'll do anything to save a beloved franchise from its own success...

EDIT: Comments and further research have shown that whether or not the game runs fluently has less to do with the power of your PC but hardware lottery. Some people with terrible machines have it run just fine, while others with beastly monstrosities have experienced all sorts of issues. There seem to be a lot more people with problems than without, so you may not even be able to have this game run fluently if you do have a supercomputer.
ATTENTION: If you work at NASA or have access to the computing power of IBM's WATSON, you will find this to be a fantastic game. Otherwise, you will have big problems with performance where there should be none, not to mention the fact that this game is buggier than a square kilometre of the Amazon rainforest.
XCOM 2 is, gamewise, a worthy successor to XCOM. It may not feature the full range of contents yet, and the story is a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor as you'd expect, but if you bought this expecting something on par with Mass Effect, you should not have. XCOM is about shooting aliens, machines, and alien-human hybrids (seeing as the players cannot be expected to simply be fighting human soldiers who have threwn their lot in with the alien overlords), and if good turn-based tactics and moments of euphoria followed by indomitable rage are what you're into, this game is for you.
Sadly, it seems Firaxis somehow managed to do many of the things it did right terribly wrong. Yes, there is full modding support (as in: the tools the devs had, we had available on day 1), but the documentation on it is spotty at best. The character pool was a great idea, but it turned out to be an unweildy and unecessarily complicated feature. Not saying you wont get the hang of it, but once the ranger guy you carefully worked out to be an insane brute becomes a specialist because the game refuses to use the class you specified you'll be quite mad, I assure you.
This is also one of the better sides of the game: the mods. The community is already hard at work, and some fantastic groundwork has been laid out, so you can be sure great things will follow. Firaxis loves the modders already, and maybe that is because they hope they can figure out a way to improve the horrendous performance, but the encouragement people are getting can only be rivalled by Bethesda. And seeing as EVERYTHING is moddable, workarounds for everything you don't like about the game will be available soon enough.
Still, I cannot recommend the game in its current state. Wait until they fixed the performance and the modding scene is a little bigger, and this will be well worth your money.

It's so sad to see one of my favorite games turned into this. XCOM2 does shine in a few areas, but overall comes across as trying far too hard to recreate the difficulty of the original XCOM series, only to feel forced and disingenuous in doing so.
It confuses the player with a flaky interface, it's unpredictable with erratic visibility mechanics, and generally feels wildly inconsistent when it comes to its own in-game rules. I'm not against difficult games, but XCOM2 goes well beyond believability and enjoyability in order to create situations that simply require multiple attempts to get right. The resulting game experience is one where you feel like you're fighting against the developers instead of the in-game enemy.
Edit:
I said at the beginning that this game shines in some areas, and it deserves to have those pointed out. Like XCOM (both the original and the new remake), XCOM2 creates some amazing, fist-pumping moments of joy and awesomeness. The graphics are generally great, the storyline is interesting and compelling, and the core game mechanics are solid and just plain fun.
So it's quite frustrating that there these moments of inconsistency, like mentioned above, that force me to reload every other turn. I get that XCOM should be a brutal game, but that brutality should come from in-game experiences within the player's expectations, not from an interface glitch, broken line of sight on grenade launchers, or the fact that I can't tell if my character can shoot from a particular position before moving him/her there.
Clarified recommendation: I recommed it, but only if you're ready for a very frustrating experience.

I nominated Darkest Dungeon for the category "Villain Most In Need of a Hug" and I wanted to take a moment to explain my choice. Darkest Dungeon instills in players a sense that the enemy lurks around every darkened corner, even the ones in our hearts and minds. The foul evil that eminates from the ruins, the blood-thirsty mercenaries who dwell in the weald, the unknowable horrors of the Darkest Dungeon itself; they all pose a grave threat to the player's party, but nowhere near as much as the player's party poses a grave threat to themselves. The stress and anxiety of fighting evil monsters in cramped spaces will loosen their resolve and tempt their darkest, most secret urges to come to the suface. They'll steal, self-sabotage, and occasionally screw over your party when it counts the most but can you really blame them? They're only human, trying their best to stay alive and restore glory to your family's name in the Darkest Dungeon. Go over there and give that trembling Highwayman or weeping Vestal a great big hug. For all you know, it could save a life.

Not recommended. But it has potential, so it may – possibly – be good once it's finished.
The biggest reasons why you shouldn't get it yet:
– It's pretty boring. Yeah yeah, some fanboys say they've invested 500 hours into Starbound, but unless you're also a fanboy, you'll probably run out of interesting things to do pretty fast.
– There is a pretty high risk that your worlds and/or characters will be wiped or corrupted in software updates, which is pretty disencouraging for investing time and effort into this game.
There are some troubling aspects about Starbound. Some of those things have to do with the failed promises of the developer. Around 6 months after it was released as Early Access, it's still basically in alpha, and who knows when it's going to be released? With few major updates, it's also hard to know if the game is on the right track. Put simply, I don't think we should reward developers who can't live up to their promises.
But I also have some deeper concerns about the concept of Starbound itself. Starbound is basically Terraria in space, and one reason it's taking so long to finish is because it's so damn ambitious. An endless amount of planets with lots of various biodomes, what's not to like? Even in the Early Access, there's a lot of variety, but unfortunately it seems to be rather superficial. And that is the problem: that despite the massive amount of content, most of it may ultimately feel rather generic and not especially meaningful. In other words, my concern is about quantity vs. quality. And furthermore, why invest time in building stuff on a planet, if you're going to move on to other planets anyways? As a result of these things, both exploration and building are hurt – arguably two of most fun things do to in games of this genre.
Can they solve this, and create both quantity AND quality? I.e. create a good game? It should definitely be possible, but we can't know until they've gotten further into the development. As of now, they haven't solved it.

As a Minecraft player, I was skeptical to try this game out at first, but a friend sent me a copy anyway.
Playing by myself, I only played for about 5 minutes before closing the game, since I knew nothing about what to do or where to go, but when playing with a group of friends, this game becomes extremely addicting.
Finding out what keys perform what action was quite entertaining(I only found out about the "N" key recently, adds a lot of flavour text to this game), and also what items can do unique tasks(I only found out about right-click mining to mine the background blocks about 30 hours into the game).
You can then start comparing loot, bases, ship interiors, and even home planets with each other, sharing coordinates of planets with valuable loot and exploring/mining together makes this game so much more while playing co-op so to say. And you can even race each other to see who can get to a certain boss/sector the fastest, or if you RP, who can build the most satisfying base/ship.
With a plethora of mods available and devs constantly posting updates to come on their website, this game is constantly evolving, but whether that is a good or bad thing is up to you. Keep in mind that this game is still in development, so some mods eventually become actual parts of the game, but that also means that many bugs/crashes/character+world wipes can be expected, take caution if you do not like to start anew every so often.
All in all, I thoroughly enjoy this game(72 hours on Steam and counting) and am in anticipation of where Chucklefish will take this game when it is officially completed.
P.S. If you enjoy Minecraft or Terraria, you will also probably enjoy this game as much as I did.

Disclaimer: I do not have a reviewer's touch, nor am I a good game critic.
My personal opinion on the game: I liked it, despite its many repeating glitches, its few bugs I've encountered and its memory leak issues that had me close the game every 2-3 hours just to free up my RAM.
I've so far played three campaigns with increasing levels of modding, and it lasted me some 130 hours before getting tired of it. That is decent milage, a little above 40 hours per playthrough.
But were those 40 hours fun?
Between the new mechanics, such as concealment (not stealth), new and diverse enemies, riddiculous story, expanded mission types, RNG maps and healthy mod support, I was pretty satisfied. If I say "new", I'm comparing to XCOM:EU/EW.
So, those 130 hours... were THEY fun?
Mostly. Each 40-hour campaign was enjoyable on its own: the missions got only slightly repetitive, exception being the grindfest final mission, heavier modding changed the rules enough to keep it fun for me.
You mentioned glitches and some bugs. Care to elaborate?
I count myself among those lucky enough to not encounter many bad bugs, but that is mostly because of my 2-3 hour play sessions that kept the game from falling apart. At first, it ran smoothly. Then it started stuttering a bit, some more pronounced slowdowns and here is where some of the more common glitches I've encountered appeared. Things like a soldier jumping from a rooftop to the ground below or a floor down and briefly clipping into the elevation level below that (i.e. into the ground or the 2nd floor below). Rarely did the cover indicator act weirdly, such as showing a soldier as flanked, even though nothing was left alive to flank it. More commonly, the grenade throwing/launching mechanic failed to take into account that the soldier briefly steps out of cover to throw said grenade. This resulted in some impossible to throw scenarios simply because of high cover adjacent to a building corner (and me trying to throw a grenade straight ahead, not around the corner). Towards the end of a play session, I'd start getting out of memory warnings and only once did I witness a longer final mission where the screen would start throwing colours at me, begging me to give it a break.
These are just some examples, as this is a review, not a bug report thread. That said, keep in mind that if the game is slowing down to a crawl, your RAM is almost completely used up and your soldiers always clip through the ground when jumping off of buildings, then it might be a good idea to shut the game down for 5 minutes.
Any other oddities?
Aside from the game's story? Picturing even the brainwashed ADVENT civilians not finding anything abnormal about the various alien species and later in the game, mechs patrolling city streets.
I hear about mission timers. You forgot to mention them.
True. The mission timers were pretty artificial to me, as I don't overwatch creep. I tend to send someone ahead first and then position my team accordingly. I modded the timers to be higher so they'd be less stress-inducing, but always tried to complete the missions within their original turn limit. A few experimental approaches barred, I've not had issues with the timers. I somehow never lost a "save the relay" mission, though those are the worst of the lot, giving you less time to do more (kill everything).
If I really had to give it a grade, I'd throw a 7/10 at it. It's charming, it's fun, but only before your RAM starts screaming at you. It's random, it's mod-friendly, but only as long as nothing gets taken down. It's playable, but only if you're lucky.
Closing notes: Read the minimum requirements! Put your disbelief in stasis. Configure your settings, as well as your game experience.

Personally I never owned AoE3 growing up and coming to it later on I can say it has not aged particularly well.
Unlike the new AoE2:HD release, increasing the resolution unfortunately does not allow you to see more. Usually this is typical of competitive RTS games in order to keep the playing field even. Unfortunately how much is shown to you on screen is limited at best, especially when groups of units grow beyond the screen size, a particular issue when moving across a map with multiple unit types of varying speeds.
AoE3 sports a more to-ground camera perspective causing vision to be obscured by walls or buildings to a far greater degree than the other AoE games. Not helping this is how the buildings are absolutely massive (houses are huge!) while this might make it seem like your town is more impressive than it is, navigating your town in a pinch can be very fiddly.
Combat is unbalanced and to be fair, pretty broken. units can be queued but are all produced on the same timer. For example you can make 1 musketeer, or 5 at once in the same time. This all but removes the need to spend any resources until you need them. Most games I find end very quickly both online and against a computer.
Unlike AoE3, the only realistic way to win is through combat, immeditae and unrelenting combat, removing a large portion of what an AoE game means to me. Naval combat has however improved significantly over previous installments, sporting a wide range of galleons and some very pleasing combat animations and damage manifesting visually through holes, masts falling and other immersive effects in constrast to AoE2's all-purpose flames.
Overall I cannot recommend this game however I can see how it could appeal to those looking for a more basic RTS than is typically offered by the AoE franchise.

I had never played a game like this before, and I loved it. The game is easy for new people to pick up, and you can make the game harder if you want to. The "Extra" modes, the Shadow Lairs, are freaky, fun, and offer awesome prizes...that is, if you can find actual good people to do them with, leading to my cons.
Yes, I listed "Gameplay" in both categories. The gameplay is fun in most cases, but the thing I hate the most about it has to do mostly with the weapons in the game. Some of the weapons are obviously superior for stupid reasons than other weapons in their same star catagory, like how the cutter series(this is the actual set of weapons I use in the game because its fun, poses a challenge, and actually requires a strategy to use) is pointless simply due to that half of its attacks don't hit (which is supposed to be this weapon's main selling point), and some people would venture further to say that it's awful because all of its lines do pure normal damage, which means it won't do next-to-nothing against anything, but it won't do tons of damage against anything either.
Moving on to the community. I have met a group of GREAT people on this game that I hang out with alot. However, the majority of the game community is stuck up, because the people greater than other people refuse to teach the newbs how to get better, and only tell them what they mess up in. They also judge people for their weapon choices. Like how I didn't choose the statistically best weapon cuz I don't want to feel too strong and make the game too easy to beat, thus killing fun.
Becoming stronger in this game has been a pain since day one. My main problems come from all the types of rarity, for the same simple and annoying reasons. On crafting, the orbs are stupidly rare, and it's hard enough to get the specific type you are looking for. On forging, the problem mostly only applies to 5* items. The fire crystals are too rare, like before, and you need like 30 of the 5* ones to do anything with a large chance of failing, and if you can't find them, you're stuck with a weapon that is weaker than the one you had directly before it. Also, if your LUCKY,
SoLs are annoying also. Too rare, and too little benefit. The ones you get can literally be drained in one stratum, and the only benefit is the likely meh loot in that stratum.
I also mentioned the S. Lairs twice, once in each catagory. I hate it because it costs a ton to get in it, and unless you do it on the hardest possible setting, your stuck doing it yourself, while paying about 150,000 crowns to do it for the slight chance of getting epic gear at the end. AND, you will probably pay another 30,000 crowns to revive yourself.
Despite the monstrous costs, the most annoying part is the community again. As I stated before, most strong enough people won't join you unless you do it on elite, effectively slimming your chance of getting that gear your looking for. Even if you offer to let them in free on an easier difficulty level, they still mostly won't go with you. I know this from experience.
Another thing I found out is that playing the game more than once is boring, because of the cons listed above.

This game is one of the best games I have played in a while. Everything you do is OP, and so is everything the aliens do. Progress for/against the aliens is a lot less linear now, and aliens pose an actual threat. This means that early on, the game is really difficult. Later on in the game, it gets a bit easier to do regular missions, but then you get more challenging options pertaining to the story.
I have only one criticism: It needs more research and items available. I am hoping that the expansions will bring some more of that to the table, but as it stands, you are likely to run out of things to research and build. There are only 2 tiers of weapons/armor to build and 2 tiers of auxilary armour (both tiers have only 2 armor pieces, so there are only 4 auxilary armor types in the whole game) so you begin to feel a lack of content, and a limit on the development that XCOM can make. Also, the story is short if you know what you are doing, but that isn't much of a negative, because it is delivered very well.
Despite my criticism, I still think this game is worth the full cost by far, and with good workshop support, the game has a lot of potential for future development! It isn't even that hard to make your own mods without being a professional!

This is the best game I've played in a long time--it truly sratches the itch. There's always some great new, game-changing upgrade just a turn or two away; maddeningly challenging (but not unfair) battles, personality, and a scenario that you can really get into (alien occupation and human resistance).
I really liked the previous XCom as well as the classic Xcom. If you enjoyed those games, I don't see why you wouldn't like this one. If you're not familiar with the franchise, imagine a turn-based strategy version of something like Deus Ex. Don't be put off by "turn-based." This game isn't boring at all, and you will APPRECIATE the time it gives you to plan each move, because each move counts. This game isn't about actions per second; it's about contemplating every possible move and choosing the most viable option.
One last thing--most games, even ones I enjoy, I look forward to ending them and moving on to the next great game. With Xcom 2, though, I put off the story missions and tried to stretch it out as long as I could. I would've put quite happy to play for another 20-30 hours, and am already looking forward to whatever DLC is planned for it.
In short: Great buy, even at full price. Money well spent!

Marking the month anniversary of having purchase and played this game I decided to write my first game review.  Since I've invested a relatively absurd amount of time in it of late I hope I can offer some insight into what to expect.
First off, I wholeheartedly recommend this game.  That being said it will appeal to the type of gamer who enjoys playing games that are analogous to a very intricate, infintely more variate, and complex digital chess.  This game will challenge your mind, as you sit and ponder over all the tiny little details of your exact squad makeup as you hit the fateful "Launch Mission" button.  Or even as you decide the order of events in the campaign screen on how/what to prioritize.
But it is also spectacularly interesting, visually awesome, and true to the XCOM series an intruiging story to boot.  (Side note: Central does get annoying). The developers also had immense forsight in making it incredibly moddable to suit even the most idiosyncratic of desires in playstyle of those who develop and mod on top of it.  It is a remarkable game if you truly enjoy a challenging and interesting experience.  And frustrating enough at times to prevent the malaise of dominating all the time.
All of that being said, as I finish up my fifth playthrough, second on Legendary IM, there is still some polishing to be done. I love Iron Man as it is the true challenge, unfortunately some of the LOS and physics issues that you must depend on to the finest T to have any semblance of success, are sometimes, albeit rarely I must add, a little klunky.  The game is already designed (well I might add) to make even a strategically safe decision, potentially risky.  This is part of the appeal.  But when you absolutely must depend on, for instance, a proximity mine to hit all targets, or you squad wipe, it just makes IM, shall we say, more malign than it already can be.
Given the complexity and dynamic nature of objects, cover, buildings, etc, a couple small hiccups are to be expected.  And really I must stress, they are small compared to the bigger whole that is XCOM 2.  And I'll sure will be patched in a small matter of time.  And again, this really only applies to some of the hardest difficulty settings in which every tiny detail of every move makes a difference.  But also saving before every turn or "savescuming" can kind of take away from the experience a bit too.
So I still can't give XCOM 2 anything but a 10/10 since it is still a well made, overall very polished, and captivating experience.   Giving it a 9/10 due to bugs that exist currently, but will I'm sure be obsolete for those of you reading this review in say a month or two, would be a disservice to the developers and this amazing game.

Somehow it captured everything I loved about my childhood, and made it even better. The pixelated graphics may not be everyone's preference, but I think Stardew Valley does it very well. One of the biggest perks is that the developer is constantly updating the game, which is something you could've never gotten on the "own your own farm" simulators of the past. Just since I've started there have been more relationship options added, more quests added, more buildings available, and talk of a multiplayer mode coming out soon. I would not be surprised if at some point in the future the map itself was expanded to provide more content.

What this game brings new to the table, is divorce is an option, and you're not limited to what gender spouse you can have. Want to marry everyone in the game at least once? Want to be the town flirt and make your husband or wife think you're cheating? Never want to settle down at all? You can do that! You even get the choice to

I would honestly recommend picking this game up, even if you aren't big on the Simulation or casual RPG genre. It's a nice game to play just to relax some stress away, or pick up and set down between tasks. It's a great game for all ages, one you won't want to put down once you get into it.

Not gonna lie. I've played ONE MATCH thus far, and I've got to say - This game has some serious potential.
I'm not a fan of MOBA's (Though, this game is MUCH more tactical and a lot less toxic than any other I've played) yet since this is such an interesting mashup of genres, that's all I really know how to call it. And, to be frank, I love it. I'm no professional critic, nor do I write very often, so just hear me out, other simple folk of the world.
Note, this review is written during the ALPHA development phase, as of 4/16/2015.
For the TL;DR, look to the bottom.
- The game is, so far, exceedingly well made for such a small studio.
+ (Pro) The graphics are wonderfully rendered, but not overly-flashy or distracting.
+ (Pro) Not once did I lag, hitch, freeze, crash, or BSoD.
- The gameplay is... Interesting.
+ (Pro) Fun is a subjective term. I much prefer interesting, because it interests me, and is unique in this day and age. I can most-closely akin it to Rules of Engagement meets DotA. It's complex, but not exceedingly so, as every class of ship has four main abilities that, from what I saw, can be upgraded and swapped out once a certain point is reached.
+ (Mix) It's a slower paced game, as opposed to the usual frantic "pew pew-ing" of the modern FPS, yet it does this well. Thrust is a factor in your movement, momentum of the ship affects how slowly you turn, and the action gets pretty hectic when you take all this into account.
+ (Con) It can be a bit frustrating when you have a team full of new players (much like myself) that have no idea what to do or how to do it, but the built in map makes it a little simpler. I say a little, because unless you learn how to utilize the map to the fullest, you're dead in the... lack of water.
-Teamwork is ESSENTIAL.
+ (Mix) I mark this as a mix of pro and con, because it can work either way. Either you're good at cooperating and filling in where there are weaknesses, or you're going to be debris floating past the nearest station. It's really one of those make or break moments in the game that will decide whether this is good or bad, as you can have a losing situation but with a smart enough team be able to overcome the odds (mostly by having the fastest ships zip in behind the enemy and capture their base without looking, tee-hee-hee.) or just sit back and watch as your team splits in three different directions with no communication and some bloke yelling "hacker" at the enemy team when he blows up.
-Though not pay-to-win, It could certainly have that impression.
+ (Mix) Most people judge games upon first impressions. When I went into the ship market, the first thing I saw was a big "UNLOCK" button on a ship that I didn't yet own. It then presented me with two options - a teeny-weeny amount of platinum (the paid-for currency) or a (seemingly) EXORBITANT amount of credits. To a first-time player, this makes it seem like a cash-grab. However, upon closer inspection, it looks to be quite the opposite. Everything I saw was purchasable by credits, and after just one match (a victory, at that) I earned well over 15,000 credits. Knowing this, it makes the prices not seem so ludicrous, and everything much more accessable and fair.
-There is only one map currently.
+ (Mix) There have been games that have done this right, and yet, as I look at this one and see it's still in alpha, I wonder if it will hold up, or if they'll develop to have more variety. Because while the ship variety is splendid, map variety and having different layouts can be a big benefit to a game such as this, as it will keep players coming back for more.
+ (Pro) On the plus side, it makes the game much easier to learn as there's less things to study up on.
--- Overall, I think this game has tons of potential, and is definitely worth a look. Better yet, if you enjoy the game, consider purchasing one of the founders packs to help support it. It'll be worth it in the long run, in my opinion. Is it worth a try? I believe so. At least pick it up for a couple fivers and if you don't like it, you've at least helped support them in making something others will enjoy.

This game is one of the best games I have played in a while. Everything you do is OP, and so is everything the aliens do. Progress for/against the aliens is a lot less linear now, and aliens pose an actual threat. This means that early on, the game is really difficult. Later on in the game, it gets a bit easier to do regular missions, but then you get more challenging options pertaining to the story.
I have only one criticism: It needs more research and items available. I am hoping that the expansions will bring some more of that to the table, but as it stands, you are likely to run out of things to research and build. There are only 2 tiers of weapons/armor to build and 2 tiers of auxilary armour (both tiers have only 2 armor pieces, so there are only 4 auxilary armor types in the whole game) so you begin to feel a lack of content, and a limit on the development that XCOM can make. Also, the story is short if you know what you are doing, but that isn't much of a negative, because it is delivered very well.
Despite my criticism, I still think this game is worth the full cost by far, and with good workshop support, the game has a lot of potential for future development! It isn't even that hard to make your own mods without being a professional!

This is the best game I've played in a long time--it truly sratches the itch. There's always some great new, game-changing upgrade just a turn or two away; maddeningly challenging (but not unfair) battles, personality, and a scenario that you can really get into (alien occupation and human resistance).
I really liked the previous XCom as well as the classic Xcom. If you enjoyed those games, I don't see why you wouldn't like this one. If you're not familiar with the franchise, imagine a turn-based strategy version of something like Deus Ex. Don't be put off by "turn-based." This game isn't boring at all, and you will APPRECIATE the time it gives you to plan each move, because each move counts. This game isn't about actions per second; it's about contemplating every possible move and choosing the most viable option.
One last thing--most games, even ones I enjoy, I look forward to ending them and moving on to the next great game. With Xcom 2, though, I put off the story missions and tried to stretch it out as long as I could. I would've put quite happy to play for another 20-30 hours, and am already looking forward to whatever DLC is planned for it.
In short: Great buy, even at full price. Money well spent!

Marking the month anniversary of having purchase and played this game I decided to write my first game review.  Since I've invested a relatively absurd amount of time in it of late I hope I can offer some insight into what to expect.
First off, I wholeheartedly recommend this game.  That being said it will appeal to the type of gamer who enjoys playing games that are analogous to a very intricate, infintely more variate, and complex digital chess.  This game will challenge your mind, as you sit and ponder over all the tiny little details of your exact squad makeup as you hit the fateful "Launch Mission" button.  Or even as you decide the order of events in the campaign screen on how/what to prioritize.
But it is also spectacularly interesting, visually awesome, and true to the XCOM series an intruiging story to boot.  (Side note: Central does get annoying). The developers also had immense forsight in making it incredibly moddable to suit even the most idiosyncratic of desires in playstyle of those who develop and mod on top of it.  It is a remarkable game if you truly enjoy a challenging and interesting experience.  And frustrating enough at times to prevent the malaise of dominating all the time.
All of that being said, as I finish up my fifth playthrough, second on Legendary IM, there is still some polishing to be done. I love Iron Man as it is the true challenge, unfortunately some of the LOS and physics issues that you must depend on to the finest T to have any semblance of success, are sometimes, albeit rarely I must add, a little klunky.  The game is already designed (well I might add) to make even a strategically safe decision, potentially risky.  This is part of the appeal.  But when you absolutely must depend on, for instance, a proximity mine to hit all targets, or you squad wipe, it just makes IM, shall we say, more malign than it already can be.
Given the complexity and dynamic nature of objects, cover, buildings, etc, a couple small hiccups are to be expected.  And really I must stress, they are small compared to the bigger whole that is XCOM 2.  And I'll sure will be patched in a small matter of time.  And again, this really only applies to some of the hardest difficulty settings in which every tiny detail of every move makes a difference.  But also saving before every turn or "savescuming" can kind of take away from the experience a bit too.
So I still can't give XCOM 2 anything but a 10/10 since it is still a well made, overall very polished, and captivating experience.   Giving it a 9/10 due to bugs that exist currently, but will I'm sure be obsolete for those of you reading this review in say a month or two, would be a disservice to the developers and this amazing game.

Age of Empires 3 is the third and (seemingly) final game in the Age of Empires series. If you  don't know already, it's a traditional real-time-strategy game set in the colonial and imperial ages of European history, with a little of flair of Asia for kicks. Although Age of Empires games traditionally feature a very strong campaign, the replay factor in AOE is always the multiplayer and skirmish options, and this time players are given a multitude of options to suit their gameplay preferences. As a "turtle" (high defense, weak offense) player, I especially like the "treaty" mode, which turns off combat for a set number of minutes at the beginning of each round and also forces players to build their base within a confined space during that time period. As with previous games in the series, AoE3 features 4 different "age" milestones that allow your civilization to access new technologies and units.
* Trading cards enabled.
* Different civilizations, especially those from different continents, have entirely separate styles of play, giving the game different "flavors" of play and replayability.
* Rather than just giving each civilization unique units and technologies, AOE3 takes "Uniqueness" a step further by giving every play 21 "bonus cards," which can be used to dramatically alter your play choices. Two players can conceivably play as the same civilization and require completely different strategies and playstyles due to the bonuses given to them by their cards.
* Vastly more multiplayer options than the predecessors in the series.
* Some Civs, such as the Sioux, are fairly simplistic. This is a positive attribute as it allows differently-skilled players to enjoy the game in their own way.
* There is a "home city building" side-game that is a little enjoyable.
* I feel like a game that supports 1000+ units on the screen and 1920x1080 resolution should let me zoom the map out a bit further. My town center annoyingly takes up way too much of my view!
* No Steam achievements.
* Antiquated map controls - the only way to scroll the map is by moving your cursor to the edge of the screen. RTS games should support WASD map scrolling and/or click 'n' drag.
* The final "age" is rarely ever needed in a match, and costs more than it benefits your team, in my opinion.
* Map-editing is nowhere near as easy and intuitive as it was in previous AOE games.
* Weak AI. It seems like a 1 vs. 1 AI opponent always focuses strictly on cavalry, which in turn focuses me to only focus on building one type of unit.
* Horribly WRONG launcher screen. When starting the game, you are given the choice of loading (a) Age of Empires III: Complete Collection, (b) Age of Empires III: The War Chiefs, and (c) Age of Empires III: Asian Dynasties. However, option "A" is not complete at all: choosing it gives you access to
of the two expansions. Option B gives you access to the War Chiefs Expansion (but not Asian Dynasties), and Option C gives you access to ALL game content: the base game and both expansions.
* Not as fun as AOE2. A sequal should be a step forward, not a step back. The differences are noticeable in all sorts of small areas, which individually would not be a problem, but lend to an overall diminished quality. Some examples are unit formations being nowhere near as "tight," and units having a tendency to WALK into battle if they are grouped with a slower unit.
* At the time of this writing, the base price for AO3 is $39.99. That is overpriced, especially since AO2-HD is a more solid and overall better game and comes for the same base price.
, I do think AOE3 is worth checking out if you can get it on sale. I have had a lot of fun with this game, perhaps 100 hours or so, before it ever became available on Steam. But now that AO2-HD has come out, I see little reason to play AO3.
