I have tried to love Fallout 4. From the onset: the shooting seemed much better & settlements were fun at first. But...
The feeling of eking out life as an outsider in a desperate wasteland was gone, replaced by just endlessly building pointless settlements and becoming the beloved leader of pretty much everyone at once; but I persisted.
The incredible agency & openness one felt in both the wasteland and in the story itself was gone, replaced by a ham-fisted narrative with ultimately very little choices; but I persisted.
The fun dialogue of other Fallout games was gone, replaced by four bland options you have to choose blindly; but I persisted.
The incredible worldbuilding & quests of other Fallout games were gone, replaced by hand-waving the past and just doing whatever seemed to fit; but I persisted.
The many unique & quirky character options along with the massive arsenal of weapons were gone, replaced by a bland options board and making only minor adjustments to existing guns; but still I persisted!
And now, under the guise of paying it forward towards the modding community, Bethesda or perhaps Zenimax has begun to try and earn a hefty profit off of existing mods for even the smallest of items; and now I'm done.
Now I'm just another idiot whining on the internet like it means something! Another poor fool thinking this'll do anything to save a beloved franchise from its own success...

I truly loved my playthrough of xcom 2 & being a big fan of the first, as well as reading the interceding book I wasn't surprised.
First game in some time that I bought on disc rather than through Steam but for a 5 pound difference I thought why not? Installation was pretty straightforward maybe took an hour or so then got into playing.
First problem was like GTA 5 the game seemed to have set itself up on max settings so took an age to load, I play on my laptop its above the minimum specs but not by a huge amount. Just seems funny that they do that, could at least auto detect. Fine when I got it sorted though.
Second problem, tutorial mission has a bug where it gets stuck so you cannot move or complete the mission. On the Tutorial. Thats pretty bad, especially if you weren't experienced with the game.
Getting into the game I really enjoyed the new way the tactical map works & it really feels a lot more like you are the resistance, the sneaking around in cover & setting traps makes it feel a bit fairer. As you play new enemies appear pretty quick & every time it was a bit like 'woah' & then you have to find a way to deal with them. Shooting helps most of the time, but they all seem pretty fair probably apart from the range of the snake tongue chaps which seems a bit ridiculous & i'm not sure if it ever triggers overwatch which makes it a bit unfair. It also is something that bugs out quite a bit with characters disappearing and reappearing on different levels.
Third problem, after playing for a couple of days. It stopped working. Totally. I tried lots of things from faq but the only thing that seemed to work is deleting local files then downloading it from Steam. This was fine for me but i'm not sure if you bought the discs because you didn't have a great internet connection whether that would cause a problem.
After this and a patch it seemed to run a fair bit better and by and large carried on fine to the end. No game ender bugs but it does autosave about 3 different saves rolling which I think is because they do corrupt. Small issues being one guy in my squad just getting stuck after being revived, stood there and couldn't do anything. The last mission can bug out with crazy coloured graphics too but a reload sorted that.
Truly its a different experience to Enemy Unknown & after an initial bit of hate to the timer missions I got into it as it forces you to get a move on, and to be fair once you get used to them you know what kind of troops work best - not slow ones!
Now the procedurally generated maps really give the variety back like the old Micropose edition, and its really a game that will stand multiple playthroughs. Not sure about going ironman yet though as I don't quite trust it which is a shame, maybe after a bit more patching.
Which does lead me to a bit of a general point on pc gaming at the moment, really I loved this game which kept me going. But there are too many bugs for a finished product & even if you are playing on minimum it should work ok especially as its a turn based game otherwise put higher settings on the box. Huge amounts of people had problems with this game, even with powerful machines so optimisation was poor & if it takes longer to iron out the problems. Do that, knock it back a few weeks as its not often I will buy a game on release now mostly due to everything being super buggy.

Short Version: A pile of wasted potential and shattered promises. A thoughtlessly-designed mess of features that all look great on screenshots but fall very short in execution. While the hope with Early Access titles is that they will be improved and the issues will be fixed, I have no hopes for this happening. Despite the claim of "thick and fast" updates, the last meaningful one was six months ago.
To go into detail: Despite being a sci-fi title, most of your weapons will be swords or hammers. There are guns, but they're rare and impotent. If you want a mobile light source you can craft a candle-lantern-on-a-stick, rather than a shoulder-mounted LED or similar. These are examples of things that end up making the setting feel more like a fantasy setting with spaceships arbitrarily tacked on.
Exploration, which should be the game's strong point, is ruined by the sheer vastness of the randomly generated planets, the tier system, and the coordinates system. Why should I build a house on this planet, over the one next to it? Why should I build a house on this tier-2 planet which only has iron on it, when I can wait and build it on a tier-5 planet with better materials? Why even explore at all, when I could just go on the forums and look up the coordinates of a planet with amazing weapons?
Combat is weak, and floaty. Can best be described as two people on a trampoline hitting each other with pool noodles. Progression consists of mining ore (with a pickaxe, of course. What do you think this is, the future??) to get armor and weapons. When you first enter a new tier, enemies will be killing you in only a few hits. When you get the armor of that tier, you become very resistant to their attacks. It results in a game where you're never properly challenged: You are either fleeing helplessly from the sky demons, or crushing them in one hit.
On top of all of this, the game is bizarrely resource-intensive for a 2d platformer. I have a fairly powerful system capable of playing full 3d games (Crysis 2, Max Payne 3), yet I have gotten consistently poor framerate.

I am not going to review the game itself here, but I want to give some info that I feel was not clear enough. The game in itself is fun, period. I like the graphics, the gameplay and the feel of the game and I think it is easy enough to find info on the gameplay itself. Steam forces me to chose wether I recommend it or not, though, so I have to chose to not recommend it. Here is why:
What you have to know is that upon release the game is going to be __Free to Play__. Admittedly this is written in the Early Access Statement here on the store page that I did not read, cause I did not expect a paid  game that will later become free. Is this bad? Not necessarily, but it is unexpected.
According to their forums [1] their plans include non-exclusive ships that have bonus boosts and "an exclusive crew member". Is this Pay2Win? Not necessarily, but it could be.
The extra copies (Scavenger Keys) bought with the Fleet packs are only Game-Access-Keys. Once the game is released your gifted friends have nothing more than everybody else using the Free2Play-Version. Add to that stats-wipes could happen (if anybody knows a clear statement from the Devs about this, I would be glad for a hint in the comments) and I kind of feel some regret for having bought the game now to gift the extra copies to friends.
I do not blame myself for having been under the impression of buying a normal early access game with extra copies, but neither do I blame the developers, it was just unexpected and it happens. I take them by their word that the money spent will be worth it, not doubting that, but I cannot be sure at this point either.
What I complain about though is that the necessary information is not easy to find or emphasized. It is there, but scattered and hidden in the early access description, as well as their own forums (which were not working this evening when I wanted to read up on their plans and what the packs actually mean). It takes a bit of reading to understand what you are buying for real.
My opinion is: As long as it is not 100% clear how the boosts and paid extras will work and affect the game it may be better to wait for clarity. Especially, because of one of their statements found at [2] is:
"There are a few other things we’re currently discussing (i.e. possibly making soft currency purchasable, and the potential for a subscription model)"

It's a weird one.
And a good one.
The best analogy for this game I could think of is some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of World of Tanks/War Tthunder and Smite that  somehow ended up looking like Elite: Dangerous.
Basically what Fractured Space is, it's 5 versus 5 arena TDM much like DotA or any other MOBA. You pick your ship, crew loadout and jump into battle. Pretty simple. Once there, you have yourself a map with grand total of 5 sectors you can jump between. Top and bottom sectors are respectevely enemy's and yours bases, 2 sector on left and right are where the actions usually is and center one is something that makes this game unique and not just "DotA in space". In the moddle of the sector there is a big capture point that is inactive most of the time. Once in awhile this point activates and anyone can cap it. Whoever caps it gets team wide buff that increases cap rate, damage and resistance. This buff can turn around whole game if played right. The leveling mechanic is also different from most MOBAs. On the map you have mining outposts that give resources to whichever team has the outpost. Your level depend on ammount of resources your team has so everyone on the team has the same level.
That seems a lot for a short explanation of the game. But all those mechanics are easy to follow once you play couple of matches.
For the ships there aren't that many ships right now but more is coming surely and even what is already there has a lot of variety in gameplay and strategy plus you have loadouts that change gameplay. Ships besides guns have 4 abilities. For example, some ships have blink (there are 2 different kinds of blinks), some have boosts, some shields etc. etc. Some ships are good against some ships and not so against other. Overall the game is balanced quite well so far.
A few words about looks: this game looks pretty darn good, especially for an early acces game. Most textures are very detailed, models are too, especially ships. Lighting is very good. Overall the graphics remind me of E:D.
The game looks very promising and if you are a fan of either Smite (or MOBAs in general) or WoT\WT (and likes) or you are just like space as much as me, I would recomend you to get this game. Not only you'll get some good and unique expirience, you'll help the game grow. Right now there is around 50-100 players online at all times and it's not a problem to find a match.
That's my 2 cents.

The idea of the Creation Club is disruptive to modding and will clearly result in the theft of work for modders by less scrupulous people that can then profit from their theft, with Bethesda's blessing.
To add to this, the Creation Club appears to download it's entire archive to the player's harddrive, cluttering our machines and effectively sabotating anyone who runs games in smaller SSDs or HDDs. The need to download unnecessary files would also limit those players with limited bandwith or on slower internet.
The Creation Club means that I cannot recommend any of Bethesda's games that uses it, as it will not only disrupt the modding community around the game, one of the major selling points of Bethesda's RPGs, but it will also occupy unnecessary space in a player's drive and force unnecessary updates.

First, don't buy this game expecting Age of Empires II. The difference between this game and the one before it are almost night and day. The core of the game is unchanged, but almost everything else in completely different.
That said, Age of Empires III is a great game, even though it hasn't stood the test of time like the second game in the series. My favorite feature, which if you ask me makes the game, is the new Home City mechanic. As you play, your home city levels up, allowing them to send you new units, supplies, or even powerful upgrades and buildings while you're in a match. As you gain experience from playing, you will recieve points to spend in your home city, consuming a "Deck Card" in exchange for a shipment that will help you along in your current game.
Another interested addition to Age III is Mercenaries. Mercs are simply more powerful, more expensive versions of other units, such as Sweedish Pikemen, Black Riders, or Outlaws. Certain civilizations are able to produce enough money to build entire armies of these units, and they're just plain fun to play with.
Naval combat is another nice update to this franchise. In certain maps and game modes, controlling the water is a requirment for victory, though the waters won't become as cluttered as in AgeII. Each unit, be it a ship, a musketman, or a hussar, takes up population. Horsemen usually take up 3 or more pop, while foot soldiers take 1 or 2. Ships have thier own limit on the numer you can contruct, so even on smaller maps with just a lake things will never get too crowded. Ships also have unique uses. One can spawn units right at the enemy's shores, while another can bombard enemy buildings from great distances.
Native Tribes are yet another addition to the game play. Across the map, trading posts are available for a player to construct an Outpost at. Depending on the type of trading post, this Outpost will offer different units, upgrades, or even revenue once it is complete. Trade routes will allow the owner to select a shipment of Gold, Wood, Food, or even Experience to quicken your progress towards a new Home City shipment. Native settlements offer new units, which do not count towards total population, giving your army a nice boost from the cheap and affective native warriors. Asian monk settlements or Spanish Missions are also available with the Asian Dynasty expansion.
And finally, Explorers make an appearance in AgeIII. These powerful, one of a kind units spawn from the get go. Think of them as your scout from AgeII, only much more powerful. These units are able to fight nutral enemies such as outlaws, wild animals, or natives to gain access to treasures that are scattered across the map. Treasures increase your supplies, give you a free unit, or even give a sizable buff to your settlement. The Explorer can also be upgraded by your Home City. Cards to increase your Explorer's health, speed, and damage are available, as well as cards that grant him the ability to become stealthed, spawn units, or reveal a portion of the map from far away.

Although I relly enjoyed the environments and interactions of Starbound. The actual gameplay and crafting mechanics fell short of the execution and simplicity that I was expecting.

An amazing game, even in it's early Alpha build (and, in all honesty, with how many new features and revamps as are being worked on it really should be considered a stable Beta).
The premise is simple. You find yourself ship disabled and orbitting an alien world. What to do? Beam down to the surface and use your ingenuity and wits to try and scavenge or build what you need of course! At least enough to break orbit and explore the rest of the universe and its endless variety of worlds, creatures, and resources.
Following the simple premise of Minecraft and Terraria, the player is allowed to interact with just about any object or brick in the game. While that's a tried and true success formula what really makes Starbound stand out is just how much FUN exploration is! Every alien world is a surprise. Will the rain be acid and melt the flesh from your bones, forcing you to dig a network of tunnels to mine the rich coal veins? Will the creatures come at you like an insane asylum lunatic, gibbering and bouncing around like a pogo stick possessed? Or will it be a quiet jungle world where the tree foliage is nothing but eyeballs that simply watch as you go about your business terraforming the world and building a mighty fortress that stretches from the stars all the way down to the core of the planet?!
Chucklefish Studios is currently reworking how game advancement and core mechanics work so expect a lot more goal oriented activity and polishing to come.
Seriously, if you only buy one game this year, make it Starbound.

In a sentence, yes, I do recommend this game to both people that enjoy space combat games and any MOBA fans.
But that's going to be my main point here, because I disagree with a lot of the other reviews here. If you're into pure space sims, of which there aren't that many of, then you might be a little surprised by Fractured Space.
Fractured Space, at its core, is a MOBA. It has more in common with LoL or DoTA than space combat sims. In fact, I'd hesitate to call this a space sim. I simply say that because, while yes, you do control huge starships with a variety of weapons and 'abilities', and yes the armour on each side of your starship is tracked, other than that the game doesn't really try to go into any deeper 'simulation'. Movement is entirely free, but it's not realistic in terms of space physics. Your health is tracked by a simple number.
In many ways you'll find traditional LoL/DoTA mechanics 'translated' so that they make sense on a sci fi starship theme. If you've played Beyond Earth, you'll probably understand that already.
I bought into the game not really sure what to expect, and I'm not a MOBA fan. I don't enjoy LoL or DoTA. At first I was disappointed at what appeared to be fairly shallow sim mechanics, but the deeper and more interesting parts of the game lie in teamwork and co-ordination, as well as pulling off a successful move or combo that sends your opponent up in flames.

TLDR; from my perspective, even though it's a bit disappointing for someone who was expecting an in-depth multiplayer starship sim game, it can still be incredibly fun as a space themed MOBA and will be a totally viable alternative in the MOBA market when it releases.
I would recommend, though, that unless you wish to directly support the developers, avoid 'buying' the game before it releases. Simply my opinion on F2P games that require purchase to access early-access. It's early, it's not finished and is a little content light at the moment.

As a FPS player with 15 years of ‘experience’ this is my review:
Pros:
-	If you're into F2P shooters then this is a safe bet as it has relatively decent gameplay.
-	NO PAY2WIN! It is all based on skill. Within 3 matches I could consistently come top of leader board!
Cons:
-	No replayability - As much as I appreciate the lack of pay2win, it still has all of those ANNOYING features designed to make you dedicate your life (and cash) towards only playing this game. For me, this is a cheap way of making the game replayable. This game isn’t replayable because of good mechanics; rather, it is replayable because you are stuck in an endless grind to gather more points for a cosmetic upgrade.
-	Even if you REALLY enjoy the gameplay there is ultimately nothing to work towards. I got bored of coming top and there isn’t any incentive to continue to play. As mentioned, all unlocks are cosmetic – meaning that there is no tactile benefit to grinding or spending money.
-	I understand that this type of ‘grindy’ F2P game is popular in the Asian market; however, I STRONGLY disagree with this type of attitude as it ultimately stifles the efforts of other game developers who put much more effort into making the experience replayable by investing in solid gameplay mechanics.
Summary: Enjoyable for the first few hours but then you realise there’s nothing to work towards and that there are much higher quality games with a price point. Other game developers put effort into developing unique gameplay mechanics whereas this offers nothing new whatsoever.
Recommendation:
-	Play the game for a few hours and then leave it alone.
-	Encourage the devs to up their game by developing unique gameplay mechanics rather than spending their time on new cosmetic items which ‘cheapen’ the gaming market on a whole.
-	Pay for your games…

*EDIT* The problem explained below is, on further inspection, limited to a marginally small number of the unlocks available. I'm changing my recommendation accordingly.
Fractured Space is a game i've been waiting for for years. The mechanics are solid, the gameplay is fun and rewarding when  things go right. I had a lot of fun in the early access period.
However,
I cannot recommend the game right now, and here's why.
Firstly, the developers have designed the game as a space combat MOBA, essentially. But the upgrade system is permanent; a rank based ladder instead of a progressive session-to-session system like in any other MOBA. This means that higher level players can have a distinct advantage from the very start of each match, and the differential between them and lower level players is a gap that seems uncloseable within the match, no matter how long it lasts or how well each player does.
Secondly, hand-in-hand with the above problem is the fact that so few servers actually have enough players, meaning that you're likely to find a rank difference that spans the entire spectrum, from Captain (entry-level rank) to Admiral (The highest I've seen so far), exacerbating the first problem.
Hopefully, they remove the current upgrade system and implement a proper MOBA one, where upgrades are similar to Items in other MOBA's.

I never particularly liked Harvest Moon.  I really WANTED to, but I just couldn't get into it for whatever reason.  I played it some anyhow, but just eventually gave up because I felt directionless and wasn't engaged with the characters or setting.  Animal Crossing was even worse, at a glance even.
Something about Stardew Valley transcends that, at least for me.  The characters are engaging and interesting, even the ones that are not all that deep.  They just feel... unique.  I don't know, it feels like there's a real living town here and there aren't just a lot of random chibi people that I can't relate to.  Sometimes imagination is better than a lot of explicit backstory that is told in excruciating depth, anyhow.  That said, at the time of this review I'm only 7ish hours in and that's clearly just scratching the surface here.
The main things that keep me engaged are the setting, the interesting quests and activites, the people of the town, the various things to explore and the mysteries that are present, and... probably some other things.  That's one of the things about this game -- it has a bit of that "one more turn" feel that games like Civilization have.  You've always got a variety of things in progress at once (crops growing, gifts giving, season winding down, time-based quests and longer-term ones,  things you want to gather, etc).  Jumping between activities helps keep anything from becoming stale.
THAT said, you really should look into using mods for the game, as there is a robust system for that and the game is in sore need of certain tweaks.  The movement speed is abysmal, even when running, and sucked a lot of the fun out of the game for me.  The "Auto Speed" mod fixes that up easily.  Other things can be annoyingly slow, too.  "Fast Animations" fixes up things like the geodes and whatnot.  You can also have it tune up the time-to-catch-a-fish speed, becausee that is annoying as well.
Fence decay is super annoying, and there's a mod that fixes that.  I like the more rain mod, but that's just personal preference.  A mod that lets you see the sell price for goods is really useful.  Another that dynamically lists your daily tasks is also a big help.  I had no idea I needed to water my cat's bowl or pet it every day until that.  The save backup mod is really really a good idea.  The simple crop label mod, and skip intro mod, are helpful.  The "did you water your crops" mod is pretty much essential.  The fruit trees mod is helpful.  Quest delay mod can be nice if you want to keep things relaxed a bit more.  UI Info Suite tells you SO much without being cheaty -- boy that one is useful.  It overlaps a bit annoyingly with a couple of those other mods at certain times, but it's livable.
I haven't gotten into animal coops and whatnot yet, but it looks like the mood guard and loved labels and possible auto animal doors, animal sitter, auto gate, and better hay might be good.  I have them earmarked for checking out later.
There's also an "improved quality of life" mod that aims to help with a lot of things in general.  I wound up not installing that one yet, because I got pretty much all those things from the other mods listed above.  But a variety of people like it.
And that's before you get into mods that add content or change content or change mechanics in a more funadmental way.  There are plenty of those, but something tells me you need to be 100+ hours in before any of those even start being remotely a problem.  This game has a ridiculous amount of content.
But for the love of all that is holy, use the speed increase mod to save yourself some grief. ;)

I Am Bread I guess would best be defined as a puzzle/adventure game, for it certainly has aspects of both genres. You may or may not like this game. If you're like me, you brought the game because of the interesting title name and backstory.
That said backstory is that you literally play as bread. You are some guy's bread, and you need to move around his house haphazardly in order to 'toast' yourself. I thought this title would be worth a look, so I went ahead and brought it, and soon found out that this was a hard game.
I'm not opposed to challenge. Some of the best games of all times were also the hardest. Challenge however shouldn't come in the form of bad camera angles and shoddy controls.
The idea behind I am bread is interesting, but once the novelty wears off, you'll probably find the game to be lackluster. Spending ages climbing up a fridge only to have you work undone by the punishing game mechanics isn't fun. It's tedious and boring. And once you get to the top of the fridge, you have to  proceed down a linear path in order to climb the next obstacle.
Ultimately, my point is this. You are apiece of bread which climbs things. There are literally only three or four game play elements that provide challenge. These game play elements are nothing new or exciting, and certainly not worth the price of this game.
If you can get it on sale, it might be worth a try. As it stands however, I Am Bread leaves a lot to be desired with me. This could have been an interesting game, but it is just so... boring, repetitive and tedious.

Dota in SPACE*ominous voice*
Fractured space is a 5 vs. 5 team battle on areas of space that has been divided in various sectors. All sectors have control points you need to capture in order to advance and eventually make your way to enemy base. During combat you can freely fly in the battlefield, warp into sectors where the combat is currently going on and warp back to base to regroup or to run away with your nearly destroyed ship for repairs.
There's currently 15 different ship types in game, 3 of them unlocked right at the start. Ship types fit for many roles: long range, hard hitting sniper boat, heavily armored flagship for more close range combat, sneaky & stealthy assassin ship, fast moving frigate etc. As the game is currently in it's early stages, it understandably might have some balance issues between various ship designs - though I personally feel like every ship has their own use and an organized group will easily take down those solo snipers or assassins who think they can/should be able to kill everything themselves.
PROs:
Awesome ship design
Well made level
Graphics, sfx
CONs
1(one) level
Very low playerbase (seen max of 54)
Level Matching system(isn't one)
No real training/tutorials

I'll continue to update this review, but I have spent 10+ hrs playing this game and I've had it just over 24 hrs. This game has been on my wishlist since release and I finally pulled the trigger when it recently went on sale. A lot of the negative reviews can be put into 2 categories from what I can tell. The second category is that the game is too hard/too RNG-based. Maybe the game seems easier to me because I spent some time watching streamers play it at release, so I already had an idea of what I wanted to do and what to expect. It is worth mentioning that I have very little experience with turn-based RNG games as I have only played Hearthstone and This War of Mine (great game as well). If you're on the fence about this game, get it. You will not be disappointed as it is very well put together and very much worth the full asking price. Worst case scenario, you find the game "grindy" after 20-50 hours (still get your money's worth IMO). Best case scenario, you find a new favorite game.

Half-Life revolutionized how the industry looks at gaming. At the time of release in 1998 one of the major popular FPS games were Quake by id Software, a superb masterpiece, but what it was missing was what Valve had in mind.
An immersive storyline experience.
Rather than doing cutscenes like all of the rest, they felt that the only way you could actually feel like you were part of the world was by placing you in it instead of a character controlled by you. They achieved this by making sure you would always see from the eyes of Gordon Freeman, a theoretical physicist at the age of 27, from the very beginning to the end.
There is no narrator, no one telling you what's going on. It's just you experiencing and learning the plot. The level design is beautiful, you weren't playing just another level with another environment, what it did was it progressed the story by using the environment to make you think you were actually a part of the world, instead of using the arbitrary concept of levels like so many others.
It convinced you that this isn't a game anymore, this is entertainment at its highest.
When a monster would come at you in other games, it would usually scare you, but when you realized that all of the monsters AI was in fact just cardboard cutouts homing in on you, sometimes getting stuck on corners, it somehow took away from the experience.
The Half-Life AI was the most advanced on the market, but there were certainly monsters designed to be stupid by choice, such as the headcrabs.
But where it shines the most on is the HECU soldiers. They can flank, toss grenades, take cover and spit out information to other team mates. Another great AI is the houndeyes, they work in groups attacking together. Even the cockroaches were advanced, moving away from light, seeking food and running away from larger creatures. It's even possible to feed bullsquids. All of this to try and enhance the experience of you actually being there.
Scripting made everything more immersive, it made sure that the plot mattered to you, and that the outcome of the ending was satisfying to keep you wanting more. It also made sure cutscenes wasn't necessary as it would take away from the experience.
Every time you see a great scripted character in a game you have Half-Life and Half-Life alone to thank for it.
The levels never became stale and boring since they kept changing them all the time. They mixed around with different mechanics and weapons to keep you interessted, weapons would be lying on logical places or dropped by someone rather than at a random place where the devoloper thought "This place is empty, lets place a weapon or powerup here".
One example of excellent design is a place where you find something reffered to as snarks, they are essentially small bugs that you could throw away and they would jump around attacking, even yourself if you weren't careful enough. You're not really sure where they could be useful, but valve just introduced you to them so that you now know how they work. Later on you come across this ventilation filled with these, you crawl forward a bit and realize soldiers are shooting the ventilation down, it collapses and creates a large gap in front of you.
Your only instinct is to load the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s with snarks. This is one of so many examples that the game just keeps letting you try out new interessting things and it becomes a fun ride all the way through.
Other games would either have a handfisted tutorial, which to me is like looking at the answers to a puzzle, why even bother doing the puzzle in the first place... or the mechanics would for the most part be the same, making the game boring after a while.
It's the solutions to new problems that gives you satisfaction and enjoyment to a discovery. Which is something most games, even today, seems to have lost. Because, what else is there really to make a game enjoyable?
It's not just the weapons that mix it up, but also the enemies, you never fight the same enemies all the way through, it's constantly variating, not to mention all of the enemies are unique.
Vortigaunts needs to charge before firing which means you can take cover in between, bullsquids charge when close and spit on long range, houndeyes are lethal in groups and need to charge to fire a damaging blast radius around them and headcrabs and zombies need to be timed with the crowbar to avoid taking damage. However, later on you recieve weapons so that killing them becomes much easier.
Enemies actually react properly when you shoot them, sometimes they'll moan when they are hurt and grunts will run away from your grenades instead of just standing there. You can't just strafe left and right to dodge incoming nades like you can dodge linear hitscan fire, this creates a different experience than most other games at the time.
Because that Half-Life is running on GoldSrc, a modified Quake engine, it recieved an infamous exploit, bunnyhoping. While it technically has nothing to do with the intended game it feels worth mentioning as it has created one of the most entertaining games to run and watch. It has a very high skill ceiling so there's no doubt Single Segments will always be improved.

This game is not for the faint of heart. It is frustrating, difficult, rng based and at times it can seem unfair. This is a game where your characters will die, you'll have a dungeon run screwed up because of one rng boss spawn when you're not ready (i'm looking at you collector) and chance dodges, crits, and status effects will make or break your day sometimes. For me, i like it this way. Without the difficulty this game loses a lot of it's charm and character. It has an overall fantastic audio and visual style (in my opinion) and the gameplay, difficulty adn mechanics just back it up. Yes the rng may seem unfair at times but this game is about making the best of bad situations when they arise. You have to know when to retreat and cut your losses and when to try to forge ahead and eek out a victory. Dont get me wrong, once you get used to the game and mechanics, you can have some easy runs, some may even seem comfortably easy but this game has a way of keeping you on your toes. DD has great replayability in the sense that it has a rogue-lite feel to it. You have several different dungeon paths with different objectives to complete in each with the purpose of finding loot, leveling up your characters and leveling up your dungeon experience with the goal to make your team strong enough to face the different bosses, then eventually traverse the Darkest Dungeon. This game forces care management of finances and materials as higher level character become more costly to maintain as they develope different quircks, habits and contract diseases along with the increasing cost of equipment and upgrades. Each time you embark on a dungeon crawl you must carefully stock your party's limited inventory with items that might mean the difference between life and death or profit and disaster. Overall, I have really enjoyed this game and eventhough it has had its moments when it has frustrated me to no end, i keep returning to it.

EDITED:  Thumbs Up due to Long War 2.
Original Review:
XCOM EU is my favorite game. I love it, and like many others here, I really like what XCOM 2 is doing.  I have beaten XCOM EU twice on XBOX in Ironman mode.  I also LOVE "The Long War" mod.   I love Ironman mode, and as frustrating as it is to lose some of your best soldiers, or get a squad wiped out, I appreciate the struggle.    With all of this being said, I am not a newbie to XCOM.  So I feel I should be able to play the game with a reasonable amount of success on the Veteran setting.  Nothing pretentious.  Just take yer lumps and try to save humanity with whoever can survive.  I also am very familiar with Confirmation Bias, so I don't think missing a 92% shot is ruining the game with difficulty nor is the game cheating.
My problem with XCOM 2 is the seemingly overwhelming odds against my troops.  I have lost 11 ironman games in a row.  I didn't just have a bad battle or two, or just lose my highest ranking soldier on occasion...   My games are done. Game Over, man.   And there seems to be nothing I can change about the situation unless I want to stop playing Ironman and scout maps and reload saves constantly.   I cannot get plated armor any faster than I've been getting it.  I can't get more engineers than I've gotten, I dont' see a way to change anything I'm researching or building to make anything any better.
I love when my 4 man crew has 1 strangled by a snake, 1 mind controlled, 1 in forced panic and the other in actual panic.  You just sit and watch them run around on the screen.  (One got so scared he actually dropped a grenade on himself and died.  I laughed at that one.)
The latest 6 man squad I've sent in to rescue civilians ran into a new Alien.  A Berserker (My first time getting this far in the game.), a Shield Advent and a Regular Advent.    So I'm trying to rescue civilians and at the same time, I am unloading on this huge beast of an alien which is not dying even though I'm hitting it.  I manage to kill it on the second round, but it takes a full two rounds and every trick i can think of to deal max damage. (Blowing up walls so others get shots, shooting propane tanks to kill the shield advent... that sort of thing.)  However, in the scond round, while flanking, I somehow unlock two groups of aliens.  1 Advent Officer with his mark of death, two Mutons, 1 snake, 2 Stun Lancers AND ANOTHER BERZERKER! UPDATE: I can't honestly recommend this game *at this time* and had to change my review. Core issue? Lack of updates and a host of excuses from the developer. It's a fun game, it can be much better, and honestly the mods are about all that holds it together still if that. I suggest waiting until it gets out of beta and/or the developer gets it together. I still stand by the rest of my review but just keep this main part in mind.
---
First I want to start off by saying this is a beta review and everything in it may be subject to change as the game is completed. Given how many folks are picking it up, I thought a mini review would be useful!
- Unlimited planets to explore and build on
- Insane number of decoration items for your builds as well as block types, colors, etc
- Pretty much everything you like abou Terraria is here... but in SPACE!
- Mod friendly! Mostly. If you play single player mods work wonderfully. If you play multiplayer... not always so.
- It's $15. That's the cost of a movie. Play it for a few hours and you've already broke even on your entertainment value. :)
- Your spaceship is tiny. I've ran a character from start to finish [top tier gear] using only my ship but it required very, very good space management and I had to skip some things to make it all work, like expansive storage. Since this game is mod-friendly, you can simply get a mod to let you edit your ship [you cant by default] or replace it with a different ship [also a mod] -- future versions promise upgradable ships so hopefully this con goes away
- Planet tracking. There is none. Want to know where you've been? Keep paper and pencil handy. The game gives you no way to know. You *can* set your homeworld which lets you basically bookmark a single planet but... you can also easily reset your home world accidently and your base is lost forever.
- Tier progression [1-10] isn't quite as linear as you'd think. The first few are but the second half can be cleared out incredibly fast getting to the top tier stuff. This *will* change in final as they take out the placeholders for crafting tier advancement. Of course, once you get to X sector you can go to level 5-10 planets and just go find high level items... but I digress.
- Monsters are a bit meh. After you've seen the same monsters just in different colors a hundred times it gets a bit boring
- Quests aren't in yet other than the tutorial so the game "story" doesnt really exist. Same with bosses as there are only 4 currently.
- Money goes from incredible sparse at first to a joke later in the game when you have a refinery and more pixels [the ingame currency] than you know what to do with. Said item can be gotten fairly early on as well which just adds insult to injury.
- Mob AI is not that bright and/or block placement is a bit too lenient. Want to avoid a monster or poke safely through a hole at a boss? Surround them in blocks. It's really that easy and with the fluid and fast block placement of 2x2 blocks [default size] it takes literally nothing to do. This facilitates "world raiding" once you open up X Sector to immediately find level 10 planets and bombard through them to find good loot in chests on the surface or in buildings. This is on the "may not ever be fixed" list.
- Player wipes.  Its beta and this still happens and is expected to continue tho they are working to lock that in. Not a huge deal for me but for many it is so be forewarned.
- The game often feels disjointed with so many planets and no real attachment to any of them. A good number of players simply live in their ships. Add in planet-losing bugs and you can probably guess why tho those are getting shored up quickly. Having no idea of where you've been makes it hard to "come home" again and turns every planet into a random faceless stranger that you really dont care about after you've finished looting it.
- Inventory management is a nightmare when you have 30 colors of dirt and 10 types of sand.
- Bugs. It has to be said. While the game is pretty stable and bugs are fairly low, the ones you will find are fairly bad. This should improve over time as the game progresses into its next stages.
Hopefully you find this helpful. I could write a novel on this game as it features so much but I'll leave you this list for now. If Chucklefish can manage to shore up the gameplay and solidify the core components, Starbound will be a solid game at release. If you want to play a fully working, fully implemented, no bugs version... wait until it gets out of early access. As for me, I've got aliens to kill!

I never particularly liked Harvest Moon.  I really WANTED to, but I just couldn't get into it for whatever reason.  I played it some anyhow, but just eventually gave up because I felt directionless and wasn't engaged with the characters or setting.  Animal Crossing was even worse, at a glance even.
Something about Stardew Valley transcends that, at least for me.  The characters are engaging and interesting, even the ones that are not all that deep.  They just feel... unique.  I don't know, it feels like there's a real living town here and there aren't just a lot of random chibi people that I can't relate to.  Sometimes imagination is better than a lot of explicit backstory that is told in excruciating depth, anyhow.  That said, at the time of this review I'm only 7ish hours in and that's clearly just scratching the surface here.
The main things that keep me engaged are the setting, the interesting quests and activites, the people of the town, the various things to explore and the mysteries that are present, and... probably some other things.  That's one of the things about this game -- it has a bit of that "one more turn" feel that games like Civilization have.  You've always got a variety of things in progress at once (crops growing, gifts giving, season winding down, time-based quests and longer-term ones,  things you want to gather, etc).  Jumping between activities helps keep anything from becoming stale.
THAT said, you really should look into using mods for the game, as there is a robust system for that and the game is in sore need of certain tweaks.  The movement speed is abysmal, even when running, and sucked a lot of the fun out of the game for me.  The "Auto Speed" mod fixes that up easily.  Other things can be annoyingly slow, too.  "Fast Animations" fixes up things like the geodes and whatnot.  You can also have it tune up the time-to-catch-a-fish speed, becausee that is annoying as well.
Fence decay is super annoying, and there's a mod that fixes that.  I like the more rain mod, but that's just personal preference.  A mod that lets you see the sell price for goods is really useful.  Another that dynamically lists your daily tasks is also a big help.  I had no idea I needed to water my cat's bowl or pet it every day until that.  The save backup mod is really really a good idea.  The simple crop label mod, and skip intro mod, are helpful.  The "did you water your crops" mod is pretty much essential.  The fruit trees mod is helpful.  Quest delay mod can be nice if you want to keep things relaxed a bit more.  UI Info Suite tells you SO much without being cheaty -- boy that one is useful.  It overlaps a bit annoyingly with a couple of those other mods at certain times, but it's livable.
I haven't gotten into animal coops and whatnot yet, but it looks like the mood guard and loved labels and possible auto animal doors, animal sitter, auto gate, and better hay might be good.  I have them earmarked for checking out later.
There's also an "improved quality of life" mod that aims to help with a lot of things in general.  I wound up not installing that one yet, because I got pretty much all those things from the other mods listed above.  But a variety of people like it.
And that's before you get into mods that add content or change content or change mechanics in a more funadmental way.  There are plenty of those, but something tells me you need to be 100+ hours in before any of those even start being remotely a problem.  This game has a ridiculous amount of content.
But for the love of all that is holy, use the speed increase mod to save yourself some grief. ;)

I love how every ship looks and feels very unique so far and how they all have unique weapons and abilities. There is also a nice tech tree for abilities that allows for players with the same model ship to still be different in that they have upgraded there ship differently or have different crew members operating it. I think allowing players to feel unique is crucial to the success of any game, so i'm glad to see it present in Fractured Space.
I would like to see more ships developed as well as more crew options, there are really only 2 options per position atm. Also, you would have to weigh a much higher risk to pursue a fleeing target if the teams were larger. Currently, most skirmishes are only between 2 and 3 ships because you need to split up to capture and defend sectors so devs please consider increasing the team size.
Anyway i really see alot of potential for this game to be successful. All it needs is more exposure. You have my support.

EDIT AS OF 02-APR-2017:
I am... very disappointed. The newest update has brought with it sweeping changes to the way the game flowed, and it's not all good. By only changing one thing, this game has gone from a thoughtful, pace yourself style game into a much faster paced melee of ships, and all by changing the map size. One of the things I loved this game for was the feeling of actually commanding a massive ship in the cold void of space, fighting over resource stations in asteroid belts or the rings surrounding a gas giant, and the massive rush for the mining center at its core. Now It's... very World of Warships in feeling. Right now, I will still recommend this game only because it is still a good game, but it has lost one of its key core elements that gave it that sense of identity. I pray they bring it back one day.

The Music is also really good, its very calming but also very... Lonely, I can only really compare it to Chrono Trigger's music it just has that same feel...
All in All its a pretty amazing game for Early Access, I'd recommend it.

XCOM 2 is a turn-based strategy game based around aliens invading earth and winning. it was overall a good game but their were some problems which can be overlooked.
Story:
Pros
the story for the game was interesting and different and showed a perspective that not many games or movies ever cover. It allowed for interesting character development and brought back a few familiar faces, names and voices. Unlike enemy unknown it gave us a much more fleshed out story about why the alien are here and what they are planning to do.
Cons:
However the ending was satisfying i feel that it could of had a bit more to it since the ending felt short for how much time and effort you put into the game.
Gameplay:
Pros
The game play for the most part was pretty solid. It had the same feel and style to that of XCOM EU but built upon that with more mission types, more map destruction (always good) and procedurally generated maps, which added a nice feeling having played through the entire game not seeing the same map twice. A big change the game play however was concealment, which is undoubtedly one of my favourite new editions. it allowed the player to sneak up to the aliens and set up elaborate ambushes which could be very satisfying.
The game also made changes to the base management side of the game, changing it up to how it previously was in EU. however for the first look it seemed somewhat complicated but after a read through the room descriptions it made complete sense.
Cons
In the game there were two annoying factors about the missions. Firstly the fact that a majority of the turn-based parts of the game a turn limit which was not necessarily the worst but could get annoying when you wanted to have a nice methodically plan but are forced into quick eight turn games.  Secondly there was the bugs which deserve their section.
The felling when everyone misses their overwatch shots on a stun lancer
BUGS:
in the game there were numerous bugs that at times could affect the gameplay and it also has some gam breaking glitches such as the game for me wont start up or stay open if i have my razor kraken headset plugged in. It also suffers from fps problems (i know its not technically a bug) 	even with computer specs above the recommended. this however does not have as big as affect due to the game being turn-based.
Overall:
in conclusion i would recommend this game to most people especially if you were a fan of EU. it builds upon everything that it did right and adds some new ideas to the mix. It does have its fair share of bugs but they should hopefully be fixed soon.

The AI system is very well written and, depending on the difficulty, will always provide a challenge. This game is often compared to Starcraft II yet there is a lot of differences between them. In Starcraft I always found myself rushing and trying to be the best, and if you were bad at the game, you were in for a lot of stress. But in AOE players can find servers with their own skill level which makes this game one of my favorite strategy games.
In my opinion, you don't HAVE to play online like most competitive games. This game actually has a very good Skirmish mode where you go against bots. It may seem boring but if you give it a chance, it will not disappoint you. As for aesthetics, the graphics are great considering it was a game made in 2009 but this is just a small factor since the game's mechanics draw you away from noticing. There is rarely glitches, units walk with great animation, and the battle scenes have you urging to see what team will win.
The only downfall the game has is that there is no cross-platform multiplayer support and it lacks an intriguing storyline. It is common for an AOE game to have a blan or boring storyline. And you can see that when looking at its predecessors. But don't let this change your opinion. The game wasn't really made with a basis on heartwarming or intense storyline experiences but more of a play-with-friends or AI and just have a great time.
Overall, I wish they made a AOE 4. Their progression from each Age of Empires have only been big leaps in the gaming industry. But I will happily settle for AOE 3 and look forward to playing it many, many years from today. If you are in to strategy games like StarCraft, Warcraft, and Command & Conquer, this is no doubt a game worth adding to your arsenal!

Fractured Space does have a promise to be a good MOBA game, mainly through its innovative idea - space battles. Content in menu is so far very limited, but game is capable of being played and provides excellent audiovisual experience.
Also, I have to say, that guns do have sound effects according to their nature, strong canon shows "recoil" sound efffect. I know, there is the vacuum in the space, but it is very important for players to feel the power of the weapon and this is present here. Strategy is a key for winning  and community is good so far.
There has been a wipe to set everyone equal starting conditions after bringing economics to the game. You have to earn reputations with manufacturers and unlock new ships and loadouts, I rate this as positive feature, which is still being evaluated and getting better.
Free weekend had a great impact on community grow and new players are seeking for new stratiegies with a help of veteran players. Also in-game shop emerged, content will be released soon. These changes increased requirements for the servers, so you can expect some engine glitches and a need of lower resolution, but this is only a temporary issue. Also be preparde for increased effort to play together, because servers are filling fast and team matchmaking is to be implemented soon.
Also, teamplay is now crucial for the victory and even with basic loadout you can do pretty messy things. But forget about one single overpowered ship. Good combination can beat anything, solo ships are sentenced to be easily neutralized.
I recommend this for everyone, who had ever desired to command his own ship and lead it to a furious battle.
Note, that this is an Early Access Game. Be ready for bugs and features in development, creators are eager to discuss and implement it in patches. If you are not willing to contribute in developing the game, better wait for full release.

Remeber  StarTrek: Generations? Kirk keeps giving suggestions to the new Captain about how to rescue the stranded vessels, but major components won't be installed until Tuesday......this is a lot like that. Still, I've enjoyed the game enough I thought I should write a short review of what you can expect so far.
The combat is great! Each ship varies in its armament, capabilities and how it's most effective. You can hop in a quick and agile frigate and dart in between asteroids and make quick hit runs against a slow moving Flagship or man a giant rail gun and smash ships all the way across the map. There is enough variety between the ships, that each offers its own experience.
Remember the 2009 Star Trek? When the Enterprise first encounters the mining vessel and♥♥♥♥♥♥really goes down? Phasers and torpedoes flying everywhere, pieces of hull flying off into space. That's what this game feels like. When you execute your strategy perfectly and unleash hell on your enemy, chewing away a good portion of his hull....Sweet Baby Jesus it's awesome.
The game play is great. I've not played DOTA, but I understand it's similar in objectives. There are a few key points you should try to cap, with the ultimate objective being the capture of your enemy's gate that leads to their home base. It's set up in a way that forces you to think tactically and you'll have to work as a team to push in strategic areas. As you collects key resource points, your ships get stronger and stronger, as they tier up.
Of course, there is a lot missing, but that comes with the territory of an Early Access game.

If you liked XCOM: Enemy Unknown / Enemy Within, you'll like XCOM 2. Classes have been changed significantly, there's a new tech path,  procedurally generated maps [save for some missions], and it just generally improves upon the formula of the first game. The only gripes I have are that it's still a bit buggy, but nothing game breaking has happened for me. I also kind of miss gene modding and MEC troopers from Enemy Within, but lore wise it makes sense why they're absent.
The game has an even stronger focus on tactics, I've found. Enemy units now play significantly into what soldiers you'll want to bring, so no more squad of 6 flying snipers all with scopes. You have to actually plan for what you'll encounter. Sectopod? Bring EMP grenades/bombs, or bluescreen/armor piercing rounds. Vipers? Better keep your squad close together. Etc.
Overall I love this game even more than I did the first one (and I played the hell out of the first one). Highly recommend if you enjoyed XCOM 1.

XCOM2 is a solid turn-based strategy game, and I really wish I could give it a full recommendation. However, as it currently stands there are a number of glaring issues with the game that need to be addressed before I can do so.
1.) The game is a poorly optimized buggy mess.
Frame rates are wildly inconsistent, and character animations are hilariously buggy (falling through the ground, breaking already-shattered windows, guns firing while on the back of the soldier, teleporting to another part of the map while being strangled by a viper ect...). The kill-cam is arguably even more buggy now than in XCOM: Enemy Unknown, especially when using abilities that initiate multiple attacks at once.
2.) The UI is genuinely awful.
Fraxis chose a concise and "stylish" look for all the important information in the game at the cost of the players. Damage estimates always show the highest possible outcome causing players to make poor attacks, what constitutes as flanking is completely unclear and not apparent before making a move, soldier skills are not viewable in the deployment menu,  the difference between "one-time" projects and "for all soldiers forever" projects in the workshop are not made clear, and information regarding the aliens outside of their health on the battlefield is never viewable by the player (what does "battle frenzy" even do?). No wonder many of the most popular mods are simply UI fixes.
3.) Gameplay is enjoyable, but suffers from some minor issues.
For the most part, the gameplay is enjoyable. If you liked the previous XCOM's gameplay, you will like XCOM2's gameplay. However, it carries with it the same problems of its predecessor. Firing angles are still bizarre and unclear; sometimes you can shoot through walls, other times your soldier cannot fire at an enemy clearly within range/view. Difficulty remains wildly inconsistent, with the early game being challenging, the mid-game unbearablely hard, and the end game being a bit too easy.
The most controversial new gameplay decision is the addition of various turn timers to most of the missions. Whether you would like this or not really depends on how you play the game. If you like slow and methodical gameplay, you will probably hate it. Thankfully, not all missions are timed, so you still have some diversity in playstyle.
In conclusion: unless you are a huge XCOM: Enemy Unknown fan, wait for a sale before buying this game. Right now it is an unpolished product that needs a lot of time and work before being worth full price.

Overall a very mediocre game. Graphics are decent, sounds boring, simplistic gameplay, painful control scheme.
Gameplay is overly simplistic with far less options than typical fps or moba style games. This is primarily left-click or right-click on a target to shoot and like 1 or 2 very uninspired special attacks. Capturing stations is simply a matter of flying near them as they are all completely undefended. The level up system is also rather simplistic and yields little more than bonus hps and damage. Loadouts are also uninspired with weapon options having little more variety than for example average laser, laser that shoots fast and does lless damage and big laser that shoots slow and does extra damage; nothing that really affects your gameplay in an substantial way.
Ships are surprisingly weak for a game that bills itself on capital ship duels which tends to make the game feel very fps-ish. Many battles are over in just a few shots. Many movie/tv battle sequences last longer and they are paying like $1M a minute for cgi. This might be ok for if it was a fighter sim but feels totally wrong in a capital ship context. Also, the respawn timers are far too long making for too much idling. Ship balance is also very poor for an early access game that has been out this long. The support type ships seem generally unplayed and unuseful.
Immersion is very poor due to virtually no consistency in the styling of the various ships. They all look decent but there is little stylistic consistancy like they were just ripped at random from
or someting. Many of the battles take place at ranges where its difficult to even make out the appearance of the ships so you feel like you are mostly just attacking hitboxes.
Currently, in Early Access there is only 1 map and once again it is a very uninspired symetrical 2-lane map.
The only victory condition is to cap your opponents home base. Unfortunately, they made a very dubious design decision in that there is no way to decap your home base meaning that rushing the enemy base is a pretty easy win especially with the short cap time needed and really long respawn timers. Its not unusual to see matches end after simply 1 or 2 clashes not much room for strategy or comebacks.
Hopefully the game gets better - there is certainly some potential here.

Great RPG and dungeon crawler that is presented in side-scrolling fashion, with a unique art style that is held intact consistently throughout the entire game and everything you come across.
The game provides a rather simple set of rules and presents its content mostly in a randomly generated way. While in most randomly generated games this is the quick recipe for mindless grind and a low skill cap, with Darkest Dungeon the random elements serve to provide a chilling and almost fear-inducing, hopeless vibe to your dungeon adventures.
Darkest Dungeon is built on the idea that dungeon delving is a stressful, painful and not-so-glorious quest for inevitable doom, with perhaps some riches if you get really lucky along the way. Only if you get that into your head and act accordingly, will you have a successful progression through the game. And even with the utmost care in resource management, party setup and a step-by-step dungeon crawling approach, you will find yourself in many a situation where you will want to cut losses and run away in fear. Darkest Dungeon plays with that emotional struggle within you.
This game allows you to get really attached to your party members as you hone their skills, upgrade their weapons and level them up. At times, it even seems like you've found the cure-all, kill-all party make up, so you get a bit overzealous, and think 'Let's do this one last room, surely there's a treasure box I can still snag before going back to camp' and you end up with three permanently dead and number four heavily traumatized and bleeding.
Any player who goes into Darkest Dungeon comparing it to any of their previous dungeon grinds, thinking 'I'll do this quickly now, I'll grind to max level and destroy this content' will be rating this game Not Recommended. It's the wrong mindset. What you need to play Darkest Dungeon? You need balls, you need wit, you need to plan two or three runs ahead of your progression, and you need to grasp every little mechanic in all its glorious perfection.
Ladies and gents, this is proper, clever game design with a véry cruel twist. Come prepared, and discover an infinitely replayable game full of emotional and memorable moments. The only question is how long it will take before you finally surrender to desperation and uninstall. As with many games, this game is not about the end goal, but the road towards that goal.

XCOM2 brings a lot of new wrinkles to the formula laid down by XCOM:EU. It retains an art style that is somewhere between cartoon and realistic but manages to pack in more detail than the previous XCOM game.
The game play is fresh and yet familiar with new twists and a level of tension that could be lacking on the easier difficulty settings of EU.
Overall XCOM2 is a great game but still feels very familiar to XCOM:EU. That is both it's best and worst quality. On one hand it is a still a thrilling TBS and one that left me deeply satisfied. On the other hand in many ways I felt like in many ways it was too similar to EU while in others it had complicated systems that didn't need to be tweaked.
This is all nitpicking for what really is a fantastic game. I'll definitely be putting many more hours into it.

If you're a fan of the XCOM series this game certainly has a lot to commend it. I found the balance of familarity and new elements to be just right and the plot line was good enough to keep me engaged. I read a lot about bugs and crashes and I played the game all the way through without experiencing either so I can't comment to how pervasive those problems are.
I liked the new base format but felt there was just way too little to do. Most of the time my engineers and scientists just sat idle while the grunts did all the work.My main gripe though was that it was just too easy and too quick.
I initially thought I was struggling against the aliens, especially when I blew all of my intel on the black market before understanding it's importance. I played without any reloads and lost a far share of troops (I believe the end of game stats showed 17 killed) including my first two Captains to the same grenade. I saw the steady increase in the Avatar project and I hadn't made contact with more than three continents so it all looked pretty helpless. Then suddenly I find that I'm at the end game and the final two missions were a walk in the park. I kept expecting the game to put me back in my place but I finished the final mission with only one soldier wounded. 30 hours total gameplay (including tutorial, cut scenes, snack breaks etc) seemed very quick when compared to the 80+ hours I invested in XCOM. I was just left feeling that there should have been more and it should have been harder. There was no real sense of satisfaction in finishing the game as it came so easy.
I'm sure I'll play again on the highest difficulty setting once some DLC is released but right now I think I'll fire up the original XCOM again and see whether it lasts as long the second time around.
Having said all of that I have to recommend this game. If you're a fan of the series, you'll like it and if you're new to the series then start with XCOM (and all the DLCs) and then jump straight in to this. Even with the relatively short play time and challenge it's still worth every penny.

First Look/Impressions - Fractured Space
Me and moba like games such as LOL and Dota have a long storied history. I play them for a bit, get frustrated at peoples inability to read a minimap and eventually get obliterated by some out of control hypercarry(Tryndamere...).
Not only do those games have a massive learning curve, they also have mechanics that are a bit out of date, the games power snowball too early on(LOL) or theres so much gear combinatiosn that you need  months of study to pick what item when.
So my general experience has been avoid them like they have Ebola, I don't like them and in turn people that play them typically don't like me.
That's not been the case with Fractured Space, at least not in the 20+ games I have played so far. Before I go any further I must warn that this is early Alpha and it still has a chance to turn into a bucket of dolphin♥♥♥♥♥♥later on, but for now I'm actually enjoying myself with the game (I know, angry bitter me enjoying a moba? And no this isn't a evil double doing this post).
I won't touch much on the graphical fidelity of the game or the sound assets much since it is just an early alpha, but for what's there, it's all rather good looking(for alpha).
That just leaves the gameplay and balance. Each ships has it's own role and from what I can tell the game seems to run on a rock paper scissors-ish kind of system. A fine example of this is Flagships get tyranasourousrekt by snipers, but snipers get rektified by smart frigates and assasins.
From what i can tell, the weakest ship class in game is the flagship by far. It is a monster to deal with close range for both the hunter and enforcer classes, but even alone the flagship doesn't really hardcounter anything. Frigates and corvetes are too fast to be threatened by it and will typically run away unless they have the power of numbers and hunters/enforcers CAN kill them 1v1 if they use their blinks properly.
There are balance issues at this early stage. Both the flagship and disruptor feel rather weak compared to hunters, enforcers, frigates and assasins. Hopefully that will be fixed.
Gameplay wise, it's a blast to play. winninga  fight you had no business winning is always exilerating and getting away with crap you shouldn't have(like the video) is also fun. Each ship uses different tactics to win each engagement in terms of 1v1. Smaller faster ships can use hit and run tactics to whittle down a stronger enemys (corvettes, frigates and assasins).
While the larger ships, if they catch you alone without support or in a  team fight can absolutely obliterate you. The game really comes together in team fights however. I had a team of 2 frigates, 1 enforcer, 1 hunter and a corvette ship entirtely destroy a team with superior upgrades that consisted of 2 flagships, 1 sniper and 2 hunters.
The frigates used shields to keep the fire of the forward gunships while we chased down and killed all the flagships support. Frigates dived behind rocks for repairs while me and the enforcer alpha damaged the underside of a flagship, the enforcer blinking around like a madman to avoid big guns.
We eventually both died, only managing to seriously injure 1 flagship and destroy the other. The frigates did good cleanup work with corvette support and managed to cap 1 entire lane and most of the next one(as well as the gas station).
I want to go into deeper detail about the resource system in game, but it's still being tweaked right now and has undergone many changes. I will say this about it; getting snowballed is very, very rare.
I think the biggest attrataction to this game is that there isn't as much non-sense management. No boring cookie cutter rune pages, no gear management, no farming creeps or trying to block creeps. It's just you, your team coposition and how you position yourself that ultimately determines the winner.
I'll go into more detail once the game releases, but for now I'll just sit back and enjoy the game and pray it doesn't turn into another LOL.﻿

First Look/Impressions - Fractured Space
Me and moba like games such as LOL and Dota have a long storied history. I play them for a bit, get frustrated at peoples inability to read a minimap and eventually get obliterated by some out of control hypercarry(Tryndamere...).
Not only do those games have a massive learning curve, they also have mechanics that are a bit out of date, the games power snowball too early on(LOL) or theres so much gear combinatiosn that you need  months of study to pick what item when.
So my general experience has been avoid them like they have Ebola, I don't like them and in turn people that play them typically don't like me.
That's not been the case with Fractured Space, at least not in the 20+ games I have played so far. Before I go any further I must warn that this is early Alpha and it still has a chance to turn into a bucket of dolphin♥♥♥♥♥♥later on, but for now I'm actually enjoying myself with the game (I know, angry bitter me enjoying a moba? And no this isn't a evil double doing this post).
I won't touch much on the graphical fidelity of the game or the sound assets much since it is just an early alpha, but for what's there, it's all rather good looking(for alpha).
That just leaves the gameplay and balance. Each ships has it's own role and from what I can tell the game seems to run on a rock paper scissors-ish kind of system. A fine example of this is Flagships get tyranasourousrekt by snipers, but snipers get rektified by smart frigates and assasins.
From what i can tell, the weakest ship class in game is the flagship by far. It is a monster to deal with close range for both the hunter and enforcer classes, but even alone the flagship doesn't really hardcounter anything. Frigates and corvetes are too fast to be threatened by it and will typically run away unless they have the power of numbers and hunters/enforcers CAN kill them 1v1 if they use their blinks properly.
There are balance issues at this early stage. Both the flagship and disruptor feel rather weak compared to hunters, enforcers, frigates and assasins. Hopefully that will be fixed.
Gameplay wise, it's a blast to play. winninga  fight you had no business winning is always exilerating and getting away with crap you shouldn't have(like the video) is also fun. Each ship uses different tactics to win each engagement in terms of 1v1. Smaller faster ships can use hit and run tactics to whittle down a stronger enemys (corvettes, frigates and assasins).
While the larger ships, if they catch you alone without support or in a  team fight can absolutely obliterate you. The game really comes together in team fights however. I had a team of 2 frigates, 1 enforcer, 1 hunter and a corvette ship entirtely destroy a team with superior upgrades that consisted of 2 flagships, 1 sniper and 2 hunters.
The frigates used shields to keep the fire of the forward gunships while we chased down and killed all the flagships support. Frigates dived behind rocks for repairs while me and the enforcer alpha damaged the underside of a flagship, the enforcer blinking around like a madman to avoid big guns.
We eventually both died, only managing to seriously injure 1 flagship and destroy the other. The frigates did good cleanup work with corvette support and managed to cap 1 entire lane and most of the next one(as well as the gas station).
I want to go into deeper detail about the resource system in game, but it's still being tweaked right now and has undergone many changes. I will say this about it; getting snowballed is very, very rare.
I think the biggest attrataction to this game is that there isn't as much non-sense management. No boring cookie cutter rune pages, no gear management, no farming creeps or trying to block creeps. It's just you, your team coposition and how you position yourself that ultimately determines the winner.
I'll go into more detail once the game releases, but for now I'll just sit back and enjoy the game and pray it doesn't turn into another LOL.﻿

ALPHA REVIEW:
First off, if you're thinking of getting this game, please understand that it is, at its core, a MOBA. (Think LoL in space.) It is however, a very unique MOBA; it is very different from say, LoL or DOTA, and it's not just because it's in space.
Right now, there are not very many ships to choose from, but this is likely to change as the game develops. "Creeps" or "minions" are replaced by stations that have to be captured and "towers" are replaced by simple damage taken when you're in range of the enemy base. Upgrades, as of now, consist only of gathering resources from captured stations and gaining a universal upgrade every level gained. This will probably be changed to specific upgrades later. The middle fuel station buff is extremely helpful, so get that when you can. Warping in a fight is dangerous as it leaves you extremely vulnurable to damage. Choose the right time to warp. Teamwork is essential to victory, and this is tied to having a team with balanced ship types. A well coordinated attack can completely turn the tide of a game and to that end, use the warp paths wisely. Controls may seem sluggish or sticky, but this is mostly due to ship stats. This brings up the important point, know your ship! The strengths and weaknesses of each ship are made very clear after a few games. Knowing the capabilities of each ship during a fight can make the difference between wiping the enemy team and a 60 second respawn.
The game asks a lot from your computer on the performance end. Lag is also a pretty big problem right now. Connecting to the servers is always a gamble and crashes happen quite frequently. These things are likely to be fixed in time
The game is still in alpha, so don't expect this to be anything close to the final product. A lot of what I consider cons will likely change later on.
TL;DR Pros-Cons
Pros:
+Solid gameplay
+Clear strengths and weaknesses between ships and loadouts
+Teamwork a must
+Great, detailed ship graphics(Alpha)
+/- No way to cancel warp jumps (Alpha?)
Cons:
-High computer performance demand
-Crashes 1/5 times (Alpha)
-Few ship choices (Alpha)
-Disconnect/can't connect to server 1/5 times (Alpha)

One of the coolest things about the game is that there is now mod support so if you want your units to run around with a Stormtrooper or Boba Fett helmet you can. Overall if you liked the first game and are thirsting for more alien killing action get this game.
