I have always loved Star Wars, Star Trek, Gundams, and so on. I love the enormous fleet battles. I love it when the Millenium Falcon trades fire with a star destroyer. I thrilled to the final episodes of Gurren Lagann. Legend of the Galactic Heroes is in my backlog. I've become jaundiced with dota-likes, MOBAS, ASFAGGTS, whatever you want to call them, but I do enjoy them-over a thousand hours of Dota logged should attest to just how receptive I am to that kind of game. So, it seemed initially that Fractured Space could be a great game for me, as I've been on a gradually intensifying Sci-Fi kick for three months.
So, after convincing my buddy to buy it so I have somebody to play with, I discover that I have purchased a game with cumbersome controls (you must use both WASD -and- the arrow keys to navigate your ship), nonsensical balance, the skeleton of the worst, most flamboyantly avaricious sort of pay/grind-to-win microtransaction content restriction system conceivable, one map, which is boring and virtually empty, a matchmaking system combining all of the worst elements of automated matchmaking and room-based matchmaking (To elaborate: the game automatically maintains some twenty or so games which players can join at any time, even after a game begins. It is possible for a game to start with only four ships and then fill to a full house of five on five. The problem with this is that you can't play together with friends, because the team picker will automatically sort you onto different teams, or avoid playing with the people who have ten to a hundred more hours of gameplay logged than you do.) and no strategy whatsoever. The only meaningful choice the player has is their choice of ship, which they determine before joining the game. Because there is no way (that I found, anyway) to see what ships are already in the game, or even which side you would be placed on if you joined the game, from the outside, it is entirely possible to wind up with a team consisting of three snipers, one hunter and a frigate. There is no way to change your ship once you are in the game, either, so enjoy being the fourth flagship on a team. Despite the fact that the game is constructed in such a way that a player leaving should not be a big issue as long as somebody else joins the game promptly after, there is still an anti-leaver honor system, which I suppose is a good thing, although a player disconnecting or connecting is not nearly as disruptive as in games like Dota.
In-game, teams squabble over little starbases that provide money to the team that captures them, and block incoming fire. When some threshold of money is passed, a team gains access to upgrades for their ship, provided when they return to a friendly starbase. Every five minutes or so a large starbase in a central sector activates and can be fought over and captured for a temporary bonus. What this bonus might actually do is not particularly clear. Because the upgrades are just a generic boost to a ships' capabilities, there can be no strategic decisions in how you choose to upgrade a ship, and no way to do any of the planning, reacting, and improvising that makes space battles in shows entertaining. Just go capture the bases and fight the ships, which you will do in pretty much the same way every game.
The majority of the actual gameplay is at least based around flying a big spaceship and shooting at other spaceships. This turns out to be much less fun than it sounds like it ought to be, with enormous swathes of mostly empty airspace through which ships ponderously glide with all the handling and finess of a crippled whale, their players holding the mouse over each other's ships with the mouse buttons held down, occasionally striking a number key. There's not really a sense of immediacy, for all the flashing lights, obnoxious klaxons, and noisy lasers, the last of which I wouldn't comment on if it weren't for the fact that the ships look like they're trying to look realistic. It's very slow and boring. For some reason the devs thought it would improve my gaming experience to have a recording of a british woman scold or mock me every time I die. No option to turn this "feature" off.
All customization is done blind, outside of a battle. This means that if your ship's loadout turns out to be poorly chosen that's just too bad, enjoy waiting for the game to end so you can change weapons. Additionally, most of the options are locked. Some of these are probably not implemented at the time of this review, which is fine and what I expect in an alpha, but the screen design seems to imply that players will have to grind or pay to unlock this content in the future. Already something like a third of the ships require in-game currency grinding to buy. Even this would not all be so worrying if not for the fact that many of the loadout options seem to merely be tiered upgrades, with the newer, higher-ranked item always outperforming the lower. I will forever maintain that grinding for an advantage in a game built around match-based pvp is an abomination.
The visuals are all rendered very lavishly if you happen to be running a powerful enough computer to support high graphics settings and maintain a good framerate. Unfortunately there isn't any reason to do so, since the ships are all built on a hard science fiction aesthetic and therefore aren't all that interesting to look at, and the map is an asteroid field. The game is amply supplied with what I can only describe as spectacle, with an abundance of prety lights and  two teams of half a dozen crewmembers, all individually voiced and waiting to tell you things you already knew. All of them have a glimmer of personality in some of the flavor quotes accessed from the hub menu only, but that doesn't matter in game, since everything they say in the actual game is terse and to-the-point, which is appropriate for the situation, I suppose, but when your "setting" consists of three generic shipbuilder names and a dozen portraits hooked up to sound bites, it's certainly not adding any extra entertainment.
2/10, I have to concede that this is at least a game.

GameSpot said it best: "Age of Empires III has some very big shoes to fill".
It is a very good game, and there are barely any real flaws to speak of, but I still prefer its predecessor, even though almost everything that was good about
is improved here, most noticeably the A.I. and the graphics.
Perhaps the historical era covered by the game and its heavy focus on gunpowder in later stages isn't as compelling, and the scenario editor (which played a big part in
's prolonged success) is a little more complicated to use.
But the core gameplay, which is easy to understand, but hard to master, remains pretty much the same, with some interesting additions like the "Capital City" and the ability to choose different bonuses as you advance through the ages, a similar system to the one seen in
.
If you're a fan of the "
" series or you just enjoy well-designed, polished real-time strategy games, or are looking to get into the genre,
is definitely worthy of your time and money.

It is inescusable how unpolished and buggy this game is now and has been since it launched. It is utter garbage how terribly optimized this game is. The bugs, the crashing, the god damned everything about it that is so ♥♥♥♥ing awful despite struggling, trying so hard to get things to stabilize and play better. It's so god awful that you almost need to download player made fixes. It's so bad that there are even sections of the final level, yes final level mind you, where things are so bugged out that it's possible to have unskippable cutscenes play multiple times, not be able to shoot grenades anywhere and even have the final boss die to a bug (YOU HEARD RIGHT).
WITH ALL THAT SAID.
When the bugs are fixed and when the game is actually polished then yes I recommend it, but make sure you understand that I am only recommending this to you 'when that happens'.
Now that I have that out of the way, the game is quite good mechanically, barring a few silly things such as units barreling through walls or breaking the ladder they are climbing on and then falling. I think they did a good thing emphasizing modding so much as it's good for the community as a whole. Maybe too much which would explain their lack of fixing the game up.
I found the game itself to be pretty damn nice. Again the mechanics all work well, the main plot of the game is fairly interesting (up until the ending which in my opinion was mediocre). I liked moving around the globe and I loved combat, loved building up my force as always and the character customization is pretty good (though pretty sparse without mods).
Overall the game is actually decent, but really doesn't do much that xcom didn't. It just sorta refines the forumla a good bit and fixes some issues the first game had.
I do have quite a few complaints about the overall functionality, like the number of turns you get on timed missions, the sheer volume of timed missions and the generally annoying avatar project looming off in the distance. While I thought the avatar project thing was going to be something where I was slowly being pushed towards the end inexoribly, it actually turns out to literally be a 'how you lose the game' counter and the big reason that's super lame is because it doesn't loom so much later down the line as it pokes at you to move forward. It becomes annoying more than threatening like having a ghost in your house, but all he does is spoil movies for you or other stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥and you just can't get rid of him until you put together the pieces surrounding his death and help him to move on.
And whether you want to admit it or not, there are TONS of bugs and some of them are almost gamebreaking. Not only that but I turned my graphics to the lowest I could and the game ♥♥♥♥ing soaks up my god damned ram to the point that it causes other programs crash as well. It crashes on menu navigation. It crashes on mission loading. It crashes when I pull up the global interface. IT CRASHED WHEN I WAS WATCHING THE FINAL CUTSCENE I♥♥♥♥♥♥YOU NOT.
At first I was pretty down with the 'you lost the war' until I realized it was a lame excuse to stay on earth.
In the end I think this will be the last xcom I buy, unless they proceed forward into outer space or do something drastic to make the game generally cooler. Fights on space ships you own? Yes please. Own multiple space ships and colonies? yes. Why isn't this game moving in that direction? It really felt like I was going somewhere special in this game only to snag on an invisible string and realize that the depth of the pond isn't nearly as deep because I've got strings attached to me.
TL;DR - I feel frustrated with the game overall because I am really upset that I have to not recommend this game! It is just not good enough of a game to recommend in it's current state. I will change the review to positive when the game is polished because overall it's a damn good game. Bug fixes and optimizations are neccessary for this game to be worth the price. Save your money until it's polished or on a pretty big sale.

A game that is so painfully hard to grasp and after around 40 hours of gameplay I could say that this game is a well-polished turn-based RPG that stresses careful strategizing, planning and tactics for you to become successful. Even at higher levels, your heroes could die so easily if you become careless, and each move you make should always be thought hard on.
For the characters, there's a deep pool of characters that you could choose from to make your party of 4. As of the moment, there are 15 classes to choose from. The base stats and skill pool of each class is the same for every character for that class. What sets them apart are their character traits, called "quirks", which may be positive (Increased damage versus certain kind of enemies) or negative (some characters are kleptomaniacs). The fact that each hero can have up to 8 skills in his pool with 4 skills being active at a time allows for some specialization and flexibility on how you could form your party. Party-building is a very important part of the game as it is important to play on the synergy of the classes to be able to survive. Some characters are inherently weak when working alone, but when paired with the right party, they make up for their frailty by offering lots of bonuses for their teammates.
The design part of the game, aesthetically, is fantastic. The artwork fits the mood and the theme quite well, and the designs of the monsters, the characters, the items, the dungeons and the bosses are wonderfully dark and gloomy. Tremendous amount of attention to detail might make up to the fact that the only customization to the looks of your heroes available is a simple color palette change and name change.
Story-wise, the plot is presented slowly to you through excerpts in your ancestor's journal. If you're looking for a very deep story, with complex and relatable characters, you won't find them here. But the lore itself is rich in its own way, and whatever it lacks in depth, it makes up in cohesiveness and design.
The soundtrack also fits the game well, with a very sombre theme while in town and a very foreboding theme inside the dungeons.
Gameplay-wise, the game is split into three parts: Combat, Exploration, and Preparation. Combat is turn-based 4v4 that goes the way of traditional RPGs. Each character is placed in one of four tiles, and their positioning affects the effectiveness, range and skill availability. Some skills will only be usable on some tiles, for example, while some skills can only hit certain tiles. A lot of the game's calculations use RNG, so if uncertainty frustrates you, this game will certainly will too.
Exploration sends your party on the dungeon to accomplish quests. The quests are simply made, which could range from simply exploring most of the rooms in the dungeon, or to defeat a certain enemy on the map, or to activate a number of curious laid out in the dungeon. The dungeons are always randomly generated as you enter them, and are separated into rooms and hallways. One party would move from room to room and traverse hallways set with traps, curious and random encounters. There is a chance that your party would be able to scout ahead to tell you what lies in the next room or corridor, but most of the time you will have to stay on your toes for any surprises.
Finally, preparation tasks you to take care of your party outside of combat in the form of a simple town management and supply management system. The town management part has you developing the hamlet where the party stays when they're not exploring, where they could use various town amenities to relieve stress or to cure the diseases and to treat the quirks they receive inside the dungeon. You can also upgrade the weapons, armor, skills and even buy new equipment called trinkets that do various stat changes to your heroes. You may also recruit more heroes if you find your roster lacking. As for developing the town, you pay for the development through items you find in the dungeon called "heirlooms". Trading the heirlooms in to make your town more caring will be pivotal to exploring the dungeon completely. Then before entering the dungeon, you will be asked to choose four heroes from your roster, then asked to purchase supplies that they will take with them, such as food, bandages, antitoxins, holy waters and most importantly, torches. Torches are used to give the party light while exploring, which also affects a number of gameplay elements such as stress.
Stress is a very pivotal part of the game, and it acts as a sort of secondary life bar to your units. Aside from keeping in mind not to get them killed physically, you also have to keep everyone sane. This extra depth to your characters allows for increased challenge to the game. It's also actually great to see a cool mechanic such as this - where else do you see characters losing their minds from fighting horrors? You don't usually see that as a game mechanic, although it is indeed very sensible to think that people would lose their minds being exposed to these kinds of Lovecraftian creatures. Which I think really captures the heart of Lovecraftian literature, where the horror is as much as in the mind as it is in the flesh.
Overall, I really love the game and would buy it in full price. I got it on a sale and I wish I could spend more money on the game to show my support to the developers. So far, they have made updates that add so much to the game and yet they make them available to all owners for free. An upcoming expansion/DLC is coming up, and given their performance in updates, I'm thrilled on how much content they'll be releasing for the expansion/DLC. Grab the game this coming Steam Holiday Sale and then grab the DLC once it gets released this January.
TO SUMMARIZE: If you like traditional RPGs, Lovecraftian Horror, a decent challenge, and learning the ropes as you progress the game, get this. However, be warned that the game's mechanics are complex but not at all very deep, and that the story is rich but is very shallow.

XCOM2 does a lot of things right. It smoothes a lot of the rough edges of the first game, and there is no doubt it is fun to play. As turn based tactical games go, it doesn't have a whole lot of competition, but it is still objectively a very well-crafted gaming experience presuming you enjoy this genre.
Base-building is much more streamlined (you're not going to reach turn 150 and realize you fatally misplaced three rooms 100 turns ago); character management is simpler; and the combat interface while it has a few irritations remains very solid. Graphically also it is very pretty.
So as a tactical game there is a lot to recommend it. I'd say it is definitely best-in-class.
Having said that it does have some limitations. Here are a few that bugged me in particular.
First of all, although it ran smoothly enough on my machine, it does (as did XCOM1) have weird pauses at some points. No doubt important things are happening in the background, but it is weird when the game decides to wander off and make a coffee in the middle of a combat move. Load times are also a little on the long side, but I can live with that.
Second, the story is pretty terrible. The climax is very flat, in particular - you don't get the feeling of having achieved anything in particular. Now, you couldn't say the story was especially affecting in XCOM1 either; but for me at least the end of the story did pack some emotional impact. XCOM2 was all the way very meh. To be honest most of the time I just ignored the story portions as they didn't affect the game and were mostly technobabble of one sort or another. I realize XCOM2 is not an RPG but even so, I feel like they could have thrown a little more money at the script-writing dept.
Third, I felt like the game was a little on the easy side. Now I say this with some caution, as after all I am now used to playing Long War XCOM1 which is it's own experience; and having played so much XCOM1 I am much more careful and deliberate with my play in XCOM2 than a first-timer would be. Even factoring this in however the game did not take so long to finish. And more than this, I didn't feel like there was much variation in the way the game played out. In XCOM1 when you discovered a new enemy not only was it stronger, it had a range of abilities which mandated a change in strategy. I didn't really experience that in XCOM2. Although again, perhaps this is simply a reflection of the fact that I have played XCOM1 so/too much.
So my summary point really is that it is a very successful game and polishes XCOM1 nicely; but it isn't a substantially different gaming experience. My advice for XCOM3 would be to work a little more at the plot and narrative that you are building around the maps.

From what I've played so far, I am quite impressed. it's worth pointing out that this is in Alpha, so a lot of features are missing, but I'll update my review as the game evolves. For now, let's focus on what is actually there.
Pros:
+ Capitol ships are huge, and insanely fun to pilot
+ Great effects for a game at this stage
+ Great core gameplay
+ The reward; nothing beats the feeling of single handedly anihilating a Flagship closing on your base in your teeny-tiny little Frigate
+ Each ship works differently, and has very clear strengths and weaknesses
+ The fact that you can use 3 dimensions in each sector (similar to lanes) makes tactical manouvres far mor rewarding.
+ Spaaaaaaaace
Cons:
- Servers range from "tolerable" to "how did I get here, exactly?" levels of lag
- Only one map/skybox
- Some issues with mouse tracking, especially in Sniper Mode
- Hiding behind asteroids at the far end of a sector you just jumped to because the opposite end has two Snipers decimating your team way out of range of your weaponry
- Some movement controls seem to get lost, like when turning right I sometimes stop accelerating deespite holding W down firmly
- Textures are a bit... "conservative" as of now. Everything looks kinda like Lego
- Some ships/upgrades are locked (assumed to be added in updates)
- Level/XP/Credits mean nothing/have no use as of yet
- Minimap takes a bit of getting used to
- No description of weapons/abilities (I moved my Frigate from Kingfisher Missles to a SKUA Torpedo and had literally no clue what it did. Still don't. Moved back to KF's since I could actually see those.)
- Snipers. A well-placed pair of Snipers will wreck you. The damage:range ratio is through the roof, and they still have more health than some other close range attack craft
- The Assassin follows the issue I said above, with lower health than the Sniper and a lower damage output. Surely the point of an assassin would be to get in ASAP,
, and jump to a safe distance?
- No smaller AI enemies (not sure if this is planned or not)
- Fleet "upgrades" are poorly explained in game (I saw my health go up once, but I have no idea about other parameters/buffs)
That's everything so far.
Yes, there are issues, but what you get as of this moment is a well put-together, fairly barebones 5v5 experience where you fly giant capitol ships through space and into other ships, where you shoot them with your cool weapons, with one of you inevitably being reduced to a really cool heap of smoldering wreckage. Enjoy!

XCOM 2 follows it's predecessor in many ways.  Too many ways, in my opinion.  The best upgrade in the game is the Strategic Map and Base Building aspects. There are always many choices to make and you can agonize over picking the correct one for what you intend to do on harder difficulties. The enemy abilities and AI are much expanded from previous games, and the concealment factor is a fun new improvement. Setting up ambushes are a great deal of fun.
What detracts from this game is that they played it safe. I expected a game that had you scrounging for equipment and resources in true guerilla style warfare, but in the end you just follow the first XCOM reboot's system of research and facility building. In the tactical combat, the same old 'find a pack of enemies and dispatch them' is the exact same as the first in just about every mission.  It's rare to get ambushed yourself unless you are playing poorly, and objectives are rather easy to complete with a skilled hacker. In the first XCOM games there were solo enemies hiding, groups of enemies, and you never knew what to expect on any given map. This is not the case in XCOM2.
I hope that in a future expansion, the RPG inventory system where you can create your own style of class through gearing up your squad makes a return, and isn't completely overwhelmed by the skill trees.  Want to make a ranger?  Find a soldier with high mobility and give them a sword and shotgun. Want a heavy soldier? Give him heavy armor and a much greater assortment of weapons with their own pros and cons rather than the new tradition of '2 upgrades of the same weapon that hit harder and look slightly different'.
This is definitely a dumbed down/streamlined version of XCOM and while it's incredibly fun, it's very little short of 'babies first tactical squad game'. It's the Civilization: Revolutions of the Civiliation games.
More ability to customize characters beyond straight upgrades would be a great deal of fun. Classes and skills can be kept in, but not as the pinnacle of tactical choice. If you combine weaker skills with a great deal of inventory management you will have a deeper system with much more ways to make each soldier different and memorable.
When compared to the XCOM reboot, this is a straight upgrade.  When compared to XCOM reboot + Long War, this is a game that needs another Long War mod in order to get this game into excellent status.  If you don't want to add a true inventory system, at least give us more classes to play as. Playable MEC's in XCOM: Enemy Within was a step in the right direction if you think sales will take a drastic hit if you make this game more complex.  Long War would bring this game to excellent status.
Each new game of XCOM2 feels exactly the same as a previous game. So what if some maps are randomized? Cover is always available and there is very little reason not to build 'optimal' builds for your classes, rather than interesting new builds by using inventory to modify and specialize a soldier.
When compared to old XCOM: 5/10.  When compared to new XCOM: 8/10. This is not the game I expected it to be.
It is recommended as an entry point into tactical strategy games.

While still a good game, there is a LOT wrong with Xcom 2.  I had to put my graphical settings to "paper and cardboard cut-outs" option just to keep the game from crashing on the main menu.  Even then, gameplay flows like a river of magnets and a super-glue covered sloth could pour 5 gallons of molasses by the time a mission gets around to loading.
The menu navigation is slow and laggy, and it takes around nine years for the aliens to look up from their hideous torture of God's beatiful creatures and realize it's their turn to move.  Doing ANYTHING (building, researching, training, healing, and most importantly, SCANNING) is impossible without being interrupted by a flood of urgent missions.  SERIOUSLY!  I had up to five missions come in in less than three in-game days!  Most scans take at least 4 days (I think), and scans are required to get ANY currency, even supplies given to you by the council.
Much like the first game, playing a mission through without save-scumming is like trying to get a seven-ten split after undergoing a quadruple amputation and a botched lobotomy.  That being said, there are mods that speed up menu navigation and other side-effects of poor optimization, and despite everything wrong with this game, I've still played WAYY too much of it, so it's doing something right.  So basically, if you liked Xcom UE or just have an extra bit of money laying around, definitely get this game.

Realm of the mad god is a nice little 2D MMO game to play with friends.
The game can be seen as a pay to win type, mainly because dying in this game is fatal, as you lose everything when you die. The game tries to divide its "Realm" into difficulty levels so players can stay where they will not be killed easily, however there is a large gap between players who have maxed stats and the best items and those who have just started out, its the combination of these major factors and others that tempt players to spend money into overpriced in-game items.
The only things I recommend buying (if you do plan to spend money) are for character slots vaults and maybe feed for your pet. The game also features its own trading system, though even if you are careful you still can be scammed, personally I feel its terrible, but to help traders out there have a look at "RealmEye" the tf2outpost/ebay of Realm.
If you have a bunch of friends who will play the game with you, a lot of patience, do not mind pixel art, willing to spend some money on the game and plan on playing this game in the long term (to get to that dream 8/8 stats) then I would recommend this game for you!
EDIT: All the time you spend into strengthening your character can all disappear, thanks to a little mistake, or simply lag. The creators of the game have also conveniently made the game very "pay to win", so when you do die, you can easily be forced into spending money.

I would really like to be able to promote this game, but I can't. If it was about 2+ years ago I could, but that is not the case.
First thing, do not be mislead by my amount of hours played. I started SK before it was brought to Steam, and refused to link my main account to my Steam account due to perpetual connectivity issues between the two. I have more hours logged on SK than I have on Terraria and Mincraft combined.
They have changed the tutorial area from when I started, it is admittedly much better now. Has a minor storyline and teaches you how to use your various abilities. The game is much more approachable for newbies. Which is a definite plus. The removal of the energy system to do levels also means that newbies aren't restricted to 10 floors at max before they have to quit for about 24 hours (or pay money). That is all definite pluses.
The issues start about mid-tier, or 3-star gear. 3-star fire crystals and alchemy orbs are incredibly hard to find. Too early and you get 2-star stuff, if you do the boss areas odds are you will get 4-star stuff... and you don't get the recipe to downgrade the 4-star fire crystals to 3-star until AFTER a mision that requires you to level up 3-star gear enough to be in full 4-star gear. This is a minor setback, the big setback is high tier equipment. You need 5-star alchemy orbs and fire crystals for that, and unlike earlier tiers you can not downgrade higher crystals to make them. To fully level a single piece of 5-star equipment is going to cost you 453 fire crystals... or about 50 runs of the boss mission. You have at minimum a shield, 2 weapons, armor, and helmet, at maximum 2 more weapons. So that is a minimum of 250 boss mission runs, or 350 at maximum. And that is just for your starting set of gear.
But they don't want you to grind all that... they want you to buy the crystals. 50 5-star fire crystals costs 700 energy (cash shop currency), which is about 10-12 runs of the boss mission I mentioned, converting in game currency to cash shop currency (via a player run market). AKA NOT CHEAP!
They introduced pets at one point, reworking the mineral system (which originally were used to help influence the dungeons and get you some easy currency as well) into a way to feed and level the pets. There are 3 color pets: red, purple, and yellow. There are 5 colored minerals... 2 of which, blue and green, have absolutely zero use.
There are floors that are just horribly annoying to do, too high difficulty for too little payout. They're nice to experience, but a lot of groups will actively avoid them, to the point of waiting at the elevator at the end of a floor for 10 minutes to avoid such bad floors. Some floors, are amazingly fun. A lot of people hate Candlestick Keep, where an immortal ghost chases you, but I find them fun. Arenas are a blast, along with various other areas. But in comparison you can get Treasure Vaults... which are junk ironically, Compounds that are full of minis and are incredibly annoying, or Fiend floors... which a lot of people despise.
The last constantly available boss was introduced well over 2 years ago. There are minor bosses you can fight once for daily missions, but actual bosses you can just decide to go fight there has not been a new one in ages. There has been more gear added, but it is mostly reskins of other weapons with stat changes. And its hard to level due to the incredibly annoying fire crystal system.
PVP is even worse, it is dominated by people that have quite literally dropped $100s into the game by now. They have the best gear possible, my gear is high end (and I can do fairly well against them) but their stuff puts mine to shame, for the casual player you are just going to get beaten into the ground repeatedly. In addition to that if you don't have accessory slots (cash shop only!) than you are going to be at an even bigger disadvantage as everybody runs with health booster accessories.
On a sadder note, the game is dying. It started when the chief developer left, and now various other devs have as well. At one point it was not uncommon to see a dozen instances of the town going. For one event my guild saw over 70 instances running. Now you are lucky to get 3, and none of them are showing as full.
I really, REALLY want to be able to recommend this game... but I can't, not anymore. I love the art style, it is unique and cute and colorful. I love the music, Candlestick Keep has incredibly creepy but whimsical sounding music, the Wildwoods has beautifully fitting music for how its designed. I greatly like the atmosphere of the game, especially some of the areas created during the game's prime. The Wildwoods look amazing, as much as I dislike Compounds they look fantastic, and the Void is nicely threatening. The combat is fairly balanced in PVE until you hit high end. But I still can't recommend the game. Too many things have changed that just make it not player friendly anymore, and it shows.
Edit: And the game just got bought from Sega by a company called Grey Havens. Hopefully it will be good for the game, but it might be too little too late, only time will tell on that one.

In a sense, there are plenty of new features to keep long time fans of Age of Empires interested, while retaining the same core gameplay. Build stuff, gather stuff, advance Ages, kill baddies. Only this time, with more cannons.

Unturned is a free-to-play (at time of writing), open world, zombie survival game. The game includes crafting (of many, many recipes), base building, driveable (and customizable - in the sense of 'building' things like shelves, crates, lights, and so on, onto the vehicles) vehicles - including cars, motorbikes, bicycles, planes, helicopters, tanks, and boats, multiplayer and singleplayer experiences, mods, weapons (many different kinds - from melee to numerous guns), character design, hunger/thirst/stamina, and much, much more. The game is constantly being updated and there are several official maps, as well as unofficial and Workshop maps, to play.  Go anywhere on the map at any time, play on a variety of difficulties, explore, fight or run from zombies, be stealthy, stick to only one type of weapon, or run in guns blazing. Explore towns, find resources and food, on some maps even do missions, and build your own base (literally anywhere) to store your stuff and survive zombie attacks.
What more can I say?
At first I had no interest in playing the game as I really don't like 'zombie' games. However after watching a LP on Youtube (thank you Paulsoaresjr, once again!) I found it really interesting and loved how much there is to do in the game and the freedom you are given. So I gave it a go - it is F2P after all! - and was so impressed that not only could I not stop playing for the first 40 hours (I've had other things to do since) but I also decided to buy the optional DLC. This is mostly multiplayer focused DLC and, as I don't play MMO, I didn't really want it. BUT, I bought it regardless simply because I wanted to support the game/developer and give something back for such a great experience and for a game that I KNOW I will come back to again and again. I would happily pay for this title.
So in short: great game, lots to do, worth a try (as it costs nothing but time), constantly updated with new and exciting things, and a whole lot of fun.
Want to know more? Check other reviews, or, better yet, give it a shot and decide for yourself!

Game is pretty damn fun. XCOM 2 is more
than Enemy Unknown: Stripped down base management, removal of aircraft, and there are no longer country-specific panic bars, but instead a single global one.
That's not to say that they haven't added in anything new. Some missions will start you off in a stealth-based concealment status. Instead of groups of enemies gaining a turn as soon as you spot them, they'll only trigger once you enter their line of sight (which, once you spot them, will be displayed on the map when you move your mouse around. Unfortunately, this is currently bugged, and enemies may be able to spot you outside of the visible zone). I really like this concept, but generally the missions you start in this condition will have a lower turn counter. It makes sense for
missions, but it's a slap in the hand to give you this freedom and being unable to utilize it. On the bright side, there are some mods that change the way the timer works.
And mods for just about everything else, actually. XCOM 2 is miles ahead of Enemy Unknown when it comes to mod support. If you go on to the Steam workshop (or elsewhere, if you prefer), and you'll find new classes, cosmetics, weapons, enemies, gameplay tweaks, the works. Making this game so mod friendly may be the best change to XCOM 2. Firaxis definitely deserves some praise for their improvements. The only downside is that if you decide you no longer want a mod during a campaign, you won't be able to use that save. On the bright side, there's a mod that lets you bypass that! (though your save may have issues or make your game crash).

Coming back to this over a decade and a half later; Half Life is like the first act of the origin story of an infamous villain.
Witness the birth of the now much maligned "scripted, linear, FPS." Wonder at Valve's story of no story technique. Remark at how it shows signs of being intersting towards the end and question why it wasn't more like this in the first two acts.
It's alright fun and there are a few interesting weapons to mess around with. Pretty much required playing for anyone who cares to see the beginning of the beginning of the end of story driven FPS.

Enemy Unknown = Half Life 1
XCOM 2 = Half Life 2
If that sounds good to you, then get this game.
First off, XCOM 2 has a fantastic premise that appropriately raises the stakes without dismissing what happened in the first game. It's much more story driven and wants to lead you down a certain path, which I personally think goes against what made EU so good. It still has the XCOM spirit of fighting a daunting, unfair, overall superior enemy, but you don't really see that at face value. It's more of a long checklist of missions, and intel. Again, if that sounds good to you, then get this game.
The game is still a patch or two from being fully optimized, but I've only had the occasional dip in framerate so far. What really slows the game down is the interface, and the push for better graphics (they are MUCH better looking btw) and fancy transistions means every action takes a fraction of a second longer. Maybe that's just a nitpick, maybe it'll wear on you like it did me, I don't know.
There's a handful of new ideas thrown into the game, some are insubstantial as far as I've seen, but my favorite is stealth elements. At the start of most missions, you are undetected by the aliens, and can ambush them if you're savvy enough, but that's equally hindered by the fact that almost every mission also has a timer, and I honestly don't know why that's a mechanic. It just further forces people to save-scum and go for a perfect run rather than face adversity. Just my opinion, but I hope some of you agree.
It's a PC game from the ground up, to the point that gamepad controls are really messy and it doesn't respond well to analog controls (if you got a gamepad to work, please tell me how). If you've succesfully weathered the original XCOM games, this will probably make you feel right at home.
I wish I could just post this as a neutral review because even though I personally don't recommend this game, there's more than enough here that most XCOM fans will love it, and I thouroghly acknowledge that. However you felt about the things I mentioned here is probably how you'll feel about them in the game, so if it's your thing, buy it.

Simliar to Terraria, because the creator/lead dev here actually previously worked as a dev on the Terraria team, and after its release struck out on his own notch style to create his own passion project, Starbound. A sci-fi themed 2d platformer in the same genre as Terraria, yet unique and much more than simply a 'clone' or 'copy'.
It's sci-fi, space, technology themed rather than fantasy, medieval, magical themed. And as such, instead of being limited to a single earth like world like Terraria, you get a space ship and are able to use it to travel to an endless number of procedurally generated (randomly created) worlds, that can vary in their alien or earthish feel, in an infinate procedurally generated universe. Due to that procedural generation of the universe, the worlds vary massively from each other in all sorts of ways from the types of creatures that live there, the trees & plants that grow, the types of terrain & biomes on them, their size which effects gravity (how high you can jump), and even the tint, brightness, color and contrast of the light coming for that planets unique sun! There really are no two planets that are identical, though there are planet types like forest/snow/arid "type" planets. Another neat thing is how unlike Terraria where the world was flat and simply had an invisible wall at the 'end' of the world map on both the far left and far right where you couldn't keep going farther. Here in Starbound the planets are round like rl so if you just go left you will eventually make it all the way around that planet and come back to where you started!
The game is still in an early beta state (stage 1 out of 3), and is lacking alot of the planned content (which is an absurd amount of content they have planed, just like terraria has). Though it is beta, it's now stable and fairly bug free and there is more than enough content to be quite enjoyable and not run out of things to do for quite sometime. The devs are constantly working on adding, changing, balancing, tweaking and polishing content & features. The updates slowed for the last month or two from the devs, which were scattered through the world in several countrys, all moving to London to work together face to face in a proper office. But that is now over and they are cracking on working on the game 9-5, 5 days a week and expect more patches to start rolling out soon. They are commited to the game and are planning on doing regular free updates to the game even after the beta has ended, similar to the way Minecraft does things.
All in all it's a very fun game with an Excellent building system that is far better than Terraria's tbh, even at this beta version point as well as the overall controlls. It's a solid base to add more and more content and features onto and I can't wait to see how things will change over time. I'm pretty sure too that once the beta stages/early access is over and it's to 'release' version the price will go up (it's only $15 atm). So if you're a fan of building/crafting/adventure, sandbox games then Starbound is a solid must get title which will only get better over time and you can't beat that indie game price!

You ever play a tabletop game like DnD where it's obvious the GM's only interest in running the game is murdering your whole party and revelling in your frustration?  That's this game.  It's not fun.
Its bones are awesome, I like the turn based play-style, I like the gritty theme, I like the brass voiced narrator.  I even like the city management and dealing with managing a crumbling team of mercenaries.  The same randomly generated dungeons over and over again is something I could get over if I could get through the game a decent pace.
But, no.  The RNG in this game ramps up from "stress inducing difficulty" to "relentlessly murdering all your players" in one level.  That's not fun.  When you can prepare perfectly, run 80% of a dungeon, then have a random encounter with a bone collector who kills your whole team in one fight - that's not fun.
This game is specifically built for the players to lose, long and hard.  That's not what games are supposed to be.  Games are meant to be won by the players in entertaining and dramatic fashion.
Instead of playing this game go get a handful of whatever dice you can get your hands on.  Roll them over and over again until you get max rolls on every die.  That's the fun-equivalent of playing this game.

I just invested 100+ of gameplay hours that was made single-handedly by Eric Barone. Man, ConcernedApe sure made me concerned with my Stardew Valley addiction.
-There are loads of possibilities! Stardew Valley is known as a farm simulator game but it doesn't stop there! Don't like farming? You can invest more of your time in the mines and go deep in the skull cave. Don't like mining either? why not go fishing and catch every fish?
- Lovable characters! As you may know, you can get married in this game and have kids (you can adopt if you married the same gender so that's a really good added feature) You can tell that ConcernedApe really took the time and effort in making the characters as each has their own back stories. ConcernedApe really did not spare his sense of humor in this game lol (keep an eye out for Marnie and Lewis).
- Stardew Valley is a great escape to the reality you live in. In this game you are able to create your own world, and make friends with the characters. It's just you, your farm and your family.
- Great Soundtrack. ConcernedApe also made the entire soundtrack of this game and that is amazing. Each season has its own music going on.
- Replayability. After your evaluation in your 3rd year, you can go on for another 50 years. You can also make several files for several farms if you're feeling productive, as you can go for different paths, either you join the Joja Co. or rebuild the Community Center all by yourself. I suggest that you take the Community Center path as it is more challenging and more rewarding. Also, there are loads of secrets in this game that you have to discover.
- There is no multiplayer feature in this game yet but I've heard that it is under development.
- It gets repetitive. Yes you can continue playing but after a several years, you might find yourself stuck in a loop of waking up, farming sleeping and then waking up. However, if you are attached with your farm then that wouldn't be a problem.
- There are needed features that are not in this game that would make your experience quite inconvinient but there is a modding community to fix that problem
Stardew Valley might be a typical farming game while there are loads of similar games but there is something about this Stardew Valley that just stands out among the rest. For a pixelated game you might find it expensive but let me tell you that the experience you get is worth every penny.
I'll be back to make another review after 1k hours, see you.

You ever play a tabletop game like DnD where it's obvious the GM's only interest in running the game is murdering your whole party and revelling in your frustration?  That's this game.  It's not fun.
Its bones are awesome, I like the turn based play-style, I like the gritty theme, I like the brass voiced narrator.  I even like the city management and dealing with managing a crumbling team of mercenaries.  The same randomly generated dungeons over and over again is something I could get over if I could get through the game a decent pace.
But, no.  The RNG in this game ramps up from "stress inducing difficulty" to "relentlessly murdering all your players" in one level.  That's not fun.  When you can prepare perfectly, run 80% of a dungeon, then have a random encounter with a bone collector who kills your whole team in one fight - that's not fun.
This game is specifically built for the players to lose, long and hard.  That's not what games are supposed to be.  Games are meant to be won by the players in entertaining and dramatic fashion.
Instead of playing this game go get a handful of whatever dice you can get your hands on.  Roll them over and over again until you get max rolls on every die.  That's the fun-equivalent of playing this game.

Darkest Dungeon is an interesting mashup of dungeon crawling with turn based combat and hero roster management.
It takes you to a gloomy world, filled with H. P. Lovecraft-inspired imagery and monsters, where you inherit an estate from a distant relative, located near a secluded hamlet. With the help of infinite supply of outlaws dimwits and other ragtag lowlifes you start to uncover the history and lore of Darkest of Dungeons.
As I mentioned before the game is two phased:
First, you manage your heroes in the hamlet i.e. making sure they snap out of their catatonic states and get rid of their more than justified phobias with a small help of church, booze, ♥♥♥♥♥s and shrinks. Then you choose four
most fitting candidates and after a quick visit at blacksmith/armory you supply them with week's supply of food, torches and other possibly useful items and kiss them goodbye as they descent into depths of whatever charming destination out of the possible five you picked.
In the second phase you control the four unlucky fellas/gals in the dungeon. All dungeons in the game are randomly generated and consists of series of hallways and rooms. Whether your mission is to scout the rooms or collect food/supplies for the hamlet your heroes will traverse through trying to kill everything in their path. In this stage the game is all about keeping your party healthy and sane at the same time which might prove to be more difficult than it sounds. Avoiding death is easier if there is any sort of healer in the group but holding group's sanity together is harder as enemies, traps, darkness and insane party members inflict stress. Hell, even walking through an empty hallway can by quite stressful.
After successfully completing the quest, whatever is remaining of the heroes crawl out just to be sent back for another mission and the first phase starts again. It is your choice whether you want to keep and tend there poor souls back to decent adventuring condition or do you just send them on their way and hire a new batch. After all, these fools are on unlimited supply.
Darkest Dungeon is an extremely atmospheric game with its distinct, gothic art style and eerie sound design. As a cherry on the top it's fully narrated by illustrious Wayne June, whipping you with quips and remarks on both failures and triumphs. The combat is well balanced and brutal giving enough challenge even for a seasoned dungeoneer and if it feels too easy one can always make it harder for extra reward. As writing this, the game has no less than 15 unique heroes and over a hundred different trinkets, providing enough possible party compositions to keep gameplay fresh and experimental minds as myself entertained.
Overall I give to Darkest Dungeon 9/10 with
8/10 for combat and fisticuffing
9/10 for milieu and lore
9/10 for immersivity and ambience
8/10 for challenge and adversary
10/10 for narration

I bought the game while it was still in Early Access and I've been on top of the updates ever since then.
Take no heed of the Metacritic score, a lot of "professional" reviewers are IGNorant. They bash the controls for the game, the objectives and so forth leaving it with the verdict that it is simply "YouTube bait".
That analysis couldn't be more wrong. I am Bread is an original idea that not only continues with Bossa Studios' satire of simulator titles and the joke simulator ones too (*cough* Goat Simulator *cough* Rock Simulator *cough* Grass Simulator *cough* Air Control *cough*).
The plot is about a slice of bread living in Bernardshire and its quest to toast itself. This highly disturbs Mr. Bob Murton, who happens to live in the same house as the slice of bread, who sees a therapist and is informed that bread does not do things on its own.
The controls, as mentioned, are awkward, but only to the new player. Within half an hour, one should be able to master the movement of bread and the game mechanic. Frustration will be a part of the game, but those who ragequit and then complain only have their lack of patience to blame. The game will remind you of Surgeon Simulator 2013 in that respect.
Outside of the story mode, you have a free roam mode, a crispbread mode, a bagel mode, baguette mode and zero g mode a la Surgeon Simulator 2013. All these game modes add extra to the already interesting game.
Oh and give Starch Wars a go, it's possibly the best space battle you may experience since Battlefront all those years ago.

Age of Empires III was one of the few strategy games that I played through every campaign.  There are definatly some awful story lines and arcs (The entire 1st game), but you almost have to play it to make sure you get a good foundation for the first and second expansions.
The main campaign has you following the story of one family from the turkish invasion of Malta too finding settling the west.  A ton of liberties are taken with history in this campaign(Defeating a russian army in the wilderness...).  Ultimately you find yourself in a base building spree attempting to defeat your enemies.  Some variance in mission structure is provided throughout the game to make it a little more interesting.
If you only had 10 hours though I would start on the second campaign, which follows the son of one of the first members of the family.  As you play as the native american you actually engage in the history of the era's that the game represents.  There are some memorable battles such as Trenton, and Little big horn(!) to relieve during the expansion, and it definatly makes it worth it to stick it out.
But, then there is, 'The Asian Dynasties,' which I looked at and said, "How could they link these two games together in one cohesive story?"  The answer is they don't!  And really for the better as each campaign follows seperate leaders as they conquer, explore, or rebel against their enemies.  Ultimately I feel like the AOE series saved one of my favorite campaigns for last in the Indian one.  In the indian campaign you play as a soldier who must choose between military loyality and nationalism for his home land.  The resulting campaign is fun and gives you some level of purpose on building up bases and fighting your enemy.

Here's another great game on Steam with less support than it deserves. I don't often play Unturned, but I do love playing it whenever I get the chance. I hate to be the one to make this comparison, but if you love Minecraft's graphics, Call of Duty's Zombies mode, and the entire Steam Workshop at your disposal, this is probably going to be an enjoyable game for you. You can customize your character with clothes and weapon skins, which brings me to another thing: weapons. There are a lot of guns in the game normally, but then there's everything on the Workshop. Its pretty damn simple to get something from the workshop into your game, be it a map, weapon, vehicle, item, or anything else really in the game. However, you probably won't start off the game with finding a gun. Especially a good one, like the Honey Badger. If you're insanely lucky, a zombie might drop an Ace, which is a revolver, with a few shots in it. But to kill that zombie that might drop a handgun for you, you'll want to probably pick up a melee weapon, such as a hockey stick, rake, or kitchen knife. There is so much design in this game, with few problems. There are also... I think five or six official maps: PEI, Russia, Washington, and Germany from my *horrible* memory. I know there's at least one more. There are several cities, farms, airports, and army bases throughout these maps.
I'll personally admit, the game does have some flaws. Sometimes the game lags for absolutely no reason, but if you have a good PC unlike me, you should be getting 30 frames easily. I'm lucky to pick up 10 frames. Sometimes, the zombies will do things they shouldnt be able to do. Like phase through a goddamn wall to kill you. But, other than a few optimization problems, small bugs, and slightly unfavorable design choices, the game is amazing. I do recommend you download it and play it for a bit.

I had forgotten just how good this game was. Like many people i'd bought it years ago, only to find my playing days cut short thanks to it being incompatible with Windows Vista onwards. Not any more! I can confirm the Steam version works perfectly on my Windows 8.1 Pro 64-bit system.
Fans of the first two games will immediately be able to dive straight in, although there have been some major changes in the third installment compared to the first two. Firstly there's not so much emphasis on micro management now. Instead you get to concentrate on the exploration and battle elements, which makes this game the most enjoyable of the three. Secondly there is the new home city section which allows you to ship units and supplies to the new world during the game. Between games you can customise your home city to change which units and supplies can be sent out to you, along with the appearance of the city itself.
Visually this game absolutely trounces the two previous games, and indeed almost any other game in the genre, it is graphically amazing. Sound-wise it's not much different to the first two, with the sound being good but not excellent, and not too intrusive. Pros:
-Its early alpha so there is time to fix whats wrong with this game.
-I got it on sale?...
Cons:
-Server side lag made playing nearly impossible. With no way to see server ping before joining i couldnt find one suitable to my specific area ("U.S. east" is not helpful at all). Made hitting anything a guessing game.
-The play area is tiny. For being a game with apparently infinite amounts of space, the actually space used by players (including snipers) wasnt very much, making mid-range ships that much more effective.
-As a level 6 sniper i was taking twice as much damage from a level 7 sniper even as he was under fire from another ship. There are clear balancing issues that need to be addressed.
-There is some system by which parts of your ship become damaged and either retreating or turning your ship becomes necessary, but how this works and in what way is beyond me. There is no explination in-game.
-The crew members ramblings became a burden and i quickly jettisoned them.
-Their bodies did NOT slow the enemy.
-half the abilites seemed to do nothing. In cases where i used a weapon and it did little to no damage, maybe a message explaining the effective range of the weapon is in order?
-You cant change your ship mid-game. So once you get into a game and realize the ship you picked is a floating crap-pile, you are stuck with it the entire game. Have fun being a burden to the rest of your team.
-hate to bring this up but THERE IS NO AIR IN SPACE. having the ships slow to a stop once i cease using thrusters is not realistic nor fun. Too many space games do this and i find it annoying even if they have a plot device for it. (at least have it as an option you can deactivate or a "full stop" button you can key bind)
-warping is a mess. you can WARP! (yay!) but only to this square foot or this square foot. (boo!) (you are forced to warp into a specific area, meaning enemies know where to look to ambush you.) you are also locked out of certain destinations if you dont own the arrival base, making coming up behind your enemy impossible.
Things to improve:
-The large shields attached to the A1/A2/B1/B2 stations should be destructable. In fact, everything should have HP and could potentially be destroyed given enough firepower.
-allow free ship movement. having "up" as always "up" isnt what space is about and limits the creativity of the player.
-put rams on the damn ships already. i want to penetrate things.
-maybe a mode by which multiple players control one ship (pilot, gunner, etc.)
-at least a couple of the weapons didnt have a form of targeting. for a game set really far in the future, i find it silly that anyone would go into combat with "fire and forget" weapons willingly.
-fix warping. maybe make a ship type (scout?) that can warp anywhere? or just remove the current limitations.
-give the smaller bases some kind of defenses, even if its basic guns. its too easy to flood a side.
-limit the number of each ship type per team until the balancing issues are addressed
-increase overall ship shields by 20-40% until connection issues are fixed. the buffer will help players survive those nasty lag spikes.
tl;dr: skip it and revisit once its release.

XCOM 2, from a gameplay standpoint, is an improvement in many ways from Enemy Unknown/Within. The addition of the concealment system was my personal favorite, although the trade-off for such a boon seemed to be very, very brisk timed missions. Then you've got the revamped Geoscape where you fly around the world in your Avenger to make contact with resistance cells, which I found invigorating. The trade off there was that your new primary concern was the Avatar project, which could quickly pile the pressure on in a less than fun way if you even try to deviate from the seemingly linear development path in your campaign. Then you've got the revamped classes alongside enemies new and old, each changed or developed in interesting ways to make it feel as though you're really starting at the bottom of the barrel against an enemy that is superior in every way. All this makes me want to recommend the game, and I will. However...
See, I like the game quite a bit for what it does right. What it does wrong (in the vanilla game at least) can really turn you off. As I said above, timed missions only serve to unfairly punish the slow and steady players who don't wish to burn through their limited human/technological resources carelessly. I've had maybe one mission where I actually got everyone to evac 1 turn before the end in a way that felt 'clutch'. Every other time involved me making a mad dash between half-cover points to play a futile game of catch-up with the timer, playing 'find the sight-line' with hacking objectives, chasing down Dark VIPs in need of a punch or a bullet, or determining whether or not a miss might destroy that stuff I need right behind [Insert Fully Covered Enemy Here].
I know that may all sound disheartening, but I assure you that the game is still great. The game gets the feeling of a lowly resistance group coming off of a great windfall doing its best to be everywhere at once. The tense consumption of time as you hop between your HQ and far-off resistance cell groups makes every scan feel like a risk, and the simplification of Scientist/Engineer usage serves to make every decision you make when acquiring new allies or tech feel all the more poignant, as you could be deciding how quickly a room or research project you desperately need gets completed. Add to that the concept of desperately picking your battles against a global super-power's foreboding new project using your amply customizable recruits, and you've got the recipe for some very personal stories of in-game turmoil and triumph.
These pros and cons combine to make a good game that reeks of potential. The devs must've realized this, as they have made modding a central aspect of the game. I for one am partial to the mod that removes timers from most missions, alongside a few voice packs and some very welcome helmets and accessories. I've yet to delve into custom classes or the like, I'm saving that for a separate playthrough, but this ease of access only serves to extend the game's ability to hold your interest.
Gameplay aside, I must say that the technical issues are pretty baffling. I just recently gained access to a much better computer than I'm used to. 3.5Ghz processor, 4gb of VRAM, 16gb of RAM, all this after having dealt with playing Enemy Unknown on a junker hand-me-down laptop for years. Needless to say, I was excited when I saw the recommended requirements for this game, especially after seeing how well EU/EW ran. What I got was stuttering at MSAA 2x with most other taxing settings off and texture quality at medium. Ultimately I settled on FXAA with high quality textures and plenty of decals, and I still get some pretty heavy framedrops after getting full-squad size and entering mission prep. One can only hope Firaxis actually optimizes this game well. After seeing what happened to the PS3 port of Enemy Within, in which it got dropped after its most recent patch caused a game-breaking bug during the invasion of XCOM's HQ no matter what happened, my faith in Firaxis' QA is less than stellar.
TL;DR: The game itself is good, but it is held back by some of its less fair mechanics and limiters. The mods are already making it better, but the performance issues take a bit of the fun out of it. Here's hoping Firaxis steps up their game as XCOM 2's community grows.

I have played this game for about 12 hours thusfar and I am going to offer up a concise, honest review at this point:
This game is a hell of a lot of fun. Not even "For an alpha" or "Taking into consideration how early it is in development." It is a hell of a lot of fun for a game, period. Having said that, it IS an alpha. There are some balance issues, missing features, and it is a bit rough around the edges......but it's an alpha....that is the point. Updates are frequent, issues get addressed quickly, and engagement with the community is high. This game is quite clearly going to turn into something very special, and to be able to jump in on the fun now, for under 8 bucks, is an absolute steal.
Some meat: The ship types are varied and interesting, with distinct roles, functions, and designs. The designs are bit more realistic than what people are typically used to, so they will look weird at first...but they grow on you. The combat is smooth and the game mechanics are solid. Essentially you fight via 2 side lanes to lock down a jumppoint at the end of the lane that enables you to jump to the enemy base and cap it. Along the way in the lane there are 3 cappable points that give resources, which are used to level up. The third middle "lane" is a capturable station that gives your team a buff when capped, but only becomes cappable every so often. Other game modes are being worked on, as are other maps.
Combat is insanely fun, wheather you play as a railgun toting Sniper, a cloaking and ambushing Assassin, a floating fortress Flagship, a run and gun Frigate, a bullying Enforcer, or one of the other classes (8 in all, lots more coming). Snipers can see and shoot clear across the lane, but the lane is literred with asteriods that allow ships to approach via cover.....unless they want to cap one of the points, in which case they must skirt across the open for a bit. But while they are doing that, an Assassin is inevitably making his way to the Sniper, using a combination of cloaking and asteriod cover. Some classes have the ability to blink (teleport) , others can speed up cap speeds, others can snare/immobilize enemies, others can heal, others can detect cloacked enemies....to name just a few. It all unfolds with surprisingly good rock-paper-scissor balance....except way more complicated. Each of the 8 classes bring a unique feel and purpose.
Anyways, I wanted this to be short, but I see I could not do that. Too many good things to say about this game. In short, if you love space combat, get this game.

Darkest Dungeon is an interesting mashup of dungeon crawling with turn based combat and hero roster management.
It takes you to a gloomy world, filled with H. P. Lovecraft-inspired imagery and monsters, where you inherit an estate from a distant relative, located near a secluded hamlet. With the help of infinite supply of outlaws dimwits and other ragtag lowlifes you start to uncover the history and lore of Darkest of Dungeons.
As I mentioned before the game is two phased:
First, you manage your heroes in the hamlet i.e. making sure they snap out of their catatonic states and get rid of their more than justified phobias with a small help of church, booze, ♥♥♥♥♥s and shrinks. Then you choose four
most fitting candidates and after a quick visit at blacksmith/armory you supply them with week's supply of food, torches and other possibly useful items and kiss them goodbye as they descent into depths of whatever charming destination out of the possible five you picked.
In the second phase you control the four unlucky fellas/gals in the dungeon. All dungeons in the game are randomly generated and consists of series of hallways and rooms. Whether your mission is to scout the rooms or collect food/supplies for the hamlet your heroes will traverse through trying to kill everything in their path. In this stage the game is all about keeping your party healthy and sane at the same time which might prove to be more difficult than it sounds. Avoiding death is easier if there is any sort of healer in the group but holding group's sanity together is harder as enemies, traps, darkness and insane party members inflict stress. Hell, even walking through an empty hallway can by quite stressful.
After successfully completing the quest, whatever is remaining of the heroes crawl out just to be sent back for another mission and the first phase starts again. It is your choice whether you want to keep and tend there poor souls back to decent adventuring condition or do you just send them on their way and hire a new batch. After all, these fools are on unlimited supply.
Darkest Dungeon is an extremely atmospheric game with its distinct, gothic art style and eerie sound design. As a cherry on the top it's fully narrated by illustrious Wayne June, whipping you with quips and remarks on both failures and triumphs. The combat is well balanced and brutal giving enough challenge even for a seasoned dungeoneer and if it feels too easy one can always make it harder for extra reward. As writing this, the game has no less than 15 unique heroes and over a hundred different trinkets, providing enough possible party compositions to keep gameplay fresh and experimental minds as myself entertained.
Overall I give to Darkest Dungeon 9/10 with
8/10 for combat and fisticuffing
9/10 for milieu and lore
9/10 for immersivity and ambience
8/10 for challenge and adversary
10/10 for narration

I have played this game for about 12 hours thusfar and I am going to offer up a concise, honest review at this point:
This game is a hell of a lot of fun. Not even "For an alpha" or "Taking into consideration how early it is in development." It is a hell of a lot of fun for a game, period. Having said that, it IS an alpha. There are some balance issues, missing features, and it is a bit rough around the edges......but it's an alpha....that is the point. Updates are frequent, issues get addressed quickly, and engagement with the community is high. This game is quite clearly going to turn into something very special, and to be able to jump in on the fun now, for under 8 bucks, is an absolute steal.
Some meat: The ship types are varied and interesting, with distinct roles, functions, and designs. The designs are bit more realistic than what people are typically used to, so they will look weird at first...but they grow on you. The combat is smooth and the game mechanics are solid. Essentially you fight via 2 side lanes to lock down a jumppoint at the end of the lane that enables you to jump to the enemy base and cap it. Along the way in the lane there are 3 cappable points that give resources, which are used to level up. The third middle "lane" is a capturable station that gives your team a buff when capped, but only becomes cappable every so often. Other game modes are being worked on, as are other maps.
Combat is insanely fun, wheather you play as a railgun toting Sniper, a cloaking and ambushing Assassin, a floating fortress Flagship, a run and gun Frigate, a bullying Enforcer, or one of the other classes (8 in all, lots more coming). Snipers can see and shoot clear across the lane, but the lane is literred with asteriods that allow ships to approach via cover.....unless they want to cap one of the points, in which case they must skirt across the open for a bit. But while they are doing that, an Assassin is inevitably making his way to the Sniper, using a combination of cloaking and asteriod cover. Some classes have the ability to blink (teleport) , others can speed up cap speeds, others can snare/immobilize enemies, others can heal, others can detect cloacked enemies....to name just a few. It all unfolds with surprisingly good rock-paper-scissor balance....except way more complicated. Each of the 8 classes bring a unique feel and purpose.
Anyways, I wanted this to be short, but I see I could not do that. Too many good things to say about this game. In short, if you love space combat, get this game.

Do you need a break from all the violent games? Do you want to feel like a productive human being who grows their own food and earns an honest living through constant hard work while never leaving the comfort of your own living room?
If you enjoy Harvest Moon, you'll enjoy this game too. You play as a city kid who inherits a farm and must build it up from nothing. You can raise animals, grow crops, fish, and go exploring in mines. You can also marry a local (of either gender) and have kids if you want. You can also get divorced, according to a friend who decided she didn't like her character's spouse after they began living together. The villagers have surprisingly interesting storylines, and there is a little more drama in town than one would find in Harvest Moon. The music is delightful and calming, the game is addictive, and I swear I blinked and 7 hours passed by.  Basically what I'm getting at is this: I suspect the creators took the best elements of Harvest Moon and improved upon it to make a superior delightful game.

XCOM 2 is a tough game, even on Rookie difficulty. However, once you dig in and learn the mechanics, what you have is a mostly brilliant turn-based strategy game that has no equal in terms of fun and style, at least not that I have played. There’s a lot to love here. Even after playing it several times, I can always find new things to try, like playing a mission with a squad of only Spark units.
It does get frustrating at times, and sometimes that frustration stems from what I see as fairly cheap moments. You can set up what seems like the perfect ambush and still miss every shot in a turn. Some might say “That’s just XCOM” but at some point, a game needs to be a game.
The War of the Chosen expansion has a lot of neat new things in it, like zombies and some fun new classes. However, after failing several missions that I felt were not particularly well-designed, I had to put the game down. Please note that while I received the core game for free from a friend, I paid for the expansion and all the DLC.
I still think the standard XCOM 2 campaign is brilliant. I’ve put in several hundreds of hours on this game over three platforms. If that is not a ringing endorsement, I don’t know what is.

XCOM 2, from a gameplay standpoint, is an improvement in many ways from Enemy Unknown/Within. The addition of the concealment system was my personal favorite, although the trade-off for such a boon seemed to be very, very brisk timed missions. Then you've got the revamped Geoscape where you fly around the world in your Avenger to make contact with resistance cells, which I found invigorating. The trade off there was that your new primary concern was the Avatar project, which could quickly pile the pressure on in a less than fun way if you even try to deviate from the seemingly linear development path in your campaign. Then you've got the revamped classes alongside enemies new and old, each changed or developed in interesting ways to make it feel as though you're really starting at the bottom of the barrel against an enemy that is superior in every way. All this makes me want to recommend the game, and I will. However...
See, I like the game quite a bit for what it does right. What it does wrong (in the vanilla game at least) can really turn you off. As I said above, timed missions only serve to unfairly punish the slow and steady players who don't wish to burn through their limited human/technological resources carelessly. I've had maybe one mission where I actually got everyone to evac 1 turn before the end in a way that felt 'clutch'. Every other time involved me making a mad dash between half-cover points to play a futile game of catch-up with the timer, playing 'find the sight-line' with hacking objectives, chasing down Dark VIPs in need of a punch or a bullet, or determining whether or not a miss might destroy that stuff I need right behind [Insert Fully Covered Enemy Here].
I know that may all sound disheartening, but I assure you that the game is still great. The game gets the feeling of a lowly resistance group coming off of a great windfall doing its best to be everywhere at once. The tense consumption of time as you hop between your HQ and far-off resistance cell groups makes every scan feel like a risk, and the simplification of Scientist/Engineer usage serves to make every decision you make when acquiring new allies or tech feel all the more poignant, as you could be deciding how quickly a room or research project you desperately need gets completed. Add to that the concept of desperately picking your battles against a global super-power's foreboding new project using your amply customizable recruits, and you've got the recipe for some very personal stories of in-game turmoil and triumph.
These pros and cons combine to make a good game that reeks of potential. The devs must've realized this, as they have made modding a central aspect of the game. I for one am partial to the mod that removes timers from most missions, alongside a few voice packs and some very welcome helmets and accessories. I've yet to delve into custom classes or the like, I'm saving that for a separate playthrough, but this ease of access only serves to extend the game's ability to hold your interest.
Gameplay aside, I must say that the technical issues are pretty baffling. I just recently gained access to a much better computer than I'm used to. 3.5Ghz processor, 4gb of VRAM, 16gb of RAM, all this after having dealt with playing Enemy Unknown on a junker hand-me-down laptop for years. Needless to say, I was excited when I saw the recommended requirements for this game, especially after seeing how well EU/EW ran. What I got was stuttering at MSAA 2x with most other taxing settings off and texture quality at medium. Ultimately I settled on FXAA with high quality textures and plenty of decals, and I still get some pretty heavy framedrops after getting full-squad size and entering mission prep. One can only hope Firaxis actually optimizes this game well. After seeing what happened to the PS3 port of Enemy Within, in which it got dropped after its most recent patch caused a game-breaking bug during the invasion of XCOM's HQ no matter what happened, my faith in Firaxis' QA is less than stellar.
TL;DR: The game itself is good, but it is held back by some of its less fair mechanics and limiters. The mods are already making it better, but the performance issues take a bit of the fun out of it. Here's hoping Firaxis steps up their game as XCOM 2's community grows.
