It took me a while to write this review as I was on the fence on whether I could recommend this game to a friend, or not. I eventually came to the realization that I cannot recommend this to a friend in it's current state. I really enjoy this game personally, but due to certain issues which arise in competitive game play that this game does nothing to address I cannot in good faith recommend anyone pick this game up, when the competition this game has (other titles) address these issues.
Black squad is a free to play competitive tactical shooter developed in Korea with the goal of not offering an edge to those who chose to support the game with money. Everything aside from cosmetic items can be earned inside the game with enough playtime. This, black squad does well, and I have no complaints with as they've done a good job in doing so. Nothing is too unbalanced, and the devs change guns as needed to keep this balance.
The main con this game has going for it, is the same con that most free to play shooters have. They allow access to players not included in their region allowing an unfair advantage to those playing outside the server area, and they have a poor anti cheat system in place. These seem like small complaints, but when the game markets itself as a competitive tactical shooter those two aspects need focused more than the next weapon or map being added. On any given day during morning time in NA, 250 is the average ping of the people playing on NA servers:
Their also also quite a few cheats floating around for the game, that have been here since launch. I'm not here to point any fingers, but those who are blatant stay active within the game with no seen repercussions. The worst part about this is no in game offered support to report said players. We all know cheats are a thing when it comes to any game, but at least give us the option to tell the devs which players are suspicious, so action can be taken against those players instead of having to fight them multiple times through matches throughout game.
I know the game is still in early access, but if the devs implement changes to these regards I will update my review accordingly. The game has potential, but is in a pretty bad state at the moment. IF these issue don't get addressed soon, I don't forsee a future for this title. I can't honestly say I want to invest too much time into a game that might not exist in 6 months. Most of the time, what keeps this style of games alive is the community. With the state the game is in now, there isn't much of a community.
TL:DR
Game play is awesome, but is suppressed by the issues that community makes clear that development doesn't address. Without serious changes I cannot recommend this game with other titles like Counter Strike, Team Fortress 2, Rainbow 6, Dirty Bomb and Blacklight Retribution exist.

Basically a slow-paced capture-the-flag with big space ships.
Currently there are a few ships to choose from (I think 8 or so), each with its own characteristics and weapons. You can further customize them with different loadouts, changing or rather adjusting abilities and weaponry. More ships seem to be unlockable (through in-game currency?) but that doesn't seem to be implemented right now.
It's 5 vs 5 on a map divided into five sectors: Your base, the enemy's base, two side-sectors and a special sector in the middle where a gas mining facility is located. You reach each sector by jumping, making only adjacent sectors available as jump destinations. Initiating a jump makes you very vulnerable and needs a few seconds to complete. Both side-sectors have minor objects to capture and also two larger ones (where you can also repair). The more objects are captured by your team, the more resources you gain. From what I can tell, this helps faster respawning, faster repairs etc. While in-game your ship will be able to level up at certain points (indicated in the upper right corner of the HUD) and you'll either have to get to one of the larger stations or your home base to aquire that upgrade. Basically this means more shield power and that is important as capturing the enemy home base will drain your health a lot. The capture level for both home bases can't be reset or decreased and you'll have to watch out for rogue enemies that might try to (partially) capture your home base while your team is busy counting the stars.
The main goal obviously is to capture the enemy's home base. Combat is rather slow-paced as those ships' movement is really ponderous. This makes you think twice before going anywhere; considered movement is a must and you really have to take into account what ship you're maneuvering and how to best use its abilities and weapons. I really like that. Also, going alone is almost always a bad idea. Taking on two enemies at the same time will have you respawning at your base in most cases. But there's always the possibility to flee a lost battle by jumping home or to another sector and try to get repairs.
Ship movement and controls seem awkward at first but you'll get the hang of it after having played a few rounds and eventually you're going to like it. You'll feel like a boss when you've spotted an enemy,
behind an asteroid to hide, let them pass and then ascend to attack. Capturing the enemy's home base in a suicide run scratching on my last bars of health with my repair drones fixing stuff up and a lot of enemy fire hitting my rear also felt epic.
Unfortunately key bindings seem to be fixed right now and I don't quite like them (abilities mapped to 1-5, R and F unmapped in combat). I hope being able to customize them will be implemented later on.
What I didn't like on my first impressions is that it seems that the game isn't balanced so well right now. Hitting ships with your weapons isn't so easy as they spread fire quite a bit (most will fire rockets or plasma beams or whatever that is) and then there are some that'll hit you from far away and there's little you can do besides taking cover or leaving the scene. Though I haven't fully explored each ship type and its abilities yet and that might be due to that, inexperience and plain incompetence.
Also, besides some tutorial on YouTube you pretty much are on your own to figure out what's going on. Weapons and abilities have no descriptions at the moment and you just have to try everything out.
All in all a rather refreshing experience for me and a welcome break from all the hectic twitch shooting that's around everywhere.
Finally, considering its current form (already very playable, a few crashes and minor bugs here and there), this makes me think there's still hope in Early Access. Well done and done right.

I personally prefer the first two AoE games to this one, but it's still worth a look. The gameplay and UI is completely different, though. You still have population caps, but individual troop types use different amounts of space; i.e. cavalry use 2 pop, cannons use 3-6, etc. You also can't dominate games with infinite towers, or massive ocean fleets, like in the other games. Buildings have caps as well, and you can only build a certain amount of each ship type; i.e. 8 galleons, 4 cannon ships, etc.
I wouldn't advise buying the game unless you can get the complete set, as the base title feels like an incomplete demo. Unlike the first two games, this one only has a single campaign for each title, which is disappointing. But the new game features, units, and civs make this title a great next step in the series. Cons aside, this is a good game to add to your collection.

After playing for 3 days I can already write a review.
The game looks good, enough for what a shooter should look. The focus on a shooter has to be smooth gameplay, not graphics.
I like that the game modes, brings forth other games like Battlefield 3(Destruction), Call of Duty MW3 (TDM) and Counter-Strike(Demolition). I played all 3 games and I can say the game successfully brings them back.
The only major flaw in this game is balance. There is no balance whatsoever. All guns shoot the same. Rifles are more accurate than Snipers or enjoy similar feel of accuracy. You can be sniped by ARs in sniper spots by people strafing, running and jumping. Also there is no stamina penalty for running, ducking or jumping. It makes really hard for the game to find its own balance since everyone moves too fast(BF3 suffered from this) and spams jumping, strafing and ducking. Your character feels like rambo. If you are good enough, you can take whole waves of respawn with an AR, more if you are using SR-47.
I don't mind dying fast for ARs, but dying to SR-47 or other medal weapons feels always like 1 shot episodes, even in greater distances like sniper exchanges. I don't mind rewarding players with better guns, I fact I like the idea. What I don't like is putting guns in the game and forgetting to balance it out. Some guns don't have recoil and others have their in-game accuracy set too high and combined with no movement penalty,♥♥♥♥♥♥just hits the fan.
I really liked the game. It is not heavy on your PC. Everything from is very clear from the get-go. You get a tutorial, you learn about skills(really nice system) and you get your guns. But after some time you start to feel the inconsistencies.
I think the game need to sit with professional and other players and really make a huge improvement on gameplay to patch up stuff. To get an idea what I'm talking about, what Lidiel(Korean?) youtube montages of him playing Black Squad. He wields around several guns with same results, many headshots.

Stardew Valley is a game where you get to live out the urban fantasy of escaping the daily rat race of the city by becoming the local farmer of a small community. The game does have objectives such as restoring the local community center, however the player is given the freedom to do whatever he/she wants and whether to complete this objectives or ignore them. The activities the player can do is diverse and can be everything from farming, fishing, mining, fighting monsters in the caves to befriending the locals.
Most of all the game has strong on atmosphere and works excellent as a stress reducer.  All in all, it is a virtual escape from the city.

A good number of annoying bugs are present, although i never ran into anything gamebreaking in 4 playthroughs. The graphical glitches are exceptionally annoying given that those same glitches were around in Enemy Unknown / Within.
There are also a handful of gameplay elements that needs a bit of balancing, like the mimic beacon and the Avatar Project which is virtually impossible to lose to once you figure it out.
To those that complain about timed missions: the real problem there is one of expectation. I treat each game like a new and unique challenge, whether the game is a sequel or not. So rather than being frustratring, i found it to be refreshing and a step in the right direction. So no problems there. Not in and of itself anyways... more on that later.
After all, there is nothing strategic about inching yourself across tactical maps like a narcoleptic slug addicted to overwatch. In order to effectively negotiate a mission with a timer, you need to be able to be able to formulate manuevers and execute them in an efficient manner.
The final large criticism I have for this game is.. the apparent laziness and lack of creativity in a few areas.
IE Guerrilla ops. Your guaranteed to get one of these every 20 in game days or so, and they are all pretty much the same thing. Reach a static objective within a time limit, interact with it minimally via a quick hack or shooting at it, clear the area.
Also, how about that item retrieval guerilla op? Why would the aliens move the item into a secure crate, load that crate onto a train, and then rig that crate to explode in 8 turns? Does the miracle of trash compaction or paper shredding elude this intestellar collective that cured all of humanities diseases as easily as blowing a bubble with your spit?
VIP operations? Find the operative (sometimes), move him to an extraction point in within a time limit.
And how about this large resistance network that you're building up? Slight income increases and meta game bonuses. IE your grenades and bathroom sundries build slightly faster. Can be great but ulitimately a little boring.
With this game being a sequel, i was sort of hoping for more. IE instead of having an inexplicably rigged trash bin that you need to reach in 8 turns.... How about catching a VIP that is slowly leaving the AO with the item in question? That would not only make the game make a little more sense, but that would open the game up to more tactical strategies. Do you chase after the guy, cutting a path of destruction in  your wake? Or do you carefully wait in ambush like some kind of oily flasher and evac immediately with the goods?
How about mounted heavy weapons or moving vehicles?
Maybe the game could feature some questionable secondary targets. IE a bank that you could potentially rob for instant gain, or prisoners that you could free to bolster the resistance in the given area. The execution of the secondary targets may fit well with XCOMs decision/consequence paradigm, where robbing a bank make may give you some instant cash, but may turn public opinion against you and make things harder for you in the long run. Makes sense given that XCOM is being painted as terrorists by the ADVENT coalition.
There has been a lot added to EU/EWs gameplay... but almost not enough IMO.
That being said, this is still one of the best strategy games to have been released in a long while, so I still give it a thumbs up.

The game looked interesting from the store page, so on a whim I took a chance and was pleasantly surprised.  I love capital ships in games, and this game doesn't disappoint.  Some have compared it to a MOBA, but its more like a team-based shooter like TF in space.  Once I got the controls down, gameplay was pretty smooth, and the strategies and tactics started becoming apparent.
Pros:  Gameplay is very fun, there's a TON of potential here.  With care, it could become a real hit.   Battlefield "terrain" (asteroids) was actually very useful for me for the first time in a space game, ducking and rushing from cover to cover.  Good teamwork leads to victory; smaller ships are useful too (I just helped win a game in a frigate because I could run and hide, eventually rushing in to cap the enemy base.)  Doesn't seem pay-to-win...yet.  Games are relatively quick but deep, they seem to have hit a sweet spot as far as game length goes.
Cons: Only 5v5?  C'mon, lets have 10v10 or more - the EPIC space battles that would result would be amazing.  Really small ships like the corvette are useless; they're so fragile that in a 5v5 game, even though they have some healing powers and team buffers, they die so fast that they're not worth taking.  But in bigger games, smaller ships like the corvette could become a real asset, as the more targets increase their chances of survivability.  With so few ships on a side, it seems like ships like the Hunter and Sniper are especially powerful.
In the end, it boils down to the question - "Am I having fun?"  In short, yes.  I'm an older gamer and have played a lot of space games over the years.  Some were great, some were frustrating and some were just awful.  This one is a very fun game that I hope will get better as they move on to beta and beyond.

All around, it's a pretty great game.  They really nailed a unique style, and it's been pretty polished.  Even in Early Access it was in better shape than many games, and it's been improving since with mechanics and updates.  Things like bugs and typos have been scarce, which is a very good sign of quality work (it warms my nitpicky software tester heart).
Personally, I have trouble with the difficulty.  I'm one to try to hoard resources and hold on to people.  But these characters facing those horrors, I'm finally learning that you pretty much have to grind through those mercenaries (heroes seems...overly strong) along with other resources.  Trying to keep them all well is an impossible task with what they face.  Getting some characters up to higher levels will definitely take a lot of work and careful shepherding.
On the one hand, it's going to take a lot of grinding type effort to build up resources (especially if you expend resources trying to hold on to early recruits).  But that difficulty does make it satisfying to see your town and roster slowly expanding.  One day you can look forward to very capable mercenaries, destroying monsters while fighting through a long list of debilitating flaws...

If all along the game the story telling is good, the end and some references are weird and at the end, something is missing. I even did not need developping Psi soldier to finish the game.
Thankfully, mods are here to help the game beeing better (or to finish the game...you choose).
As for the first X-Com, I understand the use of Unreal engine, but something can be done here too. Maybe using Unreal 4 next time or moving to the DICE BF one, so the customization and characters are much more realistic and less "Unreall gross". And while playing, I was wondering all along why this game hasn't be release on console, because the gameplay allows it as much as the last X-Com verison....budget restriction maybe, but I may have enjoyed it more on console, than on my aging laptop.
If you are a die hard fan, play it. If you discover this game, wait for prices cut and enjoy your time.

This is a MOBA game with big spaceships and even bigger potential.
Whether the developers will achieve that potential is another matter, but they're definitely on the right track. If the premise sounds appealing to you, you will enjoy the game and it is worth the price of admission. It's very well done.
However, it is early access, and as such, there are a lot of missing functions, some balance issues, bugs, and a lack of content which appears to be in the process of being addressed. My biggest concern at the moment, in terms of "I want to have fun right now," is the lack of tooltip details.
Let me explain. You get choices on which weapons/abilities to load your ship with. However, there is absolutely zero description of what any of the weapons do aside from the name. So you kind of have to try them all and figure out how they're supposed to work.  Yes, this will obviously be addressed, but in the game's current state, there's sort of an unnecessarily high learning curve.
Still, once I figured things out, I started having a ton of fun, and I'm glad I paid the $10. I'm having fun finding new ways to sneak up on enemies and blow them to pieces.

TL;DR: So far it looks great, it has some flaws but is overall a worthy successor to XCOM: Enemy Unknown.
Worldmap:
One of the less satisfying things of the game.
It doesn't give you options. If you get a mission while all of your well trained soldiers are wounded, you can't decide to just skip it, because it would backfire so hard...
The Base:
It looks great and has a nice design, but most importantly the basebuilding stayed pretty much the same.
Sure, you can or rather need to put an engineer to work, to speed up the process, which can be nice but can also be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥if you want to excavate a site, but also want to build something and you don't have enough engineers.
Sure, it makes it harder which is ok, but I didn't really like it THAT much.
UI:
Meh. Just meh, as some people already explained it, you can't access anything without the game having to zoom in on it... it just kills it.
Missions:
Again, pretty much the same as in EU. I liked the Concealment feature, but feel like it could have been more than it actually is. I also like it how they are completely randomized, makes it less predictable but also more vulnerable to bugs.
I didn't actually have any gamebreaking bugs, but many minor ones...
Performance:
Again, meh... although I do have recommended specs (i5 4690k, 8GB DDR3 1600Mhz, HD7970 OC'd to 1100/1500) I can't even play the game on High with a consistent framerate. It only gets worse in the base, where it drops to maybe 15fps on max settings.
Overall visual look:
GREAT! Even on medium it looks really good (when not zoomed in... there it gets kinda ugly-ish). It's not a graphical wonder, but it looks good and doesn't give you eye-cancer.
If you like strategic games, BUY IT.
If you liked XCOM: Enemy Unkown, YOU'LL LOVE IT, SO BUY IT!
If you want to play this game without any problems at all, or just really minor ones, wait half a year or a year and get it in some steam sale.

I love this game. Being kind of a newbie to XCOM and top down stratagy games in general, I was quite clueless when I bought this game, but boy can I tell you, this is worth the price.
Lets start off with the pros-
-Nice graphics
-Permadeath makes it quite a thrill
-Lots of classes (I will go more in-depth later)
-Full modding support
-A story that is endlessly satisfying to complete
-Full character customization (Yes that means you can make your soldiers you ex and get them kills in awful ways
-Pretty good replayability
-Random map design
Now that we got the pros out of the way, lets go to the cons.
-This is my main one, it gets TERRIBLE Fps sometimes, and I have heard that this only happens to certain people, so don't be turned away. Its a bit of a gamble, and it kind of seems random who will get lag. I have read though that they are well on their way to fixing the problem, so hey, it might already be fixed.
-Percentage hitting system that can be quite annoying (For instance twice in my playthrough I missed a 99% hit)
-Missions are almost manditory, and if you don't do some of them, you will lose a part of your resistance force
-Going back to the percentage hitting system, a lot of the game relies on chance. This is not a huge problem for me, because usually I am pretty lucky in video games, but I can see people getting annoyed by this.
-Really basic weapon upgrades. For modifications, you have regular, advanced, and superior, which are all direct upgrades of each other. Same with regular, magnetic, and beam weapons.
Alright, so those were mainly notes. Now lets get a bit more in-depth, starting with the classes.
There are 5 classes without mods who can go down 1 of 2 paths or merge the two, giving them special abilities. You have the:
Ranger, who has a sword and shotgun and can get around quickly. You can build them focusing on their sword, or you can build a sealth ranger, who will sneak around unseen. Hell, as I said before, you can merge the two, making a sword/stealth hybrid
Grenadier, who has a grenade launcher and a minigun. You can level up the grenadier to focus on grenades and defence, or massive damage with your minigun.
Sharpshooter, who has a pistol and sniper rifle. This is my personal favourite class, because you can build them up to get really close, or stay back. If you want to be battle sniper as I call it, you full focus on the pistol, and you can deal some serious damage. If you go regular sniper, you can go on a murder rampage, dealing up to 16 damage shots! (To put that into focus the rangers shotgun with the best shotgun deals around 8-9 damage
Specialist, who can be your field medic, or an anti-robot unit. The field medic is pretty self-explanitory, and the anti-robot specialist pretty much focuses on dealing massive damage or even taking control of enemy robotic units. This class just uses the basic assault rifle.
And then you have the Psi Op, who specializes in MiNd CoNtRoL! This is an extremely strong unit, and when they are fully upgraded they are some of, if not the best class. Unlike all the other classes, you can get every single ability, and you don't rank up by being in the field of battle, but by training in your base.
There is so much more I could talk about, but this review would take me HOURS to write. Its a game thats better experienced, than told about.

Theres a few stuff to know before playing this game
-A few cheaters
-People from far away countries joining your region with 300 ping or more (lately you can even see 999 ping....)

Pros
>Imrpovement from EU/EW: Lots of customization, different languages and voices to choose from
>Classes: They kind of bundled everyone up all nice and neat but they are basically your Heavy, Sniper, Medic, and Trooper classes but each are stylized to fit their needs. Grenadiers blow stuff up, Sharpshooters deal with pistols and sniper rifles, Specialists are Combat Medics/Hackers, and Rangers are your stealthy assault. Psi Troopers are fun, too.
>Enemy Variety: From your basic human-like trooper to enemy Avatars there is enough variety to keep you on your toes. Sectoids haven't changed too much as far as tactics go, Vipers will yank you out of cover, MECs launch rockets but can be hacked but with Psi Troopers ANYONE can be hacked.
>Character Pool: You can save units from one game to a character pool and when you play through another game you have a chance to get your units in another game or recruit them as Rookies.
>Weapons/Armor: There's a lot and combining certain classes with certain armors and loadouts will give you a force that even the most ballsy Berserker will run the other way from. Magnetic Rifles and Exo Suits are fun to play with. It does require a♥♥♥♥♥♥whack ton of research though. Get as many Engineers and Scientists as you can.
>The Avenger: Addons work better, have more upgrading power, it just all fits more seamlessly than a building you can't leave.
Cons
>Bugs Gallore: From graphical bugs to game glitches, no game is without them on the first release. I did find some exploits in the game that can help you along the way but yeah, expect bugs
>Hit Detection: Ever get a critical hit at 1% or a critical miss at 100%? Both times...with the same sniper...
>Multiplayer: It's not that exciting and you can't import your character pool units or customize the ones in your character pool.
>AI: Early in the game the AI (From Vet and up difficulties) takes shifts. It might be another bug but I have had enemies just stand there and do nothing while my units unload bullets into them. Didn't happen on Rookie mode and I played it to the end on Rookie and Vet. Currently going Commander and it's happened twice in the beginning levels. Like I said, might be a bug or a minor glitch but it was kind of like entering a pitbull in a♥♥♥♥♥♥fight.
Final Verdict: If you liked XCOM EU/EW or even if you played the super old XCOM games you'll love this game. I know I did and regardless of what Yahtzee says about it the game is still fun as hell. I just can't wait for the DLC to see what other classes they can add aside from the five they have now. Do yourself a favor and play it to the end and do not skip the final scene of XCOM 2. You'll see what I mean.

If you want to play an RTS game and actually be able to stand a chance against the highest level of AI... While not as good as Age of Empires II, Age of Empires III is severely underrated for just how good it is. I'd recommend it to any gamer, RTS player or otherwise.

I love this game. Being kind of a newbie to XCOM and top down stratagy games in general, I was quite clueless when I bought this game, but boy can I tell you, this is worth the price.
Lets start off with the pros-
-Nice graphics
-Permadeath makes it quite a thrill
-Lots of classes (I will go more in-depth later)
-Full modding support
-A story that is endlessly satisfying to complete
-Full character customization (Yes that means you can make your soldiers you ex and get them kills in awful ways
-Pretty good replayability
-Random map design
Now that we got the pros out of the way, lets go to the cons.
-This is my main one, it gets TERRIBLE Fps sometimes, and I have heard that this only happens to certain people, so don't be turned away. Its a bit of a gamble, and it kind of seems random who will get lag. I have read though that they are well on their way to fixing the problem, so hey, it might already be fixed.
-Percentage hitting system that can be quite annoying (For instance twice in my playthrough I missed a 99% hit)
-Missions are almost manditory, and if you don't do some of them, you will lose a part of your resistance force
-Going back to the percentage hitting system, a lot of the game relies on chance. This is not a huge problem for me, because usually I am pretty lucky in video games, but I can see people getting annoyed by this.
-Really basic weapon upgrades. For modifications, you have regular, advanced, and superior, which are all direct upgrades of each other. Same with regular, magnetic, and beam weapons.
Alright, so those were mainly notes. Now lets get a bit more in-depth, starting with the classes.
There are 5 classes without mods who can go down 1 of 2 paths or merge the two, giving them special abilities. You have the:
Ranger, who has a sword and shotgun and can get around quickly. You can build them focusing on their sword, or you can build a sealth ranger, who will sneak around unseen. Hell, as I said before, you can merge the two, making a sword/stealth hybrid
Grenadier, who has a grenade launcher and a minigun. You can level up the grenadier to focus on grenades and defence, or massive damage with your minigun.
Sharpshooter, who has a pistol and sniper rifle. This is my personal favourite class, because you can build them up to get really close, or stay back. If you want to be battle sniper as I call it, you full focus on the pistol, and you can deal some serious damage. If you go regular sniper, you can go on a murder rampage, dealing up to 16 damage shots! (To put that into focus the rangers shotgun with the best shotgun deals around 8-9 damage
Specialist, who can be your field medic, or an anti-robot unit. The field medic is pretty self-explanitory, and the anti-robot specialist pretty much focuses on dealing massive damage or even taking control of enemy robotic units. This class just uses the basic assault rifle.
And then you have the Psi Op, who specializes in MiNd CoNtRoL! This is an extremely strong unit, and when they are fully upgraded they are some of, if not the best class. Unlike all the other classes, you can get every single ability, and you don't rank up by being in the field of battle, but by training in your base.
There is so much more I could talk about, but this review would take me HOURS to write. Its a game thats better experienced, than told about.

You see, when I first heard of Stardew Valley, I thought it was some farming simulator on an alien planet.  My description of it was "Farmville except on another planet".  I kept seeing "Overwhelmingly Positive" on the Steam page and I thought "I guess nearly everyone enjoys farming sims, huh".
Then I went to my friends house and watched him play the game a bit, and bought the game the instant I came back home.
It's been almost 10 years since I've genuinely enjoyed a video game.  There was Super Mario Sunshine back when I was 7, Sonic Adventure 2 when I was 8, Super Mario Galaxy when I was 10 and my first CoD game when I was 11.  Right then and there, I don't think I could say I enjoyed another game afterwards.  Sure, there were games like Undertale, but I enjoyed the story more-so the game itself, and there was CSGO, but that was because I played with friends.
Then along comes Stardew Valley, and it meets quite literally, down to every exact detail, all the things I could ever possibly expect out of a Legendary tier game:
- Story
- Genuine progression
+ Great progression flow
- Lots of things to do
+ Each of these things are very detailed (Nothing is in the game with little to no meaning)
- Characters WITH character
+ Lovable characters
++ Quite literally :^)
- Beautiful graphics that could run on almost any computer after 2010
- Perfectly challenging (Simple enough to keep the game fun, but challenging enough to keep you feeling accomplished)
- Doesn't demand too much of your time (Not addictive, but also not a game you would stop playing and forget about)
- Accepts players who prefer any type of other game (I'm personally more into FPS' and VN's, but here I am.)
- Very low price for the massive amount of playability
And I'm sure there are other things I'm missing.
There is almost no reason NOT to get Stardew Valley.  I mean, you can marry a handful of the characters, too.  How awesome is that?
Everything is flawless in this game, and there are more than enough things in the game to keep up with.  Sure, I won't be getting my FPS action in this game, but that's where the non-addictive part comes in.  This game is one that you can always come back to not out of a sense of obligation, but out of a sense of "I want to have fun right now and relax, let's play Stardew Valley!"
This game could probably cure depression.

There's a loaf of puns to find in this game - I love it.
The controls are somewhat simple, though it can get challenging depending on how fast and how much control you have over movement at a given time.
You can choose to challenge yourself or go about solving levels (at least the story ones) in an easy way. The tutorial gives a simple overview, but can teach you a couple things, though it also leaves out some stuff; such as flying (which I find to be the "easy" way to finish a level and get a non-'E' level rating). The complaint I have about it is that it doesn't tell you how useful gripping items can be; if you're on a skateboard, locking a hold is important for movement (and the locked grip vs manual grip actually acts differently)
If you've played surgeon simulator and liked it, I would guess you'd like this game a lot. I found Surgeon simulator to be difficult and hard to master (I never really did master it), but I am Bread accepts people of all skill levels (There is magic marmalade that makes you invulnerable to death for a level - this comes up after continually failing a level without quitting). There is also a chronograph that keeps track of how long it took you to finish the level, and an "edibility" scale; burning toast lowers this, resulting in a lower score, as does hitting the floor, walking into bugs, going onto bird poop, etc.
The game seems absolutely silly, and it is, but the developers did a very good job. A somewhat notable gameplay issue occurs when objects get "stuck" in you. While a rare issue, it can also cause the bread to stretch to awkward dimensions and end up flinging you somewhere you don't want to go.
I would say this game is pretty unique; it has an aBUNdance of puns, you play as a slices of bread, and you have to navigate around dangerous areas while keeping track of your gripping power.
The developers seem to have spent a pretty enormous amount of time working on the game, and it has ended up as being a really fun and unique game.
If you see this game on sale, or have a coupon for it, I would definitely get it. At full price, it is still a pretty good deal, though the amount of time you get out of it may not be enough for some people. I would say it's a good game to have as part of a selection of games; It would be hard to play this and only this because being bread has its frustrations.

This is a huge wall of text for this review, Before people say "OH DIS GAEM IS ONLEH GRINDIN EEEEFLBFLBFLFBFLBFLBFLBF" Everyone who plays this game knows that, We love the game because of it because it drives us to get better stuff. Now sit back and read this Wall of China esque text.
Trove is a Sandbox massively multiplayer online role-playing game developed and published by Trion Worlds. The game was released on Microsoft Windows on July 9, 2015.
On Launch Day, the game was launched with issues of queue wait, in response the admins to restart the servers three times. Some players were also unable to join Club Worlds or login to the game, But eventually they fixed that issue and the game was much more enjoyable after that point.
The player assumes the role of a Trovian of multiple classes, There are 13 classes within Trove. Currently, these are The Lunar Lancer, Tomb Raiser, Boomeranger, Pirate Captain, Shadow Hunter, Ice Sage, Candy Barbarian, Neon Ninja, Dracolyte, Fae Trickster, Gunslinger, the Knight, and the Revenant. Each Character has their own strengths and weaknesses making the play style for each varied.
Most classes are designed to resemble a particular Biome whilst others are said to be "Roamer" classes which do not originate from any particular biome, according to in game lore.
Each Character has a selection of unique abilities which unlock within the first few levels of play. Each Character has a main attack, secondary attack, unique passive ability, and 2 extra skills which can be triggered when desired and have in built cooldowns, limiting their use. The Unique passive ability allows the class to utilize their class mechanics, for example the Tomb Raiser class obtains charges called 'souls' either when a set period of time has passed or when an enemy is defeated. The Tomb Raiser can store up to 3 of these charges at any one time and can expend them using their secondary attack ability to summon NPC character minions to help him in combat. Each classes mechanic is unique and allows for a variety of play styles.
There are houses, They are very mobile via signs. These are called "Cornerstones" they are homes of a Trovian where they do their basic things like crafting, forging and Loot Collecting and the other sorts. Other Trovians can walk in to your Conerstone and use your things, But not take your items. The Cornerstones are not like Safe Havens, Monsters of the world can walk in to your Cornerstones.
I know most of you people like having costumes and stuff on your characters, Your Trovian's can have that too! Any Weapon, Hat or mask that is placed in the craft station known as the Loot collector, will be destroyed but the style of that item will be added to the players library allowing the player to choose to use that items image as a vanity, instead of the item currently equipped. This applies to masks, hats and weapons only. The new image only affects the appearance of the character and provides an altered visual appearance only. Additionally any item which is destroyed in the loot collector also provides the player with resources, useful in upgrading other items or in crafting.
Players can also alter their characters' face, skin and hair styles using The Barbershop without limit, penalty or cost, which can be crafted or found at the Hub zone.
This allows for great variety as each player can customize their characters appearance to a high degree.
The Hub zone is the central Zone in Trove and acts as a meeting place for all players as well as a way of accessing the lower level worlds until players are able to craft their own world portals.
The Hub also includes a selection of crafting stations and an NPC who sells items used for fishing, an in game semi-profession, and sailing.
Each world zone contains various biomes that focuse on a specific theme. These include Neon City, a world with structures designed to resemble a fictionalised image of the insides of a computer, Highlands, designed to resemble fields and forests, The Fae Forest, a dark fairy tale like zone and many, many others.
Each biome is connected seamlessly to each other and each world zone is open world in its construction allowing players to travel from biome to biome seamlessly within each world zone.
The biomes themselves each have their own unique NPC enemies which will attack the player if they get too close, as well as their own unique flora. One of the main features of each biome is their themed dungeons. For example the Candoria biome, a theme based on sweets, chocolate and other such items can have dungeon's shaped like giant cakes, gumball machines or a myriad of other themed objects related to the biome.
Each dungeon contains a single 'mini-boss' who upon defeat rewards the player with a large amount of experience, and causes the spawning of a reward chest. The chest contains 1-3 items which are usually the matching quality of the zone but have a small chance to be of higher quality as well as various other resources useful to the player.
There are also large dungeons which appear less frequently than normal dungeons and can have 2 'mini-boss' encounters each with their own reward chest and one main boss encounter who is significantly harder but has significantly better rewards.
Clubs are like Guilds, But they have their own world! The Club world is a zone without dungeons or enemies and is meant to be a central meeting area for members of the club. The Club leader and any other member of sufficient rank can freely build within the zone and can place items normally only placeable within player built homes. Additionally there are some items which can only be placed in Club Worlds.
Players can instantly travel from anywhere within the game straight to their club world.
Club chats allow members within a club to chat to each other. The club chat is accessed through typing "/c#" in chat
Initially the Club world consists of a small island complete with grass and trees. The Island is surrounded on all sides by a unique biome called the Sea of Regret which, when entered, is harmful to the players. However, players can built and deploy devices which, when activated, can convert areas of the sea into additional land mass. This allows players to increase the size of the Club World as desired.
Players may join up to a maximum of 5 clubs at any one time.
The Community is generally very nice and helpful to new players, But to those who spam the chat asking stuff like "HOW DO I CRAFT!?!?!" will just get Ignored and Reported for Spam. So if you want to ask people stuff, Don't spam.

Well, it got a long way to go but from what i played it has ALOT of potential
First off, this IS NOT a space sim, don't come in thinking its Elite dangerous or the X Series, its not.
Rather what we do have is a very interesting twist on the MOBA genre.
Lanes are replaced with sectors of space, classes with different ship types and towers with space stations.
You capture resources bases in sectors of space for resources, that are spent on upgrades to level your ship in game. These are all very basic and I will assume what you spend will be expanded in the future, like upgrading just your engines  or buying stronger lasers etc. Right now thats all stat based.
Loadouts are very basic at the moment with only a few options for weapons and abilites.
There are 6 ships out as of now, but all have a unique playstyle and can counter each other, for example assassins have a inital advantage vs flagships due to there long range weapons, but up close a flagship will be able to do much more damage.
The performance sadly is were this game falls short, I have a GTX 760 and 8GB of ram and im struggling, but im sure this will be patched out in time.
TL;DR Very interesting MOBA style space game, wait for more patches before you buy.

Ok, where do i start... without spoiling to much ofc. :)
probably wall of text incoming so be aware:
I have just finished (and started a new one O.o) my first campaign on normal difficulty and had my share of fun the whole time. the Final battle was challenging enough and left me with a satisfying end but also intresting little cliffhanger. all in all the ending was well done and not as weird as in its predessecor is what i can say now so far.
First on, XCOM2 is quite an eyecatcher in my oppinion. the cities and different terains you see during your fights are well made. Fighting uses the known mechanic from the previous xcom game which is: move and attack, just attack or use support skills like 2x healing etc while you try to keep your soldiers in good cover and flank the enemy. one new thing that XCOM2 gives the player is the concealment mechanic. unless youre not launching a counterattack for some alien assault on civilians, you start the map always concealed. which gives you quite the advantage and makes it easier to set up traps but you need to be aware of being spoted by enemy patrols or even civilians if you dont walk careful around the map.
Even you are a XCOM veteran or not i recommend you to play the turorial since its well done and gives a good start on how to play and also comes up with a nice surprise :)
however, in the begining of your campaign, the game can be somewhat unforgiving and frustrating since you start ofc with crap gear and need to catch up with research new stuff while your soldiers hopefuly rank up and get new abilities. once you even that out some, you can more enjoy the battles and try various tactics to win over the aliens.
For me it seemed, getting closer to the end, the fights where sometimes to easy.
once you know how to fight the all the different aliens its not a big deal to kill a sectopod (mech like alien unit) during one turn.  but it seems to be quite random within various parameter, depending on the map setup since the map is generated at the start of your first turn and will be different every time you fly to the same mission location. to give you an idea, the various missions range from simple seek and destroy to hack enemy data terminal and free or even catch/kill VIP persons.
most time, all this need to be done within a turn limit of 8-12 turns per mission. alot people arguing about it makes the game unfair but serious, this isnt a TB trade sim. without a little pressure from the limited turns, the game would be just like a walk in the park and then leave you with a boring game experience without any challenge. but iam sure there are mods around if you want an easy peasy game.
back to  flying, your home base is now not a stationary "bunker" it is a big old alien "hovercraft" called the "Avenger" (somewhat like those huge carrier from the avenger movie if you know what i mean) which you move over the world map to reach all the different locations. you can upgrade your ship with new rooms like a base but your technican will have to remove obsolete alien tech first to make space for those. that gives you some ressources as well btw.
during your playtime you are able to free advent occupied territory to gain more supplies every month which is your main currency together with information points.
while days and week passing, you need to be aware of the mysterious avatar project the aliens trying to finish. once its done that means game over for the resistance and you dont want that to happen! every few weeks there will be "dark events" you need to attend to. there you have a way to slow down the avatar project and delay or prevent other anoying events from affecting your campaign.
One last point here: since the last patch that was applied before this review was made i experienced  more graphic stuttering during cut scenes because of bad performance then i had before the patch. and i even had to restart my game during final battle when the whole textures in the game went mad and painted everything pink.
but this was the only major negativ experience i had.
everything went normal again after restart and gave me a  satisfying final =)

Of the numerous silly physics simulators, this one is the most artificially difficult and has the worst actual physics implementation: most movable objects will cause you to spaz out and possibly get launched across the level when you grab them, and your slice of bread has *way* too much mass -- I was able to hold a floor lamp by the lightbulb and Jerry Lewis it around the room with just my wiggling movements. That's one thing if I'm holding like an empty box, but a metal lamp? Few things behave like you expect them to, making each level less of a physics sandbox/puzzle and more of a trial and error hellscape. The final straw is the controls: mouse+kb is almost unusable, but you can rebind the keys, while a gamepad works pretty well, but is not rebindable -- so have fun with the god-awful default binds: you have to keep your fingers on the triggers *and* bumpers the whole time. This basically limits your gameplay time to 10-20 minutes, as any more than that will turn your hands into arthritic claws permanently.
There are things to like about this game, but I wouldn't recommend spending more than $5 on it, and only then if you have a soft spot for goofy physics games. If they ever patch the physics to be less broken, it could be great, but as it stands, the physics are just too unpredictable.

Whenever someone asks for gear, if they offer energy, no matter how tantalizing it may seem, don't do it.
If you want your crowns to mean something, then use those instead of trading for energy. Trade a sword for crowns, or use the crowns to buy things. Not energy.
That is all.

Age of Empires 3 takes an already established concept, and expands and improves it greatly.  The game features "cards" -upgrades that you can send whenever you reach another experiance tier.  Cards allow you to specialize your nations units, which are sharded between all of the nations, with one or two expections.  There are also playstyle differences between nations, with the ottomans getting free yet slow settlers, or the duty settlers costing gold instead of food.  The core gameplay is similar to AoE 2, other then this new card mechanic and trading posts.  Trading posts can be built on trade routes or on Indian villages.  Both of them are worth it.  Trade routes supply you with either resources or exp, and indian villages grant you powerful units and upgrades.
Overall, it is better then AoE 2, the card system is unique, and it is worth getting.

The XCOM series has been a long favorite of mine, and XCOM 2 is an amazing addition with only some slight discomforts.
You really feel indepth with the storyline, as you fight a guerilla style war against this overwhelming alien force. You quickly get attached to your units and want to keep driving the story line forward.
PROS
1. Character Customization is amazing, you quickly get connected to each unit and the game helps give life to each of them.
2. The set of enemies is unique, ever adapting and changing so there is no real dry spell when it comes to combat.
3. The base building has been simplified some so its more streamlined, brings in the addition of set engineers and scientists with names so its no longer a numerical value.
4. Cutscene and storyline is enhanced from the previous XCOM
CONS
1. Timers, Timers and more Timers. All missions seem to have this set time until completion which means that the usual strategy is to bum rush the objective and just charge through enemies.
2. The enemies, are annoying as hell. It feels as if they came is diliberatly trying to screw you over. Most have Huge AOE attacks that not only cancel your units attack but also deal damage, while that same unit teleports and clones itself, and thats only on the second mission. Not to mention the tactics is to forget whatever objective they are guarding and just rush your units and deal as much damage as possible regardless of strategy, just to get one of your guys killed.
In the end mods are amazing and fix my complaint on the times ( i understand it and yes it does help add a sense of urgency to the missions, its just i hate EVERYTHING having a mission) but above an amazing XCOM game do buy

If you don't have many games to try or you want something new, how about Spiral Knights?
It's a top-down action-adventure dungeon crawler, in which you fight monsters with swords (obvciously), bombs and guns.
You level up your character as you play and obtain better equipment for your character.
There are four boss raids and many hidden and rare content. Most of them are event-only items.
If you like collecting rare stuff, this game has it all.
The intro for the game is great and levels are really detailed. After that the game loses dynamizm and level are procedurally generated, so there are instances that you'll end up in the same corridor. That's the main thing about the levels. Most of them are made from patterns, so there are a lot of combinations, but in-game you feel that's the same level. The music is really memorable and atmospheric. I can't forget the Jigsaw Valley and the menu music.
Because it's a F2P game, there are instances where packing money is useful, but the only gameplay changing
elements are weapon slots. You can also buy weapons and armor, but that's only for quicker progress. And here is my issue with the game:
Around Tier 3, you HAVE TO upgrade your equipment in order to continue the game. And the orbs required to craft them are really rare and can go for thousands of crowns. If you are lucky, you'll get there eventually. I had no luck and after two months of grinding, I finally got my FIRST 5-star weapon. Now I have to get my armor and a shield. That's another 8 months to spend, but I didn't had the patience to do this all. Soon, the game got boring.
I played this game for around 2 years and I think it wasn't wasted in any bit.
My most proud one is when I attempted the most difficult boss raid designed for 5-star sets. I only got 4 star equipment and I carried my whole 4 member team on my back. They called me the Gordon Freeman of Spiral Knights. That was epic. I died at the final boss, but it was worth it. Tier 3 is pretty challenging. The game gets relatively harder as you play and you can choose harder difficulty for more loot, which is fair.
Get the game, play it for some time. If you like rogue-like games, you'll probably like it.

I have tried to enjoy this game. However, the mechanics of it just don't allow me to. This game is directed towards those who jump around corners and then proceed to "spray and pray". Low-recoil guns have too much of an advantage over guns that the player has to work to control properly. This should never be the case. For those players attempting to use harder weapons, they need to be given the benefit of having an upper hand if they learn how to use harder weapons effectively. This is a dumbed down FPS game for which I cannot determine the intended audience. I appreciate what they're trying to do (create new FPS games), but they're going about it the wrong way. Games do not stay alive without a competitive scene, and this game does not support a competitive scene with the low skill-cap. You can disagree with my recommendation, but I don't see a future for this game. The only redeeming feature of the game currently is that it is resisting being a "pay-to-win" game. However, with every free-to-play game, this is bound to change over time. You're more than welcome to try this game out for yourself, but I will not recommend it. I will continue to play it to see if anything improves, but as of now... I do not find my experience on this game enjoyable.

DO NOT shell out for this until it's in a later, later, later stage of development (For an estimation, I'd say about two years in the least).
At first there's plenty to do (or rather the illusion of such,) with the various materials and planets you can pillage, working towards advancing on the gear scale. However, once you've hit the loot roof, that's it - there's nothing else to do. Building becomes tiresome, and the combat is non-existent. Tackling old bosses has no reward factor. Visiting old tier planets introduces you to a set of cut and paste biomes, with each planet likely having some pre-generated buildings or village. Yes, I realise this is not a handcrafted universe but a generated one - and it shows. None of the planets have any special nuances, and the layouts for things like glitch castles and avian villages don't seem to differ at all. I'd rather eat a small cake that's well prepared than stuff countless, hastily baked cupcakes into my face.
Things do not improve with online play - you are just introducing the same, boring lack of gameplay onto a multi-person stage. The game simply doesn't have the functionality of Minecraft or the soul of Terraria to make it worth coming back to in its present state (and likely for a long, long, long time to come).
Most of the roleplay communities I've visited over the course of my Starbound travels are simply awful, infested with 'demons', early teenagers who too busy roleplaying 'oh we are suddenly in love', or just erotic roleplay. Else, there's simply people making use of the game as a chatroom, imprinting modern day culture on what should be an alien, exotic environment. Granted, this isn't one of the problems I can blame on Chucklefish - independent servers and their populations are out of Chucklefish's control. Regardless, my encounters with those communities have been less than fulfilling, making the prospect of using Starbound as a roleplaying platform grim.
Ultimately, this game at present is just a set of bones which doesn't need anybody else's money being pumped into it. The 12 million Chucklefish already has should be enough to fund their work, but evidently the mistake of giving them dosh before the game's release has fostered a group of indolent, whinging babies, who think they do not need to live up to their promises of FREQUENT updates (thick and fast? an adequate description of the disappointment myself and other like-minded consumers have developed, and with good reason).
At the same time, they're working on other game projects irrelevant to this one, and publishing the games of other developers no doubt so the CF dev team can accumulate more money that they won't use for game development. It's a shame, I like the look of some of these CF published games - but that this excuse-making, undeserving bunch would reap some of the profits makes me kind of physically ill.
IN SHORT: Do not think you are going to get frequent updates, do not think you are going to have a lot to do, and don't expect any (re)playability. The game is so very far from even nearly completed, and Chucklefish's abyssmal management won't solve that soon. Let them use the money they already have to do something with Starbound, rather than whatever they're doing to♥♥♥♥♥♥it away at the moment.
EDIT: Also they need to sort out their launcher so that it closes by itself - I suspect a lot of 'time played' for people is being falsely attributed to them neglecting to close the launcher, even when the main game window is shut down. I had to launch the game from the .exe directly in order to bypass that pesky, misleading launcher.

The XCOM series has been a long favorite of mine, and XCOM 2 is an amazing addition with only some slight discomforts.
You really feel indepth with the storyline, as you fight a guerilla style war against this overwhelming alien force. You quickly get attached to your units and want to keep driving the story line forward.
PROS
1. Character Customization is amazing, you quickly get connected to each unit and the game helps give life to each of them.
2. The set of enemies is unique, ever adapting and changing so there is no real dry spell when it comes to combat.
3. The base building has been simplified some so its more streamlined, brings in the addition of set engineers and scientists with names so its no longer a numerical value.
4. Cutscene and storyline is enhanced from the previous XCOM
CONS
1. Timers, Timers and more Timers. All missions seem to have this set time until completion which means that the usual strategy is to bum rush the objective and just charge through enemies.
2. The enemies, are annoying as hell. It feels as if they came is diliberatly trying to screw you over. Most have Huge AOE attacks that not only cancel your units attack but also deal damage, while that same unit teleports and clones itself, and thats only on the second mission. Not to mention the tactics is to forget whatever objective they are guarding and just rush your units and deal as much damage as possible regardless of strategy, just to get one of your guys killed.
In the end mods are amazing and fix my complaint on the times ( i understand it and yes it does help add a sense of urgency to the missions, its just i hate EVERYTHING having a mission) but above an amazing XCOM game do buy

AFter playing Starbound extensively for a while now, I can safely say that it is probably one of my new favorites, because in my honest opinion Starbound is incredible in every aspect with a few minor short-comings.
+ PROS:
Gameplay: Although accused of being a Terraria clone in terms of gameplay, Starbound is much more in-depth than its counterpart, with more survival elements like requiring warm clothing to avoid freezing to death in harsh cold climates. A lot more RPG elements, like quests, random NPC encounters and a ton, (I mean like Borderlands-level here) amount of loot to find in the various dungeons scattered around the planets that dwell within the solar systems. More weapon variety and an open world that's a lot less linear.
Soundtrack: You have to hear it yourself, all I can say is that the soundtrack is beyond amazing.
Graphics: The graphical level of Starbound is your typical indie game affair and even though I believe the retro style has been done to death, Starbound sets itself apart from others with a unique science fiction/fantasy art style and I have to say that the sci-fi and fantasy elements within the aestethics merge perfectly here.
Lore: The lore of Starbound is quite simple, Earth is basically a wreck and you have to find a new home, although the various logs, books and journals you will find in the game world go a lot deeper in terms of story.
- CONS:
Running issues: Now I'll admit my PC isn't a beast, but when it can max out games like Borderlands 2, Far Cry 3 and Sleeping Dogs yet still gets FPS drops in this game, I'd call that an issue. Although, FPS drops only occur every so often so I wouldn't consider this a particularly huge issue.
Over all, Starbound is a great experience and I highly recommend it.

My opinion about the game overall:
If you were expecting a funny/punny review then you came to the wrong review. I decided to make an actual helpful/serious review for the game. Let me start off saying this is a really great game and is a real and serious game despite looking like a joke, back when I saw this game in Greenlight I laughed and gave it a vote expecting it to be a game that wouldn't even get to a full release, when it first came out my friend bought it so I went to his place and played it for a few hours, after playing it a few times I decided to buy i. Aas it got more and more updates it got better. A lot of people say the game is hard to play with a keyboard but I disagree, back when I first played the game I didn't have a controller so I played it with a keyboard, after a while, I got a controller, and the only thing that was hard about playing with a controller was that sometimes I got confused with the buttons' names, overall it's better with a controller. Awesome game, they really put a lot of work to it and listened to the community throughout the making of the game.
Cons and pros:
+Remappable keyboard controls
+Changable sensitivity
+Graphic options also pretty customizable
+Great graphics
+Great support from the devlopers of the game in issues you might run into
+Achievements
-Controls can take time to get used to
-New players can sometimes be annoyed by the game's challenge but that's pretty subjective
Gamemodes:
Story mode: At the beginning of each level you are presented with some sort of letter about an insane guy who's also the house owner, you finish reading it or skip it and you then spawn as a  piece of bread at the start of the level, at some levels you have extras you can add to yourself like jam and butter which have some side effects. You travel through the level possibly using various objects on the way to eventually get to the toaster or pan or whatever else you want to fry yourself on, in most levels there is more than one way to toast yourself. You get a grade based on your edibility, tastiness and possibly your time but I'm not sure about that, grades are from A++ from F(you only get f if you didn't finish the level). Story mode is overall challenging and my personal favorite. There are 8 levels in the story mode game mode.
Bagel Race: In this gamemode you spawn as a bagel in a different spawn than your spawn points at Story Mode, you need to run through the map using 3 and 4 keys(by default assuming you're using the keyboard) and the mouse and pass through checkpoints on the way to the end, you get a grade based on how fast you completed the race. There are 8 levels in the bagel race game mode. You have no edibility in this game mode.
Rampage: In this game mode you play as a baguette. In this mode your goal is to cause as much damage as possible to various objects around the level, the more damage you cause the better grade you are gonna get. You have multiplier for everytime you smash a few things at once. You have no edibility in this game mode. Rampage has 8 levels. You have a time limit at this game mode.
Cheese hunt: In this game mode you play as a crackbread. In this game mode you spawn as crackbread and start wandering around to find cheese and touch it so it sticks to you, as far as I know there are 5 pieces of cheese in each level. you lose ediblity by falling and/or hitting something too hard. You have no time limit in this game mode. There are 8 levels to Cheese Hunt.
Zero G(ravity): In this game mode you play as a slice of bread. This game mode is pretty much the same as the regular gamemode only there isn't gravity and you need to fly around with jets attached to you. I cannot explain the controls to this game mode as they are very complicated to explain, the main difference from the main game mode is that your grade is also based off the amount of fuel you've used up(You have infinite fuel, you use up fuel when you use your jets). You have edibility in this game mode, you lose ediblity when you touch the floor as far as I know. There is no time limit in this game mode. There are 8 levels to Zero G(ravity).
I'll edit this to explain about the gamemodes left soon.

My wife, siblings and I play this all the time, and have been on a rather consistent basis for upwards of a year. The gameplay is quite balanced, as each civilization has their own unique strengths and weaknesses.
Connecting a multiplayer game across the web is an absolute nightmare; I host my own Minecraft and Terraria servers all the time, but this game refuses to cooperate for more than two people. The only way we've been able to do it is via Hamachi, and by overriding the IP address the game uses in a txt file. Unfortunately this disables internet play, but we don't use that at all.
Despite the half-baked multiplayer connection functionality, the game itself is extremely immersive, and the computer AI poses a fun challenge for all of us. This is an excellent pick for anyone who enjoys RTS games, and comes with a little bonus of historical figures tossed into the mix.

What I love about this game is that it gives the player so many elements to control, but remains at the same time fundamentally unpredictable.
You can feel like you do everything right in terms of upgrades, provisions for a quest and curing of your party members' various ailments (there are likely to have many, and getting rid of them comes at a price) - then you start a mission and two of them die. Just like that. And there is no saving them.
The art is beautiful and the basic mechanics are easy to understand (there are some useful tips embedded in the game), but there is a good level of "complexity" that prevents it from getting boring. Every dungeon is different, and that keeps it interesting. It can also get a little frustrating when everything seems to go wrong, but that's part of what makes this game so unique.
The narration, while a little repetitive, is amazing. Overall I have no complaints about this game aside from the fact that combat has, of late, seemed to have gotten a little easier. But maybe I have just been lucky!

XCOM 2 is, ultimately, more of the same.  Did you like Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within?  You'll like XCOM 2.  Did you like Long War for either of those games?  You'll like XCOM 2, but probably find it a little bit threadbare at some points.
XCOM 2 is still host to an array of bugs and performance issues, though Firaxis has been hard at work on them and I've definitely seen better performance in recent play than in the first week.
XCOM 2 is still maddeningly random at times, just like the previous titles.  After playing Hard West, it's something I'm not convinced the genre needs or something that necessarily even adds anything fun to the game.  But modding will, hopefully, give us a lot of options towards tweaking the game to be how we want it.  It's already quite possibly to do simple numbers adjustments by directing edting the game's .ini files, though I'm not sure how that will affect things in multiplayer.
I haven't been able to get my friends to play multiplayer with me yet, but the setup seems a bit more robust than in EU/EW.  That's good, because I always thought that XCOM multiplayer could end up being a lot of fun.  I guess we'll have to see, huh?
It's worth buying at the regular $60 if you're a fan of the series or the genre.  People who aren't fans of the genre can probably wait until it goes on sale, or may skip it entirely.  XCOM, like many games in the turn-based tactical genre, seems to be a love it/hate it kind of game.  If you aren't sure you'll love it, it might be worth waiting a bit.  For me, though, I don't regret buying it three days after release, bugs and all.

== Review Based on 13/12/2014 version of the game ==
Fractured Space is just excellent as a concept, I love the idea of cap ships just slugging away at one another.
The game feels incomplete but the core game mechanics are a Lot of fun in its current state; well worth the really low price.
Here’s the good;
•	Core game mechanics are in place and they are fun. The combat is immensely satisfying, intense, kills feel good and deaths don’t feel cheap.
•	The game has a strange, methodically slow pace to it. You are encouraged to think laterally and plan manoeuvres – some may complain about this but I think it is a very good thing.
•	The verity of ships and different roles they play all feel significant, no one ship ‘feels’ gimped, all have their strengths and weaknesses.
•	The devs are proven and have a clear plan for development of this title.
There are a couple of caveats at the moment though;
•	The game does not currently support pre-made teams; this will be a problem if you want to play on the same team as your friends.
•	You will feel the FPS drop on occasion – this is fairly normal for a game in development, optimisation will come with time.
•	While the core game mechanics are (mostly) done and really quite fun, a lot of the meta – inter-match gameplay and higher level mechanics are currently missing, this makes the game feel incomplete and may be a deal-breaker for many. To those people I’d highly recommend waiting and seeing what happens as development progresses.
•	Those who don’t like Dota style 5v5 3-lane combat may be put off as the game appears to draw some influence from the likes of Smite.

I really enjoy this game, it is an improvement on almost every aspect of 2012 re-imagining. However, there are some aspects which may put you off of buying it.
Pros:
- New procedural maps are awesome. The system they used makes it so you can't just cheese your way through a map while playing ironman, while also not doing stupidly random design placements like streetlights inside of a mall.
- Soldier classes are well balanced. Soldier types in EU had quite a few skills that were must-haves compared to the alternative (Flush vs Rapid Fire, HEAT Ammo vs Rapid Reaction etc). Here the options for your soldiers are much better, as they can drastically change the way you play with any given class (Medic vs Combat Hacker, Swordsman vs Ninja Shotgunner etc).
- Aliens types are very cool as well as varied. No two aliens are really the same and each one requires a different tactical approach to both survive, and defeat it.
- Base building and Geoscape are are vastly improved. It's no longer a case of needing to build a satellite at the 21st of each month and responding to only one alien abduction because no one knows how to build another skyranger. You get supplies for clearing the debris of your ship, which you can use however you feel fit. Once cleared you can insert any building of your choosing, and all have very different effects and provide drastic improvements to both the base, and the soldiers abilities in combat. Geoscape is also a different view on overall tactics, basically now you are attacking instead of defending and can choose how and where to attack the aliens.
- The moddability in this game is incredible, and already the modding community is coming out with excellent mods ranging from camera improvements to grenade damage overhauls to new hats.
- Actual fighting of the aliens is now even more intense, with new mission types and objectives differing from the classic "kill all aliens" seen in the last game, really driving home the new theme that you are a resistance movement countering the alien invaders schemes.
Cons:
- You are CONSTANTLY getting stopped in the middle of scanning within the geoscape by an alert telling you about a new opportunity. This can get really annoying as there is never a 3 day lull where you can just scan the area to get your supplies without the game fully stopping you with an alert message saying something can be done somewhere else. This can be argued that the amount of content in the game is overflowing, however the game doesn't need to fully stop your progress to tell you about it, a nice little note on the bottom right would have sufficed.
- Where are the UFO's? I get this is a resistance movement and you don't really have an opportunity to shoot down big battleships but.... why not? Let's have the ability to strap some aerial weapons on the avenger and risk the ship to take some of the larger UFO's down. As it stands, you only really encounter one UFO breaching mission per playthrough, and its the equivalent of a medium UFO from the last game.
- Alien appearances. The aliens in this game for some reason don't come fast enough, I had fully upgraded equipment by the time Chryssalids started showing up, at which point they were cannon fodder. Not to mention the Gatekeeper, which I saw twice outside of the final mission.
Mixed Feelings:
- Timers. I like them, It makes me adapt and create a whole new plan of attack for an operation, especially if its a prison rescue. However, I do get that some people find them very unnatractive and I can see why, they do force you to take bolder, riskier decisions, something which usually will get you killed in XCOM.
- Story. I loved the way how the story unfolded... right up until the ending. Sort of spoiler: It basically has the same ending as EU with the same cliffhanger, just with a few differences, and the fact that you know why the elders are doing what they're doing.
- Base Defence. It's... really not as good as I hoped it would be. They take place outside of the base, so it really doesn't feel any different than a mission where you hunt an objective, it just is a much higher stakes mission. I would have loved something along the lines of a terror mission within the avenger, needing to save your staff from several squads of breaching aliens. As it stands, the missions themselves are ok.

Finally an interesting spaceship-themed multiplayer combat!
Fractured space is a 5 vs. 5 team battle on areas of space that has been divided in various sectors. All sectors have control points you need to capture in order to advance and eventually make your way to enemy base. During combat you can freely fly in the battlefield, warp into sectors where the combat is currently going on and warp back to base to regroup or to run away with your nearly destroyed ship for repairs.
There's currently 15 different ship types in game, 6 of them unlocked right at the start. Ship types fit for many roles: long range, hard hitting sniper boat, heavily armored flagship for more close range combat, sneaky & stealthy assassin ship, fast moving frigate etc. As the game is currently in it's early stages, it understandably might have some balance issues between various ship designs - though I personally feel like every ship has their own use and an organized group will easily take down those solo snipers or assassins who think they can/should be able to kill everything themselves.
All ships have 6 different skills at the start, some more offensive, some more defensive. As you play and get more experience, you can unlock more skills and customize your ship's loadout. There's currently 2 different crews to choose and it looks like you could probably fine tune the crew skills in future too, though I'm not 100% sure of that.
There aren't currently any tutorials, tips or guides in-game and everything feels like they're subject to change. Figuring out the skills on the fly is doable, but Steam's community hub has already some starting guides to help you avoid the Trial and Error-method.
Game is very enjoyable, fun and has a lot of potential.

After a couple of matches and having played other space battle simulation games many times before, I have a couple of things to say.
I realize this game is in early alpha. With that said, I would honestly like to see the control system redone. In space, there is no down and no up. The ships in game are strictly anchored to the X,Y, and Z planes with no ability to move otherwise. A good example of this is the game Star Conflict. Instead of playing chase-me-around-the-capture-point, Star Conflict allows players to take cover behind physical structures and move without restriction in any direction and greatly increases maneuvering abilities. Another game which can also exemplify this is Air Brawl. (keep in mind both of the forementioned games are still in alpha and beta stages, and can be downloaded and played for free.)
Again, I understand the game is still in early alpha, and I realize that new features can and will be emplimented, but the control format and limitations are my biggest concerns. At this point, I wouldn't really reccommend the game to anyone with a lot of experience in dynamic motion games. I have faith that it can improve.

What I love about this game is that it gives the player so many elements to control, but remains at the same time fundamentally unpredictable.
You can feel like you do everything right in terms of upgrades, provisions for a quest and curing of your party members' various ailments (there are likely to have many, and getting rid of them comes at a price) - then you start a mission and two of them die.
