PSA ABOUT P2W: I have seen many people complain about how p2w the game is in the reviews here but this is simply not true, this game follows the world of tanks model but is even better than it. First off the ships you get when you go up the tiers are not all around better than others, just more specialized. I see people complaining about how you can buy overpowered ships but in realty only 2 actually exists that you can, and they would be premium tanks going by the world of tanks analogy. here; however, they are exact copies of normal ships off of the main tech tree except they are        un-upgradeable, and if a noob tries to play them they fail, hard. you can also buy normal ships with platinum (gold/money bought currency etc) however you have to unlock them with xp just like everything else and as the experience is locked in a tech tree you normally have the money you want to buy them far before you have the xp.
I have seen some people talk about how the grind is only bearable if you use money but this Is completely false, you can buy boosts with platinum that when applied after a game will increase what you got in the game, but it still relies on what your skill is and the base rewards. these are also single use, unlike world of tanks premium time.
You can also get purely cosmetic skins with it.
why I say it is less so than wot is you cannot make "free xp" with it, as anyone who plays it would know. now on to the review (this was written after I finished)
While some of the ships are designed to defeat others as well as long respawn times and no changing class, it makes it kind of annoying when playing but other than that it is a fantastic game.
EDIT: wow its been a long time since I first made this, time for some more detail.
Fractured space is very fun, while the matches last a long time its gameplay is superb leading towards very fun encounters. There are issues with this game that seem almost impossible for the devs to fix, however. their option to lock the ships into what you originally pick is still a problem, but less so as there are a great deal of them now so the counters that I spoke of in the first review do not really stick as hard. however there are new problems as you cannot connect to a game in progress if someone else disconnects which causes a lot of unbalanced gameplay, framerate is also a problem with your game freezing for a few seconds every minute or so in some lobbies.
The balance in the game also needs a lot of work, you will have those people yell that everything is perfectly balanced and you just don't know how to use it correctly (which is disproven by the fact that 1. the devs aren't gods and 2. every time there is a balance patch it proves that they weren't balanced before.) and the ones who go full retard that say teamwork beats any op ship ignoring the fact that two balanced teams playerwise would be affected. In reality due to the massive update awhile ago balance isn't close to perfect, with some ships suffering immensely as they rely entirely on missiles for damaged that are blocked 100% of the time when someone activates point defense, which can now be on practically forever until you run out of energy which has never even gotten close to happening to me. others such as the protector can completely heal ships much faster than multiple people can put out damage. this may not seem like a big deal at the start as healers are a common theme in these games but due to the fact that they're healing ability is massive and they have a shield that absorbs almost all damage, they are impossible to deal with unless multiple people all attack at once, and if the enemy ships are even semi competent, because you are going after the support they will rip you to shreds. combine this with the fact you cannot change classes and no one can come in once it starts and you have a huge disadvantage if one team has one and the other does not, and while not having a medic should be a bad thing, when there are only a few people every bit of unlockable xp is precious it makes it much more difficult than it should be.
Im sure you have heard this from every review and that is the grind. due to the problems with the number of ships the majority are locked behind a number of games that while they would be quick for most games suffer due to the time of the match, this leads to playing the same ships over and over until you can get ones that you like, however unlike what most say this is not a huge pain as the starter ships are very well rounded and teach you the game. I myself have been playing practically all pioneer since the major update and despite what people say about it being♥♥♥♥♥♥I have a damage ratio of over 2. I am disappointed that they took away a lot of the ships I had with only a few tiny boosts and skins as rewards but it should not impact your decision to buy the game, and I understand why they did it.
once I got through slamming the bad behind this game you have to ask why do I still recommend it?the reason is when this game does good, it really shines. I have been here since there were 6 ships (on a side note please change the name of the "ghost" back to assassin devs, I mean I can understand changing things generic as flagship and sniper but assassin sounds so much better) and what kept me hooked this entire time was this game is fun as hell, from the unique experience of the objectives and jumping, to the intense feeling behind the fights and the thrill of out maneuvering an enemy, this game kicks♥♥♥♥♥ the issues I said above are problems and do take away, but not nearly enough to make me regret buying this and the fun I have had, sure it has problems and due to the nature of the game they are difficult to fix, but seeing how far this game has come I am confident that they will find a way through them, and make it even better.

Let me start off by saying that this game needs a LOT of polish.  Let me also say that it is currently day two of alpha early access, and we've already seen SUBSTANTIAL polish with a patch.
I first heard about Fractured Space by watching a video on Youtube from The Mighty Jingles.  If you haven't already seen it, it's definitely worth a watch.  The dev team behind this game is a hard working machine.  I've been a part of several different alpha tests/early accesses, and I've never seen a dev team put together a patch on day two.  To drive my point home, the newest expansion for Warcraft just dropped, and they're STILL having problems, and Blizzard has an almost infinite number of resources throw at its problems.
All of that being said, if you're a fan of DOTA-types or World of Tanks/War Thunder, then this game will be a definite download.
However...
There are still currently a lot of bugs.  A LOT OF THEM.  I have been playing off-and-on since official early access release last night, and I've only been able to fully complete one match.  This is the nature of the beast when signing on not only to any early access game, but especially one that is this young.  I knew it was going to be like this going in, so please don't take this as a complaint.  The game is MAGNIFICENT.  The gameplay is fantastic, and tactics and patience are well rewarded.
So, should you buy into the early access?  Only if you want to support the dev team as they continue development.  If you are easily frustrated by constant game crashes and unbalanced powersets, then please wait until the game has been developed further.  Also, if you just want to pay to be able to play the game early, you should probably rethink your decision.  I would, at this time, only recommend this game to people who genuinely enjoy testing games in early alpha and having their voices heard by the dev team in order to enhance further development.

Personal Thoughts/What's It Like To Play? :
This is absolutely one of my favorite games. I've never been much of a fan of the Harvest Moon styled games, but something about Stardew Valley hooked me in and didn't let go.
Your options of what you can do are extremely diverse, with everything from farming (of course), to fishing, to fighting monsters in caves.
Even if you tend to do the same thing over and over, there's so much room for personal improvement (before you max out your levels) that your experience is constantly shifting (albeit slowly, at times).
The optional Junimo rewards are not only extremely satisfying to complete (watching those cute little apple creatures jump around in excitement), they're also quite useful in your ongoing quest to become more efficient in what you do.
The characters are fun to talk to, even if they repeat some of their lines. The relationship cutscenes are enjoyable and once again a very satisfying sight.
I think that last part sums up the game very well. While it may tend to be a little grindy at times, every single thing you acheive feels VERY satsifying, no matter how small.
The atmoshpere of the game is very very calming and peaceful. The music is always pleasant to hear, and the sound effects compliment every situation in the game. I can't think of a single noise in this game that has ever startled or agitated me.
-----
Does It Deserve The Hype?
When I purchased this game, I was extremely skeptical. There was a lot of hype about it going on between my friends, and I usually distance myself from hyped things, as they tend to never be as good as the hype makes them sound. While I stayed away from all of the actual gameplay details, all I ever heard was good things about this game. I finally got around to purchasing it after a little bit of "ehhh, should I really? Seems like maybe it doesn't deserve all this hype," but it definitely does in its entirety.
-----
Should You Get This Game? :
If you're just kind of considering getting the game and aren't very sure, you should definitely get it. It's only 15 dollars, so I would suggest purchasing it at full value and supporting the dev, as I would love to see more games where he is in control. If you absolutely hate it, you can just refund it, but I give you a 99% chance you won't even consider a refund.

I can't really recommend the game, though I don't think it's bad. It is just... the Darkest Dungeon, a game that gives me stress-induced nightmares.
This game is great for those old-school turn-based RPG/Crawlers who love to grind levels and upgrade skills. If you loved collecting and composing a squad in Suikoden, for instance, you might like this.
That said, it is INSANELY difficult, even bordering on masochistic. One small slip and you can lose your entire party, basically, and be done with the game from a mental standpoint. I would suggest starting with some of the options put on newb-friendly settings.
If you want to try this game, BE AWARE that you will die a ton, and probably want to die right there at your keyboard. But there is a lot of substance there that might give the very organized and detail-oriented players some fun. Just don't go in thinking there's a story.
***Pros***
Lots of hero/player options. A great mix of available team compositions makes it a worthwhile game for people who like  putting substantial time investment into team setup more than simple hack-n-slash flair. You can choose to buff your group with complementing skills (full-on bleed/stun, Buff ACC and heals, tank with marks, etc.)
Tons of trinkets to use, all of which can be combined based on team makeup.
Artwork is really magical. It's dark and dreary and even whimsical at times.
Soundtrack is equally great, and the narration is top notch.
Feels like a great homage to turn-based RPGs of its heyday. Lots of strategy necessary to be good at the game.
***Cons***
There aren't a ton of tips that are accessible. There's a nifty appendix for terms, but you really don't know what to expect going into certain boss fights, and tool tips and the UI aren't super helpful all in all.
Level 0 dungeons seem just as difficult with level 2+ heroes as level 0. And level 3 heroes simply won't even go into level 0 dungeons...
The team composition interface could use some serious buffing, as organizing it is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
Quirks and afflictions are never really explained, but they are important. When you level up or finish quests, you are sometimes given positive or negative quirks. Which seems entirely DUMB AS HELL. You put in the time to level up, and you're given some bogus -20% resistance to bleed, or worse? DUMB. DUMB. DUMB.
There are crates and other items in the dungeon hallways, but they aren't all good. Actually, I find that they're almost always 50/50. Either you get screwed with blight, bleed, or stress, or you get some heirloom that becomes money and can be used for upgrades to your town. Depending on your team comp, you might altogether skip opening these.
As youre grinding, you're really limited with item use. Unlike other RPGs, you can't pump your HP post-fight with potions (unless you fill up on food, and even then, you can't use that many), so you really have to plan your battles with that in mind. Sometimes extending a victory just to top off your heroes' HP is necessary.
If you don't use torches (you must BUY them as provisions before each dungeon crawl, which is a ridiculous concept since money is a luxury once your heroes need to relieve stress, etc) it becomes much more difficult to survive, especially in medium-length dungeons. Your stress adds up so fast that you can hardly make it through if you screw up. (So BUY TORCHES, NEW PLAYERS!)
Speaing of which, the STRESS element in this game are very obnoxious, and I think the game's true downfall. It mounts up significantly, and for seemingly any reason. If you backtrack in a hallway, you get stress. Hell, walking in a hallway gives you stress, even with full torches, I feel.  If you get crit in combat, you get stress as an entire party. Once someone reaches 50% stress level, you're at their will for the entirety of the dungeon. If they get a very bad case, like "Abusive," you're just going to get berated until everyone is depressed and suicidal, begging to lose.
When you're in town, that stress can be relieved doing various tasks. But it's only based on in-game time, so you must go adventure again with another group before those stressors are removed. This is also obnoxious.
No real story. It takes so long to just level up to the point where any story progression begins, that you forget what happened before it.

While I didn't play for very long, it was like a complication due to the manner in which I was playing (over a verizon dsl network, streaming from a windows 7 pc to a windows 8 laptop). The main problems I encountered were a slow network connection (from the router, not the game), fuzzy graphics that did not want to play nice and display properly on my laptop (likely a result of not configuring them properly on my desktop first, or even having to do with the router again), and dropping from games in the middle of a fight (Which I can blame on verizon, once more, but it may have had to do with the game itself).
Overall, I would recommend this game. The gameplay I did experience had a focus on teamwork, on strategic maneuvering to enable you to appropriately apply the force you had at your disposal from flying a capital ship, and, well, 3 dimensional movement in space combat is always nice.
This game is for you if: You have the patience to play a moderately paced game, are willing to work with your team mates (even if they are strangers), and have been looking for something that focuses on large ship space combat.
This game will not scratch your itch if: you are looking for a game like tie fighter vs x wing. You will not by flying small, fast, fightercraft and engaging in dogfights. And that's okay. There are other games that do that, some in space, some not so much. War Thunder (last I played) did a very good job in giving you planes to fly around and dogfight in.
Overall, it looks like a game with a good amount of potential that has already lived up to a fair bit of it. It's an early access game, so expect bugs, but the features that are already in (from what I've seen) lay out the foundation for a solid game.

Before Half-Life, most first person shooters of the time were just run and gun and find the way out of the maze of the level. Half-Life threw that concept out and set a new level for future FPS's to meet.
Set in the Black Mesa underground research facility in the New Mexico desert the player takes the role of Dr. Gordon Freeman, a MIT graduate in theoretical physics, who is helping do research on teleportation but one experiment goes wrong and opens a portal to another planet whose inhabitants attack and try taking over the facility. All the while, Gordon Freeman’s goal is close the portal and escape alive.
Gameplay is standard fair for a FPS, the player has weapons to shoot and gains a better arsenal as the game progresses. But what set Half-Life apart from all the other games of the time was that Half-Life integrated a thorough storyline that unfolded just as if the player was actually there.
The graphics look blocky by today's standards but was a graphical powerhouse back in 1998 with clear faces of the NPC’s and moving mouths during dialogue all in real time with the game’s engine.
Sound in the game is sparse to convey the idea that the player is stuck in a underground facility but some music is heard during boss or major actions scenes and are quite memorable because of the situations.
In the end Half-Life was a major release that no one saw coming and changed the way other FPS’s, and some other game genres, were made and told stories.
9/10

Updated for alpha version .75
Gameplay: Fairly standard map layout. In the middle there is a buffing station that activates at certain points. On the sides are the Alpha and Beta lanes, each with one forward station for either team and 3 mining bases per lane, which provide exp for the team. The ships move as I'd expect large ships to move - sluggishly. The guns feel responsive, but can be hard to aim at times, especially if you play the assassin. The physical turret models on the ships are where the shots originate from so it is possible to miss a ship right in front of you. The health bar is easily understandable and clear, although I've had to figure out what most of the hud elements mean; top left is the team's level and top right is in-game score. You manually aim the turrets while you fly the ship which, in conjunction with the slow movement/tankiness of the ships, makes for tactical planning and maneuvering to increase your effective dps time and decrease the enemies'.
Ships can level up to level 9 as you garner resources from points your team has captured. The ships are automatically upgraded when flown near a friendly alpha or beta point.
The gas facility is now a buff that affects the entire team and presents itself in 3 stages, Gas Power I, II, and III, each one better than the former. I feel this mechanic blends very well into the game because it is fairly standard MOBA techniques.
Menu: Simple and straight forward, lacks options in general at the moment, but the devs have stated that they will provide every option they have available to themselves. The game has been optimized very well so far and only a few select people lag, usually from the hardware of the computer. The devs love this game as much as I do so so I can only see it going up :D
Community: No one's been rude, possibly because the community is not big enough, but it seems to be growing.
Ships: Eight ships in the game at the moment, dps, ranging from support, small amounts of electronic warfare, an assassin (stealthy with large amounts of damage), and a tank. They will add more ships considering there are already names/plaques for those ships in the store/upgrade menu, as well as more manufacturers. I believe the developers said they are going to expand from the normal way ships work (the way they work at the moment) and create a manufacterer (a line of ships) that is non-human. I can NOT wait to see those to say the least. The smallest ship type so far is a frigate, which has decent maneuverability and is very annoying to deal with, and the largest ship, at ~1.8 kilometers long is the flagship. One hell of a burden to lane against.
The aiming indicator, little red dots that show where each individual turret is aiming, is pretty accurate and easily noticeable. The Disruptor ship, for example, has a secondary crosshair that shows where a turret that fires an ability is aiming.
Extra: There is a tutorial, however it is outdated. Seeing as the game updates every about 2 weeks there would not be a point in redoing a new tutorial every time. The controls are 'move,' 'target,' 'use abilities,' and 'shoot,' so I don't see it as a high priority. WASD to move on the Y and X axes and space and ctrl to move on the Z axis. The devs have said they will add more controls, such as free camera control.
Among the things that will be added are drone defence systems and missile defence systems, which will help in making a Carrier ship. It's a special sight to see when two of the tankiest ships are firing endless amounts of flak at each other. It reminded me of Planetside 2 in the early stages, when they had very glowy tracers at night and it looked much more amazing than it does now. Here's hoping the devs can at least keep that flak in there cause it's shiny.

In summation; a bare bones but for the most part playable tactical spaceship game with a great foundation, that when expanded will truly make some waves.

Starbound is the uber popular 2D sandbox game that takes pages from Minecraft and Terraria. Created by British indie studio Chuckle Fish Ltd, Starbound is more a spiritual successor to Terraria than a clone. Starbound is also very successful with over 1 million copies sold compared to Terraria's 2 Million. Starbound is still in early access and as such some of the things discussed in this review might change.
Players start on a random planet in the alpha galaxy, they have to build a base, find ores and build a distress beacon which will trigger your first Boss battle. Starbound combat is more RPG like than Terraria's. playing the game was a lot like some of the popular Japanese RPG, where Terraria's combat was all about crazy weapons Starbound is more about exploring and combat feels more slow-paced. but that's not really bad. it's just different.
Starbound has a some story unlike Terraria or Minecraft. each race is different and exciting to learn about. The Humans, forced to flee their planet after a monster invasion. The Glitch a robotic race that is stuck in medieval times. the Avian a bird-like race that fight for their god. the Floran, a violent race of plant creatures who are hated by most of the galaxy. the Apex, an Ape like race that is Superior in mind. and the Hylotl a pacifist fish race.
Starbound seems to have looked at Terraira and try to do what it did but better. and in some areas it is. for example in starbound to place a wall all you have to do is right click. and the cool thing about Starbound is that with some many planets out there its hard to see them all. however Starbound's planets can start to get boring after awhile. the only types of planets are Deserts,Forest,Jungle,Moon,snow, and lava. i wish there where more water like worlds. the kind that always rain and stuff. also when on Moons the gravity doesn't seem to change that much. one cool thing in Starbound is the fact that some planets get asteroids that rain down on the surface. the not so cool thing is that these will destroy a good part of any surface buildings you may have built. in Starbound you can place NPC spawners, with this you can spawn guards, merchants and just some friendly NPCs to stay in your base. the NPCs will sit down on chairs, sleep in beds, and chat with each other. it helps to make your world feel alive.
Starbound like Terraria has a lot of furniture and objects you can place to make your house/base look any way you want. and with a unlimited galaxy you have millions of maps to mess around with. also your maps stay with you no matter who you play as. so if you build a base with one person then go make a new character and come back to the same planet the base will be there. the same thing applies for mulitplayer.
Speaking of mulitplayer, Starbound does have multiplayer but because it is in such an early state getting into games can be hard to do. but if you can connect to games the mulitplayer works fine. and allows you to have chaos with your friends.
Like Terraria, Starbound has bosses that can be summoned for you to fight. right now there are only four bosses in the game, but more are on the way. so far i have to say that the bosses are pretty bland. a giant UFO, a Robot, a jelly fish, and a dragon made out of bones. there is a fifth boss in development that looks unique but right now the bosses kinda of suck.
If you enjoyed Terraria or Minecraft then Starbound is a good choice for you. the only thing else i dislike about it is the fact that it sells for $15 during its Early Access while Terraria a fully completed game that is STILL getting new stuff sells for $10.  to be clear Starbound is in NO WAY a "clone" or a "copy" of Terraria, it is a game that was inspired by Terraria but it is its own game

This is one of those rare games that get the definition of "dark and gritty" right. The setting is among the most interesting Dark Fantasy scenarios I've ever come across. The addition of Cthulhu Myth additions in terms of game mechanics and background story give the game that little extra something.
It is always refreshing to a see a game try something new, as is the case with Darkest Dungeon. The art style is unique and suits the overall atmosphere perfectly, whereas the core gameplay element of "human resources" adds to the overall gloom of the game nicely. It should be added that the game features one of the best narrators I've come across so far in my life as gamer, even compared to the expertise of the narrators from Stanley Parable, Bastion or Portal.
As a fan of rogue-like or rogue-lite games, I found myself at home fast. Yes, your beloved characters will get mad and/or die. Yes, you will lose awesome loot. Yes, you will cry manly tears of rage when the game screws you over again and again. But every step forward, be it ever so little, will make feel like a huge accomplishment - and it is. Because this game is hard, but in a good way.
All in all I can only say that this game comes as close to perfection at what it tries to achieve as it can get. It is worth the time and money and does something rarely seen these days: innovate.

tl;dr: great game if you are an xcom fan, but it definitely needs some work.
The difficulty of the game is a bit unbalanced. Aliens progress at random in their conquest against XCOM and the way that you are forced to play certain missions .... or else... is a bit intrusive.  Furthermore is the hit percentage a bit off. Pointblank flanked sometimes dont give the full 100% hit or even a miss. Which is frustrating.
A lot of performance issues and bugs. For instance if your 'my documents' folder isnt installed on the C: drive. You will definitely need google to make sure you are able to save games properly and not run into weird bugs like unwinnable maps. Next to that, even with a gamerig with a 4GB Gfx and 16gb or RAM i cannot run the game smoothly on maximum settings.
Timers, timers, timers... everything in the game is on timers. Which is ok if it was logically. But sometimes it's impossible to counter them. A lot of timed levels like the bomb disposals in the previous version. Because XCOM is being hunted by aliens they need to be faster. Fun detail, but it needs some tweaking.
Why recommend the game?
The game basics are like the previous one. Turn based combat. Different approach compared to the previous version but still good. A bit more variety in levels and randomly generated maps. A lot of mods and very good mod support from the devs. If you played  XCOM Longwar, it definitely feels a bit shallow. So mods are to be recommended.
Customization galore! There are a lot of ways to customize your troopers, which is fun (if you like that stuff anyway).
Like most people, if you like xcom its good. If you like a completely finished game, wait for a bit but that doesnt make the game bad.

Fractured Space plays in the way in which I imagine World of Warships might play if it was set in the future. Giant space vessels clobber each other while trying to take contested space stations to get resources and eventually push the enemy out of their home base. This game sticks to the classic scifi trope that in space everyone is the same way up. Out of battles, the menus are reminiscent of World of Tanks, complete with a crew system, a 'battle button' that instead states "Launch", and the beginings of a tech tree and upgrade system, along with what looks to be the framework of a free to play game. There appear to be be a few different 'classes' of space ship, each with their own abilities, weapons and purpose. I should mention that the game is early access, and does have an 'alpha' feel to it currently, with buggy menus and limited features. If they keep developing this in the right direction it may turn out to be a great game, and I suppose the only way they will manage this will be from the input of their paying 'early accesseers'.
Overall, gameplay is pretty solid, graphics are great (running on the Unreal engine), and there is the tantilising whiff of promise about it which will attract many followers. If it lives up to its potential, and its free to play model is benign (and not pay to win/overpriced), it could well end up being a game to watch out for.

Before Half-Life, most first person shooters of the time were just run and gun and find the way out of the maze of the level. Half-Life threw that concept out and set a new level for future FPS's to meet.
Set in the Black Mesa underground research facility in the New Mexico desert the player takes the role of Dr. Gordon Freeman, a MIT graduate in theoretical physics, who is helping do research on teleportation but one experiment goes wrong and opens a portal to another planet whose inhabitants attack and try taking over the facility. All the while, Gordon Freeman’s goal is close the portal and escape alive.
Gameplay is standard fair for a FPS, the player has weapons to shoot and gains a better arsenal as the game progresses. But what set Half-Life apart from all the other games of the time was that Half-Life integrated a thorough storyline that unfolded just as if the player was actually there.
The graphics look blocky by today's standards but was a graphical powerhouse back in 1998 with clear faces of the NPC’s and moving mouths during dialogue all in real time with the game’s engine.
Sound in the game is sparse to convey the idea that the player is stuck in a underground facility but some music is heard during boss or major actions scenes and are quite memorable because of the situations.
In the end Half-Life was a major release that no one saw coming and changed the way other FPS’s, and some other game genres, were made and told stories.

I can't really recommend the game, though I don't think it's bad. It is just... the Darkest Dungeon, a game that gives me stress-induced nightmares.
This game is great for those old-school turn-based RPG/Crawlers who love to grind levels and upgrade skills. If you loved collecting and composing a squad in Suikoden, for instance, you might like this.
That said, it is INSANELY difficult, even bordering on masochistic. One small slip and you can lose your entire party, basically, and be done with the game from a mental standpoint. I would suggest starting with some of the options put on newb-friendly settings.
If you want to try this game, BE AWARE that you will die a ton, and probably want to die right there at your keyboard. But there is a lot of substance there that might give the very organized and detail-oriented players some fun. Just don't go in thinking there's a story.
***Pros***
Lots of hero/player options. A great mix of available team compositions makes it a worthwhile game for people who like  putting substantial time investment into team setup more than simple hack-n-slash flair. You can choose to buff your group with complementing skills (full-on bleed/stun, Buff ACC and heals, tank with marks, etc.)
Tons of trinkets to use, all of which can be combined based on team makeup.
Artwork is really magical. It's dark and dreary and even whimsical at times.
Soundtrack is equally great, and the narration is top notch.
Feels like a great homage to turn-based RPGs of its heyday. Lots of strategy necessary to be good at the game.
***Cons***
There aren't a ton of tips that are accessible. There's a nifty appendix for terms, but you really don't know what to expect going into certain boss fights, and tool tips and the UI aren't super helpful all in all.
Level 0 dungeons seem just as difficult with level 2+ heroes as level 0. And level 3 heroes simply won't even go into level 0 dungeons...
The team composition interface could use some serious buffing, as organizing it is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
Quirks and afflictions are never really explained, but they are important. When you level up or finish quests, you are sometimes given positive or negative quirks. Which seems entirely DUMB AS HELL. You put in the time to level up, and you're given some bogus -20% resistance to bleed, or worse? DUMB. DUMB. DUMB.
There are crates and other items in the dungeon hallways, but they aren't all good. Actually, I find that they're almost always 50/50. Either you get screwed with blight, bleed, or stress, or you get some heirloom that becomes money and can be used for upgrades to your town. Depending on your team comp, you might altogether skip opening these.
As youre grinding, you're really limited with item use. Unlike other RPGs, you can't pump your HP post-fight with potions (unless you fill up on food, and even then, you can't use that many), so you really have to plan your battles with that in mind. Sometimes extending a victory just to top off your heroes' HP is necessary.
If you don't use torches (you must BUY them as provisions before each dungeon crawl, which is a ridiculous concept since money is a luxury once your heroes need to relieve stress, etc) it becomes much more difficult to survive, especially in medium-length dungeons. Your stress adds up so fast that you can hardly make it through if you screw up. (So BUY TORCHES, NEW PLAYERS!)
Speaing of which, the STRESS element in this game are very obnoxious, and I think the game's true downfall. It mounts up significantly, and for seemingly any reason. If you backtrack in a hallway, you get stress. Hell, walking in a hallway gives you stress, even with full torches, I feel.  If you get crit in combat, you get stress as an entire party. Once someone reaches 50% stress level, you're at their will for the entirety of the dungeon. If they get a very bad case, like "Abusive," you're just going to get berated until everyone is depressed and suicidal, begging to lose.
When you're in town, that stress can be relieved doing various tasks. But it's only based on in-game time, so you must go adventure again with another group before those stressors are removed. This is also obnoxious.
No real story. It takes so long to just level up to the point where any story progression begins, that you forget what happened before it.

Well completed the game (with a few mods that helped improve the vanilla, good news is these do not break achievements).
My thoughts are that the game has taken many steps forward, few side ways and a few backwards.
The graphics and sound are top notch the style looks much better than Xcom and it has a real good feel to it, great customization and presented well. Cut-scenes seem to have been cutdown dramatically, not really needed but in previous game it helped break up the main story missions from the side missions. You don't get that touch this time, not huge issue but some times cinematics can move game forward.
The micro management on the base side has taken a step back and some side ways and few forward. Now people who play strategfy games usually like a bit of micro-management, not silly wasting time micro management, proper management that shows tactics and thoughts, not wasting time sorting poor design.
Well micro management has been simplified, in a few good ways but in some bad ways. The bad ways are the lack of strategy in the base ship, yes you can build rooms in a poor order, but once you have a general idea of the best setup theres not much you can do wrong, theres no different scenerio setups or tactics that you may need to change due to an unexpected event etc.
I just felt this time the micro management had moved at all forward which for me was the last games weakness and now a sequel hasnt built upon its weakness. I think delving into this could have broken the very tight dynamics maybe, but its still a shame.
The in game combat is pretty damn good, lots of tactics can be worked, the timer did not annoy me on normal, but now Im about to up the difficulty I am concerned about it. The mod True Concealment is absolutely perfect and should have been in the beginning of the game, timers only start once discovered, hoping this helps on the harder difficulties with timed runs and helps with a bit more strategy.
Ignore people complaining about timers, yes I dreaded this when I heard the reviews but really you can still plan well, use tactics and cope with the timer. For me on normal it added to the urgency and made me use better tactics and roles. Scouting out is important. But as before mentioned worried about the harder difficulties, timers could be pain if you get caught up in a early fight with many enemies and time runs down.
The RNG is better than Xcom 1 had fewer shots miss then before, never got to annoyed.
Some lovely effects in the game, acid burning upper floors and enemies/players falling through and taking damage, some excellent physics and level destruction for a strategy turn based game.
In all I had a lot of fun and looking forward to more mods and trying Ironman.
Disappointed at the simplicity of the micro-management especially with PC only release.

This. Is. Awesome! This is the best farming simulator I have played in a long time. It's clear that Stardew Valley has drawn a lot of inspiration from other farming games especially Harvest Moon, and I immediately noticed many similarities to Harvest Moon: Back To Nature. Stardew Valley also has some great additions to it.  Memorable characters, check. Challenging dungeons and a combat system, check. Upgradable skills, check. Down to earth music, check. Great 16-bit graphic art, check. Great writing, check. Slime farming… wait who asked for that? Eh, still good, check.  Stardew Valley truly is a masterpiece.
In Stardew Valley, over time more of the world opens up. You get to meet eccentric towns people. You'll be able to befriend a monster. You'll be able to marry with one of the men/women. You can at most have 2 kids in the house which get in your way all the time. You can be lauded or denounced from the towns people depending on how you want to play. You want to poison the governor in a certain event? Go right ahead!  Want to have multiple divorcees? Do it! Or just sit back and relax while you enter a meditative like state while you play the game.
My favorite part of the game was just being able to build up my farm and design it in any way I want. There are some limitations, but I still found designing to be the most enjoyable part for me.
I urge you to buy Stardew Valley if you haven't. You will not regret the money spent here. Happy gaming!!

Well completed the game (with a few mods that helped improve the vanilla, good news is these do not break achievements).
My thoughts are that the game has taken many steps forward, few side ways and a few backwards.
The graphics and sound are top notch the style looks much better than Xcom and it has a real good feel to it, great customization and presented well. Cut-scenes seem to have been cutdown dramatically, not really needed but in previous game it helped break up the main story missions from the side missions. You don't get that touch this time, not huge issue but some times cinematics can move game forward.
The micro management on the base side has taken a step back and some side ways and few forward. Now people who play strategfy games usually like a bit of micro-management, not silly wasting time micro management, proper management that shows tactics and thoughts, not wasting time sorting poor design.
Well micro management has been simplified, in a few good ways but in some bad ways. The bad ways are the lack of strategy in the base ship, yes you can build rooms in a poor order, but once you have a general idea of the best setup theres not much you can do wrong, theres no different scenerio setups or tactics that you may need to change due to an unexpected event etc.
I just felt this time the micro management had moved at all forward which for me was the last games weakness and now a sequel hasnt built upon its weakness. I think delving into this could have broken the very tight dynamics maybe, but its still a shame.
The in game combat is pretty damn good, lots of tactics can be worked, the timer did not annoy me on normal, but now Im about to up the difficulty I am concerned about it. The mod True Concealment is absolutely perfect and should have been in the beginning of the game, timers only start once discovered, hoping this helps on the harder difficulties with timed runs and helps with a bit more strategy.
Ignore people complaining about timers, yes I dreaded this when I heard the reviews but really you can still plan well, use tactics and cope with the timer. For me on normal it added to the urgency and made me use better tactics and roles. Scouting out is important. But as before mentioned worried about the harder difficulties, timers could be pain if you get caught up in a early fight with many enemies and time runs down.
The RNG is better than Xcom 1 had fewer shots miss then before, never got to annoyed.
Some lovely effects in the game, acid burning upper floors and enemies/players falling through and taking damage, some excellent physics and level destruction for a strategy turn based game.
In all I had a lot of fun and looking forward to more mods and trying Ironman.

Starbound is the uber popular 2D sandbox game that takes pages from Minecraft and Terraria. Created by British indie studio Chuckle Fish Ltd, Starbound is more a spiritual successor to Terraria than a clone. Starbound is also very successful with over 1 million copies sold compared to Terraria's 2 Million. Starbound is still in early access and as such some of the things discussed in this review might change.
Players start on a random planet in the alpha galaxy, they have to build a base, find ores and build a distress beacon which will trigger your first Boss battle. Starbound combat is more RPG like than Terraria's. playing the game was a lot like some of the popular Japanese RPG, where Terraria's combat was all about crazy weapons Starbound is more about exploring and combat feels more slow-paced. but that's not really bad. it's just different.
Starbound has a some story unlike Terraria or Minecraft. each race is different and exciting to learn about. The Humans, forced to flee their planet after a monster invasion. The Glitch a robotic race that is stuck in medieval times. the Avian a bird-like race that fight for their god. the Floran, a violent race of plant creatures who are hated by most of the galaxy. the Apex, an Ape like race that is Superior in mind. and the Hylotl a pacifist fish race.
Starbound seems to have looked at Terraira and try to do what it did but better. and in some areas it is. for example in starbound to place a wall all you have to do is right click. and the cool thing about Starbound is that with some many planets out there its hard to see them all. however Starbound's planets can start to get boring after awhile. the only types of planets are Deserts,Forest,Jungle,Moon,snow, and lava. i wish there where more water like worlds. the kind that always rain and stuff. also when on Moons the gravity doesn't seem to change that much. one cool thing in Starbound is the fact that some planets get asteroids that rain down on the surface. the not so cool thing is that these will destroy a good part of any surface buildings you may have built. in Starbound you can place NPC spawners, with this you can spawn guards, merchants and just some friendly NPCs to stay in your base. the NPCs will sit down on chairs, sleep in beds, and chat with each other. it helps to make your world feel alive.
Starbound like Terraria has a lot of furniture and objects you can place to make your house/base look any way you want. and with a unlimited galaxy you have millions of maps to mess around with. also your maps stay with you no matter who you play as. so if you build a base with one person then go make a new character and come back to the same planet the base will be there. the same thing applies for mulitplayer.
Speaking of mulitplayer, Starbound does have multiplayer but because it is in such an early state getting into games can be hard to do. but if you can connect to games the mulitplayer works fine. and allows you to have chaos with your friends.
Like Terraria, Starbound has bosses that can be summoned for you to fight. right now there are only four bosses in the game, but more are on the way. so far i have to say that the bosses are pretty bland. a giant UFO, a Robot, a jelly fish, and a dragon made out of bones. there is a fifth boss in development that looks unique but right now the bosses kinda of suck.
If you enjoyed Terraria or Minecraft then Starbound is a good choice for you. the only thing else i dislike about it is the fact that it sells for $15 during its Early Access while Terraria a fully completed game that is STILL getting new stuff sells for $10.  to be clear Starbound is in NO WAY a "clone" or a "copy" of Terraria, it is a game that was inspired by Terraria but it is its own game

I started playing playing this game some time ago. A little while ago I decided I wanted to go back and re-experience/beat games that I previously played when I was younger. Spiral knights is a game that I always remember for it's character, weapon, and enemy designs. After putting 145 hours in this game I feel like I've given it more than enough time to determine what I like, don't like, and appreciate from Spiral Knights.
What I like.
-Character, weapon, enemy designs
-Simple, easy to grasp and understand combat
-enjoyable visuals and an amazing soundtrack
-The capability for any player to earn the pay-to-win(energy) cash through gameplay(average 10 000 crowns)
-hack n slash style gameplay/weapon combos (one attack button)
-not many top tier items can be purchased through the pay-to-win store
-Weapons being able to level up, gaining more power at higher levels
-unique atmosphere
What I don't like.
-The immense grindfest to get any pay-to-win cash(energy) average missions provide 1200-3000 crowns and take 15 minuets on average(personally with friend/s)
-the immense amount of damage you take. Even with high level high tier armour
-Due to the massive amount of damage you take it becomes more of a strategy/kiting gameplay.
Except the game throws wave upon wave of both disposable and powerful enemies at players.
-the ease that pay-to-win players have to gain high levelled equipment. As leveling up equipment requires materials purchasable through the pay-to-win store.
-online only, you can't play offline to reduce lag
-reviving a second time in any level requires an item called the spark of life. You can buy ten of them for 100 pay-to-win(energy) cash, which is about equivalent to 10 000 in-game/free(crowns) currency. So it's not terrible but also not amazing.
- Armour and weapons cost way too much, both crown and energy-wise. 25 000 for a tier 5 armour/weapon recipe is not bad, but energy the entire weapon costs 3500. You can transfer that energy to get around 350 000 crowns. Which is able to craft many more weapons than the energy purchase would cover.
Anyway, I still enjoy the game. And honestly I'd suggest playing this game if you're willing to invest alot of time grinding, but as I do not have that luxury at the moment I would suggest to try it, but not to attempt to finish it, without alot of time, and/or money investment.

Before I start, let me say that this game has A LOT of potential.
However, its potential is all it has so far. I understand this game is early access, but there are dozens of game-breaking bugs. The in-match menu is literally unusable; you can't click any of the buttons. The game also has a tendency to crash.
I've only played one ship so far, the stealth ship, and the effects of its abilities are partially broken. The ship has a tendency to dissapear completely on the player's screen while cloaking, making navigation pretty difficult. (It should display itself as a wireframe model on the player's screen.) I wouldn't be surprised if other ships shared similar bugs to their abilities. The sound effects are also questionable. And loud.
Additionally, the game mechanics are never clearly explained. There's a hangar and crew that perhaps shares similar function to War Thunder or World of Tanks' system, but I can't figure out how it works (or even if its implemented yet.) There's no tutorial. Is there an in-match shop as there is in League of Legends? I have no idea. There's  no matchmaking. If you want to play with friends, you and your friends have to pick the same server and pray that you're on the same team.
The upside is that the game is very pretty. The controls feel really nice, as do the weapons. But looking at the vast number of drawbacks, I cannot recommend this game in its current state. However, I do think that this review will change to a positive one in the near future when this game gets some patches.
Keep in mind, this is very early access. At this point, you're not paying $10 (or in my case, $20) to play a game; it's more like you're pledging your support. And, I suppose, paying to test their game for them. ...

Ever wondered what is would be like to live life as a slice of bread? Me neither, but thanks to Bossa Studios, the developer behind the hugely successful and painfully difficult Surgeon Simulator, you can now experience life as a breaded product on the ultimate mission, becoming toast in I Am Bread.
Playing an overly adventurous slice of wholemeal, your job is to make your way through multiple environments made up of specific rooms around the house, including the kitchen, the lounge and the dreaded garage. As single-minded as you’d expect a slice of bread to be, your goal is to toast yourself. Where the first level offers you a toaster for the job, you’ll soon realise that a hob or even radiator will do the job just as well.
There is a sinister side to I Am Bread as you learn the true underlying themes of the story. The story of the game is played out in a very subtle way through therapy notes displayed at the beginning of each level and what we learn through the game is that your whole grain adventures are actually driving the owner of the house to insanity as he tries to make sense of the destruction you are causing on your quest to toast. Each psychology report details the poor man’s descent into madness as he leaps from conspiracy theories about “the council” breaking into his house, through to unwittingly discovering the truth that is in fact, the bread’s fault.
The gameplay is fairly easy to grasp though near impossible to fully master, this is one of the hardest games you’re ever likely to play. With controls not unlike Octodad though as frustrating as Surgeon Simulator at times, this is definitely a game for those that are incredibly patient.
Using a controller definitely feels like the easiest way to approach this game, each trigger is assigned a corner of the bread slice and when activated that corner is gripped to the surface. If you prefer the keyboard and mouse approach then the default layout gives you the number buttons 1-4 with the arrows as directional support. You can grip any solid surface, climb walls and larger objects though you are limited to how long you can grip. Lighter objects can be grabbed and moved or even smashed, but the one thing you need to remember to keep your eye on is how edible you are.
A hud monitor at the top of the screen tells you how edible your slice is as a percentage, reach 0% and the level ends, you’ve become inedible. The biggest danger to this is the floor, drop down there and your edible level will drop sharply but that is not the only risk. Fish bones, gone off meat, band-aids and a number of other obstacles stand between you and your toasting and as you work your way through the later levels, this increases the difficulty significantly.
All that said, it’s incredibly fun learning to master the controls anyway and while you’re learning the best way to approach the problem the developers are keen to see you progress with some ease. After a certain number of failures, the game will offer you an easy way through the level, the magical marmalade which gives you infinite grip and makes your edible level invulnerable. This is actually a nice touch and a saving grace on a few of levels, it also gives you time to figure out your next move and fully master the mechanics safe in the knowledge you’re not going to fall off whatever you’re currently gripped to.
As you work your way through the story, and that poor man’s sanity, you’ll unlock other modes in the game and even other types of breaded product. The modes on offer range from basic free-roam and rampage (my personal favourite), to Bagel Racing and Zero G, you’ll even have the option to play the game as a french baguette, there’s a lot to do outside of the story.
The environments themselves are amazingly interactive, it’s impressive to say the least. Almost everything you see around you is bound by the physics of the game and can be manipulated, I didn’t realise how thorough the developers had been with this until I found myself on top of the fridge in the first level only to find it’s door swing open and my slice go butter side up to the floor. There are a few occasions where these physics could do with a little tweaking, for example the jam jar takes very little to break, just a nudge actually, but it can take some force to move a box. This is minor and barely noticeable though and will have not much impact on your experience.
Visually, this game is appealing, the bizarre theme of the game is contrasted nicely with a relatively normal home environment, albeit a little messy. The attention to detail is impressive, it’s bright and colourful, a little cartoony but never the less well above what we’ve come to expect from games of this nature. The audio also compliments the game well, it’s quirky, it’s upbeat, it somehow gives the slice of bread added personality.
Overall, I Am Bread was created to be something a little silly, not to be taken seriously, something just pure fun and it delivers exactly what it sets out to do. It’s a quirky game that won’t appeal to the mainstream but for those that have games such as Goat Simulator, Octodad and Bossa’s own Surgeon Simulator, this is a game that you will enjoy. Despite a short story, there is plenty of opportunities to explore and expand your experience through the other game modes.
A good looking game with very few faults, some might see it as purely a gimmick, others will fully embrace it for what it is, a good laugh.

Stardew Valley is basically a retro-pixel ripoff of Harvest Moon, a game series I’ve always wanted to love, but always bounced off within hours. “Ripoff” is harsh. Maybe it’s more of a love letter?
Stardew Valley eliminated the “ticking time bomb” element of Harvest Moon that always sucked the joy out of it. You no longer have to get married and save the family farm in two years or less Or Else. You can be a complete slacker and take decades of game time to explore and appreciate the subtle systems.
Despite the admittedly fantastic retro art, music, themes, and tone of the game, it takes hours and hours to figure out the birthday schedule and walking patterns – to say nothing of hopes, desires and romantic tastes – of more than two dozen NPCs. It's best compared to two superior relationship/resource farming game series – Animal Crossing and Persona.
Stardew Valley has a mining/adventuring subgame with a rudimentary combat system (think 2D Minecraft), but it interrupts your farming, gathering and wooing cycle. And it’s brutal. Get killed, and you lose a LOT of money, items and access to mine levels.
This is a stellar game for tweens and teens with time to burn. If parenthood and a subsistence career hasn’t already sucked the romantic inclinations out of you, this is your pot of escapism. I would have obsessed over this game had it been on my SNES. The tone is sweet and brisk. The music is very good. There is a ton of content. And you might not have to listen to inane Minecraft stories for a while.

Updating my review. (09 July 2017)
XCOM 2 is an excellent turn-based tactics game, I am more than 400 hours ingame and finally got 100% achievements from the vanilla version. Still, I LOVE this game so much. And there is an expansion coming at the end of August 2017, an official proper expansion!
Now, let's talk about the game.
There are many changes from the XCOM Enemy Unknown, XCOM 2 offers a lot more in depth strategy and decision making:
-Should I spend time and resources on this now or give my soldiers new weapons first?
-Save a scientist and avoid ADVENT stealing my supplies for next month OR get more Intel and stop ADVENT from advancing the AVATAR project?
Decisions, decisions...
Decisions are really difficult, specially in higher difficulties + ironman mode. Decision making is a key element here.
Also introduces a new mechanic called concealment that helps making your entrance strategy and overwatch ambush in combat, if executed well, a good ambush will give you a great advantage. Another new feature is that maps/levels are randomly generated, so you never play the same level twice! This of course add a lot of replayability, and of course, you need to adapt your tactics every single level.
There are many timed mission that pressure you in decision making and adapt your strategy according to the situation. Many people don't like the timed missions, but I enjoy it and I think it is well executed. If you don't like the timed missions there are mods that extend the timers or even remove the timers.
And yes, XCOM 2 supports mods, there are already ton of mods out there, for every taste and most important, there are mods from the Long War studio that made the best mod for the first game. And even better, they are preparing a Long War 2 mod for XCOM 2 ! That by the way, the mod Long War 2 is available right now:
Be aware that there are still some bugs to fix and also some performance issue, I have a 980ti and the game works fine, no crashes or anything weird at all, just occasional frame rate drops, still I hope Firaxis release a patch to fix the performance issues. Also it seems my game crash when I have mods activated, so be careful what you install.
I recommend this game to anyone that like the XCOM series or turn-based tactics games, personally, I think XCOM 2 is best one so far, this game a MUST HAVE.
I give this game a 9 out of 10, only negative point are the performance issues.

Darkest Dungeon is an excellent take on the dungeon crawler genre.
It employs both squad-based management and settlement growth/progression.
You will direct and (try) to keep alive a group of four adventurers who quest into the dungeons under your employ. You will manage their skills and engage in combat with them, while trying not to get too attached to them, because you could lose them at any moment. The game does not hold out on the punches.
You will also manage a hamlet which contains buildings that upgrade and keep your squad in top-notch conditon. Of course, the buildings must be restored and rebuilt to gain the full effects. You upgrade your estate through items obtained while adventuring.
There is a degree of grinding involved, but what keeps me coming back to the game is the small details and atmosphere that Red Hook has created. Did I mention the whole game is Eldritch themed? The environments and characters are exceptionally well created, and deeply grim-dark.
A final point of note is the narrator, which I recommend looking up YouTube clips of, since his dulcet voice's full splendor cannot be described properly.

Strap in for yet another MOBA, this time stripped of nearly all basic features. This is Stellar Impact, without creep farm and "advanced" mechanics. This is Star Conflict without the customization, extra game modes and large team size.
You get a big ship. You fly into circular spaces and occupy them until they turn blue, and then you move on to the next one. When you see an enemy ship, everyone mashes all the ability buttons and someone dies. Some ships have a lot of health, other ships deal lots of damage, and a couple turn invisible then fly right up next to you and instakill you. Supposedly there's an in-game upgrade shop, but damned if there was any indication of that. The keybindings didn't have a button assigned to anything resembling "use" or "open shop", and nobody else playing knew how to access it.
Each "sector" feels simultaneously cramped and completely empty. Combat areas are completely open and devoid of smaller ships/asteroids, but you're completely boxed in by asteroids in every direction. Ships can quickly and easily traverse open spaces, so fights are mostly instances of players flying directly at each  other spamming abilities. If you're playing the Sniper, you'll just sit still wherever the warp drive dumps you or behind one of the stations, pecking away at the other ships until someone breaks off to wreck you. If things are going south, you're just done. That's it. Trying to jump away takes a million years, and increases your damage taken to boot. There's no dodging, no running and hiding behind an asteroid, you just slug it out until one of you explodes.
To some extent the game looks nice, but when it comes time to interact with any of the gameplay elements or UI everything falls apart. There's little indication of health, the countdown timers are as long as winter in Game of Thrones, there is no tactical strategy to the combat and there's no meta-level strategy for the overall game. You just kill as many enemy ships as possible and sit still in circular volumes until they turn blue. To win, you gank the enemy team and turn their base blue. Granted the base has defenses, but it is the only set of defenses in the entire map. There's no "jungle". There are no "creeps" or smaller ships to speak of. There's no cover or concealment besides the stations themselves. The stations are arranged along a horizontal axis, everyone is locked to the same orientation.
This might appeal to MOBA junkies, and in time may even attract some of the Stellar Impact or Star Conflict crowd, but I for one will be avoiding this game like the plague.

Updating my review. (09 July 2017)
XCOM 2 is an excellent turn-based tactics game, I am more than 400 hours ingame and finally got 100% achievements from the vanilla version. Still, I LOVE this game so much. And there is an expansion coming at the end of August 2017, an official proper expansion!
Now, let's talk about the game.
There are many changes from the XCOM Enemy Unknown, XCOM 2 offers a lot more in depth strategy and decision making:
-Should I spend time and resources on this now or give my soldiers new weapons first?
-Save a scientist and avoid ADVENT stealing my supplies for next month OR get more Intel and stop ADVENT from advancing the AVATAR project?
Decisions, decisions...
Decisions are really difficult, specially in higher difficulties + ironman mode. Decision making is a key element here.
Also introduces a new mechanic called concealment that helps making your entrance strategy and overwatch ambush in combat, if executed well, a good ambush will give you a great advantage. Another new feature is that maps/levels are randomly generated, so you never play the same level twice! This of course add a lot of replayability, and of course, you need to adapt your tactics every single level.
There are many timed mission that pressure you in decision making and adapt your strategy according to the situation. Many people don't like the timed missions, but I enjoy it and I think it is well executed. If you don't like the timed missions there are mods that extend the timers or even remove the timers.
And yes, XCOM 2 supports mods, there are already ton of mods out there, for every taste and most important, there are mods from the Long War studio that made the best mod for the first game. And even better, they are preparing a Long War 2 mod for XCOM 2 ! That by the way, the mod Long War 2 is available right now:
Be aware that there are still some bugs to fix and also some performance issue, I have a 980ti and the game works fine, no crashes or anything weird at all, just occasional frame rate drops, still I hope Firaxis release a patch to fix the performance issues. Also it seems my game crash when I have mods activated, so be careful what you install.
I recommend this game to anyone that like the XCOM series or turn-based tactics games, personally, I think XCOM 2 is best one so far, this game a MUST HAVE.
I give this game a 9 out of 10, only negative point are the performance issues.

A fantastic take on dungeon crawling. Darkest Dungeon removes the player from the more fantastical forms of dungeoneering and sends the player down a corridor to madness along with their heroes. The will have to manage more than health bars and mana; players must manage the stress of their often very imperfect heroes and ailments that they earn on their adventures. Along the way they will need to upgrade the hamlet to allow for more powerful skills to be learned, armor and weapons to smith, and more effective stress relief activities. I wouldn't recommend this game for all dungeon crawler fans as the difficulty can spike rather hard at times and randomness is a very big part of the game; you must learn to make the best out of a bad and sometimes uncontrollable situation. I do however recommend it for the challenge, the incredible atmosphere. Battles can seem one sided at times but learning the tools to bring and heroes to use are some of the most important things in this game.

Personal Thoughts/What's It Like To Play? :
This is absolutely one of my favorite games. I've never been much of a fan of the Harvest Moon styled games, but something about Stardew Valley hooked me in and didn't let go.
Your options of what you can do are extremely diverse, with everything from farming (of course), to fishing, to fighting monsters in caves.
Even if you tend to do the same thing over and over, there's so much room for personal improvement (before you max out your levels) that your experience is constantly shifting (albeit slowly, at times).
The optional Junimo rewards are not only extremely satisfying to complete (watching those cute little apple creatures jump around in excitement), they're also quite useful in your ongoing quest to become more efficient in what you do.
The characters are fun to talk to, even if they repeat some of their lines. The relationship cutscenes are enjoyable and once again a very satisfying sight.
I think that last part sums up the game very well. While it may tend to be a little grindy at times, every single thing you acheive feels VERY satsifying, no matter how small.
The atmoshpere of the game is very very calming and peaceful. The music is always pleasant to hear, and the sound effects compliment every situation in the game. I can't think of a single noise in this game that has ever startled or agitated me.
-----
Does It Deserve The Hype?
When I purchased this game, I was extremely skeptical. There was a lot of hype about it going on between my friends, and I usually distance myself from hyped things, as they tend to never be as good as the hype makes them sound. While I stayed away from all of the actual gameplay details, all I ever heard was good things about this game. I finally got around to purchasing it after a little bit of "ehhh, should I really? Seems like maybe it doesn't deserve all this hype," but it definitely does in its entirety.
-----
Should You Get This Game? :
If you're just kind of considering getting the game and aren't very sure, you should definitely get it. It's only 15 dollars, so I would suggest purchasing it at full value and supporting the dev, as I would love to see more games where he is in control. If you absolutely hate it, you can just refund it, but I give you a 99% chance you won't even consider a refund.

The game's graphics 'looks' gorgeous, with it's high detailed mother ships which you can control, and satisfying weapon effects, and good controls. The movement is slow since they're big mother ships, but some (maybe it's just one) ships you can utilize to blink/jump short distances, which aside from looking cool, adds a good advantage to deal more damage if done correctly.
So the game at the moment (20/11/2014) has six ships and a conquest mode, pick your ship, it's crew, and go own your battle, a 5 vs 5 conquest match, with 7 major points, and 6 mini points to conquer. There isn't much else to say at the moment with the game being in alpha and all, with it comes bugs and little content, but overall I'm seeing this game hitting a good spot with it's nice price of 10 dollars, I think it's worth it, don't know if the price will go up but if you want an awesome experience I (hopefully) suspect that'll come around late beta stage, then give it a wait, but if you don't mind what you get now, then go ahead and get it.
What the game needs now is a good tutorial (also don't expect anything aside from 5 players, with their respective mother ships, against other 5 players of the same), more optimization, polish, and content. Also, this game would sell like hot cakes if there's coop, would love to have a 'assault stations' kind of coop.
All in all I had a fun time playing it, and will play more, and for the asking price for what you get now and later on, it's a nice deal.

I'm not sure what I can say about Half-Life that hasn't been said already, but I'll try anyway.
This was Valve's flagship title, and it's definitely a classic. It was revolutionary in its day - November 1998, to be precise - for its (somewhat) realistic combat and overall approach to its narrative. There were no cutscenes or voiceovers for the main character.
were put into the shoes of Gordon Freeman, PhD. That made the game all the more immersive and involving, and it is indeed both.
The plot itself is still very good and elegantly presented, if not entirely as gripping nowadays where half-realistic aliens and gundudes are more prevalent in gaming. The first section of the game involves you commuting to work in a labryinthine government research facility; the presentation and interactivity present during your commute (and preparation for the workday) make it work quite well, and it's still believable.
Then you do a big experiment and everything goes to Hell in a handbasket. Hostile aliens are teleporting in from the alternate dimension your employers were foolish enough to screw around with, and you have to fight your way out of the laboratories with a scant few weapons at first. Things only get worse from there.
This is primarily a first-person shooter, and the gunplay is good if a bit repetitive. You eventually carry a whole armory's worth of guns, from an MP5 to a rocket launcher to guns that shoot tau and gluon particles (creative license; I'm pretty sure tau and gluon particles can't actually explode people) to an alien bio-gun that shoots
. The graphics...were probably great back when it was released, and while they still seem timeless to me they haven't aged
as gracefully as
's graphics.
There's also a fair bit of puzzling to be had; mostly moving objects around, jumping puzzles and finding the right switch in an area. They're not terribly hard, but they intersperse very nicely with the shooting. Since this game is partially based off the Quake engine, your character moves rather fast by default, which is something to keep in mind.
The AI was unprecedented in its day, but not quite as stellar now. They can still put up a good fight though, and the game can become very intense if you're not careful. The
is excellent; a fitting mix of unsettling ambient electronica and rock.
The last part of the game I will not spoil as much as others might, but it involves a fairly larger amount of jumping puzzles than the rest of the game, as well as some...
designed levels. It's not exactly bad, but it's definitely a change from the rest of the game that you may not be entirely comfortable with. Which is perhaps what Valve was going for...
It's worth mentioning that the multiplayer deathmatch is still around and pretty good, if rather fast-paced. Haven't played much of it, unfortunately. This game also spawned what is perhaps the biggest mod base in video game history. Multiple multiplayer mods for this game became separate commercial releases sanctioned (and usually developed in part by) Valve themselves, such as Counter-Strike and Team Fortress.
Overall, I would recommend this as a piece of history, a classic and as a good game even after all these years. Mostly. If you want classic Half-Life with the Source engine, you could try
, or if you want a modernized version you could try
. There were also two expansions by Gearbox Software,
and
, and I'd recommend them if you liked classic Half-Life. Sven Coop is also free on Steam for co-op adventures in the original Half-Life engine, and it even comes with a complementary copy of the HL campaign.

I know other people do and that's fine. While this change is different compared to the first XCOM, it becomes a pain when every mission is timed. You have to throw caution to the wind to complete the objective, and the game punishes you for that. And if you fail, then game punishes you just as severly in a different way.
There's no slow and steady in this game, that tactic is gone. It's now balls to the wall rushing into bad cover and getting nailed. But don't forget to flank! Oh wait, you now can miss quite easily while flanking. Get used to missing even with good shots. I don't think there is even much point to flanking, as you easily get out flanked when flanking. So the risk vs reward isn't there at all. But it seems the AI doesn't have any issue hitting your troops and they will hammer you even when you're in full cover.
This game is quite different to the first XCOM, and I honestly don't like XCOM 2 at all. I'm going back to the original which had the right amount of risk vs reward to it.

The 1994 XCom was one of my very 1st computer games that I bought and I loved the crap out of it. The freedom of strategy and the random maps which gave each mission a different feel. I remember the music of the game when playing late into the night with that heart beat like sound, which seem to immerse you into the game almost made you feel the terror of the soldiers you were controlling.
Terror from the Deep did much of the same with an increase of weapons, armor and aliens. And Apocalypse had all kind of weapons, armors and research along with a good story about the aliens but was a bit cumbersome to move your squad around in turned based but worked well the real time option but then you used a ton of ammo.
And for years nothing of any real notability came about until the remake of XCOM Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within showed up. It capture many of those same aspects of the original game did but with 3D graphic and with those camera angles that brought you to the soldiers view of the battlefield, which once again gave that immersion feeling of almost being in the fight yourself.  I think I logged over 1800 hours playing that game. But there were some aspects of the 1st Xcom that I wish were present in the remake, like how you had to buy or make everything right down to the ammunition for your guns (no infinite items) and how nothing was made or researched instantly but instead you could add more personal and facilities to reduce the time it took.
Anyway as for XCOM 2……I thought the game was excellent in that it gives you that intensity level that every decision you make is critical to your success. It also answered that nagging question about what the hell the aliens were abducting people for in the first place. Now it has it clichés, like how windows would break before my guy even started running toward it or the crazy psychedelic light shown in final mission to name few. But overall I rank this game up there with some of best that I have played and I also see the potential that lie within the game to give us a wide verity different gaming angles with how many mods are already up and running.  We the players are in store for some really great gaming experiences (once all of the bugs get worked out, as with most games that have just been release.)

I love this game, and had more fun playing it than the original XCOM.      To me the funnest thing was how you find your self caring about your soldiers.   I found they had different personalities which amused me.    My favorite was Jane, a ranger from the tutorial.      When you care what happens to your people, the game becomes more interesting.
In the original XCOM I thought the air combat was very silly and glad to see it gone.

In 128 hours of gameplay I had the sound get garbled up three times (fixed by exit and then restarting it), and it did crash on me exactly once.   Not too bad.
There isn't a whole lot of variation in the missions as far what you are supposed to do, but many times the situations you get in are unique.   I never felt bored.   And there is a plot mission that occurs at some point which was spectacular.   The finale was very fun and exciting for me.   I thought they did a great job of designing mission so you could use some of your higher rank abilities.
As far as criticisms, there is much to the game that I was missing until somebody was watching me play and pointed out that I could do this or that.     I thought it was odd that after a major event in the middle of the game, when you get your soldiers back there were no cut scenes.    Also, how hard would it be to show some injury to soldiers when their health is low, both in the mission and on the Skyranger etc.
I love how there are mods for the game, but the only one I have used so far is the timer mod, because I do not like being rushed.  I would much prefer to be able to take care of my soldiers.   With the timer mod there still was some time pressure but not so much I felt forced to put my people at risk.
In conclusion, I've read a bunch of negative reviews of this game.   I just wanted to say I probably have 50 to 100 games in my library, and most I have not played much.     But this game was really fun,  so fun that I actually felt compelled to write a review.
