This is a great game with loads of great free Nexus mods available for it.  Like all Bethesda games there are a lot of glitches in the game that Bethesda never bothered patching, but the free mods at Nexus can resolve those issues.  Also the free mods at Nexus allow you to completely change the game and how it plays.  So no two playthroughs are the same and you're always discovering new things about the game in each playthrough.
There is 1 drawback though.  The Creation Club Bethesda made is thus far complete crap and you should avoid it at all costs.  The Creation Club is primarily a way for Bethesda to milk extra money from players through micro transactions for new skins and weapons.  However, you can get the same and often better mods for free on Nexus.  So avoid the CC crap and you'll be in for a great ride.
Take note that the game on PC is far superior to that of the console versions as you can mod things on PC that are not possible to mod on consoles.  So while Fallout 4 is fun on consoles... it's amazing on PC.
For those of you who don't like the FPS aspects as much as building... this game has a great settlement building system that you can spend hours upon hours losing yourself in creativity with.  When you add the nexus Mods to settlement building to that it only becomes better.
Overall I love this game, but at the moment of this review Fallout 4 is taking a lot of bad press because of Bethesda's Creation Club the same way GTA5 took hits when they attacked their modding community.
I recommend this game for everyone who likes RPGs, FPS, open world gaming, exploring and building settlements.

A fantastic take on dungeon crawling. Darkest Dungeon removes the player from the more fantastical forms of dungeoneering and sends the player down a corridor to madness along with their heroes. The will have to manage more than health bars and mana; players must manage the stress of their often very imperfect heroes and ailments that they earn on their adventures. Along the way they will need to upgrade the hamlet to allow for more powerful skills to be learned, armor and weapons to smith, and more effective stress relief activities. I wouldn't recommend this game for all dungeon crawler fans as the difficulty can spike rather hard at times and randomness is a very big part of the game; you must learn to make the best out of a bad and sometimes uncontrollable situation. I do however recommend it for the challenge, the incredible atmosphere. Battles can seem one sided at times but learning the tools to bring and heroes to use are some of the most important things in this game.

I'm not sure what I can say about Half-Life that hasn't been said already, but I'll try anyway.
This was Valve's flagship title, and it's definitely a classic. It was revolutionary in its day - November 1998, to be precise - for its (somewhat) realistic combat and overall approach to its narrative. There were no cutscenes or voiceovers for the main character.
were put into the shoes of Gordon Freeman, PhD. That made the game all the more immersive and involving, and it is indeed both.
The plot itself is still very good and elegantly presented, if not entirely as gripping nowadays where half-realistic aliens and gundudes are more prevalent in gaming. The first section of the game involves you commuting to work in a labryinthine government research facility; the presentation and interactivity present during your commute (and preparation for the workday) make it work quite well, and it's still believable.
Then you do a big experiment and everything goes to Hell in a handbasket. Hostile aliens are teleporting in from the alternate dimension your employers were foolish enough to screw around with, and you have to fight your way out of the laboratories with a scant few weapons at first. Things only get worse from there.
This is primarily a first-person shooter, and the gunplay is good if a bit repetitive. You eventually carry a whole armory's worth of guns, from an MP5 to a rocket launcher to guns that shoot tau and gluon particles (creative license; I'm pretty sure tau and gluon particles can't actually explode people) to an alien bio-gun that shoots
. The graphics...were probably great back when it was released, and while they still seem timeless to me they haven't aged
as gracefully as
's graphics.
There's also a fair bit of puzzling to be had; mostly moving objects around, jumping puzzles and finding the right switch in an area. They're not terribly hard, but they intersperse very nicely with the shooting. Since this game is partially based off the Quake engine, your character moves rather fast by default, which is something to keep in mind.
The AI was unprecedented in its day, but not quite as stellar now. They can still put up a good fight though, and the game can become very intense if you're not careful. The
is excellent; a fitting mix of unsettling ambient electronica and rock.
The last part of the game I will not spoil as much as others might, but it involves a fairly larger amount of jumping puzzles than the rest of the game, as well as some...
designed levels. It's not exactly bad, but it's definitely a change from the rest of the game that you may not be entirely comfortable with. Which is perhaps what Valve was going for...
It's worth mentioning that the multiplayer deathmatch is still around and pretty good, if rather fast-paced. Haven't played much of it, unfortunately. This game also spawned what is perhaps the biggest mod base in video game history. Multiple multiplayer mods for this game became separate commercial releases sanctioned (and usually developed in part by) Valve themselves, such as Counter-Strike and Team Fortress.
Overall, I would recommend this as a piece of history, a classic and as a good game even after all these years. Mostly. If you want classic Half-Life with the Source engine, you could try
, or if you want a modernized version you could try
. There were also two expansions by Gearbox Software,
and
, and I'd recommend them if you liked classic Half-Life. Sven Coop is also free on Steam for co-op adventures in the original Half-Life engine, and it even comes with a complementary copy of the HL campaign.

The game is amazing, but at its heart it is incomplete. The 'end-game' has been missing for several years now already, and there is not much indication of development progress with regards to that since, quantitatively, 90%+ or so of updates are either recycled events (that are still fun and relevant) or new cosmetic overrides. When you "complete" the present condition of the game, there will not be much satisfaction because the overarching storyline will not be resolved and the uncertainty of it's future existence detracts from the enjoyment of the game at that point. When you look for it, the game will give you all the challenge you want, the in-game friends you want, and all the fun you want, but in the end there is an ugly hole that scars the beauty of the game, which, after spending a lot of time being absorbed into the game world (I played mostly on the non-Steam client), hurts the feels a bit. It's the best game of its kind I've played, but it makes me sad to say that it could be a LOT more than what it is today if more game development time was invested. After completing the game, it still feels like I've only seen 75% of the Spiral Knights experience.

I wasn't here for the trip through early access, but coming into the launch version blind, my experience was one of endearment, gradually eclipsed by a roaring frustration. It's a lovely novel concept, the story (yes, there is one) is pretty good, and the level design ranges from open and flexible to linear and ♥♥♥♥ WHOEVER MADE THIS. Mercifully, there is a Super Guide equivalent to let you get through any level at the expense of a forced E rank, although even with that in place you can still be hard pressed to figure out how to toast yourself.
I realize that the game is fumblecore at its heart, but it often seems to demand just a bit too much for what you can feasibly do with its unique blend of A) the controls, B) the physics, and C) the camera. The controls in and of themselves are generally manageable, but when attempting to swing like Bread Tarzan across a string of 6 or so sunflowers and the goddamn cocking things are just flailing about as though in a typhoon because of arbitrary WACKY physics, the game just starts to fall apart. If you manage to smash open a jam jar to coat yourself, you can spend a full couple of minutes wrestling with all of the broken glass trying to actually make contact with the jam -- and once coated it can actually make movement much more challenging, to the point that you'll be unable to detach from a surface until you've swiveled the camera to an angle where the controls feel like cooperating, assuming the camera also cooperates and doesn't get stuck inside a wall pointing at the ceiling. When levels last upwards of 10 minutes and have no checkpoints, getting dicked to death by the camera and/or how it interacts with the controls is not a fun experience. The epilogue took me 5 tries alone; once because it was my fault, three times in a row because the physics made my bread clip into the car and spaz out, the third time ending with me launching into space at infinite velocity.
There's only a handful of levels in total but a few different modes to play them in and a standing possibility of more post-release content for free and/or as DLC. All in all I enjoyed it, but the physics and camera still definitely need work, and due to the prolonged format of the levels as compared to Surgeon Simulator, it's just a much more frustrating experience as a whole.
As a final caveat, none of the achievements seem to work yet either.

Xcom 2012 was a great game.  Xcom 2 aggressively changes everything that made its predecessor great.  Let me count the ways.
- This game is a turn based strategy, only when it wants to be
There are enemies that can both move and attack you on your turn.  YOUR turn!  All your troops are positioned perfectly.  You inch your way forward as safely as possible.  One soldier takes one step too far.  Suddenly (still, during your turn) an alien shows up, runs towards this soldier, attacks AND poisons them.  Your soldier will be dead in 4 turns.  That's what you get for walking.  This game hates you.  It wants all your troops to die.  It will take their lives in the most unfair ways.
- Geoscape is overly complex and confusing
Base management in Xcom 2012 was fairly straight forward.  You needed to research stuff and build stuff and grow your staff.  This was all to gain more satellites, thus increasing your income.  Apparently Firaxis didn't like how cut and dry this was, so they completely changed the base management aspect and hid every bit of information behind a wall of obfuscation.  Let's say you want to fly your base to gather supplies.  The game tells you there are supplies waiting, and that it will take 4 day to collect them.  So you fly to the supplies and start waiting.  Within seconds, a red dot is added to the alien advancement gauge.  You are one step closer to losing the game.  In reality, this gauge isn't all that important, but its inclusion stresses out players for the first 5 - 10 hours.  Whatever, you shrug it off and keep waiting for the supplies.  Seconds later, you are presented with 3 bad "Dark Events".  These happen monthly.  You get the ability to prevent one of them.  The others will happen.  Sometimes just one of them, other times both of them.  It seems random and just adds more confusion and stress.  And just to make things even more stressful, they don't tell you what the third dark event is.  You have to pay to unlock that information.  Sometimes you won't have the money to do so.
You start off with one scientist and one engineer.  You are not really told how to get more.  You can't use your knowledge of Xcom 2012 for this, because gaining staff is completely changed in this new game.
- Unlike Xcom 2012, the randomness in this game is really frustrating and it makes no sense
Due to Xcom 2's punishing nature, you will often find yourself in a situation where you absolutely NEED a shot to connect.  A group of aliens appear.  You've approached the situation perfectly.  The group was discovered at the very beginning of your turn, giving you the best chance of killing all the aliens.  Your sniper has a 82% change to hit.  MISS!  Your grenadier has a 67% chance to hit. MISS!  You re-analyze your situation, realizing that you can no longer kill all the enemies that turn.  Someone is going to take damage.  If your unlucky streak continues, the alien will do a critical hit and kill your soldier instantly.  You will come to love grenades simply because they can't miss.  You can't even rely on your ranger's sword.  Standing directly next to someone and only have a 94% chance to hit them is crazy.  Sure those are good odds, but the first time the sword misses will make you second guess using it ever again.  Later in the game you will find that enemies have ridiculous dodging ability.  Flanking an alien that is only a few tiles away will frequently give you only  a 70% - 80% chance to hit.  There is absolutely no way to improve those odds.  You just have to get lucky.  This game hates you.  It wants all your troops to die.
- Xcom 2 attempts to give the player heavy choices, but it fails
Games are all about choice.  The right choice depends on context, the state the gameworld is in.  The player has to analyze their game state and determine what the proper choice is for their situation.  A proper decision means the player made a proper analysis.  This is satisfying.  Xcom 2 tries to make it's decision making hard by witholding vital information.  This is frustrating.  You will fail and it won't be your fault.
- Ambiguity
Grenadiers gain an ability that lets them fire at all enemies in a cone-of-sight.  The game just tells you that this consumes "lots" of ammo.  How much?  You just have to figure that out on your own.  When you try it in battle, you will feel ripped off.  Not only does it use up all your ammo, but it prevents you from reloading for several turns.  Not only that, but the ability can miss.  There is absolutely no reason for the game to withhold this kind of info from the player.  THIS IS NOT THE RIGHT WAY TO MAKE A GAME DIFFICULT!  btw, this kind of thing happens a lot.  Here is another example.  Some armor only needs to be build once.  A single build cost gives you access to unlimited of that armor.  Other armor requires you to build individual sets.  There does not seem to be any indicator of which is which.  I eventually learned to save my game before doing anything new.  In fact, saving and loading is the only way the player can really come to understand what is going on.  If you are going to use a new ability for the first time, save the game and be prepared to reload once you have figured out what the consequences are.
- BUGS!
There are so many bugs in this game.  Unlike Bethesda games, these bugs aren't funny OR innocent.  I've had several soldiers burst into flame for no reason.  I had one soldier catch fire while running over a tile that had no fire on it.  Upon reloading, the tile did have fire on it.  The game simply failed to load the fire effect on that tile.  When moving your troops, an icon will appear over the tile your mouse is on.  This icon indicates that the soldier will pass through fire/acid/poison/windows/doors if they move to this location.  This is great, except when the icon fails to show itself.  This has caused me many reloads.  There are also many times when the game failed to tell me that an enemy had entered overwatch.  A linear, single-player affair has no right being so buggy.  This game honestly feels like it's still in beta.
- Conclusion
Xcom 2 has moments of greatness.  One of the earlier missions was one of the most intense and enjoyable experiences I've had gaming.  However, the confusion, frustration, and plethora of bugs strips it of all it's greatness.  One moment I loved the game, the next moment I hated it.  This is coming from someone who loved Xcom 2012 and indeed the original from the 90s.  It's unfortunate, because when the stars align and the bugs aren't an issue, a pretty good game wants to emerge.  In the end, I wish I had passed this game up.

I was heartbroken to hear Microsoft disbanded Ensemble Studios.  I loved Age of Empires 1, 2, AND 3 but I loved 3 the most.  I still love AoE 3 and here's why:
First of all, the game has a good mix of ranged units vs melee vs cavalry vs Artillery.  Where other games usually boil down to "create as many units as possible and overwhelm the enemy", that kind of strategy doesn't really cut it in AoE 3.  You might win, but it'll take you far more resources to do so.  Judicious use of your forces will make them last longer and perform better.
Secondly, the emphasis on the home cities gives you something to work for even between skirmish matches.  Normally, every skirmish would be completely isolated from the overall game, but by levelling up your home city, you can provide better "shipments" to your settlers in future games.
Third, and this is probably where most people diverge in their opinions: The explorer as a sort of "hero" unit, and various minor enemies to fight for bonuses along the way, gives the game more of Warcraft III feel to it.  Without these little distractions you would just grind your way to the 4th age, create mass amounts of units and slaughter the enemy every time.   Now you have a choice: do you want to chance fighting the bears to get that special unit?  Maybe if you attack those pirates the treasure will give you a nice boost?
Lastly: all the enemies have a nice personality to them that makes me enjoy crushing them and sometimes (with them as allies) makes me laugh at the way they choose to attack.  Others make me sad to have been put on the same team (Henry the Navigator, you wuss!)
Mostly though, the game has actually aged pretty well in my opinion.  I know the game is almost 9 years old now, but it still holds up as worth buying and worth playing.  That is just talking about the base game... there's 2 whole expansions in this package I haven't really gotten into!
My favorite nation to fight as?  The Dutch... for some reason by late game I always feel like I'm controlling everything with all that coin flowing in.  It's really awesome.

Starbound is very similar to Terraria at first glance. It offers a procedural and destructible two-dimensional enviornment in which almost everything is out to kill you, and where you will only survive by scavenging you way up the food chain. Mine ores and gather wood, build tools and a shelter - then build a means of crafting more tools and better shelters. Grow stronger by growing more knowledgeable, and pay attention as each trip outwards takes you further, earns you more, and leaves you alive just that much longer. Fight, craft, survive! The user interface is not entirely different, the mouse-and-keyboard controls will feel familiar the moment you start, and many of hte incidental details between both titles blend beautifully as well.
There is however, one big difference, and it's certainly big. The engine offers you your first procedurally generated planet, and it's only the first of many. The first of thousands, if not more. Travel!
It plays out very well - my first day with Starbound left me restless as I discovered that the planets are actually not that big, and they eventually wrap around. Regardless of that fact, I set out to explore and discovered various creatures, the majority wanting to kill me, a select few that were more passive. As a Terraria player, a short jaunt like this left my heart aching. I wanted to journey elsewhere.
Your base in Starbound is not a planet at all, in fact, despite that you can mark a planet as your "home," meaning you will always be able to travel back to it no matter how far off in the galaxy you have traveled, your true base is actually a spaceship, distinct for each of the six races that you can pick between at the start. There are a few diverse races in which you can choose from, but despite all the selection, I decided to be boring and be a "Human" whose planet (Earth) had all of its resources dried up.
There was no fuel in the tank, however, so I beamed down to the planet once more, and this time I started to go through the brief sweep of story missions that are currnetly available. These teach you the basics of gathering resources, first with a matter manipulator - useful though slow - and soon with a series of metal tools you craft for yourself. Think of it as tutorials, the next educating you about crafting things such as weapons and tools, and armors. As with Terraria, you are going to spend a lot of the early game cutting down trees for lumber, making workbenches and foundries, and paging through the lists of trinkets and knick knacks you can create with them. Truthfully, nothing about any of that is fun, and it's a chore, there's no denying it.
There is a silver lining. I'm only several hours in, and I am still exploring different planets, and seeing new things. What will you find out there? Beyond your early adventures lies an infinite plain of crafting, shaping, constructing and plundering. Bring friends and start a war. Jump on a server populated with strangers and see how long you will survive.
For a game so closely connected to one another, Starbound already differs itself to Terraria. Terraria is about exploring a single, procedurally generated world that grows stranger and more diverse as you pull back hte layers. A lot of Starbound's planets are simple at present - you can walk around them, dig down to their cores and feel as though you have got the measure of them entirely. Its rich diversity comes as you hop between one planet to another: despite having the same tools and the same objectives, there is a unique sense from being a settler and being an explorer.
The game is truly fascinating, and I have been waiting for some time to get my hands on this title. I highly recommend this title to any Minecraft or Terraria enthusiasts seeing as it provides the same interlocked chains of distraction that define each of game respectively. Whether you want to travel the cosmos solo, or bring along friends, this title provides the same joy and heartfelt elements that Minecraft and Terraria have brought to me - and with more updates to come in the near future, I recommend this game to you.

Like all Bethesda games there are a lot of glitches in the game that Bethesda never bothered patching, but the free mods at Nexus can resolve those issues. There is 1 drawback though.  The Creation Club Bethesda made is thus far complete crap and you should avoid it at all costs.  The Creation Club is primarily a way for Bethesda to milk extra money from players through micro transactions for new skins and weapons. For those of you who don't like the FPS aspects as much as building... this game has a great settlement building system that you can spend hours upon hours losing yourself in creativity with.  When you add the nexus Mods to settlement building to that it only becomes better.
Overall I love this game, but at the moment of this review Fallout 4 is taking a lot of bad press because of Bethesda's Creation Club the same way GTA5 took hits when they attacked their modding community.
I recommend this game for everyone who likes RPGs, FPS, open world gaming, exploring and building settlements.

Having played Dark Souls, Dark Souls 2, and now Dark Souls 3, I can say without a doubt that this one is my favorite. While Dark Souls (the original) holds a special place in my heart for introducing me to the stunning and interesting world, this game gave me a sense of bittersweet finality. But, I guess I should try to review this in a more piece-by-piece fashion, as I could praise its general greatness all day.
(There are going to be spoilers below for areas, but not bosses.)
Graphics: Pro
The graphics are fantastic in many areas, average in others, but never are they poorly done. Walking into Archdragon Peak, the Grand Archives, or Anor Londo gives a sense of not only the grand scale but also the accompanying attention to detail that these cames carry. Every segment of the game is finely crafted and immerses you in the action. This brings me to my next point.
Combat: Pro
The combat of Dark Souls 3 can either make or break your experience. At times it is fast paced, while in others it is methodical, however it never loses the trademark intensity of the series. This can frighten new players; many claim that this game is incredibly difficult. However, this is not necessarily the case. Becoming accustomed to the style of the combat and the mindset this game requires will reward one's dedication. The sense of pride and accomplishment one gains from defeating bosses, having died again and again to their titanic weapons or cataclysmic spells, is beyond anything I've experienced in other games. I swear I'm not a masochist.
Story/Setting: Potential Con
For those who want a story told to them that has overtly complex and riveting plots, accompanying relateable characters whose motives and actions are deeply fleshed out, and gripping twists and turns that will keep you on the edge of your seat... this game is not for you. However, I have grown to love the lore bites that one can find throughout the world. Following the trail of a bumbling knight throughout the darkest nooks and crannies of the land is enjoyable, but it is just as easy to pass right over him and hardly notice his existence. The same goes for the deep history of the many factions who have affected the world's current, decrepit state. The story of this world is covered in ash; those who seek the truth must dig deep to find it.
If you are looking for a story-driven game that appeals to your finer side, Dark Souls 3 is not for you. Overall, I'd recommend this game to any and all who enjoy high fantasy with intense combat and a stunning world.

I'm not sure what I can say about Half-Life that hasn't been said already, but I'll try anyway.
This was Valve's flagship title, and it's definitely a classic. It was revolutionary in its day - November 1998, to be precise - for its (somewhat) realistic combat and overall approach to its narrative. There were no cutscenes or voiceovers for the main character.
were put into the shoes of Gordon Freeman, PhD. That made the game all the more immersive and involving, and it is indeed both.
The plot itself is still very good and elegantly presented, if not entirely as gripping nowadays where half-realistic aliens and gundudes are more prevalent in gaming. The first section of the game involves you commuting to work in a labryinthine government research facility; the presentation and interactivity present during your commute (and preparation for the workday) make it work quite well, and it's still believable.
Then you do a big experiment and everything goes to Hell in a handbasket. Hostile aliens are teleporting in from the alternate dimension your employers were foolish enough to screw around with, and you have to fight your way out of the laboratories with a scant few weapons at first. Things only get worse from there.
This is primarily a first-person shooter, and the gunplay is good if a bit repetitive. You eventually carry a whole armory's worth of guns, from an MP5 to a rocket launcher to guns that shoot tau and gluon particles (creative license; I'm pretty sure tau and gluon particles can't actually explode people) to an alien bio-gun that shoots
. The graphics...were probably great back when it was released, and while they still seem timeless to me they haven't aged
as gracefully as
's graphics.
There's also a fair bit of puzzling to be had; mostly moving objects around, jumping puzzles and finding the right switch in an area. They're not terribly hard, but they intersperse very nicely with the shooting. Since this game is partially based off the Quake engine, your character moves rather fast by default, which is something to keep in mind.
The AI was unprecedented in its day, but not quite as stellar now. They can still put up a good fight though, and the game can become very intense if you're not careful. The
is excellent; a fitting mix of unsettling ambient electronica and rock.
The last part of the game I will not spoil as much as others might, but it involves a fairly larger amount of jumping puzzles than the rest of the game, as well as some...
designed levels. It's not exactly bad, but it's definitely a change from the rest of the game that you may not be entirely comfortable with. Which is perhaps what Valve was going for...
It's worth mentioning that the multiplayer deathmatch is still around and pretty good, if rather fast-paced. Haven't played much of it, unfortunately. This game also spawned what is perhaps the biggest mod base in video game history. Multiple multiplayer mods for this game became separate commercial releases sanctioned (and usually developed in part by) Valve themselves, such as Counter-Strike and Team Fortress.
Overall, I would recommend this as a piece of history, a classic and as a good game even after all these years. Mostly. If you want classic Half-Life with the Source engine, you could try
, or if you want a modernized version you could try
. There were also two expansions by Gearbox Software,
and
, and I'd recommend them if you liked classic Half-Life. Sven Coop is also free on Steam for co-op adventures in the original Half-Life engine, and it even comes with a complementary copy of the HL campaign.
So far this game has occupied 10 days of my life thus far, soon to be more. and all of it I will never regret. Praise the sun!

Xcom 2012 was a great game.  Xcom 2 aggressively changes everything that made its predecessor great.  Let me count the ways.
- This game is a turn based strategy, only when it wants to be
There are enemies that can both move and attack you on your turn.  YOUR turn!  All your troops are positioned perfectly.  You inch your way forward as safely as possible.  One soldier takes one step too far.  Suddenly (still, during your turn) an alien shows up, runs towards this soldier, attacks AND poisons them.  Your soldier will be dead in 4 turns.  That's what you get for walking.  This game hates you.  It wants all your troops to die.  It will take their lives in the most unfair ways.
- Geoscape is overly complex and confusing
Base management in Xcom 2012 was fairly straight forward.  You needed to research stuff and build stuff and grow your staff.  This was all to gain more satellites, thus increasing your income.  Apparently Firaxis didn't like how cut and dry this was, so they completely changed the base management aspect and hid every bit of information behind a wall of obfuscation.  Let's say you want to fly your base to gather supplies.  The game tells you there are supplies waiting, and that it will take 4 day to collect them.  So you fly to the supplies and start waiting.  Within seconds, a red dot is added to the alien advancement gauge.  You are one step closer to losing the game.  In reality, this gauge isn't all that important, but its inclusion stresses out players for the first 5 - 10 hours.  Whatever, you shrug it off and keep waiting for the supplies.  Seconds later, you are presented with 3 bad "Dark Events".  These happen monthly.  You get the ability to prevent one of them.  The others will happen.  Sometimes just one of them, other times both of them.  It seems random and just adds more confusion and stress.  And just to make things even more stressful, they don't tell you what the third dark event is.  You have to pay to unlock that information.  Sometimes you won't have the money to do so.
You start off with one scientist and one engineer.  You are not really told how to get more.  You can't use your knowledge of Xcom 2012 for this, because gaining staff is completely changed in this new game.
- Unlike Xcom 2012, the randomness in this game is really frustrating and it makes no sense
Due to Xcom 2's punishing nature, you will often find yourself in a situation where you absolutely NEED a shot to connect.  A group of aliens appear.  You've approached the situation perfectly.  The group was discovered at the very beginning of your turn, giving you the best chance of killing all the aliens.  Your sniper has a 82% change to hit.  MISS!  Your grenadier has a 67% chance to hit. MISS!  You re-analyze your situation, realizing that you can no longer kill all the enemies that turn.  Someone is going to take damage.  If your unlucky streak continues, the alien will do a critical hit and kill your soldier instantly.  You will come to love grenades simply because they can't miss.  You can't even rely on your ranger's sword.  Standing directly next to someone and only have a 94% chance to hit them is crazy.  Sure those are good odds, but the first time the sword misses will make you second guess using it ever again.  Later in the game you will find that enemies have ridiculous dodging ability.  Flanking an alien that is only a few tiles away will frequently give you only  a 70% - 80% chance to hit.  There is absolutely no way to improve those odds.  You just have to get lucky.  This game hates you.  It wants all your troops to die.
- Xcom 2 attempts to give the player heavy choices, but it fails
Games are all about choice.  The right choice depends on context, the state the gameworld is in.  The player has to analyze their game state and determine what the proper choice is for their situation.  A proper decision means the player made a proper analysis.  This is satisfying.  Xcom 2 tries to make it's decision making hard by witholding vital information.  This is frustrating.  You will fail and it won't be your fault.
- Ambiguity
Grenadiers gain an ability that lets them fire at all enemies in a cone-of-sight.  The game just tells you that this consumes "lots" of ammo.  How much?  You just have to figure that out on your own.  When you try it in battle, you will feel ripped off.  Not only does it use up all your ammo, but it prevents you from reloading for several turns.  Not only that, but the ability can miss.  There is absolutely no reason for the game to withhold this kind of info from the player.  THIS IS NOT THE RIGHT WAY TO MAKE A GAME DIFFICULT!  btw, this kind of thing happens a lot.  Here is another example.  Some armor only needs to be build once.  A single build cost gives you access to unlimited of that armor.  Other armor requires you to build individual sets.  There does not seem to be any indicator of which is which.  I eventually learned to save my game before doing anything new.  In fact, saving and loading is the only way the player can really come to understand what is going on.  If you are going to use a new ability for the first time, save the game and be prepared to reload once you have figured out what the consequences are.
- BUGS!
There are so many bugs in this game.  Unlike Bethesda games, these bugs aren't funny OR innocent.  I've had several soldiers burst into flame for no reason.  I had one soldier catch fire while running over a tile that had no fire on it.  Upon reloading, the tile did have fire on it.  The game simply failed to load the fire effect on that tile.  When moving your troops, an icon will appear over the tile your mouse is on.  This icon indicates that the soldier will pass through fire/acid/poison/windows/doors if they move to this location.  This is great, except when the icon fails to show itself.  This has caused me many reloads.  There are also many times when the game failed to tell me that an enemy had entered overwatch.  A linear, single-player affair has no right being so buggy.  This game honestly feels like it's still in beta.
- Conclusion
Xcom 2 has moments of greatness.  One of the earlier missions was one of the most intense and enjoyable experiences I've had gaming.  However, the confusion, frustration, and plethora of bugs strips it of all it's greatness.  One moment I loved the game, the next moment I hated it.  This is coming from someone who loved Xcom 2012 and indeed the original from the 90s.  It's unfortunate, because when the stars align and the bugs aren't an issue, a pretty good game wants to emerge.  In the end, I wish I had passed this game up.

Half-Life is undeniably ONE of the greatest FPS (First-Person Shooter) games to ever exist on the PC.
In my opinion and the opinion of many others, Half-Life is viewed as one of the "Founding Fathers" of shooters, helping to pioneer the First-Person Shooter genre (before it became overused). Amongst many of it's distinguishable qualities it features:
- A believable setting, combined with an enviromental-based story approach, which really brings across the necessary feel and emotion of the games story than most cutscenes.
- Very-well designed levels; allowing players to have uninterrupted play time through chapters (completely doing away with FMV), along with linear-but-non repetitive maps, each with their own suprises and fun puzzles, whilst keeping to the overall theme.
- A variety of wonderful, bizarre and frightful enemies both Human and extraterrestrial, which have fairly intelligent AI (albeit a bit clumsy at times) and an arsenal of weapons to destroy you.

Starbound is in my view a very good and enjoyable game, even in early access.
However to avoid burning through my interest for the game I decided to wait till they make a release version.
The game as it is is already quite enjoyable as it is, but there are still things that could use improvement, are too easy and/or things that will be changed as it is still in development.

Game is fun, and I do recommend it, but there are a few issues that should be addressed before full release. The game doesn't really utilize multiple threads well, so I had to lower CPU-bound settings to keep my framerate up. Not a huge issue, and I don't really expect a DX9 game to take advantage of a Core i7 CPU, but my graphics card loafs at about 60% utilization. Framerates are still in excess of 100, so I do definitely plan to play more of this game with the 144Hz monitor that's on the way, but if the game was more optimized for multi-core (again, something I don't expect of a DX9 title) I think I'd be seeing higher framerates. The most pressing issue, and I hope Neowiz addresses it, is the game heavily favors HIGH PING. I have better games on EU servers with ping reaching 200, than on NA servers with ping hovering around 50. I'm not the only person who has seen this issue in action. Otherwise, this game has loads of potential.
I highly recommend it to anyone who likes roguelikes, resource management, JRPG combat, or roleplaying games. The Narrator in this game is the best I can recall from any game, movie, or otherwise.

Xcom 2012 was a great game.  Xcom 2 aggressively changes everything that made its predecessor great.  Let me count the ways.
- This game is a turn based strategy, only when it wants to be
There are enemies that can both move and attack you on your turn.  YOUR turn!  All your troops are positioned perfectly.  You inch your way forward as safely as possible.  One soldier takes one step too far.  Suddenly (still, during your turn) an alien shows up, runs towards this soldier, attacks AND poisons them.  Your soldier will be dead in 4 turns.  That's what you get for walking.  This game hates you.  It wants all your troops to die.  It will take their lives in the most unfair ways.
- Geoscape is overly complex and confusing
Base management in Xcom 2012 was fairly straight forward.  You needed to research stuff and build stuff and grow your staff.  This was all to gain more satellites, thus increasing your income.  Apparently Firaxis didn't like how cut and dry this was, so they completely changed the base management aspect and hid every bit of information behind a wall of obfuscation.  Let's say you want to fly your base to gather supplies.  The game tells you there are supplies waiting, and that it will take 4 day to collect them.  So you fly to the supplies and start waiting.  Within seconds, a red dot is added to the alien advancement gauge.  You are one step closer to losing the game.  In reality, this gauge isn't all that important, but its inclusion stresses out players for the first 5 - 10 hours.  Whatever, you shrug it off and keep waiting for the supplies.  Seconds later, you are presented with 3 bad "Dark Events".  These happen monthly.  You get the ability to prevent one of them.  The others will happen.  Sometimes just one of them, other times both of them.  It seems random and just adds more confusion and stress.  And just to make things even more stressful, they don't tell you what the third dark event is.  You have to pay to unlock that information.  Sometimes you won't have the money to do so.
You start off with one scientist and one engineer.  You are not really told how to get more.  You can't use your knowledge of Xcom 2012 for this, because gaining staff is completely changed in this new game.
- Unlike Xcom 2012, the randomness in this game is really frustrating and it makes no sense
Due to Xcom 2's punishing nature, you will often find yourself in a situation where you absolutely NEED a shot to connect.  A group of aliens appear.  You've approached the situation perfectly.  The group was discovered at the very beginning of your turn, giving you the best chance of killing all the aliens.  Your sniper has a 82% change to hit.  MISS!  Your grenadier has a 67% chance to hit. MISS!  You re-analyze your situation, realizing that you can no longer kill all the enemies that turn.  Someone is going to take damage.  If your unlucky streak continues, the alien will do a critical hit and kill your soldier instantly.  You will come to love grenades simply because they can't miss.  You can't even rely on your ranger's sword.  Standing directly next to someone and only have a 94% chance to hit them is crazy.  Sure those are good odds, but the first time the sword misses will make you second guess using it ever again.  Later in the game you will find that enemies have ridiculous dodging ability.  Flanking an alien that is only a few tiles away will frequently give you only  a 70% - 80% chance to hit.  There is absolutely no way to improve those odds.  You just have to get lucky.  This game hates you.  It wants all your troops to die.
- Xcom 2 attempts to give the player heavy choices, but it fails
Games are all about choice.  The right choice depends on context, the state the gameworld is in.  The player has to analyze their game state and determine what the proper choice is for their situation.  A proper decision means the player made a proper analysis.  This is satisfying.  Xcom 2 tries to make it's decision making hard by witholding vital information.  This is frustrating.  You will fail and it won't be your fault.
- Ambiguity
Grenadiers gain an ability that lets them fire at all enemies in a cone-of-sight.  The game just tells you that this consumes "lots" of ammo.  How much?  You just have to figure that out on your own.  When you try it in battle, you will feel ripped off.  Not only does it use up all your ammo, but it prevents you from reloading for several turns.  Not only that, but the ability can miss.  There is absolutely no reason for the game to withhold this kind of info from the player.  THIS IS NOT THE RIGHT WAY TO MAKE A GAME DIFFICULT!  btw, this kind of thing happens a lot.  Here is another example.  Some armor only needs to be build once.  A single build cost gives you access to unlimited of that armor.  Other armor requires you to build individual sets.  There does not seem to be any indicator of which is which.  I eventually learned to save my game before doing anything new.  In fact, saving and loading is the only way the player can really come to understand what is going on.  If you are going to use a new ability for the first time, save the game and be prepared to reload once you have figured out what the consequences are.
- BUGS!
There are so many bugs in this game.  Unlike Bethesda games, these bugs aren't funny OR innocent.  I've had several soldiers burst into flame for no reason.  I had one soldier catch fire while running over a tile that had no fire on it.  Upon reloading, the tile did have fire on it.  The game simply failed to load the fire effect on that tile.  When moving your troops, an icon will appear over the tile your mouse is on.  This icon indicates that the soldier will pass through fire/acid/poison/windows/doors if they move to this location.  This is great, except when the icon fails to show itself.  This has caused me many reloads.  There are also many times when the game failed to tell me that an enemy had entered overwatch.  A linear, single-player affair has no right being so buggy.  This game honestly feels like it's still in beta.
- Conclusion
Xcom 2 has moments of greatness.  One of the earlier missions was one of the most intense and enjoyable experiences I've had gaming.  However, the confusion, frustration, and plethora of bugs strips it of all it's greatness.  One moment I loved the game, the next moment I hated it.  This is coming from someone who loved Xcom 2012 and indeed the original from the 90s.  It's unfortunate, because when the stars align and the bugs aren't an issue, a pretty good game wants to emerge.  In the end, I wish I had passed this game up.

Everything about star dew valley inherits that very characteristic - the way you interact with npcs , growing and harvesting crops , the soundtrack and so on. Of course you can choose to make the game a bit more tense by trying to sell the best crops for maximum profit or trying to get every fish that roams the waters around town but i don't feel that that is the sole purpose of star dew valley.

Starbound is very similar to Terraria at first glance. It offers a procedural and destructible two-dimensional enviornment in which almost everything is out to kill you, and where you will only survive by scavenging you way up the food chain. Mine ores and gather wood, build tools and a shelter - then build a means of crafting more tools and better shelters. Grow stronger by growing more knowledgeable, and pay attention as each trip outwards takes you further, earns you more, and leaves you alive just that much longer. Fight, craft, survive! The user interface is not entirely different, the mouse-and-keyboard controls will feel familiar the moment you start, and many of hte incidental details between both titles blend beautifully as well.
There is however, one big difference, and it's certainly big. The engine offers you your first procedurally generated planet, and it's only the first of many. The first of thousands, if not more. Travel!
It plays out very well - my first day with Starbound left me restless as I discovered that the planets are actually not that big, and they eventually wrap around. Regardless of that fact, I set out to explore and discovered various creatures, the majority wanting to kill me, a select few that were more passive. As a Terraria player, a short jaunt like this left my heart aching. I wanted to journey elsewhere.
Your base in Starbound is not a planet at all, in fact, despite that you can mark a planet as your "home," meaning you will always be able to travel back to it no matter how far off in the galaxy you have traveled, your true base is actually a spaceship, distinct for each of the six races that you can pick between at the start. There are a few diverse races in which you can choose from, but despite all the selection, I decided to be boring and be a "Human" whose planet (Earth) had all of its resources dried up.
There was no fuel in the tank, however, so I beamed down to the planet once more, and this time I started to go through the brief sweep of story missions that are currnetly available. These teach you the basics of gathering resources, first with a matter manipulator - useful though slow - and soon with a series of metal tools you craft for yourself. Think of it as tutorials, the next educating you about crafting things such as weapons and tools, and armors. As with Terraria, you are going to spend a lot of the early game cutting down trees for lumber, making workbenches and foundries, and paging through the lists of trinkets and knick knacks you can create with them. Truthfully, nothing about any of that is fun, and it's a chore, there's no denying it.
There is a silver lining. I'm only several hours in, and I am still exploring different planets, and seeing new things. What will you find out there? Beyond your early adventures lies an infinite plain of crafting, shaping, constructing and plundering. Bring friends and start a war. Jump on a server populated with strangers and see how long you will survive.
For a game so closely connected to one another, Starbound already differs itself to Terraria. Terraria is about exploring a single, procedurally generated world that grows stranger and more diverse as you pull back hte layers. A lot of Starbound's planets are simple at present - you can walk around them, dig down to their cores and feel as though you have got the measure of them entirely. Its rich diversity comes as you hop between one planet to another: despite having the same tools and the same objectives, there is a unique sense from being a settler and being an explorer.
The game is truly fascinating, and I have been waiting for some time to get my hands on this title. I highly recommend this title to any Minecraft or Terraria enthusiasts seeing as it provides the same interlocked chains of distraction that define each of game respectively. Whether you want to travel the cosmos solo, or bring along friends, this title provides the same joy and heartfelt elements that Minecraft and Terraria have brought to me - and with more updates to come in the near future, I recommend this game to you.

Stardew Valley is a peaceful top-down farming simulator similar to Harvest Moon but presented to you in 32 bit graphics. You inherit an overgrown farm where you slowly fix the place up, plant seeds of various types over the seasons, and tend to your farm animals. You’d then sell the products and crops you have collected over the day to afford better equipment and even more seeds to repeat the process over again the next day. The game’s main focus leans toward farming specific resources to complete ‘bundles’. This is complemented with a simplistic marriage mechanic, skill levels, a combat system reserved for the mines, and a peaceful story experienced with the locals as you get to know them.
I managed to play over 45 hours, planting and harvesting crops, tending to my farm animals, hitting on the local hotties, and adventuring through the mine. After a while, I realised it was very repetitive doing the same thing everyday waiting for my crops to grow so I could sell them to get more seeds. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing, I was entertained the entire time and worked towards small goals. But, even missing one seasonal plant or not doing a specific thing during a scripted festival can set you back hours. It felt like skipping through each day to quickly get what I want went against the spirit of the game so I took my time playing and was rewarded for my time. Overall, I’d recommend this game to casual gamers.

Here comes my opinion of XCom2.
In Short. Can I recommend it?
No. Not at its current state.
Iam kind of sad to say this, but this game should have never been release in its state.
So, whats wrong with it?
I will start with what is right instead.
The Good:
Since the XCom:EU remake, some changes in compare to the originals from the 90's are realy good.
First of, it plays fast, action packed, and is nice to look at.
The "just one more turn" feeling is still there, and you never get bored during the missions.
The story is ok'ish, not that great but you want to know more and why things happen.
Reduction of action points to simple 2 actions per turn leads to a fast paced tactical play, skill and soldier class system feels at the right deep for this fast gameplay.
Sadly thats almost all about it.
The Bad:
-worldmap
The stratetic map has been stripped down even more since XCom:EU. You have almost no choices or alternatives, no options.
Without spoilers of some sort, every thing you can do is kind of mandatory. If you dont do the right things, you dont advance...but...you will do it because there isnt anything else to do.
In fact, you wouldnt even notice if the worldmap where not existent and this things would be done by the AI for you.
-basebuilding
Its almost the same here. You have some options of buildings, but they are not optional. You can and must build exactly 1 of the key buildings (you cant build more)
Then there are 4 facilities left you can choose to build. 2 are almost irrelevant (did complete it without even building them) and the others are also mandatory to support your base.
No real choices, no alternative approaches.
-UI
Horrible. For a PC exclusive game I was hoping for a very good and fluent UI. Insteat we got a cumbersome bunch of menus, where everytime you want to go to another menu you have to watch animations of zooming in and out for seconds. Soldier customizing is unintuitiv at best, and burred in lots of different layers till you get your dude equiped and colored.
Also there is a constant feel of lack of information. To check your current weapon, upgrades and personal stims etc. on one soldier you need to zoom in and out through a bunch of menus. In your squad overview you see fancy 3D models but almost nothing else.
Gameplay flow comes to a crawl here.
Overall presentation of information is realy bad in almost every part of the game.
-missions
The maps are now random generated, which is cool. The battles have not changed to much from :EU. But the maps are ridiculous bugged regarding line of sight, cover etc. (shooting through walls, meele through roofs etc.)
The new stealth mode in some missions is just a nice ice on the cake, but its not well thought out. After the initial stealth the enemies still getting their free movement, autospot you if you spot them etc.
Cover is now destructible, which is a good thing, except its to easy and to unpredictable to destroy. I had whole housefronts collapse to dust from swordblows, or fires expand through thin air.
-AI
The AI feels implausible. Suicide troops left and right, which you cant take out fast enough in early game, and are too easy later on. Most of the difficult comes from the unpredictable random generator and absurd skills some enmies have. In contrast the lategame feels just like a walk in the park, because your soldiers become also absurd overpowered.
So it is a very deadly beatup where you hardly can predict the exact outcome. Luck is a factor here. (even very good players are at times just had more luck then others)
Then the enemy behavior is sometimes very predictable, even in unlogic situations. If you study this you can abuse it to cancel some threats completely.
-performance
Oh my God. I dont even know what causes a turn based game to suck this much at performance at almost every aspect. Loading times, movie frame rate, animations, delay and hickups here and there. Very often complete animation sequences are skipped for no obvious reason so you have to guess what just happened. (talking about you snakeman)
The aftermission reportscreen sometimes needs longer to load then the mission itself, at least it feels like this.
You can watch how textures get loaded etc. etc. And no, I didnt play it on Max Settings, even with my very good rig.
-support
Lame. We got 1 patch till today which caused more problems then it solved. Critical flaws are still unadressed.
So in conclusion, I had my fun with one playthrough, and i had my frustration. But I cant stand to play another campaign because of the numerous flaws, bugs and the horrendous slow UI animations, constant anoying voice chat from your central and lots of other minor things.
XCom 2 could have been a precious gem, but someone forgot to polish it.

This game BLEW MY MIND.
Never before did I think an idea this vacuous at face value could lead to gameplay this masochistically enabling, and its lighthearted, obnoxiously upbeat aural and visual design was a more than welcome squeeze of originality into the mind-numbing flood of banality present in today's AAA gaming scene.
Furthermore, I did some research on
and saw that my ancestors, eons ago, were slices of bread. Based on firsthand accounts in diaries and what I could find scribbled inside our family heirloom toaster is that the struggles of their survival were startlingly similar to those we see in game. This just goes to show how accurately the life of a slice of bread is simulated in this ludological masterpiece. For example, my great-great grandfather's 11th birthday was spent getting toasted. His account of holding onto a pot with 3 corners and pulling with the 4th in order to fly across the room was expertly demonstrated through several instances in which I feel compelled to grab things and fly across the room (in-game, of course).
Finally, I am Bread has sent me to the depths of dispair, the pinnacle of ecstasy and, due to my reaction to accidentally clipping through the house in bagel race, causing my game to crash and a masochistic erection to form while I was in the living room, it led me to a great hair regrowth clinic.
Overall, 8/10.

**SPOILER FREE REVIEW**
I admit, I was concerned when I heard about the story/setting for Xcom 2. However, my fears were unfounded.
Quite simply this game is a triumph. It is a love letter to the fans of the first re-make as well as all of us old gits who have been fighting the alien invasion since 1994.
Technically the game is quite pretty, a definite upgrade from EU/EW. I have heard complaints that it is a bit unoptimised and 'shakey' in places, but barring the odd animation error (the same types you occasionally got in EU) it ran quite nicely at ultra settings on my i7 GTX980 SSD rig.
Less micromanaging and much easier production and equipping of gear. I understand this might disappoint some who loved tinkering with their base for hours, but I found it to be a great improvement, letting me get into the sweet, strategic alien murdering action much faster and more often.
The world system has been overhauled with no more panic/countries withdrawing: A great change in my opinion as countries leaving the project made no sense from a narrative point of view, and wouldn't fit with the story here anyhow.
The new weapons and classes are great and fun to use, as well as giving you a whole lot more options to deal with the Alien/Advent menace.
I particularly liked the Specialist class which are so good they are almost gamebreaking. I say 'almost' because unlike EU/EW in XCOM2 you are always in danger. There are very few aliens who are not a serious threat, even when you are kitted up to the max. A Gatekeeper and a few Codexes (Codexes? Codices? Codii?) can easily ruin your day if you drop your guard and don't plan and move tactically. Even a Snake guy can pull your plan off course (quite literally).I found this to be very refreshing and reminiscent of all the days I spent being tormented by the original game on my trusty Amiga.
The only negative thing I have to say about this game is a tiny one: The lack of David Hoffman voicing CO Bradford. That's not to say Brian Bloom doesn't do a great job, he does, it is just I really liked the original Bradford (especially after EW) and keenly missed his calm and professional tone this time around.
So to sum up: Don't worry, this most definitely is the XCOM you know and love, and it is worth every penny of the price. I would say it is the best investment of £40 I have made in a long time. The campaign is satisfying and fun with plenty of replayability. Couple that with the amazing mod support and you have really good longevity and value for money.

This game used to be fun, back in the day. But ever since SEGA stepped in, it's all gone to hell.
So, here's my two cents about this game:
Spiral Knights is a Free to Play game brought to you by 3Rings. When it was released, way back when in 2011, it drew me in instantly. I loved the aesthetics of the game, the soundtrack was pleasant to listen to, and Craddle, this world you're exploring, was interesting and colorful. Gameplay reminded me of the classic Zelda games, and since I also enjoyed those, it was all the more reason for me to play.
That was the GOOD.
Let me show you the BAD.
This game only has two servers. TWO. North America and Europe. As someone living in China, this was a major deterrent, as every level was laggier than the previous one, and enemies could kill you faster than you can shout "GODDAMN LAG SPIKES". As a result, it was a chore to play the game with a crappy latency, and facing Devilite levels was something I avoided all too entirely. Carrying on...
Eventually, there was enough of a community outcry, that we got more servers. But we had no way of transferring our characters there. Why? Because the servers belonged to a Chinese company who got the rights to distribute the game in Asia, meaning, their version of the game was standalone, and that meant RESTARTING EVERYTHING. GRINDING EVERYTHING ALL OVER AGAIN. (also, apparently, that is gone now too, no more Asian server)
Grind. Yes, grind. You need to invest a lot of time into this game, as prices are really high, and the average Crowns you earn (the mission currency) per mission is too little. Back in the day, I grinded crowns to buy recipes for better gear, as I levelled up the current gear to suit the crafting requirements. Now, you grind crowns to buy some dumb crystals in order to level your gear. In other words, before, levelling up gear was automatic, and now, you need permission. Not enough crystals to upgrade? TOO BAD. GUESS YOU'RE STUCK WITH THAT TOOTHPICK UNTIL YOU GET THE DOSH TO UPGRADE!
I think I should mention there's also PvP, but since it's such a mess, I guess I'll just sum it up as best as I can:
Blast Network - Bomberman ripoff. Enjoyable, if there are people to play with you and if your latency is stable, which, in my case, that never happens. There's never a single soul in there.
LockDown - This is the most played game mode, but it's so full of arrogant players who think using the same gear and same weapons (which are painfully simple to use and require no skill whatsoever) makes them "pros". Something as convoluted as this isn't fun for the average player, or the new player for that matter.
And here's the UGLY.
This game is being handled by SEGA. 3Rings is just a puppet. That means whatever new content that was planned by the developers is witheld by SEGA in favour of redecos of cosmetics shoved inside payed lockboxes. Because they gotta milk this cow dry, amirite? To the point the lead designer, one of the individuals who brought us this game, left back in 2013. When SEGA stepped in. From that day forward, most of the new things that arrived were just lockboxes. Lockboxes everywhere. Oh yeah there was also the pet thingamajig and some pseudo-bosses and recycled levels, but, mostly? Lockboxes.
And this is the result, a game that is a shadow of its' former self.
No new content.
No new bosses.
No new lore.
...No new nothing. Just more cosmetic redecos that would make Hasbro proud.
Might as well call this game "COSMETIC KNIGHTS", because frankly, that name does more justice than the word "Spiral".
...Yeah, I'm salty about this. Spiral Knigths had a lot of potential back in the day, and I loved it a lot, but seeing it like this, it just ticks me off. New levels, bosses, soundtracks, lore, all thrown away because SEGA wants more money and because 3Rings no longer cares.
To quote JC Denton, "What a shame."

I'd been looking forward to XCOM 2 from the very first trailer on. It did not dissapoint.
Pretty much everything that was said about it during its previews and pre-release write ups is spot on. It's XCOM: Enemy Unknown/ Within +11. It's one of the rare post-2004 games that feels like a complete package rather than something counting on DLC (even though DLC -has- been announced).
Short point by point:
- The guns look and sound cool, and customizing them is fun.
- Armor and props also have sweet visual designs, and whatever is lacking has already been taken care of by mods. My one complaint with them is that the Plated and Power Armor styles seem to have fewer customization options, but I imagine this will be dealt with soon enough via mods and DLC.
- Gameplay.... its XCOM: EU but better. Larger, less predictable maps, more abilities, improved and more impactful environmental destruction, MANY more items.
- More emphasise on mission objectives instead of just "kill things".
- The base management/ world map part of the game has been improved treamendously, with a lot of decisions to make that will pull you in multiple directions but all be just as important. Everything you do or don't do in the geoscape/ management section will have  a direct impact over what happens on ground level.
The only major gameplay complaint I have is that soldiers seem to get "gravely wounded" over the smallest injury. The game also doesn't do a  good job of explaining its various systems, so you'll likely restart your campaign a  few times just trying to figure out what is what. Fortunately, the game is HIGHLY replayable, so it doesn't get annoying.
A lot of people have complained about performance issues. I'm playing on a bellow-recommended system (graphics card is a Quadro 600), so it wouldn't be fair of me to poke at that, but I'll say this; the game is still very playable and a lot of fun even with a poor frame rate.
So yes....a good buy. Especially if you liked XCOM: EU, but even if you haven't played it, now's a good time to get a taste of XCOM!

I very much enjoy this game when I have time to play it. My friends and I always do missions together, and I absolutely love playing this game. It is free, which is a huge plus, considering all the Pros I put down. The one thing that bugs me is the small pay-to-win feature. If you go to the store, every thing costs ENERGY. Energy is obtained in certain missions I believe, but they are very hard to earn. You can buy them with real life money or trading CROWNS for ENERGY. You can also trade ENERGY with other players.
Crowns are earned in missions, they are very common. Basically, 9,000 crowns for 100 energy. Depends on what people put up in the market. But it's always expensive, which means if you want good things you have to save Crowns to trade for Energy to buy stuff in the market. That's the biggest con of this game, the worst flaw.
I really love the guilds. Sure, it costs a lot to form one, but a lot of people invite me to their guilds and my friends and I are currently in a guild, maybe someday we'll even form our own! I love how you can fight with your guild in the Colleseium, and how there are a lot of guild features.
The monsters you fight each have their own unique attacks that force you to either use a gun or a sword/shovel/axe. (Basically long range, close range)
The fighting in this game is something I very much enjoy. I abosolutely LOVE doing combo attacks by using a charge sword attack, then doing a shield bash, shooting fire from my pet, and ending it with a sword bash. I'm one of those people who likes fighting with swords, to where you can control attacks and do amazing combos.
The multiplayer feature is a good one. The loading can be so annoying sometimes. It takes my friends about 10 minutes to load into the mission I'm in. But other than that, I've experienced not much lag at all.
The missions are cool. They vary from arcade missions that are random, and to ranked missions. And two other mission categories you have to unlock. You can play them with friends, too! (As long as you're a rank that is eligible for the mission)
The graphics are very cool. I love all the colors and all the characters and designs. They really bring a uniqueness to the game that I haven't experienced with any other game.
I like the friend system. I get to interact with a bunch of different people. You can meet a lot of people, but you have to be careful who you interact with, because this IS the internet.
One of the funniest features of this game are the commands. You have MANY commands, such as /cry , /shout (message), /kiss, etc.
I really, really like how you can have 3 different Knights, because then your siblings can play on their OWN characters and not ruin your own! Or you could create 3 different characters for the 3 different pet types!
This game is for all ages! I recommend it to ANYONE!
I wish there could be like races or something. Like, you go into a space craft (COULD YOU ADD THOSE TOO!?) and you race people online. (Random people or your friends) Then you could get rewards!
Add more pet interactions! More pet choices! We want lots of pets and we want to INTERACT with them!
I have some tips for you.
Save up Energy AND Crowns. You'll need them to buy materials craft different items that are vital for more advanced missions.
Find a guild as quick as you can.
I recommend playing only with people you know. People can be rude and weird. But it's your choice.
Make sure you spend Crowns/Energy WISELY, because you never know what you'll need for specific missions.
If your friends have, in example, the Phantom and Angel Cat pets, get the Dragon one. When you play together, you'll  need different skills in battle to succeed better.
Well, that was my review! I hope I helped you! Check out my other reviews!

It was difficult for me to decide if I was going to click the yes or no button for reccomendation, simply because the game has a lot of flaws right now. And yet, despite all of these apparent flaws, i had the most fun in recent memory playing this game than anything else.
The issues with the game should be stated outright, those being bugs, performance, and to some a difficulty curve that is haphazard at best. *note that the last one I hardly noticed. There were only two difficulty spikes in my playthrough for me, those being when i first encountered a specific psionic enemy time that appears later in the game, and the final level.
The game is buggy as heck, and while a vast majority of bugs are graphical, and only serve to give rise to the occational head shake or chuckle, there are a few bugs that are frustrating. One bug has the map turn into a technicolor mess that could induce siezures, and another bug will cause a character to just die randomly. Thankfully the seccond bug only occured to me once, and was one of the few times I reloaded through my playthorugh. The game also has a lot of loading times, and performance issues like framerate are constantly put at the forefront.
NOW despite all of this, I am still reccomending the game, because the game itself is in my opinion better than previous installment by leaps and bounds. While most find the turn timer limiting, I personally liked it, as it forced me to go from an agonizing crawl to a frantic race against time where the slightest mistep is death, and while people here will complain that this leaves troops liable to getting murdered, I argue that the game gives you all the tools you need to keep tabs on the enemy. Concealment is your number one weapon against the missions with the clock, and you have it for all of them, and the options given to you when you have complete control over how you engage the enemy is amazing. It opens up even further once you unlock the upgrades in the ranger path that keep your ranger in concealment if the group breaks it, meaning you can use them as a forward scout.
As for the missions without turn timers, it basically is exactly what you would expect from Xcom 2.
Since i wasnt particularly a fan of the air game from the last game, because it essentially devolved to "do you have the required specs? if yes you get a mission, if no you get a sattelite destroyed," the lack of one here was actually not a big deal for me.
All in all, I personally enjoy this game, and if you can look past some bugs and stuff, i am sure you can too.

I really wish that I could recommend this game, but it has so many faults that I can't.
The game itself is fairly good.  It's very relaxing and peaceful, and it doesn't throw you into the water at the beginning, but instead starts you off at a pace that if you keep it up then you will succeed.
The artstyle is good as well, however, it does get a little stale after a while.
The soundtrack is great.  The music really defines all of the seasons in the game, which makes the game feel more alive.
The game doesn't limit you to doing one thing.  If you don't want to farm then you can fish.  Don't want to fish?  Then go mining.  Don't want to go mining?  Go foraging.
The game may have a time limit all the time, but that just makes it feel more realistic, as you have to plan out what you're going to plant or do every season.
Stardew Valley may seem like a good game, but trust me, it has faults that ruin it.
For starters, the villagers in the game are awful.  They each are just cliches of modern steriotypes and only grow personality wise if you become friends with them.  Even then though, they just regergitate the same duialouge every season.
There is no real sense of time in the game.  Every year is the same.  The only thing that changes is in Year 2 when a new character is introduced, but he too is another steriotype.
Just like almost every other game, this one has achievements.  Some of them are pretty good ones, like getting to the bottom of the mines.  However, others require you to craft every item in the game.  This is definitely challenging, but the only challenging part of it is getting all of the ingredients to make them, which can take many in-game YEARS to get.
The Museum in the game takes years and years and even more years to complete.  Sometimes you can get it done in just a few, but 9 times out of 10 it will take forever to complete.  Why?  Because the game doesn't like to give you the items that you need.  I myself have spent tons of real life HOURS trying to collect the artifacts that you need to donate, but since the game randomly generates how many artifact spawns there are each day and what spawns in them you pretty much have a 1/1000 chance to get what you need.
I've noticed in the last few days that this game relies too much on its bad item spawning to increase its longetivity, which is a sign that the dev didn't put a lot in the game.
Speaking of which, there isn't a whole lot to do in Stardew Valley.  Sure, you can farm, mine, fish, forage, and fight, but those all get very bland after Year 2.  There are secrets to find, but most of them are somewhat boring and either give you a useless item or a Stardrop, which increases your in-game energy.
Even though there are multiple things to do in game, the game mostly focusses on farming.  This is a bummer as it gives the game very little replay value.
The only reason that you would even want to start a new save file would be to get a certain achievement.
Lastly, I have one Pro of the game that I didn't want to mention above.  Stardew Valley has this bug where if you name yourself or an animal a certain number (like this: [XXX]) then the game spawns the item associated with that number in.  This is a lifesaver in certain situations.  An example being me trying to find the Ancient Seed (an in-game artifact) that I needed to get so that I could craft an Ancient Seed Packet for the achievement Craft Master I couldn't find legit so I had to use this exploit to get it.  This bug can also be used to get a good sum of money really quickly, so if you get the game and are short on cash, go buy a new chicken and name it [163], this gives you a very expensive fish that is worth $5k.
All in all, if you want a game that you can just play to relax then get this. If you want to get a game that you will enjoy then realize how empty it is once you reach the 40 hour mark then avoid this game.

It was difficult for me to decide if I was going to click the yes or no button for reccomendation, simply because the game has a lot of flaws right now. And yet, despite all of these apparent flaws, i had the most fun in recent memory playing this game than anything else.
The issues with the game should be stated outright, those being bugs, performance, and to some a difficulty curve that is haphazard at best. *note that the last one I hardly noticed. There were only two difficulty spikes in my playthrough for me, those being when i first encountered a specific psionic enemy time that appears later in the game, and the final level.
The game is buggy as heck, and while a vast majority of bugs are graphical, and only serve to give rise to the occational head shake or chuckle, there are a few bugs that are frustrating. One bug has the map turn into a technicolor mess that could induce siezures, and another bug will cause a character to just die randomly. Thankfully the seccond bug only occured to me once, and was one of the few times I reloaded through my playthorugh. The game also has a lot of loading times, and performance issues like framerate are constantly put at the forefront.
NOW despite all of this, I am still reccomending the game, because the game itself is in my opinion better than previous installment by leaps and bounds. While most find the turn timer limiting, I personally liked it, as it forced me to go from an agonizing crawl to a frantic race against time where the slightest mistep is death, and while people here will complain that this leaves troops liable to getting murdered, I argue that the game gives you all the tools you need to keep tabs on the enemy. Concealment is your number one weapon against the missions with the clock, and you have it for all of them, and the options given to you when you have complete control over how you engage the enemy is amazing. It opens up even further once you unlock the upgrades in the ranger path that keep your ranger in concealment if the group breaks it, meaning you can use them as a forward scout.
As for the missions without turn timers, it basically is exactly what you would expect from Xcom 2.
Since i wasnt particularly a fan of the air game from the last game, because it essentially devolved to "do you have the required specs? if yes you get a mission, if no you get a sattelite destroyed," the lack of one here was actually not a big deal for me.
All in all, I personally enjoy this game, and if you can look past some bugs and stuff, i am sure you can too.
