Just barely scratching the surface of this game and I am incredibly impressed. Have a few FPS drops during loading and Avenger flight sequences but other than that my performance has been just fine (AMD R9 290x). In addition, after playing for 6 hours I've only run into one "bug" and it was only some actions not properly playing their animations ( a reload fixed it).
There was a lot of potential for a sequel to a highly successful reboot and for the most part I believe that XCom 2 succeeded in hitting those pockets of potential. There are still some issues that carried over from the first game of the reboot, though, and that's an issue. (Why is the camera still so terrible? Why does it bug out during action camera?)
One thing I instantly dislike about this game is the fact that it is determined to be a timed event. The previous game was timed only by how long you could keep your XCom project alive. However, the sequel has mostly timed missions and a doomsday clock clicking down (you can offset and slow the doomsday clock, but it's still there.) I wish there hadn't been such a heavy emphasis on making the player rush around to do everything as it pigeon-holes you into a playstyle. All that said, you can easily and quickly download a mod to modify the time limit on missions and remove the doomsday clock if you so choose, so at least the option is there.
Character customization is greatly improved, and the character pool was a great addition. Armor and weapon additions and upgrades are great, too.

As of writing this, XCOM 2 is unplayable. The load it puts on my system is insane, resulting in ubiquitous performance issues. Including the typical load screen (soldiers sitting in the back of skyranger) and deployment animations, actually starting a mission might take me 5 - 10 minutes. Stuttering, skipping, freezing, etc. Seems like some LOS bugs too.
The ability to draw soldiers from a pre-created pool is a welcome addition in concept, yet disappointing in function. The class that you've chosen for a soldier pre-game does not stick, and they must be put through training at the Guerilla Tactics School to be assigned a class. This only applies to rookies, however, so if your soldier is promoted prior to this process, they have the usual chances of getting assigned to any specialty. "Don't deploy that soldier until they go through the GTS, then". Unfortunately, you're guarenteed to have one or more of your pool soldiers assigned to the first mission, so waiting for the GTS isn't an option for them. Pool soldiers can be encountered as rewards later on, yet even higher ranked soldiers will have specialties different from what you set for them.
Additionally, the attitudes you assign your troops are randomized as well, and for whatever reason you are not able to change them back - atleast at lower ranks. Soldiers' names, appearance, sex, and race can be changed on a wim, but something dynamic like their mindset cannot. Okay then.
Despite the inhibiting performance concerns and a flawed pre-game customization utility, I'm still going to recommend XCOM 2. Once they get this ironed out it will be atleast as good as Enemy Unknown - and that game was the sh*t. Huge potential, many additions, just not what it needs to be right now.

This is the first time I actually get around to writing a "review" on Steam - let's say I felt compelled.
I could write a thorough review where I could present my analysis of the game, and I can tell you right now that it would be mostly positive... after all, the tried and tested gameplay dynamics of EU are thoroughly implemented in XCOM 2, which is exactly what many of us were hoping for, and that alone is a major selling point (at least for me).
However, the unfortunate reality is that I find that the game as it stands is not even WORTHY of a review of that kind of nature, because it has not AT ALL been optimized... it plays like an early beta (and even that is a generous statement).
For this price tag, I expect at the very least a stable and mostly seamless game in terms of functionality (with exception to large-scale, open world games like F4, Skyrim and the likes where unique bugs are unavoidable due to the sheer magnitude of possible executions). XCOM 2 seamless? Not. Even. Close.
Aside from the annoying lack of graphics optimization which causes at times severe drops to FPS, there are shading problems, jittering and a plethora of other issues that affect gameplay... but that, folks, isn't even the worst part.
The game has a mind-bogglingly high crash-frequency, and it's impossible to determine most of the causes. Sometimes the game stops working, other times it just closes, and on rare occasions, it actually induces a fatal error in the system causing a blue screen or otherwise forcing a hard reboot. I have NEVER seen the likes of it, and I've done everything in my power on the user side to resolve, or rather mitigate the problems, to absolutely no avail.
The crashes have been a show-stopper for many users trying to get in on the noble quest to save the Earth... but, not all.
Be advised, if you buy this game, there is a very good chance it will be practically unplayable to you. If you do experience crashes early, immediately get a refund before it's too late, because you more than likely not be able to resolve the issues.
TL;DR: XCOM 2 is virtually unplayable due to terrible optimization, and I cannot with a clear conscience recommend this game to anyone at its current quality, especially at the shameful price. I look forward to the patch.
EDIT:
To date, it's been exactly six months since I made my original review, and I figured I'd try out XCOM 2 again. There's a multitude of different mods, and a series of new DLCs added since the game came out, and I wanted to give it a run.
During my first runthrough six months ago, I actually ended up pushing through the game (despite crashing an uncountable amount of times a day). Why? Well, the game IS entertaining, and even though I suffered through hours trying to fix the crashes to no avail, as well as countless restarts due to those very same crashes, I still wanted to get through it. Hey, it was too late for a refund...
Now I'm back, and I didn't dream that the game would still be suffering issues... and yet it did. After copious amounts of research (here we effing go again), there seems to be no solution or even trigger for the most common crash, the one that I'm also experiencing. In addition, there seems to be no indication that Firaxis, to be frank, gives one iota of a♥♥♥♥♥♥(it's been happening since the Shen's Last Gift DLC, it would seem).
Unbelievable. It sucks that I couldn't change my review.

Let's start with the highest acclaim that I can give a game:  It rewards intelligent play!  By this I mean, it's not just reaction time, it's not just pretty 3-D graphics, it's really hard turn-based play, and you have to fight back against the game by every means possible just to survive and certainly to have any chance of conquering!
It is hard hard hard, I rarely play games that try to kill me so much, but in this case, it's my scrabble for survival that will make the difference, unlike some games out there that are hard in boring ways.
The game obviously has a lot of depth, a lot of care, and a lot of detail put into it's development, from it's lush voice acting, it's beautifully detailed characters and classes, to it's unflinchingly dark atmosphere.
But there is a downside, and that is the RNG (random number generator).  The game is so random, that it subverts your ability to intelligently keep yourself alive.  Often events will just go bad and your whole party, that you have built so very painstakingly, will all slowly be killed by inches.  So it takes a certain mindset to even play the game (after the 3rd party wipe), but that "danger" also makes you really try your hardest to keep your beloved characters alive.  Often without success.
So go into it knowing that sometimes the randomness will kill you, and without question your characters will die some, and try to enjoy this horror game with that kind of Lovecraftian atmosphere to it.

Okay I can already say right off the bat as I am sure you will find out, I am very fond of this game. The first thing I was worried about was the economy/shop system in the game, I was deeply worried it would be pay to win. It actually isn't pay to win at all. In fact, you simply cannot just buy in-game currency for weapons at all. Instead, you get 3 types of currencies, of which I can't remember the names of all of them now. I'll break them down below.
CURRENCIES? CURRENCIES.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
So the way the buy/shop system works is that you have two in-game currencies that as far as I am aware can only be earned via playing the actual game, which is used to unlock every weapon available, and even types of grenades and skins. Then there is the actual "cash shop" side of the game. It is basically just buying the guns with specific skins to them, a lot like CSGO, as well as random boxes similar to the way cases work in CSGO. That is essentially all that I have seen that is worth mentioning in it.
Gameplay? Gameplay.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Another interesting part about the game is the fact that it seems to be inspired by CSGO missions, and shop mechanics, but it plays almost identically to the way the old Sudden Attack game did. That's right, if you, like me, really, really, loved Sudden Attack as a child, this game is absolutely worth checking out. Although, I will say, as of right now, the map variations are rather minute. As far as I have witnessed there is basically only 4 types of maps that are each different for each game mode, specifically tailored for each of mode in particular.
As a final note to my fellow Sudden Attack fans, I hope you liked the old map with all those storage containers, because it's back, and it's basically just a reskin. It's probably my favorite map in the game when I am in the right mood.

As of writing this, XCOM 2 is unplayable. The load it puts on my system is insane, resulting in ubiquitous performance issues. Including the typical load screen (soldiers sitting in the back of skyranger) and deployment animations, actually starting a mission might take me 5 - 10 minutes. Stuttering, skipping, freezing, etc. Seems like some LOS bugs too.
The ability to draw soldiers from a pre-created pool is a welcome addition in concept, yet disappointing in function. The class that you've chosen for a soldier pre-game does not stick, and they must be put through training at the Guerilla Tactics School to be assigned a class. This only applies to rookies, however, so if your soldier is promoted prior to this process, they have the usual chances of getting assigned to any specialty. "Don't deploy that soldier until they go through the GTS, then". Unfortunately, you're guarenteed to have one or more of your pool soldiers assigned to the first mission, so waiting for the GTS isn't an option for them. Pool soldiers can be encountered as rewards later on, yet even higher ranked soldiers will have specialties different from what you set for them.
Additionally, the attitudes you assign your troops are randomized as well, and for whatever reason you are not able to change them back - atleast at lower ranks. Soldiers' names, appearance, sex, and race can be changed on a wim, but something dynamic like their mindset cannot. Okay then.
Despite the inhibiting performance concerns and a flawed pre-game customization utility, I'm still going to recommend XCOM 2. Once they get this ironed out it will be atleast as good as Enemy Unknown - and that game was the sh*t. Huge potential, many additions, just not what it needs to be right now.

This is the first time I actually get around to writing a "review" on Steam - let's say I felt compelled.
I could write a thorough review where I could present my analysis of the game, and I can tell you right now that it would be mostly positive... after all, the tried and tested gameplay dynamics of EU are thoroughly implemented in XCOM 2, which is exactly what many of us were hoping for, and that alone is a major selling point (at least for me).
However, the unfortunate reality is that I find that the game as it stands is not even WORTHY of a review of that kind of nature, because it has not AT ALL been optimized... it plays like an early beta (and even that is a generous statement).
For this price tag, I expect at the very least a stable and mostly seamless game in terms of functionality (with exception to large-scale, open world games like F4, Skyrim and the likes where unique bugs are unavoidable due to the sheer magnitude of possible executions). XCOM 2 seamless? Not. Even. Close.
Aside from the annoying lack of graphics optimization which causes at times severe drops to FPS, there are shading problems, jittering and a plethora of other issues that affect gameplay... but that, folks, isn't even the worst part.
The game has a mind-bogglingly high crash-frequency, and it's impossible to determine most of the causes. Sometimes the game stops working, other times it just closes, and on rare occasions, it actually induces a fatal error in the system causing a blue screen or otherwise forcing a hard reboot. I have NEVER seen the likes of it, and I've done everything in my power on the user side to resolve, or rather mitigate the problems, to absolutely no avail.
The crashes have been a show-stopper for many users trying to get in on the noble quest to save the Earth... but, not all.
Be advised, if you buy this game, there is a very good chance it will be practically unplayable to you. If you do experience crashes early, immediately get a refund before it's too late, because you more than likely not be able to resolve the issues.
TL;DR: XCOM 2 is virtually unplayable due to terrible optimization, and I cannot with a clear conscience recommend this game to anyone at its current quality, especially at the shameful price. I look forward to the patch.
EDIT:
To date, it's been exactly six months since I made my original review, and I figured I'd try out XCOM 2 again. There's a multitude of different mods, and a series of new DLCs added since the game came out, and I wanted to give it a run.
During my first runthrough six months ago, I actually ended up pushing through the game (despite crashing an uncountable amount of times a day). Why? Well, the game IS entertaining, and even though I suffered through hours trying to fix the crashes to no avail, as well as countless restarts due to those very same crashes, I still wanted to get through it. Hey, it was too late for a refund...
Now I'm back, and I didn't dream that the game would still be suffering issues... and yet it did. After copious amounts of research (here we effing go again), there seems to be no solution or even trigger for the most common crash, the one that I'm also experiencing. In addition, there seems to be no indication that Firaxis, to be frank, gives one iota of a♥♥♥♥♥♥(it's been happening since the Shen's Last Gift DLC, it would seem).
Unbelievable. It sucks that I couldn't change my review.

First: Love the game, Love the gameplay and Xcom series is my favorite series of all time, by a very large margin.
Having said that: This game is unplayable.  I'm playing with a Nvidia 4gig 460 GTX, and a 4.7ghz 8 core AMD cpu which should run this at a reasable rate.
Min settings: caps at 27 FPS.  Max settings (excep AA is turned way down) 25 FPS.  Something is just wrong there.  This, I could actually tolerate.
However: The crashes are so prolific it's unplayable.  It crashed 3 times at different points in the tutorial, two of them during cutscenes.  Disabled tutorial, and I get 20-30 crashes per mission.  I can usually get 1-4 turns off before it hardlocks my PC.  I've went through about 40 hours of troubleshooting, and without a doubt it is the the game software.  It's not my hardware, it's not over heating, it's not drivers, it's not corrupted software.  The software itself repeatedly crashes on a significant number of people.
Judging by the overwhelming number of compliants of poor performance and random crashes, it's clear they did not beta test this properly.
**UPDATE** 09/02/17 For the first time, I was able to play through the tutorial and subsequent video without crashing.  I haven't tried since I beat the game (suffering through very frequent crashes) and wrote the original review.  I'm going to give this a positive review while I play through it again, and hopefully no crashes and it can stay positive.

I'll be honest... I LOVED XCOM:EU. So much so that I've completed it multiple times, including on Impossible/Ironman, and on Long War. Everything I saw in the build up to XCOM 2 said that I should love it just as much. But I didn't, and for most of the time, I'm not even sure WHY I don't like it. An accumulation of little things, I think.
For one thing, the story is based on the "it was all a dream" premise. In XCOM 2, the aliens won and everything you experienced from early mid-game in XCOM:EU was actually taking place in an alien simulation, as they pull tactical info and doctrine from your brain. I hate feeling like everything I did and achieved in XCOM:EU was wasted.
For another, they've implemented a turn-counter on many missions that make success or failure into a largely luck-based affair. If you're lucky, the pods are spread out, you can avoid some activations, and you'll succeed at the mission. If you're unlucky, the pods are all in/around the objective, and you'll have to fight them all which is likely to lead to soldier deaths and/or mission failure.
I was attached to my troopers in XCOM:EU, and I liked the classes. In XCOM 2, I just can't find the same level of attachment, nor do I like the classes as much. The Ranger is basically the Assault, but with a melee attack (which is minimally useful, unless you LIKE being out of cover right next to the enemy). The Sniper remains the sniper. The Grenadier is basically a weaksauce Heavy - Why the hell are you carrying a magazine-fed 'nade launcher, and only loading two of the six chambers?! Max two rockets, I could understand, those buggers are heavy... max two 'nades? Not so much. Sure, I know it's for "balance" reasons, but I'd rather have cool than balanced. And don't get me started on the Support - I detest the new hacking minigame. They could have done something really good, but instead, it's just another RNG roll.
In addition, many of the aliens are sporting new abilities, some of which are complete BS. Just one example is the Viper's tongue-grab. They can pull your dudes out of cover into the open, from ridiculously long distances, with near guaranteed hits (I've never seen a miss, although I have seen some YouTubers get some), which pulls you into a grapple for a guaranteed 3 damage, continuing to the next round unless you can succeed at 30%-40% shots. Screw that.
I'm sure there will be some "Git Guds" in response to this review, but they can sod right off. I found the game actively unpleasant to play, and frequently found myself feeling that the game was unfair - and that's coming from a dude who beat XCOM:EU on I/I, and never found it to be as unfair feeling as XCOM2. So take this for what it is.... I didn't enjoy XCOM2. If you have no problems with the issues I raised, you might. I certainly encourage you to try.

First: Love the game, Love the gameplay and Xcom series is my favorite series of all time, by a very large margin.
Having said that: This game is unplayable.  I'm playing with a Nvidia 4gig 460 GTX, and a 4.7ghz 8 core AMD cpu which should run this at a reasable rate.
Min settings: caps at 27 FPS.  Max settings (excep AA is turned way down) 25 FPS.  Something is just wrong there.  This, I could actually tolerate.
However: The crashes are so prolific it's unplayable.  It crashed 3 times at different points in the tutorial, two of them during cutscenes.  Disabled tutorial, and I get 20-30 crashes per mission.  I can usually get 1-4 turns off before it hardlocks my PC.  I've went through about 40 hours of troubleshooting, and without a doubt it is the the game software.  It's not my hardware, it's not over heating, it's not drivers, it's not corrupted software.  The software itself repeatedly crashes on a significant number of people.
Judging by the overwhelming number of compliants of poor performance and random crashes, it's clear they did not beta test this properly.
**UPDATE** 09/02/17 For the first time, I was able to play through the tutorial and subsequent video without crashing.  I haven't tried since I beat the game (suffering through very frequent crashes) and wrote the original review.  I'm going to give this a positive review while I play through it again, and hopefully no crashes and it can stay positive.

I'll be honest... I LOVED XCOM:EU. So much so that I've completed it multiple times, including on Impossible/Ironman, and on Long War. Everything I saw in the build up to XCOM 2 said that I should love it just as much. But I didn't, and for most of the time, I'm not even sure WHY I don't like it. An accumulation of little things, I think.
For one thing, the story is based on the "it was all a dream" premise. In XCOM 2, the aliens won and everything you experienced from early mid-game in XCOM:EU was actually taking place in an alien simulation, as they pull tactical info and doctrine from your brain. I hate feeling like everything I did and achieved in XCOM:EU was wasted.
For another, they've implemented a turn-counter on many missions that make success or failure into a largely luck-based affair. If you're lucky, the pods are spread out, you can avoid some activations, and you'll succeed at the mission. If you're unlucky, the pods are all in/around the objective, and you'll have to fight them all which is likely to lead to soldier deaths and/or mission failure.
I was attached to my troopers in XCOM:EU, and I liked the classes. In XCOM 2, I just can't find the same level of attachment, nor do I like the classes as much. The Ranger is basically the Assault, but with a melee attack (which is minimally useful, unless you LIKE being out of cover right next to the enemy). The Sniper remains the sniper. The Grenadier is basically a weaksauce Heavy - Why the hell are you carrying a magazine-fed 'nade launcher, and only loading two of the six chambers?! Max two rockets, I could understand, those buggers are heavy... max two 'nades? Not so much. Sure, I know it's for "balance" reasons, but I'd rather have cool than balanced. And don't get me started on the Support - I detest the new hacking minigame. They could have done something really good, but instead, it's just another RNG roll.
In addition, many of the aliens are sporting new abilities, some of which are complete BS. Just one example is the Viper's tongue-grab. They can pull your dudes out of cover into the open, from ridiculously long distances, with near guaranteed hits (I've never seen a miss, although I have seen some YouTubers get some), which pulls you into a grapple for a guaranteed 3 damage, continuing to the next round unless you can succeed at 30%-40% shots. Screw that.
I'm sure there will be some "Git Guds" in response to this review, but they can sod right off. I found the game actively unpleasant to play, and frequently found myself feeling that the game was unfair - and that's coming from a dude who beat XCOM:EU on I/I, and never found it to be as unfair feeling as XCOM2. So take this for what it is.... I didn't enjoy XCOM2. If you have no problems with the issues I raised, you might. I certainly encourage you to try.

I've owned Darkest Dungeon since it was in Early Access. It is a game thats content has grown with it over time and now provides a complete package of environments and bosses that require different party arrangements and strategies to defeat. My biggest complaint about the game is that your first playthrough will likely take an extremely long time. Having added heart attacks and bodies to the dungeon crawl portion of the game has made it very difficult. You also receive very few town upgrade materials, so the first heroes you manage to level up will not have the weapons and armor they need to reliably survive.
It's a game of frustrating grind, trying to pull in a profit from longer, more challenging missions without losing any high level heroes that will take hours to replace, but I've come to appreciate it for that. Once you start completely abandoning low level heroes that have developed some bad traits or received afflictions in order to save yourself the money it would take to cure them, you know you have the right mindset to beat this game. Once you have the foresight to flee an expensive boss mission after the first random encounter (and bad RNG) left you with badly wounded heroes and low supplies, even though it means grinding several lower level missions to replenish your coffers, you will have the wherewithal to explore the Darkest Dungeon.

After playing XCOM Enemy Unknown I had high hopes for this game. And it certainly doesn't disappoint, with exceptions.
The pure gameplay aspect of the game is a great improvement over the last in the title. It can largely be summed up by simply saying that there are more enemies, abilities, and scenarios. Base building is also a large improvement but it could be more intuitive (I couldn't find out how to destroy a building for a while because its hidden behind two menus). Soldier customization is, well, on a whole different level than the previous title which had none. And lastly one of the greatest things that they have added was proper mod support.
Some great mods are out for this game. I particularly like Sotp Wasting My Time, as the game does have some long scenes that aren't needed.
Performance wise, the game has taken a hit. I can only get 30fps regardless of settings with SLI 780s and an i5 4690k. And that isn't a terrible thing. It isn't good, but because this isn't an FPS, I really don't mind the poor framerate. Now there is some base stuttering for me that dips to single digits and that is a slight pain, but it normally goes away within a minute.
The developer has acknoledged and apologized for these issues and I have good faith they will fix them.
I would still reccommend this game. I never replayed XCOM Enemy Unknown, but I can tell I'm going to replay this. Likely more than once.
You can also make a waifu soldier squad using the character customization.

9/10.  Fixes a ton of the issues I had with the XCOM remake.
PROS:
- Base building is no longer a micromanaging hell
- More class variety (Rangers are amazing)
- Levels seem to actually do something for soldiers (IE: Rookies feel like rookies, but as they gain ranks they feel like hardened soldiers)
- Storyline isn't cringeworthy and the cutscenes are really well done
- Great graphics
CONS:
- Has some frame hiccups for no reason sometimes
- Sometimes there's a weird pause after you take an action
- Takes a little bit to get going into what feels like "XCOM" instead of a tutorial, but that could just be the tutorial mode.  Will edit when I start my second campaign to see.
- RNG God's are still a bit judgemental but no where near as bad here.  98% to hit at point blank with a shotgun doesn't seem to mean "12% and you're wearing a blindfold" anymore.
All in all this game reminds me more of the classic XCOM series both in story and fun.  It's very fast paced once it picks up and it feels more gratifying storywise.  I like the concept of "Humans failed, we are a small resistance movement vs the big conquering force" a whole hell of a lot.

A brief description: Darkest Dungeon is a game where you, the descendant of a great family, are on a quest to take back your home estate from evil monsters, with the helps of mercenaries from all over.
The early to middle part of the game is very enjoyable: the learning curve is high but it's very fun to discover characters, monsters, mechanics, items ... One important thing is to be prepared for failure. A combination of your ignorance at first, and RNG, amongst other things, will spell doom for your teams of heroes for a little while. But your losses at this phase doesn't matter that much, as the mercenaries are very dispensable. And when you managed to kill a dungeon's boss, it's a glorious feeling.
But when you reached the end-game, this is where the salts overflow. Sometimes RNG just decided to wipe your whole team of very powerful heroes that you've invested so much in, and there is little you can do about it. As your characters' level getting higher, your losses become much more devastating. Sometimes the game's reduced to a grind to get back a resemblance of a fighting force, and it's frustrating that way.
The review is subject to change as the developers add new things to the game. The lastest addition has been the Town Quest, which introduced a lot of benefits events like "no cost for stress-relieving", "no cost for medical treatment", ... until that ONE THING ...
Lastly, ♥♥♥♥ the Caretaker.

XCOM 2 or "pants ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ simulator 2016" has been one of the most tense gaming experiences i've had since it's predecessor, Enemy Unknown. The game's tutorial mission spells it out for you that people are going to die, and you're going to have to move on, but you'll still find yourself waiting on every clutch shot you make when your one team mate is pinned by 3 guys and your only hope is that the sniper threads the needle.
The game has some worthwhile fixes to the previous formula such as reloading and still being able to fire, and the skill tree has been reworked so that no two soldiers has to be exactly the same (granted it's always good to invest in a scout only ranger for worthwhile recon). On top of this, you will be researching stronger weapons/armor almost from the get go. To counter this, enemies have also gotten alot rougher, sectoids are an actual threat until stronger weapons arrive, and over the months weaker enemies will be replaced with stronger versions of the same (advent trooper > advanced advent trooper).
My favorite feature so far has been the upgrades to customization, if you want your soldier to look like someone famous or someone you know, you almost certainly can in this game. I've been using it to make my guys looks like friends, and it's been the worst/best decision i've made so far.
There ARE some issues with framerate and cinematics at times, and there are moments where during alien activity the game will take a few seconds longer than usual to process, and that can be irksome at points, however alot of the issues can be alleviated in the game/graphic settings. I'm willing to overlook some of these problems from just how much has been added, but this can really turn off some folks.
TL;DR: XCOM 2 improves on alot of areas in gameplay and customization, but the framerate at certain points ingame may annoy some people, i've been having a blast atleast. 09/10, would yell at my virtual characters for missing a 96 % shot again.

This game once again vindicates my resolution to never buy a game at release. I made the mistake of not holding to that with XCOM 2 because I loved the predecessor so much and I promptly got punished for it.
In short, XCOM  2 is a great game which improves on XCOM in multiple small ways so if you liked the first one, you will probably LOVE the second.
BUT it has so many bugs and technical problems atm that imo it should not had been released when it did. None of the bugs I encountered was game breaking, but there are so many small annoyances mounting up that I almost put it away on multiple occasions out of sheer exasperation.
The game is still great, don't you believe otherwise. But if you successfully avoided the preorder trap, wait a little longer until they have all (or at least most of) the bugs fixed. You'll get a much less tarnished experience and will enjoy the game a lot more without minutes long loading times, clipping errors, sound cutting out etc.
I am sorry to say, I cannot reccommend buying this game at this point in time.
Edit: Rejoice, for I have been shown the way. I has been made clear to me, that I wrote my review in blatant disregard of the intellectually challenged of our esteemed colleagues out there. Since you read this review, I am assuming that you have not yet bought the game. If you did, what are you doing here? Go play it, it is a good game!
I spent a three digit number of hours in this game, yes. Did I enjoy that time? Yes.... mostly. But I spent almost double that amount on XCOM and far less moments where I wanted to punch through my screen and exactly zero minutes contemplating a critical review.
So assuming you did NOT buy the game yet. From the top of my mind, there are two reasons I can think of why.
A) You desperately want it, but are broke. And while scrounging the money together, you amuse yourself by reading about how good this game is, trampling its enemies into the dust, grinding their bones for your bread and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on their graves. Yay you! Good for you, everybody needs a hobby, I guess.
B) You wanted to see if the game is worth your money and your time. For you, I wrote this review. Is the game worth it?
That depends, do you want a really good game (yes it IS good as my hours can easily testify, even if you subtract the idling time) NOW? Or do you want a great game in about half a year (where realistically at least a few bugs will have been worked out and it will probably have already been on a first 10% sale)?
Chocolate bar now or tub of ice cream later? What I am saying here is that in retrospect, I should have waited for the ice cream. But hey, it's your decision in the end.

I'll start with the pros and move to the cons, as optimism is a virtue.
+Helpful, patient admins.
+Ingame soundtrack that has its own peculiar flair. It can be somewhat of an acquired taste, but overall the soundtrack is gud.
+Really neat skyboxes. Though said skyboxes will turn your computer into a toaster if you have a crap-tier AMD graphics card.
+Chibi artstyle. I've never been really scared by any of the enemies due to this, though a few have their creepy side, such as the spectral felines you'll find in haunted zones.
+The community (ingame and on the official Spiral Knights Forums) is generally welcoming and helpful, though there are a few loud complaints about various things at times. Can hold decent, respectable conversations with other players.
+Smooth character control using the mouse.
+Makes you not want to kill the rare enemies that can occasionally drop special loot. This is something I don't see often, as it turns the killing-things cash-grab into a "this thing doesn't hurt you; are you really gonna kill it?" scenario.
+Wide variety of armor and weaponry to create, although you have to work for it.
+Every single obtainable item save for armor accessories has its own peculiar flavor text. These can be fun for trivia enthusiasts.
+The developers will occasionally take ideas from the official forums pages and incorporate them into the game, though this can be a rare occurrence.
+Lots of alliteration and a few puns here and there. Mostly in the names of different dungeons and the flavor texts of certain items.
+The storyline is fragmented, but the shards of its canon are dynamic. Spaceflight from a genocidal war, a mysterious crash-landing on a celestial body of machinery and nature, an oligarchal dictatorship bent to its rulers' own twisted design, a tortured, fiery Duke of a smoldering kingdom, forever believing his realm is under siege...all of this is part of the world the player characters live in.
+Sentient jelly cubes with mustaches
+helicopter birds
+tree physics have yet to make any sense, as the leaves aren't attached to the trunk. good stuff.
+demons throw office supplies at you. Only the disgruntled overtime-workers use pitchforks.
+I'm pretty sure that putting a rocket engine on a war-hammer is the greatest achievement weaponry has to offer.
Now for the cons.
-Development of the game has slowed to a crawl. Although the major updates are impressive, they come few and far between, and as such there hasn't been much to accomplish once endgame is reached. This is a major contention with players who lack a certain amount of patience.
-Promotional "costume" items are produced more often than game updates. This, too, leads to negative feelings toward the developers, as the costume items can only be acquired using real-world funds. Though it does lead to a huge variety of player costumes and personalized outfits. I haven't seen a single other player that dresses their character the same as mine.
-Many of the weapons have a certain niche in the game, but there is a significant quality fluctuation when it comes to how well the small group of most-effective weapons function as opposed to the great variety of others.
-Few money-making stages. There is one particular endgame dungeon that is the most effective way to earn ingame currency sans trading, but as there are no other stages to rival its payout, playing the dungeon can become increasingly repetitive.
-The comment sections on Steam for most of the promotional costume updates are a veritable maelstrom of angry players. Being a repeatedly-returning player requires extraordinary patience.
-PvP can be difficult unless you're extremely good at it.
Overall, if you play the game without expecting much new content to be released in a set period of time, it's a good 8/10. For those of you with less patience with the dev team, probably not the game for you.

This game is possibly the most infuriating thing I have ever played. Without prior knowledge of it or guides, you will repeatedly close out of this game after a bad situation, hoping that if you don't play it for long enough, the problem will go away, only to find out it's still there a month later and that it's only gotten worse.
That being said, sweaty hands, clenched muscles, and praying to various Gods you didn't believe in 13 seconds ago all come along with this game. The pure drive to beat this game is honestly insane. Never before have I wanted to finish a game solely to prove that it can't beat me. It won't beat me. And the pure, holy, joy of finding an extra torch or getting a lucky critical is only comparable to the unfathomable rage that you will feel when your best hero defies your will and opens a chest for no reason only to acquire various diseases and mental disorders.
I would wager that this game is worth playing if you enjoy RNG situations that grant you pleasure or just another challange, intense planning, and the eventual numbness you get when you finally win that makes you just want to start dancing and punch things. That or the numbess when your 2 hour mission ends in complete and total disaster, ruining your entire game and knowing theres nothing you can do about it, and there are no resets or chances to go back. Either way, for 10 bucks or even at full price, this game might not give you pure fun all the time, but you'll be addicted in no time.

There seem to be two major complaints regarding XCOM 2, those being poor performance issues, and turn limits on most types of missions. I'll quickly debunk both.
Performance issues seem to always be present with any new release, and almost always the people complaining have sub-standard specs. I can affirm that if you have the recommended specs listed on this store page, the game will run at 60fps on the high preset, with some occassional dips if you happen to blow up a wall and a ton of debris flies everywhere, but never below 30fps. I never had any CTDs in my ~40 hours of gameplay, either, and I would play up to 8 or 9 hours at a time. In short, get a better computer before spending $60 on a new game, dumbass.
As for turn limits, not only does it match the narrative of the game, as you're undertaking guerilla missions in territory fully controlled by the enemy, but it's also a neat game mechanic as it prevents overwatch camping and encouraging more aggressive tactics. There are already mods that remove turn timers because they're a "bad game decision". I'm sure there are or will be mods that raise soldier health to 999, because losing soldiers is also a bad game decision or "isn't fun". I guess being a coddled little baby is fun to some people. But my point is the option is there for those who can't handle strategic thinking.
Anyway, the game itself was fun and exciting for the entire time I played it, and didn't feel too short or too long. The new aliens were fun to encounter for the first time in the field, sure some people might whine and cry about it being "unfair" that an Andromedon caught them by surprise and wiped out their best soldier, but to me that's all part of the XCOM experience. I'd read from various sources that the game was plagued by save-breaking bugs and unfair difficulty even on lower levels, so I played my first game on Veteran difficulty, non-Ironman, and now that I've beaten it I can say that's simply not the case. I can only imagine how easy Rookie difficulty must be.
There's definitely room for expansion, and I'm sure there will be an EW-type DLC around a year from now, but as it stands XCOM 2 is a much more complete game than XCOM EU was, and in my opinion even better than XCOM EW.
Overall, XCOM 2 is a 9 out of 10, and you should definitely get it if you liked the prequel even a little bit. Do play the prequel first if you haven't, though, really.

Having played through all three Dark Souls games, I can say that Dark Souls III learns from its predecessors and incorporates what From Software did in Bloodborne to make an excellent final(?) entry into the series.
The controls are slick and the game ultimately feels polished. Although use of a controller remains king over mouse and keyboard they did try and make it viable.
The bosses are fantastic, especially in both of the DLC areas. New enemies will keep you on your toes at times and make you question what might be around a corner or a box. Remember, don't get greedy, not every treasure chest is friendly.
The new mana bar allows for a spellcaster build that can make spells very deadly and useable without having to return to a bonfire to refresh the uses like in previous games. Weapons have special abilities that can perform some really fun combos.
PVP is enjoyable as ever and there are several PVP focused covenants in the game to reward players for participating.
Anyone who has played the previous two games will likely love this one as well. Here's to hoping From Software continues developing great games.

It pains me to write this, considering that I'm a very huge fan of Enemy Unknown. I confess that I have not played any of the other titles, but that's an irrevelant point.
While the core mechanics and gameplay are solid, as well as nice visual, I cannot recommend the game in its current state. As noted, there are many instances of hiccups and awkward in-game delays. For example, after a unit is killed, there is a rather lengthy pause. I also experienced clipping/invisible enemies on the map. Some of these issues are not entirely gamebreaking though, but it is rather jarring. The pre-mission loading screen takes too long, and if you read the other reviews, you'll find out more issues.
It also doesn't help that the chance to hit relies entirely on RNG. I'm not sure where to begin. But the aim/hit system is incredibly inconsistent. Throughout the majority of the game, I lost count how many "misses" I experienced on our end. My sharshooter has missed plenty of "90% hit" shots. I also notice that enemies such as Vipers (from across the map) have better firing on my team than vice versa. I'm also not sure how the "positioning/aiming" system actually works, but there were instances where I would come around a covering, only to find that I would have a less than 70% chance of killing an EXPOSED enemy a few tiles ahead of me.
I also notice that the game really throws everything at you from the get-go. More often than not, you'll be stuck with rookie soldiers on your first playthrough. I love playing tactically, and spamming my Overwatch just to be sure, but these time-based missions force you to rush against the constant assault by the enemy. It wouldn't be so bad, but they throw in these Sectoids of whom have an extreme high range of panicking/mind controlling your squad. There is certainly an unforgiving pace, but only for the wrong reasons. The first game had a perfect balance and pace, but this just seems to really throw the nuke at you when you're not careful.
If it weren't for the mods adding a support class and allowing benched soldiers XP, I probably wouldn't have gotten as far as I did. Not only does the game need a technical patch, they really need to reevaluate some of the balancing in the enemies and allow current players some breathing room. I pity the ironmen out there.

*EDIT and UPDATE 3/15/16*
So, after the recent March 2016 patch, I'm editing my review from Not Recommended to Recommended. My original review follows this brief update.
The patch definitely made some strides in fixing the graphics optimization and speed. My rig is far from top-of-the-line, but can handle some fairly meaty games so I was surprised at the amount of stuttering, even at low settings. The patch seems to have had a positive effect; I do still notice some chugging here and there, but I can more readily admit that it's my system. They have also included a toggle on the amount of extra fancy menu graphics, which cuts down on a lot of wasted transition time between screens. I do still feel like they could shave a little more off, but this works well.
Gameplay and difficulty: I'm biting the bullet and driving my first playthrough on Rookie now, and it is much more enjoyable. It's still frustrating though, as a veteran Xcom player, to have to do so. I'm hoping that after a novice playthrough, I'll have a better idea on how to play the game on standard difficulty. Rookie is by no means easy; the Advent Dark Event timer is still breathing heavily on my back, and have managed to lose some star team members to lucky enemy shots, but the combat feels a little better at this level. Regardless, I still love to play on Ironman... no takesy-backies!
Overall, I'm really enjoying the game now, and I'm very happy that the patch put me in the position to want to change my review to Positive, where it should be.
See my original review below for addtional praise on the things the game got right!
*I generally don't write reviews, but I was such a fan of Enemy Unknown/Within and was SO looking forward to X-Com2... so it really pains me to say that X-Com2 is a huge letdown, despite everything it gets right.
Performance issues: Not everyone is having them, but enough people are, and Firaxis seems aware of the problem. Terrible framerates on a rig that while certainly not top-of-the-line, can handle some decent graphics in other games fairly well. Dialing my settings down to near-minimum seems to have no effect, other than making the game look worse than EU/EW. Delays in events (Okay, the Sectoid seems to activating a power... what's happening? Wait 10 seconds to find out!), as well as over-zealous menu transitions in the base management screens just seem like chugging wastes of time.
Balance: I loved the difficulty of EU/EW, but was never such a glutton for punishment that I would play on anything higher than Veteran. I did play with Ironman enabled though, as well as several Second Wave options. It was challenging, yet rewarding. I could build highly skilled soldiers, but sometimes lose my Golden Child or an entire squad to a misstep or bad luck. In X-Com2, it's only a matter of time before the stun-baton jerks charge across the screen and render me unconscious, or a snake-man grabs me while the rest of my squad panics or misses every conceivable shot. Setting up ambushes is fun until your whole squad misses their Overwatch shots.
Anyway. There are lots of things I love about it: It COULD look gorgeous if it weren't stuttering so badly, I love the myriad customization options, the new storyline of rebels on the run, the new base management and mission selection/scanning, the procedurally-generated maps, the new classes, enemies, destructible terrain, etc...
Ultimately, it's just too frustrating to play right now, so I'm uninstalling. With some patches that fix the technical problems, and some nerfing of some VERY overpowered early-game enemy units, I may give it another try someday.
I could very easily see this becoming my favorite game after some fixes; the potential is there, it's just a shame and a disappointment that the game was released in this state.*

Starbound. Where do I begin? There's so much to this game, and I feel like I've only scratched the surface!
Starbound is a side-scrolling game that combines elements of survival, adventure, exploration, and space travel to create a gem that certainly deserves its place in many libraries as a much-played game. Games like Terraria and Minecraft immediately come to mind, and if these games are among your favorites, then expect Starbound to feel both familiar, yet different.
As I've stated, there's a LOT to this game. With whole systems of stars, and with each of those possibly supporting MULTIPLE planets, each with different biomes, creatures, races, and numerous other features, there's a good possibility that avid players will play with the first character they create, or play as each of the six playable races, perfecting their in-game style as they go.
After creating a character to use, it's time to go down to the planet's surface! The planet you start with is often random, so you could find yourself in a forest, a desert, or the tundra. And the early game isn't going to be easy for many. Hunger, shelter, local wildlife, and especially the temperature, require you to act fast, or be killed.
Once you've established a base, hunted food, and made some basic tools, you can expand your base, or head underground, where the riches lie buried in the dark. Or you could check out that military base to the right. Or you could visit that NPC village to your left. There's plenty to keep you busy!
I could go on about the game, but I would like to go over what I think so far.
Having logged only several hours of play, I'm basing this off of what I've come across so far.
PROS:
Beautifully-done environments and terrain
Plenty of types of wildlife, both passive and aggressive
Lots of weapons and armors to choose from
Great music and sounds
Challenging yet addictive gameplay
CONS:
Awkward controls, especially for those who are used to controllers (GUILTY)
Healing requires certain foods, items, or a bed, and takes quite some time
Unclear mission objectives in the beginning
As I've said, this is all I've come across so far. Granted, each player will have their own opinions, but I'm not going to challenge anyone.
But don't let the cons I've listed or any negative reviews stop you! If you wish to buy this game, I say go right on ahead! Each time you play, there's a new story just waiting to be told. From finding yourself on an alien world, to battling a horde of alien creatures by firelight, to stopping and simply tending to your garden. There's a bit of everything for everyone in here.

First off: This is honestly the best free-to-play game you will find on Steam.
The graphics are intuitive and maintain the perfect balance between realism and cartoonishness. The community is incredibly nice and supportive (hello, Dota 2?) and the possibilities to play with others are endless.
One of the best things about this game is that even if you replay a mission over and over again, the scenario and map you are put into is never the same. There's an infinite number of possible map layouts for every mission, and the missions always have something different that makes that certain mission special and unique.
Another major plus is that it requires no grinding/farming to achieve the highest level, and even once you have the best gear and have completed all of the regular missions, there's still so much you can do. There's room to have up to three games on one account so you can always start anew, and if you really think you've accomplished everything there is to accomplish on one game, you can always delete it and start again, opening up another new world of possibilities and game-changing decisions to experiment with.
Being a Youtuber (PeaceOfMined), the guild and party options are incredibly useful and fun to record on, especially with the voice-sync (although it is kind of slow). The armor and sword combinations are endless, and with the battle sprites and all the different skills and compositions in one party comes a feeling that you're playing the perfect blend of Spiral Knights and League of Legends, where you have all the abilities and attack possibilities of League, and along with it have the intuitive control system, open-world feeling, and extra attacking options of Spiral Knights, as well as the manual team composition and chatting system.
One last thing is the addictiveness of the game itself. I'm a full time student as well as a musician, Youtuber and athlete. What you may notice is I seem to have more hours on record than would seem possible with a schedule like that. I agree. Spiral Knights is a very addicting game. If you have a steady job, be prepared to leave Spiral Knights for a week, as you won't like it one bit.

Teacher: Im secretly your friend on steam and i was in your party for five hours straight
Me: subscribe to my channel

This text isn't a review (there are enough good reviews out there), its an opinion from a long time XCOM fan. I loved Firaxis' XCOM from 2012, i loved Terror from the Deep from 1995 (wich was my first game of the series), loved Jagged Alliance 2 and so on. I am a big fan of tactical squad based combat games! So I bought this game on release day, a no brainer ;) .
I read a lot of negative comments about this game. And yes, there are some bugs, even gamebreaking ones. Wich is why i cant use my beloved ironman mode. The performance is bad, the loading time is to long and so on. The controls are... special and take some time to get used to. The strategic overlay lookes bad (WHY??) and some parts of the gameplay are a little unbalanced (especially the difficulty curve).
But! The core mechanic, the gameplay on the battlefield and the stategic overlay is just SO FREAKISHLY AWESOME. The unique mix of stratgy, rpg, siumaltion and story still workes great. Its so intense (especially on ironman), simple and jet so deep. Its very close to the original from 2012, but there are a lot of little changes (like reloading your weapon is just one action, the line of sight indicator and so on). The destructible enviroment is fantastic. The graphics and cutscenes are beautiful. Not just "for a straegy game", they really are :) .The action camera gives the game a dynamic feeling. The guerilla warfare is a nice change from the first game. The near-sims-like character customisation is also a very good idea. You grow acustomed to your team. And when someone is killed, you really mourn them :/ (At this point please observe a minute's silence for Kilobyte,my beloved hacking-specialist).
There is so much more that i like, but this should be enough.
So, in conclusion: Wonderful game. The old "addiction spiral" (is this an english word?) starts sucking you in from the first minute. And i have nearly 50 hours sunken into the game and its still as much fun as on the first day!  Thank you Firaxis for making such gems! So many AAA titles in the last year were uninspired, boring and felt like all the other games out there. This one is different. Its unique. And very well crafted. And when i think about the modability of this game, i know there will be hundreds and hundreds of hours of fun in this.
08/10 (now, because of the glitches) 9/10 (when the bugs are fixed) and expectably 12/10 when more mods are out an i can change and upgrade the game the way i like.
Buy it. Now!

XCOM is a tough act to follow, but they pulled it off. So many parts of the gameplay have been deeply refined, from map layouts (randomly generated now!), to class abilities, to enemy design--they clearly learned a lot of lessons from the last game. The completely flip-flopped campaign feels different enough to keep things fresh, too--they do a pretty good job of making you feel like you're part of a rag-tag alien resistance instead of the Men In Black. The unbelievably extensive mod support also promises a ton of play for years to come.
Now, this review was written a couple weeks after launch, and right now, the game does have pretty horrendous performance problems--you might end up just having to disable a lot of graphics options just to run at all. It's not often you find a game where the concept, gameplay, and story are all original, and it's even rarer to find one that executes all of the above in an engaging and entertaining way, but I Am Bread manages it with panache.
As the game opens, you find yourself as the titular slice of bread in a typical kitchen with one straightforward goal: to become toast. There's no tutorial and no on-screen hints to guide your progress, but a little bit of exploration will make the control scheme clear - you can grab with any combination of corners at once, and nudge, flip or fling yourself toward furniture or objects scattered about the room.
Sometimes the physics of interactive objects gets a little wonky; grabbing onto an object as it topples may sometimes hurl you in an unexpected direction, but the simulation is pretty solid otherwise. Hazardous elements of the environment are left for the player to discover; surfaces or objects that decrease the bread's "ediblility", hurting your score and eventually causing you to fail the level.
Succeeding at becoming toast unlocks a new room and a little more of the backstory, hinting at a larger meaning beyond finding a way to brown oneself. The novelty of the concept and the control scheme make a simple game very enjoyable and eminently replayable.

Even though it's an Early Access game, it's probably the best sandbox survival game I have ever played. The game is a HUGE step up from Terraria, which I only found to be somewhat okay when playing with friends. Even when I'm playing alone, I have a ton of fun exploring each planet, gathering resources, battling creatures, and overall surviving.
The game starts with a few selectable races. Each race has their own characteristics and backstory (some of which still needs to be added), but aren't wildly different in playstyle. Right now, the only difference I've noticed between races is who can eat what type of food. As the game gets updated, I'm sure the differences will be more fleshed out.
The main goal of the game is simply to survive. You start out in a stranded ship on an unknown planet, and all you can do is gather resources to survive. It's very similar to Terraria, but with a few key differences. For starters, you now have a hunger meter. Oddly enough, the game has been very generous with dropping enough meat from dead animals to keep your character alive (at least from what I've played). The game also introduces a temperature meter, which is mananageable depending on the planet you're on. Once you've got the resources ready, you can power back up your ship and explore the entire galaxy. The number of planets is huge, and the planets themselves are quite vast in themselves, and offer a ton of variety from planet to planet. One planet could be a dense jungle, where as another could be covered in ice and a lot of snowstorms.
Unlike Terraria, there is no real definite goal to the game. In Terraria, it felt as if you had to build up to fight these giant bosses, and the game is pretty much over once you've defeated the last boss that you could possibly fight. In Starbound, it encourages more exploration than any other game I've played. I could spend countless hours exploring each planet, and I would only get so far. The focus on exploration increases the longetivity, and adds to the game.
However, the game isn't without its faults. Since it's an Early Access game, some features are missing, such as backstory for some of the races, and the questline clearly isn't finished. The UI is also a bit annoying to use, as bringing up the inventory screen can easily get in the way of whatever action it is you're doing. The game's pacing also can be pretty slow at first.
Nevertheless, I love this game to pieces, and I can't wait to see what the developers do with this. Highly recommended purchase, even in its current state.

Starbound is a sandbox adventure game that has been hailed as a long-awaited successor to Terraria. Unfortunately, I am applying the "sandbox" bit very loosely.
At first glance, Starbound looks exactly as you would've expected it to look like. A game about building stuff, exploring countless alien worlds and generally killing♥♥♥♥♥♥for the hell of it. While in a literal sense, all of this is true, Starbound makes it apparent that all of these aren't going to be of any use to you throughout the game, and you're not going to have any fun trying.
Starbound's linear progression system is a blatant contradiction to the term "sandbox", and mind-numbing amounts of item/material grinding don't help either.
You see, while Starbound also bases its core elements off what has made games like Minecraft and Terraria so successful, there is also a very apparent lack of actual freedom-- the very same freedom that made the aforementioned games so enjoyable.
Starbound's not-so-subtle linear progression is basically landmarked for you in small steps, telling you what you have to do in order to get ahead in terms of equipment. And by landmarks, I mean boss fights when you've done everything that the game tells you to do in a particular sector --basically just an area of space where creatures and items are all locked on a particular "level", so to speak. The sectors themselves are essentially levels, backtracking earlier "sectors" being completely useless; as most materials/items you'd find there would be of no benefit for use or crafting equipment of your current tier. And let's not forget that because these landmark bosses drop items that are absolutely necessary for crafting items of a higher tier, in the flavor of some advanced crafting station.
Starbound also features needlessly complicated requirements for some basic items. For example, a device that allows you to breathe in space - in a game about space! - requires you to kill a mid-game boss, hunt down midgame minerals and have a crafting station that in itself requires some irrelevant materials. And mind you, this sort of pointless grind is necessary for a great deal of practical items such as armor, weapons and other equipment. While some weapons and armor are simple to create, those particular items are usually sub-par, if not utterly useless for the sector you'd be using them on.
Exploration and the gathering of resources are pointless and incredibly unenjoyable, respectively.
For a game about gathering resources and exploration, Starbound is still incredibly bland in both of those aspects. Of course hunting down minerals is a must, but Starbound seems to make even that a frustratingly boring experience. (I'm not saying it's amazing in any comparable games either, but Starbound somehow makes it even worse.) And don't even bother digging deeper into a world, it's easier to just find a different world and dig for whatever resource you need there. Also keep in mind that there are certainly no unique resources on particular worlds that would be of
use to you. And the only variation of equipment comes from the fact that most of it is randomly generated, with the exception of legendary or otherwise named items.
Speaking of other worlds, and exploring in general, I can't say Starbound doesn't make it somewhat memorable to find some secret lab or mining complex hidden beneath the ground. But overall, these really don't help you at all in the long run. Functionally, almost all worlds are the same, they have trees, they have minerals, you should look to see if there's a structure that you could loot. If so, loot it and move onto the next world, if not, just move on. The only exceptions are asteroid fields and moons, which have no air, low gravity and more minerals. NPC villages basically exist solely for you to raid them, buy things from them and/or rest in them
Combat is a slow-paced mess with unnecessary amounts of difficulty in places.
On combat, Starbound is just plain bad. There's just no other way of putting it. It's arguably the most incredibly boring part of the game, either being an awkward cover-based ranged engagement or painfully monotonous melee combat, which consists of little more than "click to swing thing" until either your enemy dies or they knock you off a cliff and you die.
Movement is teetering on 2 extremes, it's either a slow gait around your enemies with a bit of small hopping, or being knocked around at high velocity by the said enemies while completely helpless. In both cases it's extremely unenjoyable and very stiff, while some "implants" have since been added to remedy this terribly static combat (Such as higher jumping or quick bursts of speed), the fundamentals remain almost completely unaltered.
The rewards of combat are almost completely null; regular enemies will not drop
aside from a few bits of currency. Bosses will give you some necessary material to progress in the game, while mini-bosses occasionally drop some form of decent weaponry. That being said, boss fights as I've had them are crouching in a spot where the boss can't hit you and attacking them until they die, because it's simply too hard to attempt to attack them head-on. When I say hard, I mean they'll just kill you in 2 hits; combine that with the fact that combat is unredeemably boring and you're set for the most unenjoyable fighting you've had in a while.
The fact that healing pots (known as StimPaks) are inexcusably rare and expensive do not help this at all. While highly effective, you'll burn through whatever miniscule amount of them you have left incredibly quickly. And with the pathetically small health pool you're given, (which does not scale to the enemies you'll be up against, even with appropriate armors equipped) you have little choice but to rely on them.
Now, I'm going to be forthright here so pardon my unprofessional choice of wording, but Starbound's dev team is
.
Chucklefish has done a lot to show us how hard they work to make Starbound what they promised it to be. Which to say is taking
of kickstarter funds, taking a long vacation after releasing their barely passable early access game, playing bloody Mario Kart instead of working on their game, and let's not forget acquiring a puppy for the office. They had promised game updates to come incredibly quickly, yet the last big update was six whole months ago. When they attempted to work with ETAs and failed, instead of taking the inevitable backlash they got and trying to improve on it, they just used it as a further excuse to not do anything.
All official Chucklefish sites are heavily censored, any sort of criticism is flagged down as "trolling", regardless of how valid it actually is. And better yet, the devs take time out of their non-existant schedule to whine on Twitter, blaming "trolls" as the reason they're not getting their own work done.
Chucklefish should be receiving no further support through Starbound or any other game, they're irresponsible, incompetent and show what little they care for everyone who had supported them.
Feel free to disagree with me, but Starbound is a train wreck of a game. I give it a 3/10, there is enjoyment in the game, but it burns out way too fast. Linear progression in a sandbox game is downright unacceptable, grinding for items is an unnecessary meatfest, exploring nets you little reward, and combat is unreasonably hard with little health, disproportionately powerful enemies; also being painfully monotonic and boring. And it has also become quite clear that every dollar spent on Starbound is just another dollar Chucklefish is going to run away with.
Starbound is a journey into the skies and beyond, and according to Starbound, the skies and beyond aren't very enjoyable.

First off: This is honestly the best free-to-play game you will find on Steam.
The graphics are intuitive and maintain the perfect balance between realism and cartoonishness. The community is incredibly nice and supportive (hello, Dota 2?) and the possibilities to play with others are endless.
One of the best things about this game is that even if you replay a mission over and over again, the scenario and map you are put into is never the same. There's an infinite number of possible map layouts for every mission, and the missions always have something different that makes that certain mission special and unique.
Another major plus is that it requires no grinding/farming to achieve the highest level, and even once you have the best gear and have completed all of the regular missions, there's still so much you can do. There's room to have up to three games on one account so you can always start anew, and if you really think you've accomplished everything there is to accomplish on one game, you can always delete it and start again, opening up another new world of possibilities and game-changing decisions to experiment with.
Being a Youtuber (PeaceOfMined), the guild and party options are incredibly useful and fun to record on, especially with the voice-sync (although it is kind of slow). The armor and sword combinations are endless, and with the battle sprites and all the different skills and compositions in one party comes a feeling that you're playing the perfect blend of Spiral Knights and League of Legends, where you have all the abilities and attack possibilities of League, and along with it have the intuitive control system, open-world feeling, and extra attacking options of Spiral Knights, as well as the manual team composition and chatting system.
One last thing is the addictiveness of the game itself. I'm a full time student as well as a musician, Youtuber and athlete. What you may notice is I seem to have more hours on record than would seem possible with a schedule like that. I agree. Spiral Knights is a very addicting game. The loading times are long, that's a shame but acceptable, the maps are procedurally generated to an extend.
The general performance is not very good though. For example there has been times where a really long mission has required me to exit the game, to clear up some memory from all the debris and corpses hogging the frames.
Despite all of this I've completed the game, and had a fun time with it. If you enjoy strategy with some randomness thrown in, and an excellent management layer on top, then this is the game for you.

Un des meilleurs F2P FPS auquel j'ai pû jouer ces 5 dernières années.
Black Squad est un FPS assez exigent en terme de skill. Graphiquement, le jeu est très beau pour du Unreal Engine 3.
Les maps sont bien pensées et les armes sont plutôt bien équilibrées ce qui fait que l'on peut trouver son propre style de jeu parmis l'arsenal proposé.
Les devs (et c'est important de le préciser) sont très à l'écoute des joueurs et des retours qu'on leurs fait. La CBT en a été un exemple concret, par exemple, beaucoup de joueurs on demandé d'avoir la possibilité de "Maintenir pour visée", l'option a été ajouté 2 jours plus tard.
Avantages:
- Gameplay exigent
- Facilité de prise en main
- Aucuns éléments P2W (j'en ai pas parlé mais les seules options payantes avec de l'argent réel sont des cosmétiques, skins ect...)
- Jeu équilibré
- Potentiel compétitif important
Désavantages:
- A l'heure actuelle, les dégats des armes semblent +/- aléatoires mais compris dans une fourchette (par exemple un tir au torse peu aller de 30 à 40 de dégâts alors que vous tiré au même endroit avec la même arme mais les devs on dit qu'il travaille la dessus...) à suivre...
EDIT: Les dégâts ne sont plus aléatoires désormais.
- Recoil pattern là aussi aléatoire, mais ils semblent que les devs travaillent dessus aussi, à suivre...
Conclusion:
Ce jeu à un énorme potentiel, qu'il faut exploiter.
Si vous êtes habitué au FPS, Black Squad est un must have de par sa qualité.
Je recommande vivement !

Starbound. Where do I begin? There's so much to this game, and I feel like I've only scratched the surface!
Starbound is a side-scrolling game that combines elements of survival, adventure, exploration, and space travel to create a gem that certainly deserves its place in many libraries as a much-played game. Games like Terraria and Minecraft immediately come to mind, and if these games are among your favorites, then expect Starbound to feel both familiar, yet different.
As I've stated, there's a LOT to this game. With whole systems of stars, and with each of those possibly supporting MULTIPLE planets, each with different biomes, creatures, races, and numerous other features, there's a good possibility that avid players will play with the first character they create, or play as each of the six playable races, perfecting their in-game style as they go.
After creating a character to use, it's time to go down to the planet's surface! The planet you start with is often random, so you could find yourself in a forest, a desert, or the tundra. And the early game isn't going to be easy for many. Hunger, shelter, local wildlife, and especially the temperature, require you to act fast, or be killed.
Once you've established a base, hunted food, and made some basic tools, you can expand your base, or head underground, where the riches lie buried in the dark. Or you could check out that military base to the right. Or you could visit that NPC village to your left. There's plenty to keep you busy!
I could go on about the game, but I would like to go over what I think so far.
Having logged only several hours of play, I'm basing this off of what I've come across so far.
PROS:
Beautifully-done environments and terrain
Plenty of types of wildlife, both passive and aggressive
Lots of weapons and armors to choose from
Great music and sounds
Challenging yet addictive gameplay
CONS:
Awkward controls, especially for those who are used to controllers (GUILTY)
Healing requires certain foods, items, or a bed, and takes quite some time
Unclear mission objectives in the beginning
As I've said, this is all I've come across so far. Granted, each player will have their own opinions, but I'm not going to challenge anyone.
But don't let the cons I've listed or any negative reviews stop you! If you wish to buy this game, I say go right on ahead! Each time you play, there's a new story just waiting to be told. From finding yourself on an alien world, to battling a horde of alien creatures by firelight, to stopping and simply tending to your garden. There's a bit of everything for everyone in here.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown and its expansion Enemy Within successfully captured the old-school vibe of one of PC gaming's iconic turn-based strategies for a modern marketplace. XCOM 2 continues this trend, and provides everything you'd expect from a sequel to one of the greatest strategy games of all time.
The premise of the XCOM series is simple: aliens are taking over the world, and it's up to you to lead mankind's resistance. Develop your troops, outfit them with stolen technology, and deploy them in strategic locations across the world to uncover the aliens' invasion plans, and hopefully stop them.
However, an even bigger threat to XCOM 2 than aliens are its performance issues. You can expect dodgy console ports to run like bloated dogs but not PC exclusives! Firaxis says they are committed to fixing things, which is nice, but until that happens it's a case of buyer beware.
Thankfully the game is stellar despite the performance issues. It's notoriously difficult, so f you're not the kind for careful planning, the difficulty of XCOM will wear you down quite quickly. However, if you've got the time and inclination to really sink your teeth into a real challenge - and can get past the performance issues - there's really nothing else out there like it.

Some games are difficult, HARD games. The Darkest Dungeon is just UNFAIR and SADISTIC with you. And I LOVE IT.
Make no mistake, this is the kind of game that makes you loose hours of effort on the blink on an eye. No matter how much you prepare your troops, no matter how much you manage your economy, the game will always find a way to keep you on the brink of desaster. Train a group of fighters and then gaze in despair as they go insane on the middle of the battle and start messing with the rest of the group, get ill and force you to spent your hard earned gold to cure them and finally die permanently in a minor mission that you never though would be a challenge. Then, if for some reason you manage to find an efective party combination, be prepared to suffer varios RNG scenarios where you'll be ambushed in the darkness or hunted by random bosses (I'm looking at you "The Collector", you #%@!).
The at desing of the game is beutiful, Lovecraft like, dark, hopeless. And the gameplay is devastating and forces you to take risks that usually end up in tragedy. Those that enjoy watching Game of Thrones could get a nice idea of what it feels to play this: NOBODY is save at any moment, everyone can DIE at any time. And that is why every single little victory, every critical hit landed, every boss defeated and every inpired hero feels so great!

I'm really torn. The character writers clearly had a lot of fun with a lot of the characters in this game. The companions are fun, and make the world feel lived in.
Unfortunately that's about the only thing that makes the world feel lived in.
Fallout is yet another franchise where Obsidian has rolled in and made the best entry in a series. Fallout 4 is shallow, poorly optimized, and boring. Fallout 4 is a continuation of Bethesda's new business model of pushing out wire frame open world games with nothing to inhabit them, and relying on RNG "radiant quests" to fill in the gaps between the week story.
In my single 40 hour playthrough I went to the same factory somewhere around 4 or 5 times for different fetch quests. The main factions in the game are unsympathetic, and poorly fleshed out. The resolution for either faction is a simple "press this button to kill them all or betray your current faction" choice.
There are a number of fun side quests that are pretty clever, but I found myself asking "how is this any better or different when compared to New Vegas?" more often than not.
Just play Fallout 1, 2, and New Vegas. They'll provide everything this game tries to be and more. Bethesda can't write unless they leave windows open to sell DLC, and even then its pretty weak.
Also, while paid mods are a great idea to give back to the hardworking modding community, I don't feel that Bethesda would be the best vector to do so. They're a company that takes credit for everything good they haven't actually made themselves, (dishonored, DOOM, Wolfenstein TNO, etc.) and follow other anti-consumer predatory business practices (withholding review copies until release.)
