Ooookay! Time to make this more useful by expanding my review.
Fallout 4 like it's predecessors and TES games has a big world to explore, unlike FO3 and FONV Beth finally made an accessible part of the town with skyscrapers, overpasses and such. You'll see much more small details compared to previous FO games too. However, i miss subways as in FO4 there's fewer accessible stations and they are not linked together like it was in FO3. Vaults also suffered the same fate and are much smaller that those in FO3 and FONV.
Some guys at Bethesda decided to simplify interiors and now they look like dungeons in MMOs - one way from entrance to boss' room that contains reward chest and one-way exit. It's simple but i didn't buy Fallout to something MMO styled.
Combat system looks much better and closer to shooters at early levels, however, it doesn't stay that way as your character levels up: first your enemies and then your character become bullet sponges, at higher levels you'll be able to survive mini-nuke headshot and so will your enemies.
Beth finally made power armor what it should be, in FO4 you can't just fold it and put in your bag, now it's an actual exoskeleton with real armor on it, on the bad side they just retconned it's power supply and you gonna have a few spare batteries with you to keep it going.
FO4 finally got basebuilding feature. Yay? Not really. You'll need all DLCs to be able to build something better than lousy shack. If you get settlers to your settlement then you're in for babysitting as these people can't just defend themselves.
Survival games appear to be popular and Beth wanted a piece of it. Survival difficulty adds need for food, water and sleep, as well as several diseases your character can get. Unlike FONV's hardcore mode in FO4 you never know when you'll get hungry, thirsty or sleepy, diseases randomly drop on your character if you choose to sleep less than 8 each time you go to sleep. FO4's survival difficulty also removes manual saves, fast travel and console, so if you're stuck somewhere due to faulty world design or game just crashed you'll have to roll all the way back to the last time your character slept (that's when auto saves are made).
Something i always liked about Fallout games is extensive character development, Fallout 4 doesn't have it. First of all, your SPECIAL stats give you no strengths or weaknesses, for example, even with 10 INT you never gonna talk to a scientist as equal. Skills are replaced by skill perks and perks are tied only to one special attribute, that's it. Most high level perks are overpowered and your character doesn't have maximum level which means you don't need to use brain - if you messed it up this time just level up and extra superpower. With skills also disappeared skillchecks: flirting, persuation, intimidating, etc are done with charisma only, other types of check are very few.
Fallout 4 will not offer you interesting quests, all of those are linear and you're almost never given any options, you just go in, kill everything, grab your objective and return both in main and side quests. There's a whole category of radiant quests which are infinitely repeatable quests that fill in for real stories.
That's Fallout 4 as it is. If you're looking for a sandbox to build your bases and keep killing infinitely respawning hostile camps then this game is for you, otherwise, you'd better pass.

Trove is a bit-block game that is similar to Minecraft, but just like any other MMORPG out there. It still lacks that energy that will leave players hanging on and keep playing. Trove has expanded a lot since the pre-alpha stages, in terms of its UI, game mechanics, classes, and open-world generation. The character classes has adopted the same style as Firefall, where all the classes can be earned by collecting the Cubits (daily-earned currency) and redeeming them. If you're those who loves to collect the collectibles, maybe this game is good for you to continue in search of the items.
What's interesting behind the leveling system in Trove is that, the max Level that can be leveled is Level 20. But to move beyond Level 20, you need to obtain Shadow items, refining it, to further increase this capped level. Where maybe things starts to quite grinding as it goes further. Nevertheless it's not just about the leveling, but there is also Mastery system, where each items you collected or actions you have done in Trove accumulates into this system. So it is beneficial to focus on Mastery first.
Trove has a marvellous open-world generation, that you continue to explore the Uber-worlds. I'm sure none of the worlds are similiar in any sense, since it's a mega world with various biomes merged together. Besides fighting dungeon, you can also actively participate in the Club or Cornerstone, architectural building of blocks. Some of the creative worlds can be seen in forums, like Mario World or Pokemon's Pallet Town. Trove also been always very active in their server maintenance, every Tuesday. They have come out with numerous events and limited period items that allows players to hunt and collect these items.
For network wise, it is still playable for Asian players. Although you will experience a little bit of slow response in preloading of objects. Especially Trove sends objects in chunk that loads the next few segments of land, that is in your camera view. This is very adaptive, as Trove adopts the world generation feature. Similarly for dungeon when it comes to boss-battle, it is preloads it for just that instance, so don't worry about dying out.

Let me preface this by saying the paid mods is what finally pushed me over the edge to review this game. This is absolutely ridiculous and you think they'd have learned from the first time they tried convincing people to pay for mods. The modding community is just that, a
. Most of the content creators make mods because they love the game(s) and love the community, who provide them with a reputation that demonstrates their hard work. Places like the Nexus allow us to donate to the creators to show our appreciation. No one is forced to, which makes it that much more significant when they do. All this does is add a paywall to download shoddy DLC that has been "verified" by Bethesda to work (because these games are always inherently bug-free, right?).
Onto the game itself -
I simply can not get invested into this game. The story is lackluster (the only Fallout story I still haven't completed), an abundance of the RPG elements have been removed, and I may be in the minority here but I dislike the weapons system. In previous Fallouts, I enjoyed scavenging the wasteland and finding a unique weapon that changed my overall playstyle (a la AMR) rather than finding and hoarding every piece of junk I could get to turn a pistol into a sniper rifle by simply switching the stock, adding a longer barrel, and throwing on a scope.
I have 109 hours played on this game with 330 hours on New Vegas. Out of the 109 hours on this game, I don't think I've even gotten halfway through the story and, for once, that's not a good thing. A majority of it is getting a strong urge to play Fallout games, thinking "ah I still haven't beaten FO4", sitting down, making a new character, playing for a few hours, and getting bored. Judging by the character's playtime, it looks like I've spent less than half the time played in-game, meaning I likely accidentally left it minimized overnight a few times.
There's a good chance I'm just being overly cynical due to my love for the previous Fallout games (lookin' at you, New Vegas) but it just feels like they focused less on what made Fallout, well.. Fallout, and focused more on what would grab more sales from the general public (which seems to be supported by their "new" implementation of paid mods).
All-in-all, I can not recommend this game to others when asked.
Are the graphics better than previous games in vanilla comparisons? Yes.
Is the engine better? Well, not by much, if at all. I will admit that the shooting feels a bit more like an FPS, take that as a pro or a con.
Is it as fun? Not in my opinion.
Is it as RPG driven? No.

Progression feels pretty good, exploration is fun, the hub world thing is well designed, and there's plenty of items to come across, so that's all good. Crafting is pretty balanced all around, and there's no lack of cosmetics. Also the instruments are a nice touch.
Mod support is wonderful, but can get a little bit wonky in multiplayer scenarios at the time of this review.
Speaking of mulitplayer, it works pretty well. There are some occasional lag spikes from my experiecne, but the steam server setup is easy and pretty reliable, so I'll take it. Console servers are also available, but there's really no benefit to them as far as I know. Last time I ran one, there is no interaction whatsoever, but that may have changed by the time you're reading this.
Story is simplistic, no really memorable characters or plot, but that's fine. The game isn't meant for story.
Real♥♥♥♥♥♥though, exploring underground is boring as hell. I hate having to go mining, caves are boring, enemies in caves are boring, structures usually don't have anything usefull and are copy pasted all over, and there's really no point to it.
But, this is resolved with the concept that everything you can get from mining can be gotten through just normal exploring....
This concept is occurs a lot throughout the game. There's a lot of things to do, but a lot of different ways to accomplish the same thing. Many ways are just completely inferior, in terms of how fun they are and how productive they are. Farming is another pretty good example of this.
Bosses are... forgettable... alongside the combat. It's not awful, but I've never found it too engaging. Ranged weapons feel extremely underpowered, along with staves, which usually do some pretty cool stuff. There are exceptions to this, but overall that's the impression I got.
Building can be kinda fun. There's a lot you can do with the tools and materials you're given, but overall it's not too rewarding to build cool stuff. You can go pretty crazy if you enjoy building though.
Replay value for me has been... meh. I've gone back a few times and tried to play this game through again... but I only ever got all the way when 1.0 came out. I enjoyed the new additions in 1.3 (Spacefarer), but it wasn't really enough to get me all the way through again.
If the developers keep polishing this game, adding new content, and fixing any bugs that might arise, this game will continue to get better, and I'll probably come back to it.
If you enjoy games like Minecraft, Terraria, or other sandboxy voxely what have you games, you should definitely give this game a shot.

*  Great upgrade trees.  Interesting, battle-altering upgrades are available to choose from each and every level, giving your soldiers a great amount of variation if you choose.
Overall:  Great game that lacks polish.  A solid PC exclusive.

Ah Darkest Dungeon, a game that has both made me weep tears of joy and sorrow. I will start this review off by stating this game isn't for everyone, it IS an extreamly difficult game and it doesn't bother holding your hand.
BUT in those moments of depressingly bad luck and sorrow theres those one moments where everything clicks, you get a crit here an item there. Eventually you begin to grow confident, maybe even a little cocky.
You tell yourself, "I can take the next boss my guys are ready!"
So you begin you're hunt for the boss, you've bought your supplies in amples amount and have used the best combination of characters to help you in defeating the boss.
You enter the dungeon and your very first step outside of the first room is a battle.
"Okay..." You tell yourself "this will be easy."
Your fight however quickly turns and you find yourself getting critted and already running out of ideas as you watch your oh so weak healer take crit after crit. After the fifth round you find yourself with a beaten up healer barely capable of standing and your other three partner members at half health wondering why they even sighned up to clear this Estate of the darkness.
So you sit there and ponder do I risk it all and explore the next rooms in hopes of the boss appearing in one of them or do you take you're weakend party and get the hell out of dodge. You decide it's not worth losing your valuable bodies to the darkness so your abandon the quest in hopes of the RNG god smiling down at you the next time you ever venture after the boss.
The game is fun but frustrating I won't deny that but if you have patience or perhaps just love getting slammed against a brick wall with nails in by this game and just develop Stockholm Syndrome for it then you can enjoy it.
In the time I've played this game its been very enjoyable, while this won't be the case for everyone it is certainly worth it. Just make sure to do some research on it before you buy to be absolutly sure you will like this game.

I was going to write a wall of text (I actually did write one and then deleted it), but that's already been done by a lot of people who have put just as many, if not more hours, into this game than I. Instead, I will try to summarize what I want to say in a couple paragraphs (it'll still end up being longer than I want).
Spiral Knights is a simple, relaxing mmo, with a lot of potential, if the developers actually cared about the game anymore. However, they do little to retain their veteran playerbase (those who achieved getting full 5 star gear and have played around a hundred hours). Instead, they rely on those who stick with the game because they've already invested hundreds of hours (and possibly real money) into the game. As a result, most players you see have already reached end game, in a game where end game PvE barely exists. Instead, these people all flood into unbalanced PvP matches, where relatively new players (new 5 star gear players) have pretty much no chance at victory. If you don't enjoy the PvP, like me, then you really don't have much to do. If I had to estimate, I'd say around 200 of those hours I put into the game were spent socializing with guildmates.
This mmo is much more fun when you play it with friends, or make friends in game, and play with them. Enjoy your journey to end game while it lasts. There isn't much waiting for you there. The most positive thing I can say about this game is that it's excellent for introducing mmo's to those new to the genre. It has very simplified versions of various concepts you'd find in other games like Guild Wars 2, Tera, and FFXIV. It does, however, lack classes and roles (tank, dps, healer).
TL;DR GOOD GAME FOR MMO BEGINNERS AND CASUAL GAMERS, IT HAS FUN AND SIMPLE GAMEPLAY, LACKS AN ENDGAME

Now, this may not be universal but for some reason the game seems to have some performance issues occassionally. I'm going to preface this with the fact I did enjoy the game, but that was mostly due to modding and being a long time fan of the Fallout universe. Others may not have the same experience. Currently this review is negative due to Bethesda's design decisions, but also in part due to the down sides of the game. I've put a detailed list below.
TL;DR The game is poorly optimised, the engine runs like crap, and the whole thing feels unfinished. The story is horrific, as is some of the world design. It has good gameplay improvements, and crafting is nice, but get it cheap on sale, mod it, and if you want a decent story that makes sort of sense and has choice play Far Harbour.
---The Good:---
>Massive visual upgrade on previous titles. Not beautiful by modern standards, but still pretty.
>Gameplay improvement out the wazoo. Seriously, the gunplay and looting in this is so much better.
>Nice weapon customisation, and the addition of settlement building might be something you want, it might not. But regardless, the varied weapon/armour crafting is a very nice addition to the game.
>Power armour finally feels like it's done right
>As of speaking, very nice modding scene, but I'll touch on that later.
---The bad:---
>Runs really badly. Even if it doesn't and you somehow get 60FPS+, physics and animations start to break due to them being tied to refresh rate. The engine is tired, old, and showing its age really badly. There's a lot of engine issues that wont be fixed, and some optimisation issues they never bothered to fix (Downloading a modded higher res texture pack can sometimes increase framerate due to texture size issues in base game).
>Story is utterly abysmal. There're some interesting side quests, and some very interesting characters, but really not enough to go around and the main quest is so boring I've actually never finished it. Far Harbour is significantly better story wise, but then Nuka World goes back to kind of dull.
>Fantastic world... of individual locations. Whilst some pretty neat locations could be a plus, the whole world itself feels disjointed. Super mutants living literally a few yards from the main trading city etc. There's very few links between areas in lore, outside of quests, and overall the world feels unfinished. There's 4 or 5 places I can think of that could be really interesting... but they're just raiders. Some areas have actual special characters and events... but are just raiders who shoot you on site.
>Design decisions by Bethesda: I'll state it now: I'm all for Creation club as an idea. I like the thought of having new lands, or large quests added to the game constantly and with some form of reliable quality. But currently it's not worth it at all, and has actually been rather awful. For a start, almost everything was already available, and way too expensive. It also turns out the files download to begin with, and are activated later, which I hope they fix, else we'll have some horrific folder bloat.
>Dialogue: Whilst the writing of individual conversations is sort of ok, the fact it forces 4 options at all times, when sometimes 2 or 3 would do and sometimes 6 or 7 are needed, is very annoying. It means you feel like you're missing out on options, and also when you take different options that end up the same it feels like there's no choice at all. It starts to feel like a linear game, despite there being some quite varied options in some parts of it.
--------
All in all I feel as if this is a 6/7 out of 10 for the series. It's still enjoyable, and had it not been in the Fallout franchise it might have earned a solid 7. But the more you play, the more you start to realise that it's a hollow game, full of missed potential and bad writing that doesn't even feel like it takes place in a cohesive world. Negatives:
* Poor optimization.  Frame rate drops unexpectedly and illogically.
* Touchy squad commands.  Occasionally something going on in the background will cause your cursor to disappear, or not register a click, or worse causes an action you did not intend.

Positives:
*  Challenging gameplay while staying fair.  Victory or defeat is based almost entirely on your strategy and choices.
*  Sense of urgency.  The clock is always ticking, keeping you invested in each and every action.
*  Great upgrade trees.  Interesting, battle-altering upgrades are available to choose from each and every level, giving your soldiers a great amount of variation if you choose.
Overall:  Great game that lacks polish.  A solid PC exclusive.

I'm really torn. The character writers clearly had a lot of fun with a lot of the characters in this game. The companions are fun, and make the world feel lived in.
Unfortunately that's about the only thing that makes the world feel lived in.
Fallout is yet another franchise where Obsidian has rolled in and made the best entry in a series. Fallout 4 is shallow, poorly optimized, and boring. Fallout 4 is a continuation of Bethesda's new business model of pushing out wire frame open world games with nothing to inhabit them, and relying on RNG "radiant quests" to fill in the gaps between the week story.
In my single 40 hour playthrough I went to the same factory somewhere around 4 or 5 times for different fetch quests. The main factions in the game are unsympathetic, and poorly fleshed out. The resolution for either faction is a simple "press this button to kill them all or betray your current faction" choice.
There are a number of fun side quests that are pretty clever, but I found myself asking "how is this any better or different when compared to New Vegas?" more often than not.
Just play Fallout 1, 2, and New Vegas. They'll provide everything this game tries to be and more. Bethesda can't write unless they leave windows open to sell DLC, and even then its pretty weak.
Also, while paid mods are a great idea to give back to the hardworking modding community, I don't feel that Bethesda would be the best vector to do so. They're a company that takes credit for everything good they haven't actually made themselves, (dishonored, DOOM, Wolfenstein TNO, etc.) and follow other anti-consumer predatory business practices (withholding review copies until release.)

Okay... this game. It's uh... pretty good.
When version 1.0 finally came out, I played it through, and it was a ton of fun. I played it with 2 friends, and there was plenty to do, and lots of fun times.
Progression feels pretty good, exploration is fun, the hub world thing is well designed, and there's plenty of items to come across, so that's all good. Crafting is pretty balanced all around, and there's no lack of cosmetics. Also the instruments are a nice touch.
Mod support is wonderful, but can get a little bit wonky in multiplayer scenarios at the time of this review.
Speaking of mulitplayer, it works pretty well. There are some occasional lag spikes from my experiecne, but the steam server setup is easy and pretty reliable, so I'll take it. Console servers are also available, but there's really no benefit to them as far as I know. Last time I ran one, there is no interaction whatsoever, but that may have changed by the time you're reading this.
Story is simplistic, no really memorable characters or plot, but that's fine. The game isn't meant for story.
Real♥♥♥♥♥♥though, exploring underground is boring as hell. I hate having to go mining, caves are boring, enemies in caves are boring, structures usually don't have anything usefull and are copy pasted all over, and there's really no point to it.
But, this is resolved with the concept that everything you can get from mining can be gotten through just normal exploring....
This concept is occurs a lot throughout the game. There's a lot of things to do, but a lot of different ways to accomplish the same thing. Many ways are just completely inferior, in terms of how fun they are and how productive they are. Farming is another pretty good example of this.
Bosses are... forgettable... alongside the combat. It's not awful, but I've never found it too engaging. Ranged weapons feel extremely underpowered, along with staves, which usually do some pretty cool stuff. There are exceptions to this, but overall that's the impression I got.
Building can be kinda fun. There's a lot you can do with the tools and materials you're given, but overall it's not too rewarding to build cool stuff. You can go pretty crazy if you enjoy building though.
Replay value for me has been... meh. I've gone back a few times and tried to play this game through again... but I only ever got all the way when 1.0 came out. I enjoyed the new additions in 1.3 (Spacefarer), but it wasn't really enough to get me all the way through again.
If the developers keep polishing this game, adding new content, and fixing any bugs that might arise, this game will continue to get better, and I'll probably come back to it.
If you enjoy games like Minecraft, Terraria, or other sandboxy voxely what have you games, you should definitely give this game a shot.

This is one of those games that has so much wonderful potential it's difficult not to be cheering it along.
Indeed it's already a really fun experience.
As a work in progress it's a great example to those other developers out there about that think 'early access' means they can scrimp on the polish and content. It's fit to bursting already and we've been promised more.
Thankfully I missed the 'world/character wipe' issue that seemed to plague the very early adopters. As your progression/loot and attachment to your character is a large part of the games charm I could imagine how this would've been irritating. A lesson perhaps in not jumping in quite so early.
It's beautiful, quirky and occasionally funny. The systems are simple at first and although they do grow a little more complex as the map and crafting options open up, for me this games charm is not in those typical bullet points.
For me the draw of this game is in a simple yet addictive loop.
- Build and customise a character.
- Investigate a planet.
- Collect interesting loot.
- Gather resources.
- Fuel up the ship - pick a random spot on the galactic map - fly there!
If you're bored or in a bad mood you can just fuel up and see whats out there.

This is kind of a turn based squad commander game.  You assemble a squad of 4 and send them into a dungeon to complete an objective.  That's the basic component that the game revolves around.
The complexity comes from chosing a composition from the 14 heroes (including 4 of the same class) to handle the challenges of each dungeon or the bosses within.  Finding the synergy between the heroes and having a successful dungeon run can be very rewarding.
The RNG can be a daunting element.  When it cuts against you, it cuts deep and can devastate your party and waste a hero you've pumped time and resources into.  However, everything is managable; there is no factor outside your control if you prepare properly and understand your heroes, the dungeons, and the enemies.
This game will challenge you, reward you, and cheat you.  And remember, "Losing is Fun!"

I started playing this game during its various beta periods which preceded its debut on Steam, and I never paired my main account to Steam when it did, hence the low hours my review will display. I continued to play for about two years straight before I let this game fade from my mind - nothing short of what the developers had done. All activity from whomever continued to update for the past two years strips down to bi-weekly, pay-to-open cosmetic promos and years-old recycled events. That's it. Most of the actual content additions were condensed in the game's first year, and realistically, much of it was already developed during its beta period, before they had a publisher to push the game out.
Several of the reviews here already express the various issues that arose and plague the game, so I won't bother reiterating them other than the sentiment that Spiral Knights could have been far more, and most likely isn't the Zelda-like comfy co-op dungeon adventuring it once shone for.

My review is negative simply because of the direction Bethesda decided to take with, but not exclusively, the Creation Club.
Re-introducing paid mods, about which a majority of players and modders expressed their feelings quite clearly, is a big mistake in my book for the company and for both Elder Scrolls and Fallout franchises. What kept these games alive for so long was mods, free and shared by communaties and Skyrim is probably one of the best exemples.
Now as of Fallout 4, it isn't a bad game by itself, but its a bad rpg. The fps elements are great, graphics are great ( and even better with free mods). The general aspect and mechanics are fine even though some of them could use some tweaks.
What really bothers me is that so many quests and locations had so much unexplored potential that left me thinking they were expecting modders to make the stories go from average and repetitive to great and immersive wrapped up with a bit of lore (and eventually make people pay for it). To truly play this game you have to try to ignore the main quest even if the game is almost crying or yelling at you, begging for you to follow it.
The absence of a karma system and the very few options in dialogue made it frustrating at times. Kinda makes Fallout 4 feel a bit like Mass Effect 3 when in the end it doesn't change much with the decisions you made. People who have played New Vegas would be extremely disappointed. There are several videos on youtube that elaborate more on why this game is pretty much average or bad depending on the point of view and i suggest looking them up.
That being said, there are some great mods that can greatly enhance your experience and some mod projects, being worked on, that can/could make Fallout 4 a better game. If you want to get this game i suggest getting it on sale or from a humble bundle. Same goes for the dlc although the only ones really worth it are Far Harbour and Nuka World but if you can get a season past for cheap Automatron isn't half bad. Like I said Fallout 4 isn't neceassarly a bad game but its a bad Fallout game.

Fallout 3 was my first foray into a post-apocalyptic wasteland. Stepping foot outside the vault for the first time is one of my most memorable gaming experiences.  I loved the environment, the danger, and getting immersed into a world where doomsday already happened.  Even the mods were great.  Some were so impactful Bethesda even
put them into future Fallout titles.
Fallout 4, like previous titles, is a great game.  I put many hours into this game and mods added even more hours to my playtime.  Sure, it wasn't like previous titles...It was the first game in the series where the RPG part of the game took a back seat and became more of a shooter.  The DLC content (for the most part) was lackluster and probably should have been a part of the base game but that is just modern day publishing.  Putting that aside, Fallout 4 is exactly what you expect from a modern AAA title.  The controls felt nice, everything ran smooth, and the graphics were great!  What's not to love?
Bethesda has always been the publisher that
on having its consumers fix/improve their games.  Usually in the form of mods. Mods are a way to enhance a game, to increase play time, to make lasting memories that will make me more likely to buy future products.  In Bethesda's case, mods were sometimes necessary to fix certain parts of their game.  Now they are evolving into another way to leech dollars from us.  Bethesda wants to turn mods into microtransactions.
It's not going to stop either, look where we've come from.  First there were expansion packs, remember those?  Something that added a significant amount of content to a base game, sometimes doubling play time.  These usually cost half (or less) of the base game you were buying it for.  Then came the DLC.  DLC was very similar when it first came out, if you bought all of them, it was basically an expansion pack that cost more money.  Next, we have microtransactions. Microtransactions originally came from free games as a way to support the developer. Oftentimes they didn't impact the game in a significant way, maybe a new character or a weapon reskin.  They were mostly a way to say thanks for making a free game that I enjoyed, here's a couple dollars. Now they are sneaking their way into AAA games.
Well, I'm not going to support this anymore. Mods are the reason I have put so many hours into Bethesda titles and now mods are the reason I won't purchase anymore of their titles. Good on you Bethesda, you've alienated one of your biggest fans.

Ah Darkest Dungeon, a game that has both made me weep tears of joy and sorrow. I will start this review off by stating this game isn't for everyone, it IS an extreamly difficult game and it doesn't bother holding your hand.
BUT in those moments of depressingly bad luck and sorrow theres those one moments where everything clicks, you get a crit here an item there. Eventually you begin to grow confident, maybe even a little cocky.
You tell yourself, "I can take the next boss my guys are ready!"
So you begin you're hunt for the boss, you've bought your supplies in amples amount and have used the best combination of characters to help you in defeating the boss.
You enter the dungeon and your very first step outside of the first room is a battle.
"Okay..." You tell yourself "this will be easy."
Your fight however quickly turns and you find yourself getting critted and already running out of ideas as you watch your oh so weak healer take crit after crit. After the fifth round you find yourself with a beaten up healer barely capable of standing and your other three partner members at half health wondering why they even sighned up to clear this Estate of the darkness.
So you sit there and ponder do I risk it all and explore the next rooms in hopes of the boss appearing in one of them or do you take you're weakend party and get the hell out of dodge. You decide it's not worth losing your valuable bodies to the darkness so your abandon the quest in hopes of the RNG god smiling down at you the next time you ever venture after the boss.
The game is fun but frustrating I won't deny that but if you have patience or perhaps just love getting slammed against a brick wall with nails in by this game and just develop Stockholm Syndrome for it then you can enjoy it.
In the time I've played this game its been very enjoyable, while this won't be the case for everyone it is certainly worth it. Just make sure to do some research on it before you buy to be absolutly sure you will like this game.

Okay... this game. It's uh... pretty good.
When version 1.0 finally came out, I played it through, and it was a ton of fun. I played it with 2 friends, and there was plenty to do, and lots of fun times.
Progression feels pretty good, exploration is fun, the hub world thing is well designed, and there's plenty of items to come across, so that's all good. Crafting is pretty balanced all around, and there's no lack of cosmetics. Also the instruments are a nice touch.
Mod support is wonderful, but can get a little bit wonky in multiplayer scenarios at the time of this review.
Speaking of mulitplayer, it works pretty well. There are some occasional lag spikes from my experiecne, but the steam server setup is easy and pretty reliable, so I'll take it. Console servers are also available, but there's really no benefit to them as far as I know. Last time I ran one, there is no interaction whatsoever, but that may have changed by the time you're reading this.
Story is simplistic, no really memorable characters or plot, but that's fine. The game isn't meant for story.
Real♥♥♥♥♥♥though, exploring underground is boring as hell. I hate having to go mining, caves are boring, enemies in caves are boring, structures usually don't have anything usefull and are copy pasted all over, and there's really no point to it.
But, this is resolved with the concept that everything you can get from mining can be gotten through just normal exploring....
This concept is occurs a lot throughout the game. There's a lot of things to do, but a lot of different ways to accomplish the same thing. Many ways are just completely inferior, in terms of how fun they are and how productive they are. Farming is another pretty good example of this.
Bosses are... forgettable... alongside the combat. It's not awful, but I've never found it too engaging. Ranged weapons feel extremely underpowered, along with staves, which usually do some pretty cool stuff. There are exceptions to this, but overall that's the impression I got.
Building can be kinda fun. There's a lot you can do with the tools and materials you're given, but overall it's not too rewarding to build cool stuff. You can go pretty crazy if you enjoy building though.
Replay value for me has been... meh. I've gone back a few times and tried to play this game through again... but I only ever got all the way when 1.0 came out. I enjoyed the new additions in 1.3 (Spacefarer), but it wasn't really enough to get me all the way through again.
If the developers keep polishing this game, adding new content, and fixing any bugs that might arise, this game will continue to get better, and I'll probably come back to it.
If you enjoy games like Minecraft, Terraria, or other sandboxy voxely what have you games, you should definitely give this game a shot.

This is one of those games that has so much wonderful potential it's difficult not to be cheering it along.
Indeed it's already a really fun experience.
As a work in progress it's a great example to those other developers out there about that think 'early access' means they can scrimp on the polish and content. It's fit to bursting already and we've been promised more.
Thankfully I missed the 'world/character wipe' issue that seemed to plague the very early adopters. As your progression/loot and attachment to your character is a large part of the games charm I could imagine how this would've been irritating. A lesson perhaps in not jumping in quite so early.
It's beautiful, quirky and occasionally funny. The systems are simple at first and although they do grow a little more complex as the map and crafting options open up, for me this games charm is not in those typical bullet points.
For me the draw of this game is in a simple yet addictive loop.
- Build and customise a character.
- Investigate a planet.
- Collect interesting loot.
- Gather resources.
- Fuel up the ship - pick a random spot on the galactic map - fly there!
If you're bored or in a bad mood you can just fuel up and see whats out there.
I have great memories of playing Elite on my old spectrum, of Metroid on my Super Nintendo and Minecraft on this terrible laptop. Starbound is a progression of ideas from all those games yet still manages to find a voice of it's own.

I don't wish to play with anyone, nor have my game interrupted by horrid internet types. Not all of us enjoy 'social' gaming and this game gives me my own universe to play in. I do hope other people don't arrive to spoil my fun!
I have great hopes for this games future and there aren't many better ways to spend your money or time on steam.

A game that is very worth your time!
The MMORPG genre gets flak from other online gamers for being dull or boring, the kind that only lets you point and click, then you watch your avatar do the work for you.
Well here is your answered prayer. Trove is a behind-the-back, Third Person Slash/Shoot kind of adventure with soooooooo much to give.
It's set up with a voxel art style of graphics, something I sometimes see in other games, but never has it been this good.
With my gushing out of the way, let's cover Trove's positives.
This game is already much more immersive than most other MMOs. The ability to move around, jump, dodge and control your fighting style is a good deal of improvement over other games in its genre. The multiple character classes each have a very different way of battling through the Prime Realms and beyond, and new characters are becoming more welcome among them. My personal favourites go to Shadow Hunter, Gunslinger, Fae Trickster and Lunar Lancer. There is so much to explore, multiple different geographical regions which range from volcanic peaks to frozen tundras, and BOSS FIGHTS! The Shadow Tower offers players a chance to team up and take on a series of challenges leading up to a battle with one of four bosses in the game, and if that is too easy for you, try it on hard mode. Continuing updates, loads of different styles of weapons and character customization and the charm it gives off are all key selling points in this game.
Sadly, with all that praise, there are a few things I don't like about Trove. First off, some of the classes feel unbalanced in their stat setup. Many complain about the Knight, and how he isn't able to dish out the same pain he takes without hassle, but I'm not one of those people.
Classes like the Candy Barbarian sound like they should be some serious bruisers, and he kind of is, but not enough.
The new Marketplace is a very welcome addition to me, but the real problem is, unless you go to the wiki, you never know if the items being sold are on sale, or have had their prices inflated.
Lastly, the simple ways of fighting is a little bit boring. Lots of classes have a way to counter this with combos or using their abilities outside of battle (Lunar Lancer's grappling hook or Gunslinger's blast jump), but not all of them are immune to this. It's not that big of a deal, as the simple controls make it easy to get right into the game, but it would be nice to have a more complex fighting style.
Overall, this game impresses me continually, and my only hope is that it will continue to go strong, and dodge the corruption that many long-running games seem to obtain. It is a lot of fun to play either by yourself or with friends, and the adventures and laughs you can create are seemingly endless. Good on you Trion Worlds, good on you.
Final Mark: 4.5/5

Let me preface this by saying the paid mods is what finally pushed me over the edge to review this game. This is absolutely ridiculous and you think they'd have learned from the first time they tried convincing people to pay for mods. The modding community is just that, a
. Most of the content creators make mods because they love the game(s) and love the community, who provide them with a reputation that demonstrates their hard work. Places like the Nexus allow us to donate to the creators to show our appreciation. No one is forced to, which makes it that much more significant when they do. All this does is add a paywall to download shoddy DLC that has been "verified" by Bethesda to work (because these games are always inherently bug-free, right?).
Onto the game itself -
I simply can not get invested into this game. The story is lackluster (the only Fallout story I still haven't completed), an abundance of the RPG elements have been removed, and I may be in the minority here but I dislike the weapons system. In previous Fallouts, I enjoyed scavenging the wasteland and finding a unique weapon that changed my overall playstyle (a la AMR) rather than finding and hoarding every piece of junk I could get to turn a pistol into a sniper rifle by simply switching the stock, adding a longer barrel, and throwing on a scope.
I have 109 hours played on this game with 330 hours on New Vegas. Out of the 109 hours on this game, I don't think I've even gotten halfway through the story and, for once, that's not a good thing. A majority of it is getting a strong urge to play Fallout games, thinking "ah I still haven't beaten FO4", sitting down, making a new character, playing for a few hours, and getting bored. Judging by the character's playtime, it looks like I've spent less than half the time played in-game, meaning I likely accidentally left it minimized overnight a few times.
There's a good chance I'm just being overly cynical due to my love for the previous Fallout games (lookin' at you, New Vegas) but it just feels like they focused less on what made Fallout, well.. Fallout, and focused more on what would grab more sales from the general public (which seems to be supported by their "new" implementation of paid mods).
All-in-all, I can not recommend this game to others when asked.
Are the graphics better than previous games in vanilla comparisons? Yes.
Is the engine better? Well, not by much, if at all. I will admit that the shooting feels a bit more like an FPS, take that as a pro or a con.
Is it as fun? Not in my opinion.
Is it as RPG driven? No.

Still, without a doubt, one of the coolest games I own.  I'll try my best to not make this review sound too fanboyish and as objective as possible..
To start, one of the things that you will likely find striking first above all else is the outstanding narration.  It immediately drew me into the story, much the same way a great book can draw you in with a great opening or preface.  Combine this with the haunting and expertly composed music, and the unique sort of "graphic novel" style of artwork and you've already got some winning combinations for a great game.  The narrating continues throughout all moments and events in the game, and even after hearing "Executed with impunity..." for the 100th time after murdering some foul beast, one turn away from losing one of my favorite adventurers, I never get tired of it.  It feels like it belongs every time, and before long you'll find yourself uttering the same phrases just because they're fun to say..
The atmosphere is dark, grueling, gritty and violent.  I love it.
The gameplay follows suit.  In fact, in the beginning, your first set of adventurers will feel like such wimps, and everything feels like a struggle.  Whether it's impending stress levels to the point of heart attack, or snapping psyches to the point of turning on eachother--or just the lack of funds to keep your companions fed and your torches lit--all these things and more will follow you at every turn, in every quest.  What's really awesome is after those first few adventures, some will die, and others will break--but those that survive even IF they break, will soon start to become your most favored adventurers as they acquire upgrades and abilities, and traits, even in spite of their shortcomings or negative traits or any diseases they will inevitably pick up along the way.
This creates a great sense of ownership over your story and over your adventurers.  Especially since anything that transpires is permanent.  There's no reloading a save if you have a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ adventure, that's just how it goes and if you lost one or more of your favorite companions, better luck next time.  It forces you to consider all possibilities and try to be as best prepared as possible, and even then, things will change and force you to change your approach accordingly or suffer.  Every great item has the potential to have a drawback that you have to decide is worthwhile or not.  Every treasure has the potential to drag your party down with it, sometimes even for just putting in the effort to get "that extra chest" before finishing your quest.  Everything decision you make is weighing options on one level or another.  Is it worth spending the extra 1500 gold in town to upgrade your favorite champion?  Perhaps, but what if the rest of the party dies and he alone escapes?  Was it worth it?  And what is the cost of his/her survival?  How many afflictions or diseases will you have to pay to remedy?  But hey, at least your favorite champion survived right?  Right??
It is a challenging but rewarding game, and there is more to come in future updates.  I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys brutal, unforgiving challenge and strategy.  The story is awesome, the character classes are great, the mobs are pretty horrific and sometimes downright disgusting, and the narrating...so cool.  Get it.

If you have friends who are willing to play this game with you, then ignore this review and play the game.
Although I only have very few hours on this game, be assured I had much more before I had steam and I downloaded this game from the internet. It's golden time was in the spring of 2013 when people really enjoyed spending all their mist energy (ancient version of crystal energy which charged throughout the day/night and was used for the elevators in the levels) and then going to haven to trade all their loot. In the summer of 2013 a big update came along which changed the UI and the supply depot (kozma used to sell cobalt-azure stuff instead of everything, very useful) and also introduced the mission system and the forge system. It also made trips to the clockworks free so mist energy was removed from the game. Although many players liked this, most didn't because it meant the game had lost it bare-bones feel by replacing it with missions and CE purchases and grinding which ruined the game. Before this massive update, when starting the game you had to customize your character, do the basic tutorial and cross the chasm into haven, from there you were left to explore the rest of the game with the help of those who already knew. After the update, missions led to the trashy lore with razwog and other crappy characters as opposed to finding out yourself. The missions meant that visiting the clockworks was child's play and took away the dark souls difficulty to getting recon modules and finding out about what the game was about. Before the update, to buy exclusive and special items, you had to either find them yourself from boss tokens or trade at the AH for them, afterwards you could buy them more expensively from the supply depot with used to be home to the azure tree which was only available from kozma and the AH. AH prices boomed and became unpopular due to the supply depot, people could find and beat bosses by using the missions which eventually led to the tier system being demolished (the tier system was a system in the clockworks which prevented new players from farming too much and meant that it was at least possible for the tier 3 player to be able to spend his mist energy on the levels they want to farm). The forge system meant players had to constantly grind and forage the clockworks for pointless rocks which level up items, which led to players getting fed up and buying it for real money as opposed to just looting the clockworks the hard way and levelling up your items as you went along, which meant it was easier to build and buy new items. Lockdown and Bomber was introduced which was pretty pointless except for guildwars and general showing off items, after the clockworks were deemed unusable, people turned to lockdown and bomber which now is 99.99% of the game. The devs gave up after half the community left by the end of the year. No new items were introduced anymore, just the same old specials being rerun after that. Also, pointless costumes being introduced. The lore was ruined, the bare-bones feel was taken away, people didn't need or want to trade anymore and PVP was the only way out. People who couldn't keep up or wouldn't keep up decided to leave along with the devs who bailed on the game with the money they made. By mid 2014 there were only 10% of what used to be the amount of people playing. International servers were empty and 'active' guilds only had 2-3 players. The game as of the end of 2015 is now dead, there are only around 200 people playing at midday which is the peak of people online at the same time. For anyone new or old who doesn't have any friends willing to play SK along with them, leave this game alone, the devs killed it.

Trove was one of the first MMOs that I've played and remains one of the most memorable games that I have. It was, in my opinion, one of the best MMOs out there. There are a lot of classes to choose from and therefore unlocks a lot of potential ways to play the game.
However, these are thoughts from the past. And as I revisit the game recently, I was vastly disappointed at what happened to the game.
It turns out that microtransactions became VITAL for dedicated, late-gamers. Unless you are willing to spend days, even months of grinding, you will definitely need to spend a couple bucks to get stuff essential for progression. These include high level gear, gems and materials. Classes can no longer be bought using in-game currency, forcing you to use real money to try out new classes. The drop system is a bit broken so that you can never get rare loot, once again forcing you to use real money to buy items that you want.
The game may be fun early on, where you simply play for fun. As you progress later into the game, the difficulty peaks really quickly that you will need good gear to actually continue playing. Sure, you may endlessly grind dungeons to ge them, but this will become repetitive quickly and if you are not bored at this point, the sheer difficulty will force you to eventually stop playing for good.
I am 100% a free player, and it is painful to watch as my friends succumb to the temptation of spending actual money in order to impress the higher level players or guild mates. You will realize that this DOES NOT MATTER, and you just spent time and money on something useless and nonexistent.
Try the game for yourself, reach level 20 in 2 classes, and see if you can still keep playing.

So, I reviewed this game a while back and gave it what I think to be too much praise. SO, I'm redoing this review and being a lot more honest.
Trove is, at heart, a very fun action MMO RPG game, with a vast diversity between classes. Some are good, some aren't, but that's not the point. Classes will vary from player to player because of their playstyle and roles. They are all pretty much unique, though. You can equip loot to your character and try and get the most amazing loot. So, honestly, this part gets a 7/10.
Trove generally sets the game on adventuring, one of the things I like. You get to run around in a pretty open world with many different biomes, fighting monsters and collecting loot. The loot varies on the difficulty of the world you go in. So, maybe a 6.5/10?
Now, for the first part that shoots many down. To get loot, you have to kill monsters. Sometimes, these monsters don't drop very good loot. Alternatively, you can go through a dungeon to get slightly better loot, but not anything too good at the start. They are littered with monsters, though. Grinding in this game is extremely tedious, unless you are high leveled and have good loot. And really, the only way to get really good loot is to pay for it, unless you wanna go through a Shadow Dungeon. Let's say a 4/10.
And the other one. Mantle of Power. I HATE this update. It brings in rings that could be very useful, and help out a lot. But, sadly, I've not seen any difference in my combat through the rings. It adds a lot more worlds, but you have to have a specific power rank to go through a lot of them, and I don't like it just not being the difficulty worlds. The reason I'm mad about the rings, though, is because they take up so much inventory space. There are boxes you obtain from killing monsters, and when you open them, you get rings. But they're so common that I often find myself having to clear my inventory several times to get them out. So, a 3/10 for this.
Overall, Trove is a decent/good game. It's a fun, addicting game, but it does have some bumps. So, I'll give it a 7.5/10.

Starbound is a lot like Terraria when you get in really close. It offers a procedural - and destructible - 2D environment in which almost everything wants to kill you and where you'll only survive by scavenging your way up the food chain. Mine ores and gather wood, build tools and a shelter - then build a means of building better tools and better shelters. Grow stronger by growing more knowledgeable, and watch as each trip outwards takes you further, earns you more, and leaves you alive that bit longer. Fight, craft, thrive! The UI's not entirely dissimilar, the mouse-and-keyboard controls will feel familiar, and many of the incidental details between both games mesh rather harmoniously, too.

Still, without a doubt, one of the coolest games I own.  I'll try my best to not make this review sound too fanboyish and as objective as possible..
To start, one of the things that you will likely find striking first above all else is the outstanding narration.  It immediately drew me into the story, much the same way a great book can draw you in with a great opening or preface.  Combine this with the haunting and expertly composed music, and the unique sort of "graphic novel" style of artwork and you've already got some winning combinations for a great game.  The narrating continues throughout all moments and events in the game, and even after hearing "Executed with impunity..." for the 100th time after murdering some foul beast, one turn away from losing one of my favorite adventurers, I never get tired of it.  It feels like it belongs every time, and before long you'll find yourself uttering the same phrases just because they're fun to say..
The atmosphere is dark, grueling, gritty and violent.  I love it.
The gameplay follows suit.  In fact, in the beginning, your first set of adventurers will feel like such wimps, and everything feels like a struggle.  Whether it's impending stress levels to the point of heart attack, or snapping psyches to the point of turning on eachother--or just the lack of funds to keep your companions fed and your torches lit--all these things and more will follow you at every turn, in every quest.  What's really awesome is after those first few adventures, some will die, and others will break--but those that survive even IF they break, will soon start to become your most favored adventurers as they acquire upgrades and abilities, and traits, even in spite of their shortcomings or negative traits or any diseases they will inevitably pick up along the way.
This creates a great sense of ownership over your story and over your adventurers.  Especially since anything that transpires is permanent.  There's no reloading a save if you have a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ adventure, that's just how it goes and if you lost one or more of your favorite companions, better luck next time.  It forces you to consider all possibilities and try to be as best prepared as possible, and even then, things will change and force you to change your approach accordingly or suffer.  Every great item has the potential to have a drawback that you have to decide is worthwhile or not.  Every treasure has the potential to drag your party down with it, sometimes even for just putting in the effort to get "that extra chest" before finishing your quest.  Everything decision you make is weighing options on one level or another.  Is it worth spending the extra 1500 gold in town to upgrade your favorite champion?  Perhaps, but what if the rest of the party dies and he alone escapes?  Was it worth it?  And what is the cost of his/her survival?  How many afflictions or diseases will you have to pay to remedy?  But hey, at least your favorite champion survived right?  Right??
It is a challenging but rewarding game, and there is more to come in future updates.  I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys brutal, unforgiving challenge and strategy.  The story is awesome, the character classes are great, the mobs are pretty horrific and sometimes downright disgusting, and the narrating...so cool.  Get it.

PROS:
+Friendly and Helpful community. Playing with kids are quite enjoyable. It's a nice break from all the salty attitude in FPS games.
+Abundance of good players who could carry you through harder dungeons (or, in the context of the game; Clockworks)
+Friendly UI
+You may conduct in-game trading for weapons and cosmetics. Steam supports it too.
+Straight forward levels with challenges, puzzles, hidden secrets, etc.
+Game offers annual events and daily extra missions for optimal varity in gaming experience
+Free to play
+Game admins will sometimes respond to player issues by hopping in-game with you. Very nice people.
CONS:
-The community may be friendly, but it is often hard to communicate with the occasional players who speaks a different language, due to the lack of region lock.
-Although the game encourages variety in gameplay, the same events pop up every year with very minimal changes. This means that cosmetics are not as collectible as you think.
-The game will try to steal money out of your pocket at every possible corner of the street: money to revive, money for fees for selling weapons at the Auction House, money to level up your gear, and etc. Not exactly Free to Play, is it?
-The game allows trading, but never encouraged. You cannot trade away cosmetics which are worn, and you cannot trade away weapons you used without a ridiculous amount of "Unbinding" fee.
-Game has variety in levels, but only a select few can earn you good profit without spending too much time. This forces some players to have a very narrow style of gameplay. These specific levels established the fundamental procedures to farm for money, and the lack of content overall bores the player easily.
-Sometimes expected events are overhyped, which causes a general discontent amongst the players.
So, is Sprial Knights a good game? Yes, but only borderline so. There may be a great deal of friendliness to the game, but the lack of player volume and the lack of new content only bores the player.
After putting some extra time into this game, I can't help but feel that there's so much more that could be done to the game that may contribute to its possible success. I had friends and folks I could and want to play with. The community is quite friendly, the risk/reward system of levels are well balanced, and overall, I had fun. It was one of the most enjoyable and impactful games of my adolescence. The guild system was fantastic. You could always meet new people and play with them. There was a demand for companionship and sportsmanship everywhere. The User interface is fantastic. Things takes a while to get used to, but things are always there when you need then. The life I've lived in this game is the lovliest, and the love was the liveliest.
But what happened? I don't know. I can't say for sure that this is a bad game, because it really isn't. I had loved it. Were my observations also my bigotry and prejudice? Did I grow up and move away from this game genre as a whole?
Why don't you play it for a bit and tell me? I'm sure you'll love it just as much as I once had.

Used a ranger for a 100 percent chance to kill a dude? lol, have another pod of enemies! Brought your sniper along? Random map puts trees everywhere and breaks line of sight. Getting close to the enemy, boom, spotted through the floor. Originally i thought I just needed to get good, but it's not that, you have to be perfect with your combat choices, spot the pod, snipe it, blow it with grenades, and don't move anyone forward unless you absolutely know there isn't another pod right behind it.

I don't often write reviews, but I had to for xcom 2. I've put 40 hours in over the last 2 weeks since release, and it's easy to love this game if you are at all a fan of strategy gaming. The mix of great turn based combat and excellent base building/ time management mechanics is very addictive.
The risk/reward and choice and consequence nature of the combat keeps things exciting for a turn based game, and you will become invested in your squads of soldiers. This makes the permadeath aspect much more fear-inducing, and keeps you on your toes and engaged.
Another aspect that hits is that the base building portion of the game, which is constantly presenting you with choices and challenges that drag your focus away from the main goals in search of resources and even upgraded soldiers to join your small army. I felt as though most of the upgrades that become available were fed to me in a cohesive and intuitive manner, and that almost all of them gave me a meaningful benefit or a noticeable upgrade.
Not everything is perfect, however. I find that even on a decent midrange system (780gtx, 32g ram, 3770k) I'm constantly struggling on high settings at 1440 p. I have heard that this could just be an issue with optimization, and that the patches are rolling out asap. Another small issue is that the story is somewhat thin, albeit much improved from the first xcom reboot, enemy unknown. In fact, the sequel improves on the original in almost every way.
I can't speak for everyone, but this combination is addictive and rewarding in my books. Anyone interested in strategy, sci-fi, or just looking for something new should look at giving this game a shot.

Now having played the full campaign I feel I deserve writing a proper review.
This game is just awesome. Did you play XCOM EU? If you did then I have to say that XCOM 2 does it twice the better. The Long War mod did a lot for XCOM EU/EW - and the devs did take a lot of that into XCOM 2. They improved the AI, they made the game more difficult in general but where the Long War made the game unbearably difficult for many people, the devs here didn't make that mistake. They did ramp up the difficulty but a rookie can still survive the XCOM experience. In my honest opinion they did it just right, they served the old XCOM audience with a challenge and also served the new players with a challenge. In XCOM 2 playing it on the rookie level is not a shame on my books, it's a testament to the good AI and the XCOM EU/EW players will find the Veteran level quite enjoyably challenging.
The difficuly is good, the content is good, everything is good and proper with this game. The only thing that might leave you lacking is the performance department. It's really pretty but at times the FPS slows down due to lazy optimization. Fortunately as this is a turn based game, performance isn't really an issue. It's an easy thing to forgive when playability is in place, pluse it's looking like they're addressing the performance problems with patches as we speak.
I rarely give games 10/10 reviews but honestly, this game deserves 10/10 on my books, Warmly recommended.

These past two weeks, anyone that knows me probably knows how obsessed I’ve been, playing XCOM 2, pulling multiple all nighters and raging about all of my favorite characters like Kylo Ren, Wolverine, Sylvester Stallone, Eddie Murphy, Ricotta Cheese, Incognito Bandito, and even the character of myself that I created dying horrible deaths. Sometimes because of recklessness and charging ahead when I shouldn’t, but sometimes due to sheer dumb luck. Finally, after nearly losing the game a couple times when I didn’t have enough weapon or armor research, I have now completed the first playthrough of XCOM 2. It was worth all of the hours and tears put into it.
The story of XCOM basically leaves off where the first one ended. Aliens have infiltrated Earth, and now have taken over pretty much everything, and fooled the masses into believing that they are there to help rather than destroy and enslave. The XCOM forces this time are more of a guerrilla force, striking from the shadows, and slowly weakening the aliens strongholds all while trying to reunite humanity to take Earth back. It makes for a more engaging experience this time around, and offers some new elements like a stealth mechanic. Most missions start off with your team concealed from enemy eyes, and you can use this to set up clever ambushes and weaken the opposing team before starting the engagement. Your base is also mobile this time around unlike in Enemy Unkown, which I prefer greatly, and honestly it makes more sense this way. Instead of setting up satellite relays to build up resources, you have to fly your transportable base to different regions of the globe, making contact with the local resistance fighters in each section. The more contacts you make, the more resources are added to your monthly income. From here, gameplay generally follows the same route that Enemy Unknown took. You split your time between taking missions as they pop up, and managing your base: building facilities, researching upgrades, hiring new soldiers, customizing said soldiers, and building weapons/armor.
The missions this time around are much more varied than they were in Enemy Unkown. Most of them are timed, which adds a sense tension, especially when you have two turns to go and are nowhere near your target objective because you got bogged down by a group of enemies and all of your soldiers keep missing perfectly good 97% chance shots. Enemy classes are also frighteningly more difficult in XCOM 2. Sectoids, which were pushovers in Enemy Unkown, now have the ability to mind control your soldiers, reanimate the corpses of the dead on the battlefield, or inflict status effects to your characters like panic or disorientation. And those are some of the fairly easy enemies in this game. Chryssalids return too, and all of their attacks are poisonous, plus anyone killed by one will turn into a cocoon, and if the cocoon is not destroyed, it’ll hatch into more Chryssalids. I had a rather nightmarish encounter with them during a civilian rescue mission, where the Chryssalids kept killing civilians, and more and more kept hatching until my entire team was surrounded by a horde of them. Some new classes that appear include: Vipers, which can spit venom and pull your soldiers in closer so they can strangle them; The Faceless, who disguise themselves as civilians, then show their true form when you get close; And Andromedons, who are encased in armor like Big Daddies from Bioshock and revive after you kill them the first time.
Character customization is a lot of fun, but can be a bit frustrating at times too. For the most part I could make accurate representations of some well known characters like Cisco Ramon, Geralt of Rivia, Poe Dameron, Chris Evans, Natalie Portman, and even Hans from Frozen. But the major problem I ran into was that a lot of the props that you can customize your characters with aren’t unlocked for that character until they achieve a high enough rank. So for the first half of the game, Deathstroke didn’t look right at all because I hadn’t unlocked the eye-patch for him yet. Regardless, character customization is just as fun as it was in Enemy Unkown.
For all this game does right, it isn’t without it’s flaws though. There are numerous bugs that affect performance. Most aren’t too terrible. A couple times enemies would phase through walls or floors, and there were a few instances where my characters got stuck and they couldn’t move. The big problems have to do with how horribly optimized the game can be at times. I don’t have a monster of a computer, but I’m running an Nvidia GTX 960. I have twice as much VRAM as recommended to play the game, yet I can’t get much more than 25 to 30 frames per second while playing this game. Occasionally it spikes up to 60 frames, but for the most part it’s all over the place. Also, when I first attempted the final mission, there were glitches galore, include gamebreaking crashes, and crazy pixelation to the point where I couldn’t tell what was going on onscreen. Thankfully a patch came out a couple days ago and I’ve been able to beat the campaign since then, but the game still needs a lot more work. Hopefully more patches will come out soon fixing these issues, but just be warned that at the time of this review, the game is still incredibly glitchy.
That’s not to say this is a bad game. I’ve thoroughly enjoyed most of what it has to offer. Granted, I do tend to rage when my characters miss perfectly good shots, and luck seems to be against me, but it wouldn’t be XCOM without that factor, and you can’t help but love the tactical goodness that XCOM 2 provides. I can guarantee that I’ll be playing this for a long time to come, attempting to beat it at it’s higher difficulties until I’m a master. If you were a fan of XCOM Enemy Unkown/Enemy Within, you owe it to yourself to play XCOM 2. Just be sure to wait for a few more patches to come out before buying if you can. By that time, most of the problems will be fixed and you can enjoy it in it’s entirety.

XCOM 2 represents the culmination of a lot of small improvements in the XCOM formula since the original game.  Everything is streamlined; there are very few extraneous decisions, and a lot of very difficult ones.  The prevalence of effective time pressure means you can't play nearly as conservatively as you could in XCOM 2012.  They've done an excellent job of freshening up the classes - each of them feels very different, and you have enough options to build out soldiers and teams that are wildly different.
The character builds and weapon/item choices, tech trees, every part of the game is full of interesting stuff to try.  The game is difficult, but fair - and randomness tends to even itself out over time.  As someone who made it through XCOM 2012 on a reasonably high difficulty without too many problems, I was initially surprised how difficult this game felt.  It forces you to get better, to learn new tactics and adapt must faster.  The game - especially played on Ironman, which you should - creates a wonderful tension.  That tension, in turn, creates beautiful moments where you just barely escape carrying out a teammate you've grown accustomed to having.  I love the randomly generated soldiers and they're silly nicknames and different voice acting.
Everything is great; if you're at all interested in a turn based strategy game, XCOM 2 has raised the bar in pretty much every way.   Wait for a sale if you must, but you should definitely play this.

I have to recommend this game, it would be dishonest not to, but I recommend it with a lot of qualifiers. Are you fine with playing an alpha build? Because this is an alpha build, no matter what Firaxis tells you. It crashes often, loads slowly, and generally runs like Skyrim after you've downloaded too many mods. Is there anything that breaks the game? No. I've beaten it on Veteran Ironman and gotten a ways into it on Commander Ironman. Out of all the hours I've played (and you can see those hours) I've never had soldiers die due to bugs. That being said, it is unprofessional and highly disrespectful to fans to release a game in this state, and it simply cannot be ignored.
Is it still worth it? Yes. Because of the character pool, and the dozens of little touches that make your soldiers likeable. Because of the improved base management, the strategy layer that legitimately feels like fighting a war, with the juggling of resource needs versus preventing dark events and Avatar progress. The ability to evac, and the fact that you can now fail missions without a guaranteed game over (without it feeling like the game is going easy on you). The constant difficult choices, racheted up to produce anxiety on the lowest difficulties. The time limits that force those difficult choices and force you to be a more interesting player. Everything good about EU is here and amped up to 11.
I just wish that the game's difficulty was the only thing torturing me. Damn it Firaxis, either get your♥♥♥♥♥♥together, or release a worse game so we aren't compelled to deal with it.

+ Graphically, I AM BREAD gets it right, if it were extremely realistic, the game wouldn’t be as humorous and enjoyable, as when things get realistic, it feels to grown up and focused rather than fun and enjoyable. And I AM BREAD is all about enjoying being a slice of bread with a mission of getting toasted. Although the levels of I AM BREAD is very well designed, easy to distinguish which area is dirty and which is clean, and the effect it has on your bread as it comes in contact with certain substances.
+ Gameplay is rather self explanatory, four keys for each limb and an extra button for each to lock the limb, and with the compatibility of the Xbox Controller, it makes it easier to control as well. The developers do a great job on getting reactions from players, because accidents always happen, the controls can be confusing when under pressure, thus panic and overwhelming emotions, all of which make the experience enjoyable.
+- Gamemode is very simple, just get toasted, but I think they could expand on this like Goat Simulator did, which was make it an MMO, allowing for more interaction with other players. I am guessing they could make I AM BREAD larger with multiplayer modes, who could get toasted quicker or something like that, you can challenge your friends on a level at the same time. Because a singular game mode will be easy to get bored of, adding more, or specifically multiplayer, it would probably benefit the game largely.
+ The amount of room you have to be your slice of bread is good factor. Because you have multiple ways and approaches to getting toasted and what to slather yourself with before you do. Because the toy is only as good as the room you play it in.
+ And I think with the continuous involvement of the I AM BREAD community, they will continue to improve, and maybe with the addition of the Steam Workshop which could alter your type of bread, or add more levels to play, I AM BREAD will be a long lasting game.
I AM BREAD is without a doubt a very fun simulator game, it has never been done before and that is what gamers like to see, something unique and amazing. People might’ve thought of making a simulator for ridiculous things but never thought they will pull it off so they kept to the cliché simulators, which are vehicles.
But I AM BREAD has been pulled off spectacularly well; it is most definitely fun experience, playing as bread with the mission of getting toasted. The idea was ridiculous but the developers made it happen. It’s an ambitious and successful idea, which deserves all the support it gets. Well worth the price and the experience. I suggest this game to simulator lovers and people who just like to play ridiculous yet great games (Goat Sim | BroForce).

Trove is an apt name for the experience that developer Trion Worlds delivers. On the most basic level, it refers to the little troves of loot waiting at the end of the mini-dungeons that dot the landscape, yes, but it also calls attention to the sheer variety of displays. Collectible helmets and masks ranging from Viking beards and sombreros to baseball caps and kabuki masks seem to number in the hundreds or thousands, offering a wealth of cosmetic customization. Weapons share the same variety, with items like guns and swords running the gamut from fearsome to silly. The beauty of Trove is that many of these items are made by players themselves, making the looting experience far more rewarding than it would have been if Trion were responsible for it alone.
If oyu are looking for an epic journey, buy DS3, it doesnt matter if you've never played the other games. Prepare for the journey of your life!

Turn-based tactical strategic gameplay, plan ahead or get all your soldiers killed. Currently however, the game suffers from relatively poor performance on a lot of systems, consistently freezing or hanging on the long load times, and occasionally stuttering and delaying with animations. A few patches and this'll be fixed, but it remains a bugbear at the moment.
Mod support from day 1 is massive, and adds a lot to the meat of the game. Things like gameplay fixes, extra classes, more hats to choose from, anything you can imagine and I foresee this adding a long time to the lifetime of the game community and to the replayability as well.
Overall a tremendous addition to the series and extremely fun to play. Highly recommended.
