This is a change from my original review. This game is EHHH but not WOO HOO AMAZING! This game is Terraria with space ships and a interesting graphics. This game was fun for me when I first picked it up, but quickly lost its charm. I got diamond pickaxe and a giant fortress in the 8 hours I have played. That may be slower then, say MC or something, but it still.
GRAPHICS
It's a really interesting graphical build. I've never seen a game look the way this does. I really kinda like it, but just because a game looks good, doesn't mean it's a good game. I like the graphics, SUE ME!
GAMEPLAY
EHHHH... EHH... MEHH.... Not TERRIBLY good. I quickly blasted right through it. I got Diamond 3 hours in. That's faster then I can find Diamond in MC. And I know EXACTLY where to find 'em. The gameplay is mostly a Hack & Slash type game with a crafting system and building. The building is odd with that you always use four blocks instead of just one. The grid system in play here is so large, this four block per place is completely needed to play the game. Unlike Terraria, where the grid is only one block per block system. Which I prefer, in my opinion. If you KINDA SORTA A LITTLE BIT like the idea, wait until it's in a major sale.
MULTIPLAYER
It's there. There are very cool servers on here. Pretty cool, but it still doesn't excuse the crap singleplayer experience. If you are gunna get this game, do two things. One, buy it on a sale. Two, get a friend to play it with. Oh, and Skype. Or Teamspeak. Or use the crap Steam voice chat. I don't know how to make a server, Google that.
All in all, I give this a 3 out of 10. In normal terms, that's a major MEEEEHHH. You really have to be in the mood to play this game, or just love this type of game.

Edit: With the release of the Long War Studios mods, classes, the patches and the DLC's the game has gotten to a much better place than my initial playthrough. I've now completed a full playthrough and thoroughly enjoyed it, though the Long War Studios new classes mod did make it a bit easy.
Below is my initial review unchanged.

Having invested hundreds of hours into just about every game to follow the 1994 XCOM (TFTD, Apocalypse, UFO: Aftermath / Shock / Light, Extraterrestrials, etc.) and having much enjoyed the first installment of XCOM from Firaxis (300 hours into EW & LW) I was much looking forward to XCOM 2.
After about 20 hours I've decided to leave it for what it is until it's been given the TLC it still requires.
The performance issues are readily apparent but I was still able to play the game without them getting to me.
The real issue is simply the lack of strategic and tactical choice.
The world map has been dumbed down further with the removal of air combat and basically comes down to flying towards your next mission or waiting over an objective while it is being "completed".
While you're allowed to plot your own course around the globe by choosing which countries to engage the alien's own objectives force you to rush to specific locations, lest they complete their project and win the game first.
The alien's progress seems to increase randomly, going from 40% to 80% shortly after starting a new game for me. I'd nearly lost after just a few hours of play. The pace of the alien progress forces you into following paths and missions to reduce this immediately, keeping you from choosing your own path until you get it under control. With the progress being so random this can either be very frustrating or non-existant for your playthrough.
Resource collection comes down to waiting for the correct objectives to appear on the world map, after which flying over the objective location and waiting for a while completes the objective.
The only resources you'll usually be lacking are the ones you need to wait for to collect on the world map, adding a Zynga-esque energy collection vibe to the resource collection aspect of the game.
Collecting items and corpses from missions is made more difficult by only being able to take them from missions that do not have a timer (about 20% of them), however this seems to be compensated by most projects only requiring few items or corpses. In practice you'll collect everything you need without really trying (or having much of a choice in the matter).
Opposite to the previous game, getting a new armor or weapon tier now only requires you to build the item once, which is then applied to the weapons and armor of your whole squad. Strangely, there are types of armor that do need to be built 1 at a time for each soldier, however the UI does nothing to explain the difference between the two, leaving you to find this out simply by making them. Additionally there are projects that award a random weapon or item which just feels silly as it contradicts any strategic choice and just makes the game even more random.
During the ground game, timers on most missions force a play-style that have you running gung-ho towards your objective, hoping pod placement and the RNGeesus will be in your favor. There is little tactical choice when all the timer allows for is rushing. Normally I only save scum when I want to attempt a different strategy but XCOM2 had me scumming just to survive the only approach it allowed for.
This is not to say the ground game isn't enjoyable; the timers DO add something to the game and will have you at the edge of your seat, but they are often set so short that they compromise the rest of the gameplay. Having you instantly lose your soldiers also seems much too harsh. Games like Invisible Inc. find a much better balance in this respect, increasing the challenge as you exceed the time limit instead of simply making you lose.
The non-timed missions actually seem to take this approach in some cases and feel all the better for it.
Balancing is another big issue. Strong units and abilities come into play early on. Melee units can run very far and stun you. Some units pop out of nowhere to devastating effect. Mind Control will take out your squad quickly with a huge success chance. Panic is also a big feature and seems to occur fairly often, making bad things even worse. Panicked soldiers throwing grenades at their own squadmates further poke the wound. This is exacerbated by numerous bugs allowing for shots through floors and ceilings, along with the rather lenient line-of-fire through object and structures that was already present in the first XCOM.
All of this taken together just makes the ground game feel random and unfair; you're given little choice and the choices you do make can be crippled by bugs or the RNG.
XCOM 2 does make a number of positive iterative improvements, such as more destructible environments, weapon mods and some abilities that do guaranteed damage (to help alleviate the randomness somewhat). Some of the new aliens and abilities are also very cool and require new approaches to handle. Armor has been made more straightforward, becoming a simple damage reduction statistic that is displayed on each unit. The new maps are quite cool and the narrative andsetting are well done. The voice acting seems good but I've personally developed a pet-peeve with almost every unit speaking with an Australian accent regardless of race or nationality (?!). Still it's not as bad as Vahlen's German(?) accent in XCOM 1.
For every positive iteration there are also seems to be a negative, though. Units now have a chance to dodge for reduced damage after a hit has been established. This just further increases the randomness. Environments can explode and damage soldiers standing close. This makes sense for cars and other explosive objects, but can also occur on walls and such. Stray shots can also destroy the environment and I've killed my own soldiers this way.
Another minor peeve is the interface showing the max damage done to an alien when viewing its health while aiming a shot, but the actual damage is usually lower, leading to sub-optimal decisions on my part and being frustrated an alien survives when the indicator showed he should've been dead.
XCOM 2 feels like a game with all the right pieces, but not enough time to put them all together properly.
I'm hoping Firaxis will take the time to fix and balance the game and isn't afraid to make some rigorous changes where needed.
When they do, I'll give it another shot, but for now the frustration and dissapointment outweights the fun there is to be had with the game.

I've got to say that this is a fantastic game. If you're a big fan of Terraria, you'll definitely enjoy this game. It's action-packed, not to mention that you can dig underground and find some pretty huge enemies down there that'll just kill you on sight. The creation of an alien is detailed. You can pick from so many characters and customize them. Hair, clothes, and accessories is all in the touch of your fingers. But in the end, it's all about survival. Die or survive. Don't be disappointed yet though, because there are difficulties to choose from. Easy lets you respawn and your items will not drop if you die. Medium will respawn you but all your items will drop if you die, and hard, if you're looking for a real challenge, once you die - you cannot respawn and you'll have to start again. Starbound also let's you build, yes - like Minecraft too. Craft and even troll other players ships on multiplayer, the fun will never end. On multiplayer you can also steal people's valuable items. Just be aware that others can intrude your ship and even steal yours. But don't fear, it's always re-craftable. At night it might be a good idea to stay in your house. Those birds don't look so friendly... Once you get out of your house, those birds will instantly charge at you with all your might. They do very high damage, so just stay inside. Also, campfires are a way to keep you warm. When you go outside, your temperature will instantly drop dramatically if you stay outside for too long or if you stay too far away from your house. Like all survival games, you'll need food in another way in survival. Don't eat it if you're not really hungry, because food is quite rare in Starbound. You need to kill certain animals to retrieve food. Get those furnaces running, throw some meat in and eat. Dig in, fellas!
I've got to say that this one of the best games I have played in a while. I give it a 9.2/10.

Alright. My first negative review on a big title. Need I clarify that most of my playtime is on the actual launcher, which makes sense given what I say.
This review is split into 3 parts. The first part, the tl;dr, is exactly what it's for. Quick summary that gets it across to those who don't want to read a word wall. Please note, that if you plan to make any comments directed at my opinions, I expect you to read the full form so that it's better understood. It's only fair.
Last time I played was early 2014, in the beta. Rejoined, got butt****d and then some by Trion due to them smashing the effectiveness of items down over time, and adding all kinds of "pay to get better" things (I'm not going to use "pay to win" because this title is definitely free to play, and because you can still get anything for free). On top of this, my attempts to get better - which I spent about 5 days on it with a group of friends to do so - proved to be extremely slow, unyielding, and rather confusing for the first day or so. I put A LOT of effort into getting back into this game, and came out with very little return value.
To start off simply, I was a beta tester. In its earliest days, the game was pretty simple and more of a "Hey this is kinda fun!" sort of thing. Had nothing compared to what it has now. Just the basic colored blocks from terrain, a few special blocks (Mainly metallic ones, like gold/silver) and a few statues. Now they have a lot more and, in turn, a lot better content and it's pretty cool.
Now, my current-day loadout still has items that make me practically
.... For the beta. Let's just say I was shocked to realize that Rainbow-tier items are now deemed "bad" and "a waste", and that there's actually stuff higher than Shadow-tier. I was shocked about the shadow change primarily because I was around for the update that actually
shadow-tier items. They were considered a "higher level, end-game" item and behaved like any other item where they have no levelling/star system that they do today.
So to sum up what I explained above, and go into how it affected me, my knight with rainbow/shadow items is now deemed "complete garbage" by most players! To shock me even more, the value of items has
dropped - In my time, having around 5,000 or even 10,000 flux made you look like a god. People rarely broke 3500 flux in their inventory. Additionally, the value of health went down. My Knight has 6000 health, which was able to be considered about 40% god-tier back in the old days. (GOOD players had 20K HP if they really really knew how to make it work)
Finally, to top it off with this whole "Power rank" thing, my Knight was designed for U5 worlds - Note that U5 was the highest uber level in my time. Unfortunately, given the scale of the gear and such, I am now limited to U1. To add insult to injury, my beta gear is still insanely powerful for U1 due to being tailored to U5. I can two-shot anything there, and it's pretty much like going to the newbie area of a game as an end-game player. It's a complete drag, an absolute bore.
So as I did mention in the tl;dr section, I did try to get back into the game, and I truly devoted my effort into it. I loved Trove, it was very fun, and I am not the kind of person to ragequit over a few changes until I've at least put good effort into trying to learn the changes. That said, my attempts to re-learn the game were quite successful. I understand the basic ropes of how some of the new features (gems, stuff like that) work. The problem I have is getting gear - I can't pay for Trove, and even after playing for
, I was unable to get even another rainbow item. On top of that, getting shadows is likely out of the image since, while I still have 3 keys that I saved from old times, the new shadow dungeon system is ... not the same at all. Back in old times, it was actually a wild portal like any normal dungeon, but it required a key to open. Once a dungeon had started, the portal in the wild would be destroyed. In the battle itself, it was a simple 5-wave system then after 5 waves in the arena, you were done. Easy! Now it's a bit more than that. Unfortunately, from what I can gather, the game expects players to play a
long time, or spend a bit of dosh to shorten that. I can't devote myself to that in the sheer magnitude that Trove asks for.
I understand that some may have concerns about my review (It's a very strongly-negative review), so I encourage people to post things. I have no plans to silence or yell at those with criticism.

Alright. My first negative review on a big title. Need I clarify that most of my playtime is on the actual launcher, which makes sense given what I say.
This review is split into 3 parts. The first part, the tl;dr, is exactly what it's for. Quick summary that gets it across to those who don't want to read a word wall. Please note, that if you plan to make any comments directed at my opinions, I expect you to read the full form so that it's better understood. It's only fair.
Last time I played was early 2014, in the beta. Rejoined, got butt****d and then some by Trion due to them smashing the effectiveness of items down over time, and adding all kinds of "pay to get better" things (I'm not going to use "pay to win" because this title is definitely free to play, and because you can still get anything for free). On top of this, my attempts to get better - which I spent about 5 days on it with a group of friends to do so - proved to be extremely slow, unyielding, and rather confusing for the first day or so. I put A LOT of effort into getting back into this game, and came out with very little return value.
To start off simply, I was a beta tester. In its earliest days, the game was pretty simple and more of a "Hey this is kinda fun!" sort of thing. Had nothing compared to what it has now. Just the basic colored blocks from terrain, a few special blocks (Mainly metallic ones, like gold/silver) and a few statues. Now they have a lot more and, in turn, a lot better content and it's pretty cool.
Now, my current-day loadout still has items that make me practically
.... For the beta. Let's just say I was shocked to realize that Rainbow-tier items are now deemed "bad" and "a waste", and that there's actually stuff higher than Shadow-tier. I was shocked about the shadow change primarily because I was around for the update that actually
shadow-tier items. They were considered a "higher level, end-game" item and behaved like any other item where they have no levelling/star system that they do today.
So to sum up what I explained above, and go into how it affected me, my knight with rainbow/shadow items is now deemed "complete garbage" by most players! To shock me even more, the value of items has
dropped - In my time, having around 5,000 or even 10,000 flux made you look like a god. People rarely broke 3500 flux in their inventory. Additionally, the value of health went down. My Knight has 6000 health, which was able to be considered about 40% god-tier back in the old days. (GOOD players had 20K HP if they really really knew how to make it work)
Finally, to top it off with this whole "Power rank" thing, my Knight was designed for U5 worlds - Note that U5 was the highest uber level in my time. Unfortunately, given the scale of the gear and such, I am now limited to U1. To add insult to injury, my beta gear is still insanely powerful for U1 due to being tailored to U5. I can two-shot anything there, and it's pretty much like going to the newbie area of a game as an end-game player. It's a complete drag, an absolute bore.
So as I did mention in the tl;dr section, I did try to get back into the game, and I truly devoted my effort into it. I loved Trove, it was very fun, and I am not the kind of person to ragequit over a few changes until I've at least put good effort into trying to learn the changes. That said, my attempts to re-learn the game were quite successful. I understand the basic ropes of how some of the new features (gems, stuff like that) work. The problem I have is getting gear - I can't pay for Trove, and even after playing for
, I was unable to get even another rainbow item. On top of that, getting shadows is likely out of the image since, while I still have 3 keys that I saved from old times, the new shadow dungeon system is ... not the same at all. Back in old times, it was actually a wild portal like any normal dungeon, but it required a key to open. Once a dungeon had started, the portal in the wild would be destroyed. In the battle itself, it was a simple 5-wave system then after 5 waves in the arena, you were done. Easy! Now it's a bit more than that. Unfortunately, from what I can gather, the game expects players to play a
long time, or spend a bit of dosh to shorten that. I can't devote myself to that in the sheer magnitude that Trove asks for.
I understand that some may have concerns about my review (It's a very strongly-negative review), so I encourage people to post things. I have no plans to silence or yell at those with criticism.

XCOM 2  for the most part was really enjoyable. I'm not a great expert, but i was able to beat the game on normal diffculty without too much trouble.  However there are a few things i did not like about the game.  No controller support to me, was pretty big. How do game companies make a game in 2016 not have standard controller support.  I turned on my XBOX wireless controller to test it, and it works somewhat, but all the bindings were completely messed up.  When you have games like Rebel Galaxy, that come out, and have full functioning controller support, that was created by two people,  it is unaccaptable that 2K can't do it.
If you can get over the controller issue, we can start talking about the game.  For the most part i found the game to be pretty enjoyable.  I was able to beat the game on Normal without too much difficulty. Some people are upset about the timers, however in my opinion, it really doesn't hurt the player.  I was always the kind of a person who kept moving, instead of staying in overwatch.  Some missions toward the very end became hard, which causes you to take even more risks, which adds to the stress of the game, making it more enjoyable in my opinion.
I liked how XCOM was constantly throwing new enemies at the player, You really had be on guard, when i first laid eyes on the sectopod it made my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tighten.  That kind of feeling is very rare in games today. I feel most games are too easy, compaired how they were were in the 90s.
The game is a uphill battle until the very end. Once you develop the psyops characters,  it changes the demension of the game.  Those characters in my opinion were overpowered, i trained up two psyops characters completely , i could only imagine how it would be if i had a complete team of psyops characters.
But for the average gamer who is looking for a challenging RTS game, i recommend it.  Don't expect to win your first time either,  because i lost my first two runs before i understood the basic fighting mechanics.  Use Grenades to destroy cover, and know how to set up a proper ambush is key elements of playing the game sucessfully.

In all seriousness, Starbound is a game about interplanetary space travel and survival. You start out by making a character that is one of six races: Apex, Avian, Hylotl, Floran, Glitch or just a plain old human. Allow me to explain what the races of Starbound are. There are the Apex, which  are very Planet of the Apes, in the case that, they are very smart, but they are still apes. The Avians are like strange Aztec bird-people, and the Glitch are, simply put, medieval robots. Hylotl are Japanese fish-people, The Florans (my personal favourite) are cute little super-agressive plant-tribe people. And the Humans are, well, humans. This game is still in Beta Stage 1, so it is very very buggy and glitchy (no pun intended) and is constantly being updated. All six races have their own race-specific ships;  that adds a lot of immersion as to what the races are really like.
I would recommend this game to anybody who played Terraria but felt that Terraria was just a bit small and not too diverse. Starbound is very focused on space travel; as the planets can be small or large; dangerous or peaceful, or just plain old asteroid fields. You absolutely need to travel to different planets, because they can be mined out and are not infinite. Not one planet will have all the ores Starbound has to offer, so there is another reason for space travel. Starbound has multiplayer and singleplayer types, and nobody can go in your ship unless you invite them to your 'party', which is kind of like a group. You can remove people freely if you are the leader, and everyone in the party can beam to each other's ships.
I would give this game a 8.9/10 because it is still in beta, but still amazing for a beta.

Once you get past the first 50-ish hours, you quickly realize there is nothing to this game.
Beat dungeons so you can get resources so you can level up your gear. You level gear so you can beat more dungeons, get more resources, so you can level up your gear more. It's just a neverending grind.
Now, in some games this works. By supplementing that grind with cool quests, interesting npcs and a good storyline to boot, this grind can be made at least bearable, if not enjoyable.
Trove does not do this, though. There are no noteworthy npc interectings. Once you get past the tutorial, the quests are as follows; "Go to X biome. Kill Y amount of enemies. Repeat 10 times."
On top of this, no story has really been implemented into the game. There have been hints thus far, but I have no idea the real reason I'm repeatedly killing this lady named "Daughter of the Moon", supposedly the final boss, other than to... get more resources.
Now, the whole grind can just be skipped! Which sounds great, until you realize you have to pay up. It's a lackluster pay-to-progress game that leaves little to the imagination, and 254 hours I'll never get back.
I'll likely be popping in from time to time, just to see if the new updates change any of this, but at the moment, I'm less than hopeful.
**I only played these 200+ hours to see if there really was something further to the game. I regret that descision heavily.**

How is this game?
Fun? Yes.
Addictive? A lil.
Now the bad stuff:
1. Bad that players cant view range of weapons. It seems pretty arbitrary at the moment. Would be great if there's a circle (that's sensitive to the terrain, of course).
2. Bad that there're so few soldiers. End of the world, aliens control the world... and there're less than 20 in every map and reinforcements only comes in 3s? NOPE. Not good.
3. Pretty ridiculous the soldiers are so lousy at shooting and miss all the time. Considering the gravity of the whole situation (aliens rule the world), it's ridiculous to say "Let's just drop less than 10 ppl that can't hit their targets and see if they can save the world." Nope, that's weak sauce.
4. Ridiculous that the aliens get to react when the player spots it. Just because you see them, does not mean they see you. It would be nice to have a cone of view that's sensitive to terrain. And the ability for them to react gives them an extra turn. But when the aliens come to your troops, your troops don't react. Ridiculous. Unfair. But thankfully, there's a mod for that.
5. The scanning thing... Not digging that, but I get that they need to let the player pass the time. And speaking of time, the research, building and recovery times are a little too long, especially on Legendary.
6. Tiny maps. Enough said.
7. Nonsensical that every soldier only carries 1 grenade... or 2 if it's the grenadier. Sure, people would say that it's for "balance", but I say that's total crap.
---
Still, it's a fun game.

I'VE PLAYED THIS GAME FOR 5000 HOURS SO I KNOW WHAT I'M TALKING ABOUT
And by the way, if it's too long to read there is no point to play it: The Game's servers are going to close. So recommending or not, there is no reason to start it whatsoever (it has not been confirmed, but its on forums).
I would definetely give this game a thumbs up, but for its current state, it's a no from me. I don't wanna hate on the game, but what bugs me the most are the developpers that gave up on this game that it had the
to be something bigger and something everyone would enjoy playing. I would give this review a thumbs up, but I'm giving a thumbs down because of the devs. And before you trynna defend in the comments before reading this, I suggest you do. I've spent 5000 hours on this game,more than any other I've spent and you cn definetely say I enjoyed it A LOT. But I feel like I got betrayed. It would be a 10/10 if the game was active and constantly had new things to offer.
You might definetely know me if you played this game as Speedkillerr, technically still a Guild Master in Unity(an old powerfull guild). I've also made yearly Christmas Giveaways to the ENTIRE GAME! YES, I used to advertise in haven for free stuff, and over 40 people would line up to give free items to friends and strangers. So before concidering me as an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, make some research or stop assuming. To introduce you to this game, you are a knight and you must find a core, where a really old artifact was stolen by the Gremlins(a destructive enemy faction), and you must bring it back to Haven. Your Mission is also to help Spiral HQ to find the missing Alpha team that got sucked into the core. Unfortunately, the game never had the core open until few months ago and boy...the lore was disappointing. So if you are looking for story, you will not find it interesting as the gameplay progresses. Only As a 1-star player or a recruit, the story will be enjoyable.
Here is the positive part: I loooooove the costumes and the design of characters. It gives so much inspiration to designers and drawers out there. The designing part of the game is friendly. Spiral Knights on DeviantArt is a really common place for players to go. I've changed my profile picture in the past A LOT when I would find a badass or cool spiral knights pic. I even make em myself using Spiral Spy, Three Ring's software. I've made profile pictures for many friends and other peeps. I love the design and costumization of the game a lot.
What's really nice about this game is also Haven. It looks such an ideal and peaceful place for players to interact, trade, participate in events, practise, generally become better players. The design of the Town Square looks amazing and delightful! If you are going to start the game, I recommend to look around and explore the place. No wonder why most of people stay there most of their time!
The mobs-monsters are inspiring as well. Dividing them into different families and each faction-family has its own unique story and species. Personally, "the nightmare" mobs are my favourite (shadow zombies, gremlins, trojans, etc).
The game isn't challenging for you? Try out Shadow Lair! It's epic and has a lotta action!
I am also glad to see new accessories lately in early 2016. I can definetely say the design has improved A LOT. Variety expanded. But if I rant about it bellow, it's for not just that reason. The lack of new items is still a debate.
Sadly,the game is dead. I'm repeating, the game is dead. Only 500 users playing on steam. Now you're going to tell me that steam users only populate 30% of the game, but still...it is not enough. The developpers don't care about this game anymore. Some devs were playing the game and doing nothing all day. Just showing off their expensive ♥♥♥♥♥♥ items that no one can afford. The Head-Dev of the game(Nick) quit. The are almost no updates in the game.
Let's break this into two pieces now. 1-for PvE and 2-for PvP
1) Missions get repetitive, there are only 5-10 daily missions that are randomely generated. Arcade depths are empty since there is a "Mission" option where you get straight into the lore. There is no variety into the missions, that's just how I felt through out the years. Since most of the game is filled with players who finished the lore and are 5-star, the Lord Vanaduke mission is the primary selection for grinding, which is the only one that gives the most crowns(currency of the game). And yes,it's just THAT mission that you get the most money from. And it definetely gets repetitive since it's the only one that shows progress. And it takes about 30-40 minutes to complete. Either way, PvE is boring, that's all I'm gonna say,especially when you're alone.
2) The worst part of this game. Basically 99% of the game is PvP. Classic. It's called Lockdown. You just get in 2 teams and kill each other andcapturing points. OP people always playing, you see no noobs anymore. And basically the people who play PvP excessivly are the ones who live at their mom's basement and don't have anything else to play. It can be fun at some parts, but it's repetitive and BORING. More boring that Call of Duty nowadays. And everyone is using the same TWO weapons.  That's basically PvP. No variation in this game. There is also Blast Network but it has 0 players for 3 YEARS STRAIGHT. I've never seen anyone playing it. Whenever there is a match, it's surprising. It's like the most useless PvP part of the game. You just bomb others.
The prices of the items are broken. The Auction House is empty. Nothing is sold anymore, I only see 2-3 traders a day, while back in the days, there were trades everywhere. There are rarely new items anymore. Just some promo ♥♥♥♥♥♥ costumes that only difference they have is their color. NOTHING ELSE. That's what we get twice a year only.
problem in the game nowadays is the wealth gap. Now it's just rich vs poor. No in between. It's like the players have been divided in two species. The rich people monopolize everything. The bad thing also is that only 2-3 guilds are active. And the really big ones are literally ruining the game. Guild vs Guild PvP only has ONE guild which you can play against. ONE! And this one is the most hated to VS since they don't even let you play with others..and they are incredibly tryhards lol. My guild tried to vs with a friendly guild. And we didn't manage to play because that annoying guild gets in the way.
No joke, the game was full and joyfull back in 2012. It reached its climax in 2013. The servers were full. There was action going on, and the community was humble. Now it's all about competition and who is the best on LD(Lockdown). Servers are empty. There is only 1 server active and sometimes it is empty as well.
The game had full potential to become something new and different. I liked the lore and the setting at one point, but the devs don't care anymore and half of the quit. Three Rings is falling and there is nothing we can do about it. The 2 biggest guilds in the game broke and went to other games.

However to get new weapons you can either grind out gold or medals (medals are awarded for levelling up). How is this game?
Fun? Yes.
Addictive? A lil.
Now the bad stuff:
1. Bad that players cant view range of weapons. It seems pretty arbitrary at the moment. Would be great if there's a circle (that's sensitive to the terrain, of course).
2. Bad that there're so few soldiers. End of the world, aliens control the world... and there're less than 20 in every map and reinforcements only comes in 3s? NOPE. Not good.
3. Pretty ridiculous the soldiers are so lousy at shooting and miss all the time. Considering the gravity of the whole situation (aliens rule the world), it's ridiculous to say "Let's just drop less than 10 ppl that can't hit their targets and see if they can save the world." Nope, that's weak sauce.
4. Ridiculous that the aliens get to react when the player spots it. Just because you see them, does not mean they see you. It would be nice to have a cone of view that's sensitive to terrain. And the ability for them to react gives them an extra turn. But when the aliens come to your troops, your troops don't react. Ridiculous. Unfair. But thankfully, there's a mod for that.
5. The scanning thing... Not digging that, but I get that they need to let the player pass the time. And speaking of time, the research, building and recovery times are a little too long, especially on Legendary.
6. Tiny maps. Enough said.
7. Nonsensical that every soldier only carries 1 grenade... or 2 if it's the grenadier. Sure, people would say that it's for "balance", but I say that's total crap.
---
Still, it's a fun game.

Current review:  This is my all-time favorite game.  If I was stuck on a desert island with one game, this would be the game I would want.  It was good to begin with (original review below) and initially I coudn't decice if I liked Xcom or Xcom2 better, largely due to the setting.
I decided I like this one better.  The big points:
1) Procedural maps -- I'll never have them memorized and the game will always be fresh, yet I know the basic well enough I can play it waking up with coffee or having a beer.
2) Character pool - I have about 500 pre-made characters, some I've made, quite a few I've downloaded that remind me of old shows or movies, some otherwise lost to time (Space: Above and Beyond, etc).  Somebody made G.I. Joes and Cobra, really this is the closest I get to feeling like a kid playing with G.I. Joe toys.
3) Better graphics.  I want cutting edge and for Turn Based, this is it.
4) Mods -- it's a different game with mods, from comestic changes to changing some minor rule variant in my favor.  I'm playing Long War 2 now, it's like a different game.  Sure, the mods can make it more unstable, I'm writing this now 'cause it just crashed on me... no big deal I'll reload it.
5) I'm approaching 2,000 hours in it.  There's 168 hours in a week, and I've played this more than anything in two years since it came out. Sure, some of that is idle time I left the computer on... but the only game I have in my library with more hours is Team Fortress 2 (not to mention, someone ported the TF2 voices and I made them in my character pool).
Initial review below: Recommended.  The original X-Com from the 90's (not counting the sequels, of course) and the reboot Xcom are among my type 5 favorite games of all time.
I'm on my 2nd playthrough now, they advanced the game significantly.  Sure, it's a slightly different game (you are the resistance now on offense, vs. the previous game running Earth defense)  so it feels a little different but still alot of fun.
They also advanced the techinical gameplay side enough that I'll probably never play Xcom again (though I wish you could play it with this engine, there is a different vibe to it).
The character pool is great, I've already made or downloaded lots of different famous characters.
I don't buy much at full price, this one I pre-ordered.

If the above or below is helpful to you please thumb up so it can be helpful to others as well :-)
Here's the "what you need to know": Control the 4 corners of a piece of bread to navigate across levels and find a way to make yourself into toast. It's much harder than it sounds as the bread is quite difficult to control. You can move and break most anything in a level so sometimes it's fun getting sidetracked and just break stuff. As you move your way up along objects and walls your "Grip" meter diminishes and when it's empty you fall prey to gravity, but it recharges after a second of not climbing. Also, avoid gross things in a level, namely the floor, ants, etc, as coming into contact will decrease your edibility, which is the games equicalent of a health bar. THAT'S IT! That's everything you need to know to jump in and have fun with I Am Bread.

Current review:  This is my all-time favorite game.  If I was stuck on a desert island with one game, this would be the game I would want.  It was good to begin with (original review below) and initially I coudn't decice if I liked Xcom or Xcom2 better, largely due to the setting.
I decided I like this one better.  The big points:
1) Procedural maps -- I'll never have them memorized and the game will always be fresh, yet I know the basic well enough I can play it waking up with coffee or having a beer.
2) Character pool - I have about 500 pre-made characters, some I've made, quite a few I've downloaded that remind me of old shows or movies, some otherwise lost to time (Space: Above and Beyond, etc).  Somebody made G.I. Joes and Cobra, really this is the closest I get to feeling like a kid playing with G.I. Joe toys.
3) Better graphics.  I want cutting edge and for Turn Based, this is it.
4) Mods -- it's a different game with mods, from comestic changes to changing some minor rule variant in my favor.  I'm playing Long War 2 now, it's like a different game.  Sure, the mods can make it more unstable, I'm writing this now 'cause it just crashed on me... no big deal I'll reload it.
5) I'm approaching 2,000 hours in it.  There's 168 hours in a week, and I've played this more than anything in two years since it came out. Sure, some of that is idle time I left the computer on... but the only game I have in my library with more hours is Team Fortress 2 (not to mention, someone ported the TF2 voices and I made them in my character pool).
Initial review below: Recommended.  The original X-Com from the 90's (not counting the sequels, of course) and the reboot Xcom are among my type 5 favorite games of all time.
I'm on my 2nd playthrough now, they advanced the game significantly.  Sure, it's a slightly different game (you are the resistance now on offense, vs. the previous game running Earth defense)  so it feels a little different but still alot of fun.
They also advanced the techinical gameplay side enough that I'll probably never play Xcom again (though I wish you could play it with this engine, there is a different vibe to it).
The character pool is great, I've already made or downloaded lots of different famous characters.
I don't buy much at full price, this one I pre-ordered.

- Bugs - Yeah, glitches happen. Quite often. I kinda expected it and that was the reason why I didn't start in Iron Man mode. The game crashed even twice. The dev team is pushing out hotfixes, updates are underway.
All in all I will definetly recommend XCOM 2 if you like turn based games. It will keep me busy and entertained for quite some time.

This is a 2D, side scrolling, sandbox, building/exploring game. It features aspepts similar to rogue likes. The "level up" system in this game is still being worked on, so you might be at a loss for what to do at times.
I myself am a map maker of sorts, having played a decent amount of Minecraft. I enjoy spending my spare time building homes and villages for the NPCs that you can spawn and befriend. I find it nice that while in Minecraft you have to make sure to cover all 3 dimentions of your home, you only have to worry about making a cross section of your home.
NPCs are a bit limited. You can only spawn a "simple" that does nothing except greet you and "guards" that are a bit like one legged soccer players. They aren't that great, but they're better than nothing. Doctor/chef/explorer NPCs are rare finds, compared to the other two I just mentioned, so don't be too bummed out if you can't find any.
Farming is very simple. You have to till the ground once and plant seeds that you find on your journey in space.
Space exploration is simple. You start off on a planet and try to eek out an existence, staying alive just enough to scrounge up enough fuel to make the jump to a better planet with more resources. Planets can have hazardout weather like flaming meteors or harmless star showers. There are also pregenerated villages/dungeons/homes/towns that you might be lucky enough to encounter. Just don't wave around any weapons when guards are around, they get nervous around strangers.

Well... Isn't this community at a standoff with itself...
If you don't feel like reading this, here's a TL;DR:
WAKE UP SHEEPLE
Joking aside, seriously, what's up with this community? I'm actually literally confused...
I guess I should start off with when I got this game.
Now, I don't have a touching backstory to the game or anything like that, but I have been playing this game since about when it came out. The time shown isn't nearly the time played, as it only counts the time you spent in the launcher... Which I closed after the game opened from it. Alright, with that out of the way, let's get riiiight into the news! (I'm not cringe I swear)
First, lets talk about the game itself. I LOVE IT. I mean, I have been playing it for like, what is it, 3 years? Probably 2, I don't know. Anyway, love it to death. To start off, the game just feels fluid... The building is solid... All the mechanics are just nailed down. Everyone says "oh they removed this", "oh they removed that", but does anyone mention how much more optimized the game got? Or how about the (fun as heck) colony system? Fossil hunting? I could go on. As the great Keem said, I have files on top of files (of how good this game is!) ...The last part got cut from the video. Anyway, yes, this game cut a few things, but that was to appeal to the majority! Chuckle Fish wanted this game to be accessible to all, not just the hardcore, not just the 'veterans'. And because of that, I actually enjoy the current state more than the early access state. (Here come the haters.) I know I rambled on a bit, but in general, the game is good! You'll get your money's worth, and more! Just stop worrying if it's good or not, and just immerse yourself!
So, what's up with the bad reviews? Well... Like I said before, the community is in a standoff. There's the elitist on one side, mad at Chuckle Fish for trying to make profit off a game they spent 5 years on, mad they removed a few features, and just ignoring the game for what it is. I can assure you, their reviews are comparing the game to what they believed it would be, what standard they held it to, and definitely not reviewing the game itself. Instead, they're reviewing the development of the game. Reviewing the developers. On the other side, there's the new people and the people that just want to have fun with the game! The game is great fun, so just enjoy it and stop getting mad over some features being taken out! The games amazing! I highly recommend!

Its rare I play a game that I love, and hate so much at the same time as Xcom 2. The game is a non stop barrage of highs and pittfalls. There is a strange duality of quality in every facet of this game, that I have rarely seen outside of an indie game. The game looks and plays exactly the same as "Enemy Unknown" and somehow is even plagued by many of the exact same graphical, an UI issues that dragged down its predecessor. The game has grown little since its last itteration, and many of the new mechanics the game prides itself on, are so poorly fleshed out as not to add anything meanful to the experience. While there have been a number of improvements to the balance of the gameplay, the game can't seem to decide if it wants to hold your hand, or throw you to the wolves. All too often I found myself muttering "Yeah... I get it." or to the other extreme of "Where was the explination for that?" There is a lot going on in this game, with a whole slew of things to juggle if you are to succeed, and a strangley heavy handed, or an altogether detramentally late explination of many of the new resource mechanics in play. On top of this the game has an unnecessary amount of waiting built into everything. There are pauses, and cooldown timers attached to everything from animations, menu navigations, game actions (both player and enemy), and character naration, making for a frustratingly slow progression to get to the gameplay itself. At the end of it all this is less a sequal, and more of a massive expansion to "Enemy Unknown" and not a terribly ambitious one. Even in lue of all of that, it is still somehow a joy to play, thanks entirely to the modding community. They have come together to fix, many of the failings and blemishes of this tittle, and turn it into something that is a load of fun. Its a tooth and nail fight uphill all the way, as you struggle for a foot hold in the face of an overwhelmingly superiour force. The satisfaction of working your way up through alien armies, with nothing but your whits to protect you is surprisingly refreshing, in an increasingly resource oriented Strategy genre.
As it is, at the end of the day, I can't recommend this game without the heavy use of modding. The vanilla experience essentually a jar of jellybeans at the far end of a room of rock salt and broken glass. Yeah there is enjoyment to be had in it, but you have to suffer to get to it.

A lot of people will say that XCOM 2 is more of Enemy Unknown.  I can only agree with that to an extent.  I would say it's a different Enemy Unknown.  A lot of tactics that were employed in the first game will have to be widely abandoned.  Why, you ask?  Does the change in pace lend itself to effectiveness?  Well, I should elaborate.
Narratively speaking, they missed the mark.  Canonically, Enemy Unknown was nothing more than a simulated series of events.  What actually happened was a full invasion, instead of sending the rookies to fight each other.  I only mention this because, when you re-encounter some of the aliens, who have been updated, the original variants are brought up in passing mentions.  I have a problem with this because the aliens were more or less just upgrades of themselves.  Even if you strike it off as contrivance, the actual plot has its own problems.  Starting a guerilla warfare offensive is a fresh change of pace, but I was just never convinced by our team of misfits.  I think the biggest problem with the story, without spoiling anything, is the aliens being stupid, and XCOM actually not being far off from being the terrorist group that they're being propagated.
Nobody gives a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the story because the bulk of your enjoyment will be coming from the gameplay.  Let's start with base builder.  Fat was trimmed heavily.  Your facilities are fewer, the amount of facilities you can build are fewer, but all of them are more meaningful.  You could call it dumbed down, but I would rather call it streamlined.  With that said, I feel like there's a linear build path.  You're always going to want to get your Advanced Warfare Centers and Guerilla Tactics Schools ASAP.  It's easier to explain why it's so important to get those two buildings up and running almost immediately, a little later.  Research is way less vague as to what you're going to be unlocking by going into research.  You also get access to start your investigations into psionics way earlier, which fixes my biggest complaint with Enemy Unknown.  The foundry is replaced with the Proving Grounds, which has way better gear available, at the cost that some of it is randomized.  Your facilities will also have the option of being staffed, usually speeding up the process of which certain actions are done.  The scanning system is way more active, as your base is now on a flying space ship.  You can spend time scanning out at places establishing contact with regions, picking up on leads that may lead you to more goodies, or back at your main base region speeding up healing/construction, or gathering Intel (pro tip for pros only: use the medical scan option).  The defeat condition this time is the AVATAR project: a meter that fills up that you have to occasionally set back.  It's way less punishing than in Enemy Unknown, and that can make the AVATAR project pretty meaningless.  They also took out the interception mini game from Enemy Unknown, to the dismay of absolutley 0 people.
The skirmishes are where the game skews in the eyes of everybody; some love or hate the new changes.  I think everybody agrees that in Enemy Unknown, it started off hard, and got progressively easier.  XCOM 2 is way more extreme and by that, I mean that the game starts off so hard that even the devoted XCOM fans wanted nerfs, and becomes a joke once you overcome the early game hurdle.  Alien abduction missions have been replaced by Dark Events.  Dark Events will debuff you/buff aliens in any number of ways (e.g. cutting your monthly funding, speeding progress of the AVATAR project, etc.).  You get to counter one of these events.  These missions will have you coming in stealthily, allowing you to ambush unsuspecting patrols.  You could technically sneak by the patrols, but that's a terrible idea, because completing the objective blows your cover, regardless of whether or not you got caught.  The missions themselves have timers, forcing you to not spam overwatch.  These turn timers are why you get the Guerilla Tactics School and Advance Warfare Center first: you need a bunch of firepower to burn your way to the objective timely, and you're going to take heavy damage.  The enemy variety ranges from underwhelmingly weak, to being absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.  Enemies like the Shieldbearer or Lancer are priority targets, while the new crew like the Sectoids with human endoskeletons (pectoids, basically) or the faceless are gutter trash.  Late game, enemies like the Andromedon or Gatekeeper are scary, but by that point, you've probably unlocked your doomsday devices: the stock+repeater weapon attachment combo, and the psi operative.
Technically speaking, this game is probably FUBAR.  Frame drops are expected, LOAD TIMES ARE VERY LONG ON THE SKYRANGER, and the procedural generation that XCOM 2 employs gets samey before the campaign is over.  XCOM 2 is very open with mod support, and while I never consider mods in my reviews, the existence of exceptional mod support deserves to be acknowledged.
Well, can I recommend XCOM 2?  I would not recommend XCOM 2 to the newcomer to the series (start with XCOM: Enemy Unknown.  It's the most accessible of the series), but I sure as hell could to the people who loved Enemy Unknown.  There are some tough pills to swallow, yes, but I think the experience is worth it.
Final Words: "Shot failed to connect"

My review for I am Bread by Bossa Studios.
Basically, you play as a slice of bread, and your goal is to become toasted with wacky controls similar to QWOP, Octodad and Surgeon Simulator.
There are 9 levels, one is a tutorial, the next 7 are main levels and the last one is an epilogue. The levels are as follows:
Cell(tutorial)
Kitchen
Lounge
Bedroom
Bathroom
Garage
Garden
Petrol Station
Car(Epilogue, unplayable in any game mode other than Story)
However, each level gets progressively harder than the last, meaning you will probably snap your keyboard(or controller) in half in rage.
Another great thing is in the later levels, especially the Petrol Station, the heat sources require lots of thought as to what you must do to toast yourself.
There are also 6 game modes.
Story
Cheese Hunt
Rampage
Zero-G
Bagel Race
Free Roam
There is even multiple bread types! All game modes have a different bread type as the star, exept for Free Roam, which you can pick any bread, and Zero-G that uses the same bread as in Story Mode.
Wholemeal(Normal, all around)
Crackerbread(Agile, less strong)
Baguette(Agile, very strong, only 2 grip points)
Bagel(Fast, less strong, only 2 grip points)
Lets start with the HUD.
At the top left of the screen, there is an 'Edibility' meter. This is your health meter. Doing stuff like laying on the floor, touching bugs, picking up toenail cippings and band-aids and other dirty things will bring your edibility down. If your edibility goes down to 0, you lose.
At the top of the screen is the 'Grip' meter. Holding onto things bring your grip down, and you can let go of the said object will make it go back up. If the grip meter runs out, you will let go. So basically, you can only hold onto stuff for a limited time before you let go, and this can be INFURIATING at times. There have been times that I have been climbing along the wall like Spiderman, only to fall of and land on the floor and struggle to get back up.
At the top right of the screen is the timer, which times the level.
Now let's have a look at the graphics.
The graphics are very smooth and nice, lighting effects are beautiful and it's very easy to differentiate dirty things from clean things, because I have played a lot of games where you can't tell which things are okay to stand on and which things kill you.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is very similar to Octodad: Dadliest Catch, and one thing I really like about this game, is the fact that there are multiple ways to beat the levels.
You may have seen the 6 gamemodes from before, so let's see what each one has to offer.
Story mode, starring Wholemeal, is the normal game mode. Edibility, Grip and Time are here.
Cheese Hunt, starring Crackerbread, is the 2nd game mode. You must find 5 lumps of cheese hidden around the level.Edibility has been replaced with Integrity, which means you can walk on dirty stuff, but you can't get beaten around too much or you will break into pieces. Grip and Time are here.
Rampage, starring Baguette, is the 3rd game mode. You must destroy, smash, break, shatter and obliterate as many things as you can in 2 minutes. Edibility and Grip are no longer here, and the timer has been changed into a time limit.
Bagel Race, starring Bagel, is the 4th game mode. You must run through the level whilst going through checkpoints, and you must get to the finish in under 1 minute. Edibility and Grip are no longer here.
Zero-G, starring Wholemeal, is the 5th gamemode, in which Bossa has turned the old Zero-G glitch into a whole new gamemode. There are a whole bunch of new controls and grip is gone. Same goal as Story Mode. One other thing about this game mode, is the fact that they actually are in space. There are windows showing stars and nebulae, and I really like how the Garden is in a biosphere, that's really cool.
Free Roam, starring Wholemeal,Crackerbread,Baguette and Bagel! Pick any bread and roam free in any level you like, with no limits! Do whatever you like! No grip, no edibility, no integrity, no time limit, nothing! Be bread, and go on an adventure!
Conclusion:
When the game initially released, with only 1 bread type, 1 game mode and 4 levels, I didn't think this game was really worth the full price. But, then look at it now, with 6 game modes, 9 levels(7 of which are playable in all game modes) and 4 bread types, this game is actually worth it! A must have for your Steam Library.
My final rating for this is: *drumroll*
9.5/10.
It's definitely a great game if you are a fan of Octodad or Surgeon Simulator, but if even if you have not played those games, it's still worth a try. It blends 3D puzzle-platformer and adventure together, and creates a wonderful experience. If you like puzzle games, I would reccomend you buy this.
And there is even a little suprise at the end of the game, which I will leave up to you, after you buy this game.

Just finished the game after around 100 hours. The feeling is pretty mixed. But first thing first, XCOM 2 is definitely one of the few games I ever enjoy since Fallout2 and Neverwinter Nights. It has every better feature that a turn-based game can offer:
+ Friendly and well illustrated interface with pop-up information
+ Various soldier classes with distinguishable skills
+ Various types of armour, ammo and enhancement component available
+ Relatively free environment to develop your base and squad
+ Complicated and yet rich and colourful game play
Based on the original game structure, XCOM 2 introduces a new feature of ammo/armour type and enhancement components concept. With right combination of these items, you can customize different gears for each class of soldier to boost their skills. Together with newly designed class skill set, it makes the game play very rich and full of options.
The alien enemy units are well designed, too. Unlike those just-shoot-with-different-weapon types in XCOM, not only there are more classes of unit, but also they now possess own distinguishable skills. Many of them are quite powerful and dangerous. Thus combat now becomes very dynamic and challenging. Careful considerations and calculations are required all the time. From squad configuration to target priority and combat sequence, you’ll need to squeeze every single point of output that your squad can manage in order to survive. Again, it makes the game play very rich and full of options.
As for the downside of the game, there are quite a few as well. Such as:
- System requirements are little bit high.
My 2 years old rig (i5/8G/GTX760/SSD) can just manage medium graphic setting. And still lags sometimes. Considering XCOM can be played on GPU integrated Haswell, that’s quite a leap.
- Several bugs.
Such as enemy lancer can sometimes perform 4 actions instead of 2 during a turn, game freezes during reload or mission debriefing.
- Story driven and forced.
In XCOM, player can control the main story progress and enjoy the game at leisure. Now in XCOM 2, time is limited. Everything has to be rushed foward to avoid total failure. Personally I don't like such setting, it puts player under hgh tension and spoils the fun to replay.
- The last and the most: the Evil Lord RNG …
Your shots miss a lot but enemy's don't, not mentioning that 95%-and-still-miss. More, it seems the game doesn't refresh the random numbrer queue when you reload a saved file. I intentionally tried ‘hack-quick load-hack’ for 10 times, and the results were almost the same. Only after fully quit to desktop and restart the game could I get an obvious different result. I wish the RNG should be more reasonable and balanced in the future patch.
Besides of these issues, I see many people complain about the frame problem. Well, to my opinion, those people probably own top rigs already and they still want to play a turn-based game like CoD. As if to kill an enemy at 120 fps is easier than at 30 fps. For me, as long as my modest PC can run smoothly under medium graphic setting, I’m happy.

Having completed the game on Commander difficulty with Ironman on second playthrough, I don't really take people complaining that the game is too hard that seriously. Xcom is a difficult game, and not for the faint of heart. That being said, there are some issues.
The bad:
- Optimisation seems a little raw at the moment. Running a slick rig at the moment - won't bother dishing out the specs, but am running a 980 - and the framerate drops to disappointing levels at pretty much any opportunity. Have tried the game on even better top-end rigs, still encounter framerate issues. Hopefully this'll be fixed (or at least improved) with a few patches.
- Graphical issues. Had a few, ranging from funny colours requiring restart to character model positioning. Found the latter to be more annoying, particularly on downed soldiers, as they appear to be one place when they are in fact in another, on occasion.
- Elite enemy variants. I don't really have that much of a gripe on this one, but it'd be nice if the upgraded version of enemies such as the ADVENT troops and some of the other later enemies that get "Elite" variants got an additional ability or new way to fight instead of only increased health and damage. Since the "upgraded" models of these enemies look the same, it can be tricky to remember who you're dealing with (and how much damage their weapons do, since they always seem to look the same too.) The good number of new enemies you have to deal with certainly mitigates this however.
The good:
General game structure: As a reviewer put it regarding the XCOM:EU, base management and combat work harmoniously together and neither feels like they were just tacked on to the other to check some box. It's also a lot more sleek than the original Xcom those decades ago - in a way I do miss keeping track of all the supplies and managing multiple bases, but frankly I think that slimming it down like this has improved gameplay pace significantly without making it too breezy.
Gameplay: It's XCOM:EU, but sexier and with a fresh style. A faithful sequel with more than enough mechanics to keep a person interested. No MECs on your side (at this stage, at least, outside of hacking) but plenty of other ways to stick it to the ayy lmaos.
The Spokesman: He can speak for himself on this one.
There's plenty more good to write about and a fair few more issues to complain about regarding bugs (largely graphical/performance-related, as far as I know) but frankly, I'd rather get back to playing another round of Xcom 2.
I urge players to try ironman on a difficulty they're comfortable with (or at least just using autosaves, since you need to complete the game once just to unlock ironman.) It improves the pace plenty and with true permadeath, you can really feel the tragedy of your men dying due to your mistakes (or occasionally, through sheer misfortune,) and the elation of pulling off a mission in which you stuck it to the ayys flawlessly.

This is such a fun game.
The core gameplay loop is a mix of tactical ground based combat, mixed with a management game of handling resources and controlling the progress of the enemy.  These two gameplay elements work in unison to produce a truly engaging and fun gameplay experience.  On the ground tactics game, it is a well executed turn-based strategy game where mistakes cost a lot and getting perfect missions are oh so satisfying.  The management aspect of the game helps to break up the missions and helps to improve your units to make the ground combat easier.  This is a similar game to XCOM Enemy Within, which is also a fantastic game, but improves on that game in virtually all aspects.
However, at least during the first few weeks of release, there are numerous technical issues that may impact your enjoyment of the game.  Things like long loading times, long pauses where nothing happens, animation glitches, and stuff like that will be encountered while playing.  These are usually just an annoyance when they occur, so I don't think it really impacts my overall enjoyment of the game.  Another complaint that I have is with the animations.  The animations are very long for each action a unit takes, and can make things drag on for awhile.  Such as when the specialist sends a gremlin, it takes the gremlin 5 million years to get to it's destination, another 3 million years to do it's action, then 5 million more years to return.  This might be something that can be modded, but I guess we shall see.
I played through the game on Veteran, and although this was my first full playthrough of an XCOM game, I found it pretty easy to beat.  Since the story is pretty light, I would not recommend just playing this game for the story, and thus would not recommend the lowest difficulty setting.  Veteran is challenging enough that it is still fun, although I would definately bump the difficulty up a notch on my next playthrough (which I fully intend to do).
Finally, the modding support will most definately prolong the life of this game, fix issues and in general keep the game relevant.  There is NOTHING bad with mod support, and makes it all the more worth it.  I chose not to play with mods on my first playthrough, but you might want to consider at least some QOL mods.
tl; dr - game is fantastic, play it and you will not regret it, and play on Veteran or up.  Also mods.

This is a 2D, side scrolling, sandbox, building/exploring game. It features aspepts similar to rogue likes. The "level up" system in this game is still being worked on, so you might be at a loss for what to do at times.
I myself am a map maker of sorts, having played a decent amount of Minecraft. I enjoy spending my spare time building homes and villages for the NPCs that you can spawn and befriend. I find it nice that while in Minecraft you have to make sure to cover all 3 dimentions of your home, you only have to worry about making a cross section of your home.
NPCs are a bit limited. You can only spawn a "simple" that does nothing except greet you and "guards" that are a bit like one legged soccer players. They aren't that great, but they're better than nothing. Doctor/chef/explorer NPCs are rare finds, compared to the other two I just mentioned, so don't be too bummed out if you can't find any.
Farming is very simple. You have to till the ground once and plant seeds that you find on your journey in space.
Space exploration is simple. You start off on a planet and try to eek out an existence, staying alive just enough to scrounge up enough fuel to make the jump to a better planet with more resources. Planets can have hazardout weather like flaming meteors or harmless star showers. There are also pregenerated villages/dungeons/homes/towns that you might be lucky enough to encounter. Just don't wave around any weapons when guards are around, they get nervous around strangers.

It's always a pleasure, spotting a game with potential right from the start, before watching this game deliver on that potential, and then some.
Darkest Dungeon is such a game; I spotted and backed it through Kickstarter, and it is (along with The Banner Saga) two of the most special games I've had the pleasure of supporting during their development.
Darkest Dungeon is a rogue-like dungeon crawler, where the player manages several teams of adventurers, as they attempts to unravel the mystery behind the eponymus Darkest Dungeon.
From the unique art style to the unforgettable narrator (the player's deceased ancestor, whose dark experiments brought about ruin to his estate and the neighboring hamlet), Darkest Dungeon is full of memorable moments, twists and turns in the plot and hard decisions on the managements aspect of the game.
The adventurers are not heroes; indeed they are flawed creatures, with character quirks that affect their performance during the various forays into the surrounding dungeons, which are now infested by an army of foul creatures, abominations, necromancers, skeletons, beasts and other assorted nasties.
Managing the stress caused on those not quite heroic characters by their adventures (and misadventures) in the various dungeons is of paramount importance, as a high level of stress can cripple (or even kill) even the hardiest veteran.
Darkest Dungeon is a true gem, rewarding careful planning and creative thinking in the setup and management of the various teams of adenturers, throwing enough spanners in the player's plans to keep things fresh and unpredictable, but not in an unfair, arbitrary way.
I am very much looking forward to the first expansion of Darkest Dungeon, The Crimson Court, and I'll be keeping an eye out for the next game of Red Hook.
I cannot recommend Darkest Dungeon highly enough; if you haven't played it, you're missing on a classic.

XCOM 2 is an excellent follow-up to XCOM : Ennemy Unknown and XCOM : Ennemy Within. The game is tense and heavy while also giving you a realm of possibilities when it comes to killing aliens. This time around, your soldiers are on the offensive, and as such, the way you start a mission and set-up an initial ambush on your ennemies can change the odds of a mission. Fortunately or not, things do not always go as planned and the RNG makes for an entertaining but sometimes frustrating game. Ennemies are varied and all troublesome in their own, special way, but your soldiers also feel more resourceful and powerful then ever. The relatively easy to procure Psi Operative Class is so versatile and potentially devastating that you'll always want to have one in your squad. The game can be a little rough around the edges and the mission timers can be a big source of stress, but with the possibility to mod the game to suit your style of gameplay, this point is almost moot. With a few updates from Firaxis and an ongoing mod support, this game could easily be remembered as a classic of PC gaming in the years to come.

I am uninstalling Trove as of now.
I've probably put 50 hours into this game over two weeks and there is no end in sight.
The Good:
- The voxels are crunchy
- The music is not grating
- There's a ton of 'stuff' to do
- The community is hella friendly.
- The endo hits are frequent and satisfying. Finding the next best thing or popping chests and getting rare loot is incredibly satisfying.
The Okay
- The classes are largely the same, and they all have their playstyle basically dictated from level 3. As you play it's just a seesaw of power between your equips and which portal you enter.
- All uprades aside from weapons and equipment are basically cosmetic once you get past starter. Wings, mounts, boats, there's a basic one and then you unlock another by grinding. It's nice because you don't get blown out by other people with super fast mounts, but you DO need to unlock cosmetics to advance your level, and everything else.
The Bad, or "The Heart of the Review"
This game is a sugar coated addiction vampire. The bubbly exterior masks a system that encourages you to play, play play and pay, pay pay. It does this exceptionally well, and it's insidious(or good business practice).
It starts you off with a tutorial that runs you through the basics and then points you towards buying a 'free' thing from the shop. The shop button, incidentally, is 'n', right between 'b' and 'm', which are inventory and map, respectively. Controls are typical WASD/Mouse. That means you're going to be trying to hit b or m blind in game a lot and instead bringing up the store, conveniently, and there are quests that require you look at your map frequently so every mistake says 'hi, did you know we have a shop?' It comes pre-hooked into your steam account so in app purchases are very easy...
...and eventually they'll start to eat at you. Unlocking classes is cheapish, unlocking flasks is cheapish, but all the same stuff will take heaps of hours in game. You can unlock 2 extra classes with ease - after that it's grind city. You can unlock two basic 'fast' pets, but after that you need to grind 200-500 of a bunch of resources to get new ones. Unlocking that stuff, again, is a ton of grind, but it's necessary to get the resources to buy new character classes and other important gameplay items.
What's really killer is that the content really doesn't change after the first day or so of gameplay. The numbers get bigger, but 90% of the time it's just a swarm with classes not really using synergy, just trying to overwhelm bosses. If the gear+level tally is high enough you win, if you don't you lose. Some classes are force multipliers but that's really just an incidental effect. There are so many costumes that you can't tell the characters apart anyway so teamwork is a non-thing. Some classes are cheese master but who wants that?
tl;dr just another grinder

In all, if you liked XCOM, and turn based stragegy games, you'll enjoy playing the latest version.  The sound track is great, the graphics look great, the story is nice, however Bradford can get annoying at times, and the game play is enjoyable.

“Abandon all hope, ye who enter here.”
The controls, camera, and movement are all tied together and become an exercise in frustration. My rage over this, if its energy harnessed, could easily power the world three fold – but I digress. Objects here and elsewhere, fall broken into pieces as soon as you touch them (sometimes even if you don't), and everything else will move around, but never in a way that's useful.
You'll begin by planning your route, being extra careful and resetting frequently to achieve perfection. This optimism will not last. After the fatigue sets in and your initial happiness turns into bile, you'll desperately try to haul your disgusting slice as far as the game will allow. Your sighs, lamentations and loud wailings will resound through the starless air. And when the game awards all your pain and suffering with a D grade, you will not feel shame, but elation, for the struggle as finally come to an end.
An end that is short lived, as it serves only to reveal to you the next circle of hell. But, like every masochistic addict, you will not cowardly make the great refusal. You must go deeper into greater pain, for necessity brings you here, not pleasure. And when you emerge from your room to return to the bright world, without care of having any rest, you can hold your head up high and know that you could face no greater test.

Spiral Knights is, as I like to call it, a "cutesy dungeon crawler". The game takes place in various depths of a mechanical planet that is always shifting and changing. With very easy to understand gameplay and lots of replayability, Spiral Knights is a wonderful game to sit down with for a few hours and slash, shoot, and bomb things with your friends.
Overall the game has a lot going on for it, but time has left it a bit behind. Over 4000 hours in this game on Steam and I can honestly say I don't regret a single minute. It's simple, it's fun, it's cute, and it has really fun people in it. The bad and ugly parts aren't uncommon in games at this point, and if you just want to hack and slash things and have a fair amount of time to kill, this is a lovely game. This is a direct result of its controls feel as though they were poorly designed (note that I'm not referring to the default keyboard controls so much as how the controls result in your in-game movement). Unfortunetly, "I am Bread" lacks the humor of QWOP given the price tag (~$10) and amount of effort devoted to developing the game (i.e. it's been given more than the "it's a small flash game" amount of effort).
Ultimately, this game looks really amusing in YouTube videos and might work for some very small bits of humor during live streams, but isn't something particularly fun to play as a game. My suggestion is to either save your money for a different game (e.g. Banished, Democracy 3, Kerbal Space Program) or to wait until it's on a 70-90% off sale.
tl;dr: It's "QWOP 2.0 -- Bread Edition" without the humor of QWOP. Wait for it to go on a major sale or just buy a different game.

Sadly, not very well optimized from the start, no Ultrawide support, and with Bethesda trying to sell ridiculously small "mods" through the creation club I can´t really recommend to support them. There are better games.

- All guns can be bought permanently with in-game currency.
- The only thing you can buy with micro-transactions are crate skins for the guns (same stats as their original gun).
- Really optimized (i5-4460/GTX 1060 @150fps 1080p on Ultra).
- Quick matchmaking.
- Gunplay = CoD + CS:GO (perfect mix for casual play and competitive play).
- 3 ways to get in-game currency.
- Cheating
In my experience (might vary on what region you play, I play on North America), I never come across cheaters in Deathmatch, Demolition, and Assassination. But the only gamemode that I've found a cheater in (blatant, spamming rocket launchers and ends game in 2 minutes) is Battle Match. Each time I queue for Battle Match, 100% of the time I get cheaters who grind EXP.
- User Interface
Very confusing at first, and it looks like a mobile game. It's not very new player friendly, new players get confused and some don't even know how to navigate. I was very confused and astonished at how horrible it was, although the game doesn't revolve around the UI, the gameplay is still good.
- Maps are okay and basic, but perfect for this type of game: close quarter, small, and fast paced.
- No ranked system as of 8/10/17.
- Only 24 guns as of 8/10/17 (not including skins, throwables, or melee weapons).
- Level progression isn't too fast or too slow, just right and as expected, determined mostly on in-game time played.
- Gun skins are really nice and unique (except for KSG Sector 9, which is basically AWP Asiimov).
