XCOM 2, the sequel to the excellent XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within. If you played EU/EW, you learned quickly to move your squad carefully across the map, shotguns up front, heavy in the middle, snipers to the back, everyone on overwatch as individual squad members move forward.
Forget all of that. Welcome to turn limit simulator 2016. Every mission has a turn limit of between 8 and 14 turns. You will learn very quickly that you have to sprint your squad across the map like a bunch of autists in order to reach the objective in time. Forget overwatch, this is a dash or nothing game.
But at least now most missions are started in "concealment" sneaky deaky mode, right? Here is how concealment works. You have to dash across the map living on a prayer that you can get in the general area of the objective in time and maybe, just maybe, you'll be able to set up one ambush from concealment. How does an ambush work? You launch a grenade at a cell of enemies while everyone else is in overwatch. The grenade deals 3 damages and the other 3 squad members whiff their overwatch shots. That is how concealment works.
Also, getting back to grenades. This game is also 3 Damage Grenade Simulator 2016. Want your guys to use their guns? Sure, do it for keks as they whiff it 70% of the time. Go ahead and park one of your rangers with a shotgun one cell away from an enemy and watch them fire it into the air like an anti aircraft gun. I'm not talking about the first couple of missions, I'm 15 hours into the game at the time of this writing. You want to actually hit something, you have to use a grenade. Your guns are basically just for show with the exception of snipers. Oh snipers? I'm not referring to their sniper rifle, I'm referring to their pistol special abilities. Have fun doing 2 damage with that.
Let's say you get lucky and get a mission that gives you 14 whole turns on the timer. You sprint your guys into position and manage to set up a nice little ambush for that sectoid and 2 grunts. No big deal, grenade should deal with the grunts and an entire turn of follow up shots at point blank range from you autist soldiers should just barely manage to hit it one time and kill it. Good plan right? Behold as two more cells containing nothing but 3 sectoids each becomes alerted, and now it’s your four blind mice against 7 sectoids. For the uninitiated, sectoids are psychic grey alien lookalikes that have mind control and debuff psychic abilities. Each one of them can use their abilities to disorient your troopers (reduce hit chance even more), cause them to panic (they explode a loaf in their pants and run from the battle), or MIND CONTROL!!! (they take control of one of your soldiers and turn it against you).
So now you've got the new rookie puking his guts out panicked in a corner, your ranger is disoriented and is more likely to shoot her own foot off than hit the sectoid in half cover 4 blocks away, your sniper on top of the building is now lining up the rookie for a headshot (he'll actually hit it, now that the enemy controls him), and the one rookie you have left has a 40% (0%) chance of hitting one sectoid with full health (you won't be able to kill it even if you do hit it). Game over.
Maybe we should try something different. Bam. I got it. I have a ranger that by some miracle survived a mission or two because using her sword was the only option I had to kill anything once the squad ran out of grenades. She stays concealed when my other dudes start firing, so I'll bring the squad up one side of the map, initiate combat and then sneak the ranger around the other side to hack the objective. Good plan right? Great plan, except that every single objective has at least one enemy cell parked right on top of it. There is no objective in the game that a muton is not using as a suppository. Your ranger isn't sneaking up to anything. But at least it's a flanking maneuver right? You can pincer that cell and get the objective? Nope, time counter, and your soldiers can't hit the broad side of a barn. Even if you manage to take the enemies out, you won’t be able hack the objective / exfiltrate with the person/thing.
But at least the game looks good and performs well, right? It's a PC exclusive! The game looks fine, not great, and runs like liquefied dog excrement down the slopes of a glacier. Behold as an unreal engine 3 game (engine is 15 years old, not exactly obscure) runs between 20 and 30fps regardless of what video card you're running. If you don't initially have a seizure from watching all the framerate drops, you might be able to enable SLI. I mean, the game didn't launch with SLI (PC exclusive?), but as of yesterday you can really jack up performance by enabling SLI. Boom, 60fps at 4k. Awesome! Except enabling SLI somehow disables cover indicators in the game. Yep, that's right. Enable SLI and you will have to guess whether your soldiers are in half or full cover because SLI for some unknown reason removes cover indicators. Neat!
TL:DR
Turn limits on every mission ruin your ability to move carefully, meaning 1 or 2 guys on your squad will end up dead. Your soldiers truly cannot hit a thing. Concealment doesn't work, your soldiers can't set an ambush if they can't hit anything from overwatch. Grenades are the only reliable way to hit anything in the game. Extreme balancing issues with legions of sectoids controlling or panicking your entire squad. Performance issues bordering on comical, SLI removes cover indicators from the game.
This isn't XCOM. I'd say hold onto your money until they fix it, but I don't see how they can do it.

TL:DR
I'd give it a "maybe" if I could. If you liked the tactical combat of XCOM: EU/EW, you'll probably like the sequel, but you may want to wait for a sale.
Pros:
+ The tactical combat we all love is back, albeit with some minor issues/inconsistencies.
+ Steam workshop support. There are some "required" mods out there you may want to install before your first playthrough.
+ Destructible environment. See an alien standing on a roof? Take out the floor beneath it and watch it fall to its death. I wish every game would give me the option of levelling a... level... to complete a mission.
Cons:
- It seems short. I logged about 40 hours in my first playthrough, but a lot of that was afk waiting for the long load times, waiting for the inane tactical pauses (check out the "Stop Wasting My Time" mod in the workshop), and waiting for Central's 8578965786th complaint about a civilian death. With mods applied to get rid of most of these annoyances (note: most, not all), I think you can expect about 30 hours to completion.
- No more shooting down UFOs. I know, wtf, right? You're given a customized alien craft as a base and you can't even use it against them. HUGE disappointment.
- No more capturing live aliens. Even though you can mind control and hack them in a mission. Once that mission is over they're gone.
- Scientists. There's nothing for them to do in the latter half of the game. $%^*in freeloaders.
- Timed missions. 8-12 turns to rescue/capture/kill a VIP, stop a transmission, or recover data before you're forced to retreat, whether or not you started the mission in concealment (i.e. the aliens don't know you're there). There is a mod to address this.
- The whole game is on a timer. It makes sense given the lore, but I don't like being railroaded. There's no time to play with different squad compositions, or different abilities.

He was my little hero, and I fell in love with the aesthetics of the crash site.  I again was immursed with the soundtrack, and loved the bright and colorful environment.  It felt open, I was free.  Free to do what?  Hell if I knew, but this felt so good.
I can't help but wonder what went so wrong with this little gem.  All I see now are costumes and reasons to invest realworld money in the game.  I want those days back.  That's our society, isn't it?  The constant wanting of our innocence, but nobody can grant these things.
I was around 400 hours in and it was 2012.  I miss these days, Crimsonhammer was just released.  People complained of how OP the new weapons were.  Me?  Oh, I couldn't have cared less of which weapon was the best, I had my jolly little brigade, and we would delve into T2 of the clockworks, using the last of our Mist Energy on a single revive, as the living would desperately sprint from body to body, awakening our corpses to fight again.
This is not to say I didn't care of Crimsonhammer, but I had my little brigade, and I was content.  The grind was beautiful, and I could play this game forever, fighting my favorite boss, Roarmulus.  I never understood why nobody seemed to like these two.  In my messed up head, they were so beautiful.  I couldn't help but grind them, not because I had built solid Elemental Damage, but because my Fireburst Brandish had an itching for cogs that I was too eager to fulfill.
I specifically remember a conversation at the end of the T2 clockworks with some knight who had been a tremendous joy to delve with.  We would go back and forth for what must have been half an hour, discussing our experiences and dissapointments with Spiral Knight's blatant abandonment of F2P players (Crimsonhammer) (I was still F2P).
I really don't want to continue, the more I type, the more I remember.  My point is that this game holds tremendous sentimental value, but nothing I can say will ever change its longevity.
That little brigade and I went our seperate ways.  I only have contact with one, and he and I have become more distant with each passing week; I guess it really hurts that I never said goodbye to any of them.  I just dissapeared and my young mind was attracted to newer and
games.
This has been something looming over my head for around 2 years now, and I couldn't imagine a better time to look back and remember the past.  This is the season to be thankful.

I really want to like this game.
I will preface this by saying all my experience in the game is in Team Deathmatch, because that what interests me most. Call me a casual, that's just me.
God d*mn, is this game frustrating. There's a lot to like here. The gunplay is excellent, and the monetization scheme seems fair, as well as completely optional. The fatal flaw of this game, is the map design. The maps are way too small for an 8v8 Deathmatch, and they are designed like meat grinders. Sure, you have your three main alleys, like most modern shooters and MOBAs today, but they are so isolated from one another that you just end with a stalemate on one end of each lane.
Every map seems to have a long, straight hallway of some sort, that inevitably gets dominated by 1-3 people with sniper rifles. All of the other lanes are the same story, just with shorter range weapons like assault rifles and smgs. It feels extraordinaly snowbally, and flanking routes are placed poorly, if at all. There are also bizarre choke points, like on the boat map, where every single lane can be covered from 2 points. This would maybe be acceptable if those two points weren't on the same side of the map.
Honestly, I'm only giving this game a thumbs up because I think it has potential. As it stands though, the maps are just awful. I still have some risidual desire to play this game because of the tight gunplay, but I can say for certain, that interest is going to get progressively smaller every time I launch up the game because of the map design alone.

This is so stupid. It's even more stupid than Goat Simulator. But you know what? I personally believe gaming needs these kinds of games. They're fresh, interesting as hell, and super fun. Not to mention, stupid funny. Surgeon Simulator is built to challenge your (virtual) hand-eye coordination and dexterity with a keyboard and mouse. I Am Bread takes this a mile further.
It's very challenging to control the bread at first. As you play more nad more, it begins to become second nature, much like controlling the fingers on Surgeon Simulator. I Am Bread challenges your coordination in order to take control of the slice of bread.
I haven't tried this game with a gamepad, but I imagine it would be a bit easier with a gamepad. The keyboard and mosue work fine, but it is a great challenge at first. For users who are not as used to using a keyboard and mouse as dedicated PC users and veteran PC gamers, this game would be even more challenging to get the hang of.
I Am Bread is challenging, stupid, and fun. That's what gaming needs, in my opinion. The creative freedom of games like Goat Simulator, Surgeon Simulator and I Am Bread is a much needed breath of fresh air and an enjoyable step away from super serious titles like Assassin's Creed, Borderlands, and other really serious titles.

Story:

- New enemy types (turrets, robots)
Cons:
- Graphical glitches (soldiers movements, actions)

- Sometimes unfair enemy actions (for example, when an enemy soldier runs through half of the map and kill one of your soldier, then runs to cover...)

But nonetheless, I loved the game, just as I loved the previous XCOMs:

Harsh, unyielding, unforgiving, unfriendly and unapologizing for any of those.
Right off the bat, game makes it clear this is not your tabletop RPG, and goes to great lengths to crush every single staple you had come to rely on:
-You were used to a ton of items that heal anything from bleed to malaria? Bam, inventory is limited and expensive
-You were used to topping off party in between battles? Tough luck, skills are unusable out of combat
-Used to leaving a harmless fellow to top off party? Reinforcements come if you take too long to dispatch something
-Had a gold party and formation? Well crap, enemies vary, and heroes that excel in one dungeon, can be useless in another
You can't reload a save if a hero dies, there's no phoenix down to bring them back, your golden armada will outgrow their peers and refuse to explore with them in a dungeon below their expertise, and your best heroes will either need to stay behind in between quests to recover, or risk losing their mind from stress.
If you're ok with all of that, and looking for a true roguelike the way it used to be, Darkest Dungeon is the game for you. You can't let your guard down ever, as even small enemies can present a big threat to a recovering party. Leveling up does not warantee success against those either, and can be detrimental if you don't have the gold to upgrade your heroes' gear and skills, and gold will always be in short supply, barely enough to pay for the supplies and the stress relief a hero or two will need after.
Gameplay's challenging, well structured and damn addictive, history is just compelling enough to get you hooked, but honestly not the main reason to play, but the playstyle, immersion and unforgiveness is what keeps you hooked. Graphics are actually a big plus, and I don't think this would have benefited from a powerful graphics engine at all, art is what it should be and changing it would be heressy, period.
9.5/10 would definitvely be a 10 with a better history and more tidbits of information in between dungeons (history scraps are ridiculously rare and not that cool)

Darkest Dungeon is, for my personal opinion, an amazing game which is looking for it's kind.
From the beginning where you get your first two Heroes, you will get caught in the dread
atmosphere. You will be visiting places like a swamp, the ruins and in the end the Darkest Dungeon itself, facing enemys like skeletons, diseased pigs, rotten fish and bandits on the way. You will recruit new Heroes, improving their skills, upgrade their equipment, give them a name just to feel miserable when you are losing them to death's icy grip because you choose to stay in the place for it may hold even more rich loot.
There are many options and combinations for your team. You can experiment of which hero fits in with another.
For certain bosses while progressing you will have to find out the most efficient strategy so you will be able to beat them without great casualties.
There are 15 heroes recruitable at the moment. All of them come with unique combat and camping skills.
Another problem you will be facing is the amount of stress your heroes will accumulate during their exploration.
At a certain amount of stress, the heroes will be afflicted with a random negative affliction, which will "debuff" him and the others as well. But there is a chance that this affliction will become a positive one, reducing the amount of stress  and giving some perks, dependend on which affliction.
While not adventuring you are able to upgrade your facilities, upgrade the skills and equipment of your heroes as well as upgrade the facilities itself, which helps a lot. You can reduce the amount you have to pay for services as well as getting access to higher tier upgrades, increasing the amount of stress healed from certain activities and increasing the roster of heroes you can have at a time.
Of course the game has its downsides. The locations you will be visiting over and over again will feel repetitive at some point to some people. Or it can become frustrating losing your high end heroes to some random occastion. I mean you can even mourn on their graves by visiting the graveyard. You will fight some bosses and later on the same bosses upgraded with more variety and tools to make your life miserable. Though this may feel like "Whoa.. only so few bosses WOW" I can assure you will feel the difference and the increase of difficulty set in the upgraded versions.
Personally I would recommend Darkest Dungeon to anyone who is willed to take on a challenge, like rogue like games with a perma death system, a selection of 15 heroes to send to the hells near and in the Darkest Dungeon.

Personal Account:
An excellent turn-based, rogue-like, rpg, strategy game with a profound aesthetic and narrative. The game has a dark and insidious lovecraftian quality to it that creates a very immersive experience. In this game you learn of a tragic tale that has befallen a once prominent family, and now as the heirs to the manor, you must assemble the finest combatants in the land to reclaim your home.
Aesthetics:
This game has a fantastically grim and dark narrative. It's gritty and raw and there is a sense of hopelessness that is endearing. The visuals including the art style and animations are smoothe and satisfying. The sound effects, ambience, and music, are a huge part of this game, and really are what I would describe as the icing on the cake to push the game that much further.
Gameplay:
I've found that the largest criticism for the game is that it is either very grindy, or that it is very difficult, or some combination of the two. Personally I felt as though the game wasn't too difficult. Did it hold your hand and make you feel good? No it didn't. Was it unfair in it's gameplay, or not upfront about what the game is?  It most certainly wasn't. This game makes it very clear that you must choose your battles wisely. You must retreat to fight another day. You must play with caution. If you believe you can waltz in open every chest you encounter, kill every monster you fight, and not ever have a death for doing so, then you are going about it incorrectly. I can't speak much to the grindy nature of the game as I've played a little bit but not enough. I can say at this point I've only played about 17 hours, and I'm still having a ton of fun.
The game features various systems that are intriguing and bring a new experience to the table, such as the stress, and quirks that are associated with playable characters. Cons:
My only thing I can see as a negative in my opinion is eventually it may become grindy, although I'm not sure when that will be. Also I will be sad when most of the content is finished and will be craving more. But if your only complaints are that you want more of the game, then I think as a developer you're pretty well-off.
Overall:
If you like dark fantasy, RPG, or strategy games. I would give this one a go.

Fallout 4 is by all accounts a very mediocre game.
Playing through the game for the first time you will be thrust into a interactive cutscene prewar were you run to the vault followed by a family you never got time to care about, seeing people you've never met argue on the road and watch a world you know nothing about blow up in the distance.
You are then cryogenically frozen for a undetermined amount of time, only to wake up long enough to see the baby you looked at once to be stolen in front of your eyes and the spouse you talked to twice get shot by the kidnapper.
You are then after getting refrozen and rethawed expected to be invested enough in the story to chase after the kidnapper and rescue your baby.
so you go out into the Commonwealth, a ruined city were the quests are all the same, the enemies don't matter and all the "Dungeons" were copypasted.
You will then go through dialogue wheel after dialogue wheel were every answer is the same, you will build a town that doesn't tie into the rest of the game (seriously, you don't get anything out of building a settlement, you might as well just put down a bedroll, crafting stations and then forget about it) using the first person camera to place structures with illogical collision boxes.
This game has a arena with a finished questline, voices that lets you bet on fights and even fight in the arena yourself. except it was cut for no reason and a modder had to bring it back in, if you go to the arena in the unmodded game you just get shot at by more raiders.
This seems to be a recurring theme in the places you go, there's a crashed ship with people seeming to be descended from norweghian sailors in a corner of the map; your only form of interaction with them is by shooting them all.
There is a area that's set up to looking like a racing arena, but the only interaction with it is to shoot all the raiders that live there.

Another thing to point out that every time the Creation Club updates all owners of Fallout 4 download all the mods, even if they don't buy them or ever intend to buy them, this breaks all the already existing mods and forces them to update, unless bethesda fixes this the modding community will have to rush a fix every time Creation Club forces bloatware down your router.

I first played this game back in 2013 and have had many ups and downs with it.
The game is absolutely fun to play, and I've put in many hours into it (don't be fooled by my counter, I've played a lot longer on a different client).  The community is also decent too. Most people tend to solo most of the levels, but not everyone's a snob either. For the community experience, it's definitely worth checking out.
Gameplay-wise, it's a typical grind game, especially if you want to get items called Orbs of Alchemy, which are essential to leveling up equipment and even yourself. It can get tedious, but it's necessary. Or you can buy items through microtransactions, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, in fact they even have a really innovative system for converting standerd in-game money for the premium currency, which is absolutely awesome, I wish more games had a similar system.
There are only two things I dislike about the game in general:
1) Not a whole lot of players. There used to be thousands of active players, making guilds a fun thing to join, though being expensive to maintain. But as it's began to dip out of popularity, the player-base has slumped considerably, mostly populated by seasoned pvpers and pve-ers. And the reason for this is in my next point.
2) Lack of major updates. Major updates are far and in-between, sometimes lasting a whole year before OOO, the people who run the game (not Sega), release something meaningful. In fact, between 2013 and 2015, only two major updates were made: the gunner update, and extra Vanguard (max level) missions. They do have events, but they barely last a week before you have to wait 9-12 months for it to come around again.
Other than those, this game is rather promising. If only the developers put more effort into releasing quality content, instead of releasing costume designs (much like how TF2 releases hats on a constant basis), then I wouldn't have a huge issue with my last point, but the fact is OOO is really lazy when it comes to updates, so expect to have a long period of time pass before you're able to see new content.
Based on my observations, I give this game a 7.5/10.

It's finally here, the anticipated sequel to 2012's (has it already been that long?) Enemy Unknown, and its subsequent expansion pack, Enemy Within. In many ways it is exactly the sort of sequel you would expect from developer Firaxis in recent years: It is safe, sometimes overly so, and doesn't venture far from the footsteps of its predecessor. This can work to its benefit at some times, and at others leave players questioning the developer's choices.
First, the graphics received a much-needed overhaul. Characters are rendered quite well, and environments and effects are top-knotch, at least as far as turn-based strategy games are concerned. Unfortunately, the quality of the visuals are beset by unusual slowdown. While the game can be graphically impressive, attempting to run the game at higher settings with even the most expensive gaming rigs will bring FPS well below 60. Fortunately for the game graphics are not wholly integral to the experience, but they are not the last problem this game has.
The soundtrack is to be expected. You will become woefully annoyed by the Avenger's bgm, as with many of the other tunes that play throughout the game. There is some improvement on variety, and I'll admit I found myself getting pumped at some points when the music went along well.
The gameplay, obviously the meat of the game, is quite similar to its predecessors. The player is tasked with assembling a team of rag-tag alien-killers and move through a campaign, killing aliens by the dozens and researching technologies to better kill aliens by the dozens. Most notably, the game's XCOM organization is no longer tethered to a single, secretive underground base. Instead, the entire group is housed inside of the Avenger, a repurposed alien ship that flies from continent to continent in search of missions and resources to meet goals.
This can be a positive and negative aspect to the game. Whereas before there was a variety to base layout, with careful management of adjacency bonuses, players now instead have a very small number of facilities which are placed (with small exceptions) in any area of the ship the player wishes. The player has to remove old structures from the ship and recycle them for parts before they install new rooms, which is likely intended to give the feeling of constructing a base in the same way the original did, but it mostly falls flat.
In addition, the Avenger's mobility isn't used to great effect. While the player can move from location to location while following leads or searching for other resistance fighters, it ultimately feels entirely similar to the first game. Sure, there is an event wherein the Avenger can be shot down and invaded, much in the same way the base was invaded in the original, but it is an equally rare event and a poor thing to build the game around. In the end, the constant moving from place to place feels more like a time-waster than a gameplay innovation.
One of the key differentiations from EU/EW lies in XCOM 2's character-building. First and foremost, character trees have been strictly delineated into 2 separate trees. For example, the Sharpshooter class is divided into a Sniper and Gunslinger tree, with skills on each made with that specific sub-class in mind. There are always exceptions where a player may feel this or that ability is strictly inferior to another, but this title has made greater effort to simply divide classes into more distinct roles.
Like its forebears, XCOM 2 makes gratuitous use of research and production to fight the alien menace. The player will gather resources and conduct missions, improve their squads, and produce newer, deadlier equipment to better survive and finish objectives. There is a similar level of gradation in technology levels, i.e. Ballistics --> Laser --> Plasma, with the game's new Magnetic weapons technology taking the place of laser technology for some baffling reason. Players returning from EW will be sad to learn that the game's two notable inclusions, MECs and gene mods, are missing. In their place powered armor and a reworked psi-training system somewhat emulate these gameplay facets, but do so in a poor fashion.
The game can be, much like the rest of the series, quite frustrating. Breaking away from its predecessors, XCOM 2 can be quite difficult even in the first stretches of the game. Moreso than before, combat is quite lethal. Even with lategame armor and equipment, two well-placed shots from an opponent will leave the character in dire need for medical attention. And because XCOM 2 calcuates wounds on a much harsher system, characters will be judged as gravely wounded much, much more often. Much as in the previous titles facilities can be built to reduce time on the bench, but not until some time into the game.
And while it can be lethal for the player's characters, it is anything but for most aliens. Players are greeted by familiar sectoids at the outset of the game, but in the twenty years that have passed, it appears they have taken to lifting. Gifted with a plethora of psi attacks to disorient characters and revive dead enemies, these aliens are no longer susceptible to a simple grenade. Instead, players must devote a considerable amount of firepower in their direction to defeat them.
And it's not just sectoids: Virtually any non-grunt alien enemy will require more than a shot to kill with most weaponry, even at the end of the game. In addition, the game makes use of a new mechanic known as Dodge. Working in a similar way to conventional Aim vs. Defense mechanics, if a random number rolled is below the Dodge stat the damage taken is heavily reduced. It can be an incredible annoyance to flank an enemy with a charging shotgun blast with a 100% hit chance, only to have them dodge the attack anyways, receiving 2 damage instead of 12.
In the end, the game is as much an addictive romp as its two predecessors. While the ways in which it attempts to innovate can fall flat, and its poor optimization can lead to a severe drop in performance, it is an altogether enjoyable game. Much like other Firaxis titles, however, the game feels incomplete.  With a much needed companion in the form of a Terror From the Deep expansion, and with a good patch to fix graphical issues, I am sure the game will feel every bit a match for the series it draws its name. Until then, it is simply good instead of great.

Harsh, unyielding, unforgiving, unfriendly and unapologizing for any of those.
Right off the bat, game makes it clear this is not your tabletop RPG, and goes to great lengths to crush every single staple you had come to rely on:
-You were used to a ton of items that heal anything from bleed to malaria? Bam, inventory is limited and expensive
-You were used to topping off party in between battles? Tough luck, skills are unusable out of combat
-Used to leaving a harmless fellow to top off party? Reinforcements come if you take too long to dispatch something
-Had a gold party and formation? Well crap, enemies vary, and heroes that excel in one dungeon, can be useless in another
You can't reload a save if a hero dies, there's no phoenix down to bring them back, your golden armada will outgrow their peers and refuse to explore with them in a dungeon below their expertise, and your best heroes will either need to stay behind in between quests to recover, or risk losing their mind from stress.
If you're ok with all of that, and looking for a true roguelike the way it used to be, Darkest Dungeon is the game for you. You can't let your guard down ever, as even small enemies can present a big threat to a recovering party. Leveling up does not warantee success against those either, and can be detrimental if you don't have the gold to upgrade your heroes' gear and skills, and gold will always be in short supply, barely enough to pay for the supplies and the stress relief a hero or two will need after.
Gameplay's challenging, well structured and damn addictive, history is just compelling enough to get you hooked, but honestly not the main reason to play, but the playstyle, immersion and unforgiveness is what keeps you hooked. Graphics are actually a big plus, and I don't think this would have benefited from a powerful graphics engine at all, art is what it should be and changing it would be heressy, period.
9.5/10 would definitvely be a 10 with a better history and more tidbits of information in between dungeons (history scraps are ridiculously rare and not that cool)

In Starbound, you take on the role of a character who’s just fled from their home planet, only to crash-land on another. From there you’ll embark on a quest to survive, discover, explore and fight your way across an infinite universe.

You’ll encounter procedurally generated creatures and weapons, discover populated villages and abandoned temples. Explore planets dotted with dungeons, eyeball trees and treasure. Make use of over a hundred materials and over one thousand in-game objects to build a sprawling modern metropolis or a sleepy secluded cabin in the woods, and do all of it alone or with friends!
Starbound lets you live out your own story of space exploration, discovery and adventure. Settle down and farm the land, hop from planet to planet claiming resources, or make regular visits to populated settlements, taking on jobs and earning a living. NPCs are scattered about the worlds, offering quests and challenges for those looking for a little extra excitement in their lives.

While still in early beta, Starbound has a good amount of content going for it and has a lot planned.  Starting out can be a bit rough, but the handful of starter quests help give the player some direction.  Part of the difficulty, as well as part of the fun, is figuring out which monsters are friendly and which are hostile on each planet you travel to before they decide to maul you.  The monster generator can create a wide variety of creatures and they can be neutral or hostile and you won't know until you're almost in melee range.  Aside from blood thirsty monsters, cultists, and angered guards, there are other threats to one's safety as you travel the galaxy, these being environmental hazards (acid rain, pools of poison, traps in dungeons to name a few), the ever present threat of starvation, the need to be adequately prepared for oxygenless worlds, and the danger of simply freezing to death.  With so much trying to kill you, there's usually something you can be doing to stay alive.
Along side the official content that's in the game already, the developers have made it extremely easy to add (and to an extent make) mods to the game.  This brings the amount of content to another level entirely as there is an active community  thinking up and making mods that can be downloaded from Starbound's mods forum and the Nexus websites.
I do recommend this game if you've enjoyed Terraria and/or Minecraft, but only if you are willing to put up with the occasional bug due to still being in beta (and stay away from the unstable/extra beta builds) though the stable builds are a safer bet if you're game.

This game is definitely playable, I get 60 fps on max settings (with FXAA and no v-sync) and performance is pretty good. I have a 4790k and 390, so I'd say I'm suited for good performance. Some of these people must be playing at too demanding settings for their rigs or their particulary rig is not well suited for the game. Decent optimization, nothing terrible, but it's not super smooth all the time. There are occasional dips but usually while loading a mission (SECRET: press cap lock to speed up the process of the long load time in the mission loading screen) and when you first arrive at a mission, but gameplay wise it seems to be just fine. There are bugs, none that are game breaking in my playthroughs, but they are a bit strange and take out you out of the experience (ex. screen randomly goes black during enemy turn while UI is still on, clipping through walls/objects, shooting targets directly and bullets go STRAIGHT THROUGH THEM WITH NO DAMAGE.) With all of these things in mind, the game is still excellent. It is more difficult than Enemy Unknown (I had to restart the first mission so many times, so I would definitely recommend starting out on rookie.) It's better than it's predecessor as it's more XCOM in new exciting ways. Customization is more personal now, though I wish there could have been more English with accents and a lot more faces (or sliders so we could do it ourselves.) At it's core, it's improved the XCOM formula and made pleased to be playing XCOM again after the first one got a bit stale (after 90 hours w/ Enemy Within.)  I highly recommend it.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown successfully revived an old, mishandled series by taking the core of what made the classics so great and boiling it down into a much more accessible formula. This reboot did a good job of gently introducing its ideas and mechanics while retaining the challenge that is part of the series’ identity. If XCOM: Enemy Unknown and its expansion were a well-oiled but slightly drab machine, XCOM 2 is a relative fire-spewing monster truck that could do with a good deal of repairs. Tons of changes that seem relatively small by themselves add up to make XCOM 2 a significantly different and more daunting game, and while many of these changes hit their mark, others go a bit wide, and the entire experience is hampered by persistent technical issues.

Harsh, unyielding, unforgiving, unfriendly and unapologizing for any of those.
Right off the bat, game makes it clear this is not your tabletop RPG, and goes to great lengths to crush every single staple you had come to rely on:
-You were used to a ton of items that heal anything from bleed to malaria? Bam, inventory is limited and expensive
-You were used to topping off party in between battles? Tough luck, skills are unusable out of combat
-Used to leaving a harmless fellow to top off party? Reinforcements come if you take too long to dispatch something
-Had a gold party and formation? Well crap, enemies vary, and heroes that excel in one dungeon, can be useless in another
You can't reload a save if a hero dies, there's no phoenix down to bring them back, your golden armada will outgrow their peers and refuse to explore with them in a dungeon below their expertise, and your best heroes will either need to stay behind in between quests to recover, or risk losing their mind from stress.
If you're ok with all of that, and looking for a true roguelike the way it used to be, Darkest Dungeon is the game for you. You can't let your guard down ever, as even small enemies can present a big threat to a recovering party. Leveling up does not warantee success against those either, and can be detrimental if you don't have the gold to upgrade your heroes' gear and skills, and gold will always be in short supply, barely enough to pay for the supplies and the stress relief a hero or two will need after.
Gameplay's challenging, well structured and damn addictive, history is just compelling enough to get you hooked, but honestly not the main reason to play, but the playstyle, immersion and unforgiveness is what keeps you hooked. Graphics are actually a big plus, and I don't think this would have benefited from a powerful graphics engine at all, art is what it should be and changing it would be heressy, period.
9.5/10 would definitvely be a 10 with a better history and more tidbits of information in between dungeons (history scraps are ridiculously rare and not that cool)

I've played Spiral Knights on and off over the past 4 years, and unlike most other people who have a lot of time in it, like I do, I'm going to recommend Spiral Knights. Hear me out, for a bit, and I'll tell you why.
Let me just give a few pros:
+Amazing soundtrack
+Great art style
+Gameplay itself is really fun.
Now let's list the cons.
-Grindy. And when I say grindy, I mean REALLY grindy.
-"P2W"
You might be wondering to yourself, "Why did you put P2W in quotes?" I'll tell you exactly why: P2W stands for Pay to  Win, which implies you really can't progress unless you pay real money. You ABSOLUTELY can play without putting single cent it: Sure, it's gonna take forever, but you really don't have to pay. As for the grinding, grinding is a bit of a staple for f2p mmorpgs. I'm not saying it's in all of them, but it usually is. Sure, Spiral Knights has a ton of grinding: but the pay out of finally being able to upgrade your equipment is oh-so satisfying.
Overall, I would totally recommend this game. Definitely worth a shot, if you're willing to put the time into it.

Great game - Firaxis continues their evolution of the X-Com franchise.
X-Com Reboot and Enemy Unknown were a blast that brought back the stategic gameplay style of the original, but made it a little more pliable to today's gameplay.   X-Com 2 takes it a step further introducing the Avenger roaming base, and a few streamlined adjustments that makes it just fascinating enough to keep trying one more battle, but not different enough to really cause major issues.
There are some turn limitations, but they make sense from a story standpoint, and really are not a serious issue.   I came close only once or twice to running out (although I did end up leaving a soldier or two behind).   In the end, though, it tells a good story, provides incredibly rewarding turn-based strategy, and looks great doing it.
I didn't build laboratories or workshops and it didn't affect me, I rushed the main storyline, and then realized I probably should build the network and all, but like most X-Com games it takes some time to get the hang of it, and towards the end I had plenty of funds and intel to keep the aliens in line and ramp up the end game as best as possible.
I would suggest pushing for psionics a little earlier, I started toward late-to-end game, and just really had one Magus (which worked fine, but would have been fun to have a large number of them on the field).  I wish the Psionists would "level up" like normal soldiers, but they only rank up through training.
I liked the Proving Grounds approach of random items and separation of engineering items, but I didn't use a wide selection.  I still don't see a big deal for bluescreen ammo (vs. robots) since you can't select when to use ammo, and inventory is limited.   Battle scanner would probably be vital for Ironman mode (which I look forward to playing next), but isn't as useful as an acid bomb or proximity mine when it comes down to it.
Customizing the characters is fun, and I think my next playthrough I'll really focus on that.   I did like the little touches, like how your soldiers will automatically gain scars and burns after being wounded in fights.   The benefit of future technology, if you don't like it you can just customize them and remove it.  :)
The Rangers are incredible, and late in the game, I was able to use the Reaper mode to get about 5 kills in one turn.   Psionists can be game-changed, especially with mind controller, specialists are good at hacking, but primarily healers in my squads (I didn't care for the limitations of their combat droid lines).
But Grenadiers with Salvo (explosives as first move don't end turn), and the explosive specialty where they get two grenades in their grenade-only slot (very fun with either acid or proximity mines - especially if you can find two groups clumped together while concealed), are only beaten by Snipers with pistol skills.
I carrier two Snipers on each mission, one focused on accuracy and long distance, and one focused on pistol skills.   Nine times out of ten, my pistol-focused Sniper with Lightning Reflexes (free pistol shot), Quick Draw (first pistol shot doesn't end the turn), and Fan Fire (three pistols shots at target) was the lifesaver and highest scoring kills of my group.
Give your pistol user armor piercing ammo and you'll be amazed at what a plasma pistol can do!
Maybe we'll see an Expansion or X-Com 3 reboot of Terror From The Deep!   Which is a concept that would greatly benefit from Firaxis incredibly reboots!

In Starbound, you take on the role of a character who’s just fled from their home planet, only to crash-land on another. From there you’ll embark on a quest to survive, discover, explore and fight your way across an infinite universe.

You’ll encounter procedurally generated creatures and weapons, discover populated villages and abandoned temples. Explore planets dotted with dungeons, eyeball trees and treasure. Make use of over a hundred materials and over one thousand in-game objects to build a sprawling modern metropolis or a sleepy secluded cabin in the woods, and do all of it alone or with friends!
Starbound lets you live out your own story of space exploration, discovery and adventure. Settle down and farm the land, hop from planet to planet claiming resources, or make regular visits to populated settlements, taking on jobs and earning a living. NPCs are scattered about the worlds, offering quests and challenges for those looking for a little extra excitement in their lives.

While still in early beta, Starbound has a good amount of content going for it and has a lot planned.  Starting out can be a bit rough, but the handful of starter quests help give the player some direction.  Part of the difficulty, as well as part of the fun, is figuring out which monsters are friendly and which are hostile on each planet you travel to before they decide to maul you.  The monster generator can create a wide variety of creatures and they can be neutral or hostile and you won't know until you're almost in melee range.  Aside from blood thirsty monsters, cultists, and angered guards, there are other threats to one's safety as you travel the galaxy, these being environmental hazards (acid rain, pools of poison, traps in dungeons to name a few), the ever present threat of starvation, the need to be adequately prepared for oxygenless worlds, and the danger of simply freezing to death.  With so much trying to kill you, there's usually something you can be doing to stay alive.
Along side the official content that's in the game already, the developers have made it extremely easy to add (and to an extent make) mods to the game.  This brings the amount of content to another level entirely as there is an active community  thinking up and making mods that can be downloaded from Starbound's mods forum and the Nexus websites.
I do recommend this game if you've enjoyed Terraria and/or Minecraft, but only if you are willing to put up with the occasional bug due to still being in beta (and stay away from the unstable/extra beta builds) though the stable builds are a safer bet if you're game.

Fallout 4 is by all accounts a very mediocre game.
Playing through the game for the first time you will be thrust into a interactive cutscene prewar were you run to the vault followed by a family you never got time to care about, seeing people you've never met argue on the road and watch a world you know nothing about blow up in the distance.
You are then cryogenically frozen for a undetermined amount of time, only to wake up long enough to see the baby you looked at once to be stolen in front of your eyes and the spouse you talked to twice get shot by the kidnapper.
You are then after getting refrozen and rethawed expected to be invested enough in the story to chase after the kidnapper and rescue your baby.
so you go out into the Commonwealth, a ruined city were the quests are all the same, the enemies don't matter and all the "Dungeons" were copypasted.
You will then go through dialogue wheel after dialogue wheel were every answer is the same, you will build a town that doesn't tie into the rest of the game (seriously, you don't get anything out of building a settlement, you might as well just put down a bedroll, crafting stations and then forget about it) using the first person camera to place structures with illogical collision boxes.
This game has a arena with a finished questline, voices that lets you bet on fights and even fight in the arena yourself. except it was cut for no reason and a modder had to bring it back in, if you go to the arena in the unmodded game you just get shot at by more raiders.
This seems to be a recurring theme in the places you go, there's a crashed ship with people seeming to be descended from norweghian sailors in a corner of the map; your only form of interaction with them is by shooting them all.
There is a area that's set up to looking like a racing arena, but the only interaction with it is to shoot all the raiders that live there.
There is a lot of things wrong about this game, the only thing good I can say about it is that the gunplay is somewhat better than Fallout 3, but that's not saying much.
And then ofcourse there is the reason I'm writing this review now, the Creation Club, paid mods, I'm not as opposed to this as many others, I feel that it is a opportunity for good modders to create expansion sized content for the games with backing from bethesda, but if bethesda can't even quality control its own game, which even to today have severe LOD bugs in some areas, then why am I to expect them to quality check the mods they sell?
Another thing to point out that every time the Creation Club updates all owners of Fallout 4 download all the mods, even if they don't buy them or ever intend to buy them, this breaks all the already existing mods and forces them to update, unless bethesda fixes this the modding community will have to rush a fix every time Creation Club forces bloatware down your router.

Great game - Firaxis continues their evolution of the X-Com franchise.
X-Com Reboot and Enemy Unknown were a blast that brought back the stategic gameplay style of the original, but made it a little more pliable to today's gameplay.   X-Com 2 takes it a step further introducing the Avenger roaming base, and a few streamlined adjustments that makes it just fascinating enough to keep trying one more battle, but not different enough to really cause major issues.
There are some turn limitations, but they make sense from a story standpoint, and really are not a serious issue.   I came close only once or twice to running out (although I did end up leaving a soldier or two behind).   In the end, though, it tells a good story, provides incredibly rewarding turn-based strategy, and looks great doing it.
I didn't build laboratories or workshops and it didn't affect me, I rushed the main storyline, and then realized I probably should build the network and all, but like most X-Com games it takes some time to get the hang of it, and towards the end I had plenty of funds and intel to keep the aliens in line and ramp up the end game as best as possible.
I would suggest pushing for psionics a little earlier, I started toward late-to-end game, and just really had one Magus (which worked fine, but would have been fun to have a large number of them on the field).  I wish the Psionists would "level up" like normal soldiers, but they only rank up through training.
I liked the Proving Grounds approach of random items and separation of engineering items, but I didn't use a wide selection.  I still don't see a big deal for bluescreen ammo (vs. robots) since you can't select when to use ammo, and inventory is limited.   Battle scanner would probably be vital for Ironman mode (which I look forward to playing next), but isn't as useful as an acid bomb or proximity mine when it comes down to it.
Customizing the characters is fun, and I think my next playthrough I'll really focus on that.   I did like the little touches, like how your soldiers will automatically gain scars and burns after being wounded in fights.   The benefit of future technology, if you don't like it you can just customize them and remove it.  :)
The Rangers are incredible, and late in the game, I was able to use the Reaper mode to get about 5 kills in one turn.   Psionists can be game-changed, especially with mind controller, specialists are good at hacking, but primarily healers in my squads (I didn't care for the limitations of their combat droid lines).
But Grenadiers with Salvo (explosives as first move don't end turn), and the explosive specialty where they get two grenades in their grenade-only slot (very fun with either acid or proximity mines - especially if you can find two groups clumped together while concealed), are only beaten by Snipers with pistol skills.
I carrier two Snipers on each mission, one focused on accuracy and long distance, and one focused on pistol skills.   Nine times out of ten, my pistol-focused Sniper with Lightning Reflexes (free pistol shot), Quick Draw (first pistol shot doesn't end the turn), and Fan Fire (three pistols shots at target) was the lifesaver and highest scoring kills of my group.
Give your pistol user armor piercing ammo and you'll be amazed at what a plasma pistol can do!
Maybe we'll see an Expansion or X-Com 3 reboot of Terror From The Deep!   Which is a concept that would greatly benefit from Firaxis incredibly reboots!

Oh Darkest Dungeon, how I struggle to love thee.
Overall, this is a great game from a mechanics standpoint.  If you enjoy older Final Fantasy-styled RPG combat and some grind, it's tons of fun.  The classes are diverse and interesting, they synergize in ways that are extremely satisfying, and the resource management side of the game provides steady improvements to the experience even while the dungeons chew up characters.
My favorite features would probably be: class synergy and party building, the voice over narration of your tortured ancestor, and the camping /respite system in longer dungeons.   The latter is especially cool, but takes some time playing to really figure out and get the hang of.
But this is a brutal game.  I agree with many of the other reviews that ultimately don't recommend it -- the difficulty is tipped just a bit too far in favor of bad outcomes.  This is done by chance occurrences like crits and object interactions, causing you to have characters go from tip-top to dead or suffering from costly mental problems in a blink.  It definitely happens.  And it seems Red Hook means it to be this way.
Before pulling the trigger on this, I would ask you to consider: Do you only want games that make you feel like a badass, or is there room in your gaming experience for something that makes you as the player feel hopeless and doomed?  Darkest Dungeon is surely going for the latter.  You're never going to feel like you've reached a place where parties are safe.  In artistic terms, this game is a work of tragedy.  It's really not designed to make you feel on top of the world.  It's trying to evoke hopelessness and doom on some level, and it succeeds. Black Squad plays out like CSGO, except faster, with more weapons, attachments, and the ability to aim down sight. Basic mechanics like movement/quickswitching/inventory system, etc are almost identitcal to CSGO's. You run faster with your knife out and there is even a keybind for inspecting your weapon.
Pros:
+Shooting feels good. Kills feel satisfying and meaty. Aim and reaction time are rewarded.
+Extremely sniper-friendly. Sniper rifles are significantly more powerful than the AWP is in CSGO.
+Extremely well-optimized. 144hz supported.
+Very good graphics for a F2P game. Animations/textures/viewmodels are superb.
+Very player-friendly F2P model. Vast majority of ingame weapons are easily obtainable with normal currency.
+Decent maps. People complaining about the small maps are talking about the deathmatch maps.
+Wide set of options; decent built-in crosshair optimization.
+Multiple interesting and unique gamemodes. Defuse, VIP assassination, etc.
+Battleye anticheat is more robust than VAC.
+Pretty good netcode. Hit registration seems very solid.
Cons:
-Not enough weapons; they will surely keep adding weapons.
-Deathmatch maps are too small.
-Grenade physics/rental system are worse than CSGO's.
-No ranked competitive system; this may come in the future.
Play this game. It could easily be 15 dollars, but it's free.

Great game - Firaxis continues their evolution of the X-Com franchise.
X-Com Reboot and Enemy Unknown were a blast that brought back the stategic gameplay style of the original, but made it a little more pliable to today's gameplay.   X-Com 2 takes it a step further introducing the Avenger roaming base, and a few streamlined adjustments that makes it just fascinating enough to keep trying one more battle, but not different enough to really cause major issues.
There are some turn limitations, but they make sense from a story standpoint, and really are not a serious issue.   I came close only once or twice to running out (although I did end up leaving a soldier or two behind).   In the end, though, it tells a good story, provides incredibly rewarding turn-based strategy, and looks great doing it.
I didn't build laboratories or workshops and it didn't affect me, I rushed the main storyline, and then realized I probably should build the network and all, but like most X-Com games it takes some time to get the hang of it, and towards the end I had plenty of funds and intel to keep the aliens in line and ramp up the end game as best as possible.
I would suggest pushing for psionics a little earlier, I started toward late-to-end game, and just really had one Magus (which worked fine, but would have been fun to have a large number of them on the field).  I wish the Psionists would "level up" like normal soldiers, but they only rank up through training.
I liked the Proving Grounds approach of random items and separation of engineering items, but I didn't use a wide selection.  I still don't see a big deal for bluescreen ammo (vs. robots) since you can't select when to use ammo, and inventory is limited.   Battle scanner would probably be vital for Ironman mode (which I look forward to playing next), but isn't as useful as an acid bomb or proximity mine when it comes down to it.
Customizing the characters is fun, and I think my next playthrough I'll really focus on that.   I did like the little touches, like how your soldiers will automatically gain scars and burns after being wounded in fights.   The benefit of future technology, if you don't like it you can just customize them and remove it.  :)
The Rangers are incredible, and late in the game, I was able to use the Reaper mode to get about 5 kills in one turn.   Psionists can be game-changed, especially with mind controller, specialists are good at hacking, but primarily healers in my squads (I didn't care for the limitations of their combat droid lines).
But Grenadiers with Salvo (explosives as first move don't end turn), and the explosive specialty where they get two grenades in their grenade-only slot (very fun with either acid or proximity mines - especially if you can find two groups clumped together while concealed), are only beaten by Snipers with pistol skills.
I carrier two Snipers on each mission, one focused on accuracy and long distance, and one focused on pistol skills.   Nine times out of ten, my pistol-focused Sniper with Lightning Reflexes (free pistol shot), Quick Draw (first pistol shot doesn't end the turn), and Fan Fire (three pistols shots at target) was the lifesaver and highest scoring kills of my group.
Give your pistol user armor piercing ammo and you'll be amazed at what a plasma pistol can do!
Maybe we'll see an Expansion or X-Com 3 reboot of Terror From The Deep!   Which is a concept that would greatly benefit from Firaxis incredibly reboots!

Ok so... Let's try to be objective and leave aside events like, bethesda monetizing mods and that kind of crap... We all know they're greedy fckers (just like any other company in the world tbh).
The bad.
The game itself as a "FALLOUT GAME" fails at several points. There is so much wasted potential in this game, i really wish you had the option to be a mean son of a b*tch and also to be a mesiah... But you pretty much just have one choice which sucks because you're taking so much from the immersion of being whoever you want to be. It would've been so cool to be able to *SPOLER ALERT* side with the raiders when you first enter concord, and instead of being the hero of the minutemen, be a cruel unmerciful slaver or something like that...  The factions could've been a  little more interesting, i feel like they were just not as interesting as in the previous games..
I also remember the previous fallout games were a LOT darker. Stories of murder, kidnaping, cannibalism,♥♥♥♥♥♥ slavery etc.. And there were SOO many NPC's with very interesting backstories and interesting things to say. I wish this game had some more of that too. Obsidian really knew how to make their characters and stories. I feel like bethesda just tried to make a skyrim version of fallout. Where you're just simply the hero. DLC ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t as always was annoying as hell but oh well, we're talking about bethesda.. *SPOILER ALERT* It also really sucks that you just get the power armor super easy like with no effor.. When you actually had to have the skills to wear one on previous games.. They just hand it over to you like that.. Also the fact that you very quickly have your own little town and become a high rank leader super quickly.. whereas on the previous games you started like a hobo and had to work your way up to the top... Which felt good
However.....
The good
Overall Fallout 4 is an amazing game, it took years to develop, they made an outstanding job, the game engine is very fluent, you dont get that super clunky and glitchy feel like in the previous fallout games, the gunplay is magistral. It was actually one of the things i hated the most from previous fallout games.. The gunplay is actually a lot like doom's which is highly enjoiable and satisfying  (i've heard they brought some of the doom developers to do that ). The V.A.T.S system is the best so far from all the fallout series.. You don't just stop time but you actually have a few seconds to make up your strategy giving you enough room to think about it but without making you a god and actually adding some pressure to do it. The modding community is just wonderfuly talented and welcoming. this game would be very empty without mods tbh. Some people say that they didn't like the voice acting (Sorry if i go bias here a little bit) but i personally really enjoyed it, the voice actors are just amazing, I specially like Female sole survivor's voice, I feel like this adds a lot more personality to the character, Look at commander shepard from mass effect for example.. People never complained about that. But i guess people just were used to the silent misterious protagonist.. Maybe it coul've been an option to toggle the voice for the character.. I love crafting stuff, being able to mod your weapons and armor the way you want to give your character the personality you want was something that was really lacking on previous titles where you just had a set of armor and that was it.. No shoulder pads, no chest guard etc.. Now you cand customize pretty much every set of your armor.. The new power armor system is just amazing, you actually feel like you're a metal titan, makes you feel powerful by doing stuff like  super hero landings, using jetpacs, having a hud exclusive for it etc, besides that it's also customizable.. Whereas before it was just a fancy looking armor with high stats..
Overall..
I f*cking love fallout 4 man.. what can i tell you? I'm not gonna be a proud hipster brat and say that it isn't a good game just because it isnt a remake of the previous ones. Yes it lacked a lot of things.. But it also shines with innovation on a whole lot of other things..
So, do I recommend it ?.. F*CK  YES

Oh Three Rings, where shall I begin with this game of yours...
When I first played it, I enjoyed it immensely. I spent money on this game frequently, not because I wanted a certain item, but because I wanted them to develop it more, I wanted to help towards better graphics, new weapons and armour. I believed they could make this popular if they tried, but they didn't.
Three Rings have fell victim to one of a game developer's top predators: laziness and greed. For the past year the only 'updates' are just recolours of existing items. There are no new, fresh levels or missions, no new weapons, no new armour, just a different colour of the item you already have.
As you play through the game you'll first notice how repetitive the level designs are and eventually you get to the Vanguard rank (which isn't too hard to do if you're dedicated like I was) and you realize there's pretty much nothing for you to do anymore. No exclusive levels or missions for Vanguards, no nothing, the game sort of says "Yeah, good job completing me. I guess you can go now". You're stuck with prestige missions which, like everything else, are just repeated. Due to this and the lack of any sort of significant update (if you can even call them updates at this point), most players have quit. Three Rings have have caught on to this fact, they want to put as little effort into updates in an attempt to wring out any extra cash you have, or at least that's my only logical explaination.
As it stands today, I'm severely dissapointed.

Writing a negative review for XCOM goes against every fiber of my being, but I cannot recommend this game in it's current state. It is sad really. Another great title falls at the feet of corporate apathy and greed.
As it stands I have run into several bugs. Some are funny, some are annoying, and atleast one is preventing me from finishing the game. This is AFTER installing the patch THAT WAS SUPPOSED TO FIX THESE PROBLEMS.
I am a laid back guy, I am not going to get al hot and bothered because a game has a few bugs. The growing complexity of games has lead us to the ship a turd and polish with a patch business model so bugs are simply a part of life. The thing that bothers me about the kinds of glitches that XCOM shipped with is that they are not offhand things that the devlopers could not possibly forsee. This game is plagued by a lack of optimization. I have a 8 core processor running @ 4.9 Ghz, 2 GTX 980's SLI'd together an SSD and 32GB of RAM. My PC runs Assassins Creed Syndicate at a steady 60FPS, yet I struggle to get to 30 in XCOM 2. Cut scenes hang and lag. At times the game will hang for up to 10 - 15 seconds from issuing an order and the charachter completing the task. They are in your face problems that were surely detected during testing but Fraxis shipped the game with these problems anyway, then they pretended like they did not know about them. I really wanted to be able to give a positive review for this game since I’ve been a fan of the X-com series since I was a kid. However, after playing through veteran and beating the game, and getting partially through commander I have to admit I didn't really enjoy the game as I had hoped.
I'll start with the most frustrating part of the game. The hit percentages. Granted this is a problem that has carried over from Enemy Unknown but, it seems to have gotten much worse. This is not due to bad luck since I have tried to get my soldiers in different positions to attack an enemy and it doesn't matter if you have a 50% chance to hit or 90% chance to hit. If the AI has decided that soldier will miss on a certain target there's nothing you can do except try to attack a different target, load your game and try a different approach or be content with missing and losing a Major. This is not offering a "challenge", it is intentionally altering your chances so that you will miss now and then. This is supposed to be a strategy game. the decisions you make should not be affected by an AI that randomly decides to make you miss. It would be like playing chess and your opponent decides to randomly punt your pawns off the board. This follows into my next peeve.
The game is now half based on strategical placement. With the Codex and Avatar being able to teleport right behind your cover or the Snakeman able to grab you from 8 squares away at full cover or the Archon that just flies from a mile away and gets a critical head bash dealing 12 damage in one shot, the idea that this game is based on strategical advantages is laughable. The sharpshooters are still a great soldier to use and for that I am thankful.
The whole game is rushed. And I don't mean rushed through development (even though that is most likely the case.) The game forces you to make brash hurried decisions in 2 ways: the Avatar project on the main geoscape that will ultimately decide you will lose if you take too long accomplishing the main questline. If you make mistakes early on and decide to let that Avatar counter get to high your game will certainly be a failure and you will need to restart (my first game.) I wasn't even able to get through the tech tree or get a maxed out psionic warrior on my first victory because of that. The other rushed aspect is the turn counter in battle. It's rare when I can get a mission to 5+ turns before utter failure. Again this is another aspect where you will have to start over if you made any mistake in the beginning.
They also ditched a lot of the aspects of the game i loved. In XCOM 1,2 and EU you had a heavy weapons platform you could bring with you in place of a squad member. It was nice having those since it didn’t gain experience and could be replicated I didn’t mind it being blown up in combat and I took a much more aggressive battle strategy using them. Also, no more vehicle creation? One of the greatest aspects of the game was making your own flying saucer after a lengthy time in the research tree. Besides all that, there are plenty of bugs to find but, that is pretty normal for games that are shipped out prior to being completed nowadays.
On the brighter side of things the game offers a lot of new tech including being able to hack robotic enemies and a variety of grenades and ammunition variants that give a great amount of versatility when creating a squad (love the grenadiers in an exo-suit.) The plot line is well developed and intriguing. The addition of customizable weapons per squadmate as well as the PCS units was a nice addition but you may not get the drops you want in your limited time window.
All in all i tried to rate the game based on how much I enjoyed it and I would give it 2/5 the sheer frustration of the mechanics in this game has gotten me to abandon it and would not recommend this to a friend as I would not want them to feel the same.

As of Right now 11/7/15 If I started to play this game from scratch I would have fun up to a tier 2 (3 star) knight. When an individual reaches this rank he/she is about half way through the game. A few standing reasons of why I feel this way are as follows: Orbs of Alchemy are grindy to get, the dungeons you play on are repetitive, the game seems to be ignored by the creators and to me feels like the individuals who have made the game are now simply trying to get a little more money out of the game before they ignore it completely.
Orbs of Alchemy are commonly found in "Treasure boxes" which are scattered throughout the world you play in. However these "Treasure boxes" have an extremely low chance of giving you one of these fine orbs but rather have a higher chance of giving you a meeger sum of crowns (Capital in game) or heat (used in improving your weapons lethality). Another way of aquiring one of these mystic spheres is buying them with real money or crystal energy. Crystal energy is somewhat a remanant of the age of the "Spiral Knight" world if you will. How you acquire the substance now is buying if with real money in the "Spiral Depot" or crowns. It may not seem that bad paying 9,000 crowns for 100CE (CE=Crystal Energy) at first but the process of playing the same dungeons with the same equipment over and over for the satisfaction of getting a sword or a helmet after 4 something hours of gameplay is pathetic. To see exactly how the system works you can go to the "Spiral Wiki"
or download the game and you may see why im ranting.
To help put some of this into perspective I am a tier 3 (4 star) knight whom makes 2,000 crowns for every round I do by myself. That run takes about 15-20 mins or so if im going solo. Which I commonly do because people are constantly leaving and going making it hard to keep a friend. Out of 15 times I play this mission I get 3 of my precious orbs on good days. More commonly Out of 20 plays (or "runs") I will get nothing but alot of crowns and heat. I can use the crowns to buy CE to buy my Orbs of Alchemy which I normally do but The level of orbs I need cost up to 400 energy (which is at a current market price or 9,000 crowns per 100CE) 32,000 crowns. So out of 16 runs  I make approximately 32,000 crowns. If each round took me 15 mins to do I have just used 4 hours of my day into the game. To some gamers thats like dust on your shoulders. To people like you I say "More power to you". But to me that is an awful sum of time to waste every single day in the week. I do not have as many hours clocked in as some of these other "Fathers" of the Spiral Order but I can firmly say I have used 2/3 of my time into my current profile and I am still stuck to where I am at today.

-XCOM: Enemy Unknown mechanics are still there, vith visible upgrades
-New combat mechanics have great synergy with the gameplay
-Old enemies become a bigger threat while the new ones pose different levels of challenge

-At the moment of writing, performance is lower than a Muton's IQ. Running on a GTX 970 and still can't get constant 30FPS on the highest settings. Tried lowering settings; FPS remained unchanged. Get your
together, Firaxis.
-Loads of bugs ranging from minor graphical issues to walkthrough breakers. It's always
to watch teleporting soldiers, enemies walking through walls and so on
-Nervous breakdowns as the soliders with 90% hit chance decide to shoot for the moon, literally. But that's XCOM, baby!
Overall, if you can overlook the grave performance issue (seriously, Firaxis, what the truck?), XCOM 2 is a great game for XCOM fans and an unforgiving experience for those new to the series.

No. It's the perfect amount of frustration without satisfaction at the end. I wanted to get my 90 USD worth, so I got gud at another souls title. PvP is so, so poorly balanced. If I wanted to win in arena badly enough, all it really takes is the correct build, the correct attack spam, and the most basic sense of spacing. I made some small adjustments, started winning, and became disgusted in what I had become. It's a problem passed down from previous titles, but this time it seemed more absurd and unforgivingly unbalanced. Perhaps it was the fast-paced gameplay. Perhaps I simply had higher expectations than before.
Only good bosses are Champion Gundyr and Gael. Only area with an impressive atmosphere was the Ringed City DLC. Couldn't give a hoot for the rest. Most of the generic PvE is less so "tough but fair" and more so "actively avoid the glaring ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t". Story and motive doesn't cut it. DS1 made you a clear protagonist against impossible odds. DS2 had the theme of finding salvation for self and potential friends in a forgotten, dream-like land. BB was just interesting. DS3 makes you a pile of soot whose world has uninteresting overarching purposes, perhaps an intentional design, and uninteresting world nuances in heavily reused lore, a failure in design. I felt only few instances of being immersed or feeling wonder in this arcade-feeling Fromsoft title. Overall, the single player / PvE certainly wasn't terrible, it's arguably good, but it feels the least memorable and satisfying of Fromsoft's titles.
I guess it could be exciting for someone new to souls-like in general, but I'm disappointed as a series veteran. I found a few nuggets of exciting experience in my playtime, but I feel like it doesn't balance out.
I want my 90 USD back. I want my 180 hours back. I really, really gave it a chance.

Extremely punishing, but fun nonetheless, though I find myself quitting and restarting before I get too far in. I enjoy the combat, the paranoia, and the teambuilding; the massive setbacks, not so much. I think of myself as a frequent roguelike player, and absolutely agree with the Dwarf Fortress adage that "losing is fun," but Darkest Dungeon kills you too rarely, preferring to cripple you. I'm okay with dying; limping along for an hour beforehand, not so much.
At the same time, DD does an amazing job integrating resource management, dungeon crawling, and very real horror. Do I buy an extra slot on the wagon that brings new adventurers, or do I upgrade one of my characters, knowing that they could die the next time they go Dungeon-diving? Do I spend gold on items, or stockpile it in case of disaster? You grow to love powerful/useful characters, even when they're nearly identical to others of their class in both appearance and mechanics, and feel shock and loss when they inevitably die.
Also, the narrator is amazing.

-At the moment of writing, performance is lower than a Muton's IQ. Running on a GTX 970 and still can't get constant 30FPS on the highest settings. Tried lowering settings; FPS remained unchanged. Get your
together, Firaxis.
-Loads of bugs ranging from minor graphical issues to walkthrough breakers. It's always
to watch teleporting soldiers, enemies walking through walls and so on

Overall, if you can overlook the grave performance issue (seriously, Firaxis, what the truck?), XCOM 2 is a great game for XCOM fans and an unforgiving experience for those new to the series.
