Video Review:
Full text w/ photos:
Simulator games are in their hayday to be sure. There’s a simulator for everything you ever wanted to be, as well as games for a couple things you had no idea you wanted to be. I Am Bread has become the supreme frontrunner of the latter category in my book. The story is hysterical, told via psychiatrist statements about a man with rooms in his house being destroyed, and swearing that bread can move. The music is spot on, and the controls can take a lot of getting used to, but are completely fair. Made by Bossa Studios, it’s not a far throw from Surgeon Simulator, except that it features a wonderfully huge open world to explore, rather than just some dude’s chest cavity. You’ve been a goat, a deer, a gorilla, a farmer, a prisoner, a spaceman, and a rock. Now it’s finally time to pinch your inner loaf… Or something like that. Lets take a closer look at I Am Bread.
The first thing you’ll probably notice when you get into the game is the strange controls. Q,W,E,R (Or LT/LB RT/LB) are each assigned to a corner of your slice, pressing that button will cause the bread to grab, then you can fling yourself around using your mouse or control stick.  It sounds so simple, but much pain went into perfecting its execution… I’d say it was almost an hour before I became the ninja-bread man I never knew I longed to be. Once you finally stop nudging your bread along like Granny Gumgums, the music starts to click. It’s jazzy and quick and it makes my wall-crawling bread feel like he’s truly on the most dramatic adventure of his life. Hell, it probably is. It’s just a slice of bread after all.
Once you’ve mastered your abilities, you must complete the mission of getting toasted. Some lowly peons will tell you to use a toaster. Poppycock! I say find the nearest blow-dryer and just do what comes most natural. You also must stay off the floor, and away from gross stuff like trash and dishwater, as it will deplete your edibility bar. Once bread is no longer edible, it’s dead. Dead bread. The world is amazingly interactive. Almost everything can be broken or flung across the room via wonky physics, with delightful results! There is only one puzzle, “How can I become toast?”, but the answers are multiple, and as creative as you care to make them.
Now the ugly. The game does crash quite a bit… Which made recording at any length a bit frustrating. The controls are strange, but it’s likely on purpose, to increase the wackiness. That doesn’t do much for the extreme difficulty spike between the first level and the second, but there is time to adjust that as well. I also have to point out that the hardest part is wiggling yourself into the toaster. It caused me SO much heartache… You finally get to the toaster, only to discover that the real struggle has just begun. Overall though, I had a lot of fun with this game, and will likely return to it in the future. The environments are varied, and the freedom to solve a puzzle by riding on a rocket or skateboard, or simply scooting along the rug in a pot amuses me to no end.
Summary: A zany bread-simulator game with an open world and loads of freedom.
Final Score: 7/10 for gameplay, physics, and replayability. 9/10 with smaller difficulty curve.

Madness takes digital form in your quest to grind your brains out in Darkest Dungeon. On the surface, you will find elements of city management, a complex party system that requires you to balance not only classes but their post-spelunking ailments and illnesses, multiple tilesets with a variety of bosses that require different strategies, and a bevy of trinkets and baubles with equally weighted good and bad stats. All these elements (despite the RNG) combine into an enjoyable experience for the first dozen or so hours.
All this is fun and games until you clear the first boss for each dungeon and the problems with randomness and luck really show their ugly faces. RNG holds every gameplay aspect of DD in it's iron grip; from miserable combat accuracy (for both you and the enemy), interacting with curios, suffering from permanent debuffs, and even being able to run from battle are all randomized. I love board & card games so I'm used to rolling dice and suffering for it but when the entire game is determined by luck it gets infuriating. Imagine playing Monopoly: you land on an unowned property only to have to roll dice to determine if you can buy it, roll again to determine if you can put a house on it, and then your opponents get to roll when they land on it to determine if they have to pay you. Every step is a roll of the dice (not even counting traps) with your characters gaining stress randomly while walking and sometimes forcing you to interact with obviously bad curios because of a permanent trait they have.
Of course, RNG can always be brute forced because this is a video game and anyone who has played an RPG before knows how to brute force any kind of difficulty: grinding. In order to beat anything above the first tier of bosses, you are expected to have the best gear possible on all your characters in order for them to survive. With a max roster size of 28, characters running away or suffering from multiple crippling ailments, and permadeath (because why not?), you're looking at spending several hours grinding "easy" dungeons in the hope of bringing back some cash without your party suffering from any more permanent debuffs or dying. Near the end of the game, losing a max level key party member can spell the end of your progression and send you back to the grind mines. Since launch, they added the ability to upgrade your recruiter to occasionally bring you higher level recruits, but this also requires grinding up multiple buildings just to have the chance at buying non-unleveled heroes.
These are all complaints about how the game was "meant" to be playing though. Through the options menu you can choose to mitigate some of the RNG but it still leaves a lot to be desired. Most of the miserable elements above aren't covered in the menu and removing & replacing them would completely change the game. I don't hate the individual elements that bring this game down but when combined it just feels like Darkest Dungeon despises the player and is actively trying to stop you from playing it. I'm sure the devs thought this was some kind of clever meta-torture based on the Lovecraftian horrors you run into but I didn't find it amusing. There will be a small, masochistic audience that will sink their teeth into this and grind it for hundreds of hours (only 1.3% of the people who have bought it on Steam have beaten it, including SAM users) but for the average person I would not recommend it.

This brief review comes from an old time veteran of UFO games going all the way back to the 90s. Being a great fan of the relaunched Xcom the second installment was an autobuy. And I am very confident they will eventually patch it to where it should be, but...
Even on easiest setting some of the missions are extremely hard - mainly due to the RNG gameplay mechanics built into the core mechanics: I've had to reload for literally 2 evenings to finish one of the missions because of flaws in my team that I simply could not have prevented as a player. And that comes from a ironman player of Xcom 1. I have no qualms with being punished for stupid gameplay - in Xcom2 I am constantly reloading simply because stuff happens that I have absolutely no control over.
The alien opponents seemingly use their maximum movement range and still melee attack - or they have insane range. And why Aliens get an out of turn movement phase when they are surprised by my team beats me. Result as so often is that they can essentially flank the hell out of me without my team even being able to reposition.
The timers are extremely tight and often enough I had to restart missions all the way from the beginning simply because I had that one turn missing to finish the extraction. I even had to leave folks behind due to the constantly reapearing aliens - without my guys having a fair chance to fight their way out. No one left behind? Not in Xcom2.
And don't get me even started on the hit/cover percentages... Let's say it this way: they really need some love.
Story and core combat of the game are great and absolutely addicting. It's just not really polished for the player yet. But I am sure it will happen over time and then my hesitant "NO" will become an overwhelming "YES"... until then: you either have to be a lucky star OR masochistic. Or both...

This brief review comes from an old time veteran of UFO games going all the way back to the 90s. Being a great fan of the relaunched Xcom the second installment was an autobuy. And I am very confident they will eventually patch it to where it should be, but...
Even on easiest setting some of the missions are extremely hard - mainly due to the RNG gameplay mechanics built into the core mechanics: I've had to reload for literally 2 evenings to finish one of the missions because of flaws in my team that I simply could not have prevented as a player. And that comes from a ironman player of Xcom 1. I have no qualms with being punished for stupid gameplay - in Xcom2 I am constantly reloading simply because stuff happens that I have absolutely no control over.
The alien opponents seemingly use their maximum movement range and still melee attack - or they have insane range. And why Aliens get an out of turn movement phase when they are surprised by my team beats me. Result as so often is that they can essentially flank the hell out of me without my team even being able to reposition.
The timers are extremely tight and often enough I had to restart missions all the way from the beginning simply because I had that one turn missing to finish the extraction. I even had to leave folks behind due to the constantly reapearing aliens - without my guys having a fair chance to fight their way out. No one left behind? Not in Xcom2.
And don't get me even started on the hit/cover percentages... Let's say it this way: they really need some love.
Story and core combat of the game are great and absolutely addicting. It's just not really polished for the player yet. But I am sure it will happen over time and then my hesitant "NO" will become an overwhelming "YES"... until then: you either have to be a lucky star OR masochistic. Or both...

Madness takes digital form in your quest to grind your brains out in Darkest Dungeon. On the surface, you will find elements of city management, a complex party system that requires you to balance not only classes but their post-spelunking ailments and illnesses, multiple tilesets with a variety of bosses that require different strategies, and a bevy of trinkets and baubles with equally weighted good and bad stats. All these elements (despite the RNG) combine into an enjoyable experience for the first dozen or so hours.
All this is fun and games until you clear the first boss for each dungeon and the problems with randomness and luck really show their ugly faces. RNG holds every gameplay aspect of DD in it's iron grip; from miserable combat accuracy (for both you and the enemy), interacting with curios, suffering from permanent debuffs, and even being able to run from battle are all randomized. I love board & card games so I'm used to rolling dice and suffering for it but when the entire game is determined by luck it gets infuriating. Imagine playing Monopoly: you land on an unowned property only to have to roll dice to determine if you can buy it, roll again to determine if you can put a house on it, and then your opponents get to roll when they land on it to determine if they have to pay you. Every step is a roll of the dice (not even counting traps) with your characters gaining stress randomly while walking and sometimes forcing you to interact with obviously bad curios because of a permanent trait they have.
Of course, RNG can always be brute forced because this is a video game and anyone who has played an RPG before knows how to brute force any kind of difficulty: grinding. In order to beat anything above the first tier of bosses, you are expected to have the best gear possible on all your characters in order for them to survive. With a max roster size of 28, characters running away or suffering from multiple crippling ailments, and permadeath (because why not?), you're looking at spending several hours grinding "easy" dungeons in the hope of bringing back some cash without your party suffering from any more permanent debuffs or dying. Near the end of the game, losing a max level key party member can spell the end of your progression and send you back to the grind mines. Since launch, they added the ability to upgrade your recruiter to occasionally bring you higher level recruits, but this also requires grinding up multiple buildings just to have the chance at buying non-unleveled heroes.
These are all complaints about how the game was "meant" to be playing though. Through the options menu you can choose to mitigate some of the RNG but it still leaves a lot to be desired. Most of the miserable elements above aren't covered in the menu and removing & replacing them would completely change the game. I don't hate the individual elements that bring this game down but when combined it just feels like Darkest Dungeon despises the player and is actively trying to stop you from playing it. I'm sure the devs thought this was some kind of clever meta-torture based on the Lovecraftian horrors you run into but I didn't find it amusing. There will be a small, masochistic audience that will sink their teeth into this and grind it for hundreds of hours (only 1.3% of the people who have bought it on Steam have beaten it, including SAM users) but for the average person I would not recommend it.

I thought Dark Dungeon (DD) this would be challenging, hard and fun. This is from someone who can stomach MMO RNG. All I found here was endless punishment with little to no progression after so many hours of playtime. For a game that's selling gameplay as a feature, there was just no mid game substance.  I'll try break it down for detail.
I've haven't completed the game, but so far it's gives a light background on why the town and the narrator is so gloomy. As you progress, little diary entries can be found for extra flavour. The actual setting is fictional but things like classes that use single shot pistols and crossbows gives a 18th century feel. The game doesn't really need a strong story since most of the features were part of gameplay.
You work your way through randomly generated rooms which is the game's strongest feature. This is considering the limited graphic assets, DD gives a new feel to each new dungeon the player decides to plunder. There's also the standard RPG heroes progression, classes, renaming, and stat changing items. It's clearly simplistic by design so players can focus on the main mechanic, Stress. The more you push your heroes to do super human things, the faster you'll find a team wipe. In fact, the dev's tried a little too hard on this part and forgot about letting the players know some dungeons shouldn't be attempted. This game has punishment by the truck load.
Like I said before, it's so severe, that even recruiting new heroes is a chore. Let's start there. Heroes are randomised in terms of skill set, and alot of the time you're staring at a roster full of unplayable heroes with conflicting skill sets. You can retrain them which cost a punishing amount of money; coinage that you simply don't have at the start or mid game. In fact you earn so little money that progression slows down as you get further. Add that to the fact they come out of a dungeon with a bad trait 90% of the time means they'll lose value after 2 uses unless your spend more money. What makes this worse is that they can't cure their deseases or lose bad quirks at the same time. So this means yet another punishment since both deseases and quirks will become more severe and cost more to remove each week you put it off.
So how do you get stress and deseases? Through dungeon combat which has many great features and clever designs. Unfortunately it's eclipsed by the fact the random events are biased towards gaining stress and misses in attacks. I've had a hero miss twice in a row even though it says 90% chance to hit. Granted after playing over 100 hours, players might see rare misfortune like this, but I haven't gotten close to that much gameplay. Positioning is vital and this plays a great deal with strategy and planning before starting out into a dungeon. In fact once you got a good synergy going, most fights end favourably. That's if you can get the right people (see above). Turn order and speed is the second most critical thing in this game since it decides turn order. More speed and means your heroes go first. For what ever reason, the further you progress, there will be a boss that breaks this rule and hits you twice per turn. If the turn ends with an enemy attack, the next turn can start with their attack since they got more speed. But 2 swipes in a single turn was incredibly stupid and great waste of time. The whole 5 mins was just enemy attacking and spamming moves. 5 mins of no keyboard or mouse.
So a biased towards misses and handing the initiative to the enemy AI will always leave your party worse for wear. But all would be fine if the coin and treasure are good, right? High risk, high reward? Nope. DD doesn't even have risk since you can't tell what random things will happen inside a dungeon. At best, you can walk away with minimum stress but never enough money to remove all the bad quirks your team will stack up. At worst, you'll team wipe and lose all items, exp, and training. I don't even know they why allow renaming if they're forcing players to make 99% of heroes expendable like this.
The ambience and sound effects are absolutely amazing. It goes well with demonic design of the dungeons. Not much to rave about in terms of the music once you hear it play over 100 times. That's the same with any game soundtrack so nothing new here. The voice actor for the narrator is harder to judge. I can imagine some players would say he's a broken man, so some intonations are understandably awkward. Still, awkward is awkward. The other voice acting include gagging and spluttering which weren't over the top.
As with most 2D games, Art style is king. It was grotesque when it needs to be, intimadating when you meet a boss. With many mixed themes thrown around like despair and death, the colour pallete was mostly dark colours. Each attack animation had a comic book feel, with it's stylised expression and shading. It needs to be said that movement isn't entirely animated.
It's really hard to expect everyone to like a certain art, and this extends to DD's graphics. For me, I like it.
A game that closes the door on less than perfect set ups. It bars any attempt on recovery which is fine, but creates the illusion that players have multiple strategies to finishing the game. Plenty of unique concepts and mechanics, great art, and bug free. I only wished it they keep the punishments in check. Whoever balanced the economy should really think about decreasing the 'cost' ingame to even make it playable. Just horrible delivery even when gameplay is such a huge part of DD.

Black Squad is an interesting F2P modern military shooter in that it tries to be Counter Strike and CoD in the sense that it is very arcade-ish run n gun game play, though accuracy matters as headshotting someone in the right area can kill them instantly with most weapons due to the "Fatal Crit" system. Not to mention the game is extremely easy to pick up and play due to all weapons coming with every single attachment already and being rather affordable compared to most of the F2P games I've played...
Add the fact that getting shot doesn't slow you down, ADS does not penalize movement and hipfiring and ADS has roughly the same accuracy, and you have a formula that rewards skilled play, but is casual enough for even the most unskilled FPS player to contribute and you have a fairly unique Modern Military Shooter experience.
That being said, outside of this, there's not much else that sets it apart from other Modern Military Shooters in the market, so if you're burnt out of the genre, you're not going to find much of interest here. Worst of all however, despite the Developers saying they are working hard on fixing the issue, is that Hackers are currently running rampant in the game, using Speed hacks, wall hacks, aimbots and the like to ruin everyone's fun by not only destroying them, but their PCs as well thanks to the explosion spam often causing even the game servers to become overloaded...
You can take the Devs' word for it, but considering how many devs lie these days, I would strongly avoid this game for now... Once (if ever) the hacker situation is settled, then I will change this review to recommended as it is honestly not a bad game, it's just currently being ruined by sad trolls currently stress testing the servers as well as everyone's patience with their ♥♥♥♥♥♥ hacks...

This brief review comes from an old time veteran of UFO games going all the way back to the 90s. Being a great fan of the relaunched Xcom the second installment was an autobuy. And I am very confident they will eventually patch it to where it should be, but...
Even on easiest setting some of the missions are extremely hard - mainly due to the RNG gameplay mechanics built into the core mechanics: I've had to reload for literally 2 evenings to finish one of the missions because of flaws in my team that I simply could not have prevented as a player. And that comes from a ironman player of Xcom 1. I have no qualms with being punished for stupid gameplay - in Xcom2 I am constantly reloading simply because stuff happens that I have absolutely no control over.
The alien opponents seemingly use their maximum movement range and still melee attack - or they have insane range. And why Aliens get an out of turn movement phase when they are surprised by my team beats me. Result as so often is that they can essentially flank the hell out of me without my team even being able to reposition.
The timers are extremely tight and often enough I had to restart missions all the way from the beginning simply because I had that one turn missing to finish the extraction. I even had to leave folks behind due to the constantly reapearing aliens - without my guys having a fair chance to fight their way out. No one left behind? Not in Xcom2.
And don't get me even started on the hit/cover percentages... Let's say it this way: they really need some love.
Story and core combat of the game are great and absolutely addicting. It's just not really polished for the player yet. But I am sure it will happen over time and then my hesitant "NO" will become an overwhelming "YES"... until then: you either have to be a lucky star OR masochistic. Or both...

Black Squad is like.. COD, CSGO and Unreal thrown in a blender. The movement will throw any veteran shooter off tho.
Your insticts will be holding you back from running and gunning, while that is exactly what you should be doing in this game. Don't worry about steadying your rifle, just aim roughly at the enemy, and start your spraying while dodging, weaving and jumping to keep out of your enemy's crosshair. Classic spray and pray, baby!
The game definately still has its flaws tho, and some of them are... gamebreaking, sadly.
I'm writing this review after having played this for only two hours, but I can say I've seen enough to be able to speak about the contents of it. While keeping in mind this game is still in Beta, there's still a LOT of work to do.
The guns are, well, all in all pretty decent, even tho I'm missing some "classics" like the m4, the ak etc. The shop GUI where you "buy" new guns with the credits you earn in game could also definately use more "order". The way the different "versions" of the same base gun are shown can get a little confusing for new players, and not everyone will bother looking into them in detail.
The maps.. I feel like they're too small.. Less is more, and the lack of clutter and props does create a clean environment to just pick and shoot, but the maps could really use some extending, especially in Team Deathmatch.
Then, the players. So far, I've only played two hours on the NA servers, and most of my interactions were positive. Lots of new players at the moment trying this game out, that probably contributes as well.
But then the gamebreaking stuff..
Lobby's are just.. Weird.. The GUI could use a rework to make that part easier to access. Maybe add the abillity to make a game lobby before choosing gametypes etc, like most other FPS do it.
Once you've finally gotten into the lobby with your friends, the real pain can begin.
Everyone ready's up, and we launch the game. At this point, 3 of us flip a coin. If any of our 3 coins gets a head, we'll get a hacker in the game.
Playing online is like playing a game of chance. If you're lucky enough to get into a game that doesn't have a hacker, you'll enjoy your game.
Being a Free to Play game also means anyone can make an account, download hacks, and boom...
The lack of decent antihack software is genuinely game breaking, and needs to be addressed as soon as possible if this game is to survive.
I'm really talking, gamebreaking.. Just played three 16v16 games in a row, ONE of them we didn't have a hacker and had fun, the next game a hacker destroyed all the boxes under 2 mins. Somehow he was able to slice 15-20 times per second with his knife.
The next game another guy made the previous guy look like a newbie tho. This guy somehow managed to end the 16vs16 game under 30 seconds.
Now THAT'S impressive.
Sadly, there's no way to "flag" or report ingame at all, and there's no connection between steam and the game playerwise. As a legit player, for now, you'll just be forced to endure, and pray for that one match where you get don't get a hacker.
Pro's:
- Free to play
- Fun change from the classic FPS games most people play nowadays
- Wooden PC? NO PROBLEM!
- Solid engine, so fast loading times etc
Con's
- Messy GUI
- Run&Gun only, even with snipers
- Small maps
- No or badly functioning hack detection system which leads to a horrible online experience
Do you recommend this game?
For now.. I couldn't recommend it.. Until it makes up on the anti hack detection, where it completely missed the ball, I'd even say this game is almost unplayable.
It's a very solid base to build further on, but it's definately not there yet.

This is an interesting game, and won't be everyone's cup of tea. The premise is you use the 4 corners of the bread to move yourself towards a destination, such as the toaster. It's very difficult at the beginning but the more you play you'll find yourself moving faster and easier. Though the gameplay is simply "Get from A to B" you can do this through a bunch of different ways, like climbing the walls or trying to dash over the floor (not recommended as this effects your score) but you can also knock over skateboards to gain extra distance past long hallways.
If you have no patience for silly games with simple goals, this won't hold your attention for very long. The gameplay is a bit samey and unlike games like Mount Your Friends that have a similiar premise/control scheme, this is so far single player which I find drops replayability quite a lot.
The game has a story which I also find entertaining, I won't spoil anything but if you're the kind of person who sees a game where you play a piece of bread and think "This is my kinda game" you'll probably enjoy it.

XCOM 2 is a buggy mess, and we're not just talking about chryssalids here.  Massive load times, crashes and visual errors with the action camera.  Area effect attacks are finicky to aim, the alien POD system heavily favors alpha strike setup and penalizes you if a pod is discovered on your last move.
However, the game is still great when it comes to strategy and tension while trying to save earth from the now in power alien forces known here as ADVENT.  Whether you like it or not the timed battles ratchet up the tension and force you to play a more aggressive style than previous XCOM games.
The biggest improvements is the strategic layer that provides a much better feel of actually fighting for territory on earth, following that is the hacking options that can really turn the tide of battle with a lucky roll.  Luck is of course still a major part of this game you'll be praying for a shot to land and cursing when you deal a low damage roll.
That's XCOM.

darkest dungeon is one of the hardest rpgs one can play.
The plot is dead simple. Your ancestor decided to crack open some lovecraftian horror books and toyed with forces beyond his understanding and control. Because of this, he summoned an abomination from elderich depths by opening a door at the bottom of the ruins, which, as you can imagine, did not go too well. Now the surrounding area is infested with horrors and its up to you, the last member of your families bloodline, to fix what has been broken or go insane trying.
You yourself do not actually fight, you hire various heros of many different classes to do your bidding, go to the dungeons, and eventually go insane, die, or both. You have 15 classes to choose from, each one is entirely unique and brings many different skills to the table. When you hire one, they have a random set of four skills from the eight they can learn, as well as three of the camp skills they can also learn. Then there are the insanities. Every character, when they start off, and as they go through the game, gains various manias, some good, some bad. One will grant them an increase to crit chance, while another will cause them to gain more stress when going into the crypt.  as you send them out on missions they'll gain experience for completing them, improving in stats and sometimes going a little bit more insane, this can screw you over pretty badly sometimes. for example, my houndmaster became a ♥♥♥♥♥ hound and only wanted to visit the ♥♥♥♥♥ house to reduce stress, then got kicked out for "deviant tastes".
the gameplay is split into three parts, base management, exploration and combat. The base is called the hamlet, here you have several options to mess with. You can teach your minions new moves and improve their existing ones, improve the gear of your minions, buy trinkets, cure diseases, manage your minions insanity and reduce stress (not yours, your gonna be sweating from start to finish). your characters will gain access to more training and better gear as they level up, but you need to improve the facilities around the hamlet in order for you to get them that gear and give them access to better training. Sometimes you'll send the party out on missions just so you'll be able to get that next upgrade for the smithy or the hospital, just because each upgrade really does have a big impact.
once your done messing around in the hamlet you can go to the quest screen and decide where to send your minions to die. There are several areas, each one posing its own unique challanges. The crypt, the warren, the waeld, the cove and the darkest dungeon are your options. Each one will have one or more missions to choose from, each of varying length, varying difficulty, and offering varying rewards, usually in the form of a choice trinket, some money, and some resources to improve the hamlet. Its up to you to decide who goes off on what mission to go get you whatever resources you might need while at the same time, hoping they don't die. after that you buy some supplies so they don't die and then send them off.
now we get to the actual dungeons. Each one is randomly generated for each mission, its size depends on how long the mission is, its shape depends on what section of the land the mission is set in. You must move from room to room via corridors, trying to complete your objective(s) without dying horribly, all the while interacting with the various objects you'll encounter in the corridors and the rooms. Certain items you bring with you on the mission will help you with these objects, like the shovel being used to dig rubble away.
Finally, the combat. its an initiative based semi static style of combat. When you start your missions you decide which character goes where in a conga line of four, their placement in that line determines which abilities they can use, as certain abilities can only be used in certain spots. this also applies to enemy placement, as certain abilities will only target enemies in specific spots on their conga line. so before combat, make sure everyone is in the right spot before you go brawling. its also unlikely they'll be staying in that spot, as both enemies and allies can use abilities which allow them to change their position within the conga line, effectively resulting in some true juggling chaos depending on your party make up. every round begins with the person with the highest speed going first, then the second fastest and so on, each round you can do one of two things, change position within the conga line, or use one of the four abilities they have equipped. from there, its all in the hands of nuffle, god of random chance.
your characters have two bars, their health bar, and their stress bar. once they are out of health they go to deaths door, but they don't die. When a character is at deaths door they have a percentage chance every time they take a hit to die, its effectively a net to stop big enemies one shotting them. the downside is that they gain stress much faster and generate it every turn for themselves. Stress is bad, not just for your skin, but also your mind and heart. Attacks can deal five main forms of damage. Basic, bleed, blight, debuff and stress (you can't stress enemies though). bleed and blight are by turn on going damage status effects that stack on top of each other and themselves, which can lead to insane amounts of damage per turn on a single enemy. Stress however is a bugbear only you get to deal with. When a minion reaches 100 stress, they undergo a stress of will, either they go insane, or they become emboldened and get badass. going insane causes your characters to disobey commands and do other strange things depending on which insanity they have, becoming badass means they gain buffs, being insane or emboldened lasts until the end of the quest. However, when a character reaches 200 stress, they die. I'm not kidding, this will be the main way you will lose characters.
Darkest dungeon is a very stylized game, the visuals are bold and striking, they do a wonderful job of convaying just how bleak the situation you find yourself in is. While there is a lack of animation, the way the game gets around it is quite clever, making what would have just been two static images smooshing together look and feel like hefty impacts between two combatents. The music and narrator also hit the right chords, the narrator specifically is what gives the entire game is dramatic flare, spouting depressing or emboldening lines at just the right moments or monologing during loading screens for bosses. The music is somber and heavy, making you realize this is not a light hearted wonder through the woods, but a trudge through♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and rotten flesh.
Now, darkest dungeon is flawed, intentionally so, but that wont stop me from being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about it. The random element in this game is the devil. Many times you will be screwed over by the random elements of this game. The final dungeons of this will also make you pull teeth out in frustration for how much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t is tossed at you. There is a way to fix this in the settings....kinda, its still hard as nails, not because of a skill cap, but the nature of the game itself.
Overall, Darkest Dungeon is a very deep and complex rpg combat wise, its beautiful to look at and is addictive as hell, but suffers from an overly unfair random chance element and bosses late on that will ♥♥♥♥ you over royally. if you're looking for a punishing rpg, this is it.

For someone, who don't want to read this all:
Positives:
+ improved game mechanics
+ "new" classes of units (Grenadier, Ranger, Specialist, Sharpshooter, Psi Operative, SPARK - in DLC Shen's Last Gift))
+ many kinds of enemy units
+ more tactic possibilities than XCOM: EU or EW
+ great graphics
+ nice soundtrack
+ thrilling story
Negatives:
- unlike old x-com series you don't have to take care of many things (game is easier in some ways)
Ok, where to start. After XCOM reboot, most players were expecting, that this XCOM will be underwater. Luckily it's not like that. I mean, I like Terror from the deep, but it didn't bring anything new (but this game has a little legacy of Terror from the deep - magnetic weapons). This XCOM is really big surprise to me. It keeps game mechanics of XCOM, but it has many improvements. You are on the opposite side in this game, prepare to be an intruder. Now it's not the time to defend the Earth, but conquer it back! Your forces are hiding in flying base and it's your responsibility to make right choices. I'm disappointed with one thing. Games in this age are getting really easier. I don't mean, when you switch difficulties (you can make every game really challenging), I mean, do you remember old x-com series? There were many things that you have to take care of (richer micromanagement). In this game are only several things. However, it won't stop me to really enjoy it. I recomend this game for fans of the old series and for players of new XCOM.
Guys, just enjoy it!
P.S.: I consider XCOM 2 better than XCOM: EU or EW.

XCOM 2, the sequel to XCOM Enemy Unknown, is without a doubt one of the best strategy games I've ever played. XCOM as a franchise has always been some of the best strategy games out there and I am pleased to say that this new entry more then lives up to the legacy of its predecessors.
XCOM 2 assumes that you got your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you in Enemy Unknown(Enemy Within if you got the expansion, also reccomended), and turns the tables on you. You're now leading a resistance movement to overthrow the alien run ADVENT coalition, who are now operating a global government. 20 years have passed between this game and the last, and it shows. ADVENT is well entrenched, not only resource and infrastructure wise, but also in that they have the popular support of the people. Assuming you play the tutorial, the game begins from the perspective of Central Officer Bradford, as he leads an operation to rescue The Commander(Read: YOU) from an ADVENT facility. After the tutorial's crash course in some changes to the ground battles, such as concealment, you're taken to your new mobile headquarters.
XCOM is now operating out of "The Avenger", a re-purposed alien cargo vessel, now serving as your mobile base of operations. Striking from the Avenger, you travel the globe, uniting resistance cells and striking at ADVENT facilities wherever you can. While the previous games had you countering alien abductions, and defending populations, the new version pits you in a guerilla warfare situation. Now your missions consist of hit and run strikes against research labs, local armories, and other facilities, to rescue VIPs, hack their network for intel, destroy data-relays, or protect your own network taps. Some missions even involve kidnapping or assasinating key officials in their organiszation. Dirty Collaborators.
Maps are now procedurally generated, so that you never get the same one twice. The new maps are beautiful, and fully destructive. If you need a door somewhere, feel free to make one. Heck, you can even collapse the floor out from under an enemy's feet, or lure them into a building and with a few well placed explosives, drop the entire building on top of them.
The change in pace is noticeable. Almost every mission has some sort of time limit, either due to ADVENT actively destorying whatever you need to protect, or an actual timer untill the mission ends. This adds a sense of urgency to missions and encourages more risky play. Gameplay feels more fast paced then in previous installments. This also adds dificulty, not only must you achieve a hard task, but you need to do it in the next few turns or you won't have enough time to make it back to the evac point.
Speaking of Difficulty, XCOM 2 continues the franchise history of brutal and unforgiving gameplay. The easier difficulties are just that, easy. You can coast through them and learn the game in a more forgiving and casual environment if you want. Rookie to Veteran is a significant but manageable leap, however, the difficulty spikes hard changing from Veteran to Commander. The last of the training wheels come off at that point and it shows. The real test of your abilities comes from playing under the "Insanity" setting. The training wheels have been long forgotten, no more punches are going to be pulled. The game will officially break your nose and toss you overboard into shark infested waters to see if you can swim. That's not to say the game is unfair, because it is. You can beat insanity mode, but there is no longer any margin for error.
To win the game, you'll need to unravel the alien's true agenda. The ADVENT coalition is up to something, in the form of the AVATAR Project. This is the alien's win condition, and puts a timer on the game as a whole. If the aliens can make enough progress on the project, game over. Thankfully, you're given ample oppertunity to sabotage facilites critical to this initiative, slowing and even reversing their progress. If you can discover the truth about their agenda, and put a stop to it before they complete this plan, you will reign victorious.
A commander is nothing without his men, and to put an end to the AVATAR Project, you'll need the help of alot of them. Lucky for us, customising the soliders under your command has been greatly improved from the last game. New customisation options, incuding scars, tatoos, and individual armor pieces, can help vary the look of your troops. The Character Pool function allows you to save your favorites to share with your friends, and characters in the pool can appear at random points in your campaigns. New looks are accompanied by new skills. The Class based system is back, but has been changed dramatically. The Heavy, Support, Sniper and Assault classes of XCOM EW, have been replaced with the Grenadier, Specialist, Sharpshooter and Ranger, respectively. Each bring something new to the table, but hav roughly the same roles overall. A powerful 5th class exists now as well, if you're willing to spend the time to unlock it.
One more noteworthy feature is the extensive mod support, the steam workshop has over 500 mods already published at the time of writing, and more are on the way as modders explore deeper into the game's code.
Summary: XCOM 2 is a great game for the strategy junkies in all of us, offering compelling story, beautiful visuals, top notch gameplay, and brutal, but fair, difficulty. A solid 9.5/10, Must own for anyone interested in strategy games, or who enjoyed the previous installment in the franchise.
TL;DR: Buy it, game is good.

This game isn't for those who hate losing, it's for gamers who enjoy the challenge and seek to overcome obstacles that normal gamers would quit over.
This game deserves the respect it gets. Watch some gameplay if you're unsure, but I'd recommend this game any day over games like Heroes of Might and Magic, which I did love, but quickly learned how repetitive it was. This is a must buy for gamers who would like to call themselves "tactical masters".

darkest dungeon is one of the hardest rpgs one can play.
The plot is dead simple. Your ancestor decided to crack open some lovecraftian horror books and toyed with forces beyond his understanding and control. Because of this, he summoned an abomination from elderich depths by opening a door at the bottom of the ruins, which, as you can imagine, did not go too well. Now the surrounding area is infested with horrors and its up to you, the last member of your families bloodline, to fix what has been broken or go insane trying.
You yourself do not actually fight, you hire various heros of many different classes to do your bidding, go to the dungeons, and eventually go insane, die, or both. You have 15 classes to choose from, each one is entirely unique and brings many different skills to the table. When you hire one, they have a random set of four skills from the eight they can learn, as well as three of the camp skills they can also learn. Then there are the insanities. Every character, when they start off, and as they go through the game, gains various manias, some good, some bad. One will grant them an increase to crit chance, while another will cause them to gain more stress when going into the crypt.  as you send them out on missions they'll gain experience for completing them, improving in stats and sometimes going a little bit more insane, this can screw you over pretty badly sometimes. for example, my houndmaster became a ♥♥♥♥♥ hound and only wanted to visit the ♥♥♥♥♥ house to reduce stress, then got kicked out for "deviant tastes".
the gameplay is split into three parts, base management, exploration and combat. The base is called the hamlet, here you have several options to mess with. You can teach your minions new moves and improve their existing ones, improve the gear of your minions, buy trinkets, cure diseases, manage your minions insanity and reduce stress (not yours, your gonna be sweating from start to finish). your characters will gain access to more training and better gear as they level up, but you need to improve the facilities around the hamlet in order for you to get them that gear and give them access to better training. Sometimes you'll send the party out on missions just so you'll be able to get that next upgrade for the smithy or the hospital, just because each upgrade really does have a big impact.
once your done messing around in the hamlet you can go to the quest screen and decide where to send your minions to die. There are several areas, each one posing its own unique challanges. The crypt, the warren, the waeld, the cove and the darkest dungeon are your options. Each one will have one or more missions to choose from, each of varying length, varying difficulty, and offering varying rewards, usually in the form of a choice trinket, some money, and some resources to improve the hamlet. Its up to you to decide who goes off on what mission to go get you whatever resources you might need while at the same time, hoping they don't die. after that you buy some supplies so they don't die and then send them off.
now we get to the actual dungeons. Each one is randomly generated for each mission, its size depends on how long the mission is, its shape depends on what section of the land the mission is set in. You must move from room to room via corridors, trying to complete your objective(s) without dying horribly, all the while interacting with the various objects you'll encounter in the corridors and the rooms. Certain items you bring with you on the mission will help you with these objects, like the shovel being used to dig rubble away.
Finally, the combat. its an initiative based semi static style of combat. When you start your missions you decide which character goes where in a conga line of four, their placement in that line determines which abilities they can use, as certain abilities can only be used in certain spots. this also applies to enemy placement, as certain abilities will only target enemies in specific spots on their conga line. so before combat, make sure everyone is in the right spot before you go brawling. its also unlikely they'll be staying in that spot, as both enemies and allies can use abilities which allow them to change their position within the conga line, effectively resulting in some true juggling chaos depending on your party make up. every round begins with the person with the highest speed going first, then the second fastest and so on, each round you can do one of two things, change position within the conga line, or use one of the four abilities they have equipped. from there, its all in the hands of nuffle, god of random chance.
your characters have two bars, their health bar, and their stress bar. once they are out of health they go to deaths door, but they don't die. When a character is at deaths door they have a percentage chance every time they take a hit to die, its effectively a net to stop big enemies one shotting them. the downside is that they gain stress much faster and generate it every turn for themselves. Stress is bad, not just for your skin, but also your mind and heart. Attacks can deal five main forms of damage. Basic, bleed, blight, debuff and stress (you can't stress enemies though). bleed and blight are by turn on going damage status effects that stack on top of each other and themselves, which can lead to insane amounts of damage per turn on a single enemy. Stress however is a bugbear only you get to deal with. When a minion reaches 100 stress, they undergo a stress of will, either they go insane, or they become emboldened and get badass. going insane causes your characters to disobey commands and do other strange things depending on which insanity they have, becoming badass means they gain buffs, being insane or emboldened lasts until the end of the quest. However, when a character reaches 200 stress, they die. I'm not kidding, this will be the main way you will lose characters.
Darkest dungeon is a very stylized game, the visuals are bold and striking, they do a wonderful job of convaying just how bleak the situation you find yourself in is. While there is a lack of animation, the way the game gets around it is quite clever, making what would have just been two static images smooshing together look and feel like hefty impacts between two combatents. The music and narrator also hit the right chords, the narrator specifically is what gives the entire game is dramatic flare, spouting depressing or emboldening lines at just the right moments or monologing during loading screens for bosses. The music is somber and heavy, making you realize this is not a light hearted wonder through the woods, but a trudge through♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and rotten flesh.
Now, darkest dungeon is flawed, intentionally so, but that wont stop me from being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about it. The random element in this game is the devil. Many times you will be screwed over by the random elements of this game. The final dungeons of this will also make you pull teeth out in frustration for how much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t is tossed at you. There is a way to fix this in the settings....kinda, its still hard as nails, not because of a skill cap, but the nature of the game itself.
Overall, Darkest Dungeon is a very deep and complex rpg combat wise, its beautiful to look at and is addictive as hell, but suffers from an overly unfair random chance element and bosses late on that will ♥♥♥♥ you over royally. if you're looking for a punishing rpg, this is it.

After more than twenty hours of gameplay, I have to come to terms with the fact that this game is not for me - which is not the same as saying Darkest Dungeon is bad. It is not a bad game, but I guess it targets a player niche I’m not part of. And that is a shame, because I loved most things about it - the setting, the writing, the atmosphere, the art, and plenty of the gameplay mechanics. I sincerely wanted to see this one to its end. What dissuaded me from doing so was what I consider a serious imbalance between reward and frustration within the game - and I don’t mind difficult games, having played through FTL countless times as well as half the Souls series. What I’m not willing to deal with is how easily you can lose characters (or even have your party wiped out) despite hours of power playing, upgrading and strategizing. The challenge borders on the unfair, but fans of the game seem to revel in that (thus I do not count myself among the game’s target public). And yes, I’d been warned that I’d lose entire parties, that my favorite characters would die, etc. Still, because every other aspect of the game enticed me, I gave it a try - and now I can say, without prejudice and with pain in my heart, that the mandatory grind of Darkest Dungeon is not worth the time and aggravation it would take to beat the game. C’est la vie.
Edit: It has been interesting to watch the reaction of Darkest Dunegon fans to negative reviews, most of which come in the form of one (or a variation) of the following:
(a)  "Too hard? Git gud noob!!1!"
My reply: It's not that hard, once you learn how to optimize your parties. But that is part of the problem: In order to have a chance, you need optimization, and that leads to a joyless, variety-free grind in spite of all the interesting classes and abilities.
(b) "Only 20 hours? Cr4p review."
My reply: Much like the previous case, this translates into "waah waah you dislike my favorite game, you suck!", which is both immature and untrue. Along the same lines, you'll see people saying "this game is easy if you take the time to actually learn it", and to these people I say: Not everyone has (or is willing to spend) 100 hours to memorize game patterns, and not all reviewers should be expected to spend that long on the game before they are allowed to give their opinion. Please learn to cope with disagreement. FACT: Despite all its qualities (and there are many!), this game is grindy as hell, and dishes out massive doses of frustration to boot. Review readers will be interested in learning this, and reviews which contain this information are useful. Crying "Cr4p review" only because of the red thumb down makes you a whiny fanboy.
(c) "This game is not supposed to make you feel good."
My reply: If this is an honest statement, then we play games for very different reasons - which is fine. Granted: there are games which inspire a range of emotions both positive and negative in a way that is ultimately rewarding, but Darkest Dungeon is not one of them. And anyway, I already spend too many hours on ONE grindy game that gives me more than my fair share of grief and frustration. It's called "life", which has a mandatory mini-game called "work". Don't judge me for enjoying a little variety.

Absolutely loved this! Was a big fan of the previous game and I loved this one too. There are many changes to the game I quite like, such as the stealth mechanic and that your base is mobile, making travelling around the world and picking resources more difficult and make more sense due to the previous game it was meant to be all the nations standing up together whilst here you're a small gurilla ops team.
The one thing I HATED in this game was that many missions are "timed" with it all based on how many turns you need before a package self-destructs, a transmission gets through or a terminal shuts down and becomes unhackable. This made me rage-quit the game a few times as I find it impossible to balance between moving around stealthily and attempting to get to the objective in X amount of turns. Thankfully, the mod support has allowed me to install a mod ot remove it.
The whole campaign is based on a count-down to the Avatar project, a mysterious project the aliens are working on in the shadows for some un-seen reason. There is a mod to increase the countdown, based on difficulty which gives you more flexibility to get all your reasearch done and be ready to take down their facilities.
The ending I quite loved and, to not give away spoilers, unlike the first where you often killed the boss in 1 hit, none of that happens here. Hell, me and a friend of mine installed a mod for us to have 8 squad members and yet there was a good chance we could've lost everyone.
Psionics has been changed around and they are now REALLY awesome! They have all kinds of interesting and powerful abilities to break the will of aliens and smash machines with psionic blasts! There is quite a power-creep, but thanks to mods you can help make your game a little bit more fun, like the SMG which gives your ranger better movement, but it does less damage. A great weapon if you want to go focused with the sword.
The amount of customisation for your soldiers is absolutely amazing. My characters can look like whatever I want and you can make the character you wand with each armour tier having different and interesting customisable parts. Not to mention the new ability to upgrade your soldier's guns to improve crit rating or aim is very impressive. Especially as, when you research better weapons, the previous model is disgarded and the new model is in place with all the same upgrades.
Another down-side besides the timers is if you run out of rooms for your engineers to staff, they just do nothing and you have a warning about them being idle. This is late-game and certainly not something you should run into that soon, but I though I better mention it.
If you enjoyed the previous game you'll love this one, though you may want to modify it first before you can have any fun with it. If you were hoping they were going more classic X-COM like the origonals with the backpacks and such then I'm afraid you won't be impressed. They have added a loot system where if you kill an enemy that has loot with explosives you destroy the loot and if your soldier who was carrying the loot dies or is KOed, they drop the loot so you'd have to go back and pick it up again to finish the mission with it as the items have a timed detonation on them like many of the missions.
I certianly love it and if you have a problem with a certain issue with the game, you can always mod it and the mods don't interfer with achievements! Making this game VERY user-friendly, especially to the modding community as it allows you to remove the more irritating parts of the game to get your full enjoyment :) so far from my opinion, the mods I've taken on have not been over-powered. Especially as I stated earlier, the final battle is REALLY difficult, even with 8 soldiers of highest rank in various areas.
Update:
To this day, thanks to the various Mods the game have become highly enjoyable and unlike Bethesda, the people behind this game understand nothing is lost if you cheat in a single-player game. I've added SOOO many new enemies to my game that even on lower difficulties it's impossible (flame vipers are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s) so thank goodness for these developers who understand us gamers want to have fun :)

Spiral Knights is a hack 'n' slash style MMORPG that feels much like a top-down Zelda game, complete with pots.The paid content, which is obtained through the game's premium currency, energy, is completely optional and for the most part, out of the way. You don't have to get it but it feels nicer to have it, especially in times where it's tough.
However, do not expect to get through the game with owning one set of armor and weapons at a time. Certainplaces contain certain enemies and hazards that may make you weaker or stronger depending on your gear, and playing with friends is often a must.
It may seem at first that you don't have to put much effort into fighing, but you have to pay attention to your enemies and their projectiles. Glowing areas on the ground indicate where an enemy is going to attack, but you need to act quickly to dodge it. Projectiles need to be watched for, and may sometimes come to you a-la bullet hell games.
My only complaints are that you cannot equip many weapons at one time and to do that you have to rent, let me repeat myself, RENT, extra slots to equip more items. Often you have to resort to getting things from the community marketplace because getting them from stages can be a chore and often shops won't have what you need, thus having to deal with the sometimes ludicrous prices of greedy players.
And on a final note you will have these things called Sparks of Life. You can use them when you die more than once or use them on fallen teammates who also died more than once. However as a word of caution, use them sparingly, as they're hard to come by through normal gameplay, but can be bought with energy, which in my opinion, sparks are the stuff you should buy the most, because, if you're struggling on a level and you don't have them, you're screwed.

darkest dungeon is one of the hardest rpgs one can play.
The plot is dead simple. Your ancestor decided to crack open some lovecraftian horror books and toyed with forces beyond his understanding and control. Because of this, he summoned an abomination from elderich depths by opening a door at the bottom of the ruins, which, as you can imagine, did not go too well. Now the surrounding area is infested with horrors and its up to you, the last member of your families bloodline, to fix what has been broken or go insane trying.
You yourself do not actually fight, you hire various heros of many different classes to do your bidding, go to the dungeons, and eventually go insane, die, or both. You have 15 classes to choose from, each one is entirely unique and brings many different skills to the table. When you hire one, they have a random set of four skills from the eight they can learn, as well as three of the camp skills they can also learn. Then there are the insanities. Every character, when they start off, and as they go through the game, gains various manias, some good, some bad. One will grant them an increase to crit chance, while another will cause them to gain more stress when going into the crypt.  as you send them out on missions they'll gain experience for completing them, improving in stats and sometimes going a little bit more insane, this can screw you over pretty badly sometimes. for example, my houndmaster became a ♥♥♥♥♥ hound and only wanted to visit the ♥♥♥♥♥ house to reduce stress, then got kicked out for "deviant tastes".
the gameplay is split into three parts, base management, exploration and combat. The base is called the hamlet, here you have several options to mess with. You can teach your minions new moves and improve their existing ones, improve the gear of your minions, buy trinkets, cure diseases, manage your minions insanity and reduce stress (not yours, your gonna be sweating from start to finish). your characters will gain access to more training and better gear as they level up, but you need to improve the facilities around the hamlet in order for you to get them that gear and give them access to better training. Sometimes you'll send the party out on missions just so you'll be able to get that next upgrade for the smithy or the hospital, just because each upgrade really does have a big impact.
once your done messing around in the hamlet you can go to the quest screen and decide where to send your minions to die. There are several areas, each one posing its own unique challanges. The crypt, the warren, the waeld, the cove and the darkest dungeon are your options. Each one will have one or more missions to choose from, each of varying length, varying difficulty, and offering varying rewards, usually in the form of a choice trinket, some money, and some resources to improve the hamlet. Its up to you to decide who goes off on what mission to go get you whatever resources you might need while at the same time, hoping they don't die. after that you buy some supplies so they don't die and then send them off.
now we get to the actual dungeons. Each one is randomly generated for each mission, its size depends on how long the mission is, its shape depends on what section of the land the mission is set in. You must move from room to room via corridors, trying to complete your objective(s) without dying horribly, all the while interacting with the various objects you'll encounter in the corridors and the rooms. Certain items you bring with you on the mission will help you with these objects, like the shovel being used to dig rubble away.
Finally, the combat. its an initiative based semi static style of combat. When you start your missions you decide which character goes where in a conga line of four, their placement in that line determines which abilities they can use, as certain abilities can only be used in certain spots. this also applies to enemy placement, as certain abilities will only target enemies in specific spots on their conga line. so before combat, make sure everyone is in the right spot before you go brawling. its also unlikely they'll be staying in that spot, as both enemies and allies can use abilities which allow them to change their position within the conga line, effectively resulting in some true juggling chaos depending on your party make up. every round begins with the person with the highest speed going first, then the second fastest and so on, each round you can do one of two things, change position within the conga line, or use one of the four abilities they have equipped. from there, its all in the hands of nuffle, god of random chance.
your characters have two bars, their health bar, and their stress bar. once they are out of health they go to deaths door, but they don't die. When a character is at deaths door they have a percentage chance every time they take a hit to die, its effectively a net to stop big enemies one shotting them. the downside is that they gain stress much faster and generate it every turn for themselves. Stress is bad, not just for your skin, but also your mind and heart. Attacks can deal five main forms of damage. Basic, bleed, blight, debuff and stress (you can't stress enemies though). bleed and blight are by turn on going damage status effects that stack on top of each other and themselves, which can lead to insane amounts of damage per turn on a single enemy. Stress however is a bugbear only you get to deal with. When a minion reaches 100 stress, they undergo a stress of will, either they go insane, or they become emboldened and get badass. going insane causes your characters to disobey commands and do other strange things depending on which insanity they have, becoming badass means they gain buffs, being insane or emboldened lasts until the end of the quest. However, when a character reaches 200 stress, they die. I'm not kidding, this will be the main way you will lose characters.
Darkest dungeon is a very stylized game, the visuals are bold and striking, they do a wonderful job of convaying just how bleak the situation you find yourself in is. While there is a lack of animation, the way the game gets around it is quite clever, making what would have just been two static images smooshing together look and feel like hefty impacts between two combatents. The music and narrator also hit the right chords, the narrator specifically is what gives the entire game is dramatic flare, spouting depressing or emboldening lines at just the right moments or monologing during loading screens for bosses. The music is somber and heavy, making you realize this is not a light hearted wonder through the woods, but a trudge through♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and rotten flesh.
Now, darkest dungeon is flawed, intentionally so, but that wont stop me from being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about it. The random element in this game is the devil. Many times you will be screwed over by the random elements of this game. The final dungeons of this will also make you pull teeth out in frustration for how much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t is tossed at you. There is a way to fix this in the settings....kinda, its still hard as nails, not because of a skill cap, but the nature of the game itself.
Overall, Darkest Dungeon is a very deep and complex rpg combat wise, its beautiful to look at and is addictive as hell, but suffers from an overly unfair random chance element and bosses late on that will ♥♥♥♥ you over royally. if you're looking for a punishing rpg, this is it.

After more than twenty hours of gameplay, I have to come to terms with the fact that this game is not for me - which is not the same as saying Darkest Dungeon is bad. It is not a bad game, but I guess it targets a player niche I’m not part of. And that is a shame, because I loved most things about it - the setting, the writing, the atmosphere, the art, and plenty of the gameplay mechanics. I sincerely wanted to see this one to its end. What dissuaded me from doing so was what I consider a serious imbalance between reward and frustration within the game - and I don’t mind difficult games, having played through FTL countless times as well as half the Souls series. What I’m not willing to deal with is how easily you can lose characters (or even have your party wiped out) despite hours of power playing, upgrading and strategizing. The challenge borders on the unfair, but fans of the game seem to revel in that (thus I do not count myself among the game’s target public). And yes, I’d been warned that I’d lose entire parties, that my favorite characters would die, etc. Still, because every other aspect of the game enticed me, I gave it a try - and now I can say, without prejudice and with pain in my heart, that the mandatory grind of Darkest Dungeon is not worth the time and aggravation it would take to beat the game. C’est la vie.
Edit: It has been interesting to watch the reaction of Darkest Dunegon fans to negative reviews, most of which come in the form of one (or a variation) of the following:
(a)  "Too hard? Git gud noob!!1!"
My reply: It's not that hard, once you learn how to optimize your parties. But that is part of the problem: In order to have a chance, you need optimization, and that leads to a joyless, variety-free grind in spite of all the interesting classes and abilities.
(b) "Only 20 hours? Cr4p review."
My reply: Much like the previous case, this translates into "waah waah you dislike my favorite game, you suck!", which is both immature and untrue. Along the same lines, you'll see people saying "this game is easy if you take the time to actually learn it", and to these people I say: Not everyone has (or is willing to spend) 100 hours to memorize game patterns, and not all reviewers should be expected to spend that long on the game before they are allowed to give their opinion. Please learn to cope with disagreement. FACT: Despite all its qualities (and there are many!), this game is grindy as hell, and dishes out massive doses of frustration to boot. Review readers will be interested in learning this, and reviews which contain this information are useful. Crying "Cr4p review" only because of the red thumb down makes you a whiny fanboy.
(c) "This game is not supposed to make you feel good."
My reply: If this is an honest statement, then we play games for very different reasons - which is fine. Granted: there are games which inspire a range of emotions both positive and negative in a way that is ultimately rewarding, but Darkest Dungeon is not one of them. And anyway, I already spend too many hours on ONE grindy game that gives me more than my fair share of grief and frustration. It's called "life", which has a mandatory mini-game called "work". Don't judge me for enjoying a little variety.

There are plenty of reviews for the game, some very detailed, but I feel an "explanation" review could add a bit of value regardless.
There are a lot of high helpful negative reviews which seems very much at odds with its glowing meta critic and other support, so what is going on here?
It is about that the game has significant and potentially critical issues with RNG and its game design around it. And when these issues occur and occur in massive style.
The RNG as difficulty gets more pronounced as the game progresses until it finally tips over in "one bad roll away" at the Darkest Dungeon ("End" Dungeon) and the game becomes an at times  meaningless exercise where the not just the hapless player but also the average or good player enters the territory of "insert xx hours if unlucky" to try again.
How so? Because levelling takes a lot of time and a bad fight or bad roll, often down to dice rolled against 67% save will kill your character, will determine hours of your game, without anything you can do about it at all. And thus send you back to grinding, the same things again and again.
Add to this the brilliant thematic (in tune with the Lovecraft world theme) but also almost insane design decision that the player cannot leave the end dungeons (Darkest and Vvulf) without sacrificing a (random) character, thus 100% ensuring a angry player if (read:when) the RNG goes bad.
In fairness this is close to broken content and thus an "unfinished" game.
However, as this happens a long way in, those who do not go there, end up with a totally different impression due to the excellent art directtion, superb voice acting and general theme and quality feel.
Thus each side of the coin is utterly different and the reviews too.
However, as the bad side of the coin is the end game and any player will go there and suffer due to it eventually, the bad reviews are in fact more correct than the positive ones. But you discover it too late, when you are heavily invested and then ... then are you faced with bad choices, gridning to retry with an RNG waiting for you or giving up and cutting loses.
Solving the RNG would require a complete game overhaul, which is impossible, So the "crutch" solution would be that the latter part of the game need to be toned down - pretty much across the entire line on the mob side of things, dmg, stress, speed, hp.
Adding a difficulty slider that turned achievements off and allowed players to tone down the game could be an obvious solution and likely make both fanatic (achievements) and other 90% of world population (want hard but fair, not RNG hard and unfair) happy.
Big thumbs up for first 75% of game, huge thumbs down for last 25%.
And no, having a good beginning does not excuse a "broken" end. Not Recommended in its current state.

This is absolutely a great game, and arguably the most well-rounded souls game. However, this is the souls game I've put the least amount of playtime into, even less so than DS2.
If I had to say the reason for this, I think it's the atmosphere, and the fact that the souls series hasn't really pushed boundaries or innovated in a way that evolves the genre or the games themselves much at all.
Don't worry though, the combat is rock solid and feels the best it has in any souls game in my opinion.
Simply put, DS3 is a refinement of all the mechanics present in previous souls games. The themes have stagnated a bit since it's conception as a franchise though, and this game doesn't really add anything significant to its repertoire.
Again, it's a great game with great combat and awesome boss fights, but I came out feeling slightly unsatisfied with it.
While I partially blame the pre-release hype (which I feel happens a lot these days) there were way too many callbacks and references for no other reason than to just appeal to fans
. This level of self-awareness and the endlessly repeated themes just gets sort of tiresome and can take you out of an otherwise excellent experience.
Also - weapon arts:
While certainly cool, they often are the only thing that will differentiate a weapon from another within the same class. And even then, one weapon art will often be shared across multiple other weapons, sometimes that are in different classes. It's frustratingly counter intuitive because weapon arts should help each weapon feel unique, but what ends up happening is more or less the opposite.
I obviously still recommend that you play this game, especially if you're a fan of the series. It really is great, I'm just showing some tough love as a fan myself. Just don't expect it to be the sendoff you were hoping the series would receive.

Initially I disliked XCOM 2 as a lot of the feeling behind XCOM: Enemy Unknown and Enemy Within were missing from this. Everything seem so franticly paced where those other two games seemed to give you some degree of control over how fast you took things. Both were rather unforgiving in their own right but you didn't have the turn timers counting down nearly as often. You didn't have constant loss of control of units through stuns, panic, mind control. Seems terrible, right?
I kept playing this game though despite my annoyances at onset. Characters on my squad started to develop. I stopped worrying about the rather generous turn timer ticking down as much. It came to a point where just as my army started to really stand on it's own the advent project came close to fruition. As my forces rushed to keep up, our ship was shot down over the desert of Africa by a UFO. 10 days left until the end of the world and we're going down. So this is how it all ends.
NO!
My units gave those aliens that came to capture us what for! Not a single man down after we wiped the floor with 50 of those dirty xenos! Ships back online, we take off and head for the next alien facility. We start at the top and through wave after wave of explosives leave behind a glassy plate where those xenos lived. 2 months now back on the clock and we're taking the fight back to Advent.
Well... this is getting good!

This is absolutely a great game, and arguably the most well-rounded souls game. However, this is the souls game I've put the least amount of playtime into, even less so than DS2.
If I had to say the reason for this, I think it's the atmosphere, and the fact that the souls series hasn't really pushed boundaries or innovated in a way that evolves the genre or the games themselves much at all.
Don't worry though, the combat is rock solid and feels the best it has in any souls game in my opinion.
Simply put, DS3 is a refinement of all the mechanics present in previous souls games. The themes have stagnated a bit since it's conception as a franchise though, and this game doesn't really add anything significant to its repertoire.
Again, it's a great game with great combat and awesome boss fights, but I came out feeling slightly unsatisfied with it.
While I partially blame the pre-release hype (which I feel happens a lot these days) there were way too many callbacks and references for no other reason than to just appeal to fans
. This level of self-awareness and the endlessly repeated themes just gets sort of tiresome and can take you out of an otherwise excellent experience.
Also - weapon arts:
While certainly cool, they often are the only thing that will differentiate a weapon from another within the same class. And even then, one weapon art will often be shared across multiple other weapons, sometimes that are in different classes. It's frustratingly counter intuitive because weapon arts should help each weapon feel unique, but what ends up happening is more or less the opposite.
I obviously still recommend that you play this game, especially if you're a fan of the series. It really is great, I'm just showing some tough love as a fan myself. Just don't expect it to be the sendoff you were hoping the series would receive.
