XCOM is a weird game to me as all three iterations I've played have had the exact same effect of being simultaneously highly addictive and hole-in-wall punchingly frustrating. Aliens lying in wait in a closet for your last character to move and be 'revealed' as seen through a key-hole leads to out loud, "♥♥♥♥ YOU, you cheating ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥," only to induce a sociopathic and epic fap-session of victory when you kill every alien without getting scratched.
Overall it's startlingly similar to its former title, which is a good thing since the last game was the♥♥♥♥♥♥ but does leave me feeling like I'm playing a really good expansion rather than a new game. It point of fact, I'm not sure that the Enemy Within expansion wasn't overall a better cache of content than XCOM 2 in its entirety.
There's a new mechanism (basically a doomsday clock) that forces your overall strategic hand that seeks to prevent you from simply winning mission after mission and teching up. Basically it motivates you into fights that you're not really ready for yet to keep the timer down, but there's a way around it if you're clever or have the internet to contact others more clever than you. Also, I don't remember corpses having such integral uses after the autopsies themselves in the former game, but don't sell dead bodies until you're sure sure sure that you no longer need them; my first game - that I've since abandoned - has a bunch of no armor wearing jack-a-napes fighting mutons because I didn't keep the right dead bodies to make armor. My soldiers were doubling up in the infirmary if they weren't crumpled in plasma covered heaps on the battlefield.
The new stuff is great (weapon mods, line-of-sight indicator, updated/expanded class abilities), but again none of it feels like it couldn't have been tacked onto what was the excellent and highly stable engine of the former XCOM*. Also, with DLC and a season pass, I can't help but wonder if they're going to roll out a lot of the content introduced in Enemy Within (mechs and genetics) much the same way that The Sims rolls out its same 'new' expansions for each iteration of its core game.
*I only keep hammering this home because I personally can't see where the framerate issues are coming from. Having slightly increased graphics (?) aren't worth the admitted framerate problems Firaxis is currently promising they can fix. The game was not supposed to need a massive rig to run at full cap, but that is currently not the case. I run minimal graphics (which are fine) and still suffer some noticeable but not fun-breaking jerkiness.
Overall this is still a great game. I've got 50+ hours played already and I know I'll easily punch my ticket for another 50+. So if you liked the last XCOM and you've got the money, buy it; you'll enjoy it, I'm sure. However, if you haven't played the first XCOM and it's expansion Enemy Within, those games are each superior to XCOM 2 right now, if only because of price and the framerate problem.

I have loved this game ever sense the biggening, back when Energy was a HUGE source to the game. You had to wait hours to get MIST energy (Or also known as F2P Energy) which was only 100. After about a few years of not playing it, because my PC finally broke down and I had to wait to get a new PC, I finally returned. The new updates were amazing, the floors do not require energy, story, and hundreds of new armor sets.
Would I rate this game? Heck yeah! This game is all about adventure and is extremely fun to play with friends. What you might think will be a quick elite run to make some extra crowns (The in-game currency) will have you hunting with friends for HOURS farming money and materials.
However, for those of you who hate playing for hours on end grinding for money...This game will not be for you. The only problem I have with this new update is that back in the old days, you required Energy for crafting also. They traded this for Crafting Orbs (Flawed, Simple, Advanced, Elite, Eternal) to craft things, these are extremely hard to find and you would be lucky to find a Flawed more less a Elite or Eternal which you require to craft rank 4 or 5 armor. Not only do you need these extremely rare orbs but you might require an armor set of a lower teir to craft the teir 4 or 5 armor. If you want to get these rare orbs without finding them in Loot Crates (Very rarely Green and a O.K chance in Red) you will have to pay usually over 6K crowns for ONE. Now mind you, per regular elite run at about teir 2 or 3 you will only get about 2-4K on Teir 1 of the elevators. Then Teir 2 I think gives you a slight bit more.
Even though the new updates have added these things, to be honest, I think it is a big step. Especially in a F2P game. Do I recommend it still? Heck yes! For new adventurers of Cradle, in the 'Clockworks' (Not sure if they still call it that) be prepared to fight Slimes, Tree Ents that fly, Zombies, Grimlins, and so much more! Hope to see you newcomers soon!

Too soon to make a DETAILED call on this one but all the pros and cons of the first are present in the sequel. Basically if you liked the first revamp then you will also enjoy the second. The storyline is more interesting and the enemies more varied. RNG intrusion works both ways - you can be impossibly lucky or unlucky with percentages which CAN be frustrating but also gives you those 'YES!' moments when some under 40% chance will miraculously crit giving you a perfect mission. Loading times seem to have increased and cut scenes and transitions still cause stutter but overall it's as much a quality game as its predecessor and unit progression/customisation, along with an improved tech tree, perhaps give it a slight edge overall. Either way you have many hours of highly enjoyable tactical gameplay if you can learn to ignore the odd hiccup here and there. Ironman? Only for masochists.
*edit* It's interesting to note that being open to workshop has offset several poor design choices. I reccommend the "stop wasting my time" and "katana" mods. I haven't tried any of the map mods yet.
*2nd edit* 10th March patch has fixed all optimisation issues and the game now works as intended. This is a big plus point. Also, Stop Wasting My Time mod is no longer needed as the improvements in the patch make it superfluous.

TL:DR Black Squad is a great game if you enjoy FPS with low system requirements. It's still in EA, so there all flaws; but even having said that, it's very enjoyable.
Pros:
- Not P2W in the slightest. The only thing you can spend real money on is cosmetics for the guns.
- Very low system requirements. As a person who has a low spec laptop I am greatful for this.
- Easy to pick up and play. It's not hard for a new player who is somewhat familiar with FPS games to do well.
- The graphics are good for the requirements, all of the maps have their own little flair even on the lowest settings.
- The servers are good. I rarely get over 100 ping and there is no skittering from my player model.
- The timed DLC for the weapons is a fantastic idea. It lets people use the weapons in real games to determine what to buy with the gold they earn.
Cons:
- I found my first hacker today, I left immediately, and got a deserter token for it. (The hacker had teleport, infinite ammo, rapid grenade launcher, etc.)
- Even though the servers are good and I don't see skittering, I feel that when I peek a corner and hide back I still die from behind the wall; It might just be me, but it get's aggrivating when it happens multiple times.
- The game modes state a player count. Ex. Demolition 5v5. Even when it says 5v5, three more people can join to make it a 8v8; This is also misleading and ruins the feel of the game mode.
- The TDM maps are extrememly small. I can run out of spawn in all the maps and still get shot by people with invincibility; so I stopped playing TDM.
- While you're dead you cannot give you team callouts in chat. Hopefully this will be implemented fully or at least ranked if/when it comes out.
- There are only 2 pistols in the game that I'm aware of. I bought the deagle with metals, and it won't even kill somebody with 3 headshots; this is rediculous.

I know that by criticising this game, I may receive some criticism myself, but I'll be honest, Dark Souls 3 (in my opinion) is awful.
First of all, the camera - The camera in Dark Souls 3 is one of the worst cameras i have ever seen
in my life. I have died many times simply because the camera isn't
satisfactory. You will find yourself looking in the
opposite direction from an
enemy against your will many times. Even when the camera doesn't
freak out, you will then have to deal with targeting the enemy that you
want among a cluster of
enemies if you are dealing with a group, and my goodness, if you ever
have to deal with that, goodluck.
Second, the controls   - The tutorial is pointless on pc as none of the button prompts are pc keys,
instead, they are console controller buttons. To find out which key does
what, you will have to look into the keybinding options and slowly scan
through each key. This isn't that big of a problem, mostly just
personal expectations, and after a while, I definitely got used to this.
However, I cannot stand the fact that input lag is present, in a game
where split - second timing could make or break a play.
I'm not sure if consoles have this input lag, but it's unbelievably harsh on
pc. To solve this, you must turn off V-sync manually, but even after turning
it off, there is still a slight delay between
pressing a key and having the character engage in the action, and it
seems to have no effect on
the roll delay. (there is a delay of about 0.40 to 0.50 seconds for rolling, I
am not sure how to fix this)
Third, the "difficulty"   - Dark Souls 3 is quite "difficult" at times, I must say. However, I found the
game to be difficult mostly because of the awful input delay which is
always present. Many times I have timed a roll
perfectly only to have a 0.5s delay mess it up and get me squashed by
some giant hammer or axe. Also, I sometimes find enemies to have cheap
ways of being difficult, such as having super high hp. This can easily be
countered by understanding the game, but it tends to get boring and
frustrating if you keep dying to the same boss over and over again simply
because of technical reason like the camera.
Fourth, fov                  - This reason could tie in with reason no. 1. The fov in Dark Souls 3 is way
too low, I can't see jack at this fov, coupled with the awful camera.
There are many other dislikes I have about this game which I will not mention, but with all that said, I want to enjoy this game, I can see why people like this, but I just can't stand some of the problems this game has, including the ones listed here. Anyways, this is just my personal taste of the game, and if you have a different take on it, that's fine by me, we all have unique tastes and preferences.
Thank you very much for reading my review

Dankest Dungeon is a game that involves RNG, all who dislike this mechanic please leave and go back to games like ... wait, are there even games out there with 0 RNG? Anyway if you like a constant struggle to save your characters and maximize loot this game is for you. I have been completely boned by the RNG in the past (like losing 3 level 6 due to bad luck) however the game makes these risks very apparent. The only random chance that can negatively affect you (aside from standard rpg mechanics) is the affliction system. This could just be my luck, but I have certain characters who are guaranteed to recieve a positive effect (due to items probably) when reaching high stress. It is reasonable to dislike the system, but there are a lot, let me repeat that, A LOT of ways to reduce stress, by means of items and abilities. The person who leaves a bad review on this game (aside from those who generally dislike the genre) is someone who only leveled 4 people to 6 and lost them all to the darkest dungeon, then in a fit of rage angrily reviewed the game. This isn't a forgiving game, if you make mistakes you will be punished. If you are looking for a stress-free game then this isn't for you, in fact I'd argue the whole genre isn't for you, go back to Minecraft and risk free sandboxes. However if you enjoy a high risk, low reward game, then you will enjoy this game greatly.

How best to review this game. Its mechanics work well independantly, and for people who enjoy having their asses kicked constantly for the first 6 or so hours will certainly enjoy it.
But for the rest of us? This game will prove to be frustrating. Wheither or not you find the frustration worth it is up to you, but I'll gloss over the most glaring issues this game has:
1: The goddamned menus. Trying to sell Trinkets is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ managing your crew is annoying as they're all in a giant annoying list.
2: The Difficulty: Now, I'm not against a hard game. In fact I rather enjoy this game when its playing fair. But the problem is that there seems to be no rhyme or reason to half the games mechanics. Your characters come into the game with flaws already tacted onto their profiles, some of which are irritatingly crippling, and others seem to do nothing. There's no indicator of turn order, which is desperately needed. Half my deaths could have been prevented if I could have seen the order in which turns are going. I only made it to the Swine Prince Boss, and man was that a super annoying fight. The boss literally just spammed an AOE that hit the whole party for 10+ HP constantly in a game where most characters have like 25hp and also inflicts stun. I encountered another boss when I put a torch on some altar, but summoning him was my own fault, so I don't fault the game for that
The enemies are quite varied, but some of the classes seem relatively useless. You'll constantly be praying for more of the cleric class, and instead you'll be greeted constantly by anything but that. More example of RNG not exactly being the best concept for a game. There's little point in examining half the curio objects in the game, as it seems at least 75% of the time they slap you with some kind of negative, and the positive is rarely worth the risk.
Ugh, The RNG is so annoying. There's nothing more annoying than you playing perfectly, and being slaughtered by RNG and poorly explained mechanics. But there is a light at the end of the tunnel. As you feel this game out, and begin to understand its mechanics, it does get more fun. I hear tell that the end game grind is atrotious, but I've yet to reach it.
In conclusion: If you enjoy roguelikes and Dark Souls-esq games, and don't mind an irritating learning curve, you'll probably have some fun with this game. If not, you're wasting your money.

Going into this, I was pretty much expecting a Goat Simulator clone. However, after a few hours of playing this game I can tell that I was very wrong.
While the controls, physics, and name of this game are similar to GS, there is a rather large difference between the two. In short, unlike Goat Simulator, this oddly feels like an actual game. The music in the game is rather relaxing to play along to. The controls are awkward at the beginning but as you play on you start to get the hang of it. The combination of both the physics and controls are very satisfying, I began to notice this when I was climbing and swinging off the walls like some kind of ninja. The "grip" system in this game does an excellent job of adding a level of difficulty to what would otherwise be rather straight forward.
However, nothing is perfect, and even a game as interesting as this has a flaw or two.
The camera can be a large burden at times. If you would rather use the arrow keys to nudge the bread around as opposed to the mouse then you are forced to lift your hand from the keyboard and move it to the mouse every time you wish to adjust the camera. This is very irritating, especially when the direction and power you have when nudging the bread is pretty much determined by camera position. More so, if you are in a situation where you need to move quickly so your "grip" meter doesn't run out, leaving you helpless as you fall to the floor. There are other instances where the camera will rapidly jerk and twist around if your piece of bread falls into a crack, such as being between a box and a wall. But other than this, I haven't really had any major issue with the game this early on.
I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys casual, not-so-serious fun. You will surely enjoy it.

In this game, your heroes go mad if they spend too long in the dungeons - and I know just how they feel.
Darkest Dungeon is easy to admire, but hard to love. The music, voice-over work, art style, and over-all presentation are all *fantastic*. It builds a wonderfully compelling atmosphere that really draws you in. But oh my god does this game *HAAAAAAAAAATE* you. It frustrates you in every possible way hour after hour after hour, and as soon as you think you're starting to make progress: it will gleefully tear you down and send you back to square one. You'll spend an eternity painstakingly leveling up your characters to have a chance to take on some of the mid-level dungeons, then *bang*, all will be wiped out in a couple of minutes, with no way to recover other than to start grinding all over again.
The excellent presentation of the game grabbed and hooked me. But after 22 hours of a blood-soaked stalemate, and having just watched my best heroes brutally slaughtered ten feet from safety by a random boss-spawn: I'm starting to feel like this game relishes wasting my time.
Part of me longs to go back in and drink in more of the wonderful Lovecraftian atmosphere, but I'm just not sure I want to invest the 100s of hours of grinding it's going to take to get to the end. A simple difficulty slider would have made the game a lot more enjoyable IMO.

>The AI is still shackled, and this isn't more evident than when you get used to how Sectoids' fearsome psionics are used.
The good:
The script source is supposedly totally open, and the mod pack is as well. Modding for the game couldn't be any more supported and who can live without Hatsune Miku hair or Stop Wasting My Time.
Timers are good. Forcing the player to take action and take *some* risks made for a more interesting game. I found myself moving soldiers completely out of cover in order to commit to attacks I would not have taken in Xcom1.
The temptation of MELD, in the previous game, wasn't enough because there was no true penalty for ignoring it other than falling slightly behind in the tech race. Now, you stand to lose soldiers, and all the droppable equipment you outfitted them with.
The soldiers are given so much value through equipment and visual customization that losing them almost always hurts.
Escaping from some mission types makes for interesting choices as well. I found myself seriously considering taking on some missions, weighing the likelihood of losing soldiers, or the advantage it would earn should it be a success. Eventually recognizing when a mission is unwinnable and running away to fight another day helps write interesting personal stories that aren't just "and we won again easily!" The struggle gives depth.
The eh:
The game arc is still the same as before: The early and mid game are the most interesting segments of the game. They're the moments where you make tactical sacrifices so that the whole group can survive. They're the moments where you're rooting for a critical to land.
The late game is still a victory lap where your abilities match or exceed all the challenges the game throws at you except in being outnumbered.
It's still Xcom, so what else can I say?
Update: Some elements of this review have fallen out of date due to the recent patch in March.
Mimic Beacons were significantly balanced (Made more expensive and will now only waste 1-2 enemy actions instead of nearly a *full enemy turn*).
Framerate/graphical performance was significantly improved.

In this game, your heroes go mad if they spend too long in the dungeons - and I know just how they feel.
Darkest Dungeon is easy to admire, but hard to love. The music, voice-over work, art style, and over-all presentation are all *fantastic*. It builds a wonderfully compelling atmosphere that really draws you in. But oh my god does this game *HAAAAAAAAAATE* you. It frustrates you in every possible way hour after hour after hour, and as soon as you think you're starting to make progress: it will gleefully tear you down and send you back to square one. You'll spend an eternity painstakingly leveling up your characters to have a chance to take on some of the mid-level dungeons, then *bang*, all will be wiped out in a couple of minutes, with no way to recover other than to start grinding all over again.
The excellent presentation of the game grabbed and hooked me. But after 22 hours of a blood-soaked stalemate, and having just watched my best heroes brutally slaughtered ten feet from safety by a random boss-spawn: I'm starting to feel like this game relishes wasting my time.
Part of me longs to go back in and drink in more of the wonderful Lovecraftian atmosphere, but I'm just not sure I want to invest the 100s of hours of grinding it's going to take to get to the end. A simple difficulty slider would have made the game a lot more enjoyable IMO.

If you enjoyed over watching your way to victory in Xcom Enemy Unknown then Xcom 2 will be something of a culture shock.  You really cannot afford to rest on your laurels when the resident alien force outnumbers and outguns you severely in the early stages. I found it surprisingly punishing on normal difficulty compared to its predecessor.
The tactical game play remains intact; there’s better mission variety, a more involving narrative, better soldier customization, randomly generated maps, a wide variety of aliens and weapons and on the whole it’s shinier, prettier and more difficult.
There’s already a substantial number of mods available on the Steam workshop so if you’re not keen on those timed objective missions (of which there were a lot) or fancy a new hat  your needs will be met.
A word of caution however because the game really would benefit from some bug fixing and better optimization. No-one likes crashing to desktop Firaxis; not even the aliens.
